title: Investigators return to ‘House of Horrors’ in search for evidence tied to missing women
text:
PHILADELPHIA (WPVI) - Federal investigators returned to a Philadelphia home known as the “House of Horrors” to search for evidence.
Authorities believe the home may be connected to the disappearances of at least five women who are feared dead.
The home is where Raymond Horsch and his son Eugene lived.
Raymond Horsch died in 2025, and Eugene Horsch is in police custody.
Investigators suspect Raymond Horsch may have been a serial killer.
Last week, police removed items from the home. In the coming weeks, authorities are expected to bring in heavy equipment to take apart sections of the house as they search for more evidence.
So far, searchers have not found any human remains at the home.

title: Federal appeals judges don't reveal how they'll rule on Saudi Arabia's effort to end 9/11 litigation
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Family members of victims of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks packed a federal appeals courtroom in New York City on Wednesday as three judges heard arguments over whether legal claims against Saudi Arabia can proceed.
The judges revealed through their questions that there are still many legal issues to be decided in the lawsuit even though it has dragged on for almost a quarter-century.
They didn’t say when they might rule on whether claims can proceed to trial alleging that Saudi Arabia provided aid to at least two of the 19 men who hijacked planes and crashed them into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field that day.
Still, Terry Strada, whose husband Tom Strada was killed in the attacks, said she was encouraged that more than 100 family members of 9/11 victims turned out and by the judges’ questions.
“It really was a good day for us,” she said afterward. “The judges asked really meaningful questions and hammered the Saudi attorneys and didn’t let up. They weren’t buying what the Saudis were selling.”
In lawsuits, hundreds of victims’ relatives and injured survivors, along with insurance companies and businesses, claim that employees of the Saudi government directly and knowingly assisted the hijackers and other plotters and fueled al-Qaida’s development into a terrorist organization by funding charities that supported them.
Some defendants, including Iran, the Taliban and al-Qaida, already have been found in default.
On Wednesday, lawyers from both sides were questioned repeatedly by the appeals judges who seemed unsure exactly how they would respond to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia’s claims that it should be dismissed as a defendant on sovereign immunity grounds.
Lawyers for Saudi Arabia say the nation and the U.S. were partners in the 1990s against terrorism, al-Qaida and its founder, Osama bin Laden.
Although 15 of the 19 attackers on 9/11 were Saudis, the Saudi government has long denied any involvement in the attacks.
Lawyers for victims’ relatives claim that a group of extremist religious leaders in Saudi Arabia aided the hijackers.
The appeal by Saudi Arabia stemmed from an August 2025 ruling by U.S. District Judge George B. Daniels, who decided that the case could proceed in federal court, though he did not rule on the merits of the claims.

title: Washington resident, 30, accused of conspiring with 18-year-old to commit one of worst school shootings in Canada’s history
text:
SEATTLE (AP) — Federal authorities said Tuesday that they have arrested and charged a 30-year-old from Washington state with encouraging an 18-year-old to commit one of the worst school shootings in Canada’s history by offering to livestream the February attack, providing money and sharing advice on how to delete online messages to keep the plot a secret.
The U.S. attorney’s office in Seattle said James Cody Bryant of Bellingham, Washington, communicated with Jesse Van Rootselaar in British Columbia for at least six months ahead of the shooting. Bryant, who identifies as female, did not report Van Rootselaar’s plans to authorities, authorities allege.
W. Mike Herrington, the special agent in charge of the FBI’s Seattle office, said without Bryant’s “misplaced loyalty” and willingness to livestream the killings, officials didn’t know if Van Rootselaar would have gone through with the attack.
“We certainly know the shooter was concerned that not enough people would see the livestream without Bryant broadcasting it and was depending on Bryant to amplify the livestream because the shooter did not have many followers on social media,” Herrington added.
Authorities say Van Rootselaar first killed her mother and stepbrother at home before attacking a nearby school in the mountain community of Tumbler Ridge, killing five children ages 12 and 13 at the school as well as an educational assistant. Twenty-five others were wounded.
Van Rootselaar was later found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.
Investigators accessed Van Rootselaar’s Twitch account and found that she had initiated a video livestream while sitting in her vehicle with a rifle and long gun in her lap. The livestream lasted about 20 seconds before it was disconnected, and was only viewed by one other account.
Bryant is accused of helping to plan the attack
Bryant was charged with one count of conspiracy to commit murder in a foreign country — a “novel” charge for a case like this, said Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd during a press conference.
Bryant made a first appearance in court on Tuesday afternoon and is being detained ahead of a preliminary hearing set for Oct. 20. The federal public defender’s office, which represents Bryant, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Communicating over Discord with Van Rootselaar, Bryant gave tactical advice on how to carry out the killings to have the strongest impact, according to the complaint.
“Hallways also mean a lot of ways people can escape,” Bryant wrote, the complaint said. “Corners to turn. Wide open spaces means numbers.”
Bryant also sent Van Rootselaar money to purchase a lighter that would be used to construct an explosive device and advised Van Rootselaar about how to keep the plot a secret by deleting online messages and using virtual private networks, officials said.
According to the criminal complaint, Bryant and Van Rootselaar met online about three years ago on Omegle, a since-shuttered video chat site that connected users with strangers at random. Their communications were sporadic during the first year because she was “institutionalized” after being deemed a danger to herself, the complaint said. She was locked up again after setting her room on fire. But they spoke daily during the six months leading up to the attack, officials said.
“Van Rootselaar often spoke about planning to use guns to murder her family members and others because she felt she had been mistreated,” the complaint said.
Both Van Rootselaar and Bryant identified as trans, Herrington said. But authorities do not have any indication that’s why they stayed connected online, he said.
Bryant sometimes urged Van Rootselaar to reconsider, officials say
Bryant tried to talk Van Rootselaar out of committing the attack at various points, authorities said.
“I truly hope you reconsider today,” Bryant told her in January, according to the complaint. “I wish there were any other path for you, you shouldn’t have to do something like this.”
But ultimately, Bryant did not alert law enforcement and instead provided support for carrying out the shooting, authorities said.
When Van Rootselaar expressed concern that Bryant would “snitch” and alert authorities, Bryant repeatedly assured her that would not happen, officials said.
“I could,” Bryant wrote, according to the filing. “I don’t want to honestly. I know I can like, save lives I guess but idk,” using the abbreviation for “I don’t know.”
Canadian Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said in Ottawa that the allegations were devastating.
“Nothing will bring back the eight lives that were devastated back in February, but it is important that those who are responsible are held to account,” he told reporters.
Anandasangaree said it was too soon to say whether Bryant could also face charges in Canada, but added that Canadian prosecution would be possible if investigators determine Canadian laws were broken.
Bob Zimmer, the federal lawmaker who represents Tumbler Ridge, said the victims deserve answers.
“It is deeply troubling, the allegations that this individual coached the shooter all throughout the process in an effort to livestream the event,” Zimmer said.
Tumbler Ridge in the Canadian Rockies is more than 1,000 kilometers (600 miles) northeast of Vancouver, British Columbia, near the provincial border with Alberta. The provincial government website lists Tumbler Ridge Secondary School as having 175 students from Grades 7 to 12.
The families of victims are suing artificial intelligence company OpenAI in U.S. federal court, seeking to hold the ChatGPT maker responsible for failing to alert police to the shooter’s alarming interactions with the chatbot.
___
The story and headline have been corrected to identify Bryant as a resident of Washington. Authorities say Bryant identifies as female.
Associated Press reporter Rob Gillies contributed to this report from Toronto.

title: How all 12 Bangor City Council candidates say they would’ve voted in key council debates
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
With 12 candidates vying for three seats on the Bangor City Council, voters in the city are choosing from a crowded field — the largest, in fact, in at least four decades.
Campaign slogans and social media posts can often be vague and blend together, so the Bangor Daily News wanted to get into the details with candidates. That’s why we asked all of them how they would’ve voted on seven key measures that actually came before the council in the last year.
The chart below shows their answers to the seven yes or no questions. Candidates were also given the option to elaborate, so you can hover over their votes in the chart (or tap, if you’re using a mobile device) to read more. As the only incumbent running for reelection, we asked Joe Leonard to explain the votes he took on those proposals.
First, we asked about the 180-day ban on data center construction that passed this spring. The pause was recently extended for another 180 days. Only one candidate was opposed.
We also asked about a proposed 180-day ban on new syringe service programs and chemical dependency treatment facilities. That measure, proposed by City Councilor Carolyn Fish, was killed in committee. Candidates were relatively split on this temporary ban and expressed varying degrees of support for needle exchanges in the city.
Many of the candidates were hesitant to take a stance on several budgetary decisions that came before the council this year, saying they didn’t know the details and needed to gather more information. We asked if they would’ve supported funding for eight new firefighter positions, funding for the public health department’s homeless response coordinator and an increased school budget.
Four candidates said they would’ve supported a proposed ordinance restricting collaboration with federal immigration authorities, which ultimately failed 5-3 in a council vote.
Just three said they would’ve voted in favor of creating a TIF district and credit enhancement agreement for the Yellen Pines homeless housing development, a decision that has sparked outrage among some in the Bangor community but ultimately won council approval. The 75% tax reimbursement deal over 30 years will supplement the state money that represents the project’s primary funding stream.
The BDN has profiled all 12 candidates — you can read about them here. We also asked them a series of broader questions on camera about how they’d solve Bangor’s biggest issues. You can watch those videos for free here.

title: LA Lakers player proposes to longtime girlfriend at Bruno Mars concert
text:
Lakers’ Ziaire Williams proposes to longtime girlfriend at Bruno Mars concert
Right as Grammy-winning singer Bruno Mars sang the lyrics, "Hey, baby, I think I wanna marry you," from his hit song "Marry You," that was the cue.
Los Angeles Lakers forward Ziaire Williams got down on one knee and proposed to his longtime girlfriend Friday night during Mars' concert at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.
Awaiting an answer, Mars chimed in with a "Please say I do I do I do," from the stage.
She said yes.
Williams and his girlfriend, model Paris Timan, then hugged, prompting cheers from the audience.
You can watch the romantic moment here.

title: Data center moratorium vote postponed after fight, protests
text:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC/Gray News) — Chaos ensued during Tuesday night’s data center moratorium vote by the city council in Memphis, Tennessee.
More than 100 people showed up to the meeting to hear the outcome on the proposed ordinance.
“This is just a total hazard. We’ve basically been invaded by strangers, by people that have gotten paid, and they have not communicated with us in any way,” said Amber Lowe, a local community member. “This is hurtful, and I’m rethinking where I need to be living at.”
The decision to delay the vote until Oct. 20 led to a fight breaking out in the lobby and tense exchanges among city council members.
A fight between two women spilled into the lobby, with punches thrown while protesters chanted inside the meeting. One woman had her hair pulled and was slapped seconds later.
Councilwoman Yolanda Cooper-Sutton was pulled out of the meeting after arguing with protesters and council member JB Smiley.
“You could’ve came to see me like I asked you to... I ain’t no coward; you pipe down, baby, I clap back,” Cooper-Sutton said.
The city council halted the meeting amid the turmoil and subsequently delayed the vote.
Crowds chanted “this is our city” and “show me what democracy looks like” as the demonstration moved from the chamber into the halls of the building.
Protesters said they are not done pursuing the issue.
Memphis police were called to the disturbance at city hall, but a department spokesperson says no one was detained and no one was harmed.

title: Israelis mourn on the anniversary of the Oct. 7 attack as Palestinians live in devastated Gaza
text:
Israelis mourn on the anniversary of the Oct. 7 attack as Palestinians live in devastated Gaza
Israelis gathered on Wednesday to commemorate the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack that killed 1,200 people, saw 251 taken hostage, and sparked a devastating war in Gaza that has left much of the territory in ruins and its 2 million people living in dire conditions.
In southern Israel, families mourned at intersections, bomb shelters, and the site of a music festival that the militants overran three years ago in the deadliest attack against Israel. It is the first anniversary that all the hostages are home, marking a new stage of grief.
For Palestinians, the anniversary brings another day of misery and difficulties after an Israeli retaliatory campaign in Gaza that has killed tens of thousands of people.
Most of the population of about 2 million people lives in vast, squalid tent camps, with large parts of the strip’s cities reduced to rubble. More than half the territory remains in the hands of the Israeli military. Despite a ceasefire deal reached nearly a year ago, Israeli strikes continue almost daily.
For the region, the day highlights a startling transformation over the past three years.
Israeli troops occupy a large chunk of southern Lebanon in their conflict with the Hezbollah militant group, which began firing on Israel in 2023 in support of Hamas. Iran and the United States are locked in a confrontation that has seen attacks across Gulf Arab countries and has shaken the global economy — a conflict that Israel helped launch and that the Gaza war paved the way for, even if they weren’t directly connected.
Related video: Palestinian family split by Gaza war reunites after unimaginable loss
Families mourn at the Nova Festival site
Near the town of Reim, where the music festival was underway on the day of the attack, families gathered around photos of their killed relatives. They hugged at 6:29 a.m. — the exact time the first rockets were launched three years ago — as booms from explosions in nearby Gaza were heard.
Anya Davitashvili, who lost her 25-year-old son, Sean, said she comes to the site every Saturday because it’s where she feels closest to him.
“I have a video of him dancing here that ends at 6:29 in the morning; it’s in front of my eyes all the time,” she said. “Every morning, you wake up and there is just endless missing.”
Hundreds of people came to pay their respects to the more than 350 people killed in and around the festival site.
A released hostage marks his first Oct. 7
Elkana Bohbot, 37, is marking the anniversary in Israel for the first time, after being released after 738 days of captivity last year. For most of that time, he said, he was held 50 meters (165 feet) underground in a dark, damp tunnel.
Bohbot, who was abducted from the festival, was kept in a small cell with other hostages, given very little food, and allowed to bathe only every few weeks, he said. His captors forced him to take part in several propaganda videos, including one where he acts out a fake call to his family.
In the 11 months since his release, Bohbot has undergone physical and emotional rehabilitation. In August, his wife, Rivka, gave birth to a daughter, fulfilling a promise that Bohbot made to himself in the tunnels to give his 5-year-old son, Reem, a sibling.
The newborn Michele is “not a symbol for my people; she is more of a symbol for the enemy,” Bohbot told The Associated Press. “So this child is the message for you that we were here, and we will always be here forever.”
Palestinians in Gaza live surrounded by devastation and ruins
No events are expected Wednesday in Gaza, but Palestinians in the territory said reminders of how much their lives have changed over the past three years are everywhere.
Some 90% of Gaza’s population has experienced displacement, some multiple times.
“We witnessed death, destruction, and bombardment that we had never known before,” said Walid Akram, a Gaza City resident.
Raed Khozeiq’s coastal neighborhood in Tel al-Hawa was largely flattened. Nothing about his life now is the same, he said.
“No country in the world has gone through what we have experienced here,” he said. “A war of extermination, starvation, the absence of schools and universities — nothing remains.”
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Health Ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its figures but says around half were women and children. The numbers from the ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts.
While a ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10 has halted the heaviest fighting, Israeli strikes have continued, targeting what Israel says are Hamas militants. Since the ceasefire, 1,460 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, according to the ministry. Seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in that period. Restrictions on the entry of goods and aid have contributed to an ongoing hunger crisis, food security experts have said.
Hamas portrayed the Oct. 7 attack as a response to decades of Israeli military occupation, land seizures and settlement construction. But the Palestinians’ dream of an independent state appears even more distant.
The anniversary comes to a radically altered Middle East
A contentious election in Israel at the end of the month hangs over this year's anniversary. The government’s official memorial services took place on Oct. 5, closer to the Hebrew calendar's anniversary of the attack.
The separate commemorations reflected deep divisions over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, his handling of the war and his reluctance to launch an official inquiry into failings of the day.
Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who is hoping to unseat Netanyahu in Israel's upcoming elections, looked at the photos of the dead in Reim and spoke with sobbing family members.
Gadi Eisenkot, the head of the opposition Yashar! party, met with families at a bomb shelter in southern Israel where many were killed as they tried to flee.
The attack set in motion a cascade of events that led to wars across the Middle East as Israel confronted Hamas, Hezbollah and their backer Iran. Israel has seized swaths of territory in Syria and Lebanon, where more than 300,000 Lebanese remain displaced. The United States joined Israel in attacking Iran’s military and nuclear program in two rounds, battering Iran and upending global markets far from the battlefield.
Violence has also risen across the Israeli-occupied West Bank, where Israel’s far-right government has emboldened extremist settlers who have attacked Palestinians and destroyed their property.
___
Associated Press journalist Wafaa Shurafa in Deir al-Balah, Gaza Strip, contributed to this report.

title: What is a checking account?
text:
What is a checking account?
Key takeaways
- A checking account is a bank account used for everyday transactions, such as paying bills, making debit card purchases, withdrawing cash at ATMs, writing checks, sending money to friends and family and receiving direct deposits.
- Checking accounts are often covered by federal deposit insurance.
- There are various types of checking accounts, including free checking, interest-bearing checking, rewards checking and second-chance checking.
A checking account is a bank account that’s designed to be the hub of your financial life. It holds the money you use for everyday spending, and allows you to move funds in and out with ease. You can access your money through a debit card, ATM card, checks or online transfers, and set up direct deposit and automatic billpay to keep your finances running on autopilot.
A checking account is safer and easier than carrying cash or using prepaid products. If your account is covered by federal deposit insurance, your money is protected based on the limits and guidelines, even if the bank or credit union fails. And if your debit card is lost or stolen, you can lock it and dispute unauthorized transactions. To top it off, you won’t pay for any of this protection and access with a free checking account.
What is a checking account used for?
A checking account is meant for the money you use every day, so its features are designed to help you spend, receive and manage that money. Most accounts include these tools:
- Debit card access. A checking account provides a debit card linked to the account. This makes everyday purchases — both in person and online — and ATM withdrawals possible.
- Online and mobile tracking and budgeting. Using this feature, you can check balances, transfer money, pay bills and deposit checks. Some bank apps allow you to create a budget, set alerts and access customer support.
- Overdraft protection. If you spend more than you have available, overdraft protection helps bridge the gap by covering transactions that exceed the account balance. You typically have to opt in to these programs and some charge you a fee for this privilege, though others have eliminated or reduced overdraft fees.
- Direct deposit. Direct deposit lets you have your paycheck or other income deposited electronically into your checking account. Some financial institutions even allow early access, up to two days, to funds that are deposited using this feature.
- Check writing. Although checks aren’t as popular as they used to be, they can still come in handy. For example, some landlords may still only take payment via check.
Not every account handles these features equally well, so it pays to compare Bankrate’s picks for the best checking accounts.
Benefits of checking accounts
Checking accounts keep your money safe and accessible, and they make it easy to automate your money management.
Safety
- Safer than cash. If your wallet is lost or stolen, you can lock your debit card and dispute unauthorized transactions as long as you report them quickly. Once cash is stolen, it’s often gone for good.
- Federal deposit insurance. If your account is with a federally insured bank or credit union, your money is protected if the institution fails, within coverage limits.
- Coverage limits. The Federal Deposit Insurance (FDIC) and National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund (NCUSIF) insure funds up to $250,000 per depositor or share owner, per insured financial institution, per ownership category — such as joint or single accounts.
Ease of access
- Many ways to pay. Use a debit or ATM card, checks or online payments for everything from retail purchases to rent, mortgage payments and other bills.
- Quick transfers to others. Many accounts offer peer-to-peer payments through Zelle from your phone or computer. You can also link your account to apps like Venmo.
Automation
- Direct deposit. Paychecks land in your account automatically, so you don’t have to deposit them yourself. Some banks allow you to receive your paycheck up to two days sooner through early direct deposit.
- Automatic bill pay. Regular expenses, such as credit card and utility bills, are electronically withdrawn on a recurring basis.
- Automatic saving. Splitting your paycheck between checking and a high-yield savings account allows you to “pay yourself first” and put your savings on autopilot.
Access to overdraft coverage
Overdrafts can occur when you withdraw more money than what’s in your account and your balance dips below zero. Overdraft fees the bank charges you to cover your payment can be expensive, though some banks now offer this service free of charge.
Many checking accounts offer overdraft protection, which automatically transfers funds from your savings account or a line of credit when your checking account is overdrawn. You can easily find banks that don’t charge a fee for such transfers from a linked savings account.
Checking vs. savings accounts
A checking account is best for making day-to-day financial transactions, while a savings account is a good place for funds set aside for emergencies, or financial goals such as a vacation or a new car purchase.
Bankrate insight
You can get the best of both worlds by having your checking account at a brick-and-mortar bank and a high-yield savings account at an online-only bank. This way, you’re able to walk into a bank for checking issues or to make cash deposits while earning a competitive yield on your savings at an online bank.
How to choose a checking account
Start by deciding which type of checking account fits your needs, then compare the details that affect cost and convenience:
- Monthly fees: Maintenance fees can eat away at your balance over time. Look for a free checking account with no monthly fee, or check whether the fee can be waived with either a direct deposit you would normally make or a reasonable minimum balance.
- Other fees: Check the fee schedule for overdraft fees, out-of-network ATM fees or paper statement fees. Make sure such fees are easy for you to avoid, or choose an account that doesn’t charge them.
- Minimum opening deposit: This can vary among banks, so make sure it’s an amount you’re comfortable with. Some checking accounts don’t require any set minimum deposit.
- ATM access: The total average out-of-network ATM fee is around $4 to $5. To avoid these fees, choose a bank that offers plenty of its own ATMs or is a member of a large fee-free network, or go with a bank that reimburses ATM fees.
- Branch access: If you prefer in-person banking, find a bank with branches near you, but watch for higher fees, since banks with branches tend to charge more to cover their costs. Most also offer online banking, which works well if you want a mix of both.
- Features: Consider what you’ll actually use, such as a strong mobile app, early direct deposit, budgeting tools, peer-to-peer payment options like Zelle and overdraft protection. If you want to earn interest, check whether an interest checking account’s requirements are manageable for you.
Next steps

- Checking account fees Learn the common fees and how to avoid them.
- Second-chance checking accounts Access for those whose history may prevent them from opening a standard account.
- Best interest checking accounts These accounts earn money on the funds you use for daily expenses.

title: This Maine actor’s career has taken her from Camden to London
text:
Caitlin FitzGerald always finds a little bit of Maine, wherever she is.
She cornered Portland native Anna Kendrick at a party in London so she could talk about Maine with her. When the iconic true-life book “Lost on a Mountain in Maine” was made into a movie a few years ago, FitzGerald just knew she had to play the lost boy’s mother. She had read the book in grammar school, like most Maine kids.
And this year, while filming the second season of the Prime drama “We Were Liars” in Nova Scotia, FitzGerald was introduced to Elysia Roorbach, who will be playing the younger version of her character, Penny Sinclair. Roorbach grew up in Farmington, in Maine’s western mountains.
“I love Maine so much, it feels like such a part of who I am and it’s such a special place,” said FitzGerald, while filming in Nova Scotia this summer. “So it’s wonderful to meet people who understand.”
FitzGerald, 43, has traveled and worked all over the world during her 20-year career in film, TV and theater. She’s currently living in London and recently starred as Desdemona in a West End production of Shakespeare’s “Othello,” which was filmed and released to theaters in March.
She’s currently starring as one of the adult sisters of a wealthy, secrets-laden family in the Prime drama “We Were Liars,” based on the best-selling novel by E. Lockhart. The first season premiered in the summer of 2025 and the second season is slated for sometime next year. FitzGerald also had a recurring role on the hit HBO show “Succession,” playing Tabitha Hayes, girlfriend of Roman Roy (Kieran Culkin). About a decade ago, she played Libby Masters, the first wife of pioneering sex researcher William Masters, in the Showtime series “Masters of Sex.”
“We Were Liars” focuses on a wealthy family that spends the summer on a private island off the Massachusetts coast. FitzGerald’s character, Penny Sinclair, is the mother of Cadence Sinclair Eastman, part of a tightknit group called the Liars. Cadence suffers from memory loss due to a mysterious accident.
MAINE CONNECTIONS
The second season flashes back two decades, so new actors were cast to play the younger versions of the main characters. In a weird bit of Maine karma, Roorbach was cast to play the younger Penny. So there are two Maine actors on the show playing the same role. Earlier this year Roorbach made her TV debut playing an emergency room patient in two episodes of the hit HBO drama “The Pitt.”
FitzGerald said she didn’t know Roorbach, 26, until she was cast in “We Were Liars.” The two quickly found they had much in common, besides being from Maine. They both studied acting at New York University, and both did a semester abroad in London, focused on Shakespeare.
“There aren’t a lot of people from Maine in this industry, so it’s great that she’s here,” said FitzGerald of Roorbach. “I’m so pleased I get to work with her.”
FitzGerald lived in Lincolnville as a small child, then moved to Camden. Her father, Des FitzGerald, started a company called DuckTrap River Fish Farm, which became a nationally known purveyor of smoked fish. Her mother, Pam Allen, was the editor of a knitting magazine and started her own line of yarn, Quince & Co.
FitzGerald says she fell in love with acting in a kindergarten play, an adaptation of Rudyard Kipling’s “How the Elephant Got his Trunk.” She got involved with area children’s theater productions, including at Camden Civic Theatre.
FitzGerald says she really wanted to study the craft of acting, instead of just driving to Los Angeles and looking for work, like many people do. She chose the Tisch School of the Arts at NYU because it combined classroom academics with stage training. Being from Maine, she says living in New York City during college was also an education.
Though she’s worked steadily for two decades, FitzGerald says her career has ebbed and flowed. One of her early breaks was being cast in the 2009 romcom “It’s Complicated,” starring Meryl Streep and Alec Baldwin. She played Streep’s daughter.
“She was my hero, so I was definitely nervous to work with her, I had no idea what I was doing,” said FitzGerald. “I probably embarrassed myself a lot in front of her, but she was very generous.”
In one of those odd full-circle moments, FitzGerald is now sharing scenes with Streep’s daughter, Mamie Gummer. Gummer plays a sister of FitzGerald’s character on “We Were Liars.”
One of FitzGerald’s favorite roles was playing Libby Masters on “Masters of Sex” over four seasons. She says the writers created for her character “an amazing journey” from a typical 1950s housewife, who happens to be married to a sex researcher, to a more a indepedendent and complicated character. She eventually goes to Woodstock and also studies law.
But maybe her most personal role was playing the mother of Donn Fendler in “Lost on a Mountain in Maine.” Fendler was 12 when he got separated from his hiking party on Mount Katahdin in 1939 and survived nine days alone, lost in the woods.
The search for Fendler and his eventual rescue sparked stories in newspapers around the country. Within months, a book co-authored by Fendler and Joseph B. Egan, “Lost on a Mountain in Maine,” was published. For decades the book was taught in Maine schools as part of a lesson on Maine history. Fendler himself spoke to hundreds of classes and community groups over the years. He died in 2016, at the age of 90.
FitzGerald said she has vivid memories of the book, which portrays the danger, fear and hope of a young, lost boy. She said when her agent told her about the movie, and the part of Fendler’s mother, she said, “I have to do that one.”
Before opening in theaters nationally, the film premiered at the Maine International Film Festival in Waterville in the summer of 2024. FitzGerald attended the premiere and said she loved seeing so many teachers from around Maine who had taught the book to kids like her for years.
“It was such a lovely homegrown moment and I was really proud to be a part of it,” she said. “It was an honor to tell that story.”

title: Nancy Ouellette honored as Albion’s oldest citizen
text:
As with many towns across New England, Canaan, Maine is no exception to retain their Boston Post Cane,and award it to their oldest citizen. This year, on September 28, Canaan awarded one of their most loved and precious citizen, 96-year-old Nancy Harris Ouellette. Canaan has been Nancy’s home through out her life. During her long and wonderful lifetime, she has seen many things come and go, but the most precious things to Nancy has been her husband Norman and their children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren. This award is not new to her family in Canaan, for her grandfather, Harry B Harris was also awarded the Boston Post Cane. During her long life in Canaan, she has been a teacher in the Canaan Christian School for over 29 years, and has been a founding member of the Canaan Calvery Church. At the ceremony, the Town of Canaan also awarded Nancy with the first ever “Town of Canaan Coin #001” and as Selectman Daniel Harriman declared “It could’nt have started out with a better person.”This is Nancy’ home! Nancy’s people! It will always be Nancy’s legacy to be a kind and loving mother, grandmother and citizen of Canaan Maine! May she live long and enjoy the years ahead. Canaan will always love her.
The Boston Post Cane was awarded to men at first in 1909, but in 1930, they changed it so women could also receive the award. This too was the year Nancy Harris Ouellette was born. 1930!

title: Gorham History Is a Click Away!
text:
Oct. 1, 2026 marked the official launch of Open Access, the Maine State Archives (MSA) new online platform for publicly accessible, digitized and born-digital public records. Open Access is the public-facing side of a strategic effort to maintain a digital preservation system for records of Maine state government. which ensures the long-term preservation and accessibility of state records that are archival or subject to long-term retention.
MSA’s collections span five centuries from the 1639 royal land grant to Sir Ferdinand Gorges to the 2024 papers of the Lewiston Tragedy Commission. One section of the site is devoted to Maine history before statehood, highlighting important records such as Revolutionary War land grants and the Rolls and Rosters Book of Orders for the 8th Division of the Maine Militia. The records of Maine’s involvement in the Civil War are extensive.
Open Access currently holds just over 100,000 imaged records so far. Content will be continuously expanded as more and more collections are imaged.
“With more than 8 miles of documents in the Archives’ care, there is a long way to go to digitize them all, but it’s a great start,” said Maine State Archivist Christian Cotz. “We’re excited to continue to add records to the platform and provide Mainers from students to researchers with even more to discover each time they visit the site.”
The platform can be accessed at https://digitalarchives.maine.gov or from the Maine State Archives section of the Secretary of State website. Pay a visit to the site and enter “Gorham” in the search bar; you never know what local history you might discover!

title: Mother dies, baby critical after being pushed from 15th-floor balcony, police say
text:
NEW YORK (WABC) - A young mother died and her 8-month-old daughter was critically injured after police say they were pushed from a 15th-floor balcony in New York City.
Officers with the New York City Police Department responded around 3:30 a.m. Tuesday to an apartment building in the Bronx, where they found 23-year-old Nathaly Ramirez and her 8-month-old daughter on the ground outside the building.
Both the mother and baby were taken to the hospital. Ramirez was pronounced dead, and her daughter remains in critical condition.
Even in her final moments, Ramirez’s motherly instincts kicked in as officials say she wrapped her baby in a tight embrace, likely cushioning the impact of the fall.
Police are investigating Ramirez’s death as a homicide. Officers spent hours examining a 15th-floor balcony for evidence while canvassing for surveillance video and additional witnesses. They are also looking to speak with Ramirez’s ex-boyfriend.
Friends say Ramirez was devoted to her daughter.
“She was very happy to be a mom. She’s a new mom, and the baby was very happy,” one friend said.
The investigation is ongoing. No arrests have been announced.

title: Christa Pike is ‘speaking limitedly’ after being declared brain dead before waking up after failed execution, attorney says
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP/Gray News) — Christa Pike was declared brain dead on Monday night and was expected to be taken off life support, but woke up and started talking on Tuesday, according to her attorneys.
“I do not have an explanation for what happened between Monday night and Tuesday morning but I do know she has a long road to recovery,” attorney Randy Spivey said in a press conference on Wednesday.
Spivey said that while he was not there and did not want to speculate, he believes Pike’s first words upon waking up were, “Where am I and who are you?”
“She is angry and confused about everything right now. ... She is very aware of what they did to her up to a point,” he said.
According to Pike’s attorneys, she has a blood clot, cannot swallow and has not eaten. Her arms and hands are swollen and it is unknown at this time if she will regain function in her arms. They also said she has pneumonia.
“The swelling was extraordinary,” Spivey said.
Pike’s feet and right arm are shackled to her hospital bed. Medical staff and her attorneys have asked for some of the restraints to be removed, according to her legal team.
Pike is the only person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution, according to The Death Penalty Information Center.
This is a breaking news update. Previous story below.
Christa Pike regained consciousness roughly six days after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute her and was “speaking limitedly,” one of her attorneys said during a court hearing Wednesday.
Pike, 50, survived even after executioners tried to give her two lethal doses of pentobarbital on Sept. 30. She was sentenced to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer.
The Death Penalty Information Center says Pike is the only person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution.
At a hearing Wednesday in Nashville, Pike’s attorneys asked the court to order the Tennessee Department of Correction to save evidence in the case and provide more information about what went wrong. A judge ordered the state to preserve “anything that was in the actual room.”
“Part of the issue that we are facing is that, up until yesterday, our client was unconscious, unable to communicate with counsel, unable to communicate with medical providers, and without her consent, a new lawsuit cannot be filed, Luke Ihnen, a federal public defender, told the court.
Her legal team said Tuesday that Pike’s prognosis remains unclear and, at a minimum, she faces a lengthy recovery. Her arms were burned and blistered after the attempted lethal injection and she is handcuffed to the hospital bed, they said.
The failed execution has renewed scrutiny of how states carry out the death penalty, in particular the use of lethal injection. Texas was set to carry out Wednesday the first execution in the U.S. since Tennessee attempted to put Pike to death.
Christa Pike’s attorneys want evidence preserved
Pike’s attorneys wanted a court order to require the prison system to preserve information from the attempted execution, including drug lot numbers, needles, execution logs and other information.
Chancery Court Judge I’Ashea Myles indicated that her order to save the evidence would be sweeping, saying the state should maintain recordings, witness accounts, emails along with drugs, syringes, IV lines and other medical items.
The Tennessee Attorney General’s Office said a court order was unnecessary. John W. Ayers, assistant attorney general, said evidence from the death chamber already had been collected and logged.
Republican Gov. Bill Lee has called what happened “deeply disturbing” and ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred.” The governor postponed the state’s only other execution scheduled for this year.
The state’s prison chief resigned in the wake of the failed execution.
Christa Pike’s recovery remains uncertain
Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on the possibility that a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue rather than entering her bloodstream. Pike’s attorneys wrote in their court filing that “apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown.”
The attempted execution got underway around 7:30 p.m. on Sept. 30 when Pike was given a chance to make a final statement. About five minutes later, Pike raised her head and said her arm was hurting. At some point she appeared to lose consciousness, but she could be heard audibly breathing until media were escorted from the witness room at 8:53 p.m. An ambulance arrived at the prison at 9:14 p.m. to take Pike to a hospital.
Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike’s legal team, said it could be weeks or months before anyone knows exactly what her recovery might look like, and whether her competency could be restored so the state can try again to execute her.
___
Associated Press writers Ed White in Detroit and John Seewer, in Toledo, Ohio, contributed.

title: Maine Municipal Association marks 90 years with annual convention
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - The Maine Municipal Association is celebrating 90 years of service to Maine cities and towns with its annual convention.
The Augusta Civic Center was packed with Maine town and city officials for two days of learning and networking.
“Every year it’s important because it’s a great opportunity to bring together people for education but also with our exhibit hall for folks to engage with a number of service providers that might be of use in their municipalities,” said Peter Osborne, director of educational services for the Maine Municipal Association.
Osborne said over the last 90 years, the association has adapted what is being taught to match industry standards.
“In the training world that we do, there’s always new things coming up. They’re dealing with new legislation, they’re dealing with new pieces of technology. So, we’re talking a lot now about generative AI, of course, and how do you put that to use in municipal government. But, the needs change all the time, and we try to be really responsive to those as we can,” Osborne said.
The convention included breakout rooms for specific educational topics.
“Those kind of classroom experiences are really important. It’s really the opportunity to hear from the experts about the training and education that is really one of the most valuable things that somebody can get out of coming to the MMA conference,” said Chris Camire, chair of the Lisbon Town Council and incoming MMA executive board member.
Outside the classroom sessions, municipalities had the chance to talk through challenges together.
“That’s where the convention comes into play because it’s a real opportunity for members to network with each other. It’s a very small kind of small tight-knit community of municipalities. So, they’re always calling each other for advice or trying to look at what another town might be doing and try to adapt that to their municipalities need,” Osborne said.
Camire said he benefited from that networking in the first few hours of the convention.
“One example that I just had a conversation maybe half an hour ago was a conversation around creating tax relief programs for senior citizens. So, I was talking with the town manager in the town of Poland and he said, hey, we implemented this a while ago. We’re starting the first year of that in Lisbon. So, having a conversation about that and what are the things that you learned? What are the gotchas? What are some lessons learned that we can implement moving forward? So, it’s a stable program that can provide meaningful tax relief to the seniors in our community,” Camire said.

title: Wrong ballots distributed in one Maine House District
text:
Wrong ballots distributed in one Maine House District
The Maine Secretary of State's Office confirms to Maine's Total Coverage that some incorrect ballots were distributed to voters in Oxford.
The Secretary of State's Office says a resident contacted the Oxford town clerk on Tuesday after "receiving an incorrect ballot style, and it was addressed by the clerk."
State officials say the clerk identified that, due to a packaging error at the printer, "a small number of incorrect ballots were received and sent out."
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said she believed nine wrong ballots were distributed.
Town officials say 10 incorrect ballots were given out. The town was able to track down three of the voters and get them the correct ballot and they were working to contact the remaining seven.
"We're doing what we can to communicate with them to make sure that they continue to have their opportunity," said Adam Garland, Oxford's town manager.
The state said every voter will have the chance to vote the correct ballot. Anyone who receives an incorrect ballot, or who makes a mistake on their ballot, may request a new one. If a voter submits the wrong ballot and doesn't inform the clerk before 8 p.m. on election day, only their votes for statewide races will be counted.
Voters should have received ballots with the candidates for House District 80, which includes Republican Ernest Fitts and Azalea Cormier, who is not registered in a party and is also running for the House District 80 seat. There is no Democrat in the race.
Both candidates say they are concerned the ballot error could impact the election if it's a close race.
"Ten might not sound like much when we're talking about the scale of a Senate campaign or a gubernatorial campaign, but it's incredibly impactful for us, for the state House," said Cormier.
"We're two days into early voting, and we already have an issue. So it just makes me wonder what's going to be lying ahead," said Fitts.
District 80 includes the towns of Buckfield, Hebron, Otisfield and Oxford.

title: Why women should advocate for themselves after delays in heart disease diagnosis
text:
GREENVILLE, S.C. (InvestigateTV) — Heart disease is the biggest threat to women’s health, though studies show many people still believe it is primarily a men’s health issue.
The study also found women were less likely than men to have an echocardiogram, a non-invasive ultrasound test that evaluates heart structure and function.
A runner’s warning signs
Courtney Pace, a South Carolina mother, used to run a few miles a day. In 2024, even walking caused her pain.
“It felt like I was having chest pain, it would go down my arm, like a heart attack,” Pace said.
Pace went to the emergency room, where doctors gave her an EKG, a test that checks the heart’s electrical activity. Her results came back normal. Pace said doctors suggested stress or a hard workout might be the cause and sent her home.
“I left crying,” she said.
Research by the National Institutes of Health shows that during a cardiac event, women are less likely than men to be referred for cardiac diagnostic testing, receive timely treatment or be taken seriously. As a result, heart disease in women is often detected later, when it is more advanced and harder to treat.
UNC Health cardiologist Dr. Essraa Bayoumi said some of the pattern is rooted in historic thinking.
“Cardiovascular disease was seen more as a man’s disease and that women were somehow protected. And so that thought has been ingrained. So it unfortunately is true. We’ve really been behind in understanding and diagnosing and treating cardiovascular disease in women,” Bayoumi said.
Bayoumi said women are also consistently under-represented in landmark clinical trials.
A 2022 study published by the National Library of Medicine found that guideline recommendations for the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease are based on predominantly male participants.
Bayoumi said when tests come back normal, women’s symptoms are sometimes dismissed as something else, like anxiety or “just stress.”
“We use stress as sort of an excuse for their symptoms which is a double-edged sword because truly, stress is actually a risk factor for cardiovascular disease,” Bayoumi said.
Bayoumi said advocating for yourself starts with knowing personal risk factors, including family history, autoimmune disease, pregnancy-related complications like preeclampsia or gestational diabetes, and menopause-related changes.
“And that’s because they’ve lost that estrogen, which we believe is protective,” Bayoumi said. “And that’s why women who have menopause much earlier are at a much higher risk of having cardiovascular disease.”
Cardiologists and experts say women don’t always show “classic” chest pain, which can slow a diagnosis.
In addition to chest pain or discomfort, women may experience nausea and vomiting, unexplained weakness or tiredness, upset stomach, or pain in the shoulder, back or arm.
Experts say because some of these symptoms do not fit the standard heart attack narrative, they are frequently mistaken for panic attacks, acid reflux or bone and joint issues.
A Kentucky mother’s experience
In 2025, it took six stairs for Vivian Tandy to realize something was wrong.
She experienced shortness of breath and chest pain, which interfered with her daily routine. Doctors asked her to wear a heart monitor, but after it came back normal, Tandy still did not feel “right” and expressed her concerns to her doctor.
Her doctor listened and eventually found the cause. In October 2025, Tandy underwent open heart surgery to fix a rare genetic heart disorder.
“They essentially did what’s called an unroofing, and they literally shaved a piece of my heart — it’s really cool,” Tandy said.
Tandy said her decision to keep advocating for herself was connected to her mother, who died at age 47 from heart disease.
“I look in the mirror, and I see that scar, and I look at myself, and I’m like if it wasn’t for my mom, I wouldn’t have done the things that I did to fight for the answer, so I am super proud of my scar,” Tandy said.
A specialist finds answers
Back in South Carolina, Pace’s chest pain persisted, and she returned to the emergency room. This time, she asked to see a specialist. Interventional cardiologist Dr. Vincent Gacad had a hunch of what was going on.
Gacad performed a specialized type of catheterization, which detected coronary microvascular disease, or CMD, a condition that affects tiny vessels that deliver blood to heart tissue that a resting EKG often cannot detect.
“Traditionally, when we see chest pain we think about coronary artery disease or large vessel blockage,” Gacad said.
CMD causes prolonged chest pain, called angina, and increases the risk for heart attack, according to the Cleveland Clinic. It is more common in women, especially those with lower estrogen levels.
Thanks to medication and her treatment plan, Pace said she is feeling much better and has returned to exercising.
“I just got into more of a walk run, this weekend I did two miles, so I am starting to pick up the pace and get back into it,” Pace said.
What experts recommend
Experts suggest that if you suspect something is wrong with your heart, be persistent. Ask your doctor for further heart testing, such as an EKG, a stress test, a blood test for heart markers like troponin levels, or an echocardiogram.
Experts also recommend bringing an advocate, such as a trusted friend or family member, who can help reinforce your concerns.
If symptoms are dismissed, experts say do not hesitate to see another doctor.
Women who feel unheard can also request a female doctor or seek out a specialist, such as a cardiologist with expertise in women’s heart health.

title: Bangor school evacuated due to potential threat, which was deemed a hoax
text:
Cohen School in Bangor evacuated due to potential threat, which was deemed a hoax
The William S. Cohen School in Bangor was evacuated Wednesday due to a potential threat, law enforcement officials told WMTW media partner WABI. A Bangor school official said that the threat has been deemed a hoax.
A police officer at the scene told a WABI reporter that all students were safe and accounted for.
The school was searched and nothing dangerous was found, according to authorities.
An email from the school addressed to parents said that everyone was evacuated to the Fruit Street School at 11:30 a.m., also citing a “potential threat.”
The email went on to say that the safety and well-being of the children is the top priority, and that school officials were working with emergency responders to resolve the situation. School officials said Cohen School students had been given the choice to either return to school or be picked up by guardians.
It remains unclear where the threat came from or if anyone will be charged in connection with the incident. WABI contacted Bangor police and the Bangor School Department for more information.
The Cohen School, which is located on Garland Street, serves nearly 400 Bangor students in grades 6-8.

title: A rocky 'wonderland' in Arizona is poised to be the next US national park
text:
An area of towering rock spires in southeastern Arizona known among Native Americans as the Land of Standing-Up Rocks is poised to become the nation’s newest national park.
Legislation to create Chiricahua National Park is expected to be transmitted to the White House in coming days for President Donald Trump’s signature. It passed Congress with bipartisan backing and would be the 64th national park.
The 19-square-mile (49-square kilometer) site is within the historical territory of the Chiricahua Apache tribes. It was designated a national monument in the 1920s to preserve hundreds of pinnacle-shaped rocks formed from an ancient volcanic eruption.
“We’re the Grand Canyon state, so we know about this kind of landscape,” Rep. Juan Ciscomani, House sponsor of the Chiricahua National Park Act, said Wednesday. “It’s hard to compare anything to the Grand Canyon, but Chiricahua holds its own. This is something that really hasn’t been discovered.”
National Park Service officials declined to say if new staff would be hired to address an expected increase in visitors as the new designation elevates the site’s profile.
The park service has undergone deep cuts to its workforce under Trump. Maintenance projects at many sites — including Chiricahua — were ranked a “low priority” by officials who have instead focused on projects wanted by the White House including repairs to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
For centuries the site of the proposed park was home to the Apache, nomadic tribes who often resisted European newcomers to North America. They continued clashing with settlers until surrendering to U.S. troops in 1886 and being forcibly removed to the San Carlos Apache reservation.
The bill creating Chiricahua National Park preserves tribal access for traditional ceremonies. It allows temporary public closures within the park to protect those cultural uses, although Ciscomani said specifics have not been decided.
San Carlos Apache tribal leaders did not take a formal position on the national park designation, a spokesperson said Wednesday. In response to questions from The Associated Press, the tribe provided its 2024 testimony before Congress, where San Carlos Apache Deputy Attorney General Justine Jimmie asked for uninterrupted access to the site.
“National parks have become so packed with tourists,” Jimmie said. “In contrast, we go to our cultural areas in what are now parks to seek sanctuary, pray, and perform ceremonies.”
Early settlers called the site Wonderland of Rocks. The name Chiricahua comes from the surrounding mountains.
The area has evidence of thousands of years of human use, according to the park service. That spans from prehistoric people to the famed Buffalo Soldiers. The U.S. troops who were Black were stationed there after the Civil War during a government campaign against Apache leaders Geronimo and Cochise.
Former President Calvin Coolidge named the site as a national monument in 1924 under a federal law known as the Antiquities Act. Former President Franklin Roosevelt expanded it in 1938.
About 85% of the park is designated as wilderness. It gets roughly 60,000 visitors annually.
National monuments are designed to protect specific locations and objects, such as archaeological or historical sites, whereas national parks have a broader purpose including recreation and the preservation of vast expanses of wilderness. Parks and monuments alike are managed by the park service.
Chiricahua would be the first new national park since New River Gorge National Park and Preserve in West Virginia in 2021.
The mayor of nearby Willcox, Arizona, Greg Hancock, said the change could bring in more customers for its hotels, restaurants and small businesses.
The monument has a visitor center, campground and hiking trails. Park service officials declined to say if any immediate changes were planned.
The park service will “evaluate those matters consistent with the law, available funding and applicable planning requirements,” officials said in a statement. The Congressional Budget Office said it would cost less than $500,000 to establish the park, but did not specify how that might be spent.
House lawmakers approved the park’s creation in a voice vote in March, and the Senate passed it Sept. 30 by unanimous consent.

title: Family of late midcoast firefighter continues his legacy with nonprofit
text:
Members of fire departments in Lincoln County gathered at the Edgecomb Fire Department on Sept. 26 to pick up equipment donated by a nonprofit foundation formed to honor the founders’ late son.
The Gavin Martin Foundation is dedicated to honoring the legacy of Gavin Martin, a 21-year-old Edgecomb firefighter who died in a car crash in December 2025. At the Sept. 26 event, Monika and Joel Martin said they wanted to follow their son’s example of giving back and created a foundation to help the organizations and communities he loved.
“Having other people say his name keeps him alive for us,” Monika Martin said.
Haley Gifford, a member of the foundation’s board and one of Gavin Martin’s older cousins, said the nonprofit came together after the family was looking for a way to remember him. Originally from Verona, New Jersey, Gavin Martin had spent time volunteering for the fire department there and after college, eventually joined the Edgecomb Fire Department. Gifford said the family has a house in the town, which Gavin Martin moved into after college.
“Really supporting those dreams that he had as a young adult and being able to give back to the first responders and young people with their trades is really where the idea came from, and just continuing his name,” Gifford said.
When the nonprofit was first started earlier this year, Gifford said initiatives included a blood drive and other community events in both Maine and New Jersey. In the past couple of months, the organization dedicated a new field where Gavin Martin played baseball in New Jersey and donated to other areas he cared about.
In June, the organization gave out scholarships to graduating students in both New Jersey and Maine. Students from Boothbay Regional High School, Wiscasset Middle High School, Lincoln Academy and Medomak Valley High School were tasked with writing about how they display generosity in their daily lives. The organization gave out a total of $15,000 in scholarships, with students getting around $1,000 to $1,500 each.
The biggest event the organization has held so far was a midcoast fire training weekend in August at the Boothbay Fire Department’s training center. Gifford said the training welcomed firefighters from Maine and New Jersey, as well as others from around New England. The training brought in instructors and included ropes training, extrication activities, and other hands-on practice.
The Edgecomb Fire Department offered its firehouse for lectures and the Wiscasset Fire Department hosted other trainings.
Gifford said the Sept. 26 event was a thank-you for the participating departments, which included the towns of Alna, Boothbay, Boothbay Harbor, Edgecomb, South Bristol and Wiscasset. The foundation purchased equipment used in the training so the participating departments didn’t have to pay for it themselves.
“A lot of the attendees really didn’t know what to expect, but they were so thankful, so grateful about how great it was,” Gifford said. “Somebody actually recently emailed us and said that they continued to talk about the weekend and actually they were able to use some of the new skills they had at a recent extrication.”
The Edgecomb community that once rallied around Gavin Martin when he moved to the town alone as a young person has now rallied around his parents, both Monika and Joel Martin said.
Beyond being a first responder, Gavin Martin also had a passion for the trades. Monika Martin said her son had a background in engineering, recalling how he played with Lego blocks all of his life and enjoyed building things.
Gavin Martin graduated from Central Maine Community College and near the end of his time in school, he worked numerous jobs. His mother said he was looking for something in project management or construction, something hands-on. After not enjoying a job mowing lawns, Monika Martin said Gavin Martin went on to found his own landscaping company.
Gavin Martin also started working for the Waldoboro Public Works Department. Monika Martin said during this time, her son developed a close working relationship with Town Manager Julie Keizer.
“When we think about him, like he always helps, even though he was up here by himself,” Monika Martin said. “He had neighbors, but some of them were way older than him and he would always check in and make sure things were going on. He was always giving back.”
After serving in their fire department back home in New Jersey, Joel Martin said he recently joined Edgecomb’s department. He said the goal is to move to Maine once their daughter graduates high school.
“We have plans to be here full time, but a little painful without Gavin running around, so we’ll figure it out,” Joel Martin said.
Edgecomb Fire Chief Roy Potter said he watched Gavin Martin grow up and that his loss affected the department greatly.
Since the Gavin Martin Foundation was founded, Potter said the work the organization has done to benefit fire departments has been “incredible,” especially with the decline in volunteerism around the state. He used the example of his department, which has 17 members, three of whom are over the age of 60 and two are over the age of 70.
Having opportunities to go to a training like the one in August helps with accessibility for those interested in becoming a firefighter, Potter said. Not only were participants able to learn more about hands-on work, they were able to collaborate with members of other departments.
As the Gavin Martin Foundation heads toward one year as a nonprofit organization, Joel Martin said they plan on coordinating more training events and other ways to give back to the communities his son loved. He said he is currently in conversation with the state on getting funding to rejuvenate the fire training center in Wiscasset.
“The best part about it is it keeps Gavin’s legacy going,” Potter said.
For more information about the Gavin Martin Foundation, email info@gavinmartinfoundation.org or go to gavinmartinfoundation.org.

title: Maine needs a housing strategy. Hannah Pingree has one.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
When I turned 30, suddenly all of my friends were talking about buying houses. Or, more specifically, how hard it is to buy a house. Looking at houses on Zillow in one’s spare time is no longer a fun game; it’s just depressing. So many house prices have skyrocketed since 2020. 
Due to Maine’s housing prices, I see myself sticking to renting for a good long while. That’s not to say, of course, that renting is necessarily easier. Rents in Portland rival those in Boston. And outside of Portland, we don’t find much relief either. But at least when my dishwasher breaks, I’ll have someone to call. Hard to save for that down payment, though.
Thankfully, we have someone running for governor who knows Maine is facing a very serious housing crisis. Hannah Pingree’s housing plan will invest in housing, stop out-of-state corporations from driving up rents and cut the red tape that slows development. Hannah’s smart, clear and comprehensive housing plan gives me hope for Maine’s future.
Eloise Melcher
Portland

title: Hegseth visits the long-deployed USS Lincoln to bestow a top award before the ship returns home
text:
Hegseth visits the long-deployed USS Lincoln to bestow a top award before the ship returns home
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has given the crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln a high-level award during a visit to the aircraft carrier Wednesday, a day before the ship returns home to San Diego after a record-long deployment in support of the Iran war.
The Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive that is typically reserved for significant achievement in combat, was bestowed upon the Lincoln and accompanying ships for "40 days of combat operations and an ironclad maritime blockade against Iran in support of Operation Epic Fury," Hegseth said, referring to the Trump administration's code name for the Iran war.
The carrier endured a record 265 uninterrupted days at sea, and its extended deployment drew national attention following reports of crew stress and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products. After more than 10 months deployed, the Lincoln's crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East.
Pentagon chief visits the crew and acknowledges long time at sea
Hegseth, who flew out to the ship before its arrival Thursday in San Diego, acknowledged to the crew that "I'm the only thing standing between you and home" and that his intention was "once they pull up to the dock, we're getting out of the way."
Long deployments can tax service members who are away from their families for extended periods while facing threats, and can add wear to the aircraft carriers, which have been used for President Donald Trump's military operations in the Middle East and South America.
The Lincoln is the second carrier that has endured an unusually long and arduous deployment to support the war against Iran and the second to receive the top unit award afterward.
Hegseth in May met the crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford during its return from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era.
As for the Lincoln, it departed San Diego in late November, arrived in the Middle East in January and now will be back in its home port.
Hegseth said Wednesday that Trump "tracked your activities from day one and couldn't be more proud of what you executed."
Issues had been reported aboard the USS Lincoln
The Navy initially played down early reports of supply problems on Lincoln and Trump said its lengthy deployment was "not nearly long enough," Navy leaders, however, eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.
In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced from two to one for a short time. He said in a letter to a Democratic lawmaker seeking information that four nutritionally balanced meals were served daily.
Navy officials also said that while combat operations led to delays in scheduled resupply shipments, they prioritized the delivery of hygiene products and established a rotation to streamline distribution to different squadrons.
More recently, the service told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide while on the long deployment. Experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months.
Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the "Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission."
He said that "what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you're resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless."
Aircraft carriers have been key to Iran War operations
According to the award that Hegseth read to the crew, the Lincoln and the strike group executed 3,693 combat missions, delivered 1.37 million pounds of ordnance, launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles, shot down 77 one-way attack drones, sank 64 Iranian warships, destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles and defended against four fast attack craft and explosive-carrying ships.
There are now two aircraft carriers assigned to the Middle East. The USS George Washington, though usually based in Asia, relieved the Lincoln in August.
The other aircraft carrier, the USS George H.W. Bush, has been deployed for about six months, but it pulled into Phuket, Thailand, for a port visit several days ago.
U.S. officials have said a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, and thousands of troops aboard it and accompanying ships could join the Washington and the Bush as early as the end of October.

title: Top teams in Varsity Maine football polls are dominating
