title: Tayari Jones' novel 'Kin' wins the Kirkus Prize for fiction, earning a $50,000 award
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Tayari Jones’ “Kin,” a novel tracing the life and times of two Black friends from small-town Louisiana, has won the Kirkus Prize for fiction.
Paula Colloff’s “Catch the Devil: A True Story of Murder, Deception, and Injustice on the Gulf Coast” won for nonfiction, and Elizabeth Acevedo’s “Anger Is Only a Shadow” was awarded for young readers’ literature.
Each of the three authors receives a $50,000 cash prize.
Colson Whitehead’s “Cool Machine,” Douglas Stuart’s “John of John” and Patrick Radden Keefe’s “London Falling” were among the finalists.
The Kirkus awards, presented by the industry publication Kirkus Reviews, were established in 2014. Previous winners include Whitehead, Joy Williams and Ta-Nehisi Coates.

title: Obituary: Paul E. Hayden
text:
FARMINGDALE – Paul E. Hayden, son of the late Charles and Beatrice Hayden, passed away peacefully on Oct. 1, 2026, at the age of 95, following a brief illness. He was a kind, gentle man, a true gentleman whose sharp scientific mind, endless curiosity, boundless generosity, and deep devotion to his family defined nearly a century of a remarkably full and fabulous life.
Born on May 6, 1931, in Fort Fairfield, Paul’s early years were shaped by resilience, hard work, and the tight-knit warmth of a large Maine family. Following the tragic passing of his father, Charles, in a farming accident, Paul’s mother, Beatrice, moved the family to the Augusta-Gardiner area. They lived and worked on the Webb family dairy farm in Pittston, where Paul and his siblings attended the Colburn School, a historic one-room schoolhouse built in 1815. The family eventually settled at 11 Central Street in Randolph, the home that would become the heart of many cherished family stories. Paul often spoke with profound admiration of his mother’s faith and sacrifice, recalling how she gathered her five young children every Sunday morning to walk across the Randolph/Gardiner bridge to attend services at the Winter Street Baptist Church. When Beatrice passed away at the young age of 36 as Paul was entering high school, his 17-year-old sister, Ella, alongside her future husband, Winston (Winnie) Shepard, and “Grampy Shep,” stepped forward to keep the younger siblings housed, protected, and loved. Growing up in the post-Depression era, Paul and his brother Charles worked long, grueling days on the Burt Jamison property, clearing rocks from fields, tending livestock, and guiding plows behind massive workhorses. Yet Paul’s youth was also filled with outdoor adventures: hunting, fishing, exploring the woods along the Kennebec River, swimming at The Oaks in Gardiner, and riding ice chunks down the river with his brother Charles, the Teed brothers (Cecil and Mont), and George Shaw. Paul graduated from Gardiner High School in 1951, where he played football and basketball, served as editor of The Quill, and served in the National Guard (Company M, 103rd Infantry).
With the outbreak of the Korean War in the summer of 1950, Paul enlisted in the U.S. Navy following graduation, attending boot camp at Naval Station Great Lakes alongside his lifelong friend Delmont “Mont” Teed. Paul served as a machinist aboard the destroyer USS Ault (DD-698), providing operational screening, anti-submarine warfare capabilities, and a naval presence across the Pacific, Far East, and Mediterranean while circumnavigating the globe. It was during his Navy service that Paul taught himself to play the guitar, a gift that would bring music into his home for decades to come. Upon completing his naval service in 1954, Paul moved to California to attend Northrop Aeronautical Institute, laying the foundation for a career in engineering and aviation. Returning home to Maine, he reunited with the love of his life, Mary Joanne “Joan” Coro. They were married at the Winter Street Baptist Church in Gardiner, with Mont Teed standing as best man. They purchased a newly built home on Park Street in Hayford Heights in Farmingdale, where they settled for the rest of their lives, raising a family and building a home filled with warmth and hospitality. Paul held immense love and respect for Joan throughout their 65 years of marriage. Paul enjoyed a distinguished 32-year career as an engineer with the Maine Department of Transportation, retiring in 1989 before working an additional 15 years with Casey Godfrey Engineering.
Paul’s fascination with aviation began in childhood as he watched World War II fighters and bombers fly overhead and was cemented when his mother walked him down to the frozen Kennebec River for an airplane ride with Bill Perry of Maine Instrument Flight who was offering rides in a 1940s J-3 Cub. Bill Perry would later teach Paul to fly, setting off a lifelong aviation career during which Paul served as a commercial charter pilot and flight instructor. Over the years, Paul flew notable figures, including Ted Williams and Van Johnson in his beloved V-tail Bonanza N3077D, as well as Senator Edmund Muskie and Governor John Reed in the State of Maine Twin Beech N41ME. Decades later, Bill Perry would also issue a pilot’s license to Paul’s son, Scott. A foundational pillar of Maine’s experimental aviation scene, Paul was a founding member of Experimental Aircraft Association (EAA) Chapter 87. In 1960, he partnered with fellow aviator Al Tate to build a fully aerobatic, single-seat biplane known as “Little Toot” (N920Z) from scratch right in his basement. The four-year labor of love captured national attention, earning the coveted Best Homebuilt title at the 13th Annual EAA International Fly-In Convention in Oshkosh. Paul possessed a sharp scientific mind, constantly analyzing how things were made and breaking complex processes down into their foundational parts. Paul’s ingenuity knew no bounds. Combining his early experiences working with Winnie and Grampy Shep at Shepard’s Garage, his Navy machinist training, and his engineering background, there was little he couldn’t design, build, or repair. Paul’s favorite saying was a quote from Richard Bach, “Argue for your limitations, and sure enough, they’re yours.” After completing his aircraft, he turned his workshop into a woodworking haven. Long before store-bought kayaks were common, he hand built both a single-seat and two-seat kayak for fishing trips on Cobbossee Stream. He remodeled the family home, built a greenhouse, erected basketball hoops, and crafted custom desks, chairs, and bookcases that still adorn the homes and yards of his children and grandchildren. If a neighbor’s snowblower broke down in a snowstorm, Paul was in their driveway fixing it; if a neighborhood kid wanted a go-kart or minibike, he built one. He was truly the last of a self-reliant, generous generation.
Above all else, Paul’s greatest passion was his family, and he was a loving father figure to far more kids than just his own. Though his aviation achievements were vast, his love for Joan, his children, and his grandchildren surpassed everything. He was fully present for every chapter of their lives, never missing a game, a recital, a science fair, or a Hall-Dale sporting event. His commitment to local youth went above and beyond: Paul was a founding member and coach of the Hall-Dale Pee Wee Football League. To ensure the kids in his community had what they needed to play, he selflessly mortgaged his own home to purchase all the equipment required to outfit two complete football teams. Paul passed his love of music to his sons, filling the home with regular family jam sessions. He created a lifetime of traditions, leading annual family climbs up Mount Katahdin, camping trips to Aunt Dot’s campsite in the great Maine woods, snowmobiling outings, and skiing adventures both at Silver Hills and right on the front lawn. As his children grew, Paul and Joan spent their golden years traveling extensively throughout the United States and Europe. A passionate lifelong scholar and student of American history and ideals, Paul was an avid reader whose home was filled with books on the U.S. Constitution, the Federalist Papers, and world history. As a proud 32nd Degree Mason, he exemplified brotherhood and civic duty throughout his life, remaining an active, vibrant role model and hero to his children, grandchildren, and entire community throughout his 95 years.
Paul was predeceased by his beloved wife of 65 years, Mary Joanne Hayden; his parents, Charles Hayden and Beatrice Hayden (Tibbitts); his sister Ella Shepard and her husband Winston; his sister Erma Kendrick and her husband Cyrus; his sister Dorothy Perkins and her husband Ernest; his brother Charles Hayden; and his wife Kinuyo (Kay) Hayden, and his half-sister June Runnels Smith.
He is survived by his three children: son Russell Hayden, daughter Cathy Hayden, and son Scott Hayden and his wife Lori; his cherished grandchildren, Erin Gamache, Jessica Hayden, Amanda Hayden, and Matthew Hayden; and great grandchild Amelia, as well as many loving nieces, nephews, extended family members, and dear friends.
The Hayden family extends their heartfelt gratitude to the dedicated CNAs, nurses, hospice workers, and doctors at Gray Birches for their gentle and compassionate care of Paul. They also express their deep love and gratitude to the extended family for their steadfast support throughout Paul’s life.
In accordance with Paul’s wishes, there will be no traditional funeral services. A military graveside service to honor and celebrate his life will be held in the spring at the Maine Veterans Cemetery.
Arrangements and guidance are in the care of Staples Funeral Home and Cremation Care, 53 Brunswick Avenue, Gardiner, Maine.
Condolences, memories, and photos may be shared with the family on the obituary page of the Staples Funeral Home website, http://www.staplesfuneralhome.com

title: Jailhouse witness testifies Raymond Brown described Linda Maxwell’s death
text:
MACHIAS, Maine (WABI) - A jailhouse witness testified Wednesday that Raymond Brown, 67, described trying to have sex with an 18-year-old Linda Maxwell, holding her underwater after an argument and leaving her body at a boat landing. The witness also said Brown told him Maxwell’s clothing was later burned.
The testimony came on the third day of Brown’s murder trial. Maxwell, of Calais, was found dead in August 1984 after a night out with friends and her boyfriend at the time.
The defense questioned the witness’s credibility, citing a recorded call in which he said he might lie if his bail request was not granted.
Earlier Wednesday, a cousin of Brown testified that Brown told him his pants were wet after Maxwell’s body was found, that he had burned his clothes in a barrel and that he was frustrated with the investigation. The cousin said Brown also told him he had told police his clothes were dry.
Another person who was with Maxwell’s group the night she disappeared testified about her knowledge of Maxwell’s high school ring. Asked whether she had told police she knew another man had the ring, she said yes. Asked whether that was based on her own observation, she said no.
A former Maine State Police detective testified about Brown’s 1984 account of taking Maxwell to Milltown and returning to Calais. The defense questioned why police did not search Brown’s burn barrel and challenged how investigators considered possible scenarios.
Yet another witness, a Maine game warden testified that, based on the conditions he reviewed, it would be essentially impossible for a body to travel 14 miles down the St. Croix River.
Both sides said they expect to wrap up the case in the coming days.

text:
Mortgage rates jump to three-year high, blow past 7.5%
Current mortgage rates
The 30-year fixed mortgages in this week’s survey had an average total of 0.33 discount and origination points. Discount points are a way to lower your mortgage rate, while origination points are fees lenders charge to create, review and process your loan.
Shop smarter for mortgage rates
Bankrate connects you to the latest lender offers, tailored to you. Find your low rate today.
Explore mortgage rates
Monthly mortgage payment at today’s rates
The national median family income for 2026 is $106,800, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, and the median price of an existing home sold in August 2026 was $429,100, according to the National Association of Realtors. Based on a 20% down payment and a 7.53% mortgage rate, the monthly principal and interest payment of $2,407 amounts to about 27% of the typical family’s monthly income.
Meanwhile, home prices are still rising — the National Association of Realtors reports the median home price was up 1.6% over the past year, and the median of $429,100 was an all-time high for the month of August. However, values have begun to dip in many formerly hot markets. Still, signs are mixed. The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller index released in late September showed national home prices grew 1.9% in the year ending in July, marking an acceleration.
What will happen to mortgage rates in the rest of 2026?
Inflation held at 3.4% in August, although the Fed’s preferred measure, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) index, was 3.0% for September. Oil prices have spiked amid the conflict in Iran, pushing inflation up and lifting mortgage rates from their 2026 low of 6.09%. Rising inflation has been the main driver of higher mortgage rates — the consumer price index has pushed well above the Fed’s 2% target, and 10-year Treasury yields topped 5.3% this week, well up from earlier in the year.
“The 10-year Treasury has been battered over the last six weeks, climbing from 4.66% to 5.36% on Wednesday, a striking 70-basis-point jump,” says James Sahnger of C2 Financial Corp. “The 10-year hasn’t been this high since April 2002, and 30-year fixed rates haven’t been this high since August 2000. Normally, favorable personal consumption expenditures numbers and weak jobs data would bring at least some improvement in rates. Right now, though, too many crosscurrents and concerns are weighing on the markets for any relief to take hold.”
Housing economists no longer expect mortgage rates to fall below 6% in the near future, and even a return below 7% seems a stretch. That reality that’s affecting home sales. Higher mortgage rates, still-record home prices and persistent inflation are likely to put the brakes on home sales. Instead, rates have risen sharply, a situation only exacerbated by the Fed’s Sept. 16 rate hike.

title: Mr. Drew and His Animals Too in Poland to close at the end of the month
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
After nine months at its new location in Poland, Mr. Drew and His Animals Too will close its doors for good Oct. 31, owner Drew Desjardins said in a Facebook post.
Desjardins posted the news Wednesday morning calling it a “very difficult decision.”
“So this is where we are at — sad, anxious and heavy hearted, but I can say with confidence, that we are very proud of what we created and accomplished and there will be no other place like it,” he wrote.
Desjardins announced in May 2025 that his collection of more than 200 rescued reptiles, amphibians, insects, birds and more would be moving to Poland after his lease was not renewed at the Lewiston Mall.
The public education exhibit, which included hands-on experiences and a geological center with gemstones, bones and fossils, officially opened in Poland in early January.
According to the Facebook post, several factors played into this decision to close the Poland location, including the financial stress of moving from Lewiston.
He had hoped the new location would draw people to that area.
“We love having a facility as it was a dream come true and we truly wanted to make Poland a destination rather than a drive-through community, with the education center to be around for generations to come, far beyond myself, but alas, that will not be,” he wrote.
Desjardins made it clear they are not seeking donations to keep going.
“Please know Mrs. Drew and I have accepted this decision and we are NOT seeking a ‘Hail Mary’, any public financial support or a GoFundMe,” Desjardins wrote. “We accept the facts the economy is bad and simply put, we are not business people, we simply care about our animals and making people happy in this sad world we are living in.”
While the Poland location is closing, Desjardins plans to continue traveling the state with a mobile exhibit as he has done in the past. Much of his collection will stay with the family at their Poland home, while others will go to educational facilities and sanctuaries Desjardins trusts, he said.
“I am continuing to book birthdays, public schools, homeschools, community events, Scouting and more,” he wrote.
Until the closing, Mr. Drew and His Animals Too will be open every day through Oct. 31 from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Fans of Mr. Drew’s were commenting on the post Wednesday.
“Your effect has been undeniable,” a resident of Dresden Mills wrote. “Education, respect, humor. I cherish my trip to your place. You helped me with fear of spiders! I held your tarantulas!”
“Encounters with snakes at Mr. Drew’s led me to want to foster with HerpHaven Reptile Rescue and Sanctuary and ultimately adopt a hognose!” wrote another resident.
“The educational outreach is at the heart of your program,” one fan wrote. “We had the pleasure of your company a few years ago at the Arts Center in Waterville. It was an amazing experience and many of us were transformed to an appreciation of animals we had formerly been afraid of.”

title: Debate an even matchup says University of Maine Political Science Chair
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The University of Maine’s Political Science Chair, Mark Brewer, thinks both candidates fared well in Tuesday’s US Senate debate, but the even match-up might be a win for the challenger.
Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) is seeking a 6th term and has been on the debate stage far more than Jackson.

He doesn’t think last night’s performance will sway those small groups on the margins still trying to make up their mind on who to vote for.
He expects to see similar things in the debates ahead.

title: Shifting mindset — ‘Caregiving is the burden; your loved one is the blessing’
text:
(Aging Untold) — For many caregivers, social media has become a lifeline — a place to share their stories and find community. Ty Lewis is one of them.
She’s a certified dementia practitioner and content creator who cares for her mother, Gertrude, who is in the late stages of Alzheimer’s.
Lewis shares a powerful perspective shift that separates the true burden of caregiving from the loved one receiving the care.
“We have to shift our perspective”
Lewis says the mindset reframe starts with understanding what “burden” actually means.
“We have to shift our perspective. The care, that’s the burden, the financial piece, that is the burden. Us not being able to find resources, that’s the burden. But taking care of our loved one, being a servant leader, that is the blessing,” Lewis said.
She says it’s easy for caregivers to lose sight of that distinction on hard days.
“I think that is what a lot of us miss on this journey — that yes, it is hard. Yes, I am picking it up and carrying my cross, but also the cross is leading me somewhere special,” Lewis said. “Because our loved one depends on us so much, we have to be the ones to allow them to lean on us and help them carry that load. So, because they’re unable to do everything, we are who they need us to be. For us, caregiving is the burden. But our loved one is the blessing.”
Why some caregivers find joy — and others don’t
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said that reframing can change a caregiver’s entire outlook.
“That is a powerful perspective, and that just kind of changes your whole mood,” Ambrose said. “I think that’s the difference between people that find joy in being a caregiver versus the ones that don’t. They recognize what an honor it is, and that you do get unexpected gifts and blessings.”
See our full interview with Ty Lewis
The newborn comparison
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck said she’s taught this distinction for years, and she compares it to how people respond to a new baby.
“That’s the basis of my teaching, and it always has been — that the person is not the burden, work is. The definition of burden is that it’s work,” Cradduck said. “When you come home with a brand-new baby, how many people look at a newborn and go, ‘Man, you’re a burden’? There’s a lot of work that goes along with having a brand-new baby — there’s a ton of work — but you never impart that over on the child. You see the workload is the burden.”
She said that same logic gets lost when it comes to caring for aging loved ones.
“When we go to the aged community, we oftentimes get them confused. We hear so many of our aged community say, ‘I don’t want to be a burden.’ Honey, you can’t be a burden,” Cradduck said.
Holding both the burden and the blessing
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said caregivers don’t have to choose between the two realities — both can be true at once, drawing on her own experience caring for her father.
“I like that she said there’s a burden and there’s a blessing, that you can carry both of those things at the same time,” O’Rourke said. “I know when I was looking out for my dad with the rest of the family, there were days when I was so exhausted, I felt burdened. But then I would have times with him that I felt, ‘Oh, I’m so happy he’s with me, and I’m getting all these connections with him.’”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said she sees that same duality reflected in both ends of caregiving, from newborns to aging parents.
“I like both analogies — the newborn baby and then the elder person with whatever ailments they have. It really is the perspective,” Rogers said. “When you can shift your perspective to really zone in on the blessing — there’s a lot of people who would love to have their father or their mother, even if they have the late stages of Alzheimer’s, but they would physically be present here. And that’s the blessing.”
Grief versus joy in the caregiving role
Cradduck said the real difference between caring for a newborn and caring for an aging loved one comes down to emotional framing, not workload.
“With the newborn child, the workload is tough and you’re exhausted. There’s not a brand-new mother or father out there that aren’t exhausted, they’re tired — but they’re not imparting that over to the child, because you see that child with joy. You see that child with hope,” she said.
On the other hand, when you are caring for an older adult, you are also grieving, Cradduck said.
“When you’re over here in your caregiving, you’re grieving. That’s what changes and allows the perspective to put the burden on the person. ... When we see the person is still a human, always — the workload is the burden — then we can always see the blessing in what we’re doing. That’s what we’ve got to get back to.”
That mindset applies no matter which side of caregiving someone is on, Rogers and Ambrose added.
“I like the perspective of looking at — we’re going to be whatever they need us to be, whether that’s a child or the older person,” Rogers said.
“You’re just going to make your burden worse if you don’t make that mindset shift. Be open to the blessings that come out of it, because they are unexpected, and they are beautiful sometimes,” Ambrose said.
Key takeaways
- The workload is the burden — not the person. Ty Lewis says reframing caregiving starts with separating the tasks and stress of caregiving from the person receiving care.
- Burden and blessing can coexist. Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said caregivers don’t have to pick one feeling — exhaustion and gratitude can show up on the same day.
- The newborn comparison reveals a double standard. Parents absorb the exhaustion of caring for a baby without blaming the child. Gerontologist Sam Cradduck says aging loved ones deserve that same grace.
- A mindset shift can change a caregiver’s whole outlook. Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers who recognize caregiving as an honor are more likely to experience joy rather than only exhaustion.
- Being “who they need us to be” is a form of leadership. Lewis describes caregiving as servant leadership — stepping in for a loved one who can no longer do everything on their own.

title: Before a natural disaster, a governor’s order can free up the National Guard and medical help
text:
Before a big weather event even happens — like a hurricane, flood, or snowstorm — government officials in the United States have the power to call for a state of emergency, a fast-track way to free up resources to help with public safety during an anticipated natural disaster.
In a state, a governor usually signs an executive order that names the area expected to be affected by the pending severe weather. The order gives emergency management agencies the go-ahead to work up disaster response plans and delegate responsibilities.
Agencies that can be called into action, for example, include the National Guard for searches, rescues and overall security, the highway patrol to enforce road closures, and the health department to provide emergency medical services.
The declaration allows the state agencies to provide direct assistance to local governments. It suspends state rules and regulations that could interfere with emergency plans. And it allows for a state to form agreements with other states to seek help.
It’s also a necessary first step for the state to ask the federal government for financial aid through the Federal Emergency Management Agency. The president of the United States can issue a disaster declaration based on a governor’s request and FEMA damage assessments.

title: Trump's executive order on dyed diesel will offer little relief, farmers and truckers say
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SIOUX FALLS, S.D. (AP) — Farmers, truckers and economists say a move to cut taxes on diesel will provide little relief from record-high fuel prices that have soared since the U.S. attacked Iran months ago.
Industry groups said they appreciate President Donald Trump’s executive order expanding the use of a diesel now reserved for off-road work, but farmers already have access to the fuel and many have already wrapped up harvest. Truckers will struggle to navigate differing state rules.
“In the context of diesel prices that are over two dollars more than they were last year, it just doesn’t come close to closing that wound,” said Matt Perdue, president of the North Dakota Farmers Union.
With less than a month to go before the November election, diesel prices continue to hit record highs as some farmers transport their crops for processing and others rush to complete their fall harvest. Many have been feeling the squeeze as costs for inputs like diesel, fertilizer and seed have soared thanks to refinery constraints and supply disruptions amid the Iran war.
Diesel averaged $6.30 per gallon across the country on Wednesday, more than 70% higher than one year ago, according to motor club AAA. The executive order defers the $0.24 federal tax per gallon of regular diesel, used for road projects, until the end of the year. Most states also levy their own tax on diesel.
“Dyed” diesel is the same as regular diesel, except for its red dye to help law enforcement enforce penalties for on-road use. It’s already allowed for off-road purposes like farming equipment, such as tractors and combines, as well as construction and heating uses.
Who will see benefits
Savings can compound if states take similar actions; many have eased restrictions or waived taxes on dyed diesel, including South Dakota and Iowa. Perdue said North Dakota has waived the tax on regular diesel. But where the state decision is focused on farmers, he believes the federal decision would largely benefit those on other levels of the supply chain.
Farmers who will see the most benefit are those who haul their own product, like livestock or fresh produce, on public roads. Those who have already wrapped up harvesting won’t see savings.
“Most of our diesel use is behind us,” said Perdue, who grows spring wheat, durum and canola on his family farm.
Both trucking companies and independent truckers may not see much relief either. The effect is likely to be negligible for big trucking companies because the order is on a federal level and states make their own rules, Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, wrote in a social media post.
“The largest diesel users are the least likely to use dyed diesel,” he wrote. “A national carrier crossing five or six states in a day faces enormous risk with a patchwork of rules, legal in one state, and subject to fines in the next.”
Many states exempt road diesel from sales tax but apply sales tax to dyed diesel instead, he said.
Easing limits on red-dyed diesel will likely have a minimal effect for small truckers, who pay for fuel up front, said Todd Spencer, president and CEO of trade group the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association. He estimates every $1 increase per gallon in fuel costs independent truckers about $400 more per week.
Increased demand for dyed diesel
The savings will be small, but it could still increase competition for dyed diesel, said David Ortega, food economics and policy professor at Michigan State University.
“I think there’s a real chance this could backfire and make the situation worse for farmers,” he said. “Basically anybody that’s running a truck on the highway on regular diesel can now be using this off-highway diesel. Even someone that owns a diesel pickup truck potentially has access to this other type of diesel.”
Perdue in North Dakota said he expects a “rush for dyed diesel, and we’ll see how the supply responds.”
But not all dyed diesel pump stations are set up for larger trucks like semis, said Paul Mitchell, a professor of agricultural and applied economics at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.
“It’s going to come down to infrastructure ability to get your vehicles to a place that you can use and fill them up with,” he said.
Supply shortages persist
Henry Hanscom, American Trucking Associations chief advocacy and public affairs officer, pointed out that the executive order directs temporary penalty relief and potential tax deferral for using red-dyed diesel, not outright tax forgiveness. He said the ATA would review the Internal Revenue Service’s implementing guidance of the policy when it is available.
Last month, Trump had threatened a diesel export ban, though he later said it is off the table. On Friday, G7 countries agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products.
“One of the problems we have right now in the world is there’s not enough diesel fuel,” said Gregg Ibendahl, farm management specialist at Kansas State University.
But underlying causes like geopolitical issues won’t be solved overnight.
“The problem we’ve accumulated right now with the Strait of Hormuz and the Russia-Ukraine war, those are going to be longer term things to get fixed,” he said. “Getting that world supply back up again is going to be, I think, at least a year, even in the best cases.”
___
Anderson reported from New York.

title: PTSD doesn’t expire: How trauma resurfaces as we age
text:
(Aging Untold) — Post-traumatic stress disorder, or PTSD, symptoms can become more noticeable later in life, especially during major life changes including retirement, illness or loss.
The Aging Untold experts are breaking down why trauma doesn’t simply fade with time, and what families and caregivers can do to recognize it.
PTSD is a body and brain still on alert
“PTSD is not just something bad happened,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. “It’s basically your body and your brain are still reacting to a danger as if it’s still present, even though it’s long been gone.”
Trauma is an “invisible suffering” that’s stored emotionally, neurologically and physically, Rogers said.
“The body’s trying to move past something that the brain is not allowing. So in a sense, your body will express what your mind does suppress,” Rogers said.
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said trauma does not expire and PTSD is the past showing up and affecting your present.
PTSD is often associated with veterans and first responders, but Cradduck said it also affected health care workers who went through the COVID-19 pandemic.
“There is still a PTSD response,” Cradduck said. “That’s why we lost so many good workers from that.”
A car accident can leave a lasting physical response
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, described her own reaction after being in a serious car accident.
“My husband has had to adjust to how I’m riding in the car now, because if we get too close to a car, I get anxiety,” O’Rourke said.
Understanding a person’s full life story can explain behavior that might otherwise be misread, O’Rourke said.
She had a client who was easily irritated and startled and had to watch the front door. When he told her about his childhood, she said, she understood.
“And the more he talked, the more horrified I became at the abuse and the trauma that he went through, and it helped me really understand him and his behavior, because you could have written it off to dementia or depression or old age. We don’t always first think of trauma,” O’Rourke said.
Katherine Ambrose was also in a serious accident and said she feels more nervous in traffic than she used to be.
“I found myself, as I’m getting older, being a little more concerned in traffic and being a little more reactive,” Ambrose said. “I like to think I’m not a nervous person, but for some reason, I’m noticing a change.”
The brain stays in protective mode
Rogers said the brain’s instinct is to guard and stay in a “survival and protective mode.”
“You put up your guard, you stay in the defense until you feel like the danger is gone,” Rogers said.
That stress response keeps the body in fight-or-flight mode.
“You cannot repair or heal when you’re in fight or flight,” Rogers said.
Therapies some people turn to for relief
Ambrose said some people believe trauma and pain can become locked into the body, leading them to seek out yoga, massage, acupuncture or contrast therapy such as heat and cold treatments.
“I love that you’re seeing more and more, in many cities, different studios and clinics that you can go to for different types of therapy to see if that might help,” Ambrose said.
O’Rourke pointed to trauma-informed therapy, including EMDR, as another option.
“My goddaughter is a trauma therapist ... and she’s been wildly successful in this small town in Washington,” O’Rourke said. “For some reason, there’s a lot of trauma ... people who are suffering with trauma.”
Cradduck brought up the stresses of being part of an information community where everything’s 24-7.
“Our kids are suffering from trauma, and the anxiety levels are increasing way more now than ever before because there’s no off button, there’s no reset, there’s no rest and repair going on,” Cradduck said.
Cradduck added that service animals shouldn’t be overlooked.
“Don’t discount service dogs, don’t discount our service pets, and how rewarding they can be and how much help they can be,” she said. “Just feeling purpose and feeling connection again.”
Trauma doesn’t have to be dramatic to count
Rogers said trauma isn’t limited to major events like combat or accidents.
“I think sometimes the definition of trauma to everyone, they think it has to be something dramatic,” Rogers said. “Even for children, adverse childhood events — maybe your parents went through a divorce, or somebody went to jail. That’s still traumatic. I think we have to really look at what trauma means to different people, and their body is going to react to that differently.”
Ambrose said younger generations are sometimes judged harshly by older generations who compare today’s pressures to their own upbringing.
“They don’t understand the real pressure on kids,” Ambrose said.
Rogers said everyone has triggers and urged people in a caregiving role to know what the triggers are for the person they are caring for.
“If you’re taking care of a parent and they’re having signs of being easily irritated, think trauma also, and get them help with that, because it doesn’t come up. It’s not something that family members think of.” O’Rourke added.
Key takeaways
- PTSD is a present-tense reaction, not a memory. The brain and body respond as though a past danger is still happening today.
- Symptoms are often mistaken for dementia or depression in older adults, especially irritability or being easily startled.
- Keep a calm routine. Routines calm the body and help manage powerful sensory triggers.

title: Dennis Franchione, football coach at TCU, Alabama and Texas A&M, dies at 75
text:
Dennis Franchione, football coach at TCU, Alabama and Texas A&M, dies at 75
Dennis Franchione, the longtime college football coach who turned around Texas Christian University before stints at Alabama and Texas A&M, has died. He was 75.
Related video: Remembering those we lost in 2026
“TCU mourns alongside the Franchione family at the passing of ‘Coach Fran,’” TCU athletic director Mike Buddie said in a statement Tuesday.
The Fort Worth Star-Telegram, which first reported the news, said Franchione’s family confirmed his death, adding that he struggled with cancer for a decade. He was diagnosed with cancer in 2016 and 2021, but it had been in remission. Family friends said the cancer returned earlier this year and Franchione recently went into hospice, the newspaper reported.
“Remembering Coach Dennis Franchione and the memories he gave Alabama Football,” the Southeastern Conference school posted on social media. “Rest in peace, Coach Fran. Forever part of the Crimson Tide story.”
Franchione worked his way up the college football coaching ranks during a career that spanned more than 30 years. He was first an assistant at Kansas State from 1978-80, then worked at four lower-level schools before 20 seasons as a Football Bowl Subdivision head coach, at New Mexico (1992-97), TCU (1998-2000), Alabama (2001-02), Texas A&M (2003-07) and Texas State (2012-15).
He was one of nine FBS coaches who, in June, were announced as nominees for the 2027 College Football Hall of Fame class that will be revealed in January. The Kansas native compiled a 213-135-2 record before stepping down from Texas State in 2015 and retiring from coaching. Franchione led his teams to nine conference championships, nine bowl games, four NAIA playoff games and one NCAA Division II playoff appearance.
“Our fortunes as a department would not be what they are today without the efforts of Coach Franchione, his staff, and players,” said Buddie, the TCU AD. “Beyond his talent as a football coach, he was a beloved father, mentor, and friend to so many. Our thoughts and prayers are with his wife, Kim, and the entire Franchione family.”
TCU was coming off a 1-10 season when Franchione left New Mexico after six years to take over the Horned Frogs, where in his debut season in 1999 they had a 7-5 record capped by a Sun Bowl win over Southern California. With future Pro Football Hall of Fame running back LaDainian Tomlinson, TCU finished tied atop the Western Athletic Conference standings each of the next two seasons, going 8-4 with another bowl win in 1999 before a 10-1 regular season in 2000 that led to him being hired by Alabama.
Franchione was replaced at TCU by his defensive coordinator, Gary Patterson, who had winning records in 15 of his 21 seasons as head coach after first taking over for the 2000 bowl game, and was top 10 in the final AP Top 25 poll six times. That included an undefeated 13-0 season in 2010 when the Frogs finished second after a win over Wisconsin in the Rose Bowl.
“Good man, good friend!” Patterson wrote in a text to The Associated Press.
Patterson, now in his first season as defensive coordinator for No. 19 USC, added that “Coach Fran” gave him his first Division I coordinator job at New Mexico and that “a lot of my foundation to run a program” started with him.
Franchione was 17-8 in two seasons with Alabama and had five years remaining on his contract when he left to return to Texas and replace the fired R.C. Slocum at Texas A&M. The Crimson Tide had just had a 10-3 regular season in 2002 but weren’t bowl eligible because of NCAA sanctions handed down earlier that year for infractions that happened before Franchione’s arrival.
Texas A&M was 32-28 and made three bowl games during his tenure. The school said in a social media post that it was “Honoring the life and legacy of Coach Dennis Franchione.”
Franchione spent some time as a broadcaster after that before returning to Texas State as head coach in 2011, the school’s last season in the Football Championship Subdivision before becoming an FBS team the following season. He had previously coached the Bobcats at the lower level from 1990-91 before going to New Mexico.

title: Voter registration: Who can register?
text:
Part 2 of 4 series
Voter registration has become a major topic of discussion these days. Especially with the proposed Safeguard America Voter Eligibility Act (SAVE Act).
So, let’s take a look at voter registration.
The voter registration closed period is the 20-day period prior to and on election day when the registrar may accept only voter registration applications received in-person. The closed period begins on the 21st day before election day at the close of business.
During the closed period, any application received by mail or through a third party must be held for processing until after election day.
Notices regarding voters who register in a Maine town from another Maine town are sent electronically via Central Voter Registry (CVR).
New voters may register on election day. The process involves the voter to complete a voter registration card. The card is then reviewed by the deputy registrar to make sure it is completed accurately. At that time, proof of residence and ID must be provided to the deputy registrar. One of the questions on the applications asks if the person is a citizen of the United States. If the answer is “no”, the process ends.
State and federal law require that voters certify their citizenship by checking the box on the voter registration application. It is a crime to make a false statement on the application.
If a non-citizen knowingly submits a form certifying to be a citizen when they are not, they will be subject to prosecution.
Maine law does not require or authorize municipal officials to collect any documents related to citizenship.
Proof of identity includes a current and valid United States passport, military identification, driver’s license or state identification, a certified birth certificate or a signed social security card. It may also include a document confirming eligibility determinations for public benefits, a utility bill, a bank statement, a government check, a paycheck or other government document that shows the name and address of the voter.
If the voter has no proof of ID, the warden can look up the voter in the CVR to see if they were previously registered in Maine. If so, the voter only needs to provide proof of residence.
Proof of residence can include a driver’s license, vehicle registration, government check or payroll check, receipt of public benefit, utility bill, rent or lease receipt, check book, bank statement, or the personal knowledge by the warden or deputy registrar. If the voter cannot provide documentation to prove residency, they may take an oath pledging their place of residence, but only if they have ID with them.
If the voter’s eligibility is questioned,where they cannot provide proof of residence of identification, they can cast a challenged ballot. The voter is processed like all others, but add the “challenged” notation to that voter. The voter may cast their ballot at this time. The challenged ballot will come into play only if there is a recount and the challenged ballots may have an impact on the results.
In Maine, unlike other states, you are not denied the right to vote. Something like, “you’re innocent until proven guilty.”
A person does not lose residency if temporarily away as long as they intend to return; students who qualify as a voter in the town where the student resides while attending the institution; incarcerated persons may apply to register to vote in the municipality where they resided prior to incarceration; homeless persons may have a non-traditional residence such as a shelter or a park bench.
Roland Hallee has 40 years experience in conducting elections, the last 25 years as warden in Waterville.

It is also expensive!

title: Even retirees deserve a day off once in a while
text:
Vicki Sullivan of Portland is a retired English instructor and writing tutor.
Occasionally, when I was teaching, I would enter a classroom and be greeted by a student who would ask me, “Can we do nothing today?”
I’d reply sarcastically, “No work, no pay,” which invariably got the answer, “We’re not getting paid; we’re paying.” Or I might say, “That’s what you do every day,” to which the response would be a “Ha, ha” or an extended fake laugh.
But for those of us who have worked hard all our lives, that question can make you wonder.
For some days I wake up and ask myself, “Can I do nothing today?” And maybe I’m really asking myself for permission.
We, offspring of Depression Era parents, had a strong work ethic instilled in us. Our parents worked hard for their success and expected us to do the same. My mother frowned upon a sick day from school and personal days off from work were unheard of then.
I can hear my father saying, “Keep on digging” to anyone who might listen!
And a coach who coached at the University of Delaware with my father told his football players who complained about practicing on a holiday, “On Labor Day you labor.”
Doing nothing or having nothing to do was not looked upon favorably. Therefore, many of us who have retired expect ourselves to keep busy and have a purpose.
A friend of my father gave my father advice when he was going to retire. “Plan every day,” he suggested. My father didn’t and he found retirement a difficult transition.
Although I’m still trying to adjust to retirement three years later, I do plan every day. I make a to- do list as if I have a corporate job and cross off my completed tasks. Granted, they might be small items — mailing something or emptying the dishwasher — but at least I have accomplished something.
My friend Michael, a retired antiques shop owner, and I often text back and forth, discussing how productive we have been that day — his day spent cleaning out and organizing the many items in his garage and mine downsizing holiday items and “death cleaning.”
A former co-worker of mine, who had retired from the police department, had a full-time teaching job, a part-time consulting job and other short-term projects in his field. I remember laughingly commenting to him once, “You run around as if the devil were after you.”
He replied, “I don’t like to be idle.”
My friend Gladys,now deceased, lived to be 98. Before her death she was living independently, still keeping house and cooking, and driving. We laughed over an incident many times. At 97,at a doctor’s appointment, she told her physician that she didn’t seem to have much ambition. And her physician replied, “Why do you need to be ambitious at 97?” She was so used to keeping busy.
The only time most of us gave ourselves permission to do nothing was during COVID-19 when we really couldn’t do much of anything. I wasn’t working, as I was laid off during the spring semester when COVID hit.
However, of course, doing nothing has different meanings for different people.
But, whatever your definition, to those of us who’ve worked hard and deserve a day off, I say, “Let’s do nothing today.”

title: Florida crocodile dies from lead poisoning in first-of-its-kind case, officials say
text:
Florida crocodile dies from lead poisoning in first-of-its-kind case, officials say
A crocodile died unexpectedly following a capture in Florida, and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission officials said the cause of death was lead poisoning.
FWC said that this is Florida's first known case of lead poisoning in an American crocodile.
Video above: Only in Florida: Man open his front door to find a massive gator
The crocodile died during what FWC called a routine capture. Researchers performed a field necropsy and discovered more than 22 grams of lead in the crocodile's stomach, which is approximately the weight of an AA battery.
The lead contents included 23 air rifle pellets, one fishing weight, and other small lead fragments, FWC said. Researchers also found evidence that the crocodile had eaten at least one green iguana that had likely been shot with lead ammunition.
The crocodile showed signs and symptoms of long-term lead exposure, including major tooth loss and a high concentration of lead in its liver, FWC said.
FWC said it plans to conduct additional sampling for lead and other contaminants in American crocodiles across Florida.

title: Mr. Drew and His Animals Too in Poland to close at the end of the month
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
After nine months at its new location in Poland, Mr. Drew and His Animals Too will close its doors for good Oct. 31, owner Drew Desjardins said in a Facebook post.
Desjardins posted the news Wednesday morning calling it a “very difficult decision.”
“So this is where we are at — sad, anxious and heavy hearted, but I can say with confidence, that we are very proud of what we created and accomplished and there will be no other place like it,” he wrote.
Desjardins announced in May 2025 that his collection of more than 200 rescued reptiles, amphibians, insects, birds and more would be moving to Poland after his lease was not renewed at the Lewiston Mall.
The public education exhibit, which included hands-on experiences and a geological center with gemstones, bones and fossils, officially opened in Poland in early January.
According to the Facebook post, several factors played into this decision to close the Poland location, including the financial stress of moving from Lewiston.
He had hoped the new location would draw people to that area.
“We love having a facility as it was a dream come true and we truly wanted to make Poland a destination rather than a drive-through community, with the education center to be around for generations to come, far beyond myself, but alas, that will not be,” he wrote.
Desjardins made it clear they are not seeking donations to keep going.
“Please know Mrs. Drew and I have accepted this decision and we are NOT seeking a ‘Hail Mary’, any public financial support or a GoFundMe,” Desjardins wrote. “We accept the facts the economy is bad and simply put, we are not business people, we simply care about our animals and making people happy in this sad world we are living in.”
While the Poland location is closing, Desjardins plans to continue traveling the state with a mobile exhibit as he has done in the past. Much of his collection will stay with the family at their Poland home, while others will go to educational facilities and sanctuaries Desjardins trusts, he said.
“I am continuing to book birthdays, public schools, homeschools, community events, Scouting and more,” he wrote.
Until the closing, Mr. Drew and His Animals Too will be open every day through Oct. 31 from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Fans of Mr. Drew’s were commenting on the post Wednesday.
“Your effect has been undeniable,” a resident of Dresden Mills wrote. “Education, respect, humor. I cherish my trip to your place. You helped me with fear of spiders! I held your tarantulas!”
“Encounters with snakes at Mr. Drew’s led me to want to foster with HerpHaven Reptile Rescue and Sanctuary and ultimately adopt a hognose!” wrote another resident.
“The educational outreach is at the heart of your program,” one fan wrote. “We had the pleasure of your company a few years ago at the Arts Center in Waterville. It was an amazing experience and many of us were transformed to an appreciation of animals we had formerly been afraid of.”

title: Broken bathrooms force American Airlines flight to divert for urgent landing
text:
Broken bathrooms force American Airlines flight to divert for urgent landing
An American Airlines flight from Madrid diverted to New York Tuesday afternoon after all but two of the lavatories on the Boeing 777 stopped working.
Related video: AUDIO: 2 planes with the same flight number avoid possible disaster thanks to quick-thinking controller
The plane had 287 people onboard and was flying from Madrid to Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, a flight that often takes more than 10 hours.
"American Airlines Flight 37 landed at JFK International Airport in New York after the crew reported an inadequate number of operational lavatories," the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement.
An American Airlines Boeing 777 typically has eight lavatories onboard but only two were working.
"So (we) have only two potties operating on board for American 37," the pilot told air traffic control as they approached John F. Kennedy International Airport.
"You said only two potties. Is that right?" the controller confirmed.
"That's affirmative," the pilot responded.
With more than four hours of fuel left, the plane was over its normal landing weight, which can cause problems including overheated brakes. The pilot declared "pan-pan," an international term for an urgent problem that requires immediate attention, but not a life threatening emergency.
The plane landed safely and continued onto Dallas after more than three hours in New York, according to tracking site FlightAware.
American Airlines did not respond to CNN's request for comment on the incident.
While it's not clear what happened on this plane, aircraft toilets are complicated devices powered by air pressure that can get blocked or otherwise malfunction, experts tell CNN.
"It's only a tiny pipe, and people put things like (diapers) down – I've seen cutlery go down, and (soft drink cans) – they're fascinated to see whether it will go down or not," Nigel Jones, a former engineer for British Airways told CNN in 2024. "It can take days to rectify because there's an awful lot of pipework, and it has to be broken down to find the blockages."

title: ‘Positive thoughts’: Legendary WWE announcer reveals new health setback
text:
‘Positive thoughts’: Legendary WWE announcer reveals new health setback
Jim Ross, a longtime professional wrestling announcer, has revealed a new health setback months after brain surgery.
Ross, known by fans as "Good Ol’ J.R.,” announced this week that he is slated to undergo a second brain surgery.
“Getting another brain surgery Wednesday morning to address an issue with my shunt. Positive thoughts appreciated. Thanks,” he shared on social media.
Related video above | Hulk Hogan teamed up with Disney for a groundbreaking TV series in 1993
The news comes months after Ross underwent an operation to have a shunt inserted in his brain to drain excess fluid amid ongoing memory issues.
After the first surgery, Ross was open about experiencing “blistering headaches” that prevented him from sleeping at night.
Ross joined WWE in 1993 and became one of the company’s most recognizable voices.
He rose to prominence during the late 1990s, when his energetic calls helped shape the broadcast style of WWE’s Attitude Era.
He called matches featuring stars including “Stone Cold” Steve Austin, The Rock and The Undertaker. Ross also served as WWE’s head of talent relations, helping recruit and develop wrestlers.
He has written memoirs about his life and career, including “Slobberknocker: My Life in Wrestling.” Ross also hosts the podcast “Grilling JR,” where he discusses wrestling history and his experiences in the business.

title: Maine needs a housing strategy. Hannah Pingree has one.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
When I turned 30, suddenly all of my friends were talking about buying houses. Or, more specifically, how hard it is to buy a house. Looking at houses on Zillow in one’s spare time is no longer a fun game; it’s just depressing. So many house prices have skyrocketed since 2020. 
Due to Maine’s housing prices, I see myself sticking to renting for a good long while. That’s not to say, of course, that renting is necessarily easier. Rents in Portland rival those in Boston. And outside of Portland, we don’t find much relief either. But at least when my dishwasher breaks, I’ll have someone to call. Hard to save for that down payment, though.
Thankfully, we have someone running for governor who knows Maine is facing a very serious housing crisis. Hannah Pingree’s housing plan will invest in housing, stop out-of-state corporations from driving up rents and cut the red tape that slows development. Hannah’s smart, clear and comprehensive housing plan gives me hope for Maine’s future.
Eloise Melcher
Portland

title: Lincoln County Republicans meet July 22

title: Juniper Ridge’s contaminated wastewater to be treated in Brewer
text:
There’s another change in where contaminated wastewater from Juniper Ridge Landfill will be treated.
By the end of October, contaminated wastewater from the Old Town-based landfill will be trucked to Brewer to be treated, Wayne Boyd, general manager at Casella Waste System, said Tuesday.
“We’ve been looking hard to see what other options are, and it would appear that that option is open. We’ve had a door open for treatment in Brewer, and that’s where it will be going for now,” Boyd said during a landfill committee meeting in Old Town on Tuesday.
The wastewater will be treated in Brewer while a proposed off-site PFAS treatment system is being built in Hampden. The water, which is called leachate, is collected at Juniper Ridge after it runs through waste. It’s contaminated by harmful chemicals, including PFAS.
Casella operates the Juniper Ridge Landfill under subsidiary NEWSME Landfill Operations.
Old Town residents questioned why leachate was being treated in Brewer and Hampden after court documents showed that Casella was planning to truck the contaminated water 20 miles instead of treating it at the landfill in Old Town. A PFAS treatment system is a requirement for approval of a proposed 61-acre expansion of Juniper Ridge Landfill, but the public benefit agreement requiring the system does not say where it has to be built.
The Maine Department of Environmental Protection approved the expansion late last year, with the requirement of a PFAS treatment system. The expansion is expected to add 11 years to the lifetime of Juniper Ridge, which right now is on track to be at capacity by the end of 2028 or beginning of 2029, Boyd said.
The city of Brewer notified its intent to apply for a permit Tuesday to release 18,000 gallons of treated leachate into the Penobscot River. Details of the application, including where the treatment would occur, were not immediately available Wednesday.
The proposed treatment facility in Hampden would be at the town’s Pine Tree Landfill, which was closed earlier this year, and use technology that Casella has already implemented in Vermont, Boyd said. The technology is called the LEEF System, Boyd said.
Casella officials showed legislators and reporters a proposed location for a treatment facility at Juniper Ridge last year. Boyd did not say why leachate is being treated off site instead.
Leachate is currently being trucked to Nine Dragons Paper in Old Town, where it undergoes basic wastewater treatment. The proposed landfill expansion requires the material to have additional PFAS treatment.
The leachate will be held in a million-gallon tank at the Juniper Ridge Landfill before it’s treated. A similar tank will be used for holding the liquid in Hampden.
Once treated for PFAS, the water will be sent through a local sewer system and sewer treatment plant, Boyd said.
What will happen with the removed leachate is still being decided, Boyd said.
“There’s a couple different thoughts on the residual,” Boyd said.
The only proposed use Boyd shared is that the PFAS may be entombed in concrete blocks and sent back to Juniper Ridge. Technology for other ways the PFAS could be entombed or moved after treatment is still changing and advancing, Boyd said. Casella wants the “latest and greatest” technology available, he said.
Opponents to the landfill expansion have said treating leachate off site would create more environmental and public health risks. Old Town residents Tuesday echoed those concerns and asked Boyd and Lane Gould, landfill manager of the Maine Bureau of General Services, questions about the city’s agreement with the landfill, the safety of trucking leachate and if there are any ways for the landfill to close.
A representative from the Maine Department of Environmental Protection was invited to Tuesday’s meeting but did not attend due to the ongoing court cases, Landfill Committee Chair Laura Sanborn said.

title: 7 coffins containing human remains found at North Dakota governor’s residence
text:
7 coffins containing human remains found at North Dakota governor’s residence
Archaeologists found seven coffins containing human remains on the property of the North Dakota governor’s residence, according to media reports.
Contractors first discovered remains while doing work on the property on May 19. On Tuesday, Oct. 6, the seven coffins and an empty wooden box were found, KFYR reported.
The area where the remains were found served as Bismarck’s community cemetery in the 1870s, according to KFYR.
The state’s Office of Management and Budget told People Magazine that the remains consist of two women, two men, two teenage boys and one toddler, according to preliminary analysis.
A spokesperson for Gov. Kelly Armstrong's Office told the North Dakota Monitor that Armstrong "wants to ensure the remains are treated with the appropriate care and respect."
Archaeologists plan to review and catalog all remains, which is expected to take months. A reburial is expected in the spring of 2027.

title: 84-year-old accused of creating and selling explosives from home, deputies say
text:
LAKE CHARLES, La. (KPLC/Gray News) - An 84-year-old man in Louisiana was arrested for allegedly creating and selling explosives from his home, according to deputies.
On Oct. 2, detectives searched the home of John W. Sinkankas in relation to an ongoing joint investigation.
Investigators say Sinkakas was manufacturing and selling explosive devices from his home, which is also 500 feet away from a school.
Detectives initially learned the devices were manufactured to resemble fireworks, but after further investigation it was discovered that the devices contained an illegal amount of explosive materials.
During the search, detectives found several pounds of explosive powders, around 18 pounds of explosive precursors, numerous homemade explosives, and materials used to assemble them.
Sinkankas was arrested and booked into the Calcasieu Correctional Center and charged with manufacture & possession of delayed action incendiary device.
He was released the following day on a $150,000 bond. The investigation is continuing and more charges are possible.

title: HBCUs are underfunded. A legal effort starting in Missouri seeks to fix it
text:
An effort to address decades of underfunding at some historically Black colleges and universities kicked off Wednesday with a lawsuit against the state of Missouri.
Students and graduates of Lincoln University in the state’s capital of Jefferson City allege the lack of financial resources undercut their education and devalued their degrees.
More than a dozen other states are in the crosshairs of a newly formed group called the 1890 Project.
“It is very unfortunate that we still live in a climate where, depending on the color of one’s skin, one gets precedence over the other,” said Lincoln graduate Jeanneth Johnson, a 54-year-old from the Detroit suburb of Sterling Heights, who is a plaintiff in the lawsuit.
The University of Missouri system and the governor’s office both said in written statements that they couldn’t comment on pending litigation.
HBCUs missed out on money
Back in 2023, the administration of then-President Joe Biden found HBCUs in 16 states had missed out on $12.6 billion in funding over the last three decades. The finding and an ensuing call for the governors in those states to boost spending came one year after members of Congress also raised concerns.
At issue is the funding of land-grant universities. The first batch was established in 1862 under the Morrill Act, which gave public lands to states to pay for colleges that focused on educating students in practical fields like agriculture and engineering.
It was a departure from traditional colleges at the time, which focused mostly on classical subjects for the elite, such as Latin, Greek, philosophy and theology. But the law’s namesake, Justin Smith Morrill, a senator from Vermont, believed higher education should be accessible to all social classes.
In the wake of the Civil War, Morrill, an abolitionist, called for an update to the act. Passed in 1890, the new law required states either to open their land grants to students of all races or establish separate land grant schools for Black students.
Missouri, a border state that allowed slavery but fought with the Union during the Civil War, wasn’t about to open its flagship University of Missouri campus in Columbia to Black students. To meet the new requirement, it looked toward what was then called Lincoln Institute, which a Black Union Army unit started at the end of the war by pooling their wages.
Seventeen other mostly former Confederate states and border states established 18 other land grant schools for Black students. They included Tuskegee University, the only private 1890 land grant.
Federal law requires an equitable distribution of state funding for all of a state’s land-grant universities — whether HBCU or otherwise. But the 2023 Biden administration analysis found that only two states funded traditional and HBCU land-grants equitably — Delaware and Ohio. Lincoln University alone was underfunded by $361 million from 1987 through 2020, the newly filed lawsuit says, citing federal numbers.
Today, Lincoln’s enrollment has fallen to around 2,200 students, down from around 3,400 in 2011 and just a fraction of the approximately 32,000 enrolled on the University of Missouri’s Columbia campus, which was roiled by protests in 2015 over racial injustice, leading to the resignation of two top administrators.
“We’re not saying they should be funded equally, but they should be funded on parity,” said Don Calloway, a former Missouri state lawmaker who leads the 1890 Project. “And the feds funded Lincoln with the proper parity. The problem is that the state made an intentional choice not to match the federal appropriation. And that’s where Lincoln really was cheated.”
He blames millions in deferred maintenance on some of Lincoln’s enrollment woes.
Calloway said he also is talking to state’s attorneys general in several other states, including Virginia, Arkansas, Maryland, North Carolina, Alabama and Georgia. Over the decades, lawsuits also have been filed in several of those states over underfunding of HBCUs, including one in Maryland that led to a $577 million settlement.
Missouri is the first legal target
But those lawsuits mostly focused on state-level funding disparities between all HBCUs and non-HBCUs. There are dozens of HBCUs that aren’t 1890s land grants, often started by nonprofits and religious groups. Calloway said his legal strategy is focused just on the 1890s schools.
“We expect to negotiate and/or litigate in multiple jurisdictions over the next year,” he said. “Missouri is the first.”
Herbert Kitchen, a plaintiff whose great-great-grandfather, Caleb Lindsey, was one of the soldiers whose pay founded Lincoln, recalled his residence hall frequently was without heat and hot water when he was a student at Lincoln in the 1980s. Rumors were swirling that the school might close, and he said some employers looked at his degree as “second rate.”
Kitchen, a retired California community college administrator, thinks of his great-great grandfather as he fights for Lincoln, a school generations of his family have attended.
“I am,” he said, “the hope and dream that my great-grandfather had when he was a slave.”

title: Data center moratorium vote postponed after fight, protests
text:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC/Gray News) — Chaos ensued during Tuesday night’s data center moratorium vote by the city council in Memphis, Tennessee.
More than 100 people showed up to the meeting to hear the outcome on the proposed ordinance.
“This is just a total hazard. We’ve basically been invaded by strangers, by people that have gotten paid, and they have not communicated with us in any way,” said Amber Lowe, a local community member. “This is hurtful, and I’m rethinking where I need to be living at.”
The decision to delay the vote until Oct. 20 led to a fight breaking out in the lobby and tense exchanges among city council members.
A fight between two women spilled into the lobby, with punches thrown while protesters chanted inside the meeting. One woman had her hair pulled and was slapped seconds later.
Councilwoman Yolanda Cooper-Sutton was pulled out of the meeting after arguing with protesters and council member JB Smiley.
“You could’ve came to see me like I asked you to... I ain’t no coward; you pipe down, baby, I clap back,” Cooper-Sutton said.
The city council halted the meeting amid the turmoil and subsequently delayed the vote.
Crowds chanted “this is our city” and “show me what democracy looks like” as the demonstration moved from the chamber into the halls of the building.
Protesters said they are not done pursuing the issue.
Memphis police were called to the disturbance at city hall, but a department spokesperson says no one was detained and no one was harmed.

title: Former CIA official accused of stealing $40M in gold bars pleads guilty
text:
Former CIA official accused of stealing $40M in gold bars pleads guilty
A former senior CIA official pleaded guilty Tuesday in Virginia to a charge that he abused his position and government funds to enrich himself by acquiring Florida real estate and hundreds of gold bars worth over $40 million, according to court records.
File video from 2018 | Former CIA official accused of selling American secrets to China for $25,000
David J. Rush fabricated a "highly classified" government program to justify the acquisition of luxury property in south Florida that he intended to resell for personal profit, according to a court filing. Rush separately concocted a bogus "sensitive government activity" to obtain the gold bars, the filing says.
Rush's fraudulent conduct cost the federal government approximately $194 million in total losses, according to the Justice Department. The losses included over $1.8 million in privately chartered flights that Rush authorized for personal use at the government's expense.
Under questioning from investigators, Rush admitted that he provided a foreign government official with information about the identity of a secret source for the U.S. government, a new court filing says. The filing doesn't specify which country the foreign official represented.
Prosecutors also accuse Rush of lying to colleagues and government contractors about his military and academic credentials and the fake program that he invented, falsely claiming it was authorized by high-ranking U.S. officials.
"Rush used his legitimate government authority and manufactured personal bona fides to create confidence in his directions," the court filing says.
Rush, 49, of Ashburn, Virginia, pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud, which carries a maximum prison sentence of 20 years, court records show. District Judge Michael Nachmanoff is scheduled to sentence Rush on Jan. 28 in Alexandria, Virginia.
Several months ago, Rush tried to fraudulently authorize the release of $100 million from a government contract, according to Tuesday's filing. He directed somebody else to transfer approximately $145 million to a holding company formed at his direction, then used those funds to acquire four "luxury" properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound, Florida, the filing says.
In previous court filings, prosecutors said Rush stashed roughly $46 million worth of gold bars from the federal government at his Virginia home. They also accused him of fraudulently claiming tens of thousands of dollars in compensation for military leave after he was honorably discharged from the U.S. Navy in 2015.
"Federal employees are entrusted with serving the American people, not themselves," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe said the agency immediately referred the matter to the FBI after an internal investigation turned up evidence of Rush's crimes.
"David Rush abused his position and betrayed the public trust and should be held fully accountable for his actions," Ratcliffe said in a statement.
Rush was arrested after investigators searched his home and seized approximately 300 gold bars, roughly $2 million in U.S. currency and about 35 luxury watches, according to an FBI agent's affidavit. A judge ordered Rush to be held without bond after his initial court appearance earlier this year.
During a hearing in June, defense attorney Jessica Carmichael said Rush wasn't charged initially with any crimes related to the discovery of the gold bars, which she referred to as "basically a nonissue" and "nothing more than a sensational tidbit." She said her client properly obtained the gold bars and kept them locked in a safe in his basement.
"Mr. Rush never claimed they were his," Carmichael said.
Carmichael declined to comment on Rush's guilty plea after Tuesday's hearing.
Authorities say Rush lied about his education and military background on job applications, falsely claiming to be a former Navy pilot who graduated with a bachelor's degree from Clemson University in South Carolina and a master's degree from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in New York.
Investigators determined that he didn't serve as a Navy pilot and didn't attend either school. Rush enlisted in the Navy in 1997 and was honorably discharged from the U.S. Navy Reserve as a lieutenant in 2015, according to the FBI affidavit.

title: Trump administration proposes a $70,000 fee for international students to work in the US
text:
Trump administration proposes a $70,000 fee for international students to work in the US
The Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday proposed a $70,000 fee for international students seeking to work in the United States, the latest effort from the Trump administration to discourage students from abroad enrolling in U.S. schools.
Video above: Ed Department answers questions about student loan changes
A proposed rule would require schools to pay the fee for every student who participates in the optional practice training program, known as OPT, which allows students to work in jobs related to their major during or after their time in school. Students are generally eligible for one year of work post-graduation, though certain science, technology, engineering and math majors are eligible for an additional two years, before they must find a permanent legal status or leave the country.
Schools would be required to pay the $70,000 for each new student's initial application to the program, and a $30,000 fee for each renewal.
The change would represent a blow to American colleges and universities that heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue, as well as tech companies and other industries that hire many international students for technical roles.
The OPT program allows international students to gain hands-on experience and fill labor shortages in high-demand STEM fields, said Fanta Aw, CEO of NAFSA, an association that represents international education.
“Driving away the talents, perspectives, and aspirations of international students will only hurt American innovation, economic growth, workforce development, and global leadership,” Aw said in a written statement.
In a statement, DHS described the fee as a response to what it claims is fraud and abuse of the visa program, which it called a “pipeline for cheap foreign labor.”
The public has 60 days to comment on the proposal before DHS can finalize it and put it into effect. The proposal also could face legal challenges from higher education groups or business associations that could delay it.
President Donald Trump's administration has been putting pressure on international students in many ways as part of its wider efforts to crack down on immigration and reshape higher education.
Last year, the Republican administration began suddenly terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, detaining and deporting many of them.
This summer, the administration finalized a rule that sought to prevent international students from staying in the U.S. for more than four years without approval from the federal government. The move drew swift backlash from higher education leaders who said it would increase the burden on schools and noted that many programs are longer than four years by design. A federal court prevented the rule from taking effect in September.
