title: Texas man's scheduled execution is first in US since Christa Pike
text:
Lawyers seek to block Texas man's execution, citing failed execution of Christa Pike
Lawyers for a Texas man who fatally shot a convenience store clerk are asking a judge to stay his execution by lethal injection set for Wednesday, citing the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee last week.
This would be the first execution scheduled in the U.S. since Pike.
Related video above: How could a lethal injection go wrong?
Because the same drug used in her attempted execution — pentobarbital — would be used in Texas for Jamaal Howard, his attorneys argued that the drug poses the same risks and said they believe the state's supply had become degraded.
Pike's lawyers are seeking more information about what went wrong after the 50-year-old survived two doses of pentobarbital. She was hospitalized and, as of Tuesday, was awake and speaking.
Her attorneys have alleged her execution was marred by blown veins, where a needle goes all the way through a vein and causes a leak of blood and fluid, as well as Tennessee's deteriorated pentobarbital and a lack of emergency medical care.
"There is a similar risk," Howard's attorneys wrote, "that Texas's execution drugs are likewise degraded, as they are far past the original beyond-use dates that the pharmacopeia allows for drugs of this kind."
Texas has executed six people so far this year, with two more scheduled after Howard, which would be the 30th execution nationwide in 2026.
A killing caught on surveillance video
Howard, 46, was found guilty of capital murder in the 2000 killing of Vickie Swartout, 42, who was shot once in the chest during a robbery. Evidence presented at the trial included the store's surveillance video, which showed Howard shooting Swartout.
Howard, who was 20 at the time, took $114 and a carton of cigarettes from the store in the small, rural town of Silsbee, located about 100 miles (161 kilometers) northeast of Houston, according to court records.
His attorneys have argued that Howard is intellectually disabled and his execution should be halted. The state said that he has not presented evidence that would show he meets the requirements for a claim of intellectual disability.
He has an appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court pending to stop the execution.
The Supreme Court in 2002 had barred the execution of intellectually disabled people. But it has given states some discretion in how they determine such disabilities.
Motion to stay because of drugs
The motion filed in the Court of Criminal Appeals in Texas early Wednesday said Howard's attorneys had filed requests for information about the lethal dose of pentobarbital the Texas Department of Criminal Justice planned to use. They say the department asked for a state attorney general opinion about whether they would have to disclose that information, despite a "years-long practice of disclosing information."
The Texas attorney general opinion is not expected to be returned until after Wednesday, meaning Howard can't litigate whatever decision the state might make on releasing that information, they say.
Texas officials did not immediately return a request for comment Wednesday morning.
Executions in the US this year
Florida has carried out 16 executions so far this year, the most of any state. Most states that allow executions use lethal injection as their primary method.
Tennessee's Republican Gov. Bill Lee has halted the one remaining execution for the rest of the year.

title: LIV: The Innovation that Changed the Golf World
text:
LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the State of New Jersey on Tuesday, Sept. 8. This was the tipping point for the league that sought to revolutionize the game of golf.
For years critics have complained that golf is elitist, outdated and slow-paced. Arguably, the combination of the COVID-19 pandemic and the emergence of LIV changed that narrative. Tee times at municipal and public courses are harder than ever before to come by, and 2026 has seen a significant increase in PGA Tour viewership ratings compared to years prior.
Many felt LIV was directly competing with the PGA Tour because players were indirectly asked to choose between tradition and modernity. There was significant fear that LIV’s flamboyant nature would capture the attention of the PGA Tour’s top talent.
The rise of LIV Golf dates back to 2019 when Andrew Gardiner, a British corporate finance attorney and golf enthusiast set out to create a Premier League. Gardiner envisioned a 54-hole format as opposed to the typical 72, shotgun starts, team comradery and assured earnings for all competing players.
A major draw to LIV was money. The PGA Tour lifestyle is hard to sustain. Week after week players are forced to perform at their very best, otherwise they go home penniless. LIV’s model not only allowed players to capitalize on winnings, but also put less pressure on professional golfers by adding a team component to the highly individualized sport.
Still, the potential of a new league wasn’t at the forefront of the golf world’s mind. Tiger Woods’ victory at the 2019 Masters was a much bigger story.
By 2020 this had changed. Gardiner was no longer in the picture, but the Saudis were on track to cement Gardiner’s grand plan through their public investment fund (PIF). This enraged PGA Tour Commissioner, Jay Monahan who boldly declared that players who compete in the Saudi-backed league put themselves at risk of facing penalties from the PGA Tour.
Surprisingly, Monahan’s stance failed to deter some of golf’s biggest names. After Greg Norman was made head and later CEO of LIV Golf, the league officially got off the ground. One month after the PGA Tour publicly announced that golfers who play for LIV will be suspended, it was made known that Bryson DeChambeau, Dustin Johnson, Brooks Koepka and Phil Mickelson had joined.
For a period of time, it seemed like LIV was golf’s most avant-garde innovation. “Larger checks and smaller fields can attract players and make the fan experience significantly better” Connor Rabbitt ‘29 said. LIV is also known for its party-esque atmosphere, which made the experience appear hard to beat.
However, the cracks in LIV’s foundation worsened at an unexpected speed. Rabbitt spoke on the topic commenting, “From the start bad PR management made LIV the bad guys.” Players like Mickelson publicly defended the league in a passionate albeit intense manner, which sparked further controversy.
At the same time, LIV is owed credit for the revitalization of the game that’s near and dear to many of our hearts. “LIV has been good because it has caused the tour to lock in, look at their system and raise purse values,” Malin Adams ‘29 said. Once the PGA Tour initiated the process of catching up to the times, the future of LIV Golf became complicated.
Later Adams added, “Now that purse values are very similar there’s no point. No competitive value when it comes to playing on LIV.”
The PGA Tour’s response to LIV can be found in the organization’s restructuring. Starting in 2028, there will be both a Championship and Challenger Series. It remains to be seen whether players approve of this new two-tiered model.
When questioned about his thoughts on the fall of LIV Golf Brent Rollo ‘30 said, “Shows that money isn’t the most important thing in sports.” Koepka parting ways with LIV and rejoining the PGA Tour through its returning member program in January of 2026, corroborates this reality. It will be interesting to see who else follows in his footsteps.
Golf fans are currently in a state of limbo, as they grapple with the loss of LIV. Yet at the same time, they are eagerly awaiting the debut of the PGA Tour’s next chapter. Mehar Nijjer ‘27 spoke on this point adding, “I would’ve loved to see it grow and see what it could become, but I’m also not mad about the players potentially going back to the PGA Tour and playing more traditional golf again. I think it’ll be fun to watch.”
Even though LIV is now struggling financially, due to its eventual loss of PIF funding at the conclusion of 2026, the league’s creation pushed the PGA Tour to improve its business model, ultimately adding greater legitimacy to the well-established organization.

title: Debate an even matchup says University of Maine Political Science Chair
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The University of Maine’s Political Science Chair, Mark Brewer, thinks both candidates fared well in Tuesday’s US Senate debate, but the even match-up might be a win for the challenger.
Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) is seeking a 6th term and has been on the debate stage far more than Jackson.
Brewer said that going in there were questions about whether Troy Jackson would be up to the task of debating her.
“I think he answered those questions. I think he held his own, so in that sense I guess that’s a win for Jackson even those the debate was pretty even. They both had their moments.”
Brewer went on to say that tying Collins to Trump was clearly the Jackson campaign’s plan, along with reminding voters about the Brett Kavanaugh vote.
He doesn’t think last night’s performance will sway those small groups on the margins still trying to make up their mind on who to vote for.
He expects to see similar things in the debates ahead.
There are three more debates scheduled including one hosted by our media partner WMTW Thursday night at 8pm.
You can watch that on our streaming channels.
WABI and our sister station WAGM will host a US Senate debate next Tuesday night at 7pm.

title: Matthew T. Tilton
text:
Matthew Thomas Tilton passed away unexpectedly on July 7, 2026, at Miles Memorial Hospital due to complications from what began as an infection.
Matthew was born on Feb. 4, 1991, in Portland, Maine, to his parents, Gary Tilton and Vanessa (Hale) Betancourt. Matthew was a kind-hearted person, always looking for ways to serve others. From a young age, he pushed his lawnmower around the town of Washington, Maine, mowing yards for those who could no longer do it themselves. He never asked for or accepted money, instead always looking for ways to bless others. That spirit of generosity continued throughout his life, even shoveling snow this past winter for his newest neighbor.
Matthew grew up in the Church of the Nazarene, and while he was not always active in church, he had a personal relationship with Jesus. Though our hearts are broken and we begin the difficult reality of daily life without him, we find comfort in knowing that Matthew is with Jesus, and we will be together again.
After graduating from Medomak Valley High School with the Class of 2009, Matthew attended Washington County Community College, where he graduated from two different mechanical programs, earning special awards and recognition in both.
Matthew met the love of his life and very best friend, Brittany (Dickinson) Tilton, shortly after graduating from college. Together for more than fourteen years, they were married on Sept. 17, 2016. They enjoyed many adventures together, but their greatest joy was creating a beautiful family.
Matthew had many hobbies. He loved fishing, whether on open water or through the ice, and enjoyed countless days on the water with family and friends. He was community-minded, having served on the Boothbay Fire Department. In addition to attending every one of his children's games, he was always willing to step up and help whenever there was a need.
From an early age, Matthew's mechanical aptitude was evident. There was nothing he could not take apart and put back together exactly as it was meant to be. This talent served him well as he began his career at BIW as an outdoor machinist and ultimately was promoted to lead a team as a manager at Bath Iron Works, where he was well-liked and respected.
Most recently, with the help of their oldest son, Myles, Matthew took great pride in cutting and clearing the lot that would ultimately become the site of their beautiful new home in Boothbay.
Matthew overcame many challenges throughout his life. Yet, he would have been the first to say that his greatest accomplishments, and those of which he was most proud, were his loving marriage and his beautiful children.
Matthew was predeceased by his infant son, Cole Matthew Tilton; his father, Gary Tilton; his paternal grandmother, Janet Tilton; his maternal grandfather, Tom Hale, with whom he shared a special relationship; his maternal aunts, Valarie Hale and Viki Reed; his cousins, Jamie Lee Reed and Caleb Packard; and Brittany's grandparents, Bob Blackman and Sandy and Lee Dickinson.
In addition to his wife, Brittany, Matthew is survived by his children, Myles, Maci, and Bodie Tilton; his mother and stepfather, Vanessa and Miguel Betancourt; his father- and mother-in-law, Doug and Lori Dickinson; his maternal grandmother, Darlene Hale; his paternal grandfather, Alan Tilton; his uncle and aunt, Glenn and Lisa Tilton; Brittany's grandparents, Ron and Darlene French; his brother-in-law, Daniel Dickinson; as well as several great-aunts and uncles, cousins, other relatives, and close friends with whom he shared many special memories.
Family and friends are invited to visiting hours from 5 to 7 p.m. on Wednesday, July 15 at Hall's Funeral Home, 975 Wiscasset Road, Boothbay, ME 04537. A private family burial will be held at Shuman Cemetery in Waldoboro.
Hall’s of Boothbay has care of arrangements. To extend online condolences go to hallfuneralhomes.com.

title: Social Connections and Brain Health
text:
With all the recent talk about artificial intelligence (AI), it is important now more than ever for all of us to maintain human connections. We are social beings and our personal connections play a crucial role in shaping our well-being. Research has shown that maintaining strong social connections can enhance cognitive function, protect against cognitive decline and improve overall mental health. Social connections can be a source of emotional support, and they are vital for brain health. Interacting with others engages multiple regions of our brain and by regularly activating these areas, social interactions help maintain and strengthen neural connections.
Social interactions with others are a powerful buffer against stress, which is known to have a negative effect on brain health. Being lonely and experiencing loneliness is a significant risk factor for cognitive decline and dementia. The lack of social interaction can lead to reduced cognitive stimulation, which in turn accelerates brain aging and cognitive deterioration. The absence of social interactions and support can exacerbate feelings of sadness, hopelessness and anxiety.
Maintaining and strengthening social connections is essential for supporting brain health throughout our lives. There are numerous strategies to foster meaningful relationships and enhance cognitive well-being.
Participate in social activities such as book clubs, join a gym or do volunteer work, allowing you to meet new people, engage in conversations and form new friendships. Stay connected with family and friends through phone calls, Facetime chats or visiting in person. Schedule weekly get-togethers at a coffee shop or restaurant to share experiences, discuss challenges and have a few laughs. Explore local groups with people of similar interests such as food, hiking, yoga, photography or a game or craft.
Engage in meaningful conversations to promote active listening and problem solving, and perhaps to learn something new about yourself in the process. Engaging with people of different ages helps to promote idea exchanges and may shift your perspective or long-held opinion.
Research shows that having a smartphone nearby may distract you from having a meaningful conversation, so make a point of putting away your digital devices when engaging with others. We use all our senses when interacting with others. We process facial expressions, body language, tone of voice and emotions in their words. All this information influences how we react in return. We are exercising our brain, strengthening our brain cells and creating new brain cells, too. Being present in the conversation shows others you value them, respect them and see them.
Social interactions and staying connected can help to keep your mind and memory strong.
For more information about Alzheimer’s disease and all other dementia, contact the Alzheimer’s Association. A free 24/7 Helpline is available providing access to many resources. Call 800-272-3900 or visit ALZ.org to explore many educational programs.

title: Iraq devalues its currency as Iran-U.S. war disrupts oil shipping routes
text:
Iraq devalues its currency as Iran-U.S. war disrupts oil shipping routes
Iraq devalued its currency Wednesday, changing the official exchange rate from around 1,300 dinars to the U.S. dollar to 1,500 dinars to the dollar.
Related video: Trump expands access to tax-free fuel ahead of midterm elections
The country’s central bank said in a statement that the new exchange rate had been decided at a meeting of Iraq’s Cabinet the night before “to meet the relevant financial, economic and monetary requirements.”
The previous exchange rate was set in 2023. In practice, there has always been a gap between the official rate and the market rate used by exchange shops.
That gap had widened in recent months as a result of the U.S.-Iran war — which has sometimes spilled over into Iraq — and disruptions to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iraq’s economy relies heavily on oil exports, most of which were shipped via the strait before the war. Since the war started, Iraq has resorted to shipping oil overland through Syria for export, but the route is more expensive and less efficient.
The unofficial rate had risen to more than 1,600 to the dollar before the official devaluation was announced. After the announcement of the new official exchange rate, the market rate jumped to more than 1,700 dinars to the dollar.
At the new official rate, Iraq's Finance Ministry will sell dollars at 1,500 dinars to the dollar, while consumers purchasing from banks will pay 1,520 dinars to the dollar.

title: State says ‘packaging error’ caused ‘small number’ of incorrect ballots to go out in Oxford County
text:
Editor’s note, this story was updated on Oct. 8 to correct information about the ballots and where they were sent.
Several Oxford voters received incorrect ballots this week for the November election.
The Department of the Secretary of State said the Oxford town clerk was notified by a resident on Tuesday that that they had received a ballot meant for another town.
A relative of Ernie Fitts, who is running for an Oxford-area Maine House seat, noticed the candidate was missing from the ballot and raised the alarm on social media.
Jana Spaulding, deputy secretary of state for communications, said Wednesday afternoon that the situation had already been remedied.
“A resident did contact the Oxford town clerk yesterday after receiving an incorrect ballot style, and it was addressed by the clerk,” Spaulding said.
“The clerk identified that due to a packaging error at the printer, a small number of incorrect ballots were received and sent out. Oxford is working quickly to contact any resident who could have possibly received an incorrect ballot.”
She said anyone getting an incorrect ballot will be given a proper one.
“Every voter,” Spaulding said, “will have the chance to vote the correct ballot.”

title: Florida man in Maine to finish 12K-mile walk for mental health awareness
text:
Florida man in Maine to finish 12,000-mile walk for mental health awareness
A Florida man who has walked across America to raise mental health awareness has arrived in Maine to finish his journey.
Kyndal Ray Edwards started his journey in January 2022, walking from Jacksonville Beach, Florida, to Long Beach, Washington. He then made his way down to San Diego before walking from California back to Florida. Now, he is completing the last leg of his journey from the Florida Keys to the easternmost point in the continental United States.
Wednesday marked Day 1,006 of his journey as he walked from York to Kennebunk. Maine's Total Coverage caught up with Edwards while he was in Ogunquit.
Edwards is walking to raise money for the nonprofit organization Never Alone Recovery, which helps individuals and families break free from addiction and mental health struggles.
"People have been stopping at meet and greets that I do at hotels and showing love and support. People have been offering food and just all kinds of stuff, and people have been sharing what mental health and recovery means to them, more importantly than anything," Edwards said.
Edwards said he expects to finish his 12,000-mile cross-country trek in just a few weeks, aiming to reach West Quoddy Head Lighthouse in Lubec on Oct. 25.

title: Dolly Parton's nephew accused of implementing measures to avoid being served lawsuit, estate says
text:
Dolly Parton's nephew, Bryan Seaver, accused of using barbed wire, caution tape to avoid being served lawsuit
Dolly Parton's nephew has been accused by officials presiding over her estate of using evasive measures to avoid being served a lawsuit weeks after a temporary restraining order was granted.
Related video: Pink vehicle tribute parade rolls through Williamson County to honor Dolly Parton's legacy and life
According to Rolling Stone, lawyers for the estate said yellow caution tape and barbed wire were placed in front of Bryan Seaver's front door as a "process server was making repeated attempts to serve him with a lawsuit, accusing him of using a 'campaign of threats' to 'extract money' from Parton's business interests."
Lawyers for She's Alive, LLC, which Parton established to protect her properties and business interests, submitted court filings on Oct. 5. They filed the documents in an effort to push back Seaver's request to delay an upcoming court hearing so he would have time to meet with his new legal counsel.
On Sept. 22, SAL sued and filed a temporary restraining order against Seaver and his security company, alleging the star's nephew threatened to smear his aunt's legacy and made threats against several employees.
The allegations come over a month after Seaver— son of Parton's sister Cassie— announced his aunt's death on Aug. 25.
"This video announcement is something that she asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality," Seaver said in the video posted on Dolly's Instagram account. "As her head of security for more than two decades — a role my father Larry held before me — I have imagined the heaviness of this moment but haven't truly felt it until now."
He continued, saying, "It is an honor— an honor that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness. But sadness lies with us, not with Dolly. Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by [late husband] Carl, her parents and countless others who have watched over her and longed for her to meet them in the heavens."
Parton died following a brief battle with cancer, her spokesperson confirmed.
Among SAL's Oct. 5 filings is an affidavit from a process server alleging that around 4:35 p.m. on Sept. 24, they attempted to hand over legal filings related to the restraining order, USA Today reported. No one answered the door that day or on Sept. 25, according to the document.
Upon returning the evening of Saturday, Sept. 26, the server wrote, "there were now 'no trespassing' signs on the lawn and by the front door." They were allegedly unable to access the front door due to yellow caution tape and barbed wire "surrounding the front steps."
A photo included in the filing, USA Today and Rolling Stone said, showed barbed wire zig-zagging over the front steps leading to a home. Five pieces of caution tape are tied around the wires.
On Oct. 6, officials agreed to reschedule the hearing for temporary injunctive relief to the morning of Oct. 20. The temporary restraining order against Seaver is also extended to this date.

title: Road worker, 24, dies after being hit by 2 trucks in work zone crash, troopers say
text:
BENTON TWP., Mich. (WILX/Gray News) - A road worker was killed while on the job Tuesday afternoon in Michigan.
According to Michigan State Police, troopers were called around 2:30 p.m. to Lansing Road near Nixon Road for a reported crash in a roadwork zone.
Road crews had temporarily closed Lansing Road to northbound traffic for construction work, officials said. Flag workers were directing traffic while road commission trucks were parked at the scene.
Troopers said the crash occurred when a pickup truck was stopped on Lansing Road at the direction of a flagger, and a Kenworth sanitation truck, unable to stop while approaching the pickup, struck the back of the pickup.
The impact pushed the two trucks into an unoccupied road commission truck. Authorities said the 24-year-old worker, who was directing traffic, attempted to avoid the trio of trucks but was hit by the pickup and the sanitation truck.
The flagger was pronounced dead at the scene, according to police who called the crash heartbreaking.
“Yesterday’s tragic crash in Eaton County is a sobering reminder of the dangers our road crews face every day,” Michigan State Police Lt. Rene Gonzalez said.
The driver of the pickup and his passenger were taken to University of Michigan Health-Sparrow Hospital with injuries. The sanitation truck driver and his passenger were not injured.
“We urge every driver approaching a work zone to slow down, stay focused, and give workers the space they need to do their jobs safely. A few extra seconds of caution can save a life,” Gonzalez said.
Investigators noted that alcohol and drugs did not appear to have been factors in the crash.

title: Meet Willow, our Adoptable Pet of the Week
text:
Meet Willow, our Adoptable Pet of the Week in Greater Portland
This week's featured adoptable pet from the Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland is Willow, a 2-year-old mixed-breed dog who absolutely loves people.
Willow came to Maine from a rescue partner in Georgia, where she had been a stray. Matt Blanchard of the Animal Refuge League said the shelter's staff has learned that Willow is smart, eager to please and a big fan of belly rubs.
"Whatever she can do to be the center of attention and make you happy, that's going to make her happy, too," Blanchard said.
Blanchard said Willow has done well with children, but noted that the Animal Refuge League has not had much luck with introducing her to other dogs at the shelter. For the time being, Willow will need to be in a home without other dogs, but Blanchard said Willow could potentially have dog friends in the future once she has decompressed from shelter life.
More information about Willow is available on the Animal Refuge League's website, as long as she is still looking for her forever home.
Anyone who is interested in meeting Willow or other adoptable pets can visit the Animal Refuge League's shelter at 217 Landing Road in Westbrook between 11 a.m. and 4 p.m., except on Wednesdays, when the shelter is closed for adoptions.
The Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland does adoptions on a first-come, first-served basis. On the days the shelter is open, sign-in sheets will be placed on the front door at 9 a.m. to track the order of arrival of adopters who show up early. People who arrive early are asked to remain on the campus once they sign in.
Dog owners who are interested in adopting dogs that are older than 6 months are required to have their dogs meet the adoptable pet before a new pet can be brought home.

title: Troy Jackson details personal finances in new disclosure
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson‘s primary source of income over the last two years came from two international unions based in Maryland, according to a personal financial disclosure filed this week.
Since the beginning of last year, Jackson received $90,000 from the International Association of Machinists and $48,000 from the International Union of Painters and Allied Trades for general consulting work.
Jackson’s campaign said the candidate provided consulting and organizing help for various national and local issues. Jackson is no longer providing those services, the campaign said.
“Troy’s financial disclosure reflects a lifetime of working for a paycheck,” a spokesperson said in a written statement. “He’s a logger and union member who understands what it means to worry about making ends meet — and he would bring that experience to a Senate dominated by millionaires. Susan Collins has spent nearly 30 years in Washington. Troy has spent his life fighting for people who work for a living.”
Jackson’s disclosure was filed late Monday after he received a 55-day extension. It’s the first detailed look the candidate has provided into his personal finances.
Sen. Susan Collins‘ campaign accused Jackson of not being transparent about his finances, and of taking “dark money” and corporate PAC money as Maine Senate president, despite vows to refuse that money during his U.S. Senate campaign.
“As Senate president, he was paid by three unions and a dark money group,” Collins spokesperson Blake Kernen said in a written statement. “And rather than file his disclosure on time in August, he took the latest extension possible and filed at 9:54 p.m. on the final day.”
In 2025, Jackson reported payments totaling $5,100 from the Eastern Maine Labor Council and $4,800 from Food and Medicine, a 501 (c)(4) social and economic justice group. He served as an organizer for both Brewer-based groups, his disclosure shows.
Jackson is leaning heavily on his working-class background, including his prior work as a logger, in his race against Collins, the Republican incumbent. But his disclosure does not list any income from logging.
His campaign said Jackson worked as a logger for 15 years before joining the state Legislature in 2002, at which point he continued logging intermittently.
Jackson also listed his construction and land management firm, Jackson Associates, on the paperwork. He did not list any assets for that firm, but he did report that some of his consulting income went to his company.
It’s unclear exactly how much Jackson or Collins’ total assets are worth, since they are only required to disclose minimums and ranges on the Senate financial forms.
Jackson disclosed between $147,000 and $430,000 in assets, including between $100,000 and $250,000 in state retirement benefits from his partner.
Yet Jackson’s earnings and assets pale in comparison to Collins, who earns at least $174,000 a year as a senator and receives additional income through her husband, Tom Daffron. The couple has an estimated net worth of $7.1 million and owns between $4.2 million and $10 million in assets, according to Congressstock.com.
Collins’ personal holdings include mutual funds and bank deposits. Daffron has a robust portfolio of stocks, bonds and government securities.
Jackson reported commercial real estate in Allagash owned by his longtime partner as an asset valued between $15,000 and $50,000. But he did not report any income from that property.

title: FBI stops Mall of America terror plot by 18-year-old after agents sold him assault rifle
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — FBI agents thwarted a terror attack by a teenager on the Mall of America after monitoring him for nearly two years and ultimately supplying him with the AK-47 he planned to use, authorities said Wednesday.
The 18-year-old had been on the FBI’s radar since December 2024, when he began trading messages with a confidential informant. A criminal complaint says he initially expressed an interest in traveling to Somalia to fight for al-Shabab militants. As his plans to instead attack the mall solidified, the complaint says, agents sold him the gun and ammunition on Tuesday and arrested him on the spot.
“This was a radicalized young man who needed to be watched,” U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen said. Agents “were able to detect a threat, and disrupt it, before the defendant carried out his intention to kill, in his words, maybe 30 to 60 people.”
Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud was arrested Tuesday in a public park in Richfield, several miles northwest of the Mall of America, after he paid $600 to an undercover FBI employee posing as a member of the Islamic State group for the rifle and 200 rounds of ammunition, the agency said.
Mohamud appeared in a yellow jail uniform for his initial appearance Wednesday in federal court in St. Paul. He told the judge he did not have a job, own a house or a car, or have any money in the bank. He was represented by Siri Carlson McDowell, a federal public defender. Carlson McDowell and relatives of Mohamud declined to comment after the hearing.
Rosen said Mohamud is an American-born U.S. citizen of Somali descent.
According to an FBI agent’s sworn complaint, Mohamud repeatedly affirmed in chat messages to the informant that he intended to attack and kill non-Muslims at the mall on Oct. 24, the date of a scheduled arts celebration by the Hmong community, Minnesota’s largest Asian ethnic group.
When the informant asked if he was serious about committing the attack, Mohamud replied, “yes i am 100% sure,” the complaint said, and added: “I would have backed out by now if I wasn’t sure.”
The agent wrote that Mohamud’s messages expressed admiration for recent terror attacks as well as an interest in traveling to fight in Somalia, ultimately for the Islamic State group. He later decided he couldn’t afford to travel there and would attack the mall instead, the complaint said.
The teen first came to the FBI’s attention in December 2024, the same month the source began exchanging messages with him, the complaint said. By May 2025, agents were concerned enough that they went to his home. His mother told them he wasn’t home from school yet and called the boy’s father, who declined to speak with them and said he would give their contact information to his lawyer, the complaint said.
“What I would say to parents all over Minnesota, and all over America: If you get any indication — especially if you hear from federal law enforcement — that your son or daughter is being radicalized, to the point where federal law enforcement wants to come and give you that warning, those are warnings that ought to be heeded,” Rosen said.
Tens of thousands of people of Somali descent live in Minnesota, dating back to when refugees began arriving in the 1990s. Over the years several have been charged with attempting to join militant groups.
___
Johnson reported from Seattle. Associated Press reporter Philip Marcelo in New York contributed.

title: Woman seriously injured, 3 people hurt in Hancock crash
text:
Maine woman seriously injured, three people hurt in Hancock crash
Maine State Police officials say a woman was seriously hurt and three other people were injured in a two-vehicle crash on Route 1 in Hancock.
Investigators determined that a Ford Bronco was traveling east on Route 1 at about 2:25 p.m. Tuesday when it was rear-ended by a Hyundai Sonata.
The impact caused the Bronco to roll over, while the Sonata went off the road, crossed a small field and crashed into a tree, according to investigators.
Police said a passenger in the Bronco, Cathy Grant, 66, of Milbridge, was transported to a local hospital with serious injuries.
A passenger in the Sonata who sustained non-life-threatening injuries in the crash was also taken to the hospital. The Sonata passenger was not identified by police.
Police said the driver of the Bronco, Amy Houck, 53, of Steuben, and the driver of the Sonata, Nicholas McAfee, 36, of Little Rock, Arkansas, sustained minor injuries as a result of the crash.
Route 1 was closed for several hours while investigators worked at the crash scene, police said.
The crash remains under investigation.

title: What a former doctor says about Christa Pike being awake and talking after failed execution
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) - Christa Pike is alive, awake and talking after her botched execution, according to her legal team.
Paul Allen, a former doctor, said he was not surprised by the news.
“I wasn’t surprised at all,” Allen said.
Defense questions drug delivery
Pike’s defense team believes pentobarbital may not have been going directly into her vein during the attempted execution.
Allen said the drug probably could have still killed her the night of the scheduled execution if she did not receive medical care after. When Pike did not die in a certain time frame, doctors were called in to keep her alive.
The Tennessee Department of Correction said it followed all protocol.
“Had they just left her, I think she would have succumbed to the drug,” Allen said. “And then it was just a matter of time until the large dose of pentobarbital metabolized, came down and then she was able to respond and her breathing center worked normally.”
What’s next in the case
With Pike still alive, the focus shifts to what’s next in her case, including whether she can still be put to death.
Criminal defense attorney Josh Hedrick addressed the question.
“We have to assess what is her mental state? Under our law, you cannot execute someone who is not competent, right? While she may be awake, we don’t yet know what her mental state is. We don’t know if there’s brain damage. We don’t know how alert she is,” Hedrick said.
Pike’s failed execution is the second in Tennessee this year.
Hedrick said the future of the death penalty and executions in the state is now in question.
“So, twice in one year is a bad look. That’s unacceptable. So, to identify where things are going wrong and fix them is vital. If we’re going to have executions, we have to do them properly,” Hedrick said.
Pike’s legal team said it is calling on the governor to commute her sentence, meaning the team will ask for life in prison rather than the death penalty.

title: Biddeford graffiti demands strong condemnation
text:
The vandalism of Sen. Susan Collins’ Biddeford office should be a moment of clarity in this U.S. Senate race. Somebody spray-painted the door with a degrading, sexist slur, and a disturbing number of people online have applauded it.
That kind of politics doesn’t care about fixing Maine’s problems; it cares only about winning the fight, using whatever illegal or criminal means available.
Troy Jackson, and the national Democratic establishment backing his campaign, should condemn this clearly and without qualification. Silence, or a vague statement about “heated rhetoric on both sides,” will tell the voters all they need to know about the kind of campaign we can expect over the coming weeks.
In her nearly 30 years of serving the people of Maine in the Senate, Sen. Collins has found common ground in her diligent and unwavering advocacy of the people in our great state. I know she will not be intimidated by the reprehensible tactics being undertaken by her adversaries — and neither should Maine voters.
Theodore Politis
Biddeford

title: Hegseth visits the long-deployed USS Lincoln to bestow a top award before the ship returns home
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has given the crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln a high-level award during a visit to the aircraft carrier Wednesday, a day before the ship returns home to San Diego after a record-long deployment in support of the Iran war.
The Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive that is typically reserved for significant achievement in combat, was bestowed upon the Lincoln and accompanying ships for “40 days of combat operations and an ironclad maritime blockade against Iran in support of Operation Epic Fury,” Hegseth said, referring to the Trump administration’s code name for the Iran war.
The carrier endured a record 265 uninterrupted days at sea, and its extended deployment drew national attention following reports of crew stress and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products. After more than 10 months deployed, the Lincoln’s crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East.
Pentagon chief visits the crew and acknowledges long time at sea
Hegseth, who flew out to the ship before its arrival Thursday in San Diego, acknowledged to the crew that “I’m the only thing standing between you and home” and that his intention was “once they pull up to the dock, we’re getting out of the way.”
Long deployments can tax service members who are away from their families for extended periods while facing threats, and can add wear to the aircraft carriers, which have been used for President Donald Trump’s military operations in the Middle East and South America.
The Lincoln is the second carrier that has endured an unusually long and arduous deployment to support the war against Iran and the second to receive the top unit award afterward.
Hegseth in May met the crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford during its return from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era.
As for the Lincoln, it departed San Diego in late November, arrived in the Middle East in January and now will be back in its home port.
Hegseth said Wednesday that Trump “tracked your activities from day one and couldn’t be more proud of what you executed.”
Issues had been reported aboard the USS Lincoln
The Navy initially played down early reports of supply problems on Lincoln and Trump said its lengthy deployment was “not nearly long enough,” Navy leaders, however, eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.
In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced from two to one for a short time. He said in a letter to a Democratic lawmaker seeking information that four nutritionally balanced meals were served daily.
Navy officials also said that while combat operations led to delays in scheduled resupply shipments, they prioritized the delivery of hygiene products and established a rotation to streamline distribution to different squadrons.
More recently, the service told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide while on the long deployment. Experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months.
Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the “Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission.”
He said that “what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you’re resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless.”
Aircraft carriers have been key to Iran war operations
According to the award that Hegseth read to the crew, the Lincoln and the strike group executed 3,693 combat missions, delivered 1.37 million pounds of ordnance, launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles, shot down 77 one-way attack drones, sank 64 Iranian warships, destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles and defended against four fast attack craft and explosive-carrying ships.
There are now two aircraft carriers assigned to the Middle East. The USS George Washington, though usually based in Asia, relieved the Lincoln in August.
The other aircraft carrier, the USS George H.W. Bush, has been deployed for about six months, but it pulled into Phuket, Thailand, for a port visit several days ago.
U.S. officials have said a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, and thousands of troops aboard it and accompanying ships could join the Washington and the Bush as early as the end of October.

title: As Army moves to execute Fort Hood shooter, questions about procedure linger
text:
The former U.S. Army officer convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad in December in what would be the first military execution in more than 65 years.
The announcement stunned an attorney who had represented Nidal Malik Hasan in a civil case, and raised concerns among experts on military law about whether the Army followed its mandated process for setting an execution and notifying a prisoner they’ve been condemned to death.
President Donald Trump’s announcement on Monday that Hasan would be executed by firing squad also sparked questions about how a firing squad would be assembled and what procedure it would use. The last time the military executed someone by firing squad was shortly after World War II.
Here’s a look at what we know about the military execution process and how experts said this case may proceed.
Military officials declined to provide details
In a post on social media Tuesday, acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said he scheduled the execution for 1 p.m. on Dec. 3 at Fort Hood — the site where Hasan opened fire killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 others.
Telle confirmed in his post on X that Trump had approved the execution on Oct. 2, starting the clock in Army regulations that requires an execution date to be set no sooner than 60 days and no later than 150 days after that approval.
Telle also noted that the execution would be carried out by firing squad, but did not offer details of where on base the execution would take place, what personnel would be a part of that squad or what procedure they would follow.
The Associated Press asked both Pentagon officials and the Army for more details, but those requests were declined. A message to the Army seeking comment on the potential procedural issues was sent Wednesday.
The procedures for execution in Army regulations do not contain specific protocols for particular methods of execution. Experts said in previous iterations of the firing squad — nearly 80 years ago — one shooter would be given a blank so they all could plausibly believe they had not fired the fatal shot.
Hasan could file a Habeas petition in civil court
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building where soldiers were getting checkups, shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun.
He said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims — a defense a military judge barred him from presenting during his trial. Hasan made almost no effort to defend himself in court, telling jurors when he acted as his own counsel that evidence would show he was the shooter and describing himself as a soldier who had “switched sides.”
“What happens now, is if Dr. Hasan decides he wants to resist execution, he can go to federal civilian court for a Habeas Corpus petition … and that can last years,” said Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law.
“It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions,” he added.
Trump resumed the federal death penalty after an informal moratorium during previous administrations. The federal government executed 13 people between 2020 and early 2021, contributing to making Trump the most prolific execution president in over 130 years.
Lawyer questions if notification was done incorrectly
Death sentences are extremely rare in the military justice system, and executions even rarer. Four men, including Hasan, are currently on the military’s death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, and the last execution took place there by hanging in 1961.
John Galligan, a retired colonel and a former military judge, represented Hasan in civil matters. The attorney said Wednesday that he’s limited on what he can talk about, but called the rush to conduct the execution “horrific.”
Galligan, who spoke with Hasan on Wednesday, said he believes the Army regulation to have the facility’s Army commandant notify Hasan, accompanied by a chaplain and a Trial Defense Service attorney or civilian counsel if possible, was not followed. Galligan said that, according to Hasan, there was no legal counsel present.
“For the life of me, I don’t know what they are trying to accomplish in such a rush fashion … and by trying to conduct this execution at Fort Hood, when he has such medical issues,” Galligan said, raising questions about how Hasan, who is paralyzed from the waist down and uses a wheelchair, would be transported to Fort Hood.
Even states have spent time and money on planning
Before Hasan’s execution was set for Fort Hood, there was speculation the Army might reach out to one of the handful of states that have recently reinstated the firing squad for use in executions — particularly South Carolina or Utah, where they’ve renovated facilities and established protocols.
South Carolina has killed three prisoners by firing squad in the past 18 months, the only such executions in the U.S. in the past 16 years.
It’s unclear if the Army will borrow from the state’s protocol, but it sets out for three volunteer shooters to stand 15 feet (4.6 meters) from the condemned prisoner, who is strapped to a chair. A medical professional uses an X-ray to find the prisoner’s heart and place a target over it. A hood is placed over the prisoner’s head after his final words, and a shade is lifted so the shooters can see their target.
All three shooters have live ammunition and fire at the same time without a verbal warning. South Carolina spent about $54,000 to renovate its death chamber for the firing squad.
___
Associated Press reporter Konstantin Toropin contributed to this report.

title: Donald M. Tomlin
text:
Donald M. Tomlin, Don, passed away May 18, 2026, in Damariscotta, Maine.
Born on Dec. 17, 1943, in Atlanta, Georgia, and raised in Buckhead, Don lived a full and meaningful life shaped by family, friends, good humor, and a deep appreciation for the places and people he loved. Don graduated from the Georgia Institute of Technology with a degree in mechanical engineering and began his career with Arthur Andersen & Co. in its Information Technology Division. He became a partner in 1977. After many successful years there, he moved to Miami Beach, Florida in 1994 and joined his friend, Rob Tabb, at Ryder Systems, Inc. Their division was outsourced, and Don continued his career with Florida Power & Light.
Don was married to Ellen Sutter Tomlin, and together they had four children: David, twins Jennifer and Deborah, and Scott. They have 12 grandchildren and 5 great-grandchildren. Following a divorce, Don met Claire Wilson Tomlin, who worked in the Arthur Andersen Tax Division. Claire's daughter, Evi, became like a fifth child to Don.
Don and Claire built a wonderful life together in Miami Beach, where they bought a home on the Venetian Islands and enjoyed their subtropical garden. Don especially enjoyed the view across his pool to the colorful bougainvillea. He was active in the community, serving on the board of the Miami Beach Community Development Corporation and as its chairman for five years. In addition, he played an important role in The Market Company, Inc., Claire's South Florida business, which she started in 1996 and continues today.
In 1994, Don and Claire traveled to Southwest Harbor, Maine, with their good friends, Rob and Anita Tabb, and stayed in a house beside the Mansell Boatyard near the Hinckley Barn. The Wooden Boat Show was taking place in the harbor, and they were immediately smitten with Maine. They returned every year on vacation and, in 2014, bought a cottage in Boothbay Harbor near the Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens, which became one of their favorite attractions. They joined the Boothbay Harbor Yacht Club in 2015 and Don served on the board for two consecutive terms. He became the club's certified ACBL Bridge Director. Don loved bridge and was a marvelous teacher, always happy to share what he knew. In May 2025, Don and Claire moved into their new home on Southport Island. Don knew Claire would love her home and garden just as he loved her.
During the pandemic, Don's friendship with Paul Schacknow deepened. Rarely a day passed without their having a conversation, no matter where either was.
Don was an eternal optimist, inspiring all who knew him with his belief in a righteous and moral world. He also had a marvelous sense of humor and frequently emailed friends jokes, cartoons, and funny aphorisms that brightened their day. He is remembered for his intelligence, warmth, wit, and loyalty, as well as for the love he gave so freely to his family and friends.
Don leaves behind a rich life in relationships, accomplishments, and cherished memories. We all miss him deeply.
At the Celebration of his Life at the Boothbay Harbor Yacht Club on Monday, Aug. 17 at 4 p.m., all of Don's children will attend, giving them a glimpse of his love for Maine.
Hall’s of Boothbay has care of arrangements. To leaveonline condolences, please visit hallfuneralhomes.com.

title: Hickory Dickory Dock
text:
The mouse ran up the clock and then under the stove and who knows where else it might be hiding? Having a mouse in the house is about more than just the “ick” factor, it is a health problem and a structural issue. They really do chew electrical wires and wreak havoc with insulation; they also carry several diseases, and they are usually never alone.
As we prepare for the upcoming indoor months, we should realize that neighborhood rodents, especially here in rural Maine, are doing the same. The best advice is to keep them out before they move in.
Now is the time to do an outdoor inspection of your home and outbuildings to identify and seal up likely entry spots. Keep in mind that mice can fit through a hole the size of a dime and rats only need a quarter-sized hole. Foundation cracks, pipes, vents and around windows are likely entry points, as are garages, especially if you leave the doors up periodically. Look for droppings and gnaw marks to identify and seal up likely entries. Always wear gloves and a mask if you discover tell-tale signs, and do not vacuum or sweep up feces or urine or touch it with your bare hands. (More on handling safety below.) Place some preventative outdoor traps unless you have young children.
Experts say that not only do mice survive better indoors during cold months, they actually reproduce 400% faster than they do in outdoor environments. So this time of year they are looking for a comfy maternity ward. In fact, research shows that indoor fall mice have 6-8 babies per litter compared to 3-4 for outdoor mamas. Warmer indoor temperatures create ideal breeding conditions, which trigger accelerated reproduction. Female mice can become pregnant again within 24 hours of giving birth during fall months. A single indoor female mouse can produce up to 10 litters per year.
Mice carry and spread several serious bacterial, viral or parasitic diseases (see Sidebar). Disease transmission can occur from contact with their urine or feces and then touching your nose, eyes or mouth, or by breathing dust stirred up from sweeping or by disturbing old nesting material or insulation. Illness can also be caused by eating contaminated food, drinking unclean water or from a scratch or bite from a once wild mouse.
These diseases can be contracted while trying to clean up an infestation. Wearing gloves is a must, as are cleaning with bleach and water (9 parts to 1 part bleach) and good ventilation. Particles from dried feces can become airborne and then inhaled. Never use your vacuum or a broom for that reason. For more detailed safety precautions on the cleanup of infected furniture, rugs, clothing, insulation and more, visit the CDC Rodent Control Guide. The website also provides excellent advice on how to seal entry points around your home.

title: Christa Pike is ‘speaking limitedly’ after being declared brain dead before waking up after failed execution, attorney says
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP/Gray News) — Christa Pike was declared brain dead on Monday night and was expected to be taken off life support, but woke up and started talking on Tuesday, according to her attorneys.
“I do not have an explanation for what happened between Monday night and Tuesday morning but I do know she has a long road to recovery,” attorney Randy Spivey said in a press conference on Wednesday.
Spivey said that while he was not there and did not want to speculate, he believes Pike’s first words upon waking up were, “Where am I and who are you?”
“She is angry and confused about everything right now. ... She is very aware of what they did to her up to a point,” he said.
According to Pike’s attorneys, she has a blood clot, cannot swallow and has not eaten. Her arms and hands are swollen and it is unknown at this time if she will regain function in her arms. They also said she has pneumonia.
“The swelling was extraordinary,” Spivey said.
Pike’s feet and right arm are shackled to her hospital bed. Medical staff and her attorneys have asked for some of the restraints to be removed, according to her legal team.
Pike is the only person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution, according to The Death Penalty Information Center.
This is a breaking news update. Previous story below.
Christa Pike regained consciousness roughly six days after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute her and was “speaking limitedly,” one of her attorneys said during a court hearing Wednesday.
Pike, 50, survived even after executioners tried to give her two lethal doses of pentobarbital on Sept. 30. She was sentenced to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer.
The Death Penalty Information Center says Pike is the only person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution.
At a hearing Wednesday in Nashville, Pike’s attorneys asked the court to order the Tennessee Department of Correction to save evidence in the case and provide more information about what went wrong. A judge ordered the state to preserve “anything that was in the actual room.”
“Part of the issue that we are facing is that, up until yesterday, our client was unconscious, unable to communicate with counsel, unable to communicate with medical providers, and without her consent, a new lawsuit cannot be filed, Luke Ihnen, a federal public defender, told the court.
Her legal team said Tuesday that Pike’s prognosis remains unclear and, at a minimum, she faces a lengthy recovery. Her arms were burned and blistered after the attempted lethal injection and she is handcuffed to the hospital bed, they said.
The failed execution has renewed scrutiny of how states carry out the death penalty, in particular the use of lethal injection. Texas was set to carry out Wednesday the first execution in the U.S. since Tennessee attempted to put Pike to death.
Christa Pike’s attorneys want evidence preserved
Pike’s attorneys wanted a court order to require the prison system to preserve information from the attempted execution, including drug lot numbers, needles, execution logs and other information.
Chancery Court Judge I’Ashea Myles indicated that her order to save the evidence would be sweeping, saying the state should maintain recordings, witness accounts, emails along with drugs, syringes, IV lines and other medical items.
The Tennessee Attorney General’s Office said a court order was unnecessary. John W. Ayers, assistant attorney general, said evidence from the death chamber already had been collected and logged.
Republican Gov. Bill Lee has called what happened “deeply disturbing” and ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred.” The governor postponed the state’s only other execution scheduled for this year.
The state’s prison chief resigned in the wake of the failed execution.
Christa Pike’s recovery remains uncertain
Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on the possibility that a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue rather than entering her bloodstream. Pike’s attorneys wrote in their court filing that “apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown.”
The attempted execution got underway around 7:30 p.m. on Sept. 30 when Pike was given a chance to make a final statement. About five minutes later, Pike raised her head and said her arm was hurting. At some point she appeared to lose consciousness, but she could be heard audibly breathing until media were escorted from the witness room at 8:53 p.m. An ambulance arrived at the prison at 9:14 p.m. to take Pike to a hospital.
Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike’s legal team, said it could be weeks or months before anyone knows exactly what her recovery might look like, and whether her competency could be restored so the state can try again to execute her.
___
Associated Press writers Ed White in Detroit and John Seewer, in Toledo, Ohio, contributed.

title: ICE watchers stand guard all day, every day outside Scarborough facility
text:
SCARBOROUGH, Maine — On Sept. 28, at 8:19 a.m., two cars with black windows leave the Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility at 40 Manson Libby Road.
Two people standing outside quickly jot down the license plate numbers and note the time.
“They’re going hunting,” one of them says.
At 8:21 a.m., five more cars suddenly appear, heading in the same direction.
The watchers scramble. On clipboards and yellow legal pads, they document everything ICE agents do, taking photos of the cars, shouting out license plate numbers, reaching for their pens. They mutter curses to themselves.
Then the alerts go out.
They have a meticulous information-gathering and distribution network, as they call it, in the southern Maine immigrant community. It’s a careful system that requires constant monitoring of ICE’s only facility in the state, a small, unassuming building on a quiet road near Route 1.
Residents across southern Maine have formed groups like this to monitor ICE activity — following federal vehicles, standing guard at school bus stops, filming agents, watching out for their immigrant neighbors — since the January enforcement surge in Maine.
But after an ICE agent killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford on July 13, many have intensified their efforts. And about five core watchers have made monitoring the ICE facility their full-time job.
They’re not protesting, they said, but they’re not just watching. They’re giving immigrants rides, buying groceries, watching their kids, driving people’s cars home after they’ve been detained, and connecting them with legal resources.
Two of those watchers agreed to speak with the Portland Press Herald about why they’re doing this work, but asked not to be fully identified out of fear for their safety. Others who followed and documented ICE activity in January reported being followed home by agents, intimidated and threatened with arrest.
The watch
For almost three months, K and Allisandra have spent about 10 to 14 hours a day watching the facility. On Sept. 28, Allisandra said she felt especially tired. She had been at the facility from 5 a.m. to around 7 p.m. for several days.
They are scrupulous, almost obsessive with their notetaking. They have to be, they said, lives are on the line.
They have a printed sheet with 39 license plates they’ve seen at the facility. They know if the cars are there, hidden behind a fence covered in black fabric, or if they’re out “hunting.”
On separate sheets, they track the immigrants who come in, and those who don’t come back out.
Age. Sex. Race. Height. Hair color. Clothing. Cars. Are they carrying an umbrella? A bag?
The watchers don’t know most of their names, whether they have a family or children waiting for them to come home, friends, a lawyer.
“If there’s nothing else that we can give people, we know what happened to them,” Allisandra said.
The numbers
In August, the group said they observed about 2 ½ detainments per day. That decreased to about 1.8 per day in September. Between both months, they observed 101 detainments.
Of those, they believe eight were arrested during routine check-ins.
“This is an every-day emergency,” K said, sitting in a lawn chair across from the facility last month. “ICE is detaining people every single day. People don’t realize it.”
ICE did not respond to requests for comment or questions about the number of people detained at the facility or about the watchers.
The numbers have been decreasing, the watchers said, not because there are fewer detainments, but because they believe ICE agents have increased efforts to conceal their operations.
Before a black mesh fence was installed around the facility a few weeks ago, the watchers could see detainees with shackles locked around their feet being brought inside the facility from SUVs with tinted windows.
Sometimes, they have seen cars come and go by driving over a small ditch. There often aren’t enough watchers to have someone stand guard by that area, so they don’t know how often cars leave that way or when.
A morning on the watch
There are about 10-12 check-ins at the facility every day, watchers said, usually between 8 and 11 a.m. On the morning of Sept. 28, a reporter witnessed 12 people walk in.
It was a rainy, gray day, the impacts of a fall nor’easter still lingering. But the watchers are always there, regardless of the weather.
Normally, they set up lawn chairs across the street. On rainy days, they work out of K’s car. Allisandra rolled down the window of the back seat to get a better look, regularly wiping the car door soaked from the rain pouring in.
Throughout the morning, immigrants waited outside in the rain, sometimes for half an hour. Watchers said they have seen sick and pregnant immigrants wait for hours.
Sometimes, people are inside for just a few minutes. When immigrants are inside for half an hour or more, the watchers start to worry.
That morning, an immigrant they knew went in for a check-in.
“Have you seen him come out yet?” Allisandra asked after half an hour, panicking. They called the man’s wife, promising to let her know as soon as he returned.
After 50 minutes, when he finally came back out, they waved to him frantically, sighing with relief.
Still, they worry that each check-in could mean another detainment.
“The fear just doesn’t end,” Allisandra said. “ICE says, ‘come back in a week, come back in a day.’”
When others they didn’t recognize left the building, Allisandra hurriedly ran out in the rain to hand them a printed list of resources.
K said she knows immigrant families with newborns who have never seen the outside of their house since the ride back from the hospital.
“One person detained means one family irreparably damaged,” K said.
“Why is this on us? We’re just a couple of weirdos sacrificing everything to be out here,” she added.
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Salomé Cloteaux can be reached at scloteaux@metln.org.

title: This election is about reclaiming the federal government
text:
The ongoing Susan Collins vs. Troy Jackson debate is a great example of not seeing the forest but for the trees. The real issue for the upcoming midterm election is not which senator should represent Maine, but how do we, the citizens, wrest control back from an administration exemplified by cruelty, incompetence, corruption, self-aggrandizement and self-enrichment.
As much as I respect Sen. Susan Collins (I have voted for her in past elections), electing a Democrat to the Senate would move us closer to flipping the balance of power in the Senate. Reducing the Senate Republican majority to minority status is a prerequisite for reclaiming our government. A government of decency, fairness, competence and sanity.
As we head to the polls, let us step out of the trees so we can see the forest.
Larry O’Rourke
Sumner

title: MaineDOT Mobility Study Findings
text:
Residents from Gorham and surrounding areas converged inside Shaw Gym at the Gorham Municipal Center on the evening of Sept. 22 for an update on initial findings from the Maine Department of Transportation’s Portland West Balanced Mobility Improvements Study. The well-attended open house–style event included detailed design drawings of four possible scenarios to address congestion and improve safety and mobility in the communities west of Portland.
As they circulated through the gym reviewing each scenario, attendees had options to weigh in on the pros and cons of each scenario, which ranged from localized, targeted roadway upgrades to the building of a four-lane highway connector, a solution previously advocated by the Maine Turnpike Authority. MaineDOT staff members were on hand at each station to provide detailed explanations of the scenarios and answer questions about the study process and next steps.
MaineDOT also presented its findings via a virtual public meeting on Sept. 24.
Per information on the department’s website, MaineDOT staff will use feedback from these meetings and from responses to public surveys to revise the alternatives. Then, each alternative will be evaluated “using traffic modeling and GIS to quantify the costs and benefits across all evaluation criteria for the mobility, safety, connectivity, community, environment, and feasibility categories.”
For those who couldn’t attend either the in-person or virtual presentation, you can still keep up with developments as study efforts proceed. Detailed information about all four proposed mobility improvement scenarios is available at https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/7ae12d952d9a48e08c93713d1ab4f596

title: Trump's $90 Medicare rebate rolls out, but millions are left out. Critics say it's a political stunt
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump says his administration will make one-time payments of $90 per person to help more than 20 million Medicare enrollees pay for their Part B premiums. It will cost about $2 billion.
Less than one-third of all Medicare recipients are eligible for the payments, which are expected to be sent out this week. Not eligible are roughly 35 million Medicare Advantage enrollees, millions of other people with disabilities and low-income Medicare recipients.
The election-year promise that the Republican president made over the weekend comes as the Nov. 3 midterms are fast approaching, with the cost of living and healthcare expenses among the top issues for voters.
Some questions and answers about the payouts:
Who will benefit?
Some 20.8 million people in the original Medicare Part B who are living in the United States, not receiving premium assistance from Medicaid or not paying an income-related monthly adjusted amount.
Medicare Advantage enrollees, who make up more than half of the eligible 64.2 million Medicare beneficiaries, will not receive a payment, according to KFF, a healthcare research nonprofit. Nor will 12 million low-income older adults and people with disabilities who get premium assistance.
The Part B program covers expenses such as doctor’s visits, ambulance services and lab tests. Total monthly costs generally start at about $200 and vary with income.
When will the payments go out and how will they be disbursed?
According to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services website, eligible beneficiaries will receive one $90 rebate this month, with most getting a direct deposit on or around Friday. Others will receive a paper check from the Treasury Department later in October.
Juliette Cubanski, director of KFF’s program on Medicare policy, said the payment will be automatic.
“As far as a benefit goes, people don’t have to call or sign up — it’s just money they receive directly, but not everybody on Medicare will receive this money.”
A White House fact sheet says people can call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) to check on their eligibility for the premium rebate. To check on payment status, people should call the Social Security Administration at 1-800-772-1213.
What is the source of the money?
Payments will come out of the Medicare Improvement Fund created by Congress in 2008 and intended to make improvements to the Medicare fee-for-service program.
The fund was created to improve program management and conduct oversight of contracts and contractors, according to the Congressional Budget Office, but its purpose has expanded after various legislative changes.
This is not the first time the fund has been used.
Democratic President Barack Obama’s administration, along with Congress, redirected $20 billion to expand healthcare coverage through the Affordable Care Act.
But under Trump, it is the first time that the fund has been used to directly pay recipients.
What are critics of the plan saying?
Critics of Trump’s promise characterize the $90 payments as a preelection stunt designed to sway voters rather than address structural problems in healthcare costs and administration.
The top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, said in a statement that “this is another desperate attempt by a failed president to escape Americans’ revulsion with his failed agenda, amounting to one tank of Trump-inflated gas.”
Trump recently promised $500 rebate checks to an estimated 1 million Obamacare enrollees across 30 states whom the White House alleged were overcharged by the Biden administration for some fees.
Cubanski said the Medicare rebate payments were being doled out when Americans were feeling the bite of higher food, energy and gas prices. Surging healthcare costs are only compounding those pressure, she said.
“This might be helpful for people but it might not go very far.”

title: Coco Gauff loses after citing an 'insane' wave of racist abuse following previous match in Beijing
text:
Coco Gauff loses after citing an 'insane' wave of racist abuse following previous match in Beijing
Coco Gauff lost to a player she had beaten in all five of their previous matchups after receiving what she described as an “insane” amount of racist comments on social media following a controversial point in the preceding round.
Related video above: Game changer: Meet the woman who came before Serena Williams, Coco Gauff
The 19th-ranked Elise Mertens beat the fourth-ranked Gauff 6-3, 6-3 to reach the China Open quarterfinals on Wednesday.
In Monday’s match against home player Sun Xinran, Gauff stopped a rally after electronic advertising boards lining the court flickered during a point late in the first set.
Sun appeared about to win the point when Gauff stopped playing. The chair umpire then ordered the point to be replayed.
“Hey everyone, you can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist,” Gauff, who is Black, said in a reply on X. “The amount of racist comments/dms I’ve received in the last few hours is insane. Lastly, I‘m not a cheater or a thief.”
Against Mertens, Gauff dropped her serve four times.
Mertens reached her first quarterfinal at a WTA 1000 event — the level just below the Grand Slams — in five years.
“She’s an incredible player, of course. I knew it was going to be a very tough match,” Mertens said. “But I had motivation. My coach/boyfriend, it’s his birthday tomorrow. So this win is dedicated to him and all the work we do.”
Mertens improved to 3-3 against top-10 opponents this year. She also beat defending champion Jasmine Paolini at the Italian Open and current No. 1 Elena Rybakina in the third round of Wimbledon, where she reached the quarterfinal.
Earlier, Iga Swiatek broke Iva Jovic's serve twice in the last four games to beat the 18-year-old American 6-1, 6-3.
Swiatek, a six-time Grand Slam champion who has struggled at times this year, will next play Mertens.

title: Maine's annual Construction Career Day event drew 1,000 students
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
More than 50 vendors from construction companies, trade organizations and state agencies and close to 1,000 high school students attended the recent annual Maine Construction Career Day.
The event, in its fifth year, was held Oct. 1 at MidCoast Maine Excavation in West Bath.
It was a healthy sign for the industry and the state, which, like much of the country, has a shortage of trades professionals.
Hosted by the National Association of Women in Construction, Maine Chapter 276, and the Associated General Contractors of Maine, the immersive event introduced students to careers in an array of construction-related fields.
“Whether they’re interested in operating heavy equipment, building electrical systems, welding, surveying, engineering or project management, we want students to experience these careers firsthand,” said Brittany Widbiller, NAWIC Maine vice president, co-chair of the event, and human resource specialist at Randolph-based Coutts Brothers electrical contractors.
Working with industry professionals, students explored welding, electrical, plumbing, surveying and GPS technology, and operated mini excavators, skid steers, boom lifts and a hydraulic crane.
Man lifts, concrete forms, HVAC equipment and commercial trucks were also on hand and there were demonstrations in fall-safety and powerline cutover procedures.
Students also learned about apprenticeships, higher education and other construction industry pathways.
“We want students to have these hands-on experiences so they can decide if they want to take the next steps into the industry through a longer-term program,” said Kelly Flagg, executive director of Augusta-based AGC Maine, which founded the Maine Construction Academy.
AGC Maine highlighted pre-apprenticeship and apprenticeship options, including the 20-day Maine Construction Academy immersion program, which gives students more training and access to extensive hands-on activities.
The day’s events also supported NAWIC Maine’s scholarship program for students entering construction-related fields.
The Associated General Contractors of Maine is the state’s leading construction industry trade association, representing over 200 members including general contractors, subcontractors and suppliers. AGC Maine advocates for the industry, promotes safety and excellence and provides essential resources for professional growth.
The National Association of Women in Construction champions inclusivity and career growth for women in the construction industry through education, advocacy, networking and professional development. The organization has over 6,000 members nationwide across more than 120 chapters.
