title: How to watch Senate debate between Collins and Jackson
text:
How to watch the Maine's Total Coverage Senate debate between Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson
Maine's Total Coverage is hosting a debate at 8 p.m. Thursday between incumbent U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson.
There are a number of ways you can watch the debate, which will air on WMTW Channel 8. The debate will also be livestreamed on WMTW.com, the WMTW app (iOS and Android) and Very Local, as well as the WMTW-TV YouTube channel and the WMTW-TV Facebook page. After the hourlong debate ends, it will be available to watch in its entirety on all platforms.
Collins, a Republican, is seeking to win her sixth term in the U.S. Senate, something no senator from Maine has done before. She was uncontested in the June 9 primary, as she was the only candidate to qualify for the GOP primary ballot.
Jackson, a Democrat, has only been in the Senate race for just over two months. He finished third in the gubernatorial primary, but was chosen as the Democratic Senate nominee on July 25 at a special nominating convention. The Maine Democratic Party had to find a replacement candidate for the Senate primary winner, Graham Platner, who dropped out of the race on July 8 following allegations of sexual assault.
The Maine's Total Coverage debate will be the second debate of the week for Collins and Jackson, who had their first debate Tuesday night.
During Tuesday's debate, Collins distanced herself from President Donald Trump by arguing that she has maintained political independence by voting against his agenda.
Jackson, meanwhile, focused largely on attempting to connect Collins to Trump. In his opening statement, Jackson pointed out that Collins cast a critical vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Trump nominee who eventually helped overturn the constitutional right to abortion.
Collins countered that she has voted against Trump more than she did Democrat Joe Biden when he was president, and that she has pushed back against Trump on tariffs, immigration enforcement and the war with Iran.
Information from The Associated Press was used in this report.

title: Man accused of hiding 10 live birds in his ‘bulge’ at the airport
text:
MIAMI (CNN) — A man is accused of trying to smuggle live birds through Miami International Airport in his underwear.
Federal authorities said Alberto Hernandez Castillo, who is a legal permanent resident of the U.S., arrived from Cuba Sunday.
Customs officers sent him to a secondary inspection after noticing what they called an “unexplained bulge” near his waist.
A pat-down allegedly uncovered six plastic containers hidden in pockets sewn into his underwear.
Authorities said the containers held 10 live birds.
Hernandez Castillo allegedly said the birds were for his “personal use.”
He is charged with smuggling goods and was released on a $25,000 bond.

title: Fire leaves Aroostook home unlivable
text:
A Tuesday fire left a Van Buren home uninhabitable due to smoke and water damage.
The Van Buren Fire Department received a call at around 3:40 p.m. that a two-story Main Street home was ablaze, Chief Brian Caron said.
Firefighters arrived to see black smoke rolling from the eaves and door frames, with all the windows blackened with haze.
Caron requested mutual aid from nearby Grand Isle and from St. Leonard, across the border in New Brunswick, he said.
Crews broke a window to vent the fire and prevent a backdraft as they fought the fire. They used thermal cameras to check for further flames elsewhere in the house.
The water district helped firefighters set up a water shuttle, as the home was out of hydrant range, Caron said.
Safety personnel closed Main Street for about an hour, and the site was cleared by 9 p.m.
No injuries were reported, and no one was home at the time, Caron said.
He did not immediately respond to an inquiry about who owns the property.
The state fire marshal’s office is investigating.

title: Seth Glier: Songwriting as a tool for positive change
text:
Singer-songwriter Seth Glier will be playing the Opera House at Boothbay Harbor on Wednesday, July 22 at 7:30 p.m. He will be accompanied by fiddle player, and long-time friend, Kelly Halloran.
Glier, a Grammy-nominated artist from Western Massachusetts, says, “I think music is just, it's one of the great magic tricks of life when it comes to building whatever you need, whether it's a bridge or whether it's community, whether it's support or just a container for pain for all kinds of things.”
Recently, he has turned his musical gaze to the natural world, channeling nature’s longing for communion with humanity into song. His new album "Everything" is a collection of eight songs inviting listeners to imagine a future in which humans and the planet are re-aligned into mutual restoration. Each song presents a practical climate solution with concrete optimism.
The album’s title track was inspired by an experience Glier had while foraging. “When I picked up the chanterelle mushroom and brought it towards my nose," he says, “I first smelled sweet apricot and then my spine straightened suddenly. The feeling was like déjà vu. It was a ‘first time,’ yet somewhere inside of me I had done this once before. I was reconnecting to a knowledge I had already known.”
Glier is thrilled to be returning to Maine: “I get to come to beautiful places like Boothbay Harbor and play the Opera House. I've been playing there since I was 19 or 20 years old.” His first show here was with Livingston Taylor. “Livingston was a mentor of mine at Berklee College of Music. When I dropped out, he kind of took me out on the road, and the mentorship kind of continued. I learned a lot about stagecraft from him, everything from, like, how do you treat people when you walk into the venue to what is your sort of collegialness?” Concert veterans of his shows will attest to the fact that he has translated those lessons into his own style of welcoming and intimate shows.
Glier has shared the bill with a diverse list of artists ranging from the likes of Ronnie Spector, James Taylor, Ani DiFranco, to Glen Campbell. As a producer, music director, or studio musician he has collaborated with Sophie B. Hawkins, Tom Rush, Antje Duvekot, Richard Shindell, Doctora Qingona, Dar Williams, Nick Carter, and Cyndi Lauper. Seth Glier is a five-time Independent Music Award winner and received a Grammy nomination for his album "The Next Right Thing."
Most recently, Kelly Halloran has been touring with Foreigner. Last fall she finished a North American tour with Noah Cyrus, playing violin, acoustic guitar, and singing background vocals. She also performed with the Goo Goo Dolls at Stagecoach 2025 along with cellist Dave Eggar, and Nikki Lane.

title: Parents Navigate Communication Gap As Bangor School Clears Threat On Garland Street
text:
It was a nerve-wracking morning for parents who have kids that attend the William S. Cohen School in Bangor.
Word began to circulated via social media around 11:30 AM that a local school was being evacuated due to a threat. This was confirmed just before noon by the Bangor School District, when they alerted parents that students from the school had been moved from the school and that authorities were on- hand conducting an investigation.
Parents were notified that all the children had been taken from the Cohen School on Garland Street to the safety of a nearby facility, while authorities swept the school space for any dangers.
Raymond Phinney, spokesperson for the Bangor School Department says authorities ultimately deemed the threat to be a hoax, and when the school was deemed safe, were the students brought back. Their parents also had the option to pick them up directly.
"After completing their evaluation, first responders determined there was no credible threat and confirmed that the building was safe for students and staff to return...
The well-being of students remains the highest priority. School counselors, teachers, and administrators will be available to provide support to any student who would like to discuss today's events. The Bangor School Department appreciates the continued support and understanding of families as we work together to maintain a safe and supportive learning environment for all students."
Many parents took to social media to voice their concerns and frustrations with Maine's new "Bell-to-Bell Personal Electronic Device Policy", or as many call it school cell phone ban, stating that they couldn't reach their children and did not have details as to what was happening.
Read More: Bangor Schools Explain New Cell Phone Rules By Grade Level
Others responded by saying they were relieved the kids didn't have their phones, as the possibility of panic that would ensue from the misinformation disseminated by unverified or undearage sources was of real concern.
Mike Missbrenner, Principal of the William S. Cohen School, expressed his appreciation for the students and the staff for doing an exceptional job under intense circumstances Wednesday.
Read More: How A Former Bangor Tire Shop Is Becoming A Music Studio
"We are incredibly proud of our students for the way they responded during a challenging situation. Their cooperation, patience, and resilience were
outstanding. I also want to thank our faculty and staff for their professionalism in following emergency procedures and supporting our students throughout the day."
Throughout the day, school officials updated parents via communication avenues like email, text and the Bangor app, when they had confirmed information to share, or instructions to give.

title: Appeals court says Atlanta family cannot take the government to trial for a mistaken FBI raid
text:
ATLANTA (AP) — An Atlanta family cannot take the federal government to trial for a mistaken FBI raid on their home in 2017, but they can seek to hold the agent who led the SWAT team liable, a federal appeals court ruled Wednesday.
FBI agents broke down the front door of Trina Martin’s Atlanta home before dawn on Oct. 18, 2017, stormed into her bedroom and pointed guns at her and her then-boyfriend as her 7-year-old son screamed for his mom from another room.
The agents quickly realized they had the wrong house and left, but Martin and her boyfriend at the time, Toi Cliatt, said they were left traumatized, and they sued the government and the agent. The U.S. Supreme Court revived their lawsuit last year.
A three-judge panel of the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said Wednesday the government was shielded from liability under an exception to a federal law that allows lawsuits over wrong-house raids. But the panel reversed a decision that gave the agent immunity.
“Viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the plaintiffs, a reasonable jury could fairly conclude” that the agent had “failed to engage in reasonable efforts to avoid error, and therefore, violated the plaintiffs’ constitutional rights,” the judges said.
Jenna Sellitto, a spokeswoman for the FBI’s Atlanta office, said the agency does not comment on personnel matters.
The FBI team quickly apologized after the raid and left for the right place, with the team leader later saying that his personal GPS device had led him to the wrong address. The FBI was looking for a suspected gang member a few houses away.
Martin and Cliatt’s lawsuit accused the agents of assault and battery, false arrest and other violations.
Their attorney, Patrick Jaicomo, said in a phone interview his clients felt good about Wednesday’s ruling.
The decision on immunity for the agent was a clear win, but there was also reason to be hopeful about the ruling in favor of the government, he said.
That decision was based on 11th Circuit precedent, and the judges wrote separately to encourage the full appeals court to revisit those earlier decisions. Jaicomo, senior attorney with the nonprofit Institute for Justice in Arlington, Virginia, said he plans to seek that review, opening up the possibility that his clients could eventually be allowed to take the government to trial as well.

title: Town Hill VIS organizes cemetery cleanup
text:
TOWN HILL — Following sweeping changes to its leadership earlier this fall, the current members of the Town Hill Village Improvement Society got to work charting what they say will be a new path focused on community and collaboration. That work began with a volunteer cleanup of the Mountain View Cemetery on Sunday, Oct. 4, a site that played a prominent role in the dissolution of the previous iteration of the VIS board.
“I’m so grateful that the previous board made the decision to take the land off the market and not develop it,” said Shaiah Emigh-Doyle, who was a key voice in opposition to a plan to sell land surrounding the historic property and who now serves as Cemetery Steward. “I’m very grateful to each one of them.”

title: Maine needs a housing strategy. Hannah Pingree has one.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
When I turned 30, suddenly all of my friends were talking about buying houses. Or, more specifically, how hard it is to buy a house. Looking at houses on Zillow in one’s spare time is no longer a fun game; it’s just depressing. So many house prices have skyrocketed since 2020. 
Due to Maine’s housing prices, I see myself sticking to renting for a good long while. That’s not to say, of course, that renting is necessarily easier. Rents in Portland rival those in Boston. And outside of Portland, we don’t find much relief either. But at least when my dishwasher breaks, I’ll have someone to call. Hard to save for that down payment, though.
Thankfully, we have someone running for governor who knows Maine is facing a very serious housing crisis. Hannah Pingree’s housing plan will invest in housing, stop out-of-state corporations from driving up rents and cut the red tape that slows development. Hannah’s smart, clear and comprehensive housing plan gives me hope for Maine’s future.
Eloise Melcher
Portland

title: Quieter Wednesday Ahead, Then Showers Return Thursday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Our Wednesday will be a much quieter day as high pressure builds in... allowing the pressure gradient to relax... in turn... resulting in a much lighter wind. A warm front approaching the state will bring us more clouds and a slight chance for a few isolated showers... mainly across the north. Expect a partly to mostly cloudy sky and more seasonable temperatures with highs in the mid-50s to low 60s. Scattered showers will be possible tonight as the warm front moves through. It won’t be as cold tonight thanks to clouds and some slightly warmer air in place. Temperatures tonight will drop to the mid-40s to low 50s for overnight lows.
A cold front will cross the state during the day Thursday bringing us a chance for scattered showers... most numerous during the morning then becoming less numerous/widely scattered during the afternoon. A few thunderstorms can’t be ruled out as well. Not expecting anything in terms of severe weather but any thunderstorms that develop could produce some heavier rainfall and even some small hail. Otherwise expect mostly cloudy skies during the morning with breaks of sunshine developing during the afternoon. Temperatures will be warmer with highs in the 60s to near 70° Thursday afternoon. Cooler air will move in behind the front for the end of the week. We’ll see a nice day Friday under partly to mostly sunny skies. High temperatures on Friday will be in the 50s to near 60°. High pressure will build in to bring us a nice weekend. Saturday will feature sunshine and highs in the 50s. Sunday is looking good too with warmer temperatures. Highs on Sunday will be in the 60s. Our next best chance of showers will arrive Sunday night into Monday.
Rest of Today: Partly to mostly cloudy. An isolated shower possible across the north. Highs in the 50s to low 60s. South/southwest wind 5-15 MPH.
Tonight: Mostly cloudy with scattered showers possible. Lows in the mid-40s to low 50s. South/southwest wind 5-15 MPH.

Friday: Partly to mostly sunny and cooler. Highs in the 50s to around 60°.

title: Russia keeps a tight lid on suspected case of pneumonic plague as global concerns mount
text:
(AP) - Russian authorities are keeping a tight lid on information about last week’s suspicious death of a lab worker in Siberia that has been surrounded by secrecy and claims that it could have been caused by pneumonic plague.
While the case has raised global concerns, Russian state TV and other national state-controlled media have steered clear of the subject. Some state-sponsored news outlets withdrew earlier reports about the case.
Russia’s public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said Sunday the lab worker was diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” meaning its origin was not known.
In its official, tersely worded statements, it does not link the case to pneumonic plague, saying only that “extensive” testing found no evidence her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
A state TV station in Irkutsk reported she died Oct. 2 in a hospital in Shelekhov, a town just outside Irkutsk.
Officials have quarantined a hospital and are monitoring the contacts of the worker, who died of what unconfirmed media reports said could have been pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person.
Moscow informed the World Health Organization that no case of plague has been registered in the Irkutsk region in southeastern Siberia.
President Donald Trump said Tuesday he would speak about the issue “very soon” with Russian President Vladimir Putin and report about it “probably tomorrow.” Wednesday is the Kremlin leader’s 74th birthday.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday that a Putin-Trump call hasn’t been set yet but could be organized quickly.
Trump said the U.S. stands ready to help Russia. Asked what the U.S. intelligence community was saying about the case, Trump said the U.S. is in “very deep discussions” on the topic.
Russia is prodded for more information
In response to the WHO’s request to clarify the situation in view of media reports alleging pneumonic plague as the cause of death, Russia has declared that no case of plague had recently been registered in the Irkutsk region, the U.N. organization said.
Russian health authorities reported a full range of preventive measures had been carried out — including tracing the dead woman’s contacts, medical monitoring and lab tests, the WHO said Wednesday. The Russian note relayed to The Associated Press by the WHO said the test showed “no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens in any of the contacts.”
The Geneva-based organization said it has requested further information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures, and media reports that a second employee had pneumonia of undetermined cause.
The organization said it has remained in contact with Russian health authorities and offered technical support.
The Kremlin and other officials stay tight-lipped
Peskov referred all questions to Rospotrebnadzor, which does not mention suspected plague in its reports.
In its latest statement Tuesday, the agency said “the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region, the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov is calm.” Authorities were completing a “complex of prophylactic measures and medical observation over contacts,” it said, adding that so far they have found two cases of COVID-19 and two cases of rhinovirus.
“No other infectious pathogens have been found among contacts,” it said.
Judy Twigg, professor of political science at Virginia Commonwealth University, noted that while the measures taken by Russian health authorities “have been swift and serious,” officials sought to play down the situation and “any statements that strayed from that party line ... were edited or deleted within hours.”
“What we are watching is less a failure to respond than a failure of candor,” Twigg said in written comments.
Vasily Vlassov, professor at the department of healthcare administration and economics at Russia’s Higher School of Economics, said the measures taken appeared “sensible,” focusing on treating the sick, isolating them and their contacts, looking for new cases and carrying out final disinfection.
But he said it wasn’t clear whether more transparency was possible if those dealing with the situation didn’t have enough certainty, and “maybe, they still don’t.” Deceiving the public in these cases “always turns out to be harmful,” he added, and distrust of Russia’s official narrative is “natural” and “almost inevitable.”
In the Soviet era, crises with dangerous outbreaks of infection had “a thick veil of secrecy — people were told nothing.”
The “massive” restriction and isolation measures were “almost always completely successful,” he said.
The lab worker who died was described as highly diligent
The news outlet Lyudi Baikala — or “People of Baikal” — identified the dead lab worker as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova and said she first was hospitalized with cold symptoms Sept. 29 and died three days later.
It quoted her colleagues as saying she was a highly qualified and diligent researcher. They also emphasized that security rules at the facility, established in the 1920s to monitor and study the plague that is endemic to southeastern Siberia, are extremely strict.
The report quoted Shipilova’s neighbors as saying a team of disinfection experts did several cleanups of her apartment, leaving a strong antiseptic smell.
Shipilova’s mother, who worked as a doctor in the past, described her daughter as hard-working and dedicated to her job, according to independent Russian news outlet Glubina, adding that she had not gotten official documents describing the cause of death.
Irkutsk Gov. Igor Kobzev said she died of a “particularly dangerous infection” and everyone who came into contact with her has remained under medical supervision.
The hospital where she died was under quarantine, no longer admitting or discharging patients, although its outpatient clinic has continued operating, according to Mayor Maxim Modin.
Twigg noted that Russia has criminalized “false information” about threats to public safety in 2020 amid the COVID-19 pandemic, “so silence is the one safe move for everyone below the top.”
“Personalist regimes without electoral accountability tend to treat bad news as a loyalty problem rather than focusing on the actual problem to be addressed,” she said.
She warned that “a government that is not believed when it says ‘there is no outbreak’ will not be believed when it must actually say ‘there is one; do the following.’ We saw this with COVID.”
Pneumonic plague and the more well-known bubonic plague — also called the “Black Death” — are caused by the same bacteria, said Simon Clarke of the University of Reading in the U.K.
Pneumonic plague results from breathing in the bacteria, causing an infection in the lungs. Bubonic plague is spread by flea bites from rodents carrying the bacteria called Yersinia pestis. It had not been eliminated, but it’s not spread very easily and it is treatable with antibiotics.
“People think the plague is gone. It was something that occurred 500 years ago, and it’s not. It’s here amongst us,” Clarke said. “Unless you get rid of those wild animals, which of course is not possible, then you’re not going to get rid of the bacteria. It’s just something that is with us.”
The incubation period for pneumonic plague — the disease’s most virulent form — can be as short as 24 hours, the WHO said. The lung-based illness is a less common but severe form of plague that can spread between people via respiratory particles. If untreated, the illness can be fatal, but recovery rates are high if detected and treated in time, it said.
__
Dasha Litvinova in Tallinn, Estonia, and Jamey Keaten in Geneva contributed.

title: Maine Municipal Association marks 90 years with annual convention
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - The Maine Municipal Association is celebrating 90 years of service to Maine cities and towns with its annual convention.
The Augusta Civic Center was packed with Maine town and city officials for two days of learning and networking.
“Every year it’s important because it’s a great opportunity to bring together people for education but also with our exhibit hall for folks to engage with a number of service providers that might be of use in their municipalities,” said Peter Osborne, director of educational services for the Maine Municipal Association.
Osborne said over the last 90 years, the association has adapted what is being taught to match industry standards.
“In the training world that we do, there’s always new things coming up. They’re dealing with new legislation, they’re dealing with new pieces of technology. So, we’re talking a lot now about generative AI, of course, and how do you put that to use in municipal government. But, the needs change all the time, and we try to be really responsive to those as we can,” Osborne said.
The convention included breakout rooms for specific educational topics.
“Those kind of classroom experiences are really important. It’s really the opportunity to hear from the experts about the training and education that is really one of the most valuable things that somebody can get out of coming to the MMA conference,” said Chris Camire, chair of the Lisbon Town Council and incoming MMA executive board member.
Outside the classroom sessions, municipalities had the chance to talk through challenges together.
“That’s where the convention comes into play because it’s a real opportunity for members to network with each other. It’s a very small kind of small tight-knit community of municipalities. So, they’re always calling each other for advice or trying to look at what another town might be doing and try to adapt that to their municipalities need,” Osborne said.
Camire said he benefited from that networking in the first few hours of the convention.
“One example that I just had a conversation maybe half an hour ago was a conversation around creating tax relief programs for senior citizens. So, I was talking with the town manager in the town of Poland and he said, hey, we implemented this a while ago. We’re starting the first year of that in Lisbon. So, having a conversation about that and what are the things that you learned? What are the gotchas? What are some lessons learned that we can implement moving forward? So, it’s a stable program that can provide meaningful tax relief to the seniors in our community,” Camire said.

title: Harpist brings calm to hospital patients
text:
MYRTLE BEACH, S.C. (Aging Untold) — A harpist is offering quiet comfort to patients and families at McLeod Seacoast Hospital, playing every Thursday, the hospital’s busiest day for same-day surgery.
Peg Mann is part of the hospital’s volunteer and student services program. She has played the harp there for more than a year.
A new sound for the waiting room
Volunteer manager Peggy Skudera, who hired Mann as the harpist, said she was initially unsure about the idea.
“I wasn’t sure a harp was the best place to be in a hospital because my thought was, next stop is heaven,” Skudera said.
Skudera said watching Mann play shows her connection to the instrument.
“When you see her play it, you can see she is so in tune and so married to that harp,” Skudera said. “It’s absolutely amazing that she doesn’t know what’s going on around her. She doesn’t know all the people are listening. All the people that are looking at her.”
Playing from the background
Mann said she prefers not to be the center of attention while she plays.
“And I like it because you’re just the background,” Mann said. “You’re not the center of attention. That’s not my cup of tea.”
Mann plays relaxing and religious music on the harp, plucking each string. Her favorite song is “Angel’s Hymn.”
“I like to play relaxing music here, some religious music,” Mann said.
Mann said she also plays piano and organ. She added the harp to her repertoire in 2005 and continues harp lessons three times a month. She has also played at weddings and performed in church.
“This is what I like to do,” Mann said.
A full hospital shift
Mann starts her shift at 5:30 a.m., escorting patients and pushing the comfort cart before she plays the harp. She also takes breaks to visit with waiting families.
“Either they come up and visit, or I take the time to go and visit with them too,” Mann said. “I get lots of hugs and kisses.”
Skudera said Mann has become part of the McLeod family.
“We could not be happier to have her here,” Skudera said.
Mann said she receives something in return for her time at the hospital.
“I feel like I have new friends every day when I go home,” Mann said.

title: Collins campaign pushes back on ProPublica report on claims of pay-to-play scheme
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (WMTW) - The campaign for Sen. Susan Collins is making a renewed effort to push back against recent reporting and PAC ads that claim she accepted a big campaign donation in 2019 as part of a pay-to-play scheme.
In a report published on Sept. 22, ProPublica said that Collins, R-Maine, steered millions of dollars to defense contractor Martin Kao, the former CEO of Navatek, in return for donations to her 2020 reelection campaign. More specifically, ProPublica reported that the Collins campaign told Kao that he needed to make a campaign donation before meeting Collins, and that Kao was awarded millions in federal contracts after donating to the senator’s campaign.
The Collins campaign denied the corruption allegations on the day the ProPublica report was published, and on Tuesday, the campaign again vehemently denied ProPublica’s allegations, calling Kao a convicted felon and a liar.
On Tuesday, the Collins campaign presented what it said was proof that the ProPublica report is not true and that the senator did not accept money for favors. The Collins campaign presented a picture of Collins in a meeting with Kao, which was taken by a U.S. Senate photographer and had a timestamp of Feb. 15, 2018. The senator’s campaign said that meeting — which was held to discuss a contract Navatek had been granted through the University of Maine — took place months before Kao made any donations to Collins’ campaign.
“ProPublica reported that Martin Kao used the Navatek method: get the meeting, make the big initial donation, then have the high-priced lobbyists swoop in. As you can see, we were working with Navatek, through their partnership with the University of Maine, for two years before the big initial donation showed up,” said Steve Abbott, Collins’ campaign manager.
On Sept. 23, ProPublica published a follow-up report stating that some of the statements made by Collins and her representatives denying any wrongdoing were not accurate.

title: Loring Submits Two Sites for New Jail Proposal
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LIMESTONE, Maine (WAGM) - Two sites on Loring have been submitted as possible locations for Aroostook County’s new jail.
On the former Loring Air Force Base two sites have been submitted as potential sites for Aroostook’s new jail. LDA CEO Jonathan Judkins says they’ve worked on the proposal for years, and that it could reduce the tax burden on county residents.
Jonathan Judkins, the CEO of the Loring Development Authority said: “Loring was incredibly lucky to be considered as one of the sites for the Aroostook County jail. Limestone’s town manager Ed P ocock and I have been talking about this proposal for a number of years. It came to me as a simple idea of one taxpayer entity helping another taxpayer entity. We have an opportunity to reduce the tax burden on some of the Aroostook County people. Some of the other benefits that we found is that the centralized location to Aroostook would cut down on overtime costs for the cities and communities that are outside the range of the current jail.”
Judkins says the two sites in their proposal meet all the requirements for the new jail and have room for expansion if needed. “So, we have two potential site locations, the crows foot area and then the nose dock area. Crows foot features existing structures that could be utilized for administration or housing of the jail personnel. Not to mention world class runway access and ready-made pads of concrete that would support structures of a variety of sizes.
Judkins says a county prison had been proposed in Limestone in the past, but back then it was met with backlash. “Historically, there had been a prison proposed in Limestone. The community did not seem to embrace it. This time it seems like the community can really get behind the idea of the Aroostook County jail being located here for the savings of the taxpayers. You know, we’re all paddling in the same direction. We should try to share resources and utilize the things that already exist.”
The Aroostook County Commissioner’s Office is currently reviewing jail proposals. County voters would have to approve the proposal selected by the Commissioner’s Office before the construction of a new jail can begin. If Loring is chosen as the new jail site, voters will also need to approve moving the county seat. Any proposal selected will ultimately depend on voter support.

Oakland man sentenced in Waterville firearms burglary
text:
An Oakland man was sentenced Tuesday in federal court in Bangor after breaking into a Waterville pawn shop and stealing 20 handguns in August 2025.
Cody Smith, 25, was sentenced to two years in prison and three years of supervised release. Smith was caught on the pawn shop’s video surveillance system early Aug. 10, 2025 , and within hours of the burglary, he posted videos of himself with the stolen firearms and admitting to the theft on social media.
Smith pleaded guilty in May. The maximum sentence for the burglary was up to 10 years in prison with three years of supervised release and a $250,000 fine.
U.S. District Judge Stacey D. Neumann ordered Smith to pay $6,995 in restitution in addition to serving his sentence.
The Waterville Police Department and Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives investigated the burglary.

title: Former corrections officer allegedly killed his wife and forced his kids to help
text:
CALLAWAY COUNTY, Mo. (KOMU) - A former corrections officer from Missouri is facing charges for allegedly killing his wife 10 months ago and forcing his kids to help.
Jonathan G. Houston, 44, is charged with first-degree murder and first-degree kidnapping in his wife’s death, according to the Callaway County Sheriff’s Office. Investigators learned about the alleged crimes after receiving a 911 call Sunday morning from one of his seven children.
Whispering during the call, the child claimed her father had “captured” her and her siblings for five years and physically abused them, according to court documents.
Authorities traced the call to a hotel in Kingdom City, where they found Houston – who is a former corrections officer – and his kids.
One of the kids told deputies that Houston had allegedly killed her mother, who was also the suspect’s wife, by strangling her at the hotel on Dec. 1, 2025, while some of the siblings were in the room.
Houston allegedly directed one child to pour hot water down the victim’s legs while she was being strangled, and another covered her mouth. Prior to this, he allegedly put the three youngest children in the bathroom and played music to muffle the victim’s screams, according to court documents.
The victim was never reported missing. Houston allegedly disposed of her body in a trash bag that was tossed into a dumpster on hotel property, the probable cause statement states.
During an interview with investigators, Houston allegedly admitted to killing his wife and planning it ahead of time, according to court documents.
Houston is being held in jail without bond. He is also under prior investigations for sexual assault and the assault of other victims.
Authorities say his kids were all placed into protective custody.

title: In Virginia, Democrat hoping to oust Republican tests anti-corruption message echoing around country
text:
HAYES, Va. (AP) — U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman may have spent nearly two decades in Congress, but the Republican is emphasizing the humbler parts of his resume while running for another term this year. His advertisements talk about his work in a tomato cannery and on a fishing boat, and how he commutes to Washington from the same modest home in rural Virginia where he’s lived with his wife since 1985.
It’s a far different image than the one his Democratic opponent, local prosecutor Shannon Taylor, has been painting for voters in the red-leaning district. She says Wittman is “too busy getting rich” by trading stocks in companies he’s supposed to regulate, a characterization he says is false.
Taylor’s campaign is one of many that’s embracing an anti-corruption message in a midterm year that’s otherwise defined by high gas prices, persistent inflation and sinking confidence in the economy. With so much frustration over the cost of living, candidates see an opportunity to argue that incumbents are more interested in looking out for themselves or donors than their constituents. For some Democrats, it’s also an indirect way to remind voters of controversies surrounding President Donald Trump’s family business interests.
At a recent news conference on the U.S. Capitol steps, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said, “Anyone who is stealing from the American people, shortchanging the American people, or screwing over the American people, you are now on notice.”
An AP-NORC poll conducted in September found that registered voters nationally are more likely to describe Republicans than Democrats as corrupt. About half said “corrupt” describes Republicans “extremely” or “very” well, compared to a third who said the same about Democrats.
Virginia’s 1st Congressional District will present one of this year’s starkest tests for Democratic attempts to turn their message into a winning campaign issue, as Taylor tries to overcome Wittman’s deep experience and down-to-earth reputation with allegations of greed.
Democrats eye a flip for the first time in decades
The district hasn’t been represented by a Democrat since the late 1970s but is now part of the party’s push to flip control of the U.S. House. Trump won it by about 5 percentage points two years ago, but Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger took it by nearly 3 points last year.
Money is gushing in. Wittman — who could lead his chamber’s Armed Services Committee if Republicans hold the House — raised about $4 million to Taylor’s $2.1 million in the most recent reporting period. But Taylor has received far more support from outside groups than Wittman, and they’ve spent nearly $5 million on her behalf, with the vast majority of the money attacking Wittman, according to the nonpartisan Virginia Public Access Project.
In an interview, Wittman called Taylor “a liar” who has misrepresented the ranges and estimates in his financial disclosures, which don’t give a precise accounting of his net worth. Those records do make clear Wittman’s reported assets and individual stock holdings — he has dozens in companies with interests before Congress — have grown substantially during his time in office.
But Wittman said that’s mostly because of inheritances he and his wife received after their parents died. His campaign said he has not used nonpublic information to make investing decisions and doesn’t personally select his stock holdings, which are managed by outside advisers. It also noted that he’s voted for a bill to limit stock trading.
Wittman said he understands voters’ concerns about the cost of living and argued Taylor wouldn’t help fix the problem.
He said Republicans have addressed affordability issues through tax relief included in Trump’s “ big beautiful bill.” Wittman also said he’s “not the biggest fan” of Trump’s tariffs, which he believes have sometimes driven up costs.
“I hope this election is about ideas, about what are the solutions to the problems, and acknowledging that those problems are there,” said Wittman, who’s been endorsed by Trump and has criticized Taylor’s record as soft on crime.
Taylor, the top elected prosecutor in a suburban Richmond’s Henrico County, pledges to support a stock trading ban, term limits — something Wittman argued isn’t necessary — and a lifetime ban on members of Congress becoming lobbyists.
“Politicians in both parties are cheating the system, getting rich by trading stock while getting information only they have. Personally profiting when corporations rip us off,” Taylor said in one television advertisement.
Wittman has deep ties to the district
Bruce and Mary Halliburton, a retired married couple from Henrico County who are self-described independents, said Taylor’s message has resonated.
“He’s earned enough money,” Bruce Halliburton said of Wittman after the couple voted early for Taylor.
But voters in Gloucester County, a Republican stronghold, defended Wittman as a hard worker who knows the district, and they rejected Taylor’s corruption accusations.
“That’s a crock of lies against the man,” said Michael Greene, who sells oysters, fish and crabs at his nearby J&M Seafood Shack.
Greene said Wittman greeted him by name when the two ran into each other in late September at the Guinea Jubilee, a community festival celebrating the area’s maritime heritage.
It’s those kinds of ties that could help insulate Wittman from Taylor’s criticisms. In fact, he’s never had a close race, winning by at least 10 points in every reelection campaign.
About half of the district’s population lives in the counties surrounding Virginia’s capital city, Richmond, while the rest is comprised of smaller, more rural counties that hug the Chesapeake Bay and the rivers that flow into it.
As Wittman walked around the Guinea Jubilee, he was stopped over and over again with requests to pose for photos. One man said he’d met Wittman at a different festival. Another had run into him during a church visit. A pastor knew him from his time working in the district’s shipyards, where Wittman would visit. A child, cellphone in hand, interrupted an interview to ask Wittman to chime in on a video call.
Taylor campaigned at the same event, where she enjoyed a crab cake and talked to vendors about the impacts of Trump’s tariffs.
She easily won her primary earlier this year and defeated a Republican incumbent when she was first elected in 2011 as a prosecutor.
Last year, Taylor unsuccessfully ran for attorney general. She took corporate donations in that race but in this one isn’t accepting corporate PAC dollars, something she said in an interview is the result of listening to voters “upset about what they see as corporate and special interest influence.”
Candidates across the US harness a similar message
Allegations about corruption and self-dealing have echoed around the country this year on both sides of the aisle.
“I’ve had enough of self-serving politicians who keep getting richer at our expense,” said Democratic candidate Jamie Ager, a farmer running for an open North Carolina U.S. House seat where Republican Rep. Chuck Edwards dropped his reelection bid after an ethics investigation into improper conduct with female staff.
Rebecca Bennett, a Democratic congressional candidate in New Jersey, has criticized Republican Rep. Tom Kean Jr. over stock trading disclosures during a four-month absence from Congress. Kean didn’t disclose his hospitalization for depression until he returned to Washington, and he said it was financial advisers, not him, trading the stocks.
It’s also a major theme in Virginia’s adjacent 2nd Congressional District, a closely watched battleground where Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans is trying to stop a comeback attempt from Democratic former Rep. Elaine Luria.
Kiggans has hammered Luria for stock trades and her previous opposition to a ban on stock trading by members of Congress. Luria has since reversed herself and said lawmakers can “set an example by not owning or trading individual stocks.”
“People are tired of that type of corruption in Washington,” Kiggans said.
___
Associated Press journalists Mike Catalini in Morrisville, Pa., and Amelia Thomson DeVeaux and Lisa Mascaro in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Congresswoman Chellie Pingree seeks 10th term representing 1st District
text:
Congresswoman Chellie Pingree seeks 10th term representing Maine's 1st District
U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-Maine, is seeking a 10th term in Congress with nearly two decades in Washington already under her belt.
"There's just a lot of work to do, and it's work I've been fighting about for the last two years," Pingree said.
Pingree, originally from Minnesota, has spent most of her life on North Haven, a small island off the coast of Rockland.
Starting out as a farmer, Pingree said a life in politics was never one that she envisioned.
"We had a small farm, had three milk cows, 100 chickens and a variety of other animals, and sold vegetables," Pingree said. "It was a very good way to get to know a community."
Pingree got more involved in politics after being elected to the Maine State Legislature in 1992. She moved up to serving Maine’s 1st Congressional District after being elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in 2008.
The Democratic congresswoman faces Republican Ron Russell for a second time. Pingree defeated him back in 2024.
"I just think we're on completely opposite sides here, and this is not the year to be supporting this president," Pingree said. "We need Republicans who are willing to stand up to the president. He would not be one."
Pingree has spent a large part of the past year working with immigrant families who had someone detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. She said ICE is out of control.
"If they are willing to deal with the reforms that many of us believe are critically important, and if we can claw back some of the excessive amount of money that they have to hire officers, meet quotas, build these detention centers, I would consider allowing them to operate," Pingree said. "But I have been saying it's time to abolish ICE because their track record is horrendous."
The longtime lawmaker is hoping her party takes the majority during this midterm election, with President Donald Trump in the White House for at least two more years.
“I believe that the Republicans should be standing up much more and fighting back, and that has been left to us,” Pingree said. “In the first term, we could often work with them. We could find ways to cooperate or come to an agreement. Now, they don't negotiate. They don't reveal information. It's just a completely different world.”
If Pingree keeps her seat, she said there is a long list of what she wants to get done. That includes addressing affordability and everyday costs.
“We're going to look across the map, whether it's breaking up monopolies or helping individual farmers, doing everything we can to support the cost of food,” Pingree said.
Pingree said she hopes to rescind cuts that were made after the Trump administration's One Big Beautiful Bill went into effect, warning of changes to Medicaid.
"When the trillion-dollar cut kicks in in Medicaid after the first of the year, that will have a huge impact on who's covered and how much is there, and that directly impacts our hospitals," Pingree said. "They're already operating on very thin margins."
“We're about to face a cliff on these Medicaid cuts,” she added. “We've got to reverse that cliff and make sure that we're not putting our hospitals and people who receive those benefits in a huge problem."
Pingree calls this election the most important in our lifetime.
"This year, I truly think it's critical," Pingree said. "People are agitated and angry, and the most important voice that they have is getting out to vote."
Election Day is Nov. 3.

title: Victim’s mother reacts to Christa Pike being ‘conscious, speaking’ after botched execution, report says
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - The mother of Christa Pike’s victim spoke out after her attorneys announced Tuesday that Pike is conscious nearly a week after her botched execution.
Pike, who is convicted of the 1995 torture and murder of Colleen Slemmer, was supposed to be executed via lethal injection in Tennessee last Wednesday. However, after receiving two doses of what should have been lethal amounts of pentobarbital, she survived.
May Martinez, Slemmer’s mother, said she had a feeling Pike would survive, according to WBIR. She also said she does not think that Tennessee will make another attempt to execute her daughter’s killer.
Pike was left unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital following the failed execution. However, on Oct. 6, her attorneys reported that she is now awake and speaking.
“Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery,” they said.
When asked what her preference would be for what happens to Pike next, Martinez responded, “It doesn’t matter what I think.”
“They’re going to do what they’re going to do,” she reportedly said.
Whether the state can proceed with another execution attempt remains to be seen.
“Given what we know now, how she responds to lethal injection, and given what happened to her, Christa Pike’s lawyers have a pretty good argument that it would be a violation of the Eighth Amendment to execute her using [lethal injection],” Vanderbilt Law School professor Christopher Slobogin said.
A press conference with Pike’s attorneys will be held on Wednesday. The time for that press conference has yet to be confirmed.
Pike was one of three people found to be involved in the 1995 torture and killing of Slemmer on the University of Tennessee-Knoxville campus.
Pike’s boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, was also found guilty of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit first-degree murder. He received life in prison rather than the death penalty because he was 17 at the time.
Shadolla Peterson, who was 18 during the crime, was convicted of being an accessory and received parole after she became an informant to police.

title: Passenger steals airport vehicle on tarmac, crashes it at California airport, official says
text:
Passenger steals airport vehicle on tarmac, crashes it at California airport, official says
A Delta Air Lines passenger went out a terminal door at a Southern California airport Tuesday night, stole a vehicle on the tarmac, crashed it, and then tried to commandeer an airline truck before he was arrested, an airport official said.
Related video above: Here's what soaring jet fuel prices mean for your travel plans
The passenger, who was scheduled to fly to Seattle, went out an access door at gate 12 at John Wayne Airport in Orange County around 5:30 p.m. PT, airport spokesperson AnnaSophia Servin told CNN.
The man then stole an Alaska Airlines tug, a type of vehicle used for moving luggage trailers or planes around the airfield, and drove it to gate 7, where he crashed into another vehicle, the airport said.
The Delta passenger then attempted to steal a lavatory service truck belonging to American Airlines before he was arrested by airport police, Servin said.
“There was a security breach at the airport. Looks like someone stole a tug, so they pretty much shut down,” an air traffic controller told pilots of planes waiting on the tarmac in audio recorded by the ATC.com app.
Airport crews inspected the man’s route down a taxiway between gates 7 and 12 for any debris or other hazards, and planes quickly resumed moving around the airfield.
“Delta has zero tolerance for unlawful behavior, and we take all incidents seriously,” the airline said in a statement. “Nothing is more important than the safety and security of our customers and people, and we are cooperating fully with law enforcement.”
Jay Barr, 26, was arrested on charges of vehicle theft, trespassing and vandalism, the Orange County Sheriff’s Department said. He currently remains in custody, and CNN could not locate legal representation for him.
John Wayne Airport, in suburban Los Angeles, serves more than 11 million passengers a year and has flights to 50 destinations.

title: Appeals court reverses convictions in kidnapping and terrorism case involving 3-year-old boy's death
text:
ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. (AP) — A federal appeals court has vacated kidnapping convictions in a case involving the death of a 3-year-old boy who went missing from Georgia in 2017 and later turned up dead at a squalid compound in New Mexico.
The boy’s father and other family members were sentenced to life in prison in 2024 after jurors convicted them in what prosecutors described as a “sick end-of-times scheme.”
A panel of the U.S. 10th Circuit Court of Appeals wrote in a decision issued Tuesday that there was no evidence of a federal kidnapping crime when the family took the boy, noting that no court order or state law made it illegal for Siraj Ibn Wahhaj to take his son.
The group already was living in New Mexico when a Georgia juvenile court issued a pickup order for the boy after his mother petitioned for emergency custody. The appellate panel took issue with jury instructions that implied the mother’s lack of consent could satisfy the unlawfulness element under the federal kidnapping statute.
“This instructional error was not harmless,” the panel wrote. “Had the court correctly instructed on the law, the jury couldn’t have found unlawfulness based on the government’s evidence.”
The family members can’t be retried on the kidnapping charges, the panel ruled.
The appeals panel also vacated convictions stemming from accusations that Wahhaj and his brother-in-law were preparing for attacks against the government. It said the two men, who had represented themselves during the trial, had been excluded from bench conferences with the judge about notes jurors had sent during deliberations.
The court remanded that part of the case back to the district court, clearing the way for new trials for the men if prosecutors opt to pursue the case.
“What happened at the Taos compound was horrific. We are reviewing the case and assessing what further action may be appropriate,” the U.S. attorney’s office for the district of New Mexico wrote in an email Wednesday.
During the three-week trial in 2023, the defendants suggested that the case was the product of “government overreach” and that they were targeted because they are Muslim.
A fifth defendant — Jany Leveille, a Haitian national — avoided the trial by pleading guilty to conspiracy to provide material support to terrorists and being in possession of a firearm while unlawfully in the United States. She was sentenced to 15 years in prison.
Prosecutors alleged that it was under Leveille’s instruction that the family fled Georgia with the boy, ending up in a remote stretch of the high desert where they conducted firearms and tactical training to prepare for attacks against the government. Prosecutors said it was tied to a belief that the boy would be resurrected and then instruct the family which corrupt government and private institutions needed to be eliminated.
In a complex case that took years to get to trial, jurors heard weeks of testimony from children who had lived with their parents at the compound, other family members, firearms experts, doctors and forensic technicians.
Authorities raided the compound in 2018, finding 11 children and dismal living conditions. They also found 11 firearms and ammunition that were used at a makeshift shooting range on the property near the Colorado state line.
The remains of Wahhaj’s son, Abdul-Ghani Wahhaj, were found in an underground tunnel at the compound. Testimony indicated that the boy died just weeks after arriving in New Mexico and that his body was kept for months with Leveille promising the others he would be resurrected.
An exact cause of death was never determined amid accusations that the boy, who had frequent seizures, had been deprived of crucial medication.

title: Matthew T. Tilton
text:
Matthew Thomas Tilton passed away unexpectedly on July 7, 2026, at Miles Memorial Hospital due to complications from what began as an infection.
Matthew was born on Feb. 4, 1991, in Portland, Maine, to his parents, Gary Tilton and Vanessa (Hale) Betancourt. Matthew was a kind-hearted person, always looking for ways to serve others. From a young age, he pushed his lawnmower around the town of Washington, Maine, mowing yards for those who could no longer do it themselves. He never asked for or accepted money, instead always looking for ways to bless others. That spirit of generosity continued throughout his life, even shoveling snow this past winter for his newest neighbor.
Matthew grew up in the Church of the Nazarene, and while he was not always active in church, he had a personal relationship with Jesus. Though our hearts are broken and we begin the difficult reality of daily life without him, we find comfort in knowing that Matthew is with Jesus, and we will be together again.
After graduating from Medomak Valley High School with the Class of 2009, Matthew attended Washington County Community College, where he graduated from two different mechanical programs, earning special awards and recognition in both.
Matthew met the love of his life and very best friend, Brittany (Dickinson) Tilton, shortly after graduating from college. Together for more than fourteen years, they were married on Sept. 17, 2016. They enjoyed many adventures together, but their greatest joy was creating a beautiful family.
Matthew had many hobbies. He loved fishing, whether on open water or through the ice, and enjoyed countless days on the water with family and friends. He was community-minded, having served on the Boothbay Fire Department. In addition to attending every one of his children's games, he was always willing to step up and help whenever there was a need.
From an early age, Matthew's mechanical aptitude was evident. There was nothing he could not take apart and put back together exactly as it was meant to be. This talent served him well as he began his career at BIW as an outdoor machinist and ultimately was promoted to lead a team as a manager at Bath Iron Works, where he was well-liked and respected.
Most recently, with the help of their oldest son, Myles, Matthew took great pride in cutting and clearing the lot that would ultimately become the site of their beautiful new home in Boothbay.
Matthew overcame many challenges throughout his life. Yet, he would have been the first to say that his greatest accomplishments, and those of which he was most proud, were his loving marriage and his beautiful children.
Matthew was predeceased by his infant son, Cole Matthew Tilton; his father, Gary Tilton; his paternal grandmother, Janet Tilton; his maternal grandfather, Tom Hale, with whom he shared a special relationship; his maternal aunts, Valarie Hale and Viki Reed; his cousins, Jamie Lee Reed and Caleb Packard; and Brittany's grandparents, Bob Blackman and Sandy and Lee Dickinson.
In addition to his wife, Brittany, Matthew is survived by his children, Myles, Maci, and Bodie Tilton; his mother and stepfather, Vanessa and Miguel Betancourt; his father- and mother-in-law, Doug and Lori Dickinson; his maternal grandmother, Darlene Hale; his paternal grandfather, Alan Tilton; his uncle and aunt, Glenn and Lisa Tilton; Brittany's grandparents, Ron and Darlene French; his brother-in-law, Daniel Dickinson; as well as several great-aunts and uncles, cousins, other relatives, and close friends with whom he shared many special memories.
Family and friends are invited to visiting hours from 5 to 7 p.m. on Wednesday, July 15 at Hall's Funeral Home, 975 Wiscasset Road, Boothbay, ME 04537. A private family burial will be held at Shuman Cemetery in Waldoboro.
Hall’s of Boothbay has care of arrangements. To extend online condolences go to hallfuneralhomes.com.

title: ‘Touch grass’: Ice cream shop owner’s rant standing up for his teen employees goes viral
text:
BLACKSTONE, Mass. (WFXT) — A social media post from the owner of a Massachusetts ice cream shop has gone viral.
Dave Forgit’s strongly worded message blasting rude customers has gotten the attention of people from around the world.
“It’s supposed to be laid back. It’s ice cream. It’s supposed to be a happy place and a happy time. Settle down, take a breath, touch grass,” Forgit said.
Forgit is the co-owner of Coldstuff Ice Cream. He said he was tired of customers being rude to his employees, so he took to Facebook to post about it.
“We’re not afraid to drop a couple of colorful words on Facebook,” he said.
Forgit and his brother, co-owner Kevin Miller, said a customer yelling at a teen employee over an incorrect sundae price was the last straw.
“The amount of verbal abuse that these young kids get in a day is shocking to me. It’s wild,” Miller said.
The Facebook post said, in part, “I swear to God, stop yelling at my [expletive] employees. They are children. This job, for most of them, is their first. They are going to make mistakes ... It’s ice cream, for crying out loud. Grow up and act your age.”
Forgit said he did not expect his post to get so much attention.
He received an overwhelmingly positive response from people all over the world, including hundreds of thousands of likes and comments.
The ice cream shop has been booming since the viral Facebook post.
“I knew after seeing the post that I just had to come in and stop by and show the support,” customer Mackenzie Cahill said.
And for those who consider the owners’ message tasteless, Forgit followed up his post with a comment, writing, “And nobody gives an [expletive] if you don’t come back. We’d prefer it that way.”
The owners hope a bump in business will extend their season.

title: New nonprofit looks to raise $1 million to preserve Down East newspapers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A new nonprofit organization is seeking to preserve the future of three local newspapers in Down East Maine.
The Acadia Newspaper Trust is looking to raise $1 million to transition The Ellsworth American, the Mount Desert Islander and the Bangor Historian from private to nonprofit stewardship. The money will be used to purchase the papers and cover initial operating costs, according to a news release from the trust on Wednesday.
“We want to make sure these newspapers remain firmly rooted in the communities they serve for generations to come,” Chris Crockett, the newspapers’ publisher, said in a statement. “Local journalism is facing enormous economic pressures, and this effort is about building a sustainable future while preserving what has always defined our newspapers: local ownership, local voices and a commitment to the communities we serve.”
The Ellsworth American was founded in 1851 and the Mount Desert Islander in 2001. The Bangor Historian, a weekly publication focused on the region’s history, was launched by The Ellsworth American earlier this year.
“A community newspaper is one of a town’s most important institutions,” said Alan Baker, former publisher and owner of The Ellsworth American and Mount Desert Islander. “Its responsibility is to inform, to hold government accountable, and to tell the stories that define who we are.
“The creation of Acadia Newspaper Trust is an investment in that mission, assuring these newspapers will continue serving their communities with independence and integrity for future generations.”
The trust is aiming to acquire the publications by next summer.

title: What the Freeport-area school community owes our children
text:
I think there are few sights more endearing than a queue of new prekindergarten students learning how to line up in school. Finding the marks on the floor. Learning where to stow their things. Figuring out how to move through a hallway together. Making one of the biggest transitions of their new and promising lives. As I move through our schools in RSU 5, I am mindful of the journey our students and families make as they advance from one school to the next. Those prekindergarten students, who are just beginning to develop a sense of themselves as learners, will have countless opportunities to discover who they are and what they are capable of.
We want to nurture every latent talent, spark every curiosity and support every aspiration. That is what we owe our children. And as our district undertakes the timely and consequential work of a Systems and Sustainability Study, which will help inform the long-term decisions that will determine what those prekindergarten students experience in RSU 5 until they graduate from high school, I find myself returning to a fundamental question:
What does our community, through its stewardship of our schools, owe those children and their families?
I use the word “owe” not in the sense of financial obligation or indebtedness, although responsible financial stewardship is certainly part of that mission. I mean it more broadly. What do we owe our children as individuals? Not because they are our future, but because they are our community now.
Last week, during a meeting of our early childhood task force, we wrestled with a question that will become increasingly important as we expand our services for younger children: How do we become more efficient as a system? How can we expand the scope of services we offer to meet this need while also being mindful of the needs at every other level of education in RSU 5?
It is a natural question. We have finite resources. We have buildings with limitations. We have staffing challenges. We have growing responsibilities, including the responsibility to meet the special education needs of 3- and 4-year-olds. As I sat with the question of efficiency, I was struck that my first thoughts were not actually about dollars or buildings or staffing models. I thought about children. About children as individuals. As learners.
The greatest efficiency we can find, I believe, is to raise young children who see themselves as capable, curious learners.
That is an investment that pays dividends year after year. A child who believes that school is a place where they belong, where questions are welcomed, where mistakes are part of learning and where their interests matter is a child more likely to engage deeply in school. That confidence can carry from prekindergarten to elementary school, from middle school to high school and ultimately into whatever comes next.
So where does that begin?
It begins with a vision of school that sees children as complex individuals, right from the outset. Every child comes to us with different hopes, interests, abilities, needs, fears and dreams. That is not an obstacle to education. It is the reason education is so interesting in the first place. The magic of a school is that a child can walk through its doors not knowing yet what they will be good at, what will capture their imagination, who they will become or what contribution they might someday make. Our job is not to answer those questions for them. Our job is to create the conditions in which they can begin answering them for themselves. Fortunately, RSU 5 is a district that takes that charge seriously. It is reflected in our strategic plan, which places considerable emphasis on experiential, place-based and interdisciplinary learning and recognizes the social and emotional well-being of students as foundational to their success as learners and as people.
More importantly, it shows up in the adults who work in our schools. I cannot say enough about the culture of continuous learning and the commitment to nurturing that I see in our educators. Teaching is, of course, at the center of what schools do. But the most effective teaching helps children learn something about themselves and their capabilities. I can testify that in RSU 5, in every one of our schools, this ethos drives the way adults support children and each other.
And all of this work in our schools is, in turn, a reflection of the community that surrounds them. It reflects a deeply embedded belief that our obligation to our children is one of our deepest purposes as a community — which brings us back to the central question. What do we, as a community, owe our children?
This year, RSU 5 is undertaking a Systems and Sustainability Study that will ask fundamental questions about the future of our schools. How should our schools be organized? How do we make the best use of our buildings and resources? How do we sustain the programs and experiences we value? What will our students and families need from us five, 10 or 20 years from now? And perhaps most importantly, how do we make choices that are both educationally sound and financially responsible? These are not easy questions. They shouldn’t be.
The children standing in that prekindergarten line today will live with the consequences of the decisions we make now long after many of us have moved on. They will experience the schools we choose to sustain, the opportunities we choose to create, the buildings we choose to maintain and the tradeoffs we choose to make. This is the most important lens through which to view this hard work — not our tax bills.
Our obligation to those children is to engage in this hard work now. To listen carefully. To ask difficult questions. To be willing to challenge our own assumptions. To make responsible choices with a fair and curious frame of mind, recognizing that reasonable people can look at the same set of circumstances and see different possibilities.
When those prekindergarten students eventually walk across a stage to graduate from high school, we should be able to look back at the decisions we made today and know that we did not defer the hardest conversations or the most difficult choices simply because they were difficult. We should be able to say that we listened, that we considered the possibilities honestly, that we took seriously the resources entrusted to us, and that we kept the children in front of us as our north star. And that every decision was calculated to help every child see themselves as a learner with a bright future.
That is what stewardship means, and that is what we owe them.
Tom Gray is superintendent of Regional School Unit 5, which oversees schools in the towns of Freeport, Durham and Pownal.

title: Wife reports husband after finding child sex abuse material on his electronic devices, deputies say
text:
LINCOLN, Neb. (KOLN/Gray News) - A Nebraska man has been arrested for allegedly possessing child sexual abuse material.
According to the Lancaster County Sheriff’s Office, Timmy Lee Topil, 60, was arrested Tuesday after his wife reported finding suspected child sexual abuse material on thumb drives and a tablet belonging to him.
Topil and his wife reportedly were separated when the matter was reported to authorities.
Lancaster County authorities said Topil had been living in a camper near Branched Oak Lake, where the material was found in a backpack.
Lancaster County Sheriff’s Office Chief Deputy Ben Houchin said Topil’s wife shared with the department that she had an “inkling he was looking at improper things.”
Following an interview with Topil, the sheriff’s office said the content appeared to have been downloaded from the internet.
Topil was taken to an adult detention facility and booked on suspicion of possession of child sexual abuse material, a felony charge punishable by up to 20 years in prison.

title: Ex-Marine to face death penalty in 2025 mass shooting at North Carolina bar
text:
BOLIVIA, N.C. (AP) — A prosecutor announced Wednesday that he would seek the death penalty against a former Marine charged in a mass shooting last year that left three people dead and several others wounded.
“We are not blind to who this defendant is,” Brunswick County District Attorney Jon David said of defendant Nigel Max Edge. “He served this country in Iraq as a Marine, suffered a traumatic brain injury, and has struggled with serious mental illness. Those facts are important and they were weighed, but must be balanced against the circumstances of the crime.”
Authorities allege Edge piloted a small motorboat up to a dockside cocktail bar in Southport on Sept. 27, 2025, and opened fire with a short-barreled semiautomatic rifle. He faces three counts of first-degree murder, as well as multiple attempted murder and weapons charges.
In April, Superior Court Judge Jason Disbrow ordered Edge to undergo psychiatric treatment after it was determined he was unable to understand his legal proceedings enough to help his lawyers.
Defense attorney Matthew Geoffrion filed a motion to continue Wednesday’s hearing, arguing that the extent of Edge’s brain injury will likely make it impossible for him to stand trial. Edge was shot multiple times during a firefight in Iraq, including once in the head.
“The chances of capacity restoration in this case appear low,” Geoffrion said in his motion.
David countered that experts at the state hospital where Edge is being treated “have concluded he is likely to be restored.” But he added that the decision to proceed with a capital punishment case was not final.
“A capital designation guarantees the defendant the highest level of protection our system offers, including the appointment of a second qualified attorney and the most rigorous scrutiny our courts provide,” David said. “If evidence emerges bearing on Mr. Edge’s sanity at the time of the offense, we will reassess. If he is never restored to capacity, the death penalty would not be a lawful sentence and would be removed from consideration.”
Edge’s next hearing is scheduled for Dec. 7.

title: Charleston man wins Damariscotta pumpkin weigh-off for second straight year
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A Charleston man was the winner of this year’s Great Pumpkin-Weigh-Off contest in Damariscotta for the second year in a row.
Elroy Morgan, who has been growing pumpkins since 2002, officially won his 7th state championship at the 2026 Damariscotta Pumpkinfest
This year, his pumpkin weighed 1,847 pounds.
Morgan also achieved a new state record this year in gourd length. It measured 155.25 inches long.
Morgan shared a little bit about his process in growing big botanical fruits.
“I start them early. I got to start them already in April, and I start them inside, and then I transplant them out into the greenhouse in the month of May. Then the greenhouses come off, the plants grow, and I get a pumpkin set, and then they grow and they can grow. I had a pumpkin was growing 55 pounds a day for three straight days,” said Morgan.
His biggest pumpkin ever weighed in at 1,870 pounds.

text:
