title: Democrat files ethics complaint against Susan Collins over alleged pay-to-play scheme
text:
A former Democratic candidate for Cumberland County District Attorney on Wednesday filed a formal ethics complaint against Republican Sen. Susan Collins over pay-to-play allegations involving a defense contractor.
Attorney Valerie Adams asked the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Ethics to conduct an investigation into the allegations outlined in a recent ProPublica report that Collins agreed to steer millions of dollars in contracts to the Hawaii-based firm Navatek in exchange for political donations from its CEO, Martin Kao.
“It is difficult to conceive of behavior more improper than accepting campaign contributions in return for directing taxpayer funded government contracts to an out of state company,” Adams said in a letter to Chairman James Lankford, R-Okla., and Vice Chairman Christopher Coons, D-Del., obtained by the Portland Press Herald.
“The reporting from ProPublica suggests Senator Collins may have done just that,” she continued. “It is the Committee’s duty to get to the bottom of this.”
Collins and her campaign have repeatedly denied the allegations outlined in the ProPublica article, calling them “outrageous.”
It’s unclear what — if anything — will become of the ethics complaint. Such complaints can be filed by anybody online. The ethics committee is a bipartisan body, with three Republicans and three Democrats. Most such complaints get dismissed, although the committee has investigated senators in the past, probing then Democratic Sen. Al Franken for alleged sexual misconduct in 2017, and then-Sen. Robert Menendez of New Jersey in 2018 for improperly accepting gifts.
“This is getting to be pathetic,” Collins campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen said in a statement. “For the third consecutive week, a recently failed Democratic candidate has parroted false charges that they know nothing about against Susan Collins.”
The filing comes as Democrats are working to amplify the corruption allegations against Collins. In doing so, they are trying to put a negative light on her central argument for reelection — that she is wielding her power as chair of the appropriations committee to benefit Maine.
In her letter, Adams asked the committee to “urgently investigate whether Senator Collins engaged in improper conduct that reflects discredit upon the Senate” by:
- Steering $8 million in contracts to Navatek in exchange for political donations;
- Knowingly accepting contributions made in the name of another in violation of campaign finance law; or
- Working with President Donald Trump to stop the investigation.
In an interview Wednesday, Adams dismissed any suggestion that the complaint was politically motivated or aimed at influencing voters in Maine’s U.S. Senate race. She described herself as a former Collins supporter.
Adams said she was troubled by what ProPublica reported and believes the allegations should be looked into.
“There’s never been a more important time to demand the best of our elected officials,” Adams said. “And I truly believe that.”
In a televised debate on Tuesday, Collins said she began working with Navatek in 2017 — the year before she received any donations from Kao. The company was partnering with the University of Maine on a project for the U.S. Navy that sought federal funding.
“I worked very closely with the university. We advanced that proposal,” Collins said. “The head of Navatek at the time, unfortunately, was a crook. He is now in jail, where he belongs.”
ProPublica reported that Kao told FBI investigators that Collins would not meet with him in 2018 unless he donated to her reelection effort. But Collins’ campaign on Tuesday showed a timestamped photo of Collins and Kao meeting in the senator’s office in February 2018 — months before Kao made a donation to her campaign.
The ProPublica article also detailed how Kao told investigators that he worked with the leader of a Collins-aligned super PAC to exchange a six-figure donation to her 2020 reelection effort for millions in government contracts.
Kao made an illegal $150,000 donation to the Collins-aligned 1820 PAC through a shell company, since federal contractors are barred from contributing to campaigns. ProPublica reported that Kao told Scott Reed, the head of the pro-Collins Super PAC, about his plan to use a shell company to make the donation.
Kao pleaded guilty to charges involving money laundering and bank fraud in 2022, and is currently in federal prison. He had been cooperating with federal investigators in an effort to get his sentence reduced. Collins’ team has said he is not credible, pointing to his convictions.
Collins’ campaign manager Steve Abbott said on Tuesday that neither Collins nor her campaign were accused of wrongdoing after answering questions about Kao in 2021 — and that nobody in the senator’s office was contacted about any new investigations thereafter.

title: Teen’s resilience shines in senior photos taken amid rubble of home lost to wildfire
text:
SPOKANE, Wash. (KXLY) - A high school senior in Washington state has turned the devastation of losing his home to a wildfire into a symbol of resilience.
Weeks before his senior year of high school, Becks Bird lost his childhood home in Spokane to the Old Trails fire in August. He grew up with Riverside State Park as his backyard, and the plan was to use it as a natural backdrop for his senior photos.
“I probably ran over a thousand miles back in those trails, biked a lot with my friends,” Becks said.
But while he still needed senior photos, the backdrop had changed.
“There’s always been such good lighting there. But this year, there was no flowers. Normally, there’d be flowers,” he said.
Still, Becks chose to have his senior photos taken by what remained of his home on the morning of his last first day of high school. He stood along charred trees and debris, capturing his senior year the best he could.
Photographer Jenna Starr says the session was especially emotional for Becks’ family. One photo shows all four of them standing near the remains of their home.
“I couldn’t really look at his mom because it was so emotional for her. That was the forest her son was raised in,” Starr said. “But Becks is just resilient. He’s tough. He’s always been kind of tough.”
Like many in the Rifle Club neighborhood, the Bird family only had minutes to evacuate as the fire moved through the area. Becks, a cross-county athlete, was able to grab his medals before leaving. Those medals were also included in his senior photos.
Now, as Becks moves through his senior year and looks ahead to the future, he’s already learned some of life’s hardest lessons – and is more resilient for it.
“Don’t run away from it. You gotta live in it. You’ve got to move on at some point, so might as well make it now. So, you can get on with it faster, start trying to live a normal life again,” he said.
The Bird family is currently rebuilding their home in the Rifle Club neighborhood. More than 900 structures were damaged in the Spokane Complex fires.

title: Satirical sculpture with nude Trump unveiled outside European Parliament
text:
(CNN) - A satirical sculpture of President Donald Trump is on display at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France.
Video captures the unveiling of artist Jens Galschiøt’s sculpture of U.S. President Donald Trump titled “The Orange Plague” on the grounds of the European Parliament on Tuesday.
The sculpture depicts a naked, gold-covered Trump, covered in 23-carat gold leaf, sitting on the back of a frail man. It goes on display, the Danish artist told CNN.
The satirical sculpture of Trump also holds the scales of justice, while a golf club and a golf-ball globe lie beside him.

title: Eastern Maine Walk to End Alzheimer’s set for Oct. 10
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Hundreds of people are expected to gather at the Bangor Waterfront this Saturday for the annual Walk to End Alzheimer’s.
The walk route is 3 miles long and starts at 81 Railroad St. in Bangor.
The goal is to raise $75,000.
All funds raised through the walk go toward the care, support and research efforts of the Alzheimer’s Association, according to Brielle Hardy, with the Maine Chapter of the Alzheimer’s Association.
Participants are required to register for the walk. There is no registration fee, but every participant is asked to make a personal donation and commit to raising funds. Registration includes signing a standard waiver.
If you cannot make it to Saturday’s event but still want to donate, click here.

title: Another view of the future of American democracy
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Terry O’Connell is an entrepreneur and a former member of the Bar Harbor Planning Board and treasurer and director of the Bar Harbor Chamber of Commerce.
David Estey’s Sept. 26 commentary raises important questions about the future of American democracy. I share many of the democratic principles he identifies, but I strongly disagree with his conclusion that those principles lead to only one legitimate choice at the ballot box. After reviewing the issues he raises, I believe several of his assertions require important context, while others confuse political disagreement with a threat to democracy. The following is my point-by-point response.
Estey warns of gerrymandering, voter suppression, election interference and partisan courts. These are legitimate concerns, but they are not unique to one party. The essential tests are whether elections remain competitive, votes are counted according to law, courts can resolve disputes and lawful results are honored.
Estey calls President Donald Trump a “would-be emperor.” That is a political characterization. A president remains constrained by Congress, federal courts, elections, appropriations, federalism and the Constitution. Presidential actions should be judged individually against those restraints.
Estey describes Congress as a “cultist body” and says partisan justices have placed the president “above the law.” Congress deserves criticism when members put party loyalty ahead of constitutional responsibility, but its members are independently elected and voters can replace them. Likewise, the Supreme Court’s presidential-immunity decision did not give a president immunity for everything he does. Trump v. United States expressly states that there is no immunity for unofficial acts.
Estey criticizes “dark money.” Money unquestionably plays an enormous role in American politics, but Citizens United dealt with independent political expenditures; it did not authorize corporations to make unlimited direct contributions to candidates. Whether independent spending nevertheless exerts excessive influence is a legitimate debate.
Regarding the Epstein files, Estey refers to “endless delays and coverup.” Transparency should certainly be demanded, but millions of pages of Epstein-related material have now been released. The pertinent questions are what legally releasable material remains withheld, why it is withheld and what evidence demonstrates an intentional coverup.
On immigration, due process concerns deserve serious attention, and courts should intervene when constitutional rights are violated. But enforcing immigration law is also a lawful federal responsibility. Americans can support strong enforcement while insisting that federal agents obey the Constitution and applicable statutes.
Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security are three different programs and should not be treated as interchangeable. The 2025 Medicaid changes are substantial, and the Congressional Budget Office projects significant coverage losses. But a Medicaid change is not automatically a Medicare or Social Security cut. Each claim should be measured against the legislation affecting that particular program.
Tariffs can raise prices, and Federal Reserve research has found price effects from recent tariffs. The policy question I see is whether those costs are justified by objectives such as protecting strategic industries, countering foreign subsidies, reducing dependence on China, strengthening domestic manufacturing or gaining negotiating leverage.
On NATO, Trump’s confrontational approach toward allies is well documented. His supporters argue that pressure has encouraged greater European defense spending and burden sharing. The appropriate question is whether that approach ultimately strengthens or weakens the alliance.
My central disagreement is Estey’s conclusion that the “only choice” on Nov. 3 is an overwhelming Democratic vote to prevent authoritarian rule.
The democratic principles he identifies do not, I believe, logically establish that there is only one permissible electoral choice. They instead provide standards by which every administration and political party should be judged: Are elections competitive? Are lawful results honored? Can courts rule against the government? Does Congress retain its constitutional authority? Can citizens criticize their leaders? Is due process respected? Can voters peacefully replace their representatives?
Those are meaningful tests of American democracy regardless of which party wins an election.

title: Oct. 4–10 is Mental Illness Awareness Week
text:
BANGOR — Mental Illness Awareness Week, observed each year from Oct. 4 through 10, offers communities across Maine and the nation a focused opportunity to educate the public about mental health conditions, challenge stigma and encourage people to seek help without shame.
Mental illness touches nearly every family and community. In Maine, recent data show that roughly one in four adults experiences a mental health condition each year, and the state continues to report among the higher rates of diagnosed depression in the United States — approximately 26% of adults. Suicide rates in Maine also remain elevated compared with the national average. These numbers underscore both the need and the importance of compassionate, accessible care.
Northern Light Acadia Hospital operates under a simple, unified philosophy: “People are doing the best they can with the skills they have. They are not choosing to struggle.” This guiding belief rejects the idea that people with mental health challenges are simply not trying hard enough. Instead, it recognizes that people act with the tools and skills available to them in the moment, and that with the right support, those skills can grow.
“Stigma thrives when we assume struggle is a choice or a character flaw,” Angela Haley, LCPC, clinical director of inpatient services, Northern Light Acadia Hospital, said. “Our philosophy reminds us all that people are already doing their best. Our role is to meet them with dignity, build skills and walk alongside them toward healing. Mental Illness Awareness Week is a perfect time to share that message widely.”
Mental health is health. By educating ourselves, reducing stigma and treating one another with the understanding that people are doing the best they can with the skills they have, Maine can create communities where more people feel safe seeking support and building better days ahead.
For more information about Northern Light Acadia Hospital’s services, visit northernlighthealth.org/acadia.

title: Kimberly S. Ezzell
text:
Kimberly Sue (Baldacchino) Ezzell, 56, of Wiscasset, Maine, passed away peacefully at her home on July 8, 2026, surrounded by her loving family after a courageous battle with stage IV lung cancer.
Kim was born on Jan. 9, 1970, in Quincy, Massachusetts to Gerard and Sheila (McKnight) Baldacchino. Her family moved to Maine in 1972, before spending a brief time in Connecticut beginning in 1978. In 1980, they returned to Maine, where she would put down roots and eventually raise her own family.
On July 11, 1987, she married her husband, Paul Ezzell. Together they shared nearly 39 years of marriage.
Kim’s work reflected her strong work ethic and willingness to do whatever needed to be done. As a teenager, she scooped ice cream, before working alongside her father building fiberglass duck boats in the family shop, and then performed laundry services for Coves Edge. She later worked in janitorial services for several local businesses throughout the area before settling into a position with Damariscotta Hardware for over 20 years.
She found joy in life’s simple pleasures, a hot cup of coffee, tending to her garden, and making people laugh. She could spend hours working through word games and puzzle books, and if you ever sat down to play Scrabble with her, you knew you were probably going to lose. She was wonderfully stubborn, quick with a joke, and the kind of person who would give you the shirt off her back if you needed it. More than anything, she cherished being “Gram.” Her grandchildren, Eli and Elena, were the center of her world and her greatest source of happiness.
She was predeceased by her mother, Sheila Baldacchino; and her brother, Gerard “Jerry” Baldacchino Jr.
Kim is survived by her husband, Paul Ezzell of Wiscasset; her son, Chris Ezzell of Wiscasset; her daughter, Nicole Snyder and husband Josh of Wiscasset; her cherished grandchildren, Eli and Elena; her father, Gerard Baldacchino of Bristol; her sisters, Faith Crawford and husband Kevin of Bristol, Dawn Greenleaf and husband Michael of Damariscotta, and April Gagnon of Newcastle; her best friend, Kim Chapman of Woolwich whose unwavering friendship, compassion, and selfless care meant more than words can express; her daily visits, constant support, and loving care during Kim’s final days, and even after her passing, were extraordinary gifts that will never be forgotten. She also leaves behind many beloved nieces, nephews, extended family members, and dear friends who will miss her deeply.
Kim faced her battle with stage IV lung cancer the same way she lived her life, with remarkable strength, unwavering determination, and the stubborn spirit that everyone who loved her knew so well. Even as her illness progressed, she continued to show those around her just how strong she was. While cancer ultimately claimed her, it never diminished her love for her family, her sense of humor, or the generous heart that defined her. Though she will be deeply missed, the memories she created and the kindness she shared will live on in the hearts of all who knew and loved her.
A time of visitation will be held from 1 to 2 p.m. on Monday, July 20 at Strong-Hancock Funeral Home in Damariscotta. A service will follow at 2, also at the funeral home.
Arrangements are under the direction and care of the Strong-Hancock Funeral Home, 612 Main Street, Damariscotta, ME 04543. Condolences, and messages for her family, may be expressed by visiting: www.StrongHancock.com.

title: What a former doctor says about Christa Pike being awake and talking after failed execution
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) - Christa Pike is alive, awake and talking after her botched execution, according to her legal team.
Paul Allen, a former doctor, said he was not surprised by the news.
“I wasn’t surprised at all,” Allen said.
Defense questions drug delivery
Pike’s defense team believes pentobarbital may not have been going directly into her vein during the attempted execution.
Allen said the drug probably could have still killed her the night of the scheduled execution if she did not receive medical care after. When Pike did not die in a certain time frame, doctors were called in to keep her alive.
The Tennessee Department of Correction said it followed all protocol.
“Had they just left her, I think she would have succumbed to the drug,” Allen said. “And then it was just a matter of time until the large dose of pentobarbital metabolized, came down and then she was able to respond and her breathing center worked normally.”
What’s next in the case
With Pike still alive, the focus shifts to what’s next in her case, including whether she can still be put to death.
Criminal defense attorney Josh Hedrick addressed the question.
“We have to assess what is her mental state? Under our law, you cannot execute someone who is not competent, right? While she may be awake, we don’t yet know what her mental state is. We don’t know if there’s brain damage. We don’t know how alert she is,” Hedrick said.
Pike’s failed execution is the second in Tennessee this year.
Hedrick said the future of the death penalty and executions in the state is now in question.
“So, twice in one year is a bad look. That’s unacceptable. So, to identify where things are going wrong and fix them is vital. If we’re going to have executions, we have to do them properly,” Hedrick said.
Pike’s legal team said it is calling on the governor to commute her sentence, meaning the team will ask for life in prison rather than the death penalty.

title: Youth pastor dies after collapsing during marathon days before his birthday, family says
text:
PORTLAND Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - A 24-year-old youth pastor in Portland died after collapsing during a marathon, according to his family.
Thousands flocked to the Rose City for the annual Portland Marathon on Sunday, including Treyton “Trey” Lara.
His wife, Audrey Shin-Lara, said he trained for the marathon for several months.
“I think he’s just always just enjoyed running as just a way to like relax and release,” said Audrey.
Everything was going great that morning.
“I saw him at 18, 19. He ran over and was able to smile and give me a kiss, and then he ran off, and he looked good,” Audrey said.
Then around mile 20, Audrey said Trey collapsed.
Doctors told her he went into cardiac arrest.
Trey Lara was taken to the hospital, and Audrey said doctors did all they could to save him, but it was too late.
“The grief is coming in waves where one moment it still doesn’t feel real where we’re like I’m just gonna wake up, and he’s gonna be over there,” Audrey said.
Trey was a youth pastor. Most recently, his wife said, he was working with other youth pastors and leaders, hoping to make a change in the community around him.
“Besides loving Jesus, he loved his friends and family. He was the best big brother, Tio to so many cousins, and some of our friends’ kids would call him Uncle Trey,” Audrey said.
Audrey said Trey recently helped open a youth camp called Camp Genesis over the summer.
It was one of the many goals he had for himself.
Audrey said that, besides ambition, Trey was full of love.
And it’s the love from all those who knew Trey that’s getting Audrey through this heartbreaking time.
“He’s the love of my life, always will be. And we’ll see him again,” said Audrey.
She said Trey was as healthy as could be, with no underlying medical issues, so this loss is sudden and shocking.
A GoFundMe page has been set up to help the family during this heartbreaking time.
The fundraising page said Trey was days short of his 25th birthday on Oct 15.

title: Man accused of hiding 10 live birds in his ‘bulge’ at the airport
text:
MIAMI (CNN) — A man is accused of trying to smuggle live birds through Miami International Airport in his underwear.
Federal authorities said Alberto Hernandez Castillo, who is a legal permanent resident of the U.S., arrived from Cuba Sunday.
Customs officers sent him to a secondary inspection after noticing what they called an “unexplained bulge” near his waist.
A pat-down allegedly uncovered six plastic containers hidden in pockets sewn into his underwear.
Authorities said the containers held 10 live birds.
Hernandez Castillo allegedly said the birds were for his “personal use.”
He is charged with smuggling goods and was released on a $25,000 bond.

title: GHS Accredited by New England Association of Schools and Colleges
text:
On Sept. 18, Principal Brian Jandreau received a letter informing him that the Commission on Public Schools, at its meeting on June 22, had reviewed the Decennial Accreditation Report from a recent visit to Gorham High School and voted to award the school continued accreditation in the New England Association of Schools and Colleges. Gorham High School was congratulated for the successful completion of goals by staff and administration.
The letter from Alyson M. Geary and Carl R. Johnson highlighted the progress that GHS had made on the priority areas for growth and increased alignment with the Principles of Effective Practice, including:
-the effective use of technology to meet student learning needs
-the authentic opportunities provided through the team teaching model
-the collaborative decision-making process that is dynamic and responsive to staff and student needs
-the creative shifts in curriculum structures in English, social studies, and science to create flexibility and engagement that will enable more learners toattain the vision of a graduate
-the autonomy provided to staff through the self-selected book study to create an understanding of the “why” behind differentiation
-the collective understanding fostered through the adoption and use of the Carol Ann Tomlinson model of differentiation
-the focus on intentionally developing the instructional conceptual understanding, competency, commitment, and capacity of the staff
-the transparency and collaboration fostered through the staffing-needs process and prioritization
-the plan for long-term capital improvement projects that ensure a physically safe environment for all students and adults
-the real-world opportunities provided by the extended learning opportunities program
-the variety of pathways toward graduation requirements offered through the Social Studies and English departments
-the approach to determining the mental health and wellness needs of studentsbased on data
-the emphasis on the vision of a graduate as a living document that should guide all aspects of the school, including curriculum documents
-the expansion of learning spaces through the Modular Phase I project to better accommodate student learning needs
-the peer-to-peer learning facilitated through observations and work within
departments
The Commission also found it noteworthy that Gorham High School met all eight Foundational Elements in the Standards for Accreditation.

title: Topsham needs Annalyse Sarvinas
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Topsham is taking my property, one small bite at a time.
The 2025 inflation rate was 2.6-2.7% and the Fed forecast for 2026 is 3.7%. I just received my property tax bill that is 8.3% more than last year, more than twice the rate of inflation. I do get some COLA relief but it does not keep up with inflation — and we certainly do not need annual tax increases higher than inflation.
The property tax stabilization for seniors, a real benefit, was tabled and allowed to sunset so no one had to go on record as having voted against it. Something needs to be done to keep us elderly Topsham seniors on fixed incomes in our homes. This is an affordability issue for everyone. In this election year, at both the local and state level, please consider candidates who promote lower taxes. For Topsham, that legislative candidate is Annalyse Sarvinas. We seniors need a break.
Dan Konieczko
Topsham

title: Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities kill at least 19 in a major attack that Kyiv saw coming
text:
Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities kill at least 24 in a major attack that Kyiv saw coming
 Russian missiles and drones pounded Kyiv and a dozen other Ukrainian regions overnight into Wednesday, killing at least 24 civilians, including four children, and wounding around 60 in Moscow's latest devastating barrage, Ukrainian officials said
Related video: Could the executive order signed by President Trump Monday lower diesel costs ahead of midterms?
Three of the children killed when a Russian missile hit an apartment building were 1 year old and the other was 8 years old, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine had anticipated the attack, with Zelenskyy warning the previous day that intelligence services had concluded that Russia was building up for a “massive” strike.
Although Ukraine knew about the looming attack, which coincided with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s 74th birthday, it couldn’t fend it off completely.
The deaths and damage illustrated the difficulty Ukraine has in countering Russia’s ballistic missiles and the new jet-powered drones used in Moscow’s escalating bombardments. Without ammunition for its U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems, Ukraine can’t stop Russian ballistic weapons. It is racing to develop a new generation of interceptors fast enough to catch Moscow's high-flying jet-propelled drones.
Russia and Ukraine are engaged in a long-range aerial war as their armies remain largely deadlocked on the battlefield, more than 4 ½ years after Moscow’s all-out invasion of its neighbor. The unrelenting aerial attacks are hurting Russia but could be ruinous for smaller Ukraine.
U.S.-led peace efforts appear unlikely to bring any short-term relief, with the possibility of holding low-level technical talks still under discussion. Putin, meanwhile, is pressing ahead with the invasion in the belief that Ukrainians will buckle under the pressure and Kyiv’s Western supporters won’t stay the course, Western analysts say.
“Russia is pursuing a deliberate strategy of terror,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on X. “Trying to make daily life impossible for Ukrainians who want to live in peace.”
Russia wants Ukrainians to be afraid to fall asleep, official says
A Russian strike destroyed an apartment block in Pryluky, in Ukraine’s northern Chernihiv region, killing 18 people, including the four children, and wounding about 50, authorities said.
Deaths were also reported in three other Ukrainian cities, including the capital, Kyiv, according to Zelenskyy.
“The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” the Ukrainian leader said on social media.
Ukraine is looking worldwide for available Patriot missiles, which are in short supply due to the Iran war.
“Russian ballistic missiles remain the greatest challenge. And air defense packages for us right now are a vital necessity,” Zelenskyy said.
In Kremenchuk, in the Poltava region, two people were killed and seven injured, said Vitalii Diakivnych, head of the regional military administration, and a rescue operation was continuing.
“That is exactly what the enemy is counting on. For us to be afraid to fall asleep. To let our children out of our sight. To plan anything. So that everyone thinks: next time it could be my address,” he said.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said the military carried out a massive strike overnight targeting industrial facilities involved in the production and storage of missiles and drones across Ukraine. The ministry said that port and ship repair facilities in the southern Odesa region and ships carrying cargo for the Ukrainian military were also hit.
Ukraine strikes back with attacks on Russian oil facilities, Zelenskyy says
Ukraine has hit back at Russia by launching long-range drones and missiles at oil refineries and storage depots.
Zelenskyy said Wednesday that Ukraine targeted two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions of Russia.
Russian officials made no immediate comment.
Zelenskyy also indicated that Ukraine had struck in the Black Sea. He posted images of a fire said to show an oil tanker burning in the water near the Russian city of Sochi.
It was not possible to independently verify the images.
Some Russian online media late Tuesday also posted the images. Unconfirmed media reports said the tanker was carrying oil from Novorossiysk to India and was attacked by Ukrainian sea drones.

title: Ferry Point Bridge in Calais to close for repairs
text:
CALAIS, Maine (WABI) - The Ferry Point Bridge in Calais will be temporarily closed starting Oct. 13.
The Maine Department of Transportation says the bridge project includes deck rehabilitation and joint repair on the Maine side of the international border crossing.
The project is estimated to take six weeks, and the bridge should reopen by the end of November.
Drivers should take the Milltown International Bridge or the International Avenue Bridge during the repairs.
Commercial traffic must use the International Avenue Bridge.
Maine DOT says travelers should plan for delays and allow for extra travel time.

title: Up and Down the Kennebec Valley: Medical history in central Kennebec Valley
text:
Vassalboro
Prior articles in this subseries have described, as well as available sources allow, some of the important early doctors in the central Kennebec Valley: Moses Appleton, John McKechnie and Obadiah Williams, in Waterville, and Dr. Stephen Barton, at least part of the time in Vassalboro. This week, your writer intends to share what information (if any) she can find about other early Vassalboro doctors.
In her 1971 history of Vassalboro, Alma Pierce Robbins mentioned the following early doctors (listed in alphabetical order).
Dr. Joel Aulger “was hired ‘to transcribe the Town records'” in 1792, and was listed as a Vassalboro landowner that year. He was not in the 1800 town census, Robbins wrote; he was not named in the medical chapter in Henry Kingsbury’s Kennebec County history; and your writer found no one with that name in on-line listings.
Dr. James Bacon Robbins mentioned more than once. He seems to have spent time in Sidney, on the west side of the river, before and after it separated from Vassalboro on the east side on Jan. 30, 1792. (See below.)
Dr. Thomas Odeone, Odione, Odionne, Ordiorne (or Odiorne) was mentioned twice in Robbins’ history. In 1800, the Vassalboro assessors’ report said he “had $500 at interest”: and in 1804, the town bought John Getchell’s land between Odionne’s & the town landing for a cemetery. (See below.)
Dr. Oliver Prescott, Robbins believed, was “probably the only direct descendant of the Vassall family” who settled in Vassalboro. She mentioned him several times in her history. (See below)
Dr. Isaac Randall, Robbins said, married “the widow Percival” in 1810. (See below.)
Dr. Stephen Thayer she listed also under marriages: he and Sophia Carlton were married in 1808. (See below)
* * * * * *
When your writer included Dr. James Bacon in her Sidney history more than two years ago, he seemed to have spent more of his life in Sidney than in Vassalboro, after Sidney became a separate town on April 26, 1771.
Since then, one on-line record appears to have been updated to make it more probable that he lived – and presumably practiced medicine – on the Vassalboro side of the river, as Robbins’ list implies.
James H. Bacon was born June 30, 1738, in Bedford or Billerica, Massachusetts. By 1764, he was in the Kennebec Valley: he and Abigail Marsh (1747 -1834) were married Sept. 23 of that year, in Hallowell.
In 1766, the Vassalborough men whom Robbins listed as signing a petition to the Kennebec company requesting a grist mill included James Bacon.
Robbins said Vassalboro’s first town meeting, held May 22, 1771, was “at the house of James Bacon, physician and innkeeper.” At least one source says Bacon’s tavern was on the Sidney side of the Kennebec River.
In 1775, Robbins wrote, the Bacons bought a half-acre of land and half a “dwelling house” (John Marsh owned and occupied the other half of the house) about eight miles upriver from Fort Western, on the Sidney side of the Kennebec.
Census records show James Bacon in Vassalboro in 1790 (before Sidney became its own town) and 1800 (after the separation).
Your writer found no references to his medical education or his medical practice. He and Abigail had numerous children; sources disagree on the exact number.
James Bacon died in Sidney, in 1819. He and Abigil are buried in Sidney’s Lovejoy Cemetery.
* * * * * *
Dr. Thomas Odiorne was born in New Hampshire “about 1766” (FamilySearch). He and Elizabeth “Betsey” Tobey (born in 1776, according to Find a Grave) were married May 5, 1799, in Augusta; they had at least 4 sons.
Odiorne “lived in Vassalboro…for about 10 years,” FamilySearch says. Robbins’ list of postmasters at Vassalboro (the village on the Kennebec toward the north end of town, later Getchell’s Corner; the Vassalboro post office is there still, on Alpine Street) suggests more than 10 years.
She wrote that the post office was established April 1, 1796, with Jeremiah Fairfield the first postmaster. He was followed by Thomas Odiorne on Oct. 1, 1798; the next postmaster listed is Lathrop Chase, taking office on April 1, 1813.
Robbins’ other references to Odione/Odionne are within the same time period. She quoted an 1800 assessors’ report that said he “had $500 at interest”; and in 1804, she wrote, the town bought John Getchell’s land between Odionne’s & the town landing (on the Kennebec?) for a cemetery.
Again, aside from the title Dr., your writer found no information on Odiorne’s medical training or practice.
FamilySearch says Odiorne died August 22, 1834, in Augusta and was buried in Cony Cemetery. Find a Grave agrees, and says his wife, Betsey, who died Jan. 12, 1823, and a son, Charles Edward (birthdate unknown; died Dec. 19, 1829) are also buried there.
* * * * * *
Dr. Oliver Prescott got more mentions in Robbins’ history than did most of his colleagues, but he is even harder to find in other sources.
Kingsbury and Ancestry agree he was born in 1791. Ancestry says in Winthrop, Maine; neither gives a precise date.
Robbins wrote that in 1823, Dr. Oliver Prescott, “probably the only direct descendant of the Vassall family” to settle in the town (by then, Vassalboro was the east side of the Kennebec only) “became active in Town affairs.”
In 1829, he charged the town for damage after his chaise was upset on bad roads. In 1833, he was half a two-man committee to negotiate with Kennebec County commissioners about objections to a road from Augusta to China Village through Vassalboro. In 1840, Kingsbury added, he was elected a selectman, serving for four years.
Also, Robbins wrote (without providing a date), Dr. Oliver Prescott was appointed guardian for some orphaned children, whose name is spelled Buzel, Bussell and Buzzell.
Dr. Prescott married Lydia Chandler, born in Winthrop in 1795. They had at least one son, Oliver Danforth Prescott, who was born Aug. 20, 1834, in Vassalboro, and died May 20, 1880, in San Francisco.
In his chapter on the medical profession, Kingsbury said Prescott “practiced at Cross Hill [in southern Vassalboro, southeast of Webber Pond] before his death in 1853.” Your writer found no other information on his life as a doctor.
* * * * * *
Dr. Isaac Randall came to Vassalboro “from Cape Cod, about 1800, as a school teacher,” Kingsbury wrote. He continued:
“During his first term his knowledge of medicine became valuable to the community, and he enjoyed a successful career as a physician until his death in 1820.”
Robbins said he married in 1810, a widow named Percival. Kingsbury said their son, George L. Randall, was born in 1815; educated in town and at Kents Hill School, in Readfield; taught for 12 years; and began studying medicine under Dr. Hiram H. Hill, of Augusta.
The younger Randall graduated from Bowdoin in 1844 (apparently with a medical degree) and began practicing in Stetson. Two years later he returned to Vassalboro, “home of his wife,” a sister to Ira D. Sturgis.
Dr. George L. Randall’s son, George M. Randall, graduated from Bowdoin in 1889 and started practicing in Augusta in 1891 (the year before Kingsbury’s history was published).
* * * * * *
Dr. Stephen Thayer, Kingsbury said, was “of French Huguenot extraction.” Born Feb. 7, 1783, in Uxbridge, Massachusetts, he began practicing medicine in Vassalboro, where his first son, Albert, was born in 1808 (the same year that, according to Robbins, he married Sophia Carlton).
Soon after Albert’s birth, Thayer moved to Fairfield, where “and in all that section” he practiced until 1836, when he moved to Waterville. He died May 24, 1852.
Albert graduated from Waterville College and practiced medicine in Skowhegan until he died in 1833. His younger brother, Charles H., born in Fairfield in 1810, did not go into medicine; but the son of Charles H. and Susan E. Tobey, Frederick C. Thayer (born Sept. 30, 1844) Kingsbury called in 1892 “the acknowledged leader of the medical profession in Waterville.”
* * * * * *
The 1850 census listed six Vassalboro physicians: Oliver Prescott and George L. Randall, introduced above, plus John Bush, Robert H. Cary, Adna L. Norcross and Jonathan Smith.
Bush, Kingsbury wrote, was born in Boylston (FamilySearch says Danvers), Massachusetts, July 3, 1792. He graduated from Bowdoin; “pursued the study of medicine” while teaching at Wiscasset Academy; graduated from Bowdoin’s medical department and started practicing in Vassalboro.
Bush married Anne Wayne (1799 – 1870), either in Vassalboro (Kingsbury) or in Danvers in October, 1819 (FamilySearch). They had at least four children between 1820 and 1825, FamilySearch says all born in Danvers.
Kingsbury said that after “several years in Massachusetts,” he came back to Vassalboro and “remained in active practice” until he died, aged 84 (or, FamilySearch says, on Feb. 29, 1876, aged 83).
Your writer failed to find additional information on Drs. Cary, Norcross or Smith.
* * * * * *
Kingsbury’s medical chapter adds three more to the list of Vassalboro doctors.
Charles Bunker Cates was born in East Vassalboro Sept. 19, 1820. After graduating from Vassalboro Academy, Kingsbury wrote that he “studied medicine” and “graduated from Jefferson Medical College in 1845.”
(Jefferson Medical College was founded in Philadelphia in 1824. It is now Sidney Kimmel Medical College, part of Thomas Jefferson University.)
Kingsbury wrote that Cates practiced in Fall River, Massachusetts, for two years, and there married Margaret B. Barker. An on-line genealogy says Cates married Margaret Buffum Barker, born April 9, 1829, in Rhode Island on Dec. 3, 1846, when she was 17 years old.
The on-line source says the couple had one son, Dr. Horace Getchell Cates, born in East Vassalboro May 22, 1863.
Kingsbury said Dr. Charles Cates practiced in Vassalboro until he moved to California in 1886. He, his wife and their son all died in California, Dr. Charles on Jan. 10, 1888, Margaret on March 17, 1909 and Dr. Horace on March 27, 1911.
A doctor Kingsbury identifies as F. A. Roberts (your writer did not find out what the initials stand for), born in Jackson (Maine) in 1839, started studying medicine in Winthrop when he was 17 and received his M.D. From Dartmouth in 1860. An on-line site identifies him as a homeopathic doctor.
(A National Institutes of Health website says homeopathy is based on two “unconventional” theories: “like cures like,” or a disease can be cured by something that “produces similar symptoms in healthy people”; and the lower the dose, the more effective the medicine.)
Dr. Roberts, Kingsbury wrote, practiced in China for three years starting in September, 1862; moved to Vassalboro; and in October, 1883, moved to Waterville, dying there on May 26, 1892.
In 1869, he taught homeopathic medicine to Eli Grellet Jones, youngest son of famous Quakers Eli and Sibyl Jones.
Roberts was the grandson of Dr. Jacob Roberts, described by Kingsbury as a Quaker whose practice was in North Vassalboro the last 15 years of his life.
A history of Brooks, Maine, says Dr. Jacob Roberts was born in Buckfield on May 10, 1784. The writer called him “a self-made man” who worked on the farm, taught school and somehow learned medicine.
In 1810, he married Huldah Myrick; the couple settled in Brooks, where Roberts practiced for four decades “with great success.”
“For many years he was the most eminent physician in all that section of the state and became noted for his skill in the treatment of serious cases. He became a convert to the Quaker faith in religion and the homeopathic system of medicine….Dr. Roberts was noted for his benevolence and public spirit and had great tenacity of faith and purpose which characterizes the family.”
The couple had at least 10 children; FamilySearch says 11. Huldah died April 6, 1845.
On March 16, 1852, FamilySearch says, Jacob married Abigail Jenkins (born Sept. 10, 1820), in Vassalboro. Abigail died Aug. 7, 1852. Jacob died March 15, 1856, in Vassalboro, and is buried in the Friends cemetery in Brooks.
Main sources
Kingsbury, Henry D., ed., Illustrated History of Kennebec County Maine 1625-1892 (1892)
Robbins, Alma Pierce, History of Vassalborough Maine 1771 1971 n.d. (1971)
Websites, miscellaneous.

title: Washington resident, 30, accused of conspiring with 18-year-old to commit one of worst school shootings in Canada’s history
text:
SEATTLE (AP) — Federal authorities said Tuesday that they have arrested and charged a 30-year-old from Washington state with encouraging an 18-year-old to commit one of the worst school shootings in Canada’s history by offering to livestream the February attack, providing money and sharing advice on how to delete online messages to keep the plot a secret.
The U.S. attorney’s office in Seattle said James Cody Bryant of Bellingham, Washington, communicated with Jesse Van Rootselaar in British Columbia for at least six months ahead of the shooting. Bryant, who identifies as female, did not report Van Rootselaar’s plans to authorities, authorities allege.
W. Mike Herrington, the special agent in charge of the FBI’s Seattle office, said without Bryant’s “misplaced loyalty” and willingness to livestream the killings, officials didn’t know if Van Rootselaar would have gone through with the attack.
“We certainly know the shooter was concerned that not enough people would see the livestream without Bryant broadcasting it and was depending on Bryant to amplify the livestream because the shooter did not have many followers on social media,” Herrington added.
Authorities say Van Rootselaar first killed her mother and stepbrother at home before attacking a nearby school in the mountain community of Tumbler Ridge, killing five children ages 12 and 13 at the school as well as an educational assistant. Twenty-five others were wounded.
Van Rootselaar was later found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.
Investigators accessed Van Rootselaar’s Twitch account and found that she had initiated a video livestream while sitting in her vehicle with a rifle and long gun in her lap. The livestream lasted about 20 seconds before it was disconnected, and was only viewed by one other account.
Bryant is accused of helping to plan the attack
Bryant was charged with one count of conspiracy to commit murder in a foreign country — a “novel” charge for a case like this, said Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd during a press conference.
Bryant made a first appearance in court on Tuesday afternoon and is being detained ahead of a preliminary hearing set for Oct. 20. The federal public defender’s office, which represents Bryant, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Communicating over Discord with Van Rootselaar, Bryant gave tactical advice on how to carry out the killings to have the strongest impact, according to the complaint.
“Hallways also mean a lot of ways people can escape,” Bryant wrote, the complaint said. “Corners to turn. Wide open spaces means numbers.”
Bryant also sent Van Rootselaar money to purchase a lighter that would be used to construct an explosive device and advised Van Rootselaar about how to keep the plot a secret by deleting online messages and using virtual private networks, officials said.
According to the criminal complaint, Bryant and Van Rootselaar met online about three years ago on Omegle, a since-shuttered video chat site that connected users with strangers at random. Their communications were sporadic during the first year because she was “institutionalized” after being deemed a danger to herself, the complaint said. She was locked up again after setting her room on fire. But they spoke daily during the six months leading up to the attack, officials said.
“Van Rootselaar often spoke about planning to use guns to murder her family members and others because she felt she had been mistreated,” the complaint said.
Both Van Rootselaar and Bryant identified as trans, Herrington said. But authorities do not have any indication that’s why they stayed connected online, he said.
Bryant sometimes urged Van Rootselaar to reconsider, officials say
Bryant tried to talk Van Rootselaar out of committing the attack at various points, authorities said.
“I truly hope you reconsider today,” Bryant told her in January, according to the complaint. “I wish there were any other path for you, you shouldn’t have to do something like this.”
But ultimately, Bryant did not alert law enforcement and instead provided support for carrying out the shooting, authorities said.
When Van Rootselaar expressed concern that Bryant would “snitch” and alert authorities, Bryant repeatedly assured her that would not happen, officials said.
“I could,” Bryant wrote, according to the filing. “I don’t want to honestly. I know I can like, save lives I guess but idk,” using the abbreviation for “I don’t know.”
Canadian Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said in Ottawa that the allegations were devastating.
“Nothing will bring back the eight lives that were devastated back in February, but it is important that those who are responsible are held to account,” he told reporters.
Anandasangaree said it was too soon to say whether Bryant could also face charges in Canada, but added that Canadian prosecution would be possible if investigators determine Canadian laws were broken.
Bob Zimmer, the federal lawmaker who represents Tumbler Ridge, said the victims deserve answers.
“It is deeply troubling, the allegations that this individual coached the shooter all throughout the process in an effort to livestream the event,” Zimmer said.
Tumbler Ridge in the Canadian Rockies is more than 1,000 kilometers (600 miles) northeast of Vancouver, British Columbia, near the provincial border with Alberta. The provincial government website lists Tumbler Ridge Secondary School as having 175 students from Grades 7 to 12.
The families of victims are suing artificial intelligence company OpenAI in U.S. federal court, seeking to hold the ChatGPT maker responsible for failing to alert police to the shooter’s alarming interactions with the chatbot.
___
The story and headline have been corrected to identify Bryant as a resident of Washington. Authorities say Bryant identifies as female.
Associated Press reporter Rob Gillies contributed to this report from Toronto.

title: State says ‘packaging error’ caused ‘small number’ of incorrect ballots to go out in Oxford County
text:
Editor’s note, this story was updated on Oct. 8 to correct information about the ballots and where they were sent.
Several Oxford voters received incorrect ballots this week for the November election.
The Department of the Secretary of State said the Oxford town clerk was notified by a resident on Tuesday that that they had received a ballot meant for another town.
A relative of Ernie Fitts, who is running for an Oxford-area Maine House seat, noticed the candidate was missing from the ballot and raised the alarm on social media.
Jana Spaulding, deputy secretary of state for communications, said Wednesday afternoon that the situation had already been remedied.
“A resident did contact the Oxford town clerk yesterday after receiving an incorrect ballot style, and it was addressed by the clerk,” Spaulding said.
“The clerk identified that due to a packaging error at the printer, a small number of incorrect ballots were received and sent out. Oxford is working quickly to contact any resident who could have possibly received an incorrect ballot.”
She said anyone getting an incorrect ballot will be given a proper one.
“Every voter,” Spaulding said, “will have the chance to vote the correct ballot.”

title: FDA says its safety review of abortion pill will continue into next year
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Food and Drug Administration says its ongoing safety review of the nation’s main abortion pill will continue into next year, a timeline that was quickly condemned by abortion opponents hoping to see the drug’s use curtailed.
The FDA gave a court-ordered update on its progress in a legal filing late Wednesday, providing the first substantive information about the controversial reevaluation ordered by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Mifepristone was first approved by the FDA in 2000. The agency has repeatedly reaffirmed the pill’s safety and effectiveness over the years, in addition to easing a number of restrictions on the drug, including dropping a requirement that it be dispensed in person.
But since President Donald Trump returned to the White House, anti-abortion groups and their allies in Congress have pushed the administration to revisit the pill, in the hopes of restricting its use.
The FDA said in its filing that it expects to complete a safety study of the pill by mid-December this year. A report on the findings is expected “no later than March 2027,” after which the agency will decide whether to impose new restrictions or other changes on the drug’s use.
Gavin Oxley of Americans United for Life, an anti-abortion group, criticized the move as a lack of “true leadership” by Trump administration officials.
“The administration continues to find itself on the wrong side of women’s health, clearly uninterested in mitigating the ongoing harms caused by the abortion pill,” Oxley said.
The two-drug regimen of mifepristone, combined with a second drug misoprostol, is the most common form of abortion in the U.S.
The FDA was directed to provide the latest update by a federal judge in a case brought by the state of Louisiana alleging that mail-delivery of mifepristone undermines the state’s abortion ban. It’s one of several state lawsuits related to mifepristone winding their way through the courts.
Last month a three-judge panel for the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals questioned the merits of Louisiana’s case, including whether the state had the legal standing to challenge FDA’s oversight of mifepristone.
Any ruling from the 5th Circuit on the Louisiana case would not immediately change the landscape because the Supreme Court has blocked changes to the drug until it sees the case again.
The FDA said Wednesday it is using a “statistical data mining method” to discover “unknown safety concerns,” that may exist with the drug. The data comes from an electronic database that collects reports of medical injuries and drug side effects from major health networks and insurers.
In addition to the safety study, the agency said it is considering a number of petitions proposing changes to how mifepristone is prescribed and distributed.
Abortion opponents have focused most of their efforts on a 2021 decision allowing doctors to prescribe the drug online and send it through the mail during COVID-19. That decision, made permanent under President Joe Biden in 2023, had the effect of undermining a number of state abortion bans, since women can receive the drug through the mail.
___

title: 4 injured in Hancock crash
text:
Four people were injured Tuesday afternoon in a collision in Hancock.
Nicholas McAfee, 36, of North Little Rock, Arkansas, was driving a Hyundai Sonata east on Route 1 about 2:27 p.m. when he rear-ended a Ford Bronco driven by 53-year-old Amy Houck of Steuben, according to Shannon Moss, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety.
The collision caused the Bronco to roll over, while McAfee’s Sonata went off the road into a field, where it hit a tree, Moss said Wednesday morning.
A passenger in the Bronco, 66-year-old Cathy Grant of Milbridge, was taken to the hospital with serious injuries. A passenger in the Sonata was taken to the hospital with injuries not considered life-threatening.
McAfee and Houck suffered minor injuries in the crash, Moss said.
The crash remains under investigation.

title: FOR YOUR HEALTH: Why Natural Skin Health Matters
text:
When we hear the word anti-aging, many think of miracle creams or expensive treatments. But true skin health isn’t about turning back time – it’s about creating habits that keep your skin strong, radiant, and resilient as you age. Healthy, youthful-looking skin is the result of consistent self-care, not quick fixes.
At Glo Forward, we believe everyone deserves access to practical, affordable skin health strategies. These 10 natural anti-aging habits don’t require luxury products or complicated routines – they’re simple steps you can integrate into your daily life to support your skin and overall well-being.
1. Hydrate from the Inside Out
Your skin is the largest organ in your body, and just like every other organ, it depends on hydration to function. Drinking 6 – 8 glasses of water per day helps maintain skin elasticity, reduce the appearance of fine lines, and flush out toxins. Pairing this with a moisturizer locks in hydration and prevents dryness.
Pro tip: Look for moisturizers with ingredients like hyaluronic acid, aloe vera, or jojoba oil, which mimic the skin’s natural hydration process.
And while drinking water is essential, you can double the benefits by using a serum with hyaluronic acid. It helps the skin hold onto moisture, keeping it plump and refreshed throughout the day without feeling heavy.
2. Prioritize Restful Sleep
Nighttime is when your skin works hardest to repair itself. Skipping sleep interferes with collagen production, accelerates wrinkles, and leaves skin looking dull. Consistently aiming for 7 – 9 hours of sleep can lead to firmer, fresher skin.
Science behind it: During deep sleep, your body produces growth hormones that stimulate cell repair – making sleep a natural anti-aging remedy.
Nighttime is also the perfect moment to add a retinol serum. While you sleep, it gently encourages cell turnover, softens fine lines, and supports smoother, more even skin over time.
3. Protect Your Skin from the Sun
Up to 80 percent of visible aging signs – fine lines, dark spots, sagging – are caused by UV damage. Wearing sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher is one of the most effective anti-aging habits you can adopt.
Choose broad-spectrum protection to shield against both UVA (aging) and UVB (burning) rays, and reapply every two hours when outdoors.
4. Nourish with an Anti-Aging Diet
What you eat directly affects your skin. Foods rich in antioxidants and healthy fats can reduce inflammation and boost collagen production.
Vitamin C (citrus, berries, peppers) helps brighten and protect against free radicals.
Omega-3s (salmon, chia seeds, walnuts) keep skin plump and hydrated.
Polyphenols (green tea, dark chocolate) improve circulation and fight cell damage.
Pro tip: Limit processed sugar, which breaks down collagen through glycation.
Just like vitamin-rich foods protect your body, a vitamin C serum can protect your skin from daily stressors. Used in the morning, it brightens the complexion and shields against free radical damage.
5. Manage Stress for Healthier Skin
Stress triggers cortisol, a hormone that breaks down collagen and increases oil production – leading to acne and premature aging. Mind-body practices like meditation, yoga, or journaling don’t just calm your mind – they protect your skin from stress-induced flare-ups.
Quick fix: Even five minutes of daily deep breathing can reduce cortisol levels and support long-term skin resilience.
6. Stay Active to Boost Circulation
Exercise increases blood flow, delivering oxygen and nutrients to your skin. It also helps remove waste products that can contribute to dullness. People who exercise regularly often report brighter, firmer skin.
Pro tip: Aim for 30 minutes of moderate activity most days – even brisk walking counts.
7. Gentle Cleansing and Smart Exfoliation
Over-cleansing strips natural oils, while over-exfoliating can cause microtears. Instead, choose a mild cleanser and exfoliate one to two times per week to remove dead skin cells and boost product absorption.
Science behind it: Regular exfoliation stimulates cell turnover, a process that naturally slows as we age, keeping skin fresh and glowing.
8. Incorporate Vitamin C into Your Routine
Vitamin C is one of the most researched ingredients in skincare. Applied topically, it reduces pigmentation, protects against UV damage, and stimulates collagen production.
Pro tip: For best results, use a vitamin C serum in the morning before applying sunscreen.
9. Ditch Harmful Habits
Smoking and excessive alcohol intake accelerate aging by reducing blood flow, breaking down collagen, and depleting skin-essential vitamins. Cutting back on these habits can dramatically improve skin texture and tone.
Did you know? Smokers are up to five times more likely to develop wrinkles around the mouth than non-smokers.
10. Practice Consistent Self-Care
Anti-aging isn’t about chasing perfection – it’s about consistency. Small, daily habits have a compounding effect over time. Whether it’s your skincare routine, balanced nutrition, or mindfulness practice, the key is to stick with it.
Pro tip: Keep it simple. A 3-step routine (cleanse, moisturize, protect) practiced daily can be more effective than a complex regimen done inconsistently.
Conclusion: Empowering Aging with Confidence
Aging is natural, but premature skin damage doesn’t have to be. By focusing on hydration, nutrition, protection, and self-care, you can maintain skin that looks as youthful as it feels.

title: The Date You Can Expect to See First Snowfall in 4 Maine Cities
text:
For most people across Maine, they've already awoken to the first frost of the year. The evening temperatures are cooling and the heat is likely coming on overnight.
Those are the typical signs that winter is approaching for Maine. While the state has seen some warmer winters in recent years, the snow always falls at some point.
As winter closes in, here's a snapshot of how the snow adds up in four major cities throughout Maine, courtesy of How Much Will It Snow and Current Results.
The following data shows the average day where the first snowfall hits, the amount of snowstorms (1-5 inches) happen in each city as well as how major snowstorms (6+ inches) occur in each setting.
The First Snowfall Date For Portland, Maine, is Predicted For November 19
First Snowfall Date: November 19
Snowstorms Per Winter: 16
Major Snowstorms Per Winter: 5
For most people who live in and around Portland, Maine, it probably feels like winter keeps showing up a little bit later each year.
There's some truth to that, as the average date for the first official snowfall keeps creeping later on the calendar each year. 50 years ago, Portland's first snowfall date averaged out to be November 15.
The record for first measurable snowfall in Portland was October 10, 1979.
The First Snowfall Date for Augusta, Maine, is Predicted For November 21
First Snowfall Date: November 21
Snowstorms Per Winter: 20
Major Snowstorms Per Winter: 6
Central Maine's weather doesn't vary a whole lot from that of major cities in southern Maine. Augusta sees a handful of additional snow events that Portland doesn't, and is privy to an additional major snow event or two throughout the coldest months of the year.
The First Snowfall Date for Bangor, Maine, is Predicted For November 14
Date of First Snowfall: November 14
Snowstorms Per Winter: 20
Major Snowstorms Per Winter: 6
Bangor's data is a bit misleading because over the last five winters, the town has averaged only 15 storms per winter, four major snowstorms, and about 50 inches total snow.
The outlier was the winter of 2022-2023, where Bangor got hit with nearly 90 inches of snow.
The First Snowfall Date for Presque Isle, Maine, is Predicted For October 29
First Snowfall Date: October 29
Snowstorms Per Winter: 28
Major Snowstorms Per Winter: 8
While the mountains get the headlines when it comes to snow in Maine, 'the County' takes the brunt of the pain.
Presque Isle's first snowfall date happens well before the winter solstice, and their last snowfall date happens well after the spring solstice.
That leads to a long, grueling winter for northern Maine that features a ton of snowstorms and the most major snowstorms of any region in the state.

title: Hershey adds disclaimer to Reese’s pumpkins. This is what it says
text:

title: Maine Nursing Jobs Hit 16,900 Positions With Nearly 1,000 Openings Yearly
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
How Maine Communities Are Connecting Career Change With Accelerated Nursing Education
This content was produced in partnership with studyonline.sjcme.edu.
A career change can feel more achievable when your education connects with a clear need in the community around you.
In Maine, nursing sits at the intersection of workforce demand, demographic change and access to healthcare across urban and rural communities.
The state's 2026 healthcare workforce report covers more than 90,000 healthcare workers, clearly illustrating the scale of the sector and its importance to Maine's economy.
If you are considering a new professional direction, nursing can offer a practical route into a field with sustained demand.
Your previous education and work experience can also give you useful foundations for the transition.
Accelerated education then provides a concentrated pathway that combines academic study with laboratory learning and clinical preparation.
Exploring accelerated nursing education in Maine
When you research accelerated nursing programs in Maine, you will find pathways designed around students who already have substantial college-level education or a bachelor's degree.
These programs condense professional nursing coursework into a shorter timeframe, appealing to someone who wants to make a considered career transition without starting a traditional four-year degree from the beginning.
The faster structure also requires serious preparation, so you need to consider prerequisite courses, clinical commitments, study hours and the financial implications before applying.
Previous college coursework can help you meet some requirements, although each program establishes its own admissions criteria.
Overall, that makes careful planning useful before you commit to an accelerated pathway.
What Maine's workforce figures tell you
Current workforce projections give career changers useful context when they assess nursing as a second profession.
Maine had approximately 16,900 registered nursing jobs in 2024, while the state projects around 980 annual openings for registered nurses.
The 2025 median annual wage listed for registered nurses was $87,000, providing another relevant factor when you evaluate the financial side of changing careers.
Those figures also connect with broader demographic trends. Maine has an advancing population age structure, contributing to demand for healthcare services across several occupations.
If you are looking for a profession with a direct connection to population needs, nursing offers a particularly clear example of how workforce planning and individual career decisions can intersect.
Connecting education with local communities
Maine's geography adds another dimension to the discussion because healthcare access differs across communities.
Rural residents can face longer journeys for specialty services, while healthcare workers are distributed unevenly across the state.
That makes the development of a strong nursing workforce relevant to communities that need reliable access to care close to home.
For you as a career changer, that connection can add meaning to an educational decision.
Your eventual workplace could be a hospital, outpatient service, residential setting or community health organization, so the location and type of nursing role you choose can influence where professional capacity grows.
Clearly, your career decision can have a practical local impact.
Bringing previous experience into nursing
A second career can also bring valuable professional experience into nursing.
If you have worked in education, customer service, public administration, social services or another people-focused field, you could already have experience with communication, organization and high-pressure situations.
Those skills do not replace clinical knowledge, but they can complement the competencies you develop through nursing education.
Accelerated study also rewards disciplined preparation because the coursework moves quickly.
You will need to absorb scientific concepts, develop clinical judgment and apply classroom knowledge during practical experiences within a concentrated period.
If you understand that commitment before enrolling, you can approach the transition with more realistic expectations and a clearer plan.
Preparing for licensure and practice
Completing an accelerated nursing program represents one stage of the transition because registered nursing is a licensed profession.
Graduates must complete the applicable licensing process and pass the NCLEX-RN before they can practice as registered nurses.
Maine's Board of Nursing oversees state licensing requirements and provides guidance for applicants moving through the process.
Current examination data also shows why academic preparation matters.
During the first quarter of 2026, 216 first-time candidates educated in Maine took the NCLEX-RN, with 184 passing for an 85.19% first-time pass rate.
The national rate for U.S.-educated candidates during that period was 86.9%, giving prospective students useful context when considering the demands of nursing education.
Turning career change into community contribution
A career transition becomes more compelling when you can see how your personal goals connect with wider workforce needs.
Maine's projected demand for registered nurses, combined with its aging population and geographic differences in healthcare access, creates a strong context for people considering nursing as a second career.
If you are weighing this option, look beyond the speed of an accelerated pathway and consider prerequisites, clinical requirements, licensing, finances and the type of community where you want to work.
That broader view can help you decide whether nursing fits your professional goals while giving you a clearer understanding of what the transition will require.

title: Maine’s Fall Foliage Is Moving Fast: Catch the Colors Before They’re Gone
text:
Maine’s Fall Foliage Is Moving Fast: Catch the Colors Before They’re Gone
Hey, we’re already flying through October, so make sure you take advantage of this incredible weather and get outside. And what I mean by that is to check out the foliage before it passes you by. Because once it’s gone, you know what’s next: the white stuff.
The foliage season is cruising by, with reports now dropping weekly. According to Maine.gov, Northern Maine has just passed peak season, with mid-October being peak for Central and Western Maine, and then closer to the end of October for Southern Maine.

It feels like the season is flying by, and maybe it's due to the unseasonably warm weather we have had. Thankfully, it hasn't negatively affected the colors. It's wonderful to see the leaves starting to change quite a bit. And thanks to the Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry's Maine Foliage Report, we can see exactly where things stand.
We officially have our first regions that are past peak. It was a great run, Northern and Western Maine, but we’ll see you in 2027.
The rest of the state is a hotbed of activity, from peak conditions in parts of Central and North-Central Maine to high color levels in the south and east. However, Southeastern Maine is still holding at the midlevel. What a perfect time to hit the road and take in some amazing fall colors.

Fall temperatures should remain relatively consistent here in Maine. That basically means the rest of the foliage season is going to be absolutely ideal for leaf peeping. I mean, who doesn’t love a little crispness in the air while enjoying the outdoors this time of year?

title: Winthrop field hockey nips Spruce Mountain in Class C South showdown
text:
JAY — Winthrop’s Evelyn Mortimer saw an opening and spoiled Spruce Mountain’s senior night.
Her goal late in the first quarter was all the Ramblers needed to prevail 1-0 in a field hockey game Wednesday at Taglienti Field between the top two teams in Class C South.
After the Ramblers (10-1) transitioned from defense to offense in the midfield, Mortimer perfectly timed her move into the circle and a got a shot past Spruce Mountain goalie Kyleigh Marcotte.
“I saw a gap, and I saw my teammates, Natalie (Irwin) and Addie (Daigle), they were pushing each other up the field. So I was like, ‘You’ve got to get there and get that last touch in,’” Mortimer, a junior, said.
Winthrop/Maranacook coach Hollie Daigle said Spruce Mountain’s defense didn’t give many openings all night.
“Spruce (Mountain) does a really great job of doubling with the ball, getting their sticks low; (they) made great tackles,” Daigle said. “I thought we really started to adjust to use our passing game a little bit more and just had good communication on the field.”
Not looking ahead to the postseason
Wednesday’s game was the second of the season between last year’s Class C South finalists. The Phoenix won the 2025 regional title, but Winthrop has won both meetings in 2026.
Wednesday’s game had a postseason feel, with two teams playing a high-stakes game. But, even though the Ramblers (10-1) have beaten Spruce Mountain (9-2) twice and have a 23-point lead in the C South Heal point standings, Holly Daigle said Winthrop is focused on finishing the regular season strong, not on the postseason.
“I mean … tonight, you’re right, it was a great night, playing under the lights, beautiful night, it was exciting, and we’ve got three more games left this season,” Daigle said. “When playoff time comes, we’ll approach it then, but we know we’ve got, three more games before we close out the regular season.”
The Ramblers have games against Brunswick on Friday and Oak Hill on Oct. 14, before finishing the regular season Oct. 16 against Lisbon, which was dealt its first loss of the season by Spruce Mountain on Monday.
Mortimer said Winthrop still has things to improve before the postseason.
“I think we’ll want to work on making moves around players, marking (players better), too,” Mortimer said. “Just working on specific skills for each player, because everyone’s unique.”
Spruce Mountain staying positive
Despite her team losing to Winthrop for the second time this season, Phoenix coach Alex Bessey saw growth in things her players have been working on.
“… Communication, energy, being ready without the ball, all those little field hockey things that I think sometimes high school players just take for granted,” Bessey said. “So just realizing how important all those little things are.”
Unsung hero
There were two instances in the fourth quarter that Spruce Mountain goalie Kyleigh Marcotte prevented Winthrop from adding to its lead. First, she made back-to-back saves off a corner. Then, in the final five minutes, she again had to stop back-to-back shots.
“She was huge for us, getting on the ground, getting dirty when she needed to,” Bessey said. “I think that’s just a huge energy boost for the rest of the team.”
Statistical leaders
• Winthrop: Evelyn Mortimer (goal)
•  Spruce Mountain: Kyleigh Marcotte (seven saves)
