title: Weigh-Off Sees Most Number of Entries in Years, State Record Broken for Long Gourd
text:
At 155.25 inches, the longest long gourd in the state was measured at the Great Pumpkin Commonwealth Official Weigh-Off on Sunday, Oct. 4 at Louis Doe Home Center in Newcastle.
This is the second year in a row that Elroy Morgan, of Charleston, has broken a state record, his long gourd last year measuring a total of 151.5 inches.
“I didn’t even know I was going to be a state champion again,” Morgan said. “I just grow it and it came out the biggest in the state.”
Morgan’s long gourd is 19 inches under the world record, something he said he one day hopes to beat.
Morgan also took home two other wins at the annual kickoff to Damariscotta Pumpkinfest. He placed first in the adult pumpkin division with an entry weighing 1,847 pounds. Morgan also took home first place for adult marrow with a 99-pound entry.
Damariscotta Pumpkinfest and Regatta Executive Director Jed Weiss said the 53 pumpkins, gourds, and squash is the most the weigh-off has seen in years. The top 10 pumpkins combined weighed a total of 10,019.50 pounds.
In second place for the adult pumpkin division, Nobleboro resident Richard Powell beat his all-time record with a pumpkin weighing 1,730 pounds. Powell has approached growing the same way for the past 15 years; the former Nobleboro Select Board member said he was granted more time to work in his garden after retiring.
After weighing in his pumpkin on Oct. 4, Powell will receive recognition from the Great Pumpkin Commonwealth for having three pumpkins with a cumulative weight of at least 4,500 pounds. The smallest of the three, which Powell weighed at the Deerfield Fair in New Hampshire, weighed 1,417 pounds. His second pumpkin weighed in at 1,634 pounds at the Topsfield Fair in Topsfield, Mass. His final pumpkin and personal best brings his total score to 4,781 pounds.
“It’s just a milestone, you know,” Powell said. “You have something to push for next time.”
Sarah Whitty, of Veazie, won first place in the adult squash division for her 994-pound squash named “War Admiral.” Whitty also placed fourth for her 1,120-pound pumpkin named “Seabiscuit.” Earlier this month, Whitty broke the North American record for the largest zucchini with a 170-pound zucchini.
Whitty’s YouTube channel “Pumpkinista” has gained almost 150,000 subscribers and some of her fans ventured to Newcastle on Oct. 4 to see her in action. One of those fans was 11-year-old Ambrose Walsh, who drove down from Rockland to see Whitty. Styled in a homemade “Seabiscuit” T-shirt, Walsh said he has been watching Whitty’s videos for a few months and wanted to see her pumpkin and squash in person.
“I just really wanted to come to see her and I’ve never met a YouTuber before,” Walsh said.
In other divisions, Leon Busby placed first for adult bushel gourd, weighing in at 124.5 pounds. Bill Mackowski’s placed first in adult field pumpkin with his weighing 158.5 pounds.
For the youth divisions, Addison Harris placed first for her 220-pound squash and second for her 485-pound pumpkin. Mason Busby placed first for his 548.5-pound pumpkin and second for his 159-pound squash. Harris’ mother, Kayla Harris, placed in eighth place for the overall adult pumpkin division, weighing in at 606 pounds.
At the end of the weigh-off, Whitty’s “Seabiscuit” won the Howard Dill Award for prettiest pumpkin.
For more information, results, and the festival’s schedule, go to mainepumpkinfest.com.

title: 17-year-old accused of stabbing another student repeatedly in the neck at school, police say
text:
ROCK HILL, S.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - A 17-year-old has been charged with attempted murder after he allegedly tried to strangle and repeatedly stab another student.
Authorities in York County said the fight reportedly broke out at Northwestern High School in Rock Hill on Sept. 28.
According to Rock Hill police, during the fight, the 17-year-old tried to strangle the other student with a charging cord and stabbed him in the neck with a pencil.
Police said the other student sustained a puncture wound, but they did not say how severe his injuries were.
Officers detained the 17-year-old and allegedly found he had a THC vape. While he was detained, Rock Hill police said the teen threatened the other student and said he wanted to harm himself.
Police said the 17-year-old also damaged school property and “attempted to access items” while in a police car.
The teen was taken to the South Carolina Department of Juvenile Justice and issued a juvenile summons for assault and battery, possession of marijuana and malicious injury to property.
The assault and battery charge was later upgraded to attempted murder, with investigators noting that the 17-year-old would be charged as an adult.

title: Susan Collins’ approach to governing is the right approach
text:
Stephen Diamond is a retiree who lives in Topsham.
If Sen. Susan Collins is politically vulnerable, it is not because she has changed, but because the country has.
We live in a time when what divides us greatly overshadows what unites us. What used to be legitimate policy differences now degenerate into ugly personal attacks, and rather than push back against this development, some in public office seem happy to fan the flames of discord.
This change in our political climate has even led to calls to fundamentally transform the nature of our country, ranging from those advocating a white supremacist Christian theocracy to those arguing for a transition to socialism. Our struggle to make our religion-neutral, free-market democracy work has emboldened the advocates of extreme solutions.
Maine, along with the rest of New England, was once the ideological center of the country with little to separate Democrats from Republicans, but now Sen. Collins, as the only Republican member of Congress from this region, remains the sole heir to this tradition. Should she be voted out of office, it will be the final nail in the coffin of New England pluralism.
As someone who has known Sen. Collins for many years and who served on her staff (but who voted for the Democrat in every presidential election since 1968), I think that in addition to her legendary work ethic, her approach to governing can be summarized in three words: civility, compromise and compassion. Her civility reflects her manner of working with others, even unpleasant colleagues holding dramatically different views.
Without civility, compromise becomes impossible, and without compromise, progress becomes impossible, with our government either experiencing paralysis or vacillating between conflicting policies. Her consistent ranking as the least partisan member of the Senate and her effectiveness as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee attest to the senator’s understanding that compromise is essential to effective governing.
A less recognized feature of Sen. Collins’ approach to governing is her compassion for persons facing difficult challenges, as manifested in the importance she attaches to helping constituents dealing with personal setbacks as well as in her support for programs designed to assist those genuinely in need. A government insensitive to the suffering of persons facing hard times is not a government worth having.
What arguably most distinguishes Sen. Collins from others holding elected office is that she is a frequent target of both the extreme left and the extreme right. Ironically, nothing demonstrates more convincingly the importance of her voice.
When Rep. Jared Golden, with his impressive military record, expresses concern for the safety of his family, the problem in Washington has gone beyond mere incivility. It may be that Sen. Collins is of the old school, with an approach to governing reminiscent of that practiced by Sens. Muskie and Cohen, but we have much to learn from a past when political opponents treated each other with respect, the result of which was a functioning government.
Whether Sen. Collins is reelected has serious consequences not only for Maine but for the country. Hers is among the lonely voices in Washington pushing back against the dangerous partisanship that undermines our constitutional order. Simply put, a vote against Sen. Collins is a vote to perpetuate our national polarization while a vote for her is a vote for a healthy, civil and effective democracy.

title: Biddeford City Council signals support for ordinance to block city cooperation with ICE
text:
The Biddeford City Council could soon approve an ordinance prohibiting city employees from cooperating with federal immigration officers.
All nine councilors supported the proposal at a first reading Tuesday night. A second reading and final vote is expected to take place at the council’s next meeting on Oct. 20.
The proposal intended to limit ICE activity in the city comes about three months after Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero was shot and killed in Biddeford by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer.
“If this (ordinance) would move the needle an inch and make it 1% of 1% less likely that someone will be gunned down in the streets, I consider it absolutely worth it,” Councilor David Kurtz said Tuesday.
Biddeford’s proposal is modeled after standards set by cities like Portland and Lewiston, which both have passed ordinances limiting city employees and resources from cooperating with ICE. The state also has its own protections in place, including a law that limits police coordination with federal immigration agencies, which went into effect in July.
Biddeford police already don’t cooperate with ICE, City Attorney Harry Center said, but an ordinance strictly prohibiting any city employees — including police officers — from interacting with federal immigration agencies would strengthen the city’s approach to handling ICE.
Councilor Marc Lessard said he normally wouldn’t support a proposal that prohibits city cooperation with federal law enforcement, calling it a “dangerous precedent” that could have many unintended consequences. But Lessard was in favor of the proposal Tuesday night, citing Durán Guerrero’s killing.
“I want to say to Johan’s family and to all Biddeford families, I wish this had never happened,” Lessard said. “I want Biddeford to be the most welcoming, safe and happy place it can be.”
Lessard proposed an amendment to the ordinance that would ask the City Council to review it every six months, but that was voted down.
The ordinance is scheduled to be back before the council for a final vote in two weeks.

title: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan's firing squad execution set for Dec. 3
text:
Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan set for firing squad execution on Dec. 3
The acting secretary of the U.S. Army said Tuesday that the man convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3.
In a post on social media, acting Secretary Adam Telle said the execution of Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan will take place at Fort Hood.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had said Monday that President Donald Trump had approved the execution of Hasan. The U.S. military has not carried out the death penalty since 1961.
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, walked into a medical building where soldiers were getting medical checkups, shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. Thirteen people were killed and more than 30 injured.
He said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims and made almost no effort to defend himself at trial. He told jurors that evidence would show he was the shooter and described himself as a soldier who had “switched sides.”
Trump’s approval triggered a series of procedural steps toward carrying out the execution, but Hasan could put them on hold — potentially for years — with a habeas corpus appeal in the civilian federal court system, according to an article published in May in the magazine Army Lawyer.

title: Work to restore waterways in the Magalloway reaches far downstream
text:
Conservation work carried out by the Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust seeks to strengthen the resiliency of two waterways in the Rangeley region by replacing aging river crossings and correcting straightened waterways.
In July, more than 78,000 acres around the Magalloway River in northern Oxford County was conserved in a joint effort by four groups, Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust, Forest Society of Maine, The Nature Conservancy and Northeast Wilderness Trust, which formed the Magalloway Collaborative in spring of 2025.
The four groups have worked together to raise the $62 million needed to buy the development rights to the land.
Although the development rights have been secured by the collaborative, there is still conservation work to be done in the Magalloway, namely in its rivers and tributaries.
WORK TO BE DONE
Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust has identified many undersized or failing stream crossings that hinder the movement of fish in the preserve, which have been in place on logging roads for decades.
Brook trout are one of the dominant species in the Magalloway and Kennebago rivers. Preferring cold water, they will move upstream in the summer months as the waters warm, choosing rivers and ponds in the higher elevations on the surrounding mountains. The culverts sever access to streams in these higher elevations.
The culverts often sit high off the riverbed, meaning a fish hoping to move up or downstream would have to jump into the pipe and work their way to the other side.
“A lot of studies have shown that, you know, perhaps a few individuals that are more determined can make it through them, but the vast majority don’t,” said Jason Latham, conservation biologist for Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust.
Latham said that in surveys done by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, one side of a culvert on a brook in the nearby Kennebago conservation area, which has seen much of the same conservation techniques, held more than 130 fish while the opposite side had only two. The culvert cut off nearly four miles of upstream habitat from the majority of fish in the system.
“It was clearly a barrier,” he said.
The organization is moving to replace the culverts, opting instead to install open-bottom bridges that mimic a natural stream bed, which allow fish to freely swim through the miles of tributaries.
“By replacing these culverts and building these open-bottom bridges and replicating sort of that natural condition of the stream, we’re essentially reconnecting miles of upstream habitat for species like brook trout,” he said.
Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust has replaced nine crossings in its Kennebago preserve, with three left in the trust’s property. Work in the Kennebago will act as a model for the restorative conservation that will take place in the Magalloway in the coming years.
Replacing culverts also strengthens the area’s resiliency to heavy rains and flooding events.
When heavy rain hits the forest, like in the storms that drenched the region in 2023, the culverts can only handle so much water at a time. Latham said that when the region gets hit with multiple inches of rainfall, all of the water is moved down the mountainside and into the blocked streams.
These culverts can become overwhelmed by the water, causing soil to erode from around the pipe and polluting the downstream area with deposits from the crossing.
LOGGING LEGACY
Decades ago, lengths of rivers across Maine were straightened by logging companies. This allowed for timber harvested in the surrounding woods to easily float to the mills downstream. But now, years after the last log drive, the rivers in the region still show scars.
Stretches of water along the Magalloway and Kennebago were subject to the same treatment, creating long, channel-like stretches where water has little obstruction.
Latham said that healthy rivers often aren’t straight. Instead, they meander, with fallen trees and rocks slowing the flow of water and providing shelter to aquatic life under the surface. Above the surface, waters spill over to create floodplains that are vital to the surrounding habitat.
To correct straightened sections of water, Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust plans to fell trees into portions of waterways to help create the natural barriers the Magalloway needs for a thriving ecosystem. Similar actions were taken on the Kennebago and have been a success, Latham said.
River restoration isn’t solely benefiting the forests of the Rangeley Region. It acts as one of the first lines of defense against flooding and poor water quality in communities along the Androscoggin River.
“Everything flows down to the communities that are even more populated below us,” said Molly Shaw, communications director for Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust.
Communities such as Bethel, Rumford, Livermore Falls and Lewiston all receive water that enters the system through the Magalloway.
The Magalloway begins at the confluence of the river’s West Branch and Third East Branch in Bowman Township at the northern tip of Oxford County. It stretches 40-plus miles through the five unorganized territories south Bowman, then into New Hampshire before crossing back into Maine to become a tributary to Parmachenee Lake, Aziscohos Lake and the Androscoggin River, which flows into Merrymeeting Bay.
“There’s a million different sorts of threats to really good clean water quality that could happen up here at the top of the watershed that impact so many people downstream,” Latham said.
“The Magalloway is the source of fresh water that feeds down to Merrymeeting Bay and dumps into the Gulf of Maine,” he added.
“We have the opportunity, I’ll say, and the responsibility to practice good forest management up here,” Latham said.

title: Starbucks sued over 'sugar-free' label on protein drinks
text:
Starbucks sued over 'sugar-free' label on protein drinks
Starbucks is facing a consumer lawsuit over claims that the protein drinks labeled “sugar-free” on its cafe menus may actually contain more sugar than a Reese’s peanut butter cup.
Related video above: Consumer Reports: How much caffeine is really in your coffee?
The federal lawsuit filed late Friday in Seattle alleges that eight protein beverages Starbucks sells in the U.S. contain varying amounts of sugar, even though the company lists them as sugarless.
On Monday, the menu on Starbucks' U.S. website listed a 16-ounce (0.5-liter) Sugar-Free Caramel Protein Matcha with 16 grams of sugar and a 20-ounce (0.6-liter) version of the same drink with 21 grams of sugar. By comparison, one Reese’s cup has 11 grams of sugar.
Hagens Berman, a law firm that specializes in class action cases, filed the suit on behalf of three individual consumers who bought Starbucks’ sugar-free protein drinks in California, New York, and Washington.
“Consumers avoid sugar for various reasons, whether that be general health, diabetes and blood glucose levels or other factors, and for many, a staunch mislabeling like this is significant,” said Steve Berman, a co-founder and managing partner of the Seattle-headquartered firm.
The plaintiffs contend that Starbucks' naming and marketing of sugar-free products is “false, deceptive and unlawful” and that the company violated federal labeling regulations.
Seattle-based Starbucks said the sugar in its protein drinks comes from the protein-boosted milk it uses. The company said it doesn’t add sugar to the drinks and it uses sugar-free syrup for flavoring.
On Starbucks’ website Monday, the drinks were marketed as “sugar-free,” but the company also clearly stated the amount of sugar in each beverage and that they were made without added sugar.
“We believe these claims have no merit,” a Starbucks spokesperson said Monday. “Starbucks has consistently and clearly provided information about its protein beverages, sugar-free options, customization choices and nutritional content across product announcements, menus, marketing materials, Starbucks.com and the Starbucks app, and we intend to vigorously defend ourselves in this matter.”
Starbucks introduced its protein drinks in September 2025 to meet consumer demand for functional beverages and catch up to rivals like Dutch Bros, which launched protein-enhanced coffee drinks in 2024.
Dutch Bros also offers a lower-sugar version of its caramel-flavored Hopscotch Protein Latte, but it’s advertised as the Hopscotch Zero Sugar Added Protein Latte. The 16-ounce (0.5-liter) iced version has 7 grams of sugar and 11 grams of protein. By comparison, a 16-ounce (0.5-liter) iced Starbucks Sugar-Free Caramel Protein Latte has 9 grams of sugar and 29 grams of protein.
The lawsuit seeks damages on behalf of U.S. consumers who bought the drinks. It also wants the court to order Starbucks to stop using the label “sugar-free” on products that contain sugar.

title: Even retirees deserve a day off once in a while
text:
Vicki Sullivan of Portland is a retired English instructor and writing tutor.
Occasionally, when I was teaching, I would enter a classroom and be greeted by a student who would ask me, “Can we do nothing today?”
I’d reply sarcastically, “No work, no pay,” which invariably got the answer, “We’re not getting paid; we’re paying.” Or I might say, “That’s what you do every day,” to which the response would be a “Ha, ha” or an extended fake laugh.
But for those of us who have worked hard all our lives, that question can make you wonder.
For some days I wake up and ask myself, “Can I do nothing today?” And maybe I’m really asking myself for permission.
We, offspring of Depression Era parents, had a strong work ethic instilled in us. Our parents worked hard for their success and expected us to do the same. My mother frowned upon a sick day from school and personal days off from work were unheard of then.
I can hear my father saying, “Keep on digging” to anyone who might listen!
And a coach who coached at the University of Delaware with my father told his football players who complained about practicing on a holiday, “On Labor Day you labor.”
Doing nothing or having nothing to do was not looked upon favorably. Therefore, many of us who have retired expect ourselves to keep busy and have a purpose.
A friend of my father gave my father advice when he was going to retire. “Plan every day,” he suggested. My father didn’t and he found retirement a difficult transition.
Although I’m still trying to adjust to retirement three years later, I do plan every day. I make a to- do list as if I have a corporate job and cross off my completed tasks. Granted, they might be small items — mailing something or emptying the dishwasher — but at least I have accomplished something.
My friend Michael, a retired antiques shop owner, and I often text back and forth, discussing how productive we have been that day — his day spent cleaning out and organizing the many items in his garage and mine downsizing holiday items and “death cleaning.”
A former co-worker of mine, who had retired from the police department, had a full-time teaching job, a part-time consulting job and other short-term projects in his field. I remember laughingly commenting to him once, “You run around as if the devil were after you.”
He replied, “I don’t like to be idle.”
My friend Gladys,now deceased, lived to be 98. Before her death she was living independently, still keeping house and cooking, and driving. We laughed over an incident many times. At 97,at a doctor’s appointment, she told her physician that she didn’t seem to have much ambition. And her physician replied, “Why do you need to be ambitious at 97?” She was so used to keeping busy.
The only time most of us gave ourselves permission to do nothing was during COVID-19 when we really couldn’t do much of anything. I wasn’t working, as I was laid off during the spring semester when COVID hit.
However, of course, doing nothing has different meanings for different people.
But, whatever your definition, to those of us who’ve worked hard and deserve a day off, I say, “Let’s do nothing today.”

title: New nonprofit looks to raise $1 million to preserve Down East newspapers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A new nonprofit organization is seeking to preserve the future of three local newspapers in Down East Maine.
The Acadia Newspaper Trust is looking to raise $1 million to transition The Ellsworth American, the Mount Desert Islander and the Bangor Historian from private to nonprofit stewardship. The money will be used to purchase the papers and cover initial operating costs, according to a news release from the trust on Wednesday.
“We want to make sure these newspapers remain firmly rooted in the communities they serve for generations to come,” Chris Crockett, the newspapers’ publisher, said in a statement. “Local journalism is facing enormous economic pressures, and this effort is about building a sustainable future while preserving what has always defined our newspapers: local ownership, local voices and a commitment to the communities we serve.”
The Ellsworth American was founded in 1851 and the Mount Desert Islander in 2001. The Bangor Historian, a weekly publication focused on the region’s history, was launched by The Ellsworth American earlier this year.
“A community newspaper is one of a town’s most important institutions,” said Alan Baker, former publisher and owner of The Ellsworth American and Mount Desert Islander. “Its responsibility is to inform, to hold government accountable, and to tell the stories that define who we are.
“The creation of Acadia Newspaper Trust is an investment in that mission, assuring these newspapers will continue serving their communities with independence and integrity for future generations.”
The trust is aiming to acquire the publications by next summer.

title: 3 of Nolan Wells’ friends sue NFL Hall of Famer Terrell Owens for defamation
text:
JACKSON, Miss. (AP) — Three friends of Nolan Wells, a Black college student who went missing from a Mississippi island during a Fourth of July celebration and was later found dead, are suing NFL Hall of Famer Terrell Owens for defamation.
The lawsuit was among a handful of defamation claims the friends filed this week against content creators. They also previously indicated their intent to sue the Rev. Al Sharpton and “The View” co-host Sunny Hostin for comments they made while discussing Wells’ death.
The fathers of the three friends, who are under 21 and considered minors under Mississippi law, filed the federal lawsuit Monday on their behalf.
The lawsuit alleges Owens defamed the three friends after posting on X: “ARREST THEM IMMEDIATELY!!” Owens’ post also linked to an Instagram video, which theorized the three friends killed Wells and tampered with his phone, according to the lawsuit. The post was made days after a Mississippi grand jury declined to recommend charges in Wells’ death.
Owens has 1.2 million followers on X and had previously pledged $25,000 to a reward fund for information leading to an arrest and conviction in Wells’ death.
“Not only is he defaming them, he’s basically saying to the mob, get your pitchforks, get your torches,” said Edward Paltzik, a defamation and media attorney representing the three friends.
The Associated Press attempted to contact Owens through social media and SMAC Entertainment, which, according to its website, manages Owens, but did not immediately receive a response.
The three were part of a group of 30 friends, including Wells, who rode to Horn Island on three boats on the Fourth of July. Wells’ friends said Wells did not return to the mainland with them, choosing instead to stay behind to talk with a girl, a claim his family has disputed. His body was found two days later off the island’s coast.
Neither state nor independent autopsies have not determined Wells’ cause of death, though the grand jury found his death was “consistent with drowning.” Wells’ family and their lawyers disputed the grand jury’s findings, pointing to unexplained bruising on the back of his head and noting that his airways and stomach were devoid of water.
Images showing Wells with white friends the day he went missing fueled online speculation that racial dynamics played a role in his death.
Two of the three friends who are suing Owens were singled out online in part because they appear in a photo with Wells and one other friend on a boat, which was circulated on social media after his disappearance. The third called Wells’ mother and the U.S. Coast Guard to report Wells missing.

title: Harvest time in the State of Maine
text:
PEMBROKE — On Sunday, Oct. 11 at 1 p.m., the Pembroke Historical Society Lyceum’s “MaineSong” series will present historic songs of the Maine potato and oyster harvests.
Pembroke & Perry Schools music teacher Kris Paprocki will present “When the Taters Are All Dug” from Aroostook County, home of the Maine Potato, and the traditional Irish song “In the Garden Where the Praties Grow” which found its way throughout Maine and other parts of North America. With the revival of Maine’s oystering industry, and now that as the old folk saying has it “Oysters R in Season,” Stephen Sanfilippo, historian of songs of the maritime trades, will present “The Dredging Song” with his own musical setting. This obscure Scottish song was found in a newspaper clipping tucked into a book, now in the Pembroke Historical Society collection, that was once owned by William O. Hersey, Pembroke educator, diarist and historian.
The Pembroke Historical Society’s “MaineSong” Lyceum gatherings include performance, audience participation and discussions that lead from the local to the far corners of the world. The Oct. 11gathering is at the Pembroke Historical Society Museum. Admission is by donation. Family friendly and everyone is invited.
This is an all-volunteer event at a registered not-for-profit organization. The museum is located at the intersections of Front Street, Old County Road and Shore Road. For additional information, please write to lyceum@pembrokemainehistoricalsociety.org or phone at 207-726-4747.

title: New poll shows Jackson with lead in Senate race, Pingree with advantage in governor's race
text:
New poll shows Troy Jackson with lead in Maine's Senate race, Hannah Pingree with advantage in governor's race
A new survey from the survey research center at Marist University shows that Democratic candidate Troy Jackson has a slight lead in Maine's U.S. Senate race over Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins. The same Marist Poll also shows that Democrat Hannah Pingree has a double-digit lead in the race for Maine governor over Republican candidate Bobby Charles and independent State Sen. Rick Bennett.
The Marist Poll surveyed more than 1,500 registered Maine voters from Oct. 1-4, more than a week after ProPublica published a report about corruption allegations involving Collins — accusations that the senator and her campaign have vehemently denied.
According to the latest Marist Poll, Jackson (51%) had a four-point advantage over Collins (47%) among all surveyed voters. Among independents, Jackson (52%) had a seven-point advantage over Collins (45%). But voters older than 45 favored Collins (54%) over Jackson (44%), and 57% of all surveyed thought that Collins will win the race against Jackson (41%).
The poll found that Pingree (52%) had a 12-point lead over Charles (40%) in the governor's race, while Bennett polled at 6%. In addition, Pingree had an even bigger margin over Charles among independent voters with a 51% to 34% advantage, while Bennett gained six points (12%) among independents. The poll also found that Maine voters are nearly twice as likely to say Pingree (63%) will be victorious against Charles (34%).
The Marist Poll said that 44% of Maine voters surveyed reported that their congressional ballot is mainly a vote against President Donald Trump, while 16% said their ballot is mainly a vote for Trump and 39% said the president is not much of a factor in their vote. According to the poll, 59% of surveyed voters disapprove of the job Trump is doing while 40% approve the president's work.
The Marist Institute for Public Opinion said the poll results are statistically significant within ±3.8 percentage points. Click here to see the survey data.

title: Navigating differences in faith while supporting loved ones approaching the end of life
text:
(Aging Untold) — What happens when you and your loved one don’t share the same faith during their final days?
In this episode of The Aging Untold Podcast, our experts tackle one of the most painful, sensitive dynamics in end-of-life care: navigating clashing religious and spiritual beliefs.
When family members attempt to impose faith or force last-minute conversions, it often alienates relationships, drives up anxiety, and robs everyone of peace when comfort matters most.
Our panel breaks down how to set personal boundaries, navigate hospice and hospital chaplain visits, and prioritize presence over preaching so your loved one feels safe, heard, and supported.
According to AARP, about 80% of adults between 50 and 80 say their spiritual beliefs are important to them. At the same time, approximately 29% of Americans report no religious affiliation and are less likely to seek support from faith-based communities.
Watch this episode of The Aging Untold Podcast
Listen to the audio version of each episode
Respecting individual belief systems
Gerontologist and Aging Untold co-host Sam Cradduck said the key is honoring each person’s right to their own beliefs without imposing others’ views.
“You have to honor individual belief systems, and you have to honor their right to make their own choices and not impress your own,” Cradduck said.
Aging expert and Aging Untold co-host Amy O’Rourke said she has mixed feelings.
“If you’re really, really faithful and you really want everybody else to share your faith, you’re going to be the one that’s going to have to be extra, extra careful when you approach somebody that has a different view than yours, because it creates stress and anxiety, and it doesn’t allow room for the other person to really be where they are,” O’Rourke said.
She said people should hold onto their faith while being cautious about pushing it on others before understanding where that person stands.
Opening the conversation
Asking permission before starting a spiritual conversation can make a difference.
“Even opening up the conversation — would you like to have this conversation? Maybe they’ll say no. Maybe they’ll say yes,” O’Rourke said.
Or maybe they’ll ask about it later, aging-well coach and Aging Untold co-host Katherine Ambrose said.
Cradduck noted that religion and politics were historically considered taboo topics, but the issue is not that those conversations shouldn’t happen — it’s that people haven’t learned how to have them in a healthy way.
Asking someone what their thoughts are sets up the opportunity for conversation, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician and Aging Untold co-host, said.
“It’s open communication,” Rogers said.
Cradduck said a conversation about why the other person believes what they believe and how it brings them comfort also presents the opportunity to learn something new.
Faith differences at end of life
Cradduck said differing belief systems can become especially difficult when a loved one is nearing death.
“It’s really hard for family members sometimes to reconcile in themselves if their loved one is passing and they have a different belief system,” Cradduck said, describing a scenario in which an agnostic person is dying while a family member with strong religious beliefs tries to impose that faith.
“In doing so, you alienate that relationship,” Cradduck said.
Cradduck said family members who struggle with a loved one’s differing beliefs should seek guidance from their own spiritual counsel — a pastor, minister, or similar figure — rather than directing that pressure at the dying person.
“Don’t make them feel judged,” Rogers said. “You should not make them feel bad about what they believe. You need to be able to sit and listen and help them through their healing process, whatever that is.”
Ambrose raised the point of finding a way to hope and cope.
“Now, when it comes to taking action, what I see with a lot of people is the lack of confidence and that ‘faith it ‘til you make it’ is kind of play on ‘fake it to make it,’ like you just step into action, maybe not even quite knowing if you’re up to the task, but if you just take action and just trust that you’ll be equipped along the way, and by moving into action, it can, you know the truth will be revealed,” Ambrose said.
The value of listening
The hosts agreed that sometimes the most supportive role a person can play is simply listening and helping them through the healing process.
“Sometimes people just need to talk, and you just need to be empathetic. You don’t have to say anything. You just need to listen,” Rogers said.
O’Rourke added that reflecting on what has helped a person through difficult times in the past can be a useful tool, regardless of their specific belief system.

title: Who needs a win, and more Week 6 high school football storylines
text:
We talk a lot about the teams at the top of the Crabtree standings. This time of year, though, the games that define seasons are often not between the top teams but between those fighting for their lives.
So, what are some key showdowns this week that involve teams teetering on the brink? Let’s dive into that and Maine high school football’s other top storylines for Week 6.
Who needs a win?
Early in the season, many people tabbed Cheverus as a potential favorite in Class B. Instead, after a shocking loss Saturday against Gorham, the Stags are in last place at 1-4.
That means Cheverus would be on the outside looking in if the playoffs were to begin today. The Stags could use the points that would come with a win over Marshwood (5-0) on Friday. Otherwise, they’ll have to beat at least one of Deering or Biddeford in the final two weeks.
In Class C, York (1-4) is ninth in a statewide field that will send eight to the playoffs. The Wildcats would benefit from a win Friday against Class D Oak Hill (1-4). Belfast, meanwhile, is one spot behind Oak Hill in D South, and should the Raiders lose, the Lions have a chance to move up with a win over Madison.
In eight-man, a Large School North playoff berth might be on the line Saturday when Waterville (1-4) travels to Houlton (0-5). With both teams having tough schedules down the stretch, the winner will have the inside track to the No. 4 seed, while the loser is in peril.
If you think we forgot Class A, we didn’t — but with many key games remaining and an extra week on the schedule, these teams have more breathing room. Still, South Portland (3-2) could use a win Friday when it hosts Massabesic (4-1) or next week at Noble (2-3) as he tries to move higher than fifth place in the South.
Thursday night lights
With 11 of them having already taken place, Thursday games have been a fixture in 2026. That continues this week with five Thursday games, the most since a six-game slate back in Week 1.
A crossover clash in Freeport between Class C Wells (3-2) and Class D Freeport (4-1) highlights Thursday’s schedule. Other games feature Camden Hills (1-4) at Cony (4-1), Brewer (1-4) at Hermon (5-0), Poland (1-4) at Morse (3-2), and Traip Academy (1-4) at Old Orchard Beach (5-0).
If it seems there are more Thursday night games these days, that’s because there are. In all, 18 regular-season high school football games will be played on Thursdays in 2026. There were 12 Thursday games in 2025 and 13 in 2024. In 2023, there were only six.
Why? Dean Plante, Old Orchard Beach’s coach and a member of the Maine Principals’ Association Football Committee, believes it’s two-pronged. Sure, there’s an officiating shortage, but Plante also believes that, when OOB got permission from the MPA to open the 2019 season on a Thursday against Telstar, it started a trend.
“That was the first year of eight-man, so we wanted to showcase eight-man by having it as the first game of the season, and it kind of took off,” Plante said. “I think it’s cool; you get to be one of the only games — maybe the only game — and that gets a little exposure for the kids.”
Cony coach B.L. Lippert said the Maine Association of Football Officials asked his team to move either this week’s game or next week’s against Brunswick to a Thursday night. Because next week is senior night for the Rams, the team chose this one.
“I don’t know specifically how dire the referee shortage is, but it seems like that’s obviously an issue,” Lippert said. “It might not be 50-50 Thursday-Friday, but there might be 10 Thursday games a week next year, is what I’ve heard.”
Can the upstarts keep winning?
Every year, teams that weren’t on many radars at the start of the season capture the state’s attention. A few meet the mark in 2026: Massabesic, Biddeford, Maine Central Institute and Cape Elizabeth are all 4-1, and Lisbon is 3-2. So, what to expect from those teams in Week 6?
MCI, 2-7 a year ago, might have the toughest task of the five. The Huskies host defending Class D North champ Winslow (4-1) in a matchup between the top two teams in the region. The rivals had some fun Big 11 Conference battles between 2017-22.
Massabesic, which missed the playoffs at 3-6 last year, has the aforementioned clash with South Portland. That’s a challenging road showdown for the Mustangs against an opponent whose only losses were hard-fought defeats to Bonny Eagle and Thornton Academy — the top two teams in the Varsity Maine poll.
Cape Elizabeth, Biddeford and Lisbon all went 1-7 last year. Cape Elizabeth (at 3-2 Spruce Mountain) and Biddeford (at 3-2 Skowhegan) make long trips north to face tough opponents on Friday, while Lisbon hosts Mattanawcook Academy (2-3).

title: Don’t let Elon Musk buy Maine’s vote
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Thom Moore writes and consults in Scarborough. He is a member of Third Act.
The world’s richest person is funding Sen. Susan Collins’ campaign.
This is part of the GOP’s decades-long effort to make our government work for its wealthiest citizens. As Graham Platner noted, and Troy Jackson also appreciates, the wealthy mean to own everything and rent it to the rest of us. They already rent us the money to run our government, charging us a trillion dollars a year in interest. They should instead pay a fair share of the bills, about 24% of our GDP, especially those who made their money within our economy.
When we are paid less than we are worth, when staple prices are raised endlessly out of greed or because of unproductive wars and tariffs, when resulting inflation raises interest rates, money trickles upward.
Even when taxes are cut, deficits increase, benefits decrease and interest is paid by us to those who finance the debt, padding their estates at low risk. Those estates steadily appreciate in value from the upward trickling, and that unrealized income escapes taxation as it is passed to heirs by our wealthiest, most senior citizens.
But we must resist any impulse to make age an issue in this election, nor should we exploit, for political purposes, Sen. Collins’ exceptional seniority and respect among the most corporate-sponsored members of the U.S. Senate. She was influential in bringing defense work to Maine, but she also voted for the reduction of medical care and research support for working-class Mainers. Troy Jackson brings a fresh perspective on the kinds of development that create opportunities to keep Maine “the way life should be.”
We cannot ignore the current escalation in prices, driven by corporate profits, wars, tariffs and wasteful ego projects. Sen. Collins has done nothing to stop this. Maine’s domination by corporate utilities has caused our power costs to be among the highest in the nation. Accusations that renewable energy raises our costs are lies. Power sources get dialed back when supply exceeds demand, namely the most expensive ones, the gas plants. Who pays to oppose the transition to sustainable energy? The fuel industry and power utilities, that’s who.
Sen. Collins and the GOP oppose working-class collective bargaining and a fair minimum wage. Troy Jackson defends the right of employees to organize and assert their economic value. Maine has more than its fair share of rural poverty and hardship. The remedy for that is new businesses offering good jobs that pay a living wage. Troy Jackson understands that workers must often organize to win fair wages and working conditions from larger businesses.
Sen. Collins supported the obscene increase in the economic power of ICE. It is used to infiltrate our communities in the name of ferreting out, and in some cases assassinating, immigrants, whether properly documented or not. This is an intrusion into state and local affairs that Troy Jackson will not tolerate.
Sen. Collins supports the GOP belief that healthcare is a corporate profit center that is only for those who can afford it. They believe that profits should flow from prices determined by demand, rather than reflecting what is affordable. They do not think that the government should pay any costs. Healthcare is a trivial expense for the ultra-rich, but they want to limit what kinds of medical care everyone else can receive, including personal reproduction and body choices. Troy Jackson opposes these intrusions into privacy matters and accepts government responsibility to mitigate hardships where practical.
The government money that Sen. Collins has brought to Maine would continue to favor her corporate donors, at the expense of working-class Mainers. Troy Jackson would help working-class Mainers receive a fair share of the wealth that their work produces, in the form of higher wages and reduced expenses.

title: PTSD doesn’t expire: How trauma resurfaces as we age
text:
(Aging Untold) — Post-traumatic stress disorder, or PTSD, symptoms can become more noticeable later in life, especially during major life changes including retirement, illness or loss.
The Aging Untold experts are breaking down why trauma doesn’t simply fade with time, and what families and caregivers can do to recognize it.
PTSD is a body and brain still on alert
“PTSD is not just something bad happened,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. “It’s basically your body and your brain are still reacting to a danger as if it’s still present, even though it’s long been gone.”
Trauma is an “invisible suffering” that’s stored emotionally, neurologically and physically, Rogers said.
“The body’s trying to move past something that the brain is not allowing. So in a sense, your body will express what your mind does suppress,” Rogers said.
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said trauma does not expire and PTSD is the past showing up and affecting your present.
PTSD is often associated with veterans and first responders, but Cradduck said it also affected health care workers who went through the COVID-19 pandemic.
“There is still a PTSD response,” Cradduck said. “That’s why we lost so many good workers from that.”
A car accident can leave a lasting physical response
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, described her own reaction after being in a serious car accident.
“My husband has had to adjust to how I’m riding in the car now, because if we get too close to a car, I get anxiety,” O’Rourke said.
Understanding a person’s full life story can explain behavior that might otherwise be misread, O’Rourke said.
She had a client who was easily irritated and startled and had to watch the front door. When he told her about his childhood, she said, she understood.
“And the more he talked, the more horrified I became at the abuse and the trauma that he went through, and it helped me really understand him and his behavior, because you could have written it off to dementia or depression or old age. We don’t always first think of trauma,” O’Rourke said.
Katherine Ambrose was also in a serious accident and said she feels more nervous in traffic than she used to be.
“I found myself, as I’m getting older, being a little more concerned in traffic and being a little more reactive,” Ambrose said. “I like to think I’m not a nervous person, but for some reason, I’m noticing a change.”
The brain stays in protective mode
Rogers said the brain’s instinct is to guard and stay in a “survival and protective mode.”
“You put up your guard, you stay in the defense until you feel like the danger is gone,” Rogers said.
That stress response keeps the body in fight-or-flight mode.
“You cannot repair or heal when you’re in fight or flight,” Rogers said.
Therapies some people turn to for relief
Ambrose said some people believe trauma and pain can become locked into the body, leading them to seek out yoga, massage, acupuncture or contrast therapy such as heat and cold treatments.
“I love that you’re seeing more and more, in many cities, different studios and clinics that you can go to for different types of therapy to see if that might help,” Ambrose said.
O’Rourke pointed to trauma-informed therapy, including EMDR, as another option.
“My goddaughter is a trauma therapist ... and she’s been wildly successful in this small town in Washington,” O’Rourke said. “For some reason, there’s a lot of trauma ... people who are suffering with trauma.”
Cradduck brought up the stresses of being part of an information community where everything’s 24-7.
“Our kids are suffering from trauma, and the anxiety levels are increasing way more now than ever before because there’s no off button, there’s no reset, there’s no rest and repair going on,” Cradduck said.
Cradduck added that service animals shouldn’t be overlooked.
“Don’t discount service dogs, don’t discount our service pets, and how rewarding they can be and how much help they can be,” she said. “Just feeling purpose and feeling connection again.”
Trauma doesn’t have to be dramatic to count
Rogers said trauma isn’t limited to major events like combat or accidents.
“I think sometimes the definition of trauma to everyone, they think it has to be something dramatic,” Rogers said. “Even for children, adverse childhood events — maybe your parents went through a divorce, or somebody went to jail. That’s still traumatic. I think we have to really look at what trauma means to different people, and their body is going to react to that differently.”
Ambrose said younger generations are sometimes judged harshly by older generations who compare today’s pressures to their own upbringing.
“They don’t understand the real pressure on kids,” Ambrose said.
Rogers said everyone has triggers and urged people in a caregiving role to know what the triggers are for the person they are caring for.
“If you’re taking care of a parent and they’re having signs of being easily irritated, think trauma also, and get them help with that, because it doesn’t come up. It’s not something that family members think of.” O’Rourke added.
Key takeaways
- PTSD is a present-tense reaction, not a memory. The brain and body respond as though a past danger is still happening today.
- Symptoms are often mistaken for dementia or depression in older adults, especially irritability or being easily startled.
- Keep a calm routine. Routines calm the body and help manage powerful sensory triggers.

title: Victim’s mother reacts to Christa Pike being ‘conscious, speaking’ after botched execution, report says
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - The mother of Christa Pike’s victim spoke out after her attorneys announced Tuesday that Pike is conscious nearly a week after her botched execution.
Pike, who is convicted of the 1995 torture and murder of Colleen Slemmer, was supposed to be executed via lethal injection in Tennessee last Wednesday. However, after receiving two doses of what should have been lethal amounts of pentobarbital, she survived.
May Martinez, Slemmer’s mother, said she had a feeling Pike would survive, according to WBIR. She also said she does not think that Tennessee will make another attempt to execute her daughter’s killer.
Pike was left unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital following the failed execution. However, on Oct. 6, her attorneys reported that she is now awake and speaking.
“Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery,” they said.
When asked what her preference would be for what happens to Pike next, Martinez responded, “It doesn’t matter what I think.”
“They’re going to do what they’re going to do,” she reportedly said.
Whether the state can proceed with another execution attempt remains to be seen.
“Given what we know now, how she responds to lethal injection, and given what happened to her, Christa Pike’s lawyers have a pretty good argument that it would be a violation of the Eighth Amendment to execute her using [lethal injection],” Vanderbilt Law School professor Christopher Slobogin said.
A press conference with Pike’s attorneys will be held on Wednesday. The time for that press conference has yet to be confirmed.
Pike was one of three people found to be involved in the 1995 torture and killing of Slemmer on the University of Tennessee-Knoxville campus.
Pike’s boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, was also found guilty of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit first-degree murder. He received life in prison rather than the death penalty because he was 17 at the time.
Shadolla Peterson, who was 18 during the crime, was convicted of being an accessory and received parole after she became an informant to police.

title: Mr. Drew and His Animals Too in Poland to close at the end of the month
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
After nine months at its new location in Poland, Mr. Drew and His Animals Too will close its doors for good Oct. 31, owner Drew Desjardins said in a Facebook post.
Desjardins posted the news Wednesday morning calling it a “very difficult decision.”
“So this is where we are at — sad, anxious and heavy hearted, but I can say with confidence, that we are very proud of what we created and accomplished and there will be no other place like it,” he wrote.
Desjardins announced in May 2025 that his collection of more than 200 rescued reptiles, amphibians, insects, birds and more would be moving to Poland after his lease was not renewed at the Lewiston Mall.
The public education exhibit, which included hands-on experiences and a geological center with gemstones, bones and fossils, officially opened in Poland in early January.
According to the Facebook post, several factors played into this decision to close the Poland location, including the financial stress of moving from Lewiston.
He had hoped the new location would draw people to that area.
“We love having a facility as it was a dream come true and we truly wanted to make Poland a destination rather than a drive-through community, with the education center to be around for generations to come, far beyond myself, but alas, that will not be,” he wrote.
Desjardins made it clear they are not seeking donations to keep going.
“Please know Mrs. Drew and I have accepted this decision and we are NOT seeking a ‘Hail Mary’, any public financial support or a GoFundMe,” Desjardins wrote. “We accept the facts the economy is bad and simply put, we are not business people, we simply care about our animals and making people happy in this sad world we are living in.”
While the Poland location is closing, Desjardins plans to continue traveling the state with a mobile exhibit as he has done in the past. Much of his collection will stay with the family at their Poland home, while others will go to educational facilities and sanctuaries Desjardins trusts, he said.
“I am continuing to book birthdays, public schools, homeschools, community events, Scouting and more,” he wrote.
Until the closing, Mr. Drew and His Animals Too will be open every day through Oct. 31 from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Fans of Mr. Drew’s were commenting on the post Wednesday.
“Your effect has been undeniable,” a resident of Dresden Mills wrote. “Education, respect, humor. I cherish my trip to your place. You helped me with fear of spiders! I held your tarantulas!”
“Encounters with snakes at Mr. Drew’s led me to want to foster with HerpHaven Reptile Rescue and Sanctuary and ultimately adopt a hognose!” wrote another resident.
“The educational outreach is at the heart of your program,” one fan wrote. “We had the pleasure of your company a few years ago at the Arts Center in Waterville. It was an amazing experience and many of us were transformed to an appreciation of animals we had formerly been afraid of.”

title: New nonprofit looks to raise $1 million to preserve Down East newspapers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A new nonprofit organization is seeking to preserve the future of three local newspapers in Down East Maine.
The Acadia Newspaper Trust is looking to raise $1 million to transition The Ellsworth American, the Mount Desert Islander and the Bangor Historian from private to nonprofit stewardship. The money will be used to purchase the papers and cover initial operating costs, according to a news release from the trust on Wednesday.
“We want to make sure these newspapers remain firmly rooted in the communities they serve for generations to come,” Chris Crockett, the newspapers’ publisher, said in a statement. “Local journalism is facing enormous economic pressures, and this effort is about building a sustainable future while preserving what has always defined our newspapers: local ownership, local voices and a commitment to the communities we serve.”
The Ellsworth American was founded in 1851 and the Mount Desert Islander in 2001. The Bangor Historian, a weekly publication focused on the region’s history, was launched by The Ellsworth American earlier this year.
“A community newspaper is one of a town’s most important institutions,” said Alan Baker, former publisher and owner of The Ellsworth American and Mount Desert Islander. “Its responsibility is to inform, to hold government accountable, and to tell the stories that define who we are.
“The creation of Acadia Newspaper Trust is an investment in that mission, assuring these newspapers will continue serving their communities with independence and integrity for future generations.”
The trust is aiming to acquire the publications by next summer.

title: Jailhouse witness testifies Raymond Brown described Linda Maxwell’s death
text:
MACHIAS, Maine (WABI) - A jailhouse witness testified Wednesday that Raymond Brown, 67, described trying to have sex with an 18-year-old Linda Maxwell, holding her underwater after an argument and leaving her body at a boat landing. The witness also said Brown told him Maxwell’s clothing was later burned.
The testimony came on the third day of Brown’s murder trial. Maxwell, of Calais, was found dead in August 1984 after a night out with friends and her boyfriend at the time.
The defense questioned the witness’s credibility, citing a recorded call in which he said he might lie if his bail request was not granted.
Earlier Wednesday, a cousin of Brown testified that Brown told him his pants were wet after Maxwell’s body was found, that he had burned his clothes in a barrel and that he was frustrated with the investigation. The cousin said Brown also told him he had told police his clothes were dry.
Another person who was with Maxwell’s group the night she disappeared testified about her knowledge of Maxwell’s high school ring. Asked whether she had told police she knew another man had the ring, she said yes. Asked whether that was based on her own observation, she said no.
A former Maine State Police detective testified about Brown’s 1984 account of taking Maxwell to Milltown and returning to Calais. The defense questioned why police did not search Brown’s burn barrel and challenged how investigators considered possible scenarios.
Yet another witness, a Maine game warden testified that, based on the conditions he reviewed, it would be essentially impossible for a body to travel 14 miles down the St. Croix River.
Both sides said they expect to wrap up the case in the coming days.

title: Community rallies for 12-year-old girl killed after shots fired in fight over parking spot
text:
BALTIMORE (WJZ) - A Baltimore community is rallying for peace after a 12-year-old girl was killed when police say shots were fired during a fight over a parking spot near a youth football game.
Hundreds of people walked through the West Baltimore streets on Monday to remember 12-year-old Khloe Ishway, support her family and demand an end to the violence that took her life.
“Just remember her as a person, a loving person, a good family member, good sister, good cousin, good friend. Just want everyone to remember her,” said Khloe’s mother, Kristin Reese.
Baltimore Police say two men apparently got into an argument over a parking spot Saturday at Leon Day Park, which was packed for a youth football game. Shots were fired, and Khloe was caught in the crossfire. She was taken to the hospital, where she was pronounced dead.
Four other people – a 23-year-old man, a 25-year-old woman, a 28-year-old man and a 35-year-old woman – were injured.
At Monday’s rally, Reese had a strong message to anyone who knows who shot her daughter. No arrests had been made at the time.
“You don’t say nothing, then you must be a part of it, and being a part of it, you’re a clown,” she said.
The tragedy has left the youth football community shattered, asking how children can be kept safe while simply doing what they love. They hope Khloe’s name lives on and inspires positive change.
“May it live on. May some laws get changed. May security be at some football games, so these kids who aren’t in the streets, who don’t have guns, can play safe,” family friend Kevin Miller said.
On Tuesday, police announced the arrest of 23-year-old Tyree Reynolds in connection to Khloe’s death. He is facing charges including murder, attempted murder, assault, reckless endangerment and other offenses.

title: Jay Leach remembered as an architect of UMaine hockey’s rise to prominence
text:
The University of Maine men’s hockey team will be looking for a 21st NCAA Tournament berth this season, in the program’s 50th year.
The program has been among the nation’s elite, and one of the people who put it on the map was former coach Jay Leach.
Leach died on Sept. 30 in Saco at age 75 after having dementia for years.
When the late Shawn Walsh was hired to take UMaine into the Hockey East era before the league’s inaugural 1984-85 season, he chose Leach as one of his assistants.
And it will forever go down as one of the best decisions he ever made.
Leach was instrumental in recruiting several of the players who would form the foundation of the teams that earned UMaine its first ever NCAA Tournament appearance in 1986-87 and its initial Frozen Four appearance the following year before he moved on to become an assistant coach with the National Hockey League’s Hartford Whalers.
“He was the perfect assistant coach,” said former UMaine All-American defenseman and 17-year National Hockey League veteran Eric Weinrich. “He was a father figure to all of us. He treated all of us like we were one of his (children).”
“He meant everything to me,” said former Black Bear center and 1987-88 Hockey East Rookie of the Year Mario Thyer. “He was the only reason I came to Maine.
“I remember him coming up to Montreal and talking to me, my mother and my brother. He was always very pleasant. My mother and brother didn’t speak much English. He gave me the opportunity to come to Maine. He shaped my life and not just in hockey.”
Former University of Maine All-American defenseman and New York Islanders head coach Jack Capuano said Leach had a prominent role in him coming to UMaine.
“When he recruited me, he was totally transparent and honest. You couldn’t meet a better guy and one of the main reasons I went to Maine was the trust factor,” Capuano said. “He knew the game inside and out but, with the generational players of today, you had to be able to communicate and develop relationships with the players and that’s what Jay did.”
Capuano said Leach also cared about the families of his players and followed the careers of his players even after they left Maine and eventually retired from hockey.
Weinrich and Capuano mentioned that Leach would come on the ice before practice and play games with the players.
“He was great to be on the ice with,” Capuano said. “He’d mess around with all of us. Shawn was more serious, but Jay was a little bit opposite and that’s what you needed, that’s what kept everything together.”
”We’d play these fun games, and he would always be involved,” said Weinrich. “I loved being on the ice with him.”
After leaving UMaine for the Whalers, Leach would go on to compile an impressive resume that included head coaching jobs with the American Hockey League’s Springfield Indians and Hershey Bears and assistant coaching jobs with the NHL’s Whalers, Los Angeles Kings, Atlanta Thrashers, New Jersey Devils and Washington Capitals as well the AHL’s Portland Pirates.
He was also an assistant coach at Merrimack College and for five United States teams in the World Championships.
In 2013, he returned to UMaine after being hired as an assistant coach by the late Red Gendron. He would spend four seasons with Gendron.
“He was the architect behind the first teams that took Maine’s program to national prominence,” Gendron told the Bangor Daily News in 2013. “I’ve talked to a lot of guys who played in that era, and they said Jay Leach was the biggest reason they came to Maine. He brings an aura with him.”
As a result of his time spent in Atlanta, Leach got involved with the youth hockey programs in the area, and one of the players he coached was Mitch Fossier from Alpharetta, Georgia.
After Leach returned to UMaine, Fossier received a call from him inviting him to come on a recruiting visit to UMaine. Leach convinced Gendron to give him a full scholarship, Fossier said.
“I never would have ended up at Maine if it wasn’t for Leachy,” said Fossier, who was a two-time All-Hockey East selection and is tied for 30th on the school’s all-time scoring list with 128 points in 134 games. “He cared so much about the game and loved the game, but he made sure he took care of you as a person, first. It was such a privilege to get to know him and play for him. He was such a great man.”
Leach was also known for his sense of humor.
“It was hilarious to be around him. He was always making jokes,” Fossier said. “He was a funny fellow.”
Ben Guite, a former UMaine standout and NHLer and now men’s hockey coach at Bowdoin College, had just retired from playing pro hockey when he landed his first coaching job as an assistant at UMaine in Leach’s first season back (2013-14).
And Leach became his coaching guru.
“Red said just follow this guy around. He will show you the ropes. He will introduce you to people and teach you what it takes,” Guite said. “Jay was a big mentor of mine. He was a good and genuine person, and he connected with everyone. When he walked into a rink, everyone would bend over backwards to help him because of the way he treated people.”
“Recruits knew Jay would teach them the game and how to do things the right way in order to get them to that next level,” added Guite, who also mentioned Leach’s sense of humor.
“We shared a lot of laughter. We were getting on a flight from Philadelphia to Boston one time, and it was really crowded,” Guite said. “Everyone was ticked off. Jay said, ‘You need a shoehorn to get in here.’ The place erupted. He had that touch and timing and effect on people.”
Leach was an outdoorsman who loved to hunt and fish and had several ties to UMaine.
His parents, Chuck and Mary, were UMaine graduates, and his mother, the former Mary Healey, was from Eastport. His late younger brother Jon played on the first four UMaine teams under Jack Semler. And one of his three children, Heather, was a UMaine swimmer.
In his obituary, Leach requested that in lieu of flowers, well-wishers would consider making a donation to the men’s hockey team via the Black Bear Student Experience Fund.
He will be sorely missed.

title: South Portland having municipal ballots reprinted to fix typo on bond question
text:
The city of South Portland is having municipal ballots reprinted after a vendor informed them of a typo.
The ballots accurately stated the bond principal and estimated interest of the city’s public safety bond question, the city announced this week, but the total of the two numbers is listed inaccurately.
“While we submitted the correct total of $150,398,500, they mistakenly transposed a number and listed $105,398,500 on the ballot,” the city said in a written statement.
The ballots will be reprinted free of charge and are expected to arrive by the end of the week, the city said.
A notice will be mailed to those who voted early Monday, before the error was discovered, and those who received an absentee ballot containing the error. The inaccurate ballots will still be counted as valid, the city said, but voters may contact the city clerk’s office if they feel the error impacted their vote.
“For anyone who has already voted and would like to change their vote due to the printer’s error, City Clerk’s office staff will mark your original ballot as spoiled and issue you a new ballot,” the city said. “The clerk’s office tracks all spoiled ballots and errors to account for every ballot issued.”
Early voting at South Portland City Hall will continue as normal prior to the new ballots arriving, the city said. Voters will be informed of the error at the polls, and a notice is posted in voting booths.
Voters with questions or in need of assistance can contact City Clerk Jessica Hughes at [email protected] or 207-767-3201.
Meanwhile, state officials said Wednesday that several western Maine towns received incorrect ballots this week that excluded at least one candidate for the Maine House of Representatives running in this November’s election. The Department of the Secretary of State said that was because of a packaging error and that only “a small number” of incorrect ballots were distributed.

title: Mother dies, baby critical after being pushed from 15th-floor balcony, police say
text:
NEW YORK (WABC) - A young mother died and her 8-month-old daughter was critically injured after police say they were pushed from a 15th-floor balcony in New York City.
Officers with the New York City Police Department responded around 3:30 a.m. Tuesday to an apartment building in the Bronx, where they found 23-year-old Nathaly Ramirez and her 8-month-old daughter on the ground outside the building.
Both the mother and baby were taken to the hospital. Ramirez was pronounced dead, and her daughter remains in critical condition.
Even in her final moments, Ramirez’s motherly instincts kicked in as officials say she wrapped her baby in a tight embrace, likely cushioning the impact of the fall.
Police are investigating Ramirez’s death as a homicide. Officers spent hours examining a 15th-floor balcony for evidence while canvassing for surveillance video and additional witnesses. They are also looking to speak with Ramirez’s ex-boyfriend.
Friends say Ramirez was devoted to her daughter.
“She was very happy to be a mom. She’s a new mom, and the baby was very happy,” one friend said.
The investigation is ongoing. No arrests have been announced.

title: Sacred Heart Church in Portland to hold its final mass in late October
text:
Sacred Heart Church in Portland to hold its final mass, future of property undecided
A historic Catholic Church in Portland is preparing for its final mass; parish leaders say they can't pay the $6 million needed to fix up the Sacred Heart Church and staying at the property is "no longer feasible."
Sacred Heart Church in Portland to hold its final mass, future of property undecided
A historic Catholic Church in Portland is preparing for its final mass; parish leaders say they can't pay the $6 million needed to fix up the Sacred Heart Church and staying at the property is "no longer feasible."
Sacred Heart Church in Portland will hold its final mass on Oct. 25 as the parish prepares to vacate the building due to what leaders called significant structural concerns and the high cost of needed repairs.
Bishop James T. Ruggieri will lead the mass at 11 a.m. at the church on 65 Mellen St. alongside Rev. Seamus P. Griesbach.
The Portland Peninsula and Island Parishes announced Wednesday that the decision to leave the church and parish rectory comes after professional assessments of the property's condition. Parish leaders say there are issues with the church's facade and masonry and that the estimated repair and restorations costs are over $6 million. Leaders said the cost is beyond what the parish is able to pay and concluded that staying in the church is not feasible.
“We are heartbroken by what has happened to this beautiful church and by the reality of this situation,” Griesbach said. “My first commitment has been to care for the people of this parish.”
Parish leaders said they have spent months working with parishioners, diocesan officials and a planning committee to make arrangements for the transition and preserve the parish's ministries.
Beginning in November, a Spanish-language mass will be held at 1 p.m. at the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception in Portland. A French-English mass will be held at 11:15 a.m. at St. Pius X Church in Portland. Other existing masses will continue at parishes around the Portland peninsula.
"We've definitely made this building, this church, our home," commented parishioner Eduardo Anzurez. "But for us Hispanics, the feeling of home is found within the people."
The parish also is working to find a new location for its food pantry, which serves more than 150 families each week.
"We've served many, many, diverse communities over the many years that we've been open and that that mission won't stop for any of us," added parishioner Kimberly MacDonald. "We will continue to to serve in that way."
The future of the Sacred Heart property is still unclear. Parish officials said the building and surrounding property will be secured while decisions about the site are considered in the coming months.
Sacred Heart Church was completed in 1915 and has been a center of worship and community life in Portland for more than a century.
Ruggieri said the closing of the building would not end the parish's legacy.
“While we grieve the loss of a beloved place of worship, we also give thanks for the extraordinary legacy of faith that Sacred Heart Church has left in Portland,” Ruggieri said. “That legacy does not end with the closing of a building. It lives on in the people whose lives have been formed there and in the ministries that continue to serve our community."
