title: Christa Pike survived 2 doses of an execution drug. How is that possible?
text:
(AP) - Christa Pike regaining consciousness and speaking a week after receiving two doses of execution drugs in Tennessee has astonished even some medical professionals and left many people wondering: How did she survive?
Attorneys for Pike, 50, called her recovery “medically unprecedented” after she was placed on a ventilator following the bungled Sept. 30 attempt to make her the first woman put to death in Tennessee in 200 years. On Wednesday, they said Pike was confused, “speaking limitedly” and could not move her arms, one of which had a blood clot.
Pike, who was convicted in the 1995 torture and killing of classmate Colleen Slemmer, is the only person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Many details of the execution process remain secretive, and Tennessee officials say they are investigating what went wrong.
Still, medical experts raised a few possibilities that could explain how Pike was able to survive, including the potential drug quality and the placement of IV lines. Tennessee’s executioners had difficulties earlier this year with IV lines for another execution, leading to it being called off.
Only a small amount of the drug may have entered her bloodstream
The 5-gram dose of pentobarbital used in executions is many more times the amount that should put someone in a medical coma, said Dr. Jonathan I. Groner, a retired pediatric general surgeon at Ohio State University College of Medicine who has studied lethal injections.
“The fact that she woke, on one hand, says she got really little of it into her system. So that’s kind of shocking,” Groner said. “It says how badly they botched the execution.”
At high doses, the potent barbiturate should make a person lose consciousness and stop breathing.
Groner said the IV might have been placed improperly, or Pike’s veins could have been fragile and ruptured, causing the drug to seep into the surrounding tissue instead of flowing through the bloodstream. Pike’s attorneys have said she was poked with needles at least seven times in the state’s death chamber and that she has a blood disorder that makes it tough to get needles into her veins.
Sourcing of drugs for executions is shrouded in secrecy
Another possible problem could be the drug quality, said Michaela Almgren, a South Carolina pharmacist and educator who has consulted on several lethal injection cases.
Many major pharmaceutical companies refuse to supply drugs for lethal injections, which has raised questions about how states get them. Court orders have revealed that some states have turned to compounding pharmacies, which create custom drugs from raw ingredients and operate with less regulatory oversight.
Tennessee does not disclose its drug supplier and has not said where Pike’s supply came from. Almgren said that makes it difficult to track if a drug was prepared, tested, handled and administered properly.
That also means the public may never know exactly what happened in Pike’s case.
Pike’s attorneys asked a court to require the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence, including drug lot numbers, communications and other material from the attempted execution. A judge told prison officials on Wednesday that they must preserve “anything that was in the actual room.”
Outgoing Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has paused executions and ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred.” It’s unclear whether the state will try executing Pike again.
Hospital treatment likely involved flushing the drug from her system
Before the execution attempt, Pike’s attorneys told courts and prison officials that she had medical conditions that could complicate a lethal injection and make it agonizing.
Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike’s legal team, said Pike has a blood-clotting disorder that causes her body to produce an excess of platelets. Her lawyers had argued that the condition could cause clotting at injection sites or bleeding that could affect her lungs.
State protocol calls for a second dose of pentobarbital if the first doesn’t result in death, but it doesn’t spell out what to do if an inmate survives the second injection.
The attempted execution got underway around 7:30 p.m. At some point Pike appeared to lose consciousness, but she could be heard breathing until media were escorted from the witness room at 8:53 p.m. An ambulance arrived at 9:14 p.m. and took Pike to a hospital.
Once there, doctors likely tried to stabilize her breathing, checked how much pentobarbital was in her system and worked to quickly flush it out, said Dr. Michael Baden, the former chief medical examiner of New York City.
Pike’s lawyers said the failed attempt left her arms burned and blistered. She was unconscious and on a ventilator for several days.
“She was very fortunate that there was enough (pentobarbital) to put her into a deep sleep, but they were able to keep her breathing going and they were able to start flushing it out,” Baden said.
___
Associated Press writers Kim Chandler in Montgomery, Alabama, and Kristin M. Hall in Nashville contributed reporting.

title: America’s ‘Wonderland of Rocks’ one step away from becoming nation’s newest national park
text:
America’s ‘Wonderland of Rocks’ one step away from becoming nation’s newest national park
The United States is one step away from adding a 64th national park.
Chiricahua National Monument could soon become Chiricahua National Park, following a yearslong effort to redesignate the protected rugged mountain landscape in southeastern Arizona.
The Senate passed the bipartisan Chiricahua National Park Act on Sept. 30. A signature from President Donald Trump would make it official.
If the legislation is signed, Chiricahua would join Grand Canyon, the Petrified Forest and Saguaro to become Arizona’s fourth national park.
“Chiricahua is one of Arizona’s most extraordinary places. Designating it as our state’s fourth national park will protect this remarkable landscape for generations and bring new visitors and economic opportunities to southeastern Arizona,” said Sen. Mark Kelly, one of the authors of the legislation.
Chiricahua is best known for its “Wonderland of Rocks,” a maze of tall pinnacles, columns and balanced boulders.
The formations began as volcanic ash and debris from a massive eruption about 27 million years ago, then took shape as the rock fractured and eroded.
The Chiricahua Mountains rise above surrounding desert grasslands and support a varied mix of plants and wildlife.
The area also holds a long human history, including archaeological evidence of Indigenous communities and ties to Chiricahua Apache history. President Calvin Coolidge established the monument in 1924 to protect its distinctive landscape.
A national park is generally established by Congress to protect a broad landscape, while a national monument is designated to protect a nationally significant resource.
A national park label typically brings more visitors and economic opportunities.
The last new national park was designated in 2020, as West Virginia's New River Gorge National River was renamed New River Gorge National Park and Preserve.

title: The plague never went away. Cases are reported in parts of Africa and the US nearly every year
text:
The plague never went away. Cases are reported in parts of Africa and the US nearly every year
The plague, the rare bacterial infection infamously known for killing tens of millions in 14th-century Europe, never went away. It is now easily treated with antibiotics.
Since the 1990s, most human cases have been reported in Africa, especially Congo and Madagascar, according to the World Health Organization.
There are an average of about seven human cases per year in the U.S., according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, mostly in rural areas of the American West.
A worker at a plague research institute in Siberia recently died of pneumonia. The case has raised alarm in Russia after unconfirmed media reports suggested she might have died of pneumonic plague. Russian authorities say testing showed no evidence of plague, but the research institute has been quarantined.
"People think the plague is gone, it was something that occurred 500 years ago. It's not. It's here amongst us," said Simon Clarke of the University of Reading in the U.K. "Unless you get rid of those wild animals, which of course is not possible, then you're not going to get rid of the bacteria."
Surprised to hear the plague is still around? Here's what to know.
Pneumonic plague and the more well-known bubonic plague – also called the Black Death — are caused by the same bacteria, called Yersinia pestis.
The bacteria spread naturally among rodents like prairie dogs and rats. Fleas that jump from infected animals and bite people can spread the disease.
The bubonic plague is the most common form of the infection. It causes painfully swollen lymph nodes that are most commonly found in the groin, armpit and neck, called buboes. Other symptoms include sudden high fever and chills, headaches, and pain in the abdomen, legs and arms, according to the Cleveland Clinic.
There are two other forms of the plague: pneumonic plague, which can be caused by inhaling the bacteria, infects the lungs. Septicemic plague is an infection in the bloodstream. Both are fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization.
Bubonic plague will often advance and turn into the other two forms of plague if untreated.
Other than bites from infected fleas, people can also get plague by touching infected bodily fluids, so health experts recommend taking extra care when handling dead or sick animals.
The plague can also spread through the respiratory droplets of someone who has pneumonic plague.
"If you cough, you can spread it to another person, but that doesn't travel very far," said Dr. Glenn Wortmann, MedStar Washington Hospital Center. "So you really need to be in face-to-face contact with that person to get pneumonic plague."
That's why "the chance of this spreading widely in Russia and then extending here to the U.S. will not happen," he said.
The plague was never eradicated, but we've gotten better at preventing its spread and treating it in humans.
When treated early with antibiotics, the plague can be cured. The key is to get to a doctor fast — otherwise the plague can be deadly.
There is a vaccine, but the WHO only recommends it for people who are at high risk of infection, like laboratory and healthcare workers. But there isn't strong evidence that vaccines can work against the pneumonic form.
There's no plague vaccine available in the U.S.
AP video journalist Javier Arciga contributed to this story from San Diego.

title: Christian school employee charged with sexually assaulting student
text:
ST. CROIX COUNTY, Wis. (WEAU/Gray News) - A man is accused of sexually assaulting two students he met while working as a school employee in Minnesota.
Derrick Pfeffer, 42, is charged with 10 felonies in St. Croix County, Wisconsin:
- Repeated sexual assault of the same child (at least three violations of first- or second-degree sexual assault)
- Three counts of child enticement for sexual contact
- Three counts of sexual assault of a child by a person who works or volunteers with children
- Soliciting a child for prostitution
- Grooming a child for sexual activity by a person in a position of trust

title: Harpist brings calm to hospital patients
text:
MYRTLE BEACH, S.C. (Aging Untold) — A harpist is offering quiet comfort to patients and families at McLeod Seacoast Hospital, playing every Thursday, the hospital’s busiest day for same-day surgery.
Peg Mann is part of the hospital’s volunteer and student services program. She has played the harp there for more than a year.
A new sound for the waiting room
Volunteer manager Peggy Skudera, who hired Mann as the harpist, said she was initially unsure about the idea.
“I wasn’t sure a harp was the best place to be in a hospital because my thought was, next stop is heaven,” Skudera said.
Skudera said watching Mann play shows her connection to the instrument.
“When you see her play it, you can see she is so in tune and so married to that harp,” Skudera said. “It’s absolutely amazing that she doesn’t know what’s going on around her. She doesn’t know all the people are listening. All the people that are looking at her.”
Playing from the background
Mann said she prefers not to be the center of attention while she plays.
“And I like it because you’re just the background,” Mann said. “You’re not the center of attention. That’s not my cup of tea.”
Mann plays relaxing and religious music on the harp, plucking each string. Her favorite song is “Angel’s Hymn.”
“I like to play relaxing music here, some religious music,” Mann said.
Mann said she also plays piano and organ. She added the harp to her repertoire in 2005 and continues harp lessons three times a month. She has also played at weddings and performed in church.
“This is what I like to do,” Mann said.
A full hospital shift
Mann starts her shift at 5:30 a.m., escorting patients and pushing the comfort cart before she plays the harp. She also takes breaks to visit with waiting families.
“Either they come up and visit, or I take the time to go and visit with them too,” Mann said. “I get lots of hugs and kisses.”
Skudera said Mann has become part of the McLeod family.
“We could not be happier to have her here,” Skudera said.
Mann said she receives something in return for her time at the hospital.
“I feel like I have new friends every day when I go home,” Mann said.

title: Here’s what’s on the ballot in Freeport
text:
Freeport voters will decide in November whether to approve a controversial temporary boat launch and vote to fill three Town Council seats and two school board seats.
Election Day voting will take place at the Freeport High School gymnasium, and absentee ballots and in-person early voting are available now at Town Hall.
Here’s what’s on the local ballot in Freeport.
ISLAND ROVER REFERENDUM
A citizens’ initiative will ask residents if they would approve a temporary boat launch in the zoning district containing 0 Shore Drive, the planned site to launch the ship Island Rover.
Harold Arndt started building the Island Rover more than 30 years ago using scrap materials he got through his job at Bath Iron Works. Since then, it’s been the source of lawsuits, ownership debates and conflict between the town, neighbors and Arndt and his supporters.
Opponents have said that launching the 80-ton schooner would have a negative impact on the environment. Arndt’s supporters say it’s time that the issue was finally resolved.
This is the second time a citizens’ group has circulated a petition aimed at launching the Rover. In June, they failed to gain enough valid signatures to get the issue on the ballot.
TOWN COUNCIL
Two district seats and one at-large seat are up for grabs on the council.
At-large: Joanna Benoit
Joanna Benoit, the council chairperson, is running for reelection to her at-large post. In her responses to the Press Herald Voter Guide, Benoit said she wants to continue supporting housing and economic development, preserve the working waterfront and ensure transparent municipal processes. A Freeport resident of six years, Benoit said she wants people to be able to afford to live and stay in town.
District 2: James DeGrandpre, Steven Doran
James DeGrandpre and Steven Doran are running to replace Eric Smith in the District 2 seat.
DeGrandpre is a former school board member and has lived in town for 58 years. He said Freeport faces an affordability challenge, but a big opportunity for the town is the “smart, engaged people of Freeport and the many organizations that make Freeport a better place.” His priorities also include education, developing downtown and ensuring elderly residents can age in place.
Doran did not respond to the Voter Guide survey.
District 3: Matthew Pillsbury
Matthew Pillsbury is seeking reelection to the District 3 seat and is unopposed. He did not respond to the Voter Guide.
RSU 5 SCHOOL BOARD
Two candidates, Anna Child and Anthony McElligott, are running for two open seats for Regional School Unit 5 board, which covers the towns of Freeport, Pownal and Durham. Child is seeking reelection. The school candidates did not respond to the Voter Guide.
OTHER RACES
In addition to local and school races, two candidates are looking to replace Rep. Melanie Sachs in Freeport’s House District 102. They are Democrat Maura Pillsbury, a former RSU5 board member, and Republican Henry Lloyd Lawrence III.
Read more about Freeport’s local candidates and referendum on the Voter Guide.

title: Tropical Storm Isaias forms in the Gulf. Here’s what to know as it moves toward US
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - Tropical Storm Isaias formed Wednesday in the warm waters of eastern Mexico, and mandatory evacuations were issued for some coastal areas in Florida as forecasters predicted it would strengthen into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season before striking the U.S. Gulf Coast.
Communities in Isaias’ potential path moved quickly to prepare with landfall forecast as soon as Friday evening. Some Gulf oil wells paused production, and at least four Florida school districts canceled classes for later in the week while Okaloosa County announced mandatory evacuations for some coastal areas. Governors in Florida and Alabama declared a state of emergency for dozens of counties.
As it moves inland, Isaias might also disrupt Saturday’s college football showdown between rivals Georgia and Alabama — a game President Donald Trump has planned to attend.
Isaias could become a major, Category 3 hurricane with winds of 111 mph (178 kph) or stronger before it strikes land, said Michael Brennan, director of the U.S. National Hurricane Center.
“We’re expecting multiple dangerous, life-threatening impacts along portions of the northern Gulf Coast beginning Friday and continuing into the weekend,” Brennan said in a video briefing Wednesday.
The storm was on track to tie or break a 121-year-old record as the latest arriving initial hurricane of the Atlantic season. According to the National Weather Service, the record dates to 1905, when the first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8.
The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year because of a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over that ocean. Storm activity has been above average in the Pacific, where Tropical Storm Simon formed Wednesday off Mexico.
Storm surge threat extends from Louisiana to Florida
The Miami-based hurricane center issued a hurricane watch for the northern Gulf Coast from Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, to Indian Pass on the Florida Panhandle. The watch means hurricane conditions are possible within 48 hours.
Brennan said dangerous storm surge could affect an even wider area, from southeast Louisiana to Florida’s Big Bend. Heavy rains of 3 to 7 inches (7 to 18 centimeters) could trigger flash flooding near the coast, with accumulations of 1 to 3 inches (3 to 8 centimeters) as far inland as Tennessee and the western Carolinas.
Isaias was centered about 200 miles (325 kilometers) west-northwest of Progreso, Mexico, and about 480 miles (775 kilometers) south-southwest of the Mississippi River’s mouth, according to the hurricane center. It had maximum sustained winds of 65 mph (100 kph) and was moving east-northeast at 8 mph (13 kph).
Isaias (pronounced ees-ah-EE’-ahs, according to the hurricane center) was forecast to become a hurricane by Thursday as it turns northward toward the Gulf Coast. Though its path and timing could shift, the storm was expected to make landfall late Friday or early Saturday.
Isaias was expected to strike along a wide swath of coastline that is no stranger to major hurricanes. One of the 20th century’s worst storms, Hurricane Camille, killed more than 250 people after hitting land near Waveland, Mississippi, in 1969. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 ravaged neighborhoods in Mississippi, flooded New Orleans and killed nearly 1,400 people. And Hurricane Michael leveled homes and buildings near Panama City, Florida, in 2018.
Oil production and tourism already affected
Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the U.S.
As of Wednesday about 25% of the oil production in the region was temporarily halted, taking about 511,000 barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said eight of the Gulf’s 371 manned oil platforms were evacuated.
With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.
“I would characterize the oil market risk as moderate, but rising,” Burkhard said in an email.
In Gulf Shores, Alabama, organizers canceled the National Shrimp Festival, which had been scheduled for Thursday through the weekend. The event drew an estimated 325,000 people last year. Gulf Shores and Orange Beach issued a statement encouraging people in low-lying areas to voluntarily evacuate.
Gulf Shores resident Maranie Adams gathered water and other supplies as her family moved belongings, including a hot tub motor, to higher ground.
Adams said she, her husband and two adult sons planned to ride out the storm at home, roughly a half-mile from shore, sheltering indoors alongside their flock of chickens.
“We’re having to get crates to bring them into the house so they don’t blow away,” Adams said. “It’s going to be noisy.”
Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties, saying on the social platform X that, “While I hope for minimal impacts, we must take preparations seriously.”
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared one for 25 counties in the Panhandle and Big Bend regions. The declaration activates the state’s emergency management plan for hurricanes, allowing officials to deploy disaster responders and equipment. The state also planned to deploy a Miami-based urban search and rescue task force.
In Pensacola, electric utilities were pre-positioning crews to quickly repair any power outages. City officials provided sand for residents to fill sandbags to protect their homes against flooding. And Mayor D.C. Reeves urged people to check on older adult neighbors and others who might need help.
“Obviously no need to panic at this point,” Reeves told a news conference. “This is really about preparation.”
___
Rico reported from Atlanta, and Collins from Hartford, Connecticut. Associated Press journalists Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, Julie Walker in New York and Hallie Golden in Seattle contributed.

title: Maine writers’ anthology offers ‘nuggets of hope’ for these troubled times
text:
In this 250th anniversary of our country’s founding, when vibes of doom and gloom sadly overshadow celebration, along comes a book that offers both hope and a clear-eyed perspective on why these times are so fraught. “Ground Truth: Writing Towards Justice” is an anthology featuring 47 poets, writers and artists from Maine who collectively challenge our status quo with pointed critiques, celebrations and musings about how to make our country a better place for all.
“We are all in this together, this America,” the four co-editors write in the foreword. “It is up to us to do what we can to create a nation that is ethical, fair, responsible and, if we’re brave and lucky, a place to live peacefully, generously, and with joy.”
Claire Millikin, Mihku Paul, Karin Spitfire and Maya Williams are poets themselves, which brings to this anthology keen eyes and ears to words and phrases that not only paint pictures and evoke feelings — they also empower readers to reflect on “nuggets of hope still to be found in the present-day ground truth of our lives in this nation.”
Consider the closing stanza of the anthology’s second poem, “Ground Truth,” by Ekhlas Ahmed, a Sudanese refugee who fled the outbreak of civil war in her original homeland and resettled in Portland with her mother, father and three younger brothers: “the truest nation / is not the one imagined / from a distance / but the one assembled daily / by people who choose care.”
This is not a glib imagined sentiment. Ahmed, who currently lives in Windham with her family, has built a life in her new homeland that’s committed to helping new refugees and immigrants build new self-supporting lives for themselves and families in Maine. In the 20 years since resettling here, Ahmed earned a bachelor’s degree in international relations and a master’s degree in education from the University of Southern Maine. She has worked as an English language educator in public schools and currently works as a policy analyst for the Office of New Americans, where she supports the resettlement and integration of new Mainers across the state.
Her resumé goes much deeper, but even this brief summation should make clear that Ahmed embodies this country’s history as a nation built on the contributions of immigrants, each generation taking advantage of opportunities that came their way and adding to our cultural diversity and vitality in uniquely beautiful ways. The observation in the opening stanza of her poem, to anyone who’s knowledgeable and completely honest about our country’s tremendous debt to immigrants, rings true: “The work communities do / on the ground / is often more honest / than the stories / nations tell themselves.”
An essay by Gary Lawless, poet and co-owner of Gulf of Maine Books in Brunswick with his wife, Beth Leonard, tells of his experiences leading writing workshops with people who all too often are invisible, their voices unheard or ignored — homeless people, Vietnam veterans and adults with disabilities at the Spindleworks artists’ cooperative in Brunswick are among those he’s worked with. He shares an early insight expressed in an oft-quoted poem by the late Spindleworks artist Rita Langlois: “Handicap / I heard about it, / But I ain’t got it now.”
“The conversation of the community is not in balance, in health, unless all voices are encouraged to speak, to have their stories honored,” he writes in his essay. “And as we listen, we learn how much connection our hearts have (with each other).”
Penobscot elder Donna Loring, in her poem “It is Up to Us,” affirms the importance of storytelling from the perspective of the Wabanaki people whose presence on this land predates by more than 10,000 years Maine’s statehood in 1820 and our country’s founding in 1776. As a Vietnam War veteran, the Penobscot Nation’s representative to the Maine State Legislature from 1998-2003 and from 2007-2008 a published author, host of the monthly radio show “Wabanaki Windows” on WERU, and former senior adviser on tribal affairs to Gov. Janet Mills, she eschews victimhood in all its manifestations: “It is up to us to overcome our own invisibility. / It is up to us to use our voices to tell our stories. / It is up to us to rise from the ashes of genocide / and proclaim that We Are Still Here!! / So we will tell our own story with our voice / So you can hear us / So we can shine a light on those dark deeds that were done to us.”
In a longer poem, “We are the First People and the First Nations of this Country,” Loring offers an essential First People and First Nations perspective on the 250-year history of the United States — beginning with these core truths: “We were made foreigners in our own land. / They promised many things and delivered nothing. / First Nations were left with no land, no resources and broken treaties.”
Loring’s poem challenges each of us to confront our country’s true history in relation to “the First People.” Her poem convincingly spells out why this is so critically important. In many respects, it is the heart of this compelling and timely anthology.
“Ground Truth: Writing Towards Justice” is a carefully assembled anthology of skillful poets and essayists, each resisting “a political landscape which attempts to steal souls” — as the co-editors write in their introduction. They invite the readers of this book to ground themselves in the wonders of daily life, to be found both in community and in the bountiful natural world on which all life depends.
This book does not evade the troubled times we live in. But it also chooses not to ignore other realities essential to the daily challenge of keeping on going on. As Wolastoqey writer and visual artist Mihku Paul, one of the co-editors, writes in her poem in the “Come to Your Senses” section of the anthology: “It is a fact. / In every corner of the world, / something blooms.”
BOOK LAUNCH
Gulf of Maine Books will host a book launch for the new anthology “Ground Truth: Writing Towards Justice” at Curtis Memorial Library in Brunswick on Saturday, Oct. 10, at 2:30 p.m.
Cost of the anthology published by Huntress Press is $20.
The event, which is free and open to the public, will feature readings by the editors as well as by contributors including Linda Aldrich, Steve Luttrell, Steve Miller, Doug Rawlings, Sampson Spadafore, Panagoiti Tsolkas, and more to be announced.
For more information about the event, contact Gary Lawless or Beth Leonard at Gulf of Maine Books, 134 Maine St., Brunswick, or call them at 729-5083.
James McCarthy is a former editor of The Times Record. In 2023 he was inducted into the Maine Press Association Hall of Fame.

title: The highest-paid employees at the University of Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
University of Maine’s three highest-paid employees alone earned more than $1.2 million combined last year.
The three highest-paid employees in 2025 were UMaine President Joan Ferrini-Mundy, men’s hockey head coach Ben Barr, and Director of the Advanced Structures and Composites Center Habib Dagher, according to University of Maine System’s human resources reports.
Meanwhile, just four faculty members were in the top 25 earners last year. In total, 279 UMaine faculty members earned more than $100,000 in 2025. The highest paid was climate scientist and professor of geological sciences George Denton, who was paid $273,529.16.
UMaine is facing a $19 million budget shortfall for the next fiscal year. Ferrini-Mundy and Provost Gabriel Paquette outlined plans last month to cut more than $13 million from the budget, but the remaining $5.7 million will require layoffs and the elimination of vacant positions. It’s unclear what positions will be cut or when they will be announced.
Union representatives from across the University of Maine System last week called for administrators to conduct a parallel review of their budgets and salaries before deciding on any cuts. Of the employees who earned $100,000 or more in 2025, 73 are in administrative roles while 279 are faculty.
Administrators’ earnings made up 20% of all salaries in 2025.
University officials are looking into multiple ways to close the budget gap, according to Ferrini-Mundy and Paquette’s letter.
The university budgeted $336,842,265 in expenses for the current fiscal year, a more than $12 million hike from the previous year. Salaries, wages and benefits are projected to make up more than two-thirds of UMaine’s 2028 budget, University of Maine System spokesperson Samantha Warren said.
UMaine’s growing salary costs were reflected in its top earners. The number of UMaine employees earning more than $100,000 jumped from 373 in 2024 to 415 in 2025. The top 25 earners in 2025 were collectively paid a quarter of a million dollars more than in 2024.
The jump in six-figure earners could be attributed to multiple things, including bargained wage increases, Warren said. For example, faculty members received a 4% bump in wages on July 1, 2025.
Stipends, employees holding multiple positions across the system and faculty generally being paid for a nine-month academic year instead of a full year like administrators “can skew the actual base salary compensation data,” Warren said.
All of the included employees are listed as working at UMaine, although some may also work at other University of Maine System campuses. System employees, including Chancellor Dannel Malloy, who was paid $421,975.27 in 2025, were not included.

title: Mr. Drew and His Animals Too closing Poland location
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Mr. Drew and His Animals Too closing Poland education center
Drew Desjardins, affectionately known as Mr. Drew, announced on Facebook that he is closing his animal education center in Poland on Saturday, Oct. 31. He cites getting older and the financial challenges associated with the recent move from Lewiston to Poland.
The social media post says, "We accept the facts the economy is bad and simply put, we are not businesspeople we simply care about our animals and making people happy in this sad world we are living in."
The post explains they are not looking for financial support to keep the space open at this time and plan to transition back to a travel-only business model. The business started out of their home before expanding into a retail space 8 years ago.
"Mrs. Drew and I are looking at this as going back to our roots, as we started out of our home and it was a much simpler times," Desjardins wrote. Mr. Drew and His Animals Too is still booking visits around the state, but he will not be able to work with the same number of animals.
They are working to rehome many of them to educational facilities and sanctuaries that Desjardins trusts. He says no animal will be euthanized or adopted out publicly. Fixtures and enclosures will be sold to help cover their expenses.
Desjardins wrote, "This is where we are at - sad, anxious and heavy hearted but I can say with confidence, that we are very proud of what we created and accomplished and there will be no other place like it."
Mr. Drew and His Animals Too will be open during their regular hours until the closing date. They ask that free admission passes be used during that time, because they cannot be refunded.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Rain Continues Tonight, Thunderstorms Possible Thursday Afternoon
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Wednesday. After a chilly start to the day, clouds have continued to thicken across northern Maine as our next system moves into the region. Periods of light rain will continue to develop tonight, becoming more widespread through Thursday as a cold front approaches from the west. Rainfall amounts have trended a little higher compared to earlier forecasts, but this still does not look like enough rain to provide much meaningful improvement to the ongoing drought. One additional wrinkle in Thursday’s forecast will be the potential for a few thunderstorms across northern Maine during the afternoon.
Cloud cover and increasing southerly winds will keep temperatures much milder tonight compared to Tuesday night. Low temperatures across Aroostook County look to remain mainly in the lower to mid 40s, including around 46 degrees in Presque Isle and Caribou, with Houlton also near 46 degrees. Farther north and west, temperatures generally fall into the lower 40s.
Showers become more numerous overnight, especially across northern portions of the region. Southerly winds around 10 to 15 mph will also help prevent temperatures from falling nearly as far as they did Tuesday night.
Thursday will be an unsettled day across northern Maine, with periods of rain continuing through much of the day. High temperatures look to reach the upper 50s to lower 60s across Aroostook County, including around 62 degrees in Presque Isle and Caribou and near 62 degrees in Houlton.
As the cold front crosses the region Thursday afternoon, a little bit of instability could develop ahead of it, increasing the chance for scattered thunderstorms across northern Maine. Severe weather is not expected, but some storms could be capable of producing small hail thanks to relatively low freezing levels. Any thunderstorm activity should remain scattered rather than widespread.
Overall rainfall totals from tonight through Thursday are generally expected to remain below a half inch, with the highest amounts favored across northern Maine. That is an increase from previous forecasts, but still not enough to significantly improve drought conditions across the region.
Rain chances decrease Thursday night as the front exits the region, with cooler air moving back in for Friday. High temperatures look to fall into the lower to mid 50s across northern Aroostook County, including around 55 degrees in Caribou and 57 degrees in Presque Isle and Houlton.
Friday will also turn breezier, with west winds around 15 to 20 mph and gusts approaching 30 mph at times. A few late-day showers cannot be completely ruled out, especially across northern portions of the region, but most of Friday should trend drier than Thursday.
Looking farther ahead, Saturday looks mainly dry and cool with highs in the lower to mid 50s before a noticeable warm-up arrives Sunday. Temperatures could climb well into the 60s by the second half of the weekend.
For more details on tonight’s rainfall, Thursday’s thunderstorm potential and the cooler weather returning Friday, make sure to check out this evening’s First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening!

title: Don’t let Elon Musk buy Maine’s vote
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Thom Moore writes and consults in Scarborough. He is a member of Third Act.
The world’s richest person is funding Sen. Susan Collins’ campaign.
This is part of the GOP’s decades-long effort to make our government work for its wealthiest citizens. As Graham Platner noted, and Troy Jackson also appreciates, the wealthy mean to own everything and rent it to the rest of us. They already rent us the money to run our government, charging us a trillion dollars a year in interest. They should instead pay a fair share of the bills, about 24% of our GDP, especially those who made their money within our economy.
When we are paid less than we are worth, when staple prices are raised endlessly out of greed or because of unproductive wars and tariffs, when resulting inflation raises interest rates, money trickles upward.
Even when taxes are cut, deficits increase, benefits decrease and interest is paid by us to those who finance the debt, padding their estates at low risk. Those estates steadily appreciate in value from the upward trickling, and that unrealized income escapes taxation as it is passed to heirs by our wealthiest, most senior citizens.
But we must resist any impulse to make age an issue in this election, nor should we exploit, for political purposes, Sen. Collins’ exceptional seniority and respect among the most corporate-sponsored members of the U.S. Senate. She was influential in bringing defense work to Maine, but she also voted for the reduction of medical care and research support for working-class Mainers. Troy Jackson brings a fresh perspective on the kinds of development that create opportunities to keep Maine “the way life should be.”
We cannot ignore the current escalation in prices, driven by corporate profits, wars, tariffs and wasteful ego projects. Sen. Collins has done nothing to stop this. Maine’s domination by corporate utilities has caused our power costs to be among the highest in the nation. Accusations that renewable energy raises our costs are lies. Power sources get dialed back when supply exceeds demand, namely the most expensive ones, the gas plants. Who pays to oppose the transition to sustainable energy? The fuel industry and power utilities, that’s who.
Sen. Collins and the GOP oppose working-class collective bargaining and a fair minimum wage. Troy Jackson defends the right of employees to organize and assert their economic value. Maine has more than its fair share of rural poverty and hardship. The remedy for that is new businesses offering good jobs that pay a living wage. Troy Jackson understands that workers must often organize to win fair wages and working conditions from larger businesses.
Sen. Collins supported the obscene increase in the economic power of ICE. It is used to infiltrate our communities in the name of ferreting out, and in some cases assassinating, immigrants, whether properly documented or not. This is an intrusion into state and local affairs that Troy Jackson will not tolerate.
Sen. Collins supports the GOP belief that healthcare is a corporate profit center that is only for those who can afford it. They believe that profits should flow from prices determined by demand, rather than reflecting what is affordable. They do not think that the government should pay any costs. Healthcare is a trivial expense for the ultra-rich, but they want to limit what kinds of medical care everyone else can receive, including personal reproduction and body choices. Troy Jackson opposes these intrusions into privacy matters and accepts government responsibility to mitigate hardships where practical.
The government money that Sen. Collins has brought to Maine would continue to favor her corporate donors, at the expense of working-class Mainers. Troy Jackson would help working-class Mainers receive a fair share of the wealth that their work produces, in the form of higher wages and reduced expenses.

title: Nobel Prize in chemistry awarded to scientists who unraveled mystery of mirror molecules
text:
Nobel Prize in chemistry awarded to scientists who unraveled mystery of mirror molecules
Scientists Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in chemistry Wednesday for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs and transformed modern medicine.
Video above: FDA approves first-of-a-kind pancreatic cancer drug trialed in Boston
Many molecules come in versions that look alike but are not exactly identical, like right and left hands. Kagan, who is from France, and Soai, from Japan, found ways to make chemistry pick a side, designing reactions to produce the desired mirror image.
“The medicines we have today would not be possible without this chemistry,” said Rigoberto Hernandez, president of the American Chemical Society.
Soai was shopping at a neighborhood supermarket when he heard he had won.
“I’m very excited to receive the very nice news,” Soai told the Nobel committee and journalists by phone. “Of course, this is one of the most exciting days in my life.”
The discovery enabled most modern medicines
Mirror images of the same molecule can have different properties. For example, one version of the chemical carvone smells like mint, while the other has a whiff of caraway, a spice often used in rye bread.
The alternate versions can also behave differently when interacting with other chemicals. When designing drugs to treat diseases, scientists want to be choosy about which mirror image they get. They want the version of a molecule to treat a cold, not one that will make the sniffles worse.
The Nobel committee described Kagan and Soai’s work as a feat never previously achieved by anyone “other than life itself.”
“It might be difficult to say that this drug, or that drug, was developed using this,” said Peter Somfai, a member of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry. “I would say all of them, because we use this as a tool, we use this as an understanding, how to develop catalysts, how they function.”
In the 1980s, Kagan’s work showed there might be a way to design reactions to produce one form of a molecule over the other. Years later, Soai perfected the process. He created the first-ever chemical reaction to efficiently produce only one of a molecule’s mirror images, in what’s now known as the Soai reaction.
“This is probably the coolest experiment in organic chemistry,” Somfai said.
Even life prefers one mirror image over the other. DNA twists to the right, and the proteins in human bodies are made of mostly left-handed building blocks.
In addition to developing better medicines or perfumes, deciphering the mirror images of molecules can help scientists understand the chemical architecture of life, said chemist Holden Thorp, editor-in-chief of the journal Science.
Kagan, 95, is affiliated with the Université Paris-Sud in Orsay, France. Soai, 76, is affiliated with the Tokyo University of Science.
Neither of the universities immediately responded to requests for comment from The Associated Press.
More Nobel prizes will be awarded over the next week
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winner in Stockholm.
Last year, three scientists won the chemistry Nobel for their development of new molecular structures that can trap vast quantities of gas inside, laying the groundwork to potentially suck greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere or harvest moisture from desert environments.
This year's prizes began with the Nobel for medicine, awarded Monday to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award announced Tuesday recognized a scientist's efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos.
The literature prize is set to be awarded Thursday. After Friday’s peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates or an organization.

title: Bangor school evacuated due to hoax threat, officials say students are safe
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The William S. Cohen School in Bangor was evacuated Wednesday due to a bomb threat that school officials now characterize as a “swatting hoax.”
An officer confirmed to our reporter on scene Wednesday morning that all of the nearly 400 students were safe and accounted for.
Students and staff were evacuated to Fruit Street School around 11:30 a.m. while law enforcement searched the Cohen School property. Police told WABI nothing dangerous was discovered, and they determined that the threat was not credible. Once it was found that the building was safe, students were able to return to their classrooms, or parents and guardians had the option to pick them up early.
Parents were notified of the situation at the time of the evacuation by an email from the school that described a “potential threat.”
School officials thanked local law enforcement for their assistance in responding to the incident.
“We are incredibly proud of our students for the way they responded during a challenging situation,” said Mike Missbrenner, Principal of school. “Their cooperation, patience, and resilience were outstanding. I also want to thank our faculty and staff for their professionalism in following emergency procedures and supporting our students throughout the day.”
The Bangor School Department says counselors, teachers, and administrators will be available to provide support to any student who wants to talk about what happened Wednesday.
The Garland Street school serves students in grades 6-8.

title: New Ellsworth nonprofit seeks to raise $1M to buy Hancock County newspapers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A new Ellsworth nonprofit has set a $1 million fundraising goal to purchase a group of Hancock County-based weekly newspapers by the summer of 2027.
Acadia Newspaper Trust, a recently-created local nonprofit, said Wednesday it hopes to buy the Ellsworth American, Mount Desert Islander and the Bangor Historian from Reade Brower, a Maine newspaper businessman who previously owned several newspapers now owned by another nonprofit, the The Maine Trust for Local News.
The acquisition would mark the latest effort to reorient local newspapers under nonprofit stewardship. Brower sold 22 of his daily and weekly newspapers, including the Portland Press Herald and Lewiston Sun Journal, to the National Trust in 2023.
Brower, who currently owns the Midcoast Villager, is retiring, according to the American.
Islandport Media CEO Will Bleakey, who oversees the Camden-based newspaper, the American and the Islander, said Thursday Brower still owns the Villager and had no announcement at this time.
The funding will also go toward initial operating costs, according to the new trust.
Acadia Trust said the newspapers’ editorial independence would remain intact and be separate from the nonprofit’s fundraising efforts.
The move comes after the Ellsworth American, the largest and oldest newspaper involved in the trust, and the Islander laid off some of their staff in mid-August.
The American has been in publication since 1851, and the Islander was founded by former American owner and publisher Alan Baker in 2001. The two outlets sell roughly 8,000 print copies weekly and have 6,000 digital subscribers.
The Bangor Historian publishes historical stories to the greater Bangor area. The Historian distributes about 26,000 copies weekly, according to the nonprofit.
The three outlets employ 39 people across Hancock County, according to the group.
The new trust seeks to raise the money through gifts, pledges, grants and community partnerships, with the intention of transitioning from for-profit outlets to nonprofit newspapers, according to the group.
The trust is hosting a community event Oct. 29 at Fogtown Brewing Company in Ellsworth to raise money and awareness of the nonprofit transition.

title: GOP ad calls Troy Jackson 'corrupt' over a college funding bill. What the record shows
text:
A GOP ad calls Troy Jackson 'corrupt' over a college funding bill. Here's what the record shows
An ad by a Republican group calls Maine Democrat Troy Jackson “corrupt” and accuses him of enriching his son on the public dime.
As a state senator, “Jackson cosponsored a bill sending millions of taxpayer dollars to his son’s lobbying client,” said the ad by Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC that aims to protect the Republican majority.
A super PAC can raise and spend unlimited amounts of money to campaign for federal candidates.
The ad’s text said “Jackson’s son charged nearly $200,000 lobbying” and “$13.4 million in additional taxpayer funding.”
Using what look like explosive news clips charging “fraud and wrong doing” and “rot and corruption,” the ad zeroes in on a 2024 bill Jackson cosponsored. The bill sought funding for a public college that has long received bipartisan support from state and federal lawmakers, including Republican Sen. Susan Collins, Jackson’s campaign opponent. But the ad omits key details and charges corruption where the public record is unclear.
School information shows that Chace Jackson had a relationship with the academy involving legislative work. But his state lobbying disclosures don’t list the school as being his client and it’s not clear how much he was paid. Whether Chace influenced the Senate’s funding legislation is also unclear.
Ad includes corruption citations unrelated to Jackson
The ad begins with a clip of TV journalists referencing alarming allegations, but the actual news reports cited don’t pertain to Jackson.
- “Allegations of fraud and wrongdoing,” one news anchor says. This clip stems from WGME-TV’s (CBS 13 News) 2025 report about alleged tax fraud by a nonprofit, Gateway Community Services. The report did not mention Jackson. The state health department in December stopped MaineCare payments to Gateway because of fraud allegations. A few employees were later charged with tax fraud.
- “Rot and corruption in Augusta,” a reporter says. This is from a May 2026 report by News Center Maine from WLBZ-TV and WCSH-TV about a plan by Bobby Charles, the Republican candidate for governor, to root out corruption. It didn’t mention Jackson.
- “Another scandal in a disturbing pattern with corrupt politician Troy Jackson,” a female voice says in a third clip that shows video of Jackson. The ad did not cite the audio’s source and PolitiFact could not find it in news coverage. PolitiFact asked the Senate Leadership Fund for it and received no response to that question.
The clips set the scene for viewers, alerting them that corruption allegations will follow, but the ensuing accusations don’t prove corruption.
Bill would have provided more funding to Maine Maritime Academy
The ad quotes an August article by the Washington Free Beacon, a conservative outlet, about legislation Jackson cosponsored in January 2024. The bill would have provided $13.4 million for Maine Maritime Academy, a public college in the eastern coastal town of Castine. A spokesperson for the Senate Leadership Fund directed PolitiFact to that article.
But the ad did not mention that Jackson, who was Senate president at the time, was one of 10 of the bill’s bipartisan presenters or cosponsors. The academy sought more money because it said it faced a funding disparity relative to Maine colleges and other state maritime academies. An official with the academy testified that the school was seeking money beyond its usual appropriations and said the extra money would allow the school to increase enrollment and lead to a greater contribution to Maine’s economy.
The legislation passed the Senate unanimously. It never became law; PolitiFact did not find news coverage explaining why the bill died. The university did not receive the bill’s $13.4 million that year.
However, Maine Maritime Academy generally received an appropriation through the state budget process ranging from $9 million to $16 million during the past five years; in 2024, it received about $12.2 million.
Details thin on the role of Jackson’s son
The ad ties Jackson’s cosponsorship with his son’s employment, saying “special interests paid Jackson’s son, and Jackson pushed their agenda.”
PolitiFact found only thin public documentation about this connection and was unable to conclude whether Chace Jackson’s role influenced senators’ support for the bill.
Chace Jackson registered with the state ethics commission as the “legislative affairs coordinator” for the Maine Maritime Academy in December 2022; in January 2024, he registered as the school’s legislative coordinator for the president’s office. These public documents include no explanation about his work or payment. An academy spokesperson did not respond to our questions.
In December 2022, The Resurgam Group lobbying firm announced it had hired Chace Jackson as part of its public affairs team. BJ McCollister, Troy Jackson’s former chief of staff, founded Resurgam.
Chace Jackson’s state lobbying disclosure form shows that in 2024, his clients paid $182,500 to Resurgam Group; Maine Maritime Academy was not among the named clients. The ad’s text said that Chace “charged nearly $200,000 lobbying,” but the $182,500 disclosure does not mean he received all of that money. That’s because lobbyists report the compensation earned by the firm, not by individuals, Martha Currier, assistant director of the state’s ethics commission, told PolitiFact.
The clients listed on Jackson’s disclosure included a law firm, businesses, a gun safety coalition, environmental groups, a union and a public health association.
PolitiFact reached out to Chace Jackson with questions about his role with the academy and did not hear back. Resurgam has since merged with Frame Strategies; that firm is making ads for Jackson’s campaign.
PolitiFact also asked Jackson’s campaign for information about whether Chace Jackson encouraged his father to vote for the 2024 legislation and didn’t get a response to that question. However, the campaign noted that Chace Jackson’s lobbying disclosure did not list the academy and that Troy Jackson and other lawmakers have long supported funding the public college.
Bipartisan support of Maine Maritime Academy predated Chace Jackson’s work for the school
Jackson’s campaign pointed to the lawmaker’s votes on budgets that included academy funding years before disclosures show his son began working as the academy’s legislative coordinator in 2022.
In 2019, Jackson praised the Legislature for passing a budget that he said “invests in workforce development and education.” He didn’t single out the maritime academy, but the budget included a nearly 3.3% increase for higher education, including the academy.
In 2025, after Jackson left the Legislature, Democratic Gov. Janet Mills signed a budget that included a 4% increase for higher education, including for the Maine Maritime Academy.
The college has also received bipartisan support from Maine’s congressional delegation, including Collins, Sen. Angus King, an independent, and U.S. Rep. Jared Golden, a Democrat.
Maine doesn’t require a lawmaker to recuse himself from a vote if a family member lobbies, Currier said.
Craig Holman, who lobbies Congress on ethics at Public Citizen, a consumer advocacy organization, said to his knowledge no state requires legislators to recuse themselves if a family member worked on a bill.
PolitiFact Researcher Caryn Baird contributed to this fact-check.

title: Why your retirement plan shouldn’t depend on an inheritance
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Millions of Americans are expecting an inheritance someday, but Matt Schulz, a consumer finance analyst with LendingTree, said that money should not replace a personal savings plan.
“It’s a luxury if you have it,” Schulz said. “But it’s really, really important for people to not have that be their entire retirement plan.”
LendingTree found that homeowners 65 and older could transfer $17.2 trillion between 2026 and 2045. About a third of Americans younger than 65 expect to receive some of that money as an inheritance or financial gift, and of those expecting a payout, 43% say their retirement plan depends on it arriving.
Schulz said that money is not guaranteed to be there when it’s needed.
“It’s important for people to not assume that all the money that’s there now is going to be there in the future, because the cost of health care, the cost of assisted living and so many other things that we face when dealing with elderly parents or our own aging are so expensive,” Schulz said. “And a lot of that would-be inheritance money can go away in a pretty big hurry.”
Despite the financial stakes, Schulz said many families avoid discussing inheritance planning, even though those conversations need to happen well in advance.
“There’s so much that goes into it. Whether you’re talking about just family dynamics, but there’s also legal ramifications and tax issues and all that,” Schulz said. “And that’s all the kind of stuff that needs to be discussed going down the line here, whether that’s with professionals or with siblings or with family or what have you.”
Schulz said the bottom line is to build a retirement plan around current savings, not around money that might be passed down in the future.

title: Kittery water shortage expected to worsen as winter approaches
text:
Kittery residents are headed into the eighth week of a strict water restriction order, with no relief in sight as the district’s supply shrinks. It’s a problem that’s expected to intensify as temperatures drop and source ponds struggle to refill.
The Kittery Water District draws from four ponds to service all of Kittery, some of Eliot and the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard. Three of those ponds are at least 12 feet lower than expected for this time of year, even after a recent nor’easter that brought nearly 3 inches of rain to Kittery, district Superintendent Matthew Berube said Tuesday.
In recent months, there have also been some persistent leaks at the shipyard and a string of water main breaks in town, raising further concerns about the district’s supply.
The shortage has landed the town under a “Level 3,” or a severe conservation order, limiting some outdoor watering. A “Level 4” would constitute an emergency and an immediate ban on all outdoor water usage.
Restrictions went into effect Aug. 17 and come with fines for those who don’t comply with watering bans on certain days of the week. Berube hasn’t had to issue any fines but said he doesn’t doubt some of the district’s 6,000 customers are violating the restrictions.
“We’ve done our best to educate a few people that we’ve seen and noticed,” he said, adding that combined with persistent drought conditions, the supply “just got worse.”
The National Integrated Drought Information System indicates that 1.3 million Mainers, which is nearly the state’s entire population, are living in drought conditions, including 100% of York County residents.
SHIPYARD DEMAND
Fluctuating pond levels are an annual issue, but starting the colder months with an already low supply could spell a much longer restriction period for Kittery residents, especially with added strain from the shipyard.
The Navy facility normally demands more than half the district’s water supply. That requirement becomes more drastic in the winter months to support “industrial processes and freeze protection,” a shipyard spokesperson wrote in an email Tuesday.
Berube said an ongoing project — the Shipyard Infrastructure Optimization Program, or P1080 — will result in an even higher demand than usual.
“The whole point of the power and resiliency project is so that (the shipyard) can expand their levels of usage through 2037,” he said, adding that the end goal is to eventually fix the “extraneous water usage.”
In the past decade, ongoing system improvements and conservation measures have led to a significant decrease in water usage at the shipyard, the spokesperson wrote. Last winter, those efforts saved 55 million gallons compared to previous years. Berube said Wednesday that the shipyard’s peak usage from October 2025 to April 2026 was close to 380 million gallons.
During that time, the shipyard was also testing some new conservation infrastructure. The shipyard stopped that testing after a few months, Berube said, but he expects more conservation efforts to be implemented this winter.
The spokesperson noted that the P1080 project will expand the capacity of Kittery Water District, counteracting the increased demand for resources and describing the project as “mutually beneficial” for the Navy and residents.
“There are no indications that (Naval Support Activity Maine) and PNSY will exceed our long-term projected operational demands previously shared with Kittery Water District,” the spokesperson wrote.
Shipyard officials and the water district have been working together to find ways to mitigate the effects of the ongoing restrictions, though Berube acknowledged he’ll need to do more studies to determine how to alleviate the water strain — and what’s left for residents this winter.

title: Texas court denies request to stop execution over Christa Pike’s failed lethal injection
text:
HUNTSVILLE, Texas (AP) — A Texas man who fatally shot a convenience store clerk was put to death Wednesday evening, becoming the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year and the first since Tennessee’s failed attempt to administer a lethal injection to Christa Pike a week ago.
Jamaal Howard, 46, was pronounced dead at 8:03 p.m. after receiving a fatal dose of pentobarbital at the state prison in Huntsville. He was convicted of killing Vickie Swartout, 42, in a 2000 store robbery caught on surveillance video.
Asked by the warden if he had a final statement, Howard apologized profusely to some members of his victim’s family, who watched through a window just feet from the death chamber.
“I wish that you accept my apology and I wish for your forgiveness,” he said, shortly before the injection got underway. “I’m sorry for what happened. I wish you can learn to forgive me one of these days.”
He also thanked his friends and family and said he loved them, adding he was “in a good state of mind to find peace and the Lord, so I thank y’all.” He concluded with: “Hey, enjoy life, and peace to y’all.”
Man took a few breaths and gasped as the drugs began flowing
As the pentobarbital began taking effect, Howard took a couple of breaths and gasped. He then began making snoring sounds, coughed and resumed the snoring sounds, each time the sound becoming quieter. Within about 30 seconds, all movement stopped.
He was pronounced dead 19 minutes later.
His sister was among witnesses watching through a window from an adjacent room and became distraught, exclaiming several times: “Get me out of here.” She was assisted by corrections officers in exiting the witness room.
Texas has executed seven people so far in 2026, including Howard, and plans two more executions later this year.
Howard’s attorneys unsuccessfully sought to block the execution by arguing that he was intellectually disabled and that he faced risks similar to those in Pike’s case because both states use pentobarbital for lethal injections.
Pike’s lawyers continue to seek more information about what went wrong after the 50-year-old woman survived two doses of pentobarbital on Sept. 30. Her lawyers said she was unconscious at a hospital after the attempt but was awake and speaking by Tuesday.
Store clerk’s killing was caught on surveillance video
Howard was convicted of capital murder in the killing of Swartout, who was shot once in the chest during the robbery. Evidence presented at trial included surveillance video showing Howard shooting Swartout.
Howard, who was 20 at the time, took $114 and a carton of cigarettes from the store in Silsbee, a small, rural town about 100 miles (160 kilometers) northeast of Houston, according to court records.
A flurry of late appeals failed to stop the execution
In bidding to halt Howard’s execution, his attorneys had filed a motion hours earlier before the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals raising concerns about the quality of Texas’ execution drugs. The court denied that request and a second filing involving the drugs without comment.
His attorneys also argued unsuccessfully to the U.S. Supreme Court that Howard’s execution should be halted because he was intellectually disabled. The Supreme Court in 2002 had barred the execution of intellectually disabled people, though it gave states some discretion in determining such disabilities.
The state told the court that Howard’s lawyers did not present evidence that would show he meets the requirements for a claim of intellectual disability.
The high court late Wednesday declined to intervene, without comment, clearing the way for the execution.
Florida leads the nation in executions this year
Florida has carried out 16 executions so far this year, the most of any state. Most states that allow executions use lethal injection as their primary method.
Tennessee Republican Gov. Bill Lee has halted the one remaining execution that was scheduled to be carried out in his state this year.
___
Stengle reported from Fort Worth, Texas.

title: Group learns about trees at library presentation
text:
On Sunday September 27, Susan Cottle, Maine Master Naturalist, came to the South China Public Library to speak about trees. On Sunday, October 4, she followed up with a ‘field trip’ to the China (Schools) Forest trails, for a delightful and educational walk in the woods with some tree identification.
The group learned many things. Did you know: There are paper birches and also gray birches, and the gray birches have ‘mustaches’ on their bark? That Balsam fir, not white pine, is the most prevalent tree in Maine? That Larch is the only evergreen that sheds its needle-like leaves in winter, has cute little bumps on its branches, and is also called tamarack and hackmatack? That red pine can live 300 – 500 years, has needle bunches of two, and that its bark changes from flaky when young to scaly plates when old?
OR, that our amazing little town’s China Community Forest is a most wondrous place this time of year (as well as all the seasons), to just be present in nature?
Stay tuned for more ‘field trip’ walks with Susan sponsored by the South China Public Library. We are loving the idea of mushroom walks, fern walks, possibly bird walks. Thank you to Susan for your fun talks and for expanding learning to beyond our bookshelved walls!

title: Residents raise concerns over Juniper Ridge Landfill expansion in Old Town
text:
OLD TOWN, Maine (WABI) - Residents brought their concerns to a Juniper Ridge Advisory meeting in Old Town Tuesday night about the landfill’s potential expansion.
They wanted to know how the expansion would positively impact the local community.
Some brought up that the proposed expansion includes three acres of wetlands.
Officials said the primary contributors of PFAS at the landfill are construction and demolition debris, the highest percentage at around 35 percent, as well as ash from incinerators, special waste including discharge from fuel trucks, and asbestos.
PFAS treatment at Juniper Ridge will be centered primarily around leachate and won’t focus on other contaminants.
That leachate would be transported 20 miles down the road from Juniper Ridge to another wastewater treatment facility.
Some residents raised concerns that expansion into the wetlands, as well as transporting the leachate, could create potential hazards for the community.
“I have really deep concerns about any, I don’t think there’s any way that the landfill could expand into a wetland area and have the type of rainfall that we have these days, which is pretty sometimes very heavy, and not have runoff from the site go down into the waters. If the leachate is going to be moved from Juniper Ridge, is it going to be treated and trucked back or is it just going to stay where it’s trucked to,” a resident said.
“After it’s been treated, it will either be taken by pipeline to a wastewater treatment facility or be trucked to its further destination of a wastewater treatment facility. So they have to say, they have to get the phone up and say to us, okay, we’re putting this on bypass, something that we started doing in 2000,” an official said.
Officials stressed they would remain compliant with regulations, prioritizing public safety and taking caution when transporting cancer-causing materials like leachate.
There’s no stipulation on where the PFAS treatment will take place due to the public benefit determination under Maine law.
Juniper Ridge accepts about 52% of the state’s municipal waste.

title: In its 5th year, Portland’s Festival Champlain celebrates French language films from across the world
text:
Rarely do people witness an aspiring filmmaker, a housewife with 1 million trading stamps, a man completely indifferent to the world around him and an obstinate Canadian customs agent at the same event.
Maine’s only French-language film festival is giving people the opportunity to do just that.
“It’s a very unique event,” Lisa Scali, executive director of the Alliance Francaise du Maine, said about the fifth annual Festival Champlain, which runs Oct. 15-18 at the Portland Museum of Art.
The event has grown from 2022, when six films were screened across two days. This year, it features eight films across four days.
Festival Champlain’s schedule reflects Maine’s close, complex relationship with the French language. Maine remains the state with the highest percentage of French speakers and people with French ancestry.
Over the years, organizers have diversified their selection, searching for films from outside of Canada and France. Last year, two films from Cape Verde were screened. Of this year’s eight films, three are Canadian, three are French, one is Gabonese and one is Tunisian.
They don’t just strive to represent Maine’s French-speaking communities; festival organizers made a concerted effort to find films relevant to the whole state, Scali said.
“We are looking to speak to various communities within Maine, and if a film we think in general is relevant for the state of Maine, we’re going to choose that as well,” she said.
One movie, “Promised Sky,” which screens Oct. 16, features an Ivorian pastor living in Tunisia who allows two women to seek refuge in her home. An unconventional family is formed when the group takes in a young orphan who survived a shipwreck.
For Scali, the film touches on contemporary issues Mainers are familiar with, exploring community, relationships and immigration.
“I think this movie is important for everyone to see,” Scali said.
Scali also emphasized changes to programming outside of the screenings. This year three of the films will be followed by a series of conversations with either directors or the deputy director of the Portland Museum of Art.
There will also be a gala reception from 6-8:30 p.m. Oct. 17 at State Street Church in Portland’s West End. It is free, but people are asked to register so organizers know how many guests will attend.
Previously the gala has welcomed special guests, such as Gov. Janet Mills and members of the French and Canadian consuls.
‘A CULTURAL OFFERING’
Throughout the year, the Alliance Francaise du Maine works to promote the French language throughout Maine, hosting classes, events and trips to Canada and France. While the festival is geared toward people who enjoy French, previous attendees say the event offers films that often aren’t easily available.
“I really enjoy the Francophone African films because I don’t know those films, and I wouldn’t necessarily have access to them,” Chelsea Ray, a professor of French language and literature at the University of Maine at Augusta, said.
Watching these films is important, Ray said, highlighting the variety of “different cultural perspectives” they offer.
Scali wants to continue growing the festival.
“There’s such a creative community here in Maine, and I think a cultural offering like a film festival is attractive to that creative community,” Scali said.
Ray mentioned several of her students living near Portland have attended the festival. She hopes it grows too.
“It’d be great to grow it to make more films available at UMA because there is an interest in doing that,” Ray said.
WHERE TO BUY TICKETS
Tickets to the event can be purchased online through the Alliance Francaise du Maine’s website at afdume.org. The festival pass offers access to all films for $45 for the general public and $30 for members of the Alliance Francaise du Maine or the Portland Museum of Art. Tickets to individual films are also available for $10 for the general public and $7 for members.
Every third Thursday of the month the Portland Museum of Art offers free entry to all exhibitions, so tickets to Thursday’s screenings are available for free.
There is a reduced rate for high school and college students. They are eligible to buy a $10 festival pass which allows them to see three films. The individual ticket rate for high school and college students is $5.

title: A push to train and hire more women in the auto repair industry
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LAS VEGAS (InvestigateTV) — Most auto repair shops are staffed almost entirely by men, according to federal labor data.
A February 2026 report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics found about 1.8% of mechanics are women.
Federal data predicts about 70,000 job openings in the field by 2034 as many older workers retire. The industry is stepping up efforts to recruit and train more women to meet that demand.
Samantha Aiken is the service manager for the Midas off Tropicana in Las Vegas. The trained auto technician said some shops were skeptical to hire her. She said the family that owns the shop vouched for her, saying customer service needed a woman’s touch.
“I relate to the customers. I’m honest with them. You know, I put myself in their shoes because I was them at one point, you know,” Aiken said. “So, I just sit next to them and I show them everything. If they have questions, I bring them out here and show them the cars.”
Aiken said she has never been afraid to get her hands dirty.
After fixing cars with her boyfriend and going to parts stores by herself, she decided to pursue a new career.
Companies and shops call staff at UEI looking for students to hire. Rose White, UEI campus president, said students train in the school’s automotive lab.
“We are in the automotive lab here at my campus. This is where our students get to take the theory and the didactic part of their training and put it into hands-on, real practical practice and training,” White said.
White said students are not limited to repair work.
“They’re not looking for careers that they’re going to be sitting at a desk. You can go into the service side, into the management side, administrative,” White said. “You can break into some of the fun things like we have in Las Vegas with F1, racing. So, the sky’s the limit.”
Aiken said she hopes to go back to the classroom in the future to teach other women entering the field. “Just go for it. Don’t be afraid to get your hands dirty.”
National organizations such as Women in Automotive provide mentorship programs and connect women already working in the auto industry.

title: Peak foliage arriving in Bangor region, not quite peak south while past peak north
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Peak foliage is officially arriving in the Bangor region as well as areas around Millinocket and Houlton.
Areas to the north and west of the state have passed their peak and there was significant leaf drop the past few days with the high winds. The leaves will continue to fall rapidly with the colder temperatures we will see through the rest of the week dropping to near freezing multiple nights in the north. The rain tomorrow will also contribute to the significant fall off.
Areas to the south of Bangor and coastal portions of Washington and Hancock county haven’t quite reached their peak yet and will likely not do so until next week.
The weekend looks very comfortable right now so if you do want to see the leaves this weekend a trip to the coast is probably your best bet.
The colors have been quite vibrant this year even with the drier conditions so hopefully that trend will continue into the rest of the season.
Far southern Maine is still in the “low” zone and probably won’t reach its peak until late in the month so if you don’t get to see the peak up here there is still a chance to see some color down there later in the month.

title: Fall foliage is peaking in Bangor this week and headed for the coast
text:
We’re into the part of Maine’s fall foliage show when there are no bad seats.
