title: Singer Olivia Dean served with copyright lawsuit for track on award-winning album
text:
Singer Olivia Dean served with copyright lawsuit for track on award-winning album
The estate of deceased singer-songwriter Bill Withers filed a lawsuit against Olivia Dean over similarities between one of Dean's songs and Withers' "Just the Two of Us."
Singer Olivia Dean served with copyright lawsuit for track on award-winning album
The estate of deceased singer-songwriter Bill Withers filed a lawsuit against Olivia Dean over similarities between one of Dean's songs and Withers' "Just the Two of Us."
Olivia Dean, the British pop star known for her album "The Art of Loving," has been served with a copyright lawsuit.
Related video above: Taylor Swift's 'Showgirl Encore'
The lawsuit accuses Dean's song "I've Seen It," the closing track on "The Art of Loving," of infringing upon the copyright of the Bill Withers song "Just the Two of Us."
Mattie Music Group, the entity that holds the rights to Withers' discography, accused Dean and her publisher, Capitol Records, of copying "in large and significant part" from Withers' song, according to the lawsuit. The accusation stems from the similar lyrics and the "protectable melody" of "Just the Two of Us." The lawsuit was made public by Music Business Worldwide.
Mattie Music Group enlisted the help of an expert musicologist — Alexander Stewart, a professor of jazz studies and ethnomusicology at the University of Vermont — to analyze whether the songs were actually similar. Stewart also testified in the plagiarism case involving Ed Sheeran and Marvin Gaye's estate.
"Dr. Stewart conducted a preliminary musicological comparison and a search for similar prior art and concluded that the works contain substantial similarities in protectable musical expression, including repeated copying of the distinctively protectable melody," the lawsuit reads, though it does not mention what the comparison entailed.
Bill Withers was a legendary singer-songwriter with hits such as "Lean On Me," "Lovely Day," and "Ain't No Sunshine." Over the course of his career, Withers was awarded three Grammy Awards out of nine total nominations. Withers died in 2020.
Olivia Dean won Best New Artist at the 2026 Grammy Awards and the BET Awards. Her 2025 album "The Art of Loving" won British Album of the Year at the 2026 Brit Awards, and she was also awarded British Artist of the Year, Best Pop Act, and Song of the Year there for her single "Rein Me In" with Sam Fender.

title: 50 apartments for low-income seniors open in Bangor
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Housing
This section of the BDN aims to help readers understand Maine’s housing crisis, the volatile real estate market and the public policy behind them. Read more Housing coverage here.
A local housing agency celebrated the completion of 50 new units of affordable housing for low-income seniors in Bangor on Wednesday.
The Bangor Housing Development Corporation, a partner agency of the Bangor Housing Authority, recently completed construction of the Sunridge Senior Housing apartments on Sunset Avenue off Union Street in Bangor.
The $20 million project offers 44 one-bedroom apartments, priced at $1,163 per month, and six two-bedroom units with a monthly rent of $1,395. All utilities are included in the rent fees.
“Our senior housing waiting lists are measured in years so to open a new state of the art facility in Bangor is something we’re very proud of,” said Mike Myatt, executive director of the Bangor Housing Authority. “Sunridge gives seniors a place they can afford that is accessible to them and can adapt as their needs change.”
The building opened as developers statewide are chipping away at a gaping housing shortage largely caused by years of underproduction. A Housing Production Needs Study, completed in 2023, determined that Maine needs at least 76,400 new homes by 2030 to close the gap and meet future need.
Roughly 40 residents have already moved into the building, according to Myatt. Another 10 units are available and the housing agency is accepting and processing applications.
“We all see how the lack of housing impacts us and our families,” Myatt said. “We see the lack of affordability for working families, kids living with their parents longer or even moving out of state. We see the lack of accessible homes for seniors and sadly see Mainers sleeping on our streets.”
The housing is reserved for people ages 55 and older whose income is up to 60% of the area median income, which the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development sets annually. For one person in Bangor, this would be an annual income of up to $43,440, or $49,620 for a two-person household.
The building’s amenities include an elevator, on-site laundry, community gardens and all utilities included.
The new building provides housing for some of the thousands of low-income seniors who have been on the housing authority’s waitlists for years, according to Myatt. On average, it takes three to four years for an older resident to receive a call about an available unit after joining BangorHousing’s waitlist.
The agency has closed some waitlists for its other senior housing developments as it was “giving people false hope,” Myatt previously told the Bangor Daily News.
Aside from adding to Bangor’s insufficient housing stock, creating homes for older residents creates a trickle down effect in the region and helps make other types of housing available.
“We’ve had people sell a house to move in here,” Myatt said. “Now that house that they couldn’t get out of is available for a young family and the family’s apartment that they were overgrown in is available for a new working professional.”
The Bangor Housing Development Corporation developed Sunridge Senior Housing and the Bangor Housing Authority manages it.
BangorHousing manages nearly 900 affordable and market rate apartments across 10 developments in the region. The quasi-governmental agency is also responsible for administering housing vouchers in Bangor and surrounding communities, including Hermon, Glenburn, Hampden and Veazie.
BangorHousing hopes to later build another 50-unit apartment building for families, called Conifer Ridge, on an adjacent piece of land the agency bought from the University of Maine in Augusta Bangor campus.

title: Susan Collins says she supports women. We saw otherwise.
text:
Debra Katz and Lisa Banks are founding partners of Katz Banks Kumin LLP. They represented Dr. Ford during the 2018 confirmation hearings of Justice Brett Kavanaugh.
In September 2018, we sat beside Dr. Christine Blasey Ford as she courageously testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee. In a packed room with more than 20 million people watching live on television, Dr. Ford raised her right hand — now an iconic image — and painstakingly recounted the sexual assault she endured by then-Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh when she was 15.
Dr. Ford came forward at enormous personal and professional cost, facing such extreme threats to her safety that she and her family were forced to leave their home and retain 24-hour security services. She did so because she believed that U.S. senators, like Sen. Susan Collins, should know the character of a man who was up for a lifetime appointment to the Supreme Court.
Ultimately, Sen. Collins did not care, and pledged fealty to President Trump in casting the
deciding vote in favor of Kavanaugh’s confirmation. She voted this way despite Dr. Ford’s testimony, which Collins described as “sincere, painful, and compelling,” and despite her own avowed support of survivors of sexual assault and the importance of reproductive rights.
Collins justified her vote by explaining that she had met privately with Kavanaugh, who, in addition to denying the assault, assured her that he would honor precedent, including Roe v. Wade. She subsequently also told CNN that with regard to Dr. Ford’s sexual assault, “I do not believe that Brett Kavanaugh was her assailant. I do believe that she was assaulted. I don’t know by whom, and I’m not certain when, but I do not believe he was the assailant.”
This preposterous explanation, while politically expedient, was offensive not only to Dr. Ford but to survivors everywhere. Conveniently forgotten by Collins was Dr. Ford’s sworn testimony that she was “one hundred percent” certain that it was Kavanaugh who had assaulted her. Also ignored was the important fact that Dr. Ford had named Kavanaugh as her assailant to her friends, therapist and husband years before his nomination.
At best, Susan Collins was duped by Kavanaugh and President Trump. At worst, her actions were duplicitous, born of a desire to assure her constituents she was a moderate and supporter of women, even if her voting record says otherwise.
Beyond Kavanaugh, Collins’ voting record includes a long history of votes for extreme judicial nominees who hold regressive positions on a shocking array of rights.
Sen. Collins voted for Joshua Dunlap, who now sits on the 1st Circuit Court of Appeals, where Maine’s federal appellate matters are heard, despite the fact that he opposed marriage equality and has a history of opposition to pro-choice laws. Collins also voted to confirm Eric Tung to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, even though he too does not believe in a constitutional right to same-sex marriage. And even though Joshua Divine, now a federal judge in Missouri, once lumped homosexuality together with bestiality, she voted to confirm him too.
In total, Susan Collins has voted for 52 out of 55 of Donald Trump’s second-term judges, while voting “no” on many of the pro-choice, pro-worker Biden nominees that she claims to find common cause with.
Collins may claim to be a moderate, but she does not vote like one. And where Dr. Ford demonstrated tremendous courage, Sen. Collins has demonstrated that she will always place politics over principle.
We hope that when Mainers go to the ballot box this November, they remember that Collins’ lack of principle has led directly to the appointment of Justice Kavanaugh, the overturning of Roe v. Wade and to President Trump stocking the federal courts with extreme jurists intent on undermining our nation’s civil rights.

title: InvestigateTV+: Help for overwhelmed animal shelters
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ digs into what is driving the surge at animal shelters nationwide and unique solutions giving pets a second chance.
Then, why heart disease is too often missed in women, the diagnostic bias behind it, and how women can advocate for lifesaving care.
Plus, a group of seniors stitches together a sisterhood, creating quilts of comfort that strengthen their community.
Geography plays role in overwhelmed animal shelters
Many animal shelters across America are overwhelmed, and where animals are located is a big reason why.
In regions like the South, shelters are under-resourced and over-capacity, packed with dogs and cats waiting for adoption. For many, that wait can be fatal. In 2024, U.S. shelters euthanized more than 600,000 animals.
Experts say homes often exist for these animals, but the animals are in the wrong place.
Women advocating for themselves
Heart disease is the biggest threat to women’s health, though studies show many people still believe it is primarily a men’s health issue.
That misconception can be dangerous, as symptoms in women are sometimes mistaken for stress or something else minor, leading to delays in care.
A 2022 study published in the Journal of the American Heart Association found women who went to the emergency room with chest pain waited, on average, 11 minutes longer than men to receive medical attention.
Recruiting for the auto repair industry
Most auto repair shops are staffed almost entirely by men, according to federal labor data.
A February 2026 report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics found about 1.8% of mechanics are women.
Quilting for a cause and for fun
A group of seniors meets every Thursday morning at Cedarhurst of Tesson Heights to sew quilts from fabric scraps.
The quilting club was the idea of activities coordinator Glenette Nothum.
“I love to quilt, and I think word got out. Then the ladies were like, we wanna quilt, and I was like really...wow,” Nothum said.

title: Maine volunteer search and rescue organization finds new home in Orono
text:
A new building on Kelley Road in Orono will be a hangar and rescue station for a Maine search and rescue organization with more than 120 volunteers.
Down East Emergency Medicine Institute, a volunteer organization funded by donations, built a new hangar in Orono earlier this year after previously using a space at the Bangor International Airport for decades. The new location will allow DEEMI to store and work on one of their helicopters, their multiple drones and their two Humvees.
The hangar is unassuming from the outside but large enough for a helicopter and equipment to fit in. The building is painted blue and sports the organization’s logo, but DEEMI’s helicopters and Humvees are painted in their orange, white and yellow coloring.
DEEMI is Maine’s largest volunteer search and rescue organization, and helps state and local agencies find and rescue missing or lost people. Despite being funded by donations, the organization has technology that other search teams and police do not have access to.
During DEEMI’s open house Wednesday, the hangar showcased how heat imaging, drones and helicopter coverage can help searches. DEEMI Director Richard Bowie called their resources “simple technology that works.”
“Our big thing is that we use technology to find people,” Bowie said.
DEEMI participates in roughly 20 search and rescue missions a year, Bowie said. In recent years, the organization has sent volunteers and supplies to disasters in North Carolina and searches across Maine and other New England states, Bowie said.
It’s easier to respond to events out of the state than one would imagine because volunteers are “embedded in states across the county,” meaning some people are already where a disaster or search is taking place, Bowie said. In one instance, a volunteer living in Asheville, North Carolina, was able to help DEEMI coordinate delivering thousands of pounds of supplies during Hurricane Helene.
One of DEEMI’s helicopters, which is kept in Bar Harbor, helped deliver the supplies. Another helicopter, which is undergoing repairs, was the centerpiece for the open house.
Along the edges of the rescue station sat a drone that can upload still images to artificial intelligence to lower search times, an underwater remotely operated vehicle that can search up to 1,000 feet of water, and cameras capable of using heat imaging and night vision.
Joe Hayden, who owns and operates the underwater vehicle, said he hasn’t been involved in any searches yet. Xingda Chan, a post-doctorate researcher at UMass Amherst, also hasn’t had an opportunity to volunteer for any searches, but his research will be used to shorten search times through the use of artificial intelligence.
Chan’s research focuses on how AI can scan images to find specific things like people in black clothing standing near water, or with more generic responses, like how bad traffic is in an area. DEEMI’s imaging, which is done with quick, still images that are later searched by volunteers, gave Chan’s research a real-world application.
The AI program could shorten a 72-hour search to less than 10 minutes, he said. Its offline system means volunteers could use it in remote Maine areas.
Other volunteers, including Chief Pilot David Wight, are also searching for ways the organization can better help.
Wight, who was a helicopter pilot in California before moving to Maine, said he’s trying to find roughly $35,000 in funding for two sets of night vision goggles. The goggles could allow DEEMI to search with their helicopter during night, which is not done by other agencies.
“No one is searching at night. They have to wait for the morning,” Wight said.
Finding funding has not been an issue previously, Boyd said. People generally donate after seeing how helpful DEEMI is during searches, Boyd said. In some instances, companies have donated as much as two cars or multiple helicopter motors after seeing DEEMI’s work, he said.
“It’s really built on generosity,” Boyd said.

title: Grants fund traditional Wabanaki art, harvest practices: ‘Now that’s connection’
text:
MOTAHKOMIKUK — Standing at the narrows that separate Big and Long lakes, Matthew Dana II curled his fingers around the base of a sweet flag shoot and pried its root from the boggy earth.
He snapped it in two to reveal its light interior and release its earthen scent.
Once dried, flag root — or kiwhosuwasq, which translates to muskrat root, given the rodent’s affinity for the plant — is a traditional Passamaquoddy medicine used to treat, among other things, colds and indigestion.
Dana learned to harvest it in this patch of wetland from his late uncle.
Today, he’s teaching the next generation.
And though working with Passamaquoddy youths has been a passion of his for years, he’s made it into a full-time job thanks in part to a $25,000 grant from the Wolankeyutomone Kisi Apaciyewik Fund.
The fund, the name of which translates to “let us take good care of what has been returned,” is an endeavor of the Wabanaki Commission on Land and Stewardship and First Light.
The commission is composed of representatives of all five Wabanaki communities in Maine: the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians, the Mi’kmaq Nation, the Passamaquoddy at Motahkomikuk Indian Township, the Passamaquoddy at Sipayik and the Penobscot Nation. First Light is a group of allied nonnative organizations.
Together, they are accelerating the return of land to Wabanaki Nations.
The Penobscot Nation regained control of 11,000 acres last month and the Mi’kmaq Nation’s holdings nearly doubled when the tribe obtained title to 3,400 acres in June. These are all part of a plan to return 50,000 acres to tribal governments.
“Just getting the land back doesn’t mean that our communities are going to be properly resourced to be able to go out there and engage with the land,” said Frances Soctomah, the fund manager.
That’s where the grants come in.
Wabanaki individuals, nonprofits and governments are eligible to apply for grants of $25,000, $50,000 and $75,000, respectively. In the first two years, the fund has distributed a total of $1.35 million in 32 grants across all five communities. Projects support work around anything from food sovereignty to cultural tourism to trail building.
The fund itself, designed to support Wabanaki self-determination, breaks the mold of traditional nonprofit fundraising. Soctomah and First Light plan to grow it into a multimillion-dollar self-sustaining endowment that will support this kind of work in perpetuity.
Conservation organizations, Maine and national philanthropic foundations and individual donors all contributed in equal part in the initial fundraising. Donors in Maine included the Elmina B. Sewall Foundation, Maine Coast Heritage Trust, the Onion Foundation and the Quimby Foundation.
The application is low barrier, the grants are unrestricted and the use of donations to the fund is often undefined from the outset because it is intended to support self-determination. That’s sometimes difficult for nonnative donors to wrap their heads around.
“We are integrating more of a trust-based philanthropy approach,” Soctomah said.
But on a recent visit to Motahkomikuk, one of the two Passamaquoddy communities in Washington County, it’s not hard to find evidence of the grants at work.
QUILLS PUT A POINT ON IT
Piece by piece, Donald Soctomah can walk you through the Passamaquoddy Tribal Museum and the myriad artifacts and artworks collected there.
These things just have a way of coming home, he said.
There’s a case of stone tools people have found at their camps and, below it, a small Revolutionary War cannon gifted to the tribe by the state in 1820, in gratitude for the service of Wabanaki warriors. The cannon was once lost in the lake, discovered by a fisherman and taken to Maryland, then returned again decades later.
There are baskets, woven by artisans both famous and obscure, and a drum used by the Passamaquoddy Brass Band that toured with Buffalo Bill.
Soctomah, 71, is the Passamaquoddy Tribal Historic Preservation Officer, a former tribal state representative and Frances Soctomah’s father.
He’s been involved in three grant-winning proposals since Wolankeyutomone Kisi Apaciyewik was launched, including one that supported cultural activities through the museum he manages.
With that grant, Soctomah hired a local artist to lead workshops in porcupine quill art; he was a financial benefactor of this year’s community days to celebrate Passamaquoddy culture with drumming, dancing and a slate of native vendors; and he paid the portage drivers for the ancestral canoe journey, an annual event in which tribal members paddle from Motahkomikuk down the St. Croix River to Sipayik.
These are traditions that run in his DNA. They are traditions, he said, that must be supported.
“It’s the right thing to do,” Soctomah said.
At community days, Alisia Morin, 34, said she spotted a road-kill porcupine as she crossed Passamaquoddy lands that very morning.
She was eager to attend several of the quill workshops Soctomah organized. There, she learned to dye and soften the tubular spikes, and then thread them into a backing to create ornately detailed patterns.
“I’ve always been drawn to how beautiful quill work is,” Morin said.
She grew up in Texas and was not exposed to traditional Passamaquoddy art as a kid. Now, raising her own kids on her ancestral homelands, Morin said it’s important that they have more exposure than she did.
So when she spotted the porcupine carcass, she braked.
If Morin had a shovel, she would’ve taken the whole thing. Instead, she and her daughter, Eliana McGinley, 6, plucked just enough quills to make some earrings.
Hudson McGinley, 22 months old, shows off the medallion his mother made by threading dyed porcupine quills through a birch bark backing, at left. At right, Alisia Morin hit the brakes when she spotted the porcupine carcass that morning. (Daryn Slover/Staff Photographer)
“Mom got stuck,” McGinley pipes in, before admitting, “I was a little scared to do it.”
When she pulled out a quilled medallion she made in the workshop, her 22-month-old son Hudson insisted he wear it, and toddled back to the event grounds grasping it with both hands.
ALL ABOUT RESPONSIBILITY
That evening, Eric Bacon steadied the gunwales of his birch bark canoe as a teenager lifted the hem of her ribbon skirt and swung her leg into the shaky hull.
Bacon, who is 49 and has no kids of his own, paddled out into the channel connecting Lewy Lake to Grand Falls Flowage and made a circle.
His 23-year-old birch bark canoe was made by master builder Steve Cayard, a mentor of Bacon’s. These boats, constructed in the traditional Wabanaki style, are feather-light.
But the boats have enough gravity to pull the the course of Bacon’s life into their orbit.
He crossed under the bridge and looped back around before drifting up to the rocky shore.
“Let me get out first,” he instructed.
The girls giggled and ran off.
“I’m trying to plant the seed,” Bacon said as he strapped the boat back on his pickup.
In 1981, he dragged his mother by the hand across the grounds at Mihku Lodge to see a birch bark canoe. He was 4.
In a way, everything Bacon has done since has been about trying to nurture that passion.
He received a $25,000 grant to remodel a garage he owns and turn it into a canoe building and birch bark art space where he can host workshops.
The garage isn’t done yet, and Bacon has instead spent some of the money to rent gear for public paddling events. It’s what the community told him it wanted.
Unlike with some other grants, that’s exactly what grantees are supposed to do, Frances Soctomah said. She wants them to have the ability to pivot according to the needs of their community.
Other grant programs often come with burdensome restrictions — food distribution is often off-limits. In one case, Soctomah recalled a funder telling her they wanted to support a basket-making program, but at the 11th hour said the money couldn’t be used on sharp axes, critical tools for harvesting and processing ash trees.
Now, the fund she manages can help fill the gaps for grantees who are constrained by other programs.
There’s a new skiff parked in Matt Dana’s yard. He bought it with the grant money and, from it, harvested a porpoise as part of his goal to gather 500 pounds of protein with Passamaquoddy youth.
For Dana, all of this is about fulfilling a responsibility.
As a boy, he learned to trap muskrat from a neighbor, and from his father learned to call them in with birch bark; as a young man, Dana learned to harvest ash and weave baskets from Jeremy Frey, a nationally recognized basket-maker; in his 40s, Dana has sought out elders who can still recall how to hunt seals and process their hides.
After he was awarded a grant in 2025, Dana decided to make this a full-time job.
He’s secured funding from numerous nonprofits in Maine to support the work of Mecimi-te Nihtawehtunen — the name of his organization, which means “we have always remembered.” It’s a phrase implying that the traditions not only exist, but will continue to.
Matthew Dana made a crown from ash and sweetgrass for his 4-year-old granddaughter, Sage Dana, to wear during the community days celebration, at left. At right is sweetgrass on Dana’s kitchen sink. (Daryn Slover/Staff Photographer)
Coils of ash splints sat bound in a box outside his kitchen, and there are locks of sweetgrass in the sink.
“It’s got to be preserved,” Dana said. “The generations coming after us need to know it.”
He harvested his first moose at 11. By 18, he was out hunting with his cousins and 10 siblings, then his kids and grandkids. In the woods, Dana said placing his palms down flat on the table, he feels grounded.
Two years ago, Dana took his 21-year-old nephew out hunting and guided what was then a timid young man as he harvested his first buck. Last year, they went out again.
Dana’s nephew tracked a buck into the woods as Dana sat listening.
“And then I heard — I heard the shot.”
When they reunited, there was no more fear. There was pride and confidence and joy. His nephew shared the meat with elders in the community.
“It’s ceremony, it’s prayer, it’s connecting with the ancestors,” Dana said. “The feeling of doing something that my DNA has done for over 15,000 years in this same place? Now that’s connection.”
Reuben M. Schafir is a Report for America corps member who writes about Indigenous and rural communities for the Portland Press Herald.
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 7 to correct the amount of money that the Wolankeyutomone Kisi Apaciyewik Fund has distributed.

title: Work to restore waterways in the Magalloway reaches far downstream
text:
Conservation work carried out by the Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust seeks to strengthen the resiliency of two waterways in the Rangeley region by replacing aging river crossings and correcting straightened waterways.
In July, more than 78,000 acres around the Magalloway River in northern Oxford County was conserved in a joint effort by four groups, Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust, Forest Society of Maine, The Nature Conservancy and Northeast Wilderness Trust, which formed the Magalloway Collaborative in spring of 2025.
The four groups have worked together to raise the $62 million needed to buy the development rights to the land.
Although the development rights have been secured by the collaborative, there is still conservation work to be done in the Magalloway, namely in its rivers and tributaries.
WORK TO BE DONE
Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust has identified many undersized or failing stream crossings that hinder the movement of fish in the preserve, which have been in place on logging roads for decades.
Brook trout are one of the dominant species in the Magalloway and Kennebago rivers. Preferring cold water, they will move upstream in the summer months as the waters warm, choosing rivers and ponds in the higher elevations on the surrounding mountains. The culverts sever access to streams in these higher elevations.
The culverts often sit high off the riverbed, meaning a fish hoping to move up or downstream would have to jump into the pipe and work their way to the other side.
“A lot of studies have shown that, you know, perhaps a few individuals that are more determined can make it through them, but the vast majority don’t,” said Jason Latham, conservation biologist for Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust.
Latham said that in surveys done by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, one side of a culvert on a brook in the nearby Kennebago conservation area, which has seen much of the same conservation techniques, held more than 130 fish while the opposite side had only two. The culvert cut off nearly four miles of upstream habitat from the majority of fish in the system.
“It was clearly a barrier,” he said.
The organization is moving to replace the culverts, opting instead to install open-bottom bridges that mimic a natural stream bed, which allow fish to freely swim through the miles of tributaries.
“By replacing these culverts and building these open-bottom bridges and replicating sort of that natural condition of the stream, we’re essentially reconnecting miles of upstream habitat for species like brook trout,” he said.
Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust has replaced nine crossings in its Kennebago preserve, with three left in the trust’s property. Work in the Kennebago will act as a model for the restorative conservation that will take place in the Magalloway in the coming years.
Replacing culverts also strengthens the area’s resiliency to heavy rains and flooding events.
When heavy rain hits the forest, like in the storms that drenched the region in 2023, the culverts can only handle so much water at a time. Latham said that when the region gets hit with multiple inches of rainfall, all of the water is moved down the mountainside and into the blocked streams.
These culverts can become overwhelmed by the water, causing soil to erode from around the pipe and polluting the downstream area with deposits from the crossing.
LOGGING LEGACY
Decades ago, lengths of rivers across Maine were straightened by logging companies. This allowed for timber harvested in the surrounding woods to easily float to the mills downstream. But now, years after the last log drive, the rivers in the region still show scars.
Stretches of water along the Magalloway and Kennebago were subject to the same treatment, creating long, channel-like stretches where water has little obstruction.
Latham said that healthy rivers often aren’t straight. Instead, they meander, with fallen trees and rocks slowing the flow of water and providing shelter to aquatic life under the surface. Above the surface, waters spill over to create floodplains that are vital to the surrounding habitat.
To correct straightened sections of water, Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust plans to fell trees into portions of waterways to help create the natural barriers the Magalloway needs for a thriving ecosystem. Similar actions were taken on the Kennebago and have been a success, Latham said.
River restoration isn’t solely benefiting the forests of the Rangeley Region. It acts as one of the first lines of defense against flooding and poor water quality in communities along the Androscoggin River.
“Everything flows down to the communities that are even more populated below us,” said Molly Shaw, communications director for Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust.
Communities such as Bethel, Rumford, Livermore Falls and Lewiston all receive water that enters the system through the Magalloway.
The Magalloway begins at the confluence of the river’s West Branch and Third East Branch in Bowman Township at the northern tip of Oxford County. It stretches 40-plus miles through the five unorganized territories south Bowman, then into New Hampshire before crossing back into Maine to become a tributary to Parmachenee Lake, Aziscohos Lake and the Androscoggin River, which flows into Merrymeeting Bay.
“There’s a million different sorts of threats to really good clean water quality that could happen up here at the top of the watershed that impact so many people downstream,” Latham said.
“The Magalloway is the source of fresh water that feeds down to Merrymeeting Bay and dumps into the Gulf of Maine,” he added.
“We have the opportunity, I’ll say, and the responsibility to practice good forest management up here,” Latham said.

title: In first Maine Senate debate, Sen. Collins seeks to distance herself from President Trump
text:
Maine (AP) - Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins distanced herself from President Donald Trump during her first Maine Senate debate with Democrat Troy Jackson, arguing she has maintained her political independence by repeatedly voting against Trump’s agenda and saying that she’s “not exactly his favorite senator.”
Democrats are trying to flip the Maine Senate seat as they work to win control of the Senate. President Trump lost the state in 2024, giving Democrats hope of defeating the five-term moderate Republican, who has been targeted by Democrats in previous elections and survived.
During the hourlong debate, Jackson focused largely on attempting to connect Collins to Trump. He kicked off the night by pointing out she cast a critical vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Trump nominee who eventually helped overturn the constitutional right to abortion. Collins supports abortion rights and said Kavanaugh assured her it was settled law, but she has said recently that she does not regret her vote to confirm him.
“Would you trust her to pick the next Supreme Court justice?” asked Jackson, a former state lawmaker and logger.
He also repeatedly brought up her procedural vote to advance the president’s 2025 tax and spending bill — though Collins ultimately broke with her party to vote against it.
Collins countered that she has voted against Trump more than she did Joe Biden when the Democrat was president, and has pushed back against Trump on tariffs, immigration enforcement and the war in Iran.
“I voted against my party more than another other senator on either side of the aisle,” Collins said.
The attention on Trump comes as only 31% of U.S. adults approved of how the Republican is handling the presidency, according to a September AP-NORC poll. That’s well below where his approval stood when he took office last year.
The president has started holding rallies around the country in an effort to help GOP candidates win in November, telling voters to pretend he is on the ballot. At Tuesday’s debate, a moderator noted Trump has floated the idea of campaigning in Maine, and asked Collins if she would stand beside him if he does.
“I’m not exactly his favorite senator,” she said, adding “I would say that he’s not coming to Maine.”
Collins, who has said she didn’t vote for Trump in 2016, voted to convict the president after his 2021 impeachment over his role in the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. In January, Collins joined a handful of Republican colleagues in backing a failed effort to limit the president’s ability to unilaterally use force in Venezuela. The move prompted Trump to say on social media that they “should never be elected to office again.”
Collins argued that her seniority and experience in the Senate have resulted in money and resources for Maine, saying: “Leadership matters in Washington.”
She also spent Tuesday evening attempting to turn the focus of Maine’s high cost of energy and housing on Jackson, arguing that he had a larger role in making a difference when he was the state Senate president and criticizing “Augusta’s failed policies” as a way to connect Jackson’s to the state’s struggle to address affordability.
Other moments showed how the two candidates were approaching their appeal to working class Maine voters. For example, as Collins touted her ability to remove certain items from Trump’s trade war with Canada, including pulp, concrete and road salt. Jackson pushed back by quipping “we can’t eat road salt.”
Jackson and Collins are scheduled to participate in three more debates later this month.

title: Maine’s Fall Foliage Is Moving Fast: Catch the Colors Before They’re Gone
text:
Maine’s Fall Foliage Is Moving Fast: Catch the Colors Before They’re Gone
Hey, we’re already flying through October, so make sure you take advantage of this incredible weather and get outside. And what I mean by that is to check out the foliage before it passes you by. Because once it’s gone, you know what’s next: the white stuff.
The foliage season is cruising by, with reports now dropping weekly. According to Maine.gov, Northern Maine has just passed peak season, with mid-October being peak for Central and Western Maine, and then closer to the end of October for Southern Maine.
How is the Maine Foliage Season Going?
It feels like the season is flying by, and maybe it's due to the unseasonably warm weather we have had. Thankfully, it hasn't negatively affected the colors. It's wonderful to see the leaves starting to change quite a bit. And thanks to the Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry's Maine Foliage Report, we can see exactly where things stand.
We officially have our first regions that are past peak. It was a great run, Northern and Western Maine, but we’ll see you in 2027.
The rest of the state is a hotbed of activity, from peak conditions in parts of Central and North-Central Maine to high color levels in the south and east. However, Southeastern Maine is still holding at the midlevel. What a perfect time to hit the road and take in some amazing fall colors.
How Will the Upcoming Forecast Affect the Foliage Season?
Fall temperatures should remain relatively consistent here in Maine. That basically means the rest of the foliage season is going to be absolutely ideal for leaf peeping. I mean, who doesn’t love a little crispness in the air while enjoying the outdoors this time of year?

title: Tropical Storm Isaias forms, forecast to become a hurricane and hit the US Gulf Coast this week
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Tropical Storm Isaias formed early Wednesday in the warm waters off eastern Mexico and forecasters said it was expected to strengthen into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season before hitting the U.S. Gulf Coast later in the week.
Isaias was located about 285 miles (460 kilometers) west of Progreso, Mexico, and about 580 miles (935 kilometers) southwest of the Mississippi River’s mouth, according to the Miami-based National Hurricane Center. It had maximum sustained winds of 40 mph (65 kph) and was moving east-northeast at 8 mph (13 kph).
It was not immediately known where the storm may make landfall on the Gulf Coast. The hurricane center’s initial projections said the center of Isaias could come onshore somewhere between eastern Louisiana and the western Florida Panhandle. People in those areas were urged to prepare for the storm.
“There is an increasing risk of dangerous wind and storm surge impacts along portions of the northern Gulf Coast,” the hurricane center said. “Residents from Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle should closely monitor the latest forecast updates and ensure they have their hurricane plan in place.”
Isaias also will bring areas of heavy rain to portions of the Gulf Coast and much of the U.S. Southeast on Friday and into the weekend, forecasters said.
The storm comes as the Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year due to a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over that ocean. Storm activity in the Pacific has been above average.

title: Ferry Point Bridge in Calais to close for repairs
text:
CALAIS, Maine (WABI) - The Ferry Point Bridge in Calais will be temporarily closed starting Oct. 13.
The Maine Department of Transportation says the bridge project includes deck rehabilitation and joint repair on the Maine side of the international border crossing.
The project is estimated to take six weeks, and the bridge should reopen by the end of November.
Drivers should take the Milltown International Bridge or the International Avenue Bridge during the repairs.
Commercial traffic must use the International Avenue Bridge.
Maine DOT says travelers should plan for delays and allow for extra travel time.

title: DOJ attempts to strip citizenship from 40 people accused of criminal activity
text:
DOJ attempts to strip citizenship from 40 people accused of criminal activity
The U.S. Department of Justice announced it is moving to strip citizenship from 40 individuals accused of serious crimes, including acting as an agent for a foreign government, sexual abuse and voluntary manslaughter.
The denaturalization cases were filed between Aug. 21 and Oct. 2. Attorney General Todd Blanche called it "the largest denaturalization effort in modern history."
Some of the countries of origin for the targeted individuals include China, Mexico and Pakistan.
According to Axios, a DOJ spokesperson told the outlet that it has filed more than 200 denaturalization complaints to date.
In April, The New York Times reported that the Justice Department had identified 384 naturalized Americans whose citizenship it sought to revoke.
Federal law allows courts to strip someone of naturalized U.S. citizenship if the government proves that the citizenship was obtained illegally by concealing material facts or by intentional misrepresentation.

title: Buckwheat growers hope new markets can help it reach more tables
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PENN YAN, N.Y. (AP) — Buckwheat crops sway in the breeze as bees bop between the plants’ tiny white flowers. Underneath, small seeds begin to darken, a sign that harvest nears.
Paige Hansen leans down, holding between her fingers the plant whose seeds could soon turn into one of her food products.
“That diversity of crop in the field, I think we should be eating the same way with our diets,” Hansen said. “And ultimately that’s how I think we can shift things.”
After dealing with a dairy allergy in her adult life, Hansen traveled back and forth for about two years between her home in California and the Cornell Food Venture Center in Geneva, New York, to develop a buckwheat-based alternative milk. Now, she has partnered with New Barn Organics, launching her buckwheat milk in Whole Foods Markets across the country this month and creating a buckwheat milk powder that could be used as an ingredient in confections, snacks, crackers and other food products.
It’s part of an effort Hansen and her partners are undertaking to expand the market for buckwheat and hopefully incentivize more farmers to plant it. In the United States, some farmers already plant buckwheat as a cover crop, but many farmers avoid planting cover crops because of the costs despite the environmental benefits. Hansen and other organic farmers see buckwheat as one way to change the food system and help farmers become more resilient in the face of human-caused climate change.
“If we can grow a valuable crop it’s a lot more likely to become part of the system than if we’re growing it because there’s a subsidy payment,” said Klaas Martens, an organic farmer who has grown buckwheat for about 40 years and has worked with Hansen.
Buckwheat fields ‘feel alive’
A popular food crop in the United States until the mid-20th century, buckwheat fell out of favor as farmers turned to higher-yield crops such as corn, soybeans and wheat. Today, buckwheat is often used as a cover crop, and farmers often use the fast-growing plant to suppress weeds or rebuild depleted soils between the harvesting of other crops like corn and soybeans. As a cover crop, buckwheat can also store carbon in its roots and reduce fertilizer runoff at times when fields would otherwise be bare.
Globally, about 2 million tons of buckwheat were produced in 2024, according to data from the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization, a decrease of about half over the last two decades. Comparatively, about 1.2 billion tons of corn were produced globally in 2024, an increase of about 53% in that same time period.
China, Russia and Ukraine produce the most buckwheat, whose seeds are more akin to a fruit rather than a grain despite its name. It’s the main ingredient in soba, a Japanese noodle, and the Ashkenazi Jewish dish kasha varnishkes uses roasted buckwheat alongside pasta and sautéed onions.
Buckwheat takes between 10 to 12 weeks to produce seed. Its short growing cycle means many farmers who sell the harvested crop can plant it between a winter-planted crop and a spring-planted crop.
The plants’ roots also release an acid that can draw phosphorus out of soil and attract a diversity of microbes, creating a soil environment that is “much more favorable for some of our main food crops,” Martens said.
But little is known about how buckwheat can work best in a farmer’s crop rotation. At Cornell University, researchers are working to better understand how the plant suppresses weeds, how it grows and yields under varying conditions and how farmers could potentially add it into their rotations as a cash crop.
Dan Gladstone, who manages 800 acres (324 hectares) of organic crops in Newfield, New York, uses buckwheat as a cover to suppress weeds and rebuild soil but also sells harvested buckwheat. Its roots make the soil loose and easy to plant the following season without tilling, a technique Gladstone implements as much as possible to reduce fuel use and wear on equipment. The crop also supports a diversity of pollinators and Gladstone said he finds buckwheat fields “alive in a way that a lot of other crops don’t feel.”
But harvesting buckwheat can be challenging. It doesn’t all ripen at the same time so farmers need extra equipment to cut the crop so it can dry in fields before getting threshed and hulled.
Despite that, Martens thinks if more farmers added buckwheat into their cropping systems, it would help diversify away from corn and soybeans and could make farms more resilient against losses from extreme weather. Crop insurance, he added, is geared toward high-yield crops like corn and soybeans and adding buckwheat into a crop rotation may help farms stay profitable. Growing buckwheat, which is usually done without fertilizer or pesticides, could also help reduce a farm’s costs while providing income, he said.
“There’s a big difference between being highly productive and extremely resilient,” Martens said. “And there’s a risk in our system because it is highly dependent on a few outside inputs and if you take away some of those outside forces or they become damaged in some way, the entire system is at risk.”
Building market needs cooperation
In Penn Yan, a village of about 5,000 on the shores of Keuka Lake, The Birkett Mills have been processing buckwheat into flour and other products since the late 18th century. There, millers work with 200-year-old milling stones that grind buckwheat and a system of pulleys, wheels and belts that move and sift the buckwheat as it is further refined next to modern robots that bag and stack some finished products. To be gluten-free, the mill uses a sorter to separate buckwheat from other debris and grain.
The mill also works directly with local farmers, selling them buckwheat seed and buying back the crop at a fixed price. That financial guarantee is one way more farmers might start planting the crop.
“There’s also a home for it when they’re done with it,” said Kyle Gifford, president of The Birkett Mills. “Some of these cover crops, they just plow them back under the field because there’s nowhere to sell it.”
Gifford said the company is milling more buckwheat than it has before, working around the clock, seven days a week to meet increased demand. His father, Jeff, said he sees more farmers in the area growing the crop than he did a decade ago. They process the grain for use in their own products and for other companies, including Hansen’s.
Gladstone thinks having strong partnerships with processors and product companies will get more farmers on board with planting buckwheat as a cash crop.
“We need somebody who’s going to do the wholesale processing and turn it into an ingredient. And then we also need people who turn those ingredients into food,” Gladstone said.
And getting buckwheat into more food products as an ingredient is Hansen’s mission. Partnering with a large brand like New Barn Organics allowed her to triple the amount of buckwheat she was buying from farmers. She hopes that demand could offer farmers an incentive to plant the crop on more acres or undergo an organic certification process, she said.
And starting with the ingredients in our food is how the food system can change.
“I’ve always thought that you can’t really have innovation in food unless you have different types of crops to work with,” Hansen said. “Otherwise, you’re kind of all innovating with the same set of ingredients from the same big ingredient suppliers.”

HARMONY, Minn. (KTTC/Gray News) - A 7-month-old girl in Minnesota died after being kicked in the head by a pony, according to authorities.

Deputies responded to the scene along with Harmony Ambulance, the Harmony Fire Department and the Preston Police Department.

title: Maine’s 3 must-watch high school football games this week
text:
Playoff positioning and solidifying your current record. Those are the two themes for this week’s three must-watch high school football games in Maine.
Massabesic (4-1) at South Portland (3-2), 7 p.m. Friday
The Mustangs and Red Riots — ranked No. 8 and No. 10 in the latest Varsity Maine poll — have already shown that they are playoff-worthy teams. But South Portland is currently fifth in the Class A South Crabtree standings, one spot out of the playoffs, with a tough final four games. After this week, they play at Noble, which is ranked fourth in the Crabtree standings, then they host one-loss Winnacunnet of New Hampshire, followed by Portland (4-1).
South Portland’s Chris Salamone ran over Sanford for 227 yards last week and has been productive in every game, totaling 99 carries, 783 yards and 10 TDs. But no one has put up big numbers against Massabesic’s run defense, which is allowing 70 yards per game and stuffed Noble last week for 28 yards on 22 carries.
South Portland has the edge in the passing game. QB Shea Healy (45 of 87, 661 yards, 6 TDs, 3 interceptions) has effectively teamed up with tight end Jacoby Jellow (14 catches, 216 yards) and sophomore wideout Ben Dube (15 catches, 203 yards).
Massabesic has thrown for 215 yards total. It relies on its inside running game, with fullback Alex Harriman (100 carries, 627 yards) doing most of the work and Dustin Maley (41 carries, 278 yards) complementing him as a big-play threat, as he showed with a 75-yard sprint against Noble.
With a win, Massabesic would be in great position to finish third. A move into second would even be possible if either Thornton Academy or Bonny Eagle, the top two teams in the Varsity Maine poll and the league standings, stumble down the stretch. The Mustangs’ lone loss is to Bonny Eagle. They have winless teams Lewiston and Scarborough up next after South Portland before ending the year with a home game against Thornton.
Oxford Hills (4-0) at Bonny Eagle (5-0), 7 p.m. Friday
This game should tell us the validity of Oxford Hills’ unblemished record. Bonny Eagle’s isn’t in doubt, as the Scots beat playoff contender South Portland, Noble and Massabesic in their first three games and are averaging 34.6 points, with an a victory margin of nearly 23 points.
The Vikings, who had a Week 4 bye, have played weaker opponents in Windham (2-3), Deering (1-4), Edward Little (2-2) and Lewiston (0-5). That said, we’ve heard several coaches say something like, “Oxford Hills is looking tough.” Behind the play of dual-threat quarterback Toby Oufiero and top back Keegan Ridley, Oxford Hills has averaged 34.8 points, and the defense has allowed just 27 points total.
The Vikings are likely to have a tough time slowing a Bonny Eagle offense that is starting to hit on multiple cylinders. The Scots have theirs own dynamic QB in Lucas Klehn. Running backs Ben Noe and Ben Havu are improving weekly. Drew Gervais is a big-play threat as a receiver.
Cape Elizabeth (4-1) at Spruce Mountain (3-2), 7 p.m. Friday
Back in the preseason, Cape Elizabeth’s players were convinced they would be much better than last year’s team that went 1-7 and gave up a hideous 51.25 points per game. The Capers are certainly better under first-year coach Issiah Bachelder (though they did give up 82 points to Varsity Maine’s No. 1 eight-man team, Yarmouth).
Spruce Mountain, meanwhile, is the defending Large School South champion. Four of the six teams in Large School South make the playoffs. Right now, it looks like both Cape and Spruce will be in that mix. This game could determined which team is going to be No. 2 behind Yarmouth and get to host a playoff game.

title: FBI stops Mall of America terror plot by 18-year-old after agents sold him assault rifle
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — FBI agents thwarted a terror attack by a teenager on the Mall of America after monitoring him for nearly two years and ultimately supplying him with the AK-47 he planned to use, authorities said Wednesday.
The 18-year-old had been on the FBI’s radar since December 2024, when he began trading messages with a confidential informant. A criminal complaint says he initially expressed an interest in traveling to Somalia to fight for al-Shabab militants. As his plans to instead attack the mall solidified, the complaint says, agents sold him the gun and ammunition on Tuesday and arrested him on the spot.
“This was a radicalized young man who needed to be watched,” U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen said. Agents “were able to detect a threat, and disrupt it, before the defendant carried out his intention to kill, in his words, maybe 30 to 60 people.”
Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud was arrested Tuesday in a public park in Richfield, several miles northwest of the Mall of America, after he paid $600 to an undercover FBI employee posing as a member of the Islamic State group for the rifle and 200 rounds of ammunition, the agency said.
Mohamud appeared in a yellow jail uniform for his initial appearance Wednesday in federal court in St. Paul. He told the judge he did not have a job, own a house or a car, or have any money in the bank. He was represented by Siri Carlson McDowell, a federal public defender. Carlson McDowell and relatives of Mohamud declined to comment after the hearing.
Rosen said Mohamud is an American-born U.S. citizen of Somali descent.
According to an FBI agent’s sworn complaint, Mohamud repeatedly affirmed in chat messages to the informant that he intended to attack and kill non-Muslims at the mall on Oct. 24, the date of a scheduled arts celebration by the Hmong community, Minnesota’s largest Asian ethnic group.
When the informant asked if he was serious about committing the attack, Mohamud replied, “yes i am 100% sure,” the complaint said, and added: “I would have backed out by now if I wasn’t sure.”
The agent wrote that Mohamud’s messages expressed admiration for recent terror attacks as well as an interest in traveling to fight in Somalia, ultimately for the Islamic State group. He later decided he couldn’t afford to travel there and would attack the mall instead, the complaint said.
The teen first came to the FBI’s attention in December 2024, the same month the source began exchanging messages with him, the complaint said. By May 2025, agents were concerned enough that they went to his home. His mother told them he wasn’t home from school yet and called the boy’s father, who declined to speak with them and said he would give their contact information to his lawyer, the complaint said.
“What I would say to parents all over Minnesota, and all over America: If you get any indication — especially if you hear from federal law enforcement — that your son or daughter is being radicalized, to the point where federal law enforcement wants to come and give you that warning, those are warnings that ought to be heeded,” Rosen said.
Tens of thousands of people of Somali descent live in Minnesota, dating back to when refugees began arriving in the 1990s. Over the years several have been charged with attempting to join militant groups.
___
Johnson reported from Seattle. Associated Press reporter Philip Marcelo in New York contributed.

title: FCC considers allowing more political robocalls before midterms, including those created with AI
text:
FCC considers allowing more political robocalls before midterms, including those created with AI
The Federal Communications Commission is considering a request by a conservative group to loosen rules on political robocalls, including those with artificial intelligence-generated voices, before November's midterm elections.
Federal law currently bans most robocalls to cellphones unless the caller gets consent beforehand. The petition calls for a waiver that would allow political groups to use artificial or prerecorded voices in unsolicited wireless calls.
The Republican-led FCC advanced the request for public comment and could rule on it as soon as late October.
Consumer advocacy groups warn the proposed change could trigger a surge of unwanted, partisan and potentially misleading automated calls in the critical final days of the election, which will determine which party controls Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term.
The potential perils became evident two years ago during the presidential primary season when thousands of voters in New Hampshire received a robocall with an AI-generated voice of then-President Joe Biden. The call suggested voters should forgo casting a ballot in the primary and "save" their votes for the general election.
Under the waiver request before the FCC, some state and federal laws protecting against deception and voter intimidation would continue to prohibit certain misleading election-related messages. But granting it could weaken a major deterrent for bad actors, said Tim Harper, who leads the elections team at the Washington-based Center for Democracy and Technology.
Such a ruling close to Election Day would open "a huge opportunity for abuse during a period where harm has outsized impact," he said. "Campaigns will use this technology to target voters in deceptive ways."
A tool for better communication or misleading messages?
The Club for Growth, a right-leaning economic policy group seeking the change, said it could help political organizations better communicate with potential voters, including in more languages, and improve polling accuracy by helping groups reach more voters. It calls current federal rules outdated and argues they dampen freedom of speech.
The nation's communications regulatory body would have to act within a compressed schedule to grant the waiver in time to affect the midterm elections. Critics said it wouldn't be the first time the FCC, which has become closely aligned with the president during his second term, has bypassed procedural norms to serve its political agenda.
Its Republican chairman, Brendan Carr, launched an unusual early review of broadcast licenses for several ABC-owned local broadcast stations, prompting the company to sue. It said the review years ahead of schedule was unconstitutional, a violation of free speech and a retaliation for content Trump dislikes.
The FCC didn't respond to a request for comment on the petition.
Anna Gomez, the sole Democrat among the FCC's three active commissioners, told The Associated Press she opposes the move and thinks it would create "a tsunami of robocalls and misinformation."
"We've already seen dark money groups use AI to put candidates' likeness behind inflammatory comments ahead of this election," Gomez said. "Exempting political calls from the need for consumer consent would supercharge that strategy, and misleading messages could land directly on the handheld phone of nearly every voter in our country."
Political robocalls have caused controversies before
In past elections, deceptive political robocalls have resulted in significant fines associated with the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, the federal law at the center of the petition.
In 2020, tens of thousands of prospective voters in majority-Black areas of the U.S. received robocalls falsely warning that if they voted by mail, they could face arrest and debt collection.
The two conservative hoaxers behind the calls, Jacob Wohl and Jack Burkman, were criminally charged for the calls and fined some $5.1 million for violating the act.
The political consultant behind the 2024 New Hampshire robocalls mimicking Biden's voice said he did it to send a wake-up call about the potential dangers of AI. He was acquitted of criminal voter suppression charges but faced fines and civil damages associated with federal law.
Shortly after the New Hampshire robocall caught authorities' attention, the FCC ruled that robocalls made with AI voice-cloning tools were outlawed under the consumer protection act.
The change could boost various types of AI calling
If the commission pivots to grant the Club for Growth's petition, political groups of all stripes could amp up their use of AI to prerecord messages that play when voters pick up the phone. They also could use the technology to engage in live conversations with voters driven by AI large language models.
Mekela Panditharatne, senior counsel in the democracy program at the Brennan Center for Justice, warned that such conversations hold risks. An AI system could make false promises about a candidate or manipulate voters in conversation by providing inaccurate or incomplete information.
Harper, from the Center for Democracy and Technology, said there also could be a privacy risk for voters who might not know how an AI agent on the line with them is capturing or repurposing their data.
The Club for Growth has argued the waiver would help create a more uniform regulatory landscape, given that unsolicited automated calls to landlines are already allowed. If the waiver is granted, callers would still be limited by certain conditions, including allowing consumers to opt out and making no more than three calls within 30 days to each individual recipient.
A public comment reply period on the petition ends Oct. 19, at which point the FCC could move forward on a decision.

title: The seniors make quilts for foster children and veterans
text:
ST. LOUIS, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - A group of seniors meets every Thursday morning at Cedarhurst of Tesson Heights to sew quilts from fabric scraps.
The quilting club was the idea of activities coordinator Glenette Nothum.
People started donating fabric and sewing machines, and the quilting club was formed.
The club includes 71-year-old Barb Jackson, who has sewing experience.
“My mother was a sewer, she taught me how to sew,” Jackson said.
It also includes 81-year-old Doris Lake, a newcomer who was convinced to join by Jackson.
“I said, ‘I can’t sew like that.’ She says, ‘Come on everybody,’ and now I just love my machine,” Lake said.
Not every member of the club sews, but all members contribute.
The quilts are donated to those in need, including children in the foster care system.
“Today is a baby quilt for the foster care system,” Nothum said.
“Whoever may need it, we give it,” Lake said.
Some quilts were also given to veterans at the Jefferson Barracks VA Hospital, who sent the quilters a letter of thanks.
“The veterans love them,” Nothum said.
Club member Barb Jackson said the group is “just giving back to the community.”

title: Navigating differences in faith while supporting loved ones approaching the end of life
text:
(Aging Untold) — What happens when you and your loved one don’t share the same faith during their final days?
In this episode of The Aging Untold Podcast, our experts tackle one of the most painful, sensitive dynamics in end-of-life care: navigating clashing religious and spiritual beliefs.
When family members attempt to impose faith or force last-minute conversions, it often alienates relationships, drives up anxiety, and robs everyone of peace when comfort matters most.
Our panel breaks down how to set personal boundaries, navigate hospice and hospital chaplain visits, and prioritize presence over preaching so your loved one feels safe, heard, and supported.
According to AARP, about 80% of adults between 50 and 80 say their spiritual beliefs are important to them. At the same time, approximately 29% of Americans report no religious affiliation and are less likely to seek support from faith-based communities.
Watch this episode of The Aging Untold Podcast
Listen to the audio version of each episode
Respecting individual belief systems
Gerontologist and Aging Untold co-host Sam Cradduck said the key is honoring each person’s right to their own beliefs without imposing others’ views.
“You have to honor individual belief systems, and you have to honor their right to make their own choices and not impress your own,” Cradduck said.
Aging expert and Aging Untold co-host Amy O’Rourke said she has mixed feelings.
“If you’re really, really faithful and you really want everybody else to share your faith, you’re going to be the one that’s going to have to be extra, extra careful when you approach somebody that has a different view than yours, because it creates stress and anxiety, and it doesn’t allow room for the other person to really be where they are,” O’Rourke said.
She said people should hold onto their faith while being cautious about pushing it on others before understanding where that person stands.
Opening the conversation
Asking permission before starting a spiritual conversation can make a difference.
“Even opening up the conversation — would you like to have this conversation? Maybe they’ll say no. Maybe they’ll say yes,” O’Rourke said.
Or maybe they’ll ask about it later, aging-well coach and Aging Untold co-host Katherine Ambrose said.
Cradduck noted that religion and politics were historically considered taboo topics, but the issue is not that those conversations shouldn’t happen — it’s that people haven’t learned how to have them in a healthy way.
Asking someone what their thoughts are sets up the opportunity for conversation, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician and Aging Untold co-host, said.
“It’s open communication,” Rogers said.
Cradduck said a conversation about why the other person believes what they believe and how it brings them comfort also presents the opportunity to learn something new.
Faith differences at end of life
Cradduck said differing belief systems can become especially difficult when a loved one is nearing death.
“It’s really hard for family members sometimes to reconcile in themselves if their loved one is passing and they have a different belief system,” Cradduck said, describing a scenario in which an agnostic person is dying while a family member with strong religious beliefs tries to impose that faith.
“In doing so, you alienate that relationship,” Cradduck said.
Cradduck said family members who struggle with a loved one’s differing beliefs should seek guidance from their own spiritual counsel — a pastor, minister, or similar figure — rather than directing that pressure at the dying person.
“Don’t make them feel judged,” Rogers said. “You should not make them feel bad about what they believe. You need to be able to sit and listen and help them through their healing process, whatever that is.”
Ambrose raised the point of finding a way to hope and cope.
“Now, when it comes to taking action, what I see with a lot of people is the lack of confidence and that ‘faith it ‘til you make it’ is kind of play on ‘fake it to make it,’ like you just step into action, maybe not even quite knowing if you’re up to the task, but if you just take action and just trust that you’ll be equipped along the way, and by moving into action, it can, you know the truth will be revealed,” Ambrose said.
The value of listening
The hosts agreed that sometimes the most supportive role a person can play is simply listening and helping them through the healing process.
“Sometimes people just need to talk, and you just need to be empathetic. You don’t have to say anything. You just need to listen,” Rogers said.
O’Rourke added that reflecting on what has helped a person through difficult times in the past can be a useful tool, regardless of their specific belief system.

title: Here’s what’s on the ballot in Bath
text:
Bath residents’ ballots this November will include four uncontested City Council races, in addition to notable races for Maine governor and the Senate.
Election Day voting will be held at Bath Middle School. Absentee voting has already started, and voters can request a ballot by phone, mail, online or in-person at the city clerk’s office.
Here’s a look at what’s on the Bath ballot.
TOWN COUNCIL
Council candidates are running unopposed in Wards 1, 3 and 6. There is also one candidate running for an at-large seat.
At-large: Stefanie Veneziano
Newcomer Stefanie Veneziano said she’s looking to fill an at-large seat to “steer our city toward future success, where young people can build their careers, families can build their lives, and Bath can build a reputation as one of the most thriving communities in Maine.”
In her responses to the Press Herald Voter Guide, Veneziano said her top priorities include affordability and housing, supporting local businesses and organizations, and protecting the character of Bath.
Ward 1: Chris Marks
Ward 1 Councilor Chris Marks is seeking reelection to his seat this November.
A resident of six years, Marks said his top priorities include expanding housing and public transportation and providing property tax relief. The biggest challenge Bath faces, he said, is increasing the tax base “without fundamentally changing the things that make Bath special.”
Ward 3: Miles Burleson-Lesser
A newcomer to local office, Miles Burleson-Lesser also identified affordability as a top issue. As councilor, Burleson-Lesser said he hopes to support housing growth and walkability, and be available to his constituency.
“I’ve watched my classmates have to move away to start families, and I’ve seen my neighbors fall behind despite doing everything right,” Burleson-Lesser said in the Press Herald Voter Guide. “I want Bath to again be a city where generations of families can not only survive but thrive.”
Ward 6: Caitlin McCorkle
Current council vice chairperson Caitlin McCorkle is seeking reelection this November.
In her second term, McCorkle said she wants to be “thoughtful about how we spend while finding more ways to fund city needs without relying so heavily on residential property taxes and without postponing necessary investments.”
Her priorities also include making city government more communicative with its citizens and supporting economic development to bolster the tax base.
SCHOOL BOARD
Melissa Martin is looking to fill a vacant Bath resident spot on the seven-member Regional School Unit 1 board. Vying for the Woolwich resident seat are Jennifer Ritch-Smith, who is running for reelection, and Jamie Dorr.
OTHER RACES
State Sen. Denise Tepler, a Democrat, is running unopposed for a second term in District 24. Residents will also decide whether to reelect Democratic Rep. David Sinclair to House District 50, or choose Republican Jedediah Rice.
Read more about Bath’s local candidates on the Voter Guide.

title: Presque Isle council condemns 3 buildings in push against dangerous properties
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Presque Isle City Council Wednesday voted to condemn three buildings and work with property owners to rehabilitate two others in a series of hearings that showcased an expanded push by the city to address dangerous properties.
The council voted in favour of the immediate demolition of 31 Caron St. and designated both 63 Dupont Drive and 5 Archer St. as dangerous. The vote effectively condemns the properties and orders the owners to abate the problems within 30 days. If conditions don’t improve, the city will fine the owners $100 per day and City Manager Sonja Eyler can authorize a property’s demolition.
Speaking before the council, code enforcement officer George Howe outlined substantial damage or other issues in the three structures deemed dangerous and an unwillingness for the owners of the buildings to solve those problems.
In the case of 31 Caron St., Howe said the mobile home was full of “food, rats, raccoons, holes in the roof.”
In hearings for two other buildings, at 107 Dyer St. and 499 Caribou Road, the council gave the property owners 30 days to come up with a plan of action to fix issues with their buildings and varying timelines to follow that plan and correct the issues.
All five properties are uninhabited.
The council last designated a property as dangerous in July, and before that condemned four others in October of 2025.
Presque Isle has positioned itself on a more aggressive footing this year against dangerous properties. An ordinance aiming to prevent buildings from sitting vacant was called “government overreach” by landlords before the council approved a pared-down version in March.
The council last month advanced a sixth property, 49 Lombard St., to a dangerous building hearing. That hearing will be held on Nov. 4 at the request of councilor Debra Plummer, who said previously that she would miss the October meeting but wanted to be in attendance when that building is considered.
