title: AMHC awarded $7.5 million in federal funding
text:
ELLSWORTH — Aroostook Mental Health Services, Inc. has been awarded $7.5 million in multi-year federal grants to expand treatment, outreach, overdose prevention and recovery services across Aroostook, Hancock and Washington counties, a press release said. The awards represent a significant multi-year investment in addressing the opioid and substance use crisis in some of the state’s most rural and underserved communities.
The funding includes a $4.5 million, five-year grant from the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration and a $3 million, four-year award through the Health Resources and Services Administration’s Rural Communities Opioid Response Program. Together, the grants will strengthen AMHC’s ability to reach individuals who are often disconnected from traditional healthcare systems, including people experiencing homelessness, individuals leaving incarceration and those identified following an overdose or emergency department visit.

title: OBITUARIES for Thursday, October 8, 2026
text:
NORMAN A. DEAN
MADISON – Norman Albert Dean, 87, of Madison, passed away peacefully on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, at his home, in Madison. Norman was born on April 29, 1939, the son of Raymond and Alberta (Mantor) Dean, and was the eighth generation of the Dean family to make Madison home.
Norman’s roots in the community ran deep. He graduated from Madison High School in 1957 and the University of Maine at Orono in 1961 with a B.S. degree.
On August 5, 1961, he married the love of his life, Eleanor R. Wing. Together, they built a life on the Dean family farm and raised their two sons, Steven and Randall. Family was at the heart of Norman’s life. He took great pride in watching his family grow and especially in being “Papa” to his grandchildren. He rarely missed a game, graduation, birthday, or family celebration. His steady presence, encouragement, and genuine interest in their lives meant more to his family than words can express.
Norman dedicated 34 years to teaching at Madison High School, where he taught Vocational Agriculture, Driver’s Education, Biology, and several other science courses. He shared with generations of students not only what he knew, but also his love of the outdoors, agriculture, and the community he called home. Teaching was an important part of Norman’s life, and the relationships he formed with students and colleagues remained a source of pride throughout his life. Many students will remember “Mr. Dean” well beyond the classroom.
Legendary among family, friends, and students are the stories from the many Florida senior trips he chaperoned with longtime colleague and dear friend Ron Paquette. Just as memorable were the end-of-year teachers’ gatherings at Norman and Eleanor’s home, and later at Norm’s hunting camp, where stories were told and friendships were strengthened.
Alongside his teaching career, “Norm” owned and operated the family farm, Ray’s Dairy, delivering milk door to door. Farming was never simply a job to Norman; it was part of who he was. He loved being on his tractor, working the fields beneath the summer sun, and especially enjoyed the years when his grandson Thomas worked beside him during hay season. Special times were also shared with Norman’s cousin, Donald Morse, who came up from New Hampshire, every summer, continuing a tradition that began in childhood.
After his dairy farming days were behind him, Norman found new enjoyment in raising red deer in his pasture. Even at 85, he could still be found working the fields.
Norman believed deeply in giving back to Madison and the State of Maine. He served on the Madison Board of Selectmen from 1979 to 1991, including seven years as chairman. He served on Madison’s Charter Commission from 1979 to 1980 and was appointed by Governor John McKernan to the Maine Board of Environmental Protection.
In 2000, Norman agreed to serve as Madison’s interim town manager in what was expected to be a 30-day appointment. Those 30 days turned into 11 years. During his tenure, Norman helped guide a number of projects important to the town, including the development of the Madison Business Gateway and construction of the Preble Avenue Fields. He also worked with the developers of Backyard Farms, helping bring new investment and jobs to the community.
Norman was a member of the Kennebec Valley Grange, the Odd Fellows, and the Wood Turners Association of Maine. In retirement, he spent many joyful hours at his lathe. He made beautiful wooden bowls, salt-and-pepper shakers, music boxes, and countless other pieces, often giving them to family and friends. Each piece was made with care and became a lasting reminder of Norman’s generosity and the pleasure he found in making something special for someone he loved.
Whether he was teaching in the classroom, working a field, serving the town of Madison, or standing at the lathe, Norman found purpose in being helpful to others. He was proud of his family, deeply connected to his community, and grateful for the life he and Eleanor built together. His legacy can be found not only in his accomplishments, but in the family he loved, the students he taught, the community he served, and the many people whose lives were better for having Norman in them.
When Norman was once asked what he would change if he could do it all over again, he thought for a moment and said, “Well, I guess I wouldn’t change a thing.” For a man who found happiness in his family, his work, his farm, and his community, perhaps nothing could say “a life well lived” better.
Norman and Eleanor were especially grateful to reach their goal of having a beautiful summer together and getting to celebrate their 65th wedding anniversary on the coast of Maine.
Norman is survived by his wife of 65 years, Eleanor W. Dean, of Madison; his son, Steven Dean and his wife, Gloria, and their daughters, Erika and Jessica, and great-granddaughter, Layla; and his son, Randall “Randy” Dean and his wife, Charlene, and their children, Allison, Jennifer, and Thomas.
There will be no public funeral services. Norman’s wish was that his ashes remain with Eleanor on Thurston Hill until she joins him and then they will leave together.
GWENDOLYN H. CUNNINGHAM CASEY
WINDSOR – Gwendolyn H. Cunningham Casey, 91, passed away on Saturday, September 19, 2026, while she was in her own home. She was born April 25, 1935, in Vassalboro, the third of 10 children to Montie Senior and Marguerite Rainey Cunningham.
A memorial church service will be held at North Windsor Baptist Church, on Saturday, October 24, 2026, at 11 a.m. A celebration of life will be held at the China Legion hall, Post #179, in China, on the same day at 1 p.m. A private family committal service and burial will take place at Dyer Hill Cemetery at a later date.
Her complete obituary can be found on Plummer Funeral Home’s website at http://www.plummerfh.com.
In lieu of flowers, please send a donation to North Windsor Baptist Church, 955 Ridge Rd., Windsor.
ARLENE E. CANNON
WINSLOW – Arlene E. (Towers) Cannon, 81, of Winslow, passed away at home on Saturday, September 19, 2026. She was born May 4, 1945, in South Bristol, Maine.
She is survived by her husband, David C. Cannon Sr.; sons, David C. Cannon Jr. and Dean Kinney Sr.; daughters, Robin Kespert and Kysha Towers; along with several grandchildren and great-grandchildren.
At Arlene’s request, no services will be scheduled.
DAVID BURTON
BELGRADE – David “Dave” Burton, 78, passed away peacefully on Tuesday, September 22, 2026, following a long, courageous struggle with multiple health conditions. Dave was born in Waterville, on January 16, 1948, the first of seven children born to Donald and Leora (Edith) Burton (Williams).
He was a lifelong resident of Belgrade and graduated from Belgrade High School as salutatorian in 1966.
After attending Southern Maine Vocational Technical Institute (SMVTI) and earning an associate’s degree in electrical technology, Dave voluntarily enlisted in the U.S. Army and proudly served as a ‘missile man’ with the 65th Artillery from 1968 to 1971. Later, as a patient at the Togus VA hospital, Dave met a pleasant young hospital employee from ‘The County’ who would turn out to be his lifelong love and partner. David and Carolyn (Barnes) Burton were married on August 3, 1974, and through all the ups and downs, shared 52 years together.
A licensed master electrician for 35 years, Dave was employed by various companies, but his longest tenure was working for Digital Equipment, in Augusta, where he met many good friends. Later, his passion for hunting, fishing and the outdoors would lead him to attend schools in Iowa and Montana to learn the art of taxidermy, and he brought those skills home to operate his own business for 10 years until his declining health forced him to retire. An interest in giving back to the town he loved led him to be trained as an EMT and he spent 10 years with Belgrade Fire and Rescue, earning Rescue Person of the Year in 1999.
Dave was happiest spending time with his family and in the outdoors. He never let his health issues interfere with him being present for his family with a smile on his face. He was a huge fan of the Red Sox and Patriots, enjoyed gardening and spending quiet time on his land, often just looking at the trees. He was also thrilled to see his lifelong dream of having a camp on the water come to fruition and spent as much time as possible there with Carolyn and his family.
David was predeceased by his parents Donald and Leora; a sister Brenda (Burton) Hilliker, and a brother Brandon Burton.
He is survived by his wife Carolyn; sons Ryan and his wife Amanda, of Mount Vernon, Travis and his wife Bethany, of Belgrade; and four grandchildren, Nathaniel, Silas, Eliana and Blake; a sister, Bonnie Burton, of Winslow; brothers Terry and his wife Claudia; of Belgrade, Michael, of Belgrade, and Wayne and his wife Shirley, of Chicopee, Massachusetts; and several nieces and nephews.
In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to Belgrade Fire and Rescue Association, 990 Augusta Rd., Belgrade, ME 04917.
RAYMOND P. LOUBIER
WINSLOW – Raymond P. Loubier, 84, of Winslow, passed away on Saturday, September 26, 2026, in the home he built, following a long and determined battle with Parkinson’s Disease. He was born on October 25, 1941, the son of Paul E. and Fernande (Fortin) Loubier.
Ray was a 1960 graduate of Winslow High School where he excelled in Industrial Arts and received first place in the state for his senior project of a grandmother clock which earned him a four-year machinist apprenticeship at Keyes Fibre Co. (now Huhtamaki), in Waterville. A talented woodworker and machinist, he built a 43-year career there through two changes of company ownership, finally retiring in 2003. During that time he furthered his education in machine tooling at the International Correspondence School as well as earning credits at both Thomas College, in Waterville, and the University of Maine-Orono.
He joined the U.S. Air National Guard in 1963 and served six years as a jet engine mechanic. He also enjoyed being part of the Winslow Area Jaycees where he served in many roles including as president in 1971-72. Never one to rest, when he wasn’t accepting offers of free wood in exchange for cutting it down, he started his own company, Multi-Craft Products, where he produced custom items requiring his machinist savvy
He enjoyed his retirement as an antique car enthusiast restoring Corvettes and dabbling in side gigs as a home machinist, sailboat builder, floor monitor at Julia’s auction house, in Fairfield, packaging specialist at Winslow Gun Shop, and antique Corvette parts dealer traveling often to Corvette Carlisle.
He is survived by his children, Andrea Loubier, and Stephanie Weiss and her husband Carl; his grandchildren Winry and Benjamin Devenport, and Elizabeth, William, and Nicholas Weiss; his nephew, Clyde B. Arnold III, of Florida; and close cousin, Carroll LaFlamme.
He was predeceased by his parents; sister, Anne Arnold; special aunt, Florence Loubier; and several cousins.
A Mass of Christian Burial was celebrated on Thursday, October 8, 2026, at St. John the Baptist Catholic Church, 26 Monument St., Winslow.
Arrangements are under the direction and care of Gallant Funeral Home, 10 Elm St., Waterville. An online guestbook may be signed, condolences and memories shared at http://www.gallantfh.com
In lieu of flowers, donations may be sent to St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital, at https://www.stjude.org/ or to Maine chapter of Make a Wish Foundation, at https://wish.org./
THELMA E. GOGGIN BROOKS
WATERVILLE – Thelma E. Eye Goggin Brooks, 101, passed away on Monday, September 28, 2026, at the Oak Grove Center, in Waterville, where she recently celebrated her 101st birthday. She was born on September 10, 1925, in Calais, Maine, the eldest of three children of Chester William Eye and Mary Elizabeth “Bessie” Edmonds Eye.
At the time of her death, Thelma held the title of the longest living member of her family tree, going back generations and hundreds of years.
She was educated in the Calais school system and graduated from Calais Academy in the class of 1942. Shortly after graduation, her family moved to Gardiner and she moved to Rome, New York, where she worked for the Army Air Depot for the next three years, after which time she moved back to Maine.
She married William “Bill” Goggin, in Gardiner, in May 1946, and they began their family together, raising four children. Thelma was active in the community and with the schools, she often subbing a class, coaching a team, or teaching swimming to local children during the summers.
In 1971, due to the death of her son in Vietnam, she suddenly became a Gold Star Mother. One of the downsides of living a long life, she experienced the loss of many of her family members as well as the loss of all four of her children.
During her working years and into the early years of her retirement, Thelma was very involved with genealogy and her family tree. She also was a published author of some of her genealogy researches and families that she also did research for.
A few years before her retirement, she moved to Waterville where she met her second husband, Earl Brooks, and they married in 1979. After she retired, she worked at the library in Waterville and was active in the local stamp club and often played cards on Saturday nights with her friends, well into her 90s.
Thelma was predeceased by her father Chester in 1947 and her mother Bessie in 2003; her brother Donald Eye in 1985 and her sister Shirley Williams in 2015, Richard in 1971, Kenneth in 1994, and most recently, Chester, and her daughter Donna, both in 2024. Also predeceased by her nephew Daniel Williams in 2024; as well as both of her former husbands.
She is survived by two grandsons, Joel Goggin, of California, and Tom Stevens, of Randolph; four-great grandsons, Chris and Zachary Goggin, of Waterville; Ben and Luke Stevens, of Randolph; one nephew and Guardian, Jeffery Williams, of Portland; two nieces, Liz (Eye) Helton and Julie (Eye) Gilmore, of Nevada; one great-niece in Maine, Shannon (Williams) May, three great-nieces Jamie Richards, Carrie Arcoraci and Rachel Gilmore; and one great-nephew, Adam Gilmore, all from Nevada; and several great-nephews and -nieces, in Nevada.
Thelma requested no visiting hours and no funeral. She wished to be cremated, and her ashes buried in the family lot in Calais, where she will be laid to rest next to her parents and her son Kenneth.
Arrangements are under the direction and care of Aable Cremation Service, in Waterville. An online guestbook may be signed, condolences and memories shared at http://www.aablecremationservice.com.
RITA S. FORTIN
BENTON – Rita S. Fortin, 84, of Benton, passed away at her home on Monday, September 28, 2026, following a brief but courageous battle with metastatic breast cancer. She left this world bathed in the love of her family. Rita was born on March 24, 1942, the seventh of 10 children of Noel and Rose Bolduc.
She graduated high school from Bloomfield Academy, in Skowhegan, and went on to graduate from Augusta General Hospital’s radiology technology program.
In 1962, she married the love of her life, Gerald “Jerry” Fortin, with whom she raised her five children on their family farm, in Benton. As her family grew, Rita stepped away from her career as a radiation technologist and embraced her roles as a full-time mother and farm wife. Rita resumed her career 20 years later when her youngest child was in junior high school. She worked as an X-ray technician and mammography technologist at Inland Hospital, in Waterville, and later at Sebasticook Hospital, in Pittsfield, until her retirement in 2010.
Rita was a vivacious woman who brought her full self to everything she did. She was a fully involved and present mother who, together with Jerry, created a loving, fun and hard-working family life on the farm. She was known for wearing bright colors, fun socks, and holiday attire on every opportunity. Having taken up quilting with her sisters in the late 1980s, Rita and her sisters met every week for over 25 years to sew together. She made a point of making a hand-made quilt for each of her children and grandchildren and she also made a crocheted Afghan blanket for each of her great-grandchildren. Highly scheduled and ever on the go, she once left her own birthday party to attend a funeral of a community member.
Rita lived her life in service to others with enthusiasm, laughter and joy. She showed up for people in every conceivable way – usually with homemade food. Aside from the countless individual ways she supported family and friends throughout her life, Rita was also an active member of the Immaculate Heart of Mary Catholic Church, in Fairfield, where she taught Catechism to Catholic children for 15 years and for over 20 years, she taught Rites of Christian Initiation to adults wanting to become Catholic. She also served on the Parish Council and served as a lector and Eucharist Minister for many years. Rita was an active member of Victor Grange of Fairfield Center for over 50 years; she participated in the Grange “Senior Circle,” cooking and serving meals to the elderly well into her 80s; she was a member of Clinton Day Group of Cooperative Extension for over 50 years, serving as president for many of her last several years; a member of Somerset County Cooperative Extension, and she volunteered at the Fairfield Food Pantry twice a month for the past 10 years.
Until her death, Rita remained entrenched in the community that she loved so dearly. It was a great joy to watch her perform plays over the years through her 70s and 80s, both with Victor Grange and as a member of the Recycled Shakespeare Troupe, in Fairfield, of which she was an original member. She experienced great joy participating in a weekly sewing group over the past 10 years, and in more recent years she took up painting lessons with her friend and cribbage tournament partner, Jean Savage. Despite constantly being pulled in multiple directions, Rita never failed to make time for those she loved. When she gave a gift, she gave it with love and when she gave you her attention, she gave you every bit of it.
Rita leaves behind her five children, Judy Fortin, of Benton, and the child of her heart, Jackie; Joan Fortin and her husband, Chet Randall, of Portland, and their children Michael and Lainey Randall; Andy Fortin and his partner, Sandy Irving, of Benton, and his children Anthony Fortin and wife, Malley, Timothy Fortin and wife, Stephanie, Nakita Gangloff and husband Charles, and Gary Wilber; Jan Bancroft and her husband, Ryan, of New Orleans, Louisiana, and their children, Sarah, Rachel, and Matthew Bancroft; and Allan Fortin and his wife, Pamela, of Fairfield, and their children Madelyn McKenzie and her husband, Brody, and Jackson Fortin and his fiancéé, Victoria Dubay; and great-grandchildren, Samuel and Harrison McKenzie, Henry Fortin, and Alexandria and Charles Gangloff; her brother, Raymond Bolduc and his wife, Peg, of Auburn, New Hampshire; and an array of nieces and nephews along with their spouses.
Rita was predeceased by her husband of 56 years, Gerald Fortin; her parents, Noel and Rose Bolduc; eight of her siblings; and eight of her nieces and nephews.
Visiting hours will be a Veilleux-Redington-Lawry Brothers, 8 Elm St., in Waterville, on Friday, October 9, from 2 to 4 p.m. and 5 to 8 p.m. A Funeral Mass will be celebrated on Saturday, October 10, 2026, at 11 a.m., at Notre Dame Catholic Church, 116 Silver Street, in Waterville. A reception will follow immediately after the Mass. A private committal will take place at a later time.
Rita requested in advance that at the time of her death, in lieu of flowers, donations may be made to Covenant House at http://www.covenanthouse.org
Others Departed
DAVID WILLETT
GUNTERSVILLE, Alabama – David Willett, 78, of Guntersville, Alabama, passed away peacefully on Sunday, September 27, 2026, following a brief illness.
David lived his life the way he played golf: with patience, integrity and a deep appreciation for the company he kept. He will be remembered for the way he loved his family, his sense of humor and the 11 aces he managed to get in his lifetime.
David was born in Waterville, graduated from Waterville High School, in 1966, and Thomas College, in Waterville, and worked for Huhtamaki until his retirement.
David is survived by his wife of 57 years Pat; his three children, Jeff (Jessica), Sarah (Jon), Justin (Kristin); his six grandchildren; and his brothers Bruce and Garry.
There will be a celebration of life in Maine, in July 2027.
In lieu of flowers, the family requests that donations be made in his name to, Shepherd’s Cove Hospice, 408 Martling Rd., Albertville, AL 35951 or to, a hospice of your choice.
JAC A. CLAPP
SKOWHEGAN / SPRING HILL, Tennessee – Jac Adam Clapp, 58, of Spring Hill, Tennessee, died unexpectedly on Tuesday, September 29, 2026, at his home. He was born in Milo, on January 29, 1968, to Roger Gerald Clapp and Nora Lee Clapp.
He graduated from Skowhegan Area High School in 1986 and Thomas College, in Waterville, in 1990 with a degree in computer science. Jac was a voracious reader and greatly loved to spend time with his family at any opportunity. Even when he moved to Tennessee for a job, he constantly kept in touch through Facetime on iPads and iPhones.
Jac was predeceased by his father, Roger, who died on Jan. 8, 2010.
He is survived by his mother, Nora Lee; sister, Joy Lee Clapp; brother, Jon Peter Clapp; and uncle, Peter Webb and his family.
There will not be any services. Burial will be in the family lot in the Evergreen Cemetery, Milo.
Arrangements are in the care of the Lary Funeral Home. Messages of condolence and memories may be expressed at http://www.laryfuneralhome.com.
ESTEN H. PEABODY
WINSLOW – Esten H. Peabody, 93, of Winslow, passed away on Saturday, September 19, 2026, following a brief illness. Esten was born in Washington, Maine, on November 10, 1932, to Ulric and Esther (Lenfest) Peabody.
He was the youngest of four boys and graduated from Union High School in 1951. Growing up, he liked playing baseball and developed his passion for hunting with his family that would last a lifetime.
He enlisted in the U.S. Air Force soon after high school and was stationed in Japan during the Korean War, working as a mechanic on the bombers and fighter jets. He was very proud of his military service and had a remarkable memory full of places, stories and at times some colorful Japanese language, from his deployment.
Soon after his return to Maine, he began his 35-year career as a sprinkler fitter for Automatic Sprinkler Co., installing fire suppression systems in buildings across New England. About that time, he met Evelyn Kay Buzzell, of Benton. They were married on August 9, 1958, settled in Winslow and raised their three children. Esten loved coaching Little League baseball and would often commute back and forth a couple of hours to jobs so he could be home for the baseball games. Win or lose, there were many times the whole team would pile into the back of his pickup truck to get an ice cream at Smiley’s. He could often be seen out in the street throwing sky high pop flies for the kids in the neighborhood.
He was a very active member of the Winslow MacCrillis-Rousseau VFW Post #8835 for years. He enjoyed the many friends he made there and was quick to participate in his fellow veterans’ memorial services and parades. He was particularly proud of his time working with the high school on the VFW scholarship program. He was well liked by all, hardworking, humble and had a pretty good sense of humor. For years he would dye his beard green for St. Patrick’s Day and go about his daily work or routine. His favorite month was November, not because it was his and mom’s birthdays, but because it was hunting season. Esten loved walking through the woods and hunting with his brothers and other family members. He told, and re-told, many hunting stories over the years.
He was predeceased by his parents Ulric and Esther, his wife Evelyn (Buzzell) Peabody, and his brothers Neal, Milton, and Phillip.
He is survived by his children, Bruce (JoAnn), Dale (Sharon) and Cheryl; his grandchildren Lauren, Carolyn, Hannah (Isaac) and Luke (Kelsey); and one great-granddaughter, Charlotte.
A graveside service with military honors will be held on Friday, October 16, 2026, at noon, in the committal shelter at the Maine Veterans’ Memorial Cemetery, 143 Blue Star Avenue, Augusta. A Celebration of Life will be held on Friday, October 30, 2026, at 1 p.m., at the Winslow VFW, 175 Veteran Drive, Winslow.
Arrangements are under the direction and care of Gallant Funeral Home, 10 Elm Street, Waterville. An online guestbook may be signed; condolences and memories shared at www.gallantfh.com.
In lieu of flowers donations can be made in memory of dad to the Hospice Volunteers of Waterville Area, at www.hvwa.org.

WATERVILLE – There will be a funeral for Donald A. Toulouse on Friday, October 9, 2026, at 9 a.m., at Notre Dame Church, 116 Silver St., Waterville, Maine. A reception in the church hall will be held following the Mass.

title: Susan Collins’s committee bought trucks the Army didn’t want. Then campaign donations poured in.
text:
The U.S. Army announced last year that it had enough of a specific model of armored vehicle and that any more deliveries would be “excess.” But even so, Congress found a way to keep funding alive for the vehicle — and executives at the company that produces the vehicle found a way to flood key members of Congress with campaign donations.
In the weeks after this year’s appropriations bill passed, employees of AM General or its parent company donated tens of thousands to key appropriations committee members in both chambers, Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Rep. Ken Calvert, R-Calif.
Collins is separately facing scrutiny over a report from ProPublica that the FBI investigated an alleged pay-to-play scheme involving a major donor, an ex-defense contractor. Collins’ office denied that there was any kind of pay-to-play arrangement and said she fully cooperated with the FBI. There is no indication that AM General’s donations were part of such a scheme, but the giving nonetheless demonstrates how Collins’ campaign account has grown with help from employees at defense contractors doing business with the government.
Before the Army put the future of the vehicle in jeopardy, Collins was not a frequent beneficiary of contributions from the company’s workers. She last received campaign funds from AM General or its parent company’s employees more than a decade ago. But after the Army’s “excess” announcement last year, employees and the company’s PAC donated over $58,000 to committees associated with Collins.
One observer of money in politics said that appropriators receiving money from government contractors is a long-standing problem.
“Members of the appropriations committees in Congress are extremely powerful. These lawmakers can steer huge sums of money to private companies. Government contractors today routinely try to leverage a broken campaign finance system to their advantage,” said Michael Beckel, money in politics reform director at Issue One.
The revival of the Army’s order was supported by lawmakers in both parties, including the top Democrat on the House Appropriations defense subcommittee, Rep. Betty McCollum, D-Minn. Collins’ office said that in the Senate, decisions on the program were made not by her but by defense subcommittee chair Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and vice chair Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del. McConnell did not receive donations from employees at AM General or its parent company this election cycle. Coons received $2,500 from its employee PAC.
“Sen. Collins was not involved in this decision. The final decision was made by the Chairs and Ranking Members of the House and Senate Defense Appropriations Subcommittees,” said a Collins spokesperson, Phoebe Keller.
AM General’s CEO, John Chadbourne, said in an email that the company does not comment on campaign donations, “all of which fully comply with FEC rules and regulations.”
He added, “AM General’s focus is on the Warfighter and providing the best light tactical vehicle capabilities to the Joint Forces.”
Congress steps in
AM General is most famous for producing the Humvee, the iconic military vehicle that trawled the streets of Baghdad during the Iraq War. In 2023, the Army selected the company to produce 20,000 units of a more heavily armored successor known as the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle. The company was ramping up its production line in Indiana when then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll announced in May 2025 that he would cancel its order, saying the additional deliveries would result in an “excess.”
Driscoll’s announcement was part of a larger effort to “eliminate waste and obsolete programs.”
“Yesterday’s weapons will not win tomorrow’s wars,” he said.
The military does not always have the last say on its contracts, however.
Congress has for decades swooped in to save pricey programs with political appeal. Soon after the Army moved to kill the vehicle contract, Congress mobilized to save it.
AM General had backing from members of Congress in Indiana, thanks to the jobs on its production line there. It also found backing from legislators in states far from its home.
The House moved first: In June 2025, the House Appropriations Committee’s subcommittee on defense proposed spending hundreds of millions on the vehicle for the Army. By the time the final version of the defense spending bill passed this February, the Army had been provided with $345 million for procurement of a vehicle it said it did not need.
A joint statement from the House and Senate, which Collins’ office said was produced by the defense subcommittees, sounded a skeptical note about the Army’s decision to cancel further orders of the vehicle. The statement said that the Army had provided “inadequate supporting analysis.” One concern was that without the efficiencies from a larger order that included the Army, the cost-per-unit price of vehicles that the Marines still wanted would rise.
McCollum, the House Democrat with an influential role in the process, said in a statement that she was one of numerous members of Congress to question the Army’s decision.
“Appropriators felt the Army failed to do adequate due diligence to justify their rash budget decision to cut the JLTV program and explain the full impacts on the Army, and especially the Marine Corps, which had not been consulted,” she said.
By the time the final version of the defense spending bill passed this February, the Army had been provided with $345 million for procurement of a vehicle it said it did not need.
Collins’ campaign committees had received some money after the Army announced that it wanted to cancel the project.
In the weeks after Congress passed the appropriations bill on Feb. 3, Collins and Calvert, one of her counterparts in the House, both received a burst of donations from AM General employees and the company’s political action committee.
After the appropriations bill went through, donors associated with AM General gave a total of $50,000 to Collins’ fundraising committees.
The donors included Chadbourne, the company’s CEO, and two of KPS Capital’s managing partners. (Private equity firm KPS Capital Partners acquired AM General in 2020.) All gave money to a committee raising money on Collins’ behalf at the end of February or start of March.
Calvert, the California representative with the defense appropriations post, has also benefited from similar donations. Both AM General employees and KPS Capital employees have given $14,285 in direct contributions to Calvert for Congress this election cycle.
The AM General employee PAC has given a combined $20,000 to Ken Calvert for Congress and Eureka Political Action Committee, Calvert’s leadership PAC.
Most of the donations to Calvert associated with AM General came in the weeks immediately after Congress passed the appropriations bill. His office did not respond to a request for comment.
Those contributions put Collins and Calvert in the same league as the Hoosier politicians who were natural supporters of AM General. A fundraising committee associated with Republican Sen. Todd Young received $36,000 from AM General or KPS Capital employees. The AM General employee PAC donated another $10,000 to his main campaign committee. A Marine Corps veteran, Young has been a vocal proponent of the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle.
His Republican colleague Sen. Jim Banks’ leadership PAC received $14,375 total from AM General’s employee PAC and Chadbourne, the executive. Meanwhile, Rep. Frank Mrvan, a Democrat representing northwest Indiana, received $33,050 from AM General or KPS Capital employees, and another $10,000 from the AM General employee PAC, according to FEC filings.
A ban that isn’t
On her campaign website, Collins notes that she serves as chair of the “powerful” appropriations committee.
“This committee decides how federal dollars are spent each year, from national defense and infrastructure to medical research, education and public safety. Susan’s position gives Maine an outsized voice at the table when critical decisions are made which allows her to deliver serious results for Maine,” her website states.
Collins’ office said that in the case of the AM General vehicle, she had nothing to do with the funding decision. A spokesperson said the decision-making in the Senate was up to McConnell, the defense subcommittee chair, and Coons, the vice chair.
McConnell announced his pending retirement in February 2025. His campaign committee and leadership committee have not received donations from either KPS Capital or AM General employees this election cycle, FEC records show. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Coons’ campaign committee received a $2,500 donation from the AM General employee PAC on March 5, according to FEC records. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
McCollum’s leadership PAC received $5,000 from the company’s employee PAC last October, according to FEC records.
Government contractors have been banned from donating directly to candidates for decades. In practice, however, that ban does nothing to prevent company PACs or individual employees from giving to campaigns — even if they serve as company executives.
The contributions associated with AM General represent a sliver of the $15.8 million Collins had raised this election cycle through July, according to data compiled by the watchdog group OpenSecrets. Yet every dollar could help her in what is expected to be a tough fight with Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate candidate with a slight lead on her in recent polls, in November.
The contributions also illustrated a trend among the top contributors to her campaign. Many of them are from people affiliated with government contractors, according to OpenSecrets. Two defense contractors, General Dynamics and RTX, are also on the list of her top organizational contributors.
AM General’s owner, KPS Capital Partners, is the sixth-largest organizational donor to Collins’ campaign committee and leadership PAC, according to the group’s data.
Although AM General has cultivated connections in Congress, members appear to be growing increasingly skeptical of the JLTV vehicle program. In June, House appropriators signaled that they wanted to find a new contractor for the vehicle, citing production delays. AM General was 2,000 vehicles behind on orders from the Marines, the defense subcommittee said.
Chadbourne, the company’s CEO, issued a statement in June defending its performance and blaming a previous contractor for delays.
“Healthy competition, transparency and accountability strengthen America’s defense industrial base,” he said. “AM General remains fully committed to continue earning the trust placed in us by the Army, the Marine Corps, Congress, and the American taxpayer through performance, quality, and disciplined execution.”
By Matt Sledge and Jorge Medellin. Originally published on October 5, 2026. Republished

title: Skowhegan courthouse construction on track to start early next year
text:
SKOWHEGAN — Construction of an expanded, consolidated courthouse is on track to start by next spring.
That’s according to representatives for the state Judicial Branch who met Tuesday with the local Planning Board.
The board got its first look at plans for the $45 million Somerset Judicial Center, an expansion of the existing Skowhegan District Court at 47 Court St.
The project aims to consolidate the District Court, which has two courtrooms, and the single courtroom of the Somerset County Superior Court, which is across the street on the second floor of the county courthouse.
The District Court was built in 1997; and the Superior Court, in 1873, with additions in 1904 and 1938.
“It’s been a long time coming,” said David Woodward, of the Portland architectural and engineering firm WBRC. “It’s a big investment.”
According to a timeline presented to the planning board, the project will go out to bid later this month, an informal groundbreaking would be held by the end of the year and work would start in spring 2027. The current timeline anticipates completion by June 2028, Woodward wrote in a letter to the board.
Construction is estimated at $33 million. That number is lower than the $45 million presented previously to the Legislature and the public, but it does not include anything other than construction costs and other aspects of the project that will be bid separately, Judicial Branch spokesperson Barbara Cardone said Wednesday.
“We won’t know exact construction costs until the bid process is complete,” Cardone wrote in an email.
The planning board is expected to vote on its formal approval at its next meeting either later this month or the first week of November. The board will hold a public hearing before voting.
Plans include creating one additional courtroom, for a total of four. Other improvements include a new drop-off area, a secure parking area for judges and staff, more office space for prosecutors and defense attorneys and separate secure and public corridors for people to move about the facility.
In all, the new judicial center will be about 47,500 square feet, an increase of about 35,000 square feet from the existing District Court, with a one-story section of about 2,100 square feet and a three-story section of about 33,000 square feet.
Plans call for 106 total parking spaces, 75 of which will be public. The town’s ordinance requires 96 parking spaces for a development of this size. Parking and vehicle access will remain in the same area, on Court Street.
To accommodate construction, the Judicial Branch bought the residential property at 55 Court St., in between the District Court and the parking lot. The Judicial Branch also is in the process of purchasing a 0.31-acre strip from the north of 30 High St., owned by Hight Partnership, LLC.
Funding comes from $205 million in bonds the Legislature authorized in 2024, specifically for new court facilities in Somerset, Hancock and Androscoggin counties.
State Rep. Jennifer Poirer, R-Skowhegan, and state Sen. Brad Farrin, R-Norridgewock, were among the bill’s sponsors.
Poirier said at the time she had heard clerks were working in tight quarters, staffing security at two courthouses was a challenge for the sheriff’s office and bats had gotten into file storage on the third floor of the county courthouse.
The Somerset Judicial Center will be the latest consolidated court facility in the state. Since 2000, the Maine Judicial Branch has reduced its court facilities from 48 to 31, according to testimony before the Legislature from State Court Administrator Amy Quinlan.
Combining courthouses is more efficient, Quinlan said, because it allows court clerks to work out of one office, means judicial marshals have to staff only one entry screening and reduces the number of buildings the state has to maintain and heat.
There is also no longer a distinction between District Court and Superior Court when it comes to criminal matters, Quinlan said. The Unified Criminal Docket was created in 2015, and judges from both courts hear cases interchangeably. Appeals from the District Court to the Superior Court in criminal cases and some other kinds of matters were eliminated in 1999.
The new courthouse will be owned by the state of Maine rather than Somerset County, which owns the existing Superior Court space. A 1976 law establishing a statewide, unified court system forced some counties, including Somerset, to provide facilities for state courts — without compensation — in what was expected to be a short-term solution, Quinlan said.
“Over the years, this arrangement has led to an untenable situation: 19th century buildings occupied in great part by the state courts — but owned by the counties — are in great need of modernization and are falling into disrepair,” Quinlan said in her testimony.
In addition to the Superior Court, the county courthouse is home to the county’s administrative offices, the registry of deeds, the probate court and the district attorney’s office. The county’s communications center and emergency management agency are at County Drive in Skowhegan and the sheriff’s office and jail are off East Madison Road in Madison.
Somerset County officials have no plans yet for what they will do with the courtroom, once the Judicial Branch moves out, County Administrator Tim Curtis said Wednesday.

title: Charleston man wins Damariscotta pumpkin weigh-off for second straight year
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A Charleston man was the winner of this year’s Great Pumpkin-Weigh-Off contest in Damariscotta for the second year in a row.
Elroy Morgan, who has been growing pumpkins since 2002, officially won his 7th state championship at the 2026 Damariscotta Pumpkinfest
This year, his pumpkin weighed 1,847 pounds.
Morgan also achieved a new state record this year in gourd length. It measured 155.25 inches long.
Morgan shared a little bit about his process in growing big botanical fruits.
“I start them early. I got to start them already in April, and I start them inside, and then I transplant them out into the greenhouse in the month of May. Then the greenhouses come off, the plants grow, and I get a pumpkin set, and then they grow and they can grow. I had a pumpkin was growing 55 pounds a day for three straight days,” said Morgan.
His biggest pumpkin ever weighed in at 1,870 pounds.

title: City candidate forums to be held Wednesday evening at Bangor High School
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Residents of Bangor have an opportunity to hear from all 15 candidates running for office in Bangor on Wednesday night.
The League of Women Voters is holding two forums at Peakes Auditorium at Bangor High School Wednesday to connect candidates for city council and school committee with voters.
Beginning at 5:30 PM, the three candidates running for three open seats on the Bangor school committee will take the stage.

title: In its 5th year, Portland’s Festival Champlain celebrates French language films from across the world
text:
Rarely do people witness an aspiring filmmaker, a housewife with 1 million trading stamps, a man completely indifferent to the world around him and an obstinate Canadian customs agent at the same event.
Maine’s only French-language film festival is giving people the opportunity to do just that.
“It’s a very unique event,” Lisa Scali, executive director of the Alliance Francaise du Maine, said about the fifth annual Festival Champlain, which runs Oct. 15-18 at the Portland Museum of Art.
The event has grown from 2022, when six films were screened across two days. This year, it features eight films across four days.
Festival Champlain’s schedule reflects Maine’s close, complex relationship with the French language. Maine remains the state with the highest percentage of French speakers and people with French ancestry.
Over the years, organizers have diversified their selection, searching for films from outside of Canada and France. Last year, two films from Cape Verde were screened. Of this year’s eight films, three are Canadian, three are French, one is Gabonese and one is Tunisian.
They don’t just strive to represent Maine’s French-speaking communities; festival organizers made a concerted effort to find films relevant to the whole state, Scali said.
“We are looking to speak to various communities within Maine, and if a film we think in general is relevant for the state of Maine, we’re going to choose that as well,” she said.
One movie, “Promised Sky,” which screens Oct. 16, features an Ivorian pastor living in Tunisia who allows two women to seek refuge in her home. An unconventional family is formed when the group takes in a young orphan who survived a shipwreck.
For Scali, the film touches on contemporary issues Mainers are familiar with, exploring community, relationships and immigration.
“I think this movie is important for everyone to see,” Scali said.
Scali also emphasized changes to programming outside of the screenings. This year three of the films will be followed by a series of conversations with either directors or the deputy director of the Portland Museum of Art.
There will also be a gala reception from 6-8:30 p.m. Oct. 17 at State Street Church in Portland’s West End. It is free, but people are asked to register so organizers know how many guests will attend.
Previously the gala has welcomed special guests, such as Gov. Janet Mills and members of the French and Canadian consuls.
‘A CULTURAL OFFERING’
Throughout the year, the Alliance Francaise du Maine works to promote the French language throughout Maine, hosting classes, events and trips to Canada and France. While the festival is geared toward people who enjoy French, previous attendees say the event offers films that often aren’t easily available.
“I really enjoy the Francophone African films because I don’t know those films, and I wouldn’t necessarily have access to them,” Chelsea Ray, a professor of French language and literature at the University of Maine at Augusta, said.
Watching these films is important, Ray said, highlighting the variety of “different cultural perspectives” they offer.
Scali wants to continue growing the festival.
“There’s such a creative community here in Maine, and I think a cultural offering like a film festival is attractive to that creative community,” Scali said.
Ray mentioned several of her students living near Portland have attended the festival. She hopes it grows too.
“It’d be great to grow it to make more films available at UMA because there is an interest in doing that,” Ray said.
WHERE TO BUY TICKETS
Tickets to the event can be purchased online through the Alliance Francaise du Maine’s website at afdume.org. The festival pass offers access to all films for $45 for the general public and $30 for members of the Alliance Francaise du Maine or the Portland Museum of Art. Tickets to individual films are also available for $10 for the general public and $7 for members.
Every third Thursday of the month the Portland Museum of Art offers free entry to all exhibitions, so tickets to Thursday’s screenings are available for free.
There is a reduced rate for high school and college students. They are eligible to buy a $10 festival pass which allows them to see three films. The individual ticket rate for high school and college students is $5.

title: Who needs a win, and more Week 6 high school football storylines
text:
We talk a lot about the teams at the top of the Crabtree standings. This time of year, though, the games that define seasons are often not between the top teams but between those fighting for their lives.
So, what are some key showdowns this week that involve teams teetering on the brink? Let’s dive into that and Maine high school football’s other top storylines for Week 6.
Who needs a win?
Early in the season, many people tabbed Cheverus as a potential favorite in Class B. Instead, after a shocking loss Saturday against Gorham, the Stags are in last place at 1-4.
That means Cheverus would be on the outside looking in if the playoffs were to begin today. The Stags could use the points that would come with a win over Marshwood (5-0) on Friday. Otherwise, they’ll have to beat at least one of Deering or Biddeford in the final two weeks.
In Class C, York (1-4) is ninth in a statewide field that will send eight to the playoffs. The Wildcats would benefit from a win Friday against Class D Oak Hill (1-4). Belfast, meanwhile, is one spot behind Oak Hill in D South, and should the Raiders lose, the Lions have a chance to move up with a win over Madison.
In eight-man, a Large School North playoff berth might be on the line Saturday when Waterville (1-4) travels to Houlton (0-5). With both teams having tough schedules down the stretch, the winner will have the inside track to the No. 4 seed, while the loser is in peril.
If you think we forgot Class A, we didn’t — but with many key games remaining and an extra week on the schedule, these teams have more breathing room. Still, South Portland (3-2) could use a win Friday when it hosts Massabesic (4-1) or next week at Noble (2-3) as he tries to move higher than fifth place in the South.
Thursday night lights
With 11 of them having already taken place, Thursday games have been a fixture in 2026. That continues this week with five Thursday games, the most since a six-game slate back in Week 1.
A crossover clash in Freeport between Class C Wells (3-2) and Class D Freeport (4-1) highlights Thursday’s schedule. Other games feature Camden Hills (1-4) at Cony (4-1), Brewer (1-4) at Hermon (5-0), Poland (1-4) at Morse (3-2), and Traip Academy (1-4) at Old Orchard Beach (5-0).
If it seems there are more Thursday night games these days, that’s because there are. In all, 18 regular-season high school football games will be played on Thursdays in 2026. There were 12 Thursday games in 2025 and 13 in 2024. In 2023, there were only six.
Why? Dean Plante, Old Orchard Beach’s coach and a member of the Maine Principals’ Association Football Committee, believes it’s two-pronged. Sure, there’s an officiating shortage, but Plante also believes that, when OOB got permission from the MPA to open the 2019 season on a Thursday against Telstar, it started a trend.
“That was the first year of eight-man, so we wanted to showcase eight-man by having it as the first game of the season, and it kind of took off,” Plante said. “I think it’s cool; you get to be one of the only games — maybe the only game — and that gets a little exposure for the kids.”
Cony coach B.L. Lippert said the Maine Association of Football Officials asked his team to move either this week’s game or next week’s against Brunswick to a Thursday night. Because next week is senior night for the Rams, the team chose this one.
“I don’t know specifically how dire the referee shortage is, but it seems like that’s obviously an issue,” Lippert said. “It might not be 50-50 Thursday-Friday, but there might be 10 Thursday games a week next year, is what I’ve heard.”
Can the upstarts keep winning?
Every year, teams that weren’t on many radars at the start of the season capture the state’s attention. A few meet the mark in 2026: Massabesic, Biddeford, Maine Central Institute and Cape Elizabeth are all 4-1, and Lisbon is 3-2. So, what to expect from those teams in Week 6?
MCI, 2-7 a year ago, might have the toughest task of the five. The Huskies host defending Class D North champ Winslow (4-1) in a matchup between the top two teams in the region. The rivals had some fun Big 11 Conference battles between 2017-22.
Massabesic, which missed the playoffs at 3-6 last year, has the aforementioned clash with South Portland. That’s a challenging road showdown for the Mustangs against an opponent whose only losses were hard-fought defeats to Bonny Eagle and Thornton Academy — the top two teams in the Varsity Maine poll.
Cape Elizabeth, Biddeford and Lisbon all went 1-7 last year. Cape Elizabeth (at 3-2 Spruce Mountain) and Biddeford (at 3-2 Skowhegan) make long trips north to face tough opponents on Friday, while Lisbon hosts Mattanawcook Academy (2-3).

title: White House announces auto-enrollment in Trump accounts
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
White House announces auto-enrollment in Trump accounts
President Donald Trump announced auto-enrollment of children in Trump Accounts Wednesday afternoon.
"Now every member of the next generation will have an investment account," Trump said.
The Treasury Department says auto-enrollment eliminated the need for parents to file Form 4547 with their tax return to open an account.
The accounts automatically create investment accounts with $1,000 in seed money for every U.S. citizen child born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028. However, the Treasury clarified that accounts were opened for all eligible children — meaning citizens under 18 with a Social Security number — not just those qualifying for the $1,000 contribution.
Frank Bisignano, CEO of the Internal Revenue Service and commissioner of the Social Security Administration, said 10 million out of 70 million accounts are now funded with $4.5 billion, saying children will "now have a piece of capitalism" that "many would've never seen before." He added that the $4.5 billion figure would increase this weekend.
He said companies like Nvidia and Uber and individuals including Michael and Susan Dell have made contributions to help fund the accounts for children born during the four-year time period, automatically investing a base amount of $1,000 in each eligible child's account.
The money in the accounts is turned over to private firms that invest it in index funds, a type of mutual fund that tracks the stock market. Children can't access the money until they turn 18, and it can only be used for specific purposes, like attending school, starting a business or buying a home.
The president said the accounts would be "teaching people a little bit about entrepreneurship."
He said the accounts mean children would be "potentially very rich" when they reach age 18.
Video below: Treasury Secretary ScottBessent speaks at Trump Account auto-enrollment announcement
Texas Sen. Ted Cruz suggested that instead of an "ugly sweater," family members could make contributions to a child's Trump account as a gift.
During the announcement, Trump's speech wandered from saying the accounts have been widely praised to complaining of a lack of support from Democrats to denouncing communism. Toward the end, he passed out commemorative coins to children.
"Knowing that someone believes in you and your future, that matters just as much" as the money, philanthropist Susan Dell said. "These accounts are for you. We believe in you. We want you to dream big, because we know you can make your dream come true."
Speakers encouraged parents to claim their children's accounts using the Trump Account app and make contributions. Up to $5,000 can be added to the account per year.
"During the claiming process, a parent or guardian will verify their identity and relationship to their child, review the child’s information, and accept the account terms," the Treasury says. "Eligible children must also have their Trump Account claimed to receive the one-time $1,000 seed contribution from Treasury."
How compound interest could grow a Trump Account
The Get the Facts Data Team built a visualization that shows how a Trump Account could grow for a child over 18 years.
Since 1957, the S&P 500 has delivered an average annual return of more than 10%. Using that 10% average as a reference, a $1,000 seed investment could grow to about $5,600.
Experts say it could actually be about $3,600 after taxes and an early-withdrawal penalty.

title: Trying to execute Christa Pike again would push into uncharted legal territory, experts say
text:
After Christa Pike survived Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute her, the unsettled question of whether the state will try again could push Tennessee into uncharted legal territory, experts say.
Pike, 50, suffered burns and blisters to her arms and her prognosis remains uncertain after executioners tried to give her two lethal doses of pentobarbital, her legal team said Wednesday. She was sentenced to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer.
Although other states have moved forward with attempting to execute inmates a second time, in those cases, the first try had been halted before any drug actually began flowing.
Outgoing Republican Gov. Bill Lee has paused executions in Tennessee and ordered an outside review of the failed Sept. 30 attempt to put Pike to death. His office did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment on whether the state would try again to execute her.
Death penalty experts say it’s hard to know what will happen if the state decides to move forward with a second attempt.
“Whether or not it would be lawful for the state of Tennessee to attempt to execute her again is a complex question that will take significant time, attention and analysis of her defense team, the prosecution team, the state government in Tennessee and multiple state and federal courts,” said Stephen Johnson, a criminal defense attorney in Tennessee who is president-elect of the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers.
Mental competency could be a first hurdle
Pike regained consciousness almost six days after the failed attempt to kill her. Her legal team had believed she was brain dead, but after she woke up, she was aware of what happened and was “angry and confused,” her lawyers said Wednesday.
Her attorneys will surely explore the medical and psychiatric impact of receiving two doses of the lethal injection drug and being on a ventilator for several days to determine if she is “now legally competent to even be executed,” Johnson said. That will likely include neuropsychological and forensic psychiatric evaluations and potentially other medical tests, and then there would “undoubtedly be significant litigation” over those issues, which can take years, he said.
Other cases could serve as a guide, but none are quite the same
There have been dozens of troubled executions, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, including several attempts that did not end in death.
Alan Miller and Kenneth Smith both survived lethal injection attempts in Alabama in 2022. Both argued that a second execution attempt violated the Eighth Amendment’s prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment as applied to them individually, which courts found “plausible” in early litigation stages. However, the U.S. Supreme Court did not agree to decide this question, and both were ultimately executed by nitrogen gas in 2024.
Two other inmates, Thomas Creech of Idaho and Tony Carruthers of Tennessee, remain on death row after failed attempts to administer lethal injection drugs.
But Pike’s case is distinguishable from others where a second execution attempt was made because she “bore the brunt of lethal drugs,” said Jordan Steiker, co-director of the Capital Punishment Center at the University of Texas. He said other cases involved “the psychological trauma of facing an execution effort” but not “grievous harm.”
A similar case that predates the modern death penalty era
Louisiana executioners tried to put to death 17-year-old Willie Francis in 1946 but called off their efforts after an improperly prepared electric chair failed to kill him.
But he was executed by electrocution the following year after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that a second execution attempt did not violate double jeopardy under the Fifth Amendment or constitute cruel and unusual punishment under the Eighth Amendment, attributing part of its reasoning to the “malfunction” of the electric chair.
The court notably said, “Accidents happen for which no man is to blame.” But a dissenting justice called the experience of being subjected to a second execution attempt “death by installments.”
It’s not clear whether this case would be viewed as controlling precedent because the Court has not revisited this ruling using its modern “evolving standards of decency” approach to the Eighth Amendment, Steiker said.
“So I think the guide today would be whether or not it would be viewed as repulsive according to contemporary community standards to attempt a second execution,” he said.
Complex legal issues
Experts said they are not aware of any state or federal statute that explicitly bars a second execution attempt after a first one fails.
John Mills, a lawyer who represents people facing the death penalty, said a crucial question would be whether a second attempt to execute Pike would amount to torture.
He said federal courts have declined to intervene in “less egregious” cases, but noted that Pike’s lawyers had previously warned that her medical conditions could complicate a lethal injection and make it agonizing.
“Facing her death a second time having thought she was going to die and then instead being tortured raises a strong claim that a second attempt to kill her would amount to torture violating the Eighth Amendment,” Mills said.
Steiker said he believes Pike’s case would be “uncharted territory” if Tennessee moves forward with a second attempt.
“The most obvious way to avoid litigation over this would be for the governor to commute the sentence,” he said.
____
Associated Press writers Kim Chandler in Nashville, Tennessee, and Anna Wilder in Austin, Texas, contributed reporting.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Winds Ease Tonight, Frosty Start Wednesday Before Rain Returns
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Tuesday. It was certainly a windy day across northern Maine, with the strongest gusts topping 50 mph in parts of Aroostook County. A peak gust of 54 mph was reported near Saint Agatha, while Caribou reached 43 mph and Presque Isle topped out at 41 mph. The good news is that the strongest winds are now behind us, with the Wind Advisory allowed to expire late this afternoon. Winds will continue to ease through the evening and overnight hours, but that calmer weather will also set the stage for a very chilly night across the region.
Skies will continue to clear overnight as high pressure builds into northern Maine. With winds gradually diminishing, temperatures will be able to fall quickly, reaching the upper 20s and lower 30s across much of Aroostook County. Presque Isle and Houlton look to fall to around 30 degrees, while Caribou drops to near 32. Some of our normally colder locations could fall even farther, including the upper 20s across portions of western and northern Aroostook County.
Widespread frost is expected across northern Maine overnight and into Wednesday morning. Since the growing season has already ended across Aroostook County, Frost Advisories are no longer issued locally, but temperatures will still be cold enough for a widespread frost and even a freeze in some of the colder valleys.
After the frosty start, Wednesday remains on the chilly side. High temperatures look to reach only the lower to mid 50s across much of the region, including around 53 degrees in Presque Isle and Caribou and near 55 degrees in Houlton.
Cloud cover will gradually increase through the day as our next system approaches from the west. A few sprinkles or light showers could begin developing across northern sections by midday or during the afternoon, but most of the steadier rain holds off until Wednesday night.
Rain becomes more likely Wednesday night and continues into Thursday as a cold front moves through the region. Thursday’s temperatures will be a little milder, generally reaching the upper 50s to around 60 degrees across Aroostook County. Presque Isle and Caribou look to top out near 59 degrees, with Houlton closer to 60.
This next round of rain does not look particularly impressive when it comes to totals. Northern Maine is generally expected to pick up around one tenth to one third of an inch, with considerably less farther south toward Downeast Maine. While any rainfall is welcome, this will provide little to no meaningful improvement to the ongoing drought conditions.
Once the front moves through, shower chances decrease Thursday night, with cooler weather returning again heading toward Friday and the start of the weekend.
For more details on tonight’s frost, Wednesday’s increasing cloud cover and the next round of rain arriving Wednesday night into Thursday, make sure to check out this evening’s First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening!

title: VIDEO: Orphaned kittens meet sharks on aquarium field trip at the Mall of America
text:
VIDEO: Orphaned kittens meet sharks and stingrays on an aquarium field trip at the Mall of America
A pair of kittens gazed up through the aquarium's shimmering blue waters as a (relatively) enormous fish passed overhead. One kitten stared transfixed through the glass while the other, unfazed, was more interested in darting around playfully.
Inside a clear dome, a kitten named Turkey Leg stood up on its back legs as brightly colored clownfish — think "Finding Nemo" — darted just inches from its whiskers. Raising a paw, it batted at the glass, mewing.
For nearly two hours, about two dozen rescue kittens with names like Lottie Dottie, Bendy Wendy and Mouth Trap romped through the Sea Life aquarium at the Mall of America, the largest shopping complex on the continent, located in a suburb of Minneapolis.
Some charged down a 300-foot underwater tunnel, stopping to stare at a sand tiger shark or sea turtles. Other cats found the aquarium's dim blue environment calming and closed their eyes for a little nap.
This was the sixth year the Bitty Kitty Brigade, a rescue organization in the Twin Cities that finds foster homes for orphaned neonatal kittens, held its "field trip" to the aquarium. Some of this year's kittens had Minnesota State Fair-themed names like Funnel Cake or Apple Fries.
"We just thought it'd be a really fun, engaging thing for kittens to see," aquarium spokesperson John Sullwold said. The kittens came early Monday morning before the aquarium opened to the public.
In addition to raising awareness for the Bitty Kitty Brigade, these field trips are a great way for the young cats to socialize, said Kya Anderson, an event director with the group. That can make it easier for them to adjust to new homes if they get adopted, she said. The group is overseeing some 1,000 kittens this year.
"The kittens just get so excited to see, like, the fish swimming around," Anderson said.
Sea Life has also invited puppies from Safe Hands Rescue, another foster-based animal rescue, but obviously not on the same day as the kittens.
"Much more running involved with the puppies," Sullwold said.

title: ‘Touch grass’: Ice cream shop owner’s rant standing up for his teen employees goes viral
text:
BLACKSTONE, Mass. (WFXT) — A social media post from the owner of a Massachusetts ice cream shop has gone viral.
Dave Forgit’s strongly worded message blasting rude customers has gotten the attention of people from around the world.
“It’s supposed to be laid back. It’s ice cream. It’s supposed to be a happy place and a happy time. Settle down, take a breath, touch grass,” Forgit said.
Forgit is the co-owner of Coldstuff Ice Cream. He said he was tired of customers being rude to his employees, so he took to Facebook to post about it.
“We’re not afraid to drop a couple of colorful words on Facebook,” he said.
Forgit and his brother, co-owner Kevin Miller, said a customer yelling at a teen employee over an incorrect sundae price was the last straw.
“The amount of verbal abuse that these young kids get in a day is shocking to me. It’s wild,” Miller said.
The Facebook post said, in part, “I swear to God, stop yelling at my [expletive] employees. They are children. This job, for most of them, is their first. They are going to make mistakes ... It’s ice cream, for crying out loud. Grow up and act your age.”
Forgit said he did not expect his post to get so much attention.
He received an overwhelmingly positive response from people all over the world, including hundreds of thousands of likes and comments.
The ice cream shop has been booming since the viral Facebook post.
“I knew after seeing the post that I just had to come in and stop by and show the support,” customer Mackenzie Cahill said.
And for those who consider the owners’ message tasteless, Forgit followed up his post with a comment, writing, “And nobody gives an [expletive] if you don’t come back. We’d prefer it that way.”
The owners hope a bump in business will extend their season.

title: ‘That scares me a bit’: Bow hunter shot in chest by target shooter just days into hunting season
text:
LANSING, Mich. (WILX/Gray News) - Days into bowhunting season in Michigan, questions about safety are being raised after a hunter was shot in the chest.
The hunter was hit by an errant round from a target shooter while they were sitting inside a hunting blind, according to officials.
The injured hunter ended up being taken to an area hospital.
Brent Langenbacher, a lifelong hunter and manager at Moose Creek Sports, said what happened is concerning.
“I hunt up in Clinton County, so that scares me a bit. I hunt right up there,” Langenbacher said.
Langenbacher added that hunting blinds carry their own safety risks.
“Those are fully camouflaged. Unless you have some orange on there, someone could shoot you while you’re sitting in there and they would have no idea they even shot you,” Langenbacher said.
Michigan law requires hunters to wear bright orange, although there are exceptions, including for bow hunting.
According to the Michigan Department of Natural Resources (DNR), this is because typically there are fewer people in the woods, and the arrows hunters shoot won’t travel as far as bullets or penetrate as deeply.
Langenbacher said changes to a hunting blind could help improve visibility.
“Put a blaze orange hat on top of your hut. You can just do that, and that would let people know someone is in there hunting,” Langenbacher said.
The Michigan DNR noted that hunters do have that option.
“If you’re a bow hunter and you’re concerned that somebody is on a neighboring property, or you want people to know you’re out there, there’s nothing that says you can’t wear orange,” Michigan DNR Lt. Richard Nickols said.
State officials said all hunters are responsible for their rounds and where those rounds end up. If a shooter causes damage or recklessly fires rounds, they could be held criminally responsible.

title: Vassalboro sanitary district reports routine month
text:
Charles “Chuck” Applebee, who manages the Vassalboro Sanitary District’s facilities, called the month of September “routine,” and the same adjective could be applied to the Oct. 1 board of trustees’ meeting.
Applebee said the only non-routine event was a report of water coming out of a manhole. He assumes the cause was a stuck valve, which unstuck itself.
Daphne Paulette and Kirsten Hebert, of Watershed Maine (a subsidiary of Maine Rural Water Association), which manages VSD finances, had been reporting during the month and had nothing new to add. Board members had no comments on the reports.
Board members made three decisions.
After reviewing two quotes for work on the VSD’s Cemetery Street building, they agreed by consensus to reject both for now and to postpone work until spring.
They voted 4-0 to approve revised Standard Operating Procedures for accounting.
By the same vote, they chose Rural Water Impact, of Arlington, Texas, as their new website manager.
Paulette had sent a preliminary draft 2027-28 budget. Board members Vickie Limberger and Donald Robbins volunteered to work on it with her.
Another pending item, board chairman Lauchlin Titus said, is developing a public comment policy.
VSD trustees scheduled their next meeting for 4 p.m., Thursday, Oct. 22, in the Vassalboro town office meeting room.

title: Man arrested after 130 mph motorcycle chase across 3 counties, deputies say
text:
HINESVILLE, Ga. (WTOC/Gray News) - A man is facing multiple felony charges after leading deputies on a high-speed motorcycle pursuit through three southeast Georgia counties, authorities said.
Long County deputies were patrolling Georgia Highway 196 near Joe Kennedy Road at about 9:25 p.m. on Oct. 3. That night, a sergeant spotted a black Yamaha MT-07 motorcycle heading west at a high rate of speed, according to the sheriff’s office.
A sheriff’s office corporal farther ahead saw the motorcycle pass another vehicle in a no-passing zone and clocked it at 90 mph in a posted 55 mph zone. When the corporal tried to pull the motorcycle over near Hay Field Road, the driver accelerated and fled, reaching speeds up to 130 mph.
The chase continued into Tattnall County and then turned left onto U.S. Highway 301, with another corporal taking over as the lead unit. The chase ended on Key Howard Road in Long County when the driver, later identified as Victor Tavarez of Fort Stewart, brought the motorcycle to a stop.
As deputies tried to arrest him, Tavarez tried to flee again and struck a corporal and his patrol vehicle with the motorcycle, authorities said. He lost control after the collision and was taken into custody. The corporal was treated for minor injuries.
Tavarez was charged with:
- Wrong class of driver’s license
- Improper passing on the left
- Reckless driving
- Speeding (2 counts)
- Felony fleeing or attempting to elude
- Felony obstruction of a law enforcement officer
- Aggravated assault against a law enforcement officer
