title: Lewiston’s Alter L/A submits action plan for city’s first 24/7 shelter with Dec. 31 opening
text:
Key Takeaways Key Takeaways are written by Maine Trust staff and highlight the most important points of this article so you can get the gist at a glance.
- City councilors approved an action plan Tuesday setting deadlines for Kaydenz Kitchen to complete work needed to open the city’s first 24/7 homeless shelter at 70 Horton St.
- The plan includes permits, construction and equipment purchases to be completed by the end of December.
LEWISTON — City councilors approved an action plan Tuesday night that calls for a Dec. 31 opening for Alter L/A, the city’s first formally licensed low-barrier homeless shelter.
The city selected Kaydenz Kitchen Food Pantry to operate the city’s first shelter July 17, 2025, under a master services agreement, which city officials said had no deadlines or benchmarks.
The new action plan establishes them, including deadlines for submitting routine permit applications, completing construction work and purchasing equipment needed to run the shelter at 70 Horton St.
Under the plan, by Dec. 1, all permits must be in hand with construction to follow, beds and bedding for 40 guests ordered by Dec. 15 and sprinklers must be installed by Dec. 31.
The plan requires accounting for final building plans, which have been submitted, and for outstanding building, plumbing, electrical and fire sprinkler permits. Other outstanding projects include showers and general interior work and water lines.
City Administrator Bryan Kaenrath said the original agreement likely should have established a timeline for the shelter project. “So, I think what our attorneys put together here really just clarifies going forward.”
Ward 7 Councilor Bret Martel expressed frustration that city tax dollars have been used toward a shelter that is still nonoperational. He questioned what the city is guaranteed for its approval of $1.22 million for three years of shelter operation.
“Are we going to get an actual licensed low-barrier shelter for three years in exchange for that $1.2 million of taxpayer money?” Martel asked. “Or are we just going to get the balance of the time left? … I’m just trying to find out 16 months later when the city and the taxpayers who funded this are actually going to get what they paid for.”
Alter L/A Executive Director Kevin Boilard told the council he and his staff have been in constant contact with the city and its attorney and that “everyone is on the same page with the current status of the process.”
“We are confident that you will get the development and operation of a low-barrier shelter with that agreement,” Boilard said.
Alter L/A Administrative Coordinator Linda Scott said her organization looks forward to continued collaboration on the project with the city.
“We look forward to completing the job and working in partnership with the city and moving forward with this needed service in our community,” Scott said. “We’re proud of the work we do. We’re proud of our commitment to this community, and we’re proud of our partnership with the city.”

title: Maine’s 3 must-watch high school football games this week
text:
Playoff positioning and solidifying your current record. Those are the two themes for this week’s three must-watch high school football games in Maine.
Massabesic (4-1) at South Portland (3-2), 7 p.m. Friday
The Mustangs and Red Riots — ranked No. 8 and No. 10 in the latest Varsity Maine poll — have already shown that they are playoff-worthy teams. But South Portland is currently fifth in the Class A South Crabtree standings, one spot out of the playoffs, with a tough final four games. After this week, they play at Noble, which is ranked fourth in the Crabtree standings, then they host one-loss Winnacunnet of New Hampshire, followed by Portland (4-1).
South Portland’s Chris Salamone ran over Sanford for 227 yards last week and has been productive in every game, totaling 99 carries, 783 yards and 10 TDs. But no one has put up big numbers against Massabesic’s run defense, which is allowing 70 yards per game and stuffed Noble last week for 28 yards on 22 carries.
South Portland has the edge in the passing game. QB Shea Healy (45 of 87, 661 yards, 6 TDs, 3 interceptions) has effectively teamed up with tight end Jacoby Jellow (14 catches, 216 yards) and sophomore wideout Ben Dube (15 catches, 203 yards).
Massabesic has thrown for 215 yards total. It relies on its inside running game, with fullback Alex Harriman (100 carries, 627 yards) doing most of the work and Dustin Maley (41 carries, 278 yards) complementing him as a big-play threat, as he showed with a 75-yard sprint against Noble.
With a win, Massabesic would be in great position to finish third. A move into second would even be possible if either Thornton Academy or Bonny Eagle, the top two teams in the Varsity Maine poll and the league standings, stumble down the stretch. The Mustangs’ lone loss is to Bonny Eagle. They have winless teams Lewiston and Scarborough up next after South Portland before ending the year with a home game against Thornton.
Oxford Hills (4-0) at Bonny Eagle (5-0), 7 p.m. Friday
This game should tell us the validity of Oxford Hills’ unblemished record. Bonny Eagle’s isn’t in doubt, as the Scots beat playoff contender South Portland, Noble and Massabesic in their first three games and are averaging 34.6 points, with an a victory margin of nearly 23 points.
The Vikings, who had a Week 4 bye, have played weaker opponents in Windham (2-3), Deering (1-4), Edward Little (2-2) and Lewiston (0-5). That said, we’ve heard several coaches say something like, “Oxford Hills is looking tough.” Behind the play of dual-threat quarterback Toby Oufiero and top back Keegan Ridley, Oxford Hills has averaged 34.8 points, and the defense has allowed just 27 points total.
The Vikings are likely to have a tough time slowing a Bonny Eagle offense that is starting to hit on multiple cylinders. The Scots have theirs own dynamic QB in Lucas Klehn. Running backs Ben Noe and Ben Havu are improving weekly. Drew Gervais is a big-play threat as a receiver.
Cape Elizabeth (4-1) at Spruce Mountain (3-2), 7 p.m. Friday
Back in the preseason, Cape Elizabeth’s players were convinced they would be much better than last year’s team that went 1-7 and gave up a hideous 51.25 points per game. The Capers are certainly better under first-year coach Issiah Bachelder (though they did give up 82 points to Varsity Maine’s No. 1 eight-man team, Yarmouth).
Spruce Mountain, meanwhile, is the defending Large School South champion. Four of the six teams in Large School South make the playoffs. Right now, it looks like both Cape and Spruce will be in that mix. This game could determined which team is going to be No. 2 behind Yarmouth and get to host a playoff game.

title: The Fluffernutter Has Been a New England Favorite for Generations
text:
The Fluffernutter Has Been a New England Favorite for Generations
The simple sandwich, made with just three ingredients, is a staple in our region but is virtually unknown elsewhere.

The fluffernutter’s origins trace to Melrose, Massachusetts, where Emma Curtis published a recipe for a peanut butter and marshmallow creme sandwich called the “Liberty Sandwich” in 1918.
The recipe promoted her family’s Snowflake Marshmallow Creme and used oat or barley bread during World War I, when Americans were encouraged to conserve wheat and meat.
Separately, Archibald Query developed Marshmallow Fluff in nearby Somerville, Massachusetts, in 1917, providing the spread later associated with the sandwich.
In 1960, an advertising agency working for Fluff manufacturer Durkee-Mower coined the name “Fluffernutter” to help market the peanut butter and marshmallow combination.
The sandwich went on to become a familiar lunchbox favorite across New England for generations.
It even has its own annual observance, National Fluffernutter Day, celebrated Oct. 8.
And there you have it! With roots dating back more than a century in Massachusetts, the fluffernutter has become one of New England’s most recognizable regional sandwiches.

title: 2 lawsuits challenge Trump’s taxpayer-funded ads, alleging they violate propaganda law
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Two lawsuits filed Wednesday challenged President Donald Trump’s recent series of federally funded television advertisements, which promote his political message while costing taxpayers millions of dollars.
The Democratic National Committee was first to sue the Republican administration, alleging the ads are illegal government-sponsored propaganda and accusing Trump of personally directing them. Later Wednesday, a coalition including the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause filed a separate lawsuit, also alleging an illegal misuse of funds.
Both complaints asked federal judges to stop the use of federal funds to pay for the ads. The lawsuits represented the first legal challenges to the TV spots, which have faced bipartisan backlash for glorifying Trump and promoting his campaign message with November’s midterm elections less than a month away.
The ads, which began airing in September, already have cost more than $12 million to run, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact. The Department of Homeland Security awarded a $20 million contract for the campaign.
Responding Monday to the criticism, Trump defended them as “positive promotion for our Great U.S.A.” but said he’d start paying for them using his MAGA Inc. super PAC going forward.
But on Tuesday, a fifth ad began airing with a notice it was paid for by the U.S. government. It promoted Trump’s military actions to capture Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela earlier this year. The same day, Trump made it clear he hasn’t committed to reimbursing any money that has already been spent, telling reporters “we’ll decide.”
DNC Chair Ken Martin said in a statement that Trump is misusing taxpayer dollars in “a last-ditch attempt to save Republicans in November.”
“Americans deserve better than to have their hard-earned tax dollars used for Trump’s illegal schemes,” he added.
A person familiar with the ad campaign who was not authorized to speak publicly said the ad buys placed prior to Trump’s pledge to start paying for them with his super PAC will end this week. Outside groups will begin to pay at that point, the person said.
The second lawsuit was filed by the legal advocacy group Democracy Forward on behalf of Common Cause, a New York public employee union and a Democratic state legislative candidate in Alabama.
Taxpayers “shouldn’t have to foot the bill for the president’s politics,” said Skye Perryman, who leads Democracy Forward.
Omar Noureldin, senior vice president of policy and litigation at Common Cause, said his organization doesn’t trust that Trump will stick to outside money for future ads. He cited Tuesday’s new ad as proof that the government-sponsored ads were still being scheduled.
“Even if he said that moving forward, he plans to have his super PAC pay for this, that’s not enough for us,” Noureldin said. “We are not going to take the president’s word for it.”
Legal experts have suggested the ads run afoul of a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda,” and potentially other federal laws. The Homeland Security money tapped for the ads comes from a $175 million package Congress gave to the department as part of Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda.
The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have done to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren’t aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs. One of the ads is a near replica of a 2024 ad that Trump ran during his presidential reelection campaign.

title: How Susan Collins’ and Troy Jackson’s Aroostook roots are shaping their US Senate race
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
At a town hall in Gorham last month, Troy Jackson prefaced one line of his introduction with a joking concession.
“I think everyone probably now has heard that I’m a fifth generation logger.” Jackson, the Democratic U.S. Senate candidate, drew laughter.
If you know anything about Jackson, it’s probably that. It’s the second sentence on his campaign website and the centerpiece of many of his ads. He wants Maine voters to know that he has rural, working-class bonafides. His opponent, five-term Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, wants voters to know that she does, too.
“I am a County girl,” Collins says while sitting on a pile of potatoes in an ad released last week.
It’s a nod to Aroostook County, Maine’s northernmost and largest county, from which both Jackson and Collins hail. Larger than three U.S. states, Aroostook also has an outsized role in the runup to November’s midterm elections. In no race in the state’s modern memory have the candidates so heavily wielded their roots to lure voters.
“I don’t remember anything quite like this before in terms of a son and daughter of The County squaring off against each other in a high-level race,” Mark Brewer, chair of the political science department at the University of Maine, said.
‘You don’t bring back the guy who beats the dog’
European settlers first came to Northern Maine for its timber and fertile land. The logging industry literally shaped the region. Competing British and American claims to timberland initiated the bloodless Aroostook War, which ended with the establishment of the Maine-New Brunswick border along the St. John River in 1842.
More than 180 years later, the industry has declined in the region, but it molded the families at the forefront of this U.S. Senate race.
In 1844, two years after the signing of the Webster-Ashburton Treaty that ended the war, Samuel Wilson Collins and a business partner built a sawmill on the banks of the Caribou Stream. The Collinses became one of Caribou’s founding families, and still wield influence in the city of 7,400.
Samuel Wilson Collins’ mill eventually became S.W. Collins Co., a retail lumberyard and hardware business that now has five stores in northern Maine. The business established the family’s prominence, which it parlayed into politics.
Before Susan Collins first ran for office, her family already had a regional political pedigree. Both her parents served as Caribou’s mayor, which is essentially the chair of the City Council. Her father, Donald Collins, served five terms in the Maine Legislature. Her uncle was elected to the Maine Senate and sat on the state’s Supreme Judicial Court.
Numerous other family members have served on local boards and committees.
That level of involvement is not unheard of for prominent families in rural Maine communities, but the Collinses’ entanglement with city affairs has at times driven frustration.
Amid a tumultuous year for Caribou’s school budget last summer, Sam Collins, the senator’s brother, moderated an open meeting that helped determine whether the budget advanced to a ballot.
Collins had filled the role in prior years at the superintendent’s request. But the district’s increasing budget had reached a tipping point for some. One woman, speaking to a reporter after the meeting, tied Collins to a conspiracy to steer the budget through.
Collins laughed at the assertion that he can exert political influence in Caribou, saying that he’s always going to try to “make our community better.”
“When you see Sam Collins standing up, moderating like this, that or something, you can say, ‘Well he did it because he’s a Collins,’ or ‘He got that opportunity because he’s a Collins,” Paul Watson, a Caribou city councilor, said. “Probably. But for him to continually come back, there has to be enough respect in him as a person to have lived up to something that people thought was worthwhile. You don’t bring back the guy who beats the dog.”
Susan Collins, who has lived in Bangor for decades, often cites her family’s business and public service to underscore her connection to the working class.
“I grew up in a small business family in Caribou,” she said last month while campaigning in Naples. “I know what pride there is in multigenerational family businesses.”
Two Aroostooks
For Jackson, his opponent’s family business is an opportunity to tie Collins to an “out of touch” wealthy upper class that scarcely exists in Aroostook County, one of the poorest counties in the state. Collins and her husband personally have assets worth between $4.2 million and $10.1 million, according to the senator’s most recent financial disclosure. Jackson has not yet filed his disclosure, according to a federal database.
“We are both from Aroostook County, but the similarities end there,” Jackson, the former Maine senate president, said at a September town hall in Jay. “I am working class and she’s management. She always has been.”
That notion doesn’t land with Sam Collins, who is the president of S.W. Collins.
“Aroostook County as a whole is not a real prosperous county,” Sam Collins said. “I’m still working every day. I just stopped working Saturdays about four or five years ago … [Are] Susan and our family different in that perspective? No. I think anybody in The County works hard.”
On a jobsite in Allagash, Jackson’s hometown on the edge of the North Maine Woods, Hilton Hafford veered in the opposite direction when asked about The County’s class dynamics. Hafford is one of the loggers who blockaded the Canadian border with Jackson in 1998 in a protest against Canadian logging companies undercutting the wages of American workers.
“If people don’t understand that there’s two Aroostooks, then they just don’t understand,” Hilton Hafford said. “Forget about Aroostook, think of any small town anywhere. I think Troy understands small towns, and he understands people that are struggling … Susan Collins has been in her position for 30 years.”
A new kind of challenger
Susan Collins has never faced a challenger like Troy Jackson before.
In her 2020 election victory over Democrat Sara Gideon, Collins attacked Gideon’s out-of-state heritage — a race that defied polling.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, whom Collins defeated in 2014, often referenced her working-class upbringing in Hancock to strengthen her populist credentials. Collins still rolled to a 37-point win, which came in a poor midterm environment for Democrats.
The 2026 midterms present a polar opposite climate. Republicans are bracing for midterm losses amid President Donald Trump’s historically low approval rating. And Jackson, unlike any other Collins adversary, is from The County.
“The fact that Collins could paint Gideon as from away with her Rhode Island roots and all that was a big part of why she was able to hold on,” Brewer said. “But even if you’re accepted as a Mainer, it seems to me, as someone who’s not a Mainer, [that] it’s different to be from The County. It’s almost like that’s as Maine as you can get.”
Jackson is the first Democratic Senate nominee from Aroostook County in 60 years. He won State Senate elections in the region even as Allagash and the St. John Valley swung toward Trump and the GOP. However, he lost a race for an Allagash Select Board seat in 2023.
The deeply rural town of 237, where Jackson still lives, appears split on his candidacy. Political signs on the edges of its few main roads may outnumber residents.
“I think he’s totally sincere. He feels these things personally, and he wants to change things and make things better for people around him and people in the state of Maine,” novelist Cathie Pelletier, who is related to Jackson, said. “He did that for Aroostook County.”
Jackson is being put under the national microscope like few County people before him. His opponent is among the select handful who can relate.
“Jackson is definitely benefiting from his County lineage, Collins has been able to benefit from that for years,” Brewer said. “On the flip side, he’s not always the smoothest campaigner … he sometimes sticks his foot in his mouth.”
“The question is: are the positives going to outweigh the minuses enough and among the right groups of voters to push Jackson over the top?”
This story was inspired in part by conversations with reporters during BDN community gatherings in Fort Kent and Presque Isle.

title: Cause of death revealed for Dennis Haskins, 'Saved by the Bell' principal, who died at 75
text:
Cause of death revealed for Dennis Haskins, 'Saved by the Bell' principal, multiple reports say
The cause of death for actor Dennis Haskins, best known as Principal Richard Belding on "Saved by the Bell," has been confirmed, according to multiple reports.
Video above: Remembering those we lost in 2026
Haskins died Sept. 27 at Burbank, California's Providence Saint Joseph Medical Center. He was 75. TMZ was the first to report Tuesday night that Haskins' cause of death was Parkinson's disease, with the media outlet saying it obtained the actor's death certificate from the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health. Other media outlets also verified the information in his death certificate.
The Los Angeles Times spoke with his longtime caretaker, Kimberly Snow, who said he had quietly battled Parkinson's disease and had become ill about eight years ago.
While the death certificate lists Parkinson's as the immediate cause of death, it also lists other conditions, including irritable bowel syndrome, depression, hypertension, and benign prostatic hyperplasia, TMZ reported.
Known affectionately as "Mr. Belding" and "America's Favorite Principal" by fans of the hit 1990s television show, he had many other roles throughout the years.
He made his network television debut in 1979 on "The Dukes of Hazzard." Haskins also appeared on "Archie Bunker's Place," Magnum, P.I.," "7th Heaven," "Hot in Cleveland," and nearly 100 other shows as an actor and voiceover artist.
His death was confirmed by his longtime friend and caretaker and first reported by WTVC in his hometown of Chattanooga, Tennessee. His agent confirmed it to TMZ.
“It’s a tragic loss,” his agent, Jay Schachter, said in a statement, the Associated Press reports. “Everyone loved Mr. Belding and those of us who got to know Dennis loved him even more. He was a great person, and he loved, I mean absolutely LOVED his fans. He always had time for them, no matter what. He was my client and dear friend for over 20 years, and I will miss him terribly. I’m heartbroken.”
Haskins was born and raised in Chattanooga, Tennessee. According to a biography posted by the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, he was active in the school's drama club and helped found a community theater group.
Before his television career, he was a music manager, agent and concert promoter, and his clients included Tom Jones and Gregg Allman, according to his biography on IMDb.
Haskins was honored with The University of Tennessee at Chattanooga's Most Distinguished Alumni of 2000 award and has a regional high school academic decathlon named after him, The Dennis Haskins Open.
In recent years, Haskins traveled the country, visiting many Minor League Baseball stadiums in the summer, greeting fans, signing autographs and taking pictures.
Haskins first played Mr. Belding in “Good Morning, Miss Bliss” on the Disney Channel in 1988.
The show was renamed “Saved by the Bell” the following year and became a defining sitcom of the 1990s.
His greeting of “hey, hey, hey, what is going on here?” became one of the sitcom’s most recognizable running bits and remains associated with the character years after the show went off the air.
He is survived by his son, Dustin.
___
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Letter: Bill Cohen wrong about Susan Collins

I have tremendous respect for Bill Cohen and am grateful for his work on behalf of Maine and the United States. In his most recent column however, I believe he misrepresents Susan Collin’s voting record.
She may have been bipartisan during her five terms in office, however she voted with President Donald Trump 90% during his first term, and in 2025 she voted with Trump 95% of the time. When she voted against him, for instance the confirmation of Pete Hegseth and Kash Patel, the Republicans had enough votes, and it appears they allowed her to cast a nay vote.
Bill Cohen has great integrity; I think Susan Collins does not. A vote for Collins is a vote for Trump.
Sarah Everdell
Sedgwick

title: Trump administration proposes a $70,000 fee for international students to work in the US
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday proposed a $70,000 fee for international students seeking to work in the United States, the latest effort from the Trump administration to crack down on foreign enrollment.
A proposed rule would require schools to pay the fee for every student who participates in the optional practice training program, known as OPT, which allows students to work in jobs related to their major during or after their time in school. Students are generally eligible for one year of work post-graduation, though certain science, technology, engineering and math majors are eligible for an additional two years.
Schools would be required to pay the $70,000 for each new student’s initial application to the program, and a $30,000 fee for each renewal.
The change would represent a blow to American colleges and universities that heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue, as well as tech companies and other industries that hire many international students for technical roles.
The OPT program allows international students to gain hands-on experience and fill labor shortages in high-demand STEM fields, said Fanta Aw, CEO of NAFSA, an association that represents international education.
“Driving away the talents, perspectives, and aspirations of international students will only hurt American innovation, economic growth, workforce development, and global leadership,” Aw said in a written statement.
In a statement, DHS described the fee as a response to fraud and abuse of the visa program, which it called a “pipeline for cheap foreign labor.”
The public has 60 days to comment on the proposal before DHS can finalize it and put it into effect. The proposal also could face legal challenges from higher education groups or business associations that could delay it.
President Donald Trump’s administration has been putting pressure on international students in many ways as part of its wider efforts to crack down on immigration and reshape higher education.
Last year, the Republican administration began suddenly terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, detaining and deporting many of them.
This summer, the administration finalized a rule that sought to prevent international students from staying in the U.S. for more than four years without approval from the federal government. The move drew swift backlash from higher education leaders who said it would increase the burden on schools and noted that many programs are longer than four years by design. A federal court prevented the rule from taking effect in September.
___
Hollingsworth reported from Mission, Kan.

title: Van Buren Fire Leaves Home Uninhabitable
text:
VAN BUREN, Maine (WAGM) - A home is a total loss following a fire in Van Buren Tuesday evening.
According to the Van Buren Fire Department, on Tuesday, October 6, at approximately 3:40 p.m., the department was dispatched to a two-story structure fire at 640 Main Street in Van Buren. Upon arrival, small puffs of black smoke were visible from the eaves and door frames of the home. Fire officials say scanning the area showed that all the house windows were covered with black smoke, and the doors were extremely hot. At that time, Van Buren Fire Chief Brian Caron called for mutual aid from Grand Isle Fire and St. Leonard Fire in Canada.
Van Buren Fire made an initial aggressive attack, having to force their way inside the building. Firefighters broke a window on the north side of the home to let hot smoke and gases escape. Helping stop a dangerous backdraft, a sudden fireball that can happen when trapped smoke gets fresh air. Thermal cameras were used to look for hidden hot spots and to see if the fire had spread to other parts of the house.
Main Street in Van Buren was closed for about an hour for firefighters’ safety. The fire was outside of the hydrant district, so with the help of the water district, a water shuttle was set up. After the fire was knocked down, one lane of traffic opened. No one was home at the time of the fire, and no injuries were reported. The house is uninhabitable due to extensive heat, smoke, and fire damage. At approximately 5 p.m., the fire marshal’s office was called to investigate, and the fire remains under investigation. The scene was cleared at around 9 p.m.
The Van Buren Ambulance Service, Van Buren Water, and Van Buren Power also assisted. Van Buren Fire says they would like to thank the border agent who stopped and assisted with multiple tasks, as well as all the employers who allowed the volunteer firefighters to leave work and provide this community service.

title: Disney+ Will Stream the Super Bowl in 2027
text:
Disney+ Will Stream the Super Bowl for the First Time
The Super Bowl is coming to streaming.
ESPN is broadcasting the Super Bowl in 2027 for the first time, but Disney+ subscribers will also be able to stream the big game as well.
Disney and the NFL announced today that next year’s Super Bowl LXI will be broadcast simultaneously on ABC, ESPN, and stream on Disney+. The feed for all three will feature commentary from Joe Buck, Troy Aikman, Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge.
If you have a Disney+ subscription, you can watch the Super Bowl there; there is no special “Super Bowl tier” required, or anything like that.

title: Maine men’s hockey set to start home schedule
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - Robert Morris transfer Tanner Klimpke starred for Maine in its season-opening 4-1 win over Holy Cross on Friday with two goals.
“I think I’m kind of a good power forward who can put the puck in the net. I think a lot of my game kind of revolves around speed and taking pucks hard to the net,” said Tanner Klimpke, senior forward.
“He’s a good player. He can skate. He’s big. He’s got a ton of experience. There’s not much he can’t do. It’s just trying to round out his whole game, the little details of it. He’s gotten so much better since the day we started. He’s dynamic in open ice because he can skate and he’s got a really good stick,” said Ben Barr, head coach.
The Black Bears dropped Saturday’s matchup with the Crusaders, 3-2 in overtime after taking five penalties in the third period.
“You’ve got to be smart, and we weren’t. We start reaching. We start a little bit of the desperation where a guy is by us, and we’re going to hook him or we’re going to trip him for no reason. (There was) offensive zone penalties, that kind of stuff. We flipped a stick out of a guy’s hand. (It’s just) mental errors. We’re not going to be able to take four or five penalties a night and get through that most nights,” said Barr.
“(It’s) just not getting frustrated and not getting fed up with kind of how things are going. (It’s) just kind of sticking with the process and keep working at it,” said Klimpke.
This year’s Maine team spoke about being a part of Alfond Arena’s 50th season before this weekend’s home opener.
“It feels like this place should be older than 50 years. There’s so much history and tradition in here, and you can feel it every time you walk in. That’s a pretty cool thing to be a part of,” said Barr.
The Black Bears open Alfond Arena’s 50th season with a tough test. The No. 6 Quinnipiac Bobcats are coming to town.
“Q-pac is maybe one of the best teams in the nation, if not the best. They’re old. They’re experienced. They have four lines, and they’re good up and down their lineup. They can hurt you in a lot of different ways. For us, what a great opportunity to go play a team like that, especially at home, and see what we have. This might be one of the best teams they’ve ever had. So, it’s going to be a lot of fun,” said Barr.
Puck drop between the Black Bears and Bobcats is Friday and Saturday at 7 p.m.
Saturday’s game will serve as Cancer Awareness Night honoring the memory of Deena Renwick.
Deena was the mother of former Black Bear Nolan Renwick and passed away on July 19, 2025 after a courageous battle with cancer.
The Black Bears will wear special No. 24 jerseys during pregame skate and autograph them.
The jerseys will be auctioned off to support the Lafayette Champion the Cure Challenge.

title: Aging Untold: How to find support when trauma resurfaces with age
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we explore how trauma can resurface later in life and look at where to find essential support for managing symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder.
Plus, find out how to make peace with shifting priorities and move forward without guilt when lifelong friendships begin to fade.
Later, meet a dedicated South Carolina volunteer bringing unexpected comfort to hospital waiting rooms through the soothing sounds of her harp.
Trauma doesn’t simply fade with time, and symptoms can become more noticeable during major life changes, including retirement, illness or loss.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said trauma does not have to come from something dramatic. It’s an “invisible suffering,” and the body tries to move past something that the brain is not allowing.
The Aging Untold hosts are sharing tips on how therapies, from massage and trauma-informed therapy to service animals, could help.
Breaking up with a friend you have had for decades can be as painful as a romantic breakup, but the loss is often grieved in silence.
“Nobody’s bringing you casseroles or sending you flowers usually, and it can be really tough,” aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said.
The Aging Untold hosts are sharing their experiences and how to move forward after a friendship ends.
Caregiving can be overwhelming.
Ty Lewis, a certified dementia practitioner and content creator who cares for her mother, is sharing how a powerful shift in perspective can separate the burden of caregiving from the person receiving the care.
Lewis is a caregiver for her mother, Gertrude, who is in the late stages of Alzheimer’s disease. Her outlook is that the workload is the burden — not the person.
“We have to shift our perspective. The care, that’s the burden, the financial piece, that is the burden. Us not being able to find resources, that’s the burden. But taking care of our loved one, being a servant leader, that is the blessing,” Lewis said.
Peg Mann fills the waiting room at McLeod Seacoast Hospital in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, with gentle notes of harp music.
She is a hospital volunteer and her music provides soft, calming sounds over the monitors and footsteps.
She begins her shift by escorting patients and pushing the comfort cart before setting up to play for patients and families waiting for answers.

title: Argentina bids Messi farewell in final national team match, ending an era
text:
BUENOS AIRES (AP) — Argentina is confronting a once-unimaginable reality: a national team without soccer great Lionel Messi.
On Tuesday, 39-year-old Messi bid farewell to international soccer after 21 years, 126 goals, two Copa América titles and a World Cup championship, scoring a penalty and setting up Argentina’s other two goals for a 3-0 victory over Benin. What was otherwise an unremarkable friendly against the West African nation became a moment that this soccer-crazed country had long dreaded.
“It feels like an era is ending, knowing he won’t play for the national team anymore,” said Valentino Ruso, 17, who was heading to a friend’s house in Buenos Aires to watch the game. “I’m sad. I think everyone is upset today. He will be missed.”
Argentines had an intense, often unforgiving relationship with the shy boy who left his hometown of Rosario at 13 for the youth academy of Spanish club Barcelona. As he grew into a global icon of near-mythical stature, his compatriots adored and abused him, sometimes questioning his commitment to his home country and accusing him of indifference to it.
But by the time he ended his dazzling international career, his devotion to Argentina was no longer in question. Nor was Argentina’s devotion to its most famous export, whose triumphs reminded the country of its capacity for greatness through years of political and economic instability.
“Argentines often say, ‘Thank God I was born at a time when I could experience the miracle of watching Messi play,’” said Andrés Rabinovich, a University of Chicago scholar who has researched soccer’s role in Argentine culture. “It’s hard living in Argentina. Soccer is often one of the few things that offers you some respite, some joy.”
For years, Argentines had debated when and how Messi should leave the world stage. His Aug. 31 announcement that he’d be retiring from the national team, weeks after Argentina’s loss to Spain in the World Cup final, prompted an outpouring of gratitude and grief — even as Messi will continue to light up Major League Soccer with Inter Miami.
“I don’t know if there has ever been a love story between a player and a nation as great as the one you built,” his teammate Rodrigo De Paul wrote on Instagram.
The Argentine soccer federation turned Tuesday’s game — Messi’s 208th — into a national farewell billed as “the last tango.” More than 85,000 tickets to Buenos Aires’ largest stadium sold out in 90 minutes, seats that were originally priced around $60-$300 later fetching over $2,500 on resale sites. Players from Argentina’s 1978, 1986 and 2022 World Cup-winning squads returned to see him off.
After the final whistle, Messi’s eyes glistened as his teammates gathered around him, applauding. A rumbling chorus of “Olé, olé, olé, olé, Messi, Messi” rose from the stands as tens of thousands of fans jumped, sang and bowed toward him as if in worship. A banner at midfield proclaimed him the “Eternal Captain.”
“The truth is, I’m talking more than I ever have. I don’t want to leave here, I don’t want to leave this field,” Messi told the crowd, which roared as if he had scored. “I just want to tell you that I love you, I’m going to miss you, and I’m grateful to God to be Argentine.”
Winning over his own
During the 2000s and 2010s, Messi amassed trophies with his club and won diehard fans from Barcelona to Bangladesh. Yet a major championship for his own country eluded him.
Where the world saw a supernatural talent, some at home saw an outsider who had never played professionally in Argentina and seemed to buckle under the weight of their expectations. Argentine crowds chanted “Diego, Diego,” invoking Diego Maradona, the larger-than-life hero of Argentina’s 1986 World Cup victory, and reminding Messi of a standard he had yet to meet. Messi’s quiet reserve, so at odds with Maradona’s defiant swagger, fueled doubts about his patriotism.
After Argentina lost a third consecutive final in 2016, Messi briefly quit the national team.
“There’s some resentment by the people that stay in Argentina for those who leave, this sense of, ‘They think they’re better than us,’” said Rabinovich, adding that he identifies with Messi as a fellow teenage migrant. Rabinovich said he moved to Canada during Argentina’s 2001 economic crisis, around the time Messi left for Europe. “The old-school Argentines would say, ‘Diego is the Argentine. Messi is soft, a little Spanish boy.’”
The turning point came in 2021, when Argentina beat Brazil to win the Copa América, South America’s championship, for the first time in 28 years. Messi collapsed to the turf as his teammates, delirious, ran to hug him. The player long accused of feeling too little could not stop sobbing.
“Winning clearly disarmed his critics. That’s how soccer works in Argentina,” said Diego Murzi, a sports sociologist at Conicet, Argentina’s national scientific research council. “Criticism of things off the field goes hand in hand with defeats on it.”
The World Cup victory the following year in Qatar sealed his place as a national hero. Messi had delivered the one prize that had eluded him, and millions of Argentines poured into the streets in collective ecstasy, his name in their chants and his No. 10 on their backs.
“I’ll never forget it. I’d never experienced anything like that, being out there with everyone, celebrating together,” said Antonia Correa, 70, a kiosk owner, recalling that day as she waited for a bus in Buenos Aires on Tuesday. “We saw that he wasn’t just an extraordinary player, but an excellent human being.”
In recent weeks, newspapers have hummed with nostalgic tributes and murals celebrating Messi have sprung up across the country. La Nación, a leading Argentine daily, released “Immortal,” a documentary chronicling his final World Cup run, and published a 196-page special edition devoted to his career. Since June, a 26-meter (85-foot) statue of Messi kneeling with the World Cup trophy has towered over passing motorists in Patagonia. On Tuesday, Buenos Aires’ landmark Obelisk glowed sky blue and white, the colors of the national flag, while news sites live-blogged every minute of the Benin friendly as if it were a World Cup final.
A jersey without an heir
Across Argentina, fans who grew up watching Messi as their parents watched Maradona have covered their skin with tattooed tributes to the soccer great, portraits of him kissing the World Cup trophy. It was easy to believe the world’s greatest player would always be one of their own.
“I don’t think we’ll have somebody like him again, somebody with that sort of enduring power,” said Pablo Brescia, a University of South Florida professor who writes about Argentine culture and soccer. “Like Maradona, he’ll be unique — a figure that can’t be repeated.”
Messi’s contract with Inter Miami runs through the 2028 season. But the ritual of watching him carry Argentina’s hopes and anxieties into every match is over.
“Watching Messi play, you felt anything could happen,” Murzi said.
When Tuesday’s match finally ended, the crowd remained, their ovation roaring through the stadium. Messi took a final lap, a tiny figure beneath the lights, soaking it in. At the tunnel, he paused to lift his arms toward his fans one last time. Then he was gone.

title: The 87-year-old who became a symbol of Spain’s eviction crisis has died
text:
The 87-year-old who became a symbol of Spain’s eviction crisis has died
Maria del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her Madrid home sparked a government crisis in Spain, has died, the Madrid Tenants’ Union announced on Tuesday.
Known in Spain simply as Maricarmen, she died two weeks after being evicted from the home where she lived for more than 70 years after her rent increased from €500 ($560) to €2,650 ($2,970).
Related video above | Spanish PM Pedro Sánchez calls November election amid growing housing protests
“We regret to announce that Maricarmen has passed away today. As you all know, she was evicted on September 23, and has remained in hospital ever since,” the union said Wednesday. “Although a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return to her home, this solution came too late,” it added.
Maricarmen’s eviction sparked a wave of nationwide demonstrations over Spain’s housing crisis, with protesters setting up a large encampment at Puerta del Sol in Madrid.
There was an outpouring of grief and anger among protesters following news of Maricarmen’s death.
A video from the encampment showed large crowds of people holding a moment of silence and then applauding. Local media have reported that some of the protesters began marching towards the parliament.
Madrid’s Tenants Union, which was among the groups organizing the protests, claimed about 950,000 people took part in demonstrations across the country over the weekend.
On Monday, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called an early election for late November in an apparent effort to seize the initiative following nationwide protests.
The announcement came after Sánchez’s government last week failed to secure parliamentary backing for two proposed laws aimed at tackling the housing crisis.

The funniest wildlife photos of 2026 have finally been revealed

Have you ever seen an eagle "strut his stuff"? Or a praying mantis in a rather suggestive position?
The Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards show wild animals in funny and unexpected situations, and the moments this year's finalists have captured are truly laugh-out-loud.
Rather than urgency, the photography and videography competition relies on the "positive power of humour" to bring attention to the endangered wildlife and habitats our planet relies on.
The concept has worked well. In 2026, the competition received more than 10,000 entries – the highest number in its 11-year history – from 112 countries.
From Belgian beavers to Irish goslings to African elephants, this year's finalists depict a wide range of wild animals from all over the world, captured in hilarious and strangely relatable situations.
Diego Perez / Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards 2026"Sexy Mantis" by Diego Perez from Peru
There's a caiman – a relative of the alligator – wearing a 'toupée' and looking rather pleased about it, a little owl blinking sleepily into the setting sun, an orangutan giving the photographer a piece of its mind, and a Great Horned Owl's flabbergasted expression as it spots a protective squirrel launching an aerial attack.
The emotions and situations you see, of course, depend on your interpretation of each image, but each one compels the viewer to empathize with the wild animals depicted on a personal level.
"What began as a small effort to raise awareness of wildlife conservation has grown into something far bigger than we ever imagined," says professional photographer Tom Sullman, who co-founded the Comedy Wildlife Awards with Paul Joynson-Hicks MBE in 2015.
Kevin Lohman / Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards 2026"Are You Kidding Me?" by Kevin Lohman, USA
"The competition is now truly global, and a decade or so on, we want to make it even bigger, funnier, and more far-reaching than ever. We use humour to get people to feel empathy towards wildlife, and it's that empathy that creates behavioural change for the better."
This year's iteration supports the Born Free Foundation, an international charity rescuing and protecting wild animals from exploitation, and conserving threatened species and their natural habitats.
The competition winners will be announced on Tuesday, Dec. 8 at an awards night in London, followed by a one-week exhibition from Dec. 9-13 at the Oxo Gallery showcasing all of this year's finalists.

title: Maine Supreme Court hears arguments over deadly fall at Prouts Neck Cliff Walk
text:
Maine Supreme Judicial Court hears arguments over deadly fall at Prouts Neck Cliff Walk
The SJC heard arguments over whether an inn in Scarborough can be held responsible for a Georgia woman's death
Maine Supreme Judicial Court hears arguments over deadly fall at Prouts Neck Cliff Walk
The SJC heard arguments over whether an inn in Scarborough can be held responsible for a Georgia woman's death
The Maine Supreme Judicial Court heard arguments Wednesday over whether the Black Point Inn can be held responsible for a Georgia woman's deadly fall from the Prouts Neck Cliff Walk in 2022.
The oral arguments were held at Morse High School in Bath.
The case is before Maine's highest court after a Cumberland County Superior Court judge granted summary judgment to the owners and operators of the Black Point Inn.
The appeal centers on whether an innkeeper can owe its guests a duty of care on nearby property the inn does not own or maintain.
Both sides acknowledged that the Black Point Inn does not own or control the Prouts Neck Cliff Walk, but the attorney for the woman's estate argued that the hotel heavily marketed the Cliff Walk as an amenity.
"It's disingenuous for the Black Point Inn to have advertised this amenity, to have policed its parking lot to make sure that anyone there was paying money to it, to invite their guests to use it, to hand them maps," said attorney Charles King.
King also said the inn had a heightened duty to warn the woman of danger.
Tiffany Ottenga, the attorney representing the Black Point Inn, said the hotel "indisputably" did not owe a duty to the appellants.
"(The hotel) did not own, control, maintain or possess the cliff walk," Ottenga said.
It is unclear when the Supreme Judicial Court will make a decision.
Four years since a woman's deadly fall
The question is being asked by the family of Ramona Gowens, who was vacationing in Maine with her sister, Sonia Hall, in September 2022 when she died. According to court records, the pair walked from the inn on the Cliff Walk and stopped to take photographs near a fence overlooking the coast. When Gowens leaned against the fence, it gave way, and she fell backward through brush and into a steep, 30-foot-deep chasm. She later died from her injuries.
Claims of negligence and a "duty to warn of dangers"
The estate and Hall sued BPI Partners, LLC, which owns the property and buildings where the inn is located, and Migis Hotel Group, LLC, which operates the inn. The defendants initially sought dismissal, arguing they had no duty to the plaintiffs because the accident occurred off the inn's property. That motion was denied. After discovery, the defendants again argued they owed no duty regarding the Cliff Walk, and the Superior Court granted summary judgment in their favor. The plaintiffs appealed in February 2026.
The plaintiffs are now seeking to reverse that decision and allow their claims to proceed to trial.
Their attorneys argue Maine law recognizes a heightened duty between an innkeeper and its overnight guests and that the duty should extend to the Cliff Walk because of the way the Black Point Inn promoted it and provided access to it.
The inn's attorneys are asking the Law Court to uphold the Superior Court's ruling.
What the inn is arguing
In their brief, BPI Partners and Migis Hotel Group argue that the Cliff Walk is separate from the inn, is not necessary to access or use the hotel, and has traditionally been accessible to the public. They say the Prouts Neck Improvement Association, a voluntary homeowners association, maintains the Cliff Walk, not the inn.
The defendants' brief concludes that the Superior Court's decision should be affirmed and that the inn did not "owe its guests a duty of care while using the Cliff Walk."
The Law Court's calendar identifies the case as involving negligence, whether a "special relationship" creates a duty to warn of dangers and the question of control over premises.
The court is heard several appeals at Morse High School on Wednesday as part of its effort to bring oral arguments to Maine schools.

title: Oversized again: Second load to start journey from Jay mill with more traffic impacts
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Oversized again: Second load to start journey from Jay, Maine, mill
The first delivery of oversized equipment from the former mill in Jay to South Portland was completed on Tuesday morning. Crews will start to move the second so-called superload on Wednesday night. There are a total of nine loads to be moved the nearly 100 miles.
Barnhart Crane & Rigging will be the moving contractor for each delivery, and each load will follow the same route and timeline. Drivers should expect the same traffic impacts, delays and closures that they faced during the first transport over the last week.
The equipment, a heat recovery steam generator, is coming from the former Pixelle/International Paper mill in Jay. The property is now owned by JGT2, the company that wants to turn the site into a data center.
A heat recovery steam generator (HRSG) is an energy recovery heat exchanger that captures hot exhaust gases from a gas turbine or industrial process to produce high-pressure steam
Police said the load is just over 219 feet long, 20 feet wide, 19.5 feet high and has a gross weight of 683,530 pounds. Due to the size, the load and support team will take up most, if not all, of the road in several areas and crews from Central Maine Power will be lifting and moving power lines out of the way.
"We've got a tractor pulling and a tractor pushing because the magnitude of the load would be too great for one tractor to pull and take care of on its own," said Lucien Richard, site manager for JGT2 Redevelopment.

title: Bangor school evacuated due to hoax threat, officials say students are safe
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The William S. Cohen School in Bangor was evacuated Wednesday due to a bomb threat that school officials now characterize as a “swatting hoax.”
An officer confirmed to our reporter on scene Wednesday morning that all of the nearly 400 students were safe and accounted for.
Students and staff were evacuated to Fruit Street School around 11:30 a.m. while law enforcement searched the Cohen School property. Police told WABI nothing dangerous was discovered, and they determined that the threat was not credible. Once it was found that the building was safe, students were able to return to their classrooms, or parents and guardians had the option to pick them up early.
Parents were notified of the situation at the time of the evacuation by an email from the school that described a “potential threat.”
School officials thanked local law enforcement for their assistance in responding to the incident.
“We are incredibly proud of our students for the way they responded during a challenging situation,” said Mike Missbrenner, Principal of school. “Their cooperation, patience, and resilience were outstanding. I also want to thank our faculty and staff for their professionalism in following emergency procedures and supporting our students throughout the day.”
The Bangor School Department says counselors, teachers, and administrators will be available to provide support to any student who wants to talk about what happened Wednesday.
The Garland Street school serves students in grades 6-8.
