title: Public art can shout in protest – and remind us of our shared humanity
text:
There is a question, or riddle, which skulks and slinks in the back alleys of the art world, as it is called, trying to avoid direct confrontation. It is simple enough: Does art matter at all? Can it help normal people (read: non-artists) in real time inside their actual lives? Or is it — the making, seeing, talking, writing about art — just a luxury which serious persons cannot afford?
My answer here is a predictable “Yes!” That is: “No!” In any case, surely art matters greatly and has much to offer if only we make ourselves properly available to its mysterious and healing influences. Without such an official — and enthusiastic — reply, this column would evaporate and down would tumble so many essential psychological pillars upholding a life shot through with experiences in this domain of creative human expression. Yet the pressure, the need, to hold up the existing assumptions and structures is exactly what makes the position so questionable.
Insert the work of Rachel and Ryan Adams and their colleagues here. Their public art, often taking the form of large urban murals, make a strong and abiding case for the value of the whole enterprise. Next to and above us they float, they wink, they quiver, hum and murmur. They speak and they watch. They offer hard questions of their own which we may ignore at no small cost: Where are we going? Why are we so cruel to each other? What is the nature of a politics of separation and violence? How can we walk ourselves back onto a safer, more generous path?
Their public projects create elbow room for celebration, grief, remembering, frustration and reconsideration. They do not say that art, with its assorted and layered meanings, belongs to experts and owners and academics; it seems, rather, that it belongs to us, right here in Portland, Biddeford, Lewiston, Westbrook … if we want it.
Increasingly, it seems we do want it, more and more. The Adamses have been working, together and separately, in Maine for more than two decades. They keep a pretty busy schedule these days. Their memorial mural in Biddeford for Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero — killed last July by ICE agents who were looking for someone else — was completed in August and pointed forcefully, quietly to the need to revisit immigration enforcement protocols. A straightforward image of the victim and his daughter has been presented without narrative, identification or explanation. It automatically levitates above political language, which is incapable of capturing or amplifying its visual message. A parent who was is now — permanently, pointlessly — gone.
Deeply awful things happen, and some artists choose to reply. In their response, they present new and contradictory understandings of the events, new emotions, stories, faces, assumptions and governing images. For example, the gently smiling face of a father instead of an angry menace. Two images of the same “target,” two competing mythologies of the targeted group. In this case, an official and conspicuous assault by federal police resulted in an unofficial and conspicuous mural, which may be felt as a kind of reverberation.
As a result we, a public, receive a dialogue in the form of two speeches: one very loud, one very quiet. The first speech was delivered by federal police and it was about collective security. It was an expression of power in the form of dominance, demonstrating the impressive reach of their force. Its expression involved large expenditures of energy, equipment, money and institutional support. It generated results that retell a threadbare myth about those who belong and those who do not.
This icy speech was met by a second one, delivered by artists who spoke about collective losses. It too was an expression of power, here taking the form of heightened awareness, demonstrating the reach of their social concern. It involved large expenditures of energy, material, time, risk and community support. It generated an image that unspools the myth, reframing a bold and reckless action.
How did artists like Rachel and Ryan Adams find themselves at this podium, giving public speeches? When I bothered them with this question on the phone the other day, they scissored themselves down about 30 feet in order to explain why they keep doing this work, which can bring so many risks, headaches, dirty looks and rude confrontations.
Ryan noted that “creatively, we stand behind what we believe in. We don’t shy away from it, and we appreciate those kinds of opportunities.”
“We do what we’re passionate about,” Rachel added. “What we care about. And, you know, the community and all the people within it are a part of it.”
Fair enough. But what about the hostile comments, the pushback, the threats while working on site?
“It’s true that we’ve been in very scary situations just for painting,” Ryan said. “Not only for the political pieces, for just literally existing in the space … and that’s just what happens immediately, when we’re actually physically there. Afterwards, when the image hits whatever news cycle it’s going to hit, then you have the online side of it, where sometimes people are nasty, people are mean, people are scary. We have to be very, very, very careful. I’m like: We have a family.”
Rachel observed that “even when we’re not doing work that has a political narrative, our presence can kind of stir that up … just being black in these all-white spaces is a political act within itself.”
“When people approach us painting, we’re usually pleasantly surprised with people’s kindness, but we also can’t let our guards down, either,” Ryan said.
Sounds stressful. Asked if there were not a hundred moments when an artist working alone on a controversial mural might have been tempted to return to the safety of a studio, Ryan said “I would put that up around like maybe 500, 600 … still, you’re not going to scare me away from doing something I love. That’s definitely not happening.” A sustaining element has been their working partnership and the help of friends.
The result is a series of mural projects in Maine that hook elbows with big, difficult topics. The Adamses have designed and executed high-visibility public murals speaking to immigration, police brutality, race and civil rights throughout the state.
As for the mural for Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, “I really wanted the humanity to be highlighted,” Ryan said. “I wanted it to be mourning the fact that this was another human being who had a whole life of experiences, had family, had friends, had jobs … that is the thing that’s kind of paramount for these pieces. It is not necessarily a political statement, but more or less just: ‘Let us not forget that this was a human being who was from our community, who lived in our community, who added to our community and was killed unjustly, for no reason.’”
Some observers might call a mural representing a murder victim protest art. This seems hardly even possible, unless murder itself is something to be debated, an issue for which to vote yay or nay. Instead, the violent events in themselves appear to be a kind of protest against something very basic…could it be against due process? Against the benefit of the doubt? Against intuition? In these brutal actions, something which had been taken for granted is rejected, refuted.
The Adamses’ public responses to such actions, like the work of British street artist Banksy, are less a reply than a re-grounding of first principles. They enact a kind of humanation, a reminder that a father, a son, or a husband stands exactly where we were told we would encounter an alien, a criminal or an intruder.
Here is art insisting on complexity, representing the real, doing its job.
Jon Calame holds a master’s degree in historic preservation of architecture and is a Fellow of the American Academy in Rome. He currently teaches art history at the University of Southern Maine. This column is free to access through support by The Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation.

title: 'Something that you dream of': 1,116-pound bluefin tuna catch sets a record
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
1,116-pound bluefin tuna catch sets a record in New Hampshire
A New Hampshire fisherman broke a state record when he caught a massive bluefin tuna.
"We lifted it out of the water and immediately knew it was way bigger than what we thought and bigger than anything neither of us had seen before," Capt. Jamie Savage, of Savage Charters, said.
On Saturday night, fisherman Brandon McGirl joined Savage on board the "Out of Line" fishing boat for an overnight charter.
"It was very difficult conditions to try and fish. It was a little bit rougher than we were hoping for," McGirl said.
The pair spent hours at sea. Initially, they said it seemed like the fish were finding every line but theirs.
"They never come when you expect them to come," McGirl said.
They were ready to call it for the night when the sound they had been waiting for came. The reels started clicking, and they chased the fish for about a mile.
"But when it does happen, it's, you almost feel like your heart kind of skip a beat just a little bit," McGirl said.
The monster of a fish put up little fight until it was time to bring it on board. They ended up dragging the fish back at a slow pace, still unaware just how big of a catch they were dealing with.
It was bigger than any tuna ever caught in New Hampshire waters, coming in at 1,116 pounds, which is 154 pounds larger than the last record-breaker in 2013.
“If you tuna fish for long time, to catch a 1,000-pound fish, is, I mean, it's something that you dream of," McGirl said.
"Similar to how you would pick out a steak, you are looking for marbling in the meat, so all the marbling like a wagyu or a ribeye, and this has marbling all over it,"
The fish will now head to market, where it could be sent as far as Japan.
Staying at the harbor is the tuna's tail, which will serve as a trophy to remind them of their record-breaking catch.

title: Susan Collins’s committee bought trucks the Army didn’t want. Then campaign donations poured in.
text:
The U.S. Army announced last year that it had enough of a specific model of armored vehicle and that any more deliveries would be “excess.” But even so, Congress found a way to keep funding alive for the vehicle — and executives at the company that produces the vehicle found a way to flood key members of Congress with campaign donations.
In the weeks after this year’s appropriations bill passed, employees of AM General or its parent company donated tens of thousands to key appropriations committee members in both chambers, Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Rep. Ken Calvert, R-Calif.
Collins is separately facing scrutiny over a report from ProPublica that the FBI investigated an alleged pay-to-play scheme involving a major donor, an ex-defense contractor. Collins’ office denied that there was any kind of pay-to-play arrangement and said she fully cooperated with the FBI. There is no indication that AM General’s donations were part of such a scheme, but the giving nonetheless demonstrates how Collins’ campaign account has grown with help from employees at defense contractors doing business with the government.
Before the Army put the future of the vehicle in jeopardy, Collins was not a frequent beneficiary of contributions from the company’s workers. She last received campaign funds from AM General or its parent company’s employees more than a decade ago. But after the Army’s “excess” announcement last year, employees and the company’s PAC donated over $58,000 to committees associated with Collins.
One observer of money in politics said that appropriators receiving money from government contractors is a long-standing problem.
“Members of the appropriations committees in Congress are extremely powerful. These lawmakers can steer huge sums of money to private companies. Government contractors today routinely try to leverage a broken campaign finance system to their advantage,” said Michael Beckel, money in politics reform director at Issue One.
The revival of the Army’s order was supported by lawmakers in both parties, including the top Democrat on the House Appropriations defense subcommittee, Rep. Betty McCollum, D-Minn. Collins’ office said that in the Senate, decisions on the program were made not by her but by defense subcommittee chair Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and vice chair Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del. McConnell did not receive donations from employees at AM General or its parent company this election cycle. Coons received $2,500 from its employee PAC.
“Sen. Collins was not involved in this decision. The final decision was made by the Chairs and Ranking Members of the House and Senate Defense Appropriations Subcommittees,” said a Collins spokesperson, Phoebe Keller.
AM General’s CEO, John Chadbourne, said in an email that the company does not comment on campaign donations, “all of which fully comply with FEC rules and regulations.”
He added, “AM General’s focus is on the Warfighter and providing the best light tactical vehicle capabilities to the Joint Forces.”
Congress steps in
AM General is most famous for producing the Humvee, the iconic military vehicle that trawled the streets of Baghdad during the Iraq War. In 2023, the Army selected the company to produce 20,000 units of a more heavily armored successor known as the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle. The company was ramping up its production line in Indiana when then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll announced in May 2025 that he would cancel its order, saying the additional deliveries would result in an “excess.”
Driscoll’s announcement was part of a larger effort to “eliminate waste and obsolete programs.”
“Yesterday’s weapons will not win tomorrow’s wars,” he said.
The military does not always have the last say on its contracts, however.
Congress has for decades swooped in to save pricey programs with political appeal. Soon after the Army moved to kill the vehicle contract, Congress mobilized to save it.
AM General had backing from members of Congress in Indiana, thanks to the jobs on its production line there. It also found backing from legislators in states far from its home.
The House moved first: In June 2025, the House Appropriations Committee’s subcommittee on defense proposed spending hundreds of millions on the vehicle for the Army. By the time the final version of the defense spending bill passed this February, the Army had been provided with $345 million for procurement of a vehicle it said it did not need.
A joint statement from the House and Senate, which Collins’ office said was produced by the defense subcommittees, sounded a skeptical note about the Army’s decision to cancel further orders of the vehicle. The statement said that the Army had provided “inadequate supporting analysis.” One concern was that without the efficiencies from a larger order that included the Army, the cost-per-unit price of vehicles that the Marines still wanted would rise.
McCollum, the House Democrat with an influential role in the process, said in a statement that she was one of numerous members of Congress to question the Army’s decision.
“Appropriators felt the Army failed to do adequate due diligence to justify their rash budget decision to cut the JLTV program and explain the full impacts on the Army, and especially the Marine Corps, which had not been consulted,” she said.
By the time the final version of the defense spending bill passed this February, the Army had been provided with $345 million for procurement of a vehicle it said it did not need.
Collins’ campaign committees had received some money after the Army announced that it wanted to cancel the project.
In the weeks after Congress passed the appropriations bill on Feb. 3, Collins and Calvert, one of her counterparts in the House, both received a burst of donations from AM General employees and the company’s political action committee.
After the appropriations bill went through, donors associated with AM General gave a total of $50,000 to Collins’ fundraising committees.
The donors included Chadbourne, the company’s CEO, and two of KPS Capital’s managing partners. (Private equity firm KPS Capital Partners acquired AM General in 2020.) All gave money to a committee raising money on Collins’ behalf at the end of February or start of March.
Calvert, the California representative with the defense appropriations post, has also benefited from similar donations. Both AM General employees and KPS Capital employees have given $14,285 in direct contributions to Calvert for Congress this election cycle.
The AM General employee PAC has given a combined $20,000 to Ken Calvert for Congress and Eureka Political Action Committee, Calvert’s leadership PAC.
Most of the donations to Calvert associated with AM General came in the weeks immediately after Congress passed the appropriations bill. His office did not respond to a request for comment.
Those contributions put Collins and Calvert in the same league as the Hoosier politicians who were natural supporters of AM General. A fundraising committee associated with Republican Sen. Todd Young received $36,000 from AM General or KPS Capital employees. The AM General employee PAC donated another $10,000 to his main campaign committee. A Marine Corps veteran, Young has been a vocal proponent of the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle.
His Republican colleague Sen. Jim Banks’ leadership PAC received $14,375 total from AM General’s employee PAC and Chadbourne, the executive. Meanwhile, Rep. Frank Mrvan, a Democrat representing northwest Indiana, received $33,050 from AM General or KPS Capital employees, and another $10,000 from the AM General employee PAC, according to FEC filings.
A ban that isn’t
On her campaign website, Collins notes that she serves as chair of the “powerful” appropriations committee.
“This committee decides how federal dollars are spent each year, from national defense and infrastructure to medical research, education and public safety. Susan’s position gives Maine an outsized voice at the table when critical decisions are made which allows her to deliver serious results for Maine,” her website states.
Collins’ office said that in the case of the AM General vehicle, she had nothing to do with the funding decision. A spokesperson said the decision-making in the Senate was up to McConnell, the defense subcommittee chair, and Coons, the vice chair.
McConnell announced his pending retirement in February 2025. His campaign committee and leadership committee have not received donations from either KPS Capital or AM General employees this election cycle, FEC records show. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Coons’ campaign committee received a $2,500 donation from the AM General employee PAC on March 5, according to FEC records. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
McCollum’s leadership PAC received $5,000 from the company’s employee PAC last October, according to FEC records.
Government contractors have been banned from donating directly to candidates for decades. In practice, however, that ban does nothing to prevent company PACs or individual employees from giving to campaigns — even if they serve as company executives.
The contributions associated with AM General represent a sliver of the $15.8 million Collins had raised this election cycle through July, according to data compiled by the watchdog group OpenSecrets. Yet every dollar could help her in what is expected to be a tough fight with Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate candidate with a slight lead on her in recent polls, in November.
The contributions also illustrated a trend among the top contributors to her campaign. Many of them are from people affiliated with government contractors, according to OpenSecrets. Two defense contractors, General Dynamics and RTX, are also on the list of her top organizational contributors.
AM General’s owner, KPS Capital Partners, is the sixth-largest organizational donor to Collins’ campaign committee and leadership PAC, according to the group’s data.
Although AM General has cultivated connections in Congress, members appear to be growing increasingly skeptical of the JLTV vehicle program. In June, House appropriators signaled that they wanted to find a new contractor for the vehicle, citing production delays. AM General was 2,000 vehicles behind on orders from the Marines, the defense subcommittee said.
Chadbourne, the company’s CEO, issued a statement in June defending its performance and blaming a previous contractor for delays.
“Healthy competition, transparency and accountability strengthen America’s defense industrial base,” he said. “AM General remains fully committed to continue earning the trust placed in us by the Army, the Marine Corps, Congress, and the American taxpayer through performance, quality, and disciplined execution.”
By Matt Sledge and Jorge Medellin. Originally published on October 5, 2026. Republished
with permission from The Intercept, an award-winning nonprofit news
organization dedicated to holding the powerful accountable through fearless, adversarial
journalism. Sign up for The Intercept’s Newsletter.

title: FCC considers allowing more political robocalls before midterms, including those created with AI
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Federal Communications Commission is considering a request by a conservative group to loosen rules on political robocalls, including those with artificial intelligence-generated voices, before November’s midterm elections.
Federal law currently bans most robocalls to cellphones unless the caller gets consent beforehand. The petition calls for a waiver that would allow political groups to use artificial or prerecorded voices in unsolicited wireless calls.
The Republican-led FCC advanced the request for public comment and could rule on it as soon as late October.
Consumer advocacy groups warn the proposed change could trigger a surge of unwanted, partisan and potentially misleading automated calls in the critical final days of the election, which will determine which party controls Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term.
The potential perils became evident two years ago during the presidential primary season when thousands of voters in New Hampshire received a robocall with an AI-generated voice of then-President Joe Biden. The call suggested voters should forgo casting a ballot in the primary and “save” their votes for the general election.
Under the waiver request before the FCC, some state and federal laws protecting against deception and voter intimidation would continue to prohibit certain misleading election-related messages. But granting it could weaken a major deterrent for bad actors, said Tim Harper, who leads the elections team at the Washington-based Center for Democracy and Technology.
Such a ruling close to Election Day would open “a huge opportunity for abuse during a period where harm has outsized impact,” he said. “Campaigns will use this technology to target voters in deceptive ways.”
A tool for better communication or misleading messages?
The Club for Growth, a right-leaning economic policy group seeking the change, said it could help political organizations better communicate with potential voters, including in more languages, and improve polling accuracy by helping groups reach more voters. It calls current federal rules outdated and argues they dampen freedom of speech.
The nation’s communications regulatory body would have to act within a compressed schedule to grant the waiver in time to affect the midterm elections. Critics said it wouldn’t be the first time the FCC, which has become closely aligned with the president during his second term, has bypassed procedural norms to serve its political agenda.
Its Republican chairman, Brendan Carr, launched an unusual early review of broadcast licenses for several ABC-owned local broadcast stations, prompting the company to sue. It said the review years ahead of schedule was unconstitutional, a violation of free speech and a retaliation for content Trump dislikes.
The FCC didn’t respond to a request for comment on the petition.
Ana Gomez, the sole Democrat among the FCC’s three active commissioners, told The Associated Press she opposes the move and thinks it would create “a tsunami of robocalls and misinformation.”
“We’ve already seen dark money groups use AI to put candidates’ likeness behind inflammatory comments ahead of this election,” Gomez said. “Exempting political calls from the need for consumer consent would supercharge that strategy, and misleading messages could land directly on the handheld phone of nearly every voter in our country.”
Political robocalls have caused controversies before
In past elections, deceptive political robocalls have resulted in significant fines associated with the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, the federal law at the center of the petition.
In 2020, tens of thousands of prospective voters in majority-Black areas of the U.S. received robocalls falsely warning that if they voted by mail, they could face arrest and debt collection.
The two conservative hoaxers behind the calls, Jacob Wohl and Jack Burkman, were criminally charged for the calls and fined some $5.1 million for violating the act.
The political consultant behind the 2024 New Hampshire robocalls mimicking Biden’s voice said he did it to send a wake-up call about the potential dangers of AI. He was acquitted of criminal voter suppression charges but faced fines and civil damages associated with federal law.
Shortly after the New Hampshire robocall caught authorities’ attention, the FCC ruled that robocalls made with AI voice-cloning tools were outlawed under the consumer protection act.
The change could boost various types of AI calling
If the commission pivots to grant the Club for Growth’s petition, political groups of all stripes could amp up their use of AI to prerecord messages that play when voters pick up the phone. They also could use the technology to engage in live conversations with voters driven by AI large language models.
Mekela Panditharatne, senior counsel in the democracy program at the Brennan Center for Justice, warned that such conversations hold risks. An AI system could make false promises about a candidate or manipulate voters in conversation by providing inaccurate or incomplete information.
Harper, from the Center for Democracy and Technology, said there also could be a privacy risk for voters who might not know how an AI agent on the line with them is capturing or repurposing their data.
The Club for Growth has argued the waiver would help create a more uniform regulatory landscape, given that unsolicited automated calls to landlines are already allowed. If the waiver is granted, callers would still be limited by certain conditions, including allowing consumers to opt out and making no more than three calls within 30 days to each individual recipient.
A public comment reply period on the petition ends Oct. 19, at which point the FCC could move forward on a decision.

title: Topsham committee resigns en masse, prompting its end
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
All four members of Topsham’s Comprehensive Plan Implementation Committee resigned last month.
For the past six years, the committee had been working on a project called ReCode — a push to revise the town’s zoning codes. The former members were working through their third draft of a new code. The resignations came after a planning board meeting where the two parties reviewed the draft.
In their resignation letter on Sept. 18, the former members of CPIC said that six out of seven planning board members were against their efforts, and they saw it as a waste of time to continue working on the project.
On Oct. 1, the Select Board discussed the resignations, and next steps for the town. Town Manager Mark Waltz recognized the former members of CPIC, particularly Chair Susan Rae-Reeves, for their efforts. He also said that in doing so, he wasn’t “throwing stones” at the planning board.
“I don’t think there’s bad guys here. I think there’s different perspectives,” Waltz said.
At the end of the night, the board voted to accept the resignations and dissolve the committee.
CPIC’s role
The Comprehensive Plan Implementation Committee was tasked with helping the town implement its 2019 Comprehensive Plan — a document outlining a long-term vision for the town with recommendations for land use and development policies.
Topsham’s 2019 plan was ambitious, and included input from about 600 residents, said Rae-Reeves, the former CPIC chair who also helped develop the plan.
A major component of CPIC’s work was the ReCode project. Waltz said that a key intention of the project was to create zoning that would allow increased housing density in areas of town served by public water and sewer. The end result was supposed to be a “comprehensive code evaluation” that the town could use to revise its land use code.
The committee worked with consultants and solicited public input to create the ReCode draft. It employed elements of form-based code — a type of zoning where structure type and size are regulated but not use — to encourage development of mixed use spaces in town.
ReCode was intended to be completed in 2023, but the COVID-19 pandemic and multiple town employee departures slowed the process, said Rae-Reeves.
The resignations
Early in 2026, the planning board tried to stop the ReCode project entirely, said Waltz. The Select Board said that because the town had invested significant money in the project, it should not be scrapped. The solution was that the planning board and CPIC would meet once a month and review elements of the ReCode draft.
Rae-Reeves said she believed that the meetings meant the project was back on track, and that the planning board would meaningfully engage with the ReCode draft. But she said the board was not open-minded about the ReCode draft.
In their resignation letter, the former members of the committee said the planning board had largely ignored the comprehensive plan.
“We find it humiliating for all concerned to watch a planning board disregard the wishes of our town,” wrote the former committee.
The Sept. 10 meeting was a tipping point. The former members cited several moments from the meeting that led to their decision, including a board member stating that they were not in favor of form-based code.
Rae-Reeves said she knew there was skepticism about form-based code, but had hoped the planning board would consider the idea. “We were naive in hindsight,” she said.
Waltz said he felt badly that CPIC’s goals were not accomplished. “It was a dedicated group of people that worked really hard,” he said.
Waltz said the ReCode draft was a lot to take in. “I think the planning board was having trouble getting their hands around it. They were concerned about unintended consequences of … changing so many things at once,” he said.
Next steps
Waltz brought a memo to the Oct. 1 Select Board meeting outlining three paths forward for the town, based on what the planning board decides about form-based code.
If the planning board is open to form-based code, the process can continue as planned — a consultant can address questions and attend November’s scheduled meeting, albeit without CPIC.
Waltz said in his memo that removing form-based code from the ReCode draft would cost tens of thousands of dollars, so if the board decides against it, the current code could be amended instead.
His third option is to task Topsham’s planning director with creating a list of potential code changes that the planning board showed support for during the ReCode process. Town employees could then write potential amendments to the current code, and present them to the panning board.
Waltz will present the options at the Oct. 8 planning board meeting.

title: MAINE-LY GARDENING: Color filled days
text:
Maine’s weather watchers have told us to expect a shorter, and perhaps earlier fall foliage season this year due to the continuing drought. However, many of us have been reporting spectacular color in recent days.
Driving past the local bogs lately, I’ve been startled by the bright reds in the last week or so. The red maples, viburnums, and high bush blueberries are always reliably red. The sumac along the roadside varies from orange to bright red, with deeper red on their flower spikes at the top.
Another tree, that like the red maple, prefers wetter areas is the black gum or tupelo. At a distance, it blends in with the colorful display, but a closer look reveals it’s oval leaves. Black gums are favorites of honeybees but are less well known to New England people than some of our other native trees. Tall and straight trunked, when planted in an open yard or park Black gum make impressive wide branching shade trees. In fall their leaves become bright red a little earlier than the red maples, prolonging our colorful foliage season.
As our other trees like birches and poplars turn to yellow and orange, the oaks are generally late to bring their deeper wine reds to the display. Tamaracks, our deciduous conifer, make an impact in some large stands as their needles turn gold before dropping to reveal their handsome conical structure.
Two vines catch our eyes. The native Virginia creeper’s deep red leaves are set off by dark blue berries. We may not appreciate the colorful poison ivy, but the birds welcome its berries. Sadly, the invasive Asiatic bittersweet has been allowed to spread, in part because of its fruits –– red berries peeking out of yellow capsules. If you have delayed cutting it down to the roots (orange under the soil) to slow its growth, you can still spot it now by its yellow leaves as it climbs trees and the guy wires of power poles.
The pines, spruces, firs, and hemlocks provide contrast with their shades of dark greens as the golds and greens of fields and pastures frame the brighter colors. The picture is completed by our lovely New England Asters. With bright blue skies on cool, sunny autumn days our rainbow is complete. Enjoy the glorious color that precedes the quiet winter scenes to come.

title: 8 offerings you shouldn’t miss at Maine’s only French language film festival
text:
I took Spanish in high school, so I won’t embarrass myself by pretending I speak French. But French is the second-most spoken language in Maine, and the primary language spoken in some 3% of Maine households.
And while the storied history of the French language in Maine has long rung out in every dialect from Acadian to Québécois to that Parisian French some people learn as an elective, Maine’s influx of immigrants from French-speaking African countries like the Democratic Republic of Congo, Burundi, Rwanda, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, Chad, Djibouti, Ivory Coast and Togo have only enriched Maine’s relationship with the language.
That alive and growing contingent of French speakers in Maine has made the annual Festival Champlain film fest a vital part of our state’s cultural identity. Taking place for the fifth year at PMA Films from Oct. 15-18, Festival Champlain is Maine’s only all-French language film festival. All films are in their native French, with helpful English subtitles. With eight globe-spanning features from places like Canada, Gabon, France, and Tunisia, this year’s festival once more takes its rightful place in the Maine movie fest circuit, and offers plenty for everyone. Here’s a brief rundown.
‘Afrōtopia’
Franco-Gabonese filmmaker David Mboussou (who’ll appear in a Q&A over Zoom after the film) co-wrote and directed this powerful story about an aspiring filmmaker forced into his family’s logging business.
Discovering that his powerful father plans to cut down a forest sacred to the local Bantu people, the young man uncovers a colonial-era secret that threatens to ignite into present-day conflict. Called “an ecological manifesto by Mboussou, the film delves into African cultural prejudices, scars left by colonialism, and the shifting loyalties between generations.
‘La Venue de l’Avenir’ (‘Colors of Time’)
In this 2025 film from director Cédric Klapisch, four present-day cousins inherit the mysteriously abandoned house of their ancestor, a young woman whose journey from rural Normandy to 19th century Paris opens up even more secrets. There’s a lost Impressionist masterpiece, a trove of letters, and family lore that forces the modern relatives to reckon with their connections to the past, and to each other. Followed by a presentation and discussion with Andrew Eschelbacher, deputy director and head of art and exhibitions at the Portland Museum of Art.
‘Promis Le Ciel’ (‘Promised Sky’)
From Tunisia, this drama from Erige Sehiri couldn’t be more timely. An Ivorian pastor takes in women looking for a better life, all while bigotry, anti-immigrant raids, and the unexpected arrival of a little orphan girl threaten to topple the group’s delicate existence. Some politicians want us to forget that immigrants are people. This deeply human film acts to refute such ugly idiocy with grace and immediacy.
‘Maria Chapdelaine’
Adapted from a classic French-Canadian novel by Louis Hémon, this drama follows 16-year-old Maria as she confronts tradition, romance, and dreams of escape from her tough family life in 1910s rural Quebec. Director Sébastien Pilote will make a virtual appearance from his home in Saint-Ambroise, Quebec, to discuss his film.
‘Tous Toqués’ (‘All Stirred Up!’)
In this comedy, an upright Quebec border agent busts a French chef with a trunkful of gourmet ingredients, only for her to need the resentful expert’s help when her adorable young daughter enters a prestigious cooking competition. Having to overcome their mutual distrust and the town’s irritation with the agent’s by-the-book attitude, the pair unite in a uniquely funny and heartwarming tale.
‘Ma Mère, Dieu et Sylvie Vartan’ (‘Once Upon My Mother’)
Another heartwarmer, based on a true story, tells the tale of a Moroccan-Jewish immigrant mother who gives everything to ensure her disabled son will grow up independent, successful — and dependent on her.
‘Nos Belles-Soeurs’ (‘Sisters and Neighbors!’)
When a housewife wins a contest (and a million gold stamps), her extended family and friends all come together to help her redeem the prize — and maybe get some of it for themselves in this adaptation of Michel Tremblay’s comic play.
‘L’Étranger’ (‘The Stranger’)
The great French master François Ozon (“8 Women,” “Swimming Pool”) closes out this year’s Festival Champlain with his sumptuous black-and-white adaptation of Albert Camus’ classic novel. When an aimless young Frenchman in Algiers kills an Arab man, seemingly for no reason, the resulting trial presents a haunting, existential view of human nature. Ozon’s films are absolutely mesmerizing and enigmatic in equal measure, and his treatment of a timeless tale is not to be missed.
Dennis Perkins is a freelance writer who lives in Auburn with his wife and his cat.
The fifth annual Festival Champlain screens at the Portland Museum of Art from Oct. 15-18. Check out afdume.org/festivalchamplain for details, special events and showtimes.

title: Hancock, Maine Crash On Route 1 Sends One Passenger To Hospital With Serious Injuries
text:
Hancock, Maine Rollover Crash Leaves Several Injured
Several people were injured in a rollover crash on Route 1 in Hancock on Tuesday.
Maine Woman Seriously Injured in a Two-Vehicle Crash on Route 1 in Hancock, Maine
Maine State Police responded to the two-vehicle crash in Hancock just before 2:30 pm on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, and closed a portion of Route 1 for much of the afternoon.
Cathy Grant, 66, of Milbridge, sustained serious injuries in the crash and was transported to a local hospital.
Maine Police Report Several Injuries in a Crash Near the Hancock-Sullivan Bridge
The two drivers, 53-year-old Amy Houck of Steuben and 36-year-old Nicholas McAfee of North Little Rock, Arkansas, sustained non-life-threatening injuries.
A passenger in McAfee's vehicle, who police didn't identify, was taken to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.
Grant was a passenger in Amy Houck's vehicle.
Maine Police Say a Vehicle From Arkansas Caused a Crash in Hancock
An initial investigation indicates that Houck's Ford Bronco was traveling east when McAfee's Hyundai Sonata hit it from behind.
The impact caused the Bronco to roll over, while the Sonata continued off the roadway, crossed a small field, and struck a tree.
Route 1 was closed for several hours near the Hancock-Sullivan bridge.
This incident remains under investigation.

MOUNT DESERT — Most people on Mount Desert Island are familiar with the bustle of summer months when millions of visitors make the island and surrounding towns their homes. Businesses are booming, lobstermen are hauling, and restaurants are packed, giving everyone plenty to do. But what about the kids of MDI?

title: Winthrop field hockey nips Spruce Mountain in Class C South showdown
text:
JAY — Winthrop’s Evelyn Mortimer saw an opening and spoiled Spruce Mountain’s senior night.
Her goal late in the first quarter was all the Ramblers needed to prevail 1-0 in a field hockey game Wednesday at Taglienti Field between the top two teams in Class C South.
After the Ramblers (10-1) transitioned from defense to offense in the midfield, Mortimer perfectly timed her move into the circle and a got a shot past Spruce Mountain goalie Kyleigh Marcotte.
“I saw a gap, and I saw my teammates, Natalie (Irwin) and Addie (Daigle), they were pushing each other up the field. So I was like, ‘You’ve got to get there and get that last touch in,’” Mortimer, a junior, said.
Winthrop/Maranacook coach Hollie Daigle said Spruce Mountain’s defense didn’t give many openings all night.
“Spruce (Mountain) does a really great job of doubling with the ball, getting their sticks low; (they) made great tackles,” Daigle said. “I thought we really started to adjust to use our passing game a little bit more and just had good communication on the field.”
Not looking ahead to the postseason
Wednesday’s game was the second of the season between last year’s Class C South finalists. The Phoenix won the 2025 regional title, but Winthrop has won both meetings in 2026.
Wednesday’s game had a postseason feel, with two teams playing a high-stakes game. But, even though the Ramblers (10-1) have beaten Spruce Mountain (9-2) twice and have a 23-point lead in the C South Heal point standings, Holly Daigle said Winthrop is focused on finishing the regular season strong, not on the postseason.
“I mean … tonight, you’re right, it was a great night, playing under the lights, beautiful night, it was exciting, and we’ve got three more games left this season,” Daigle said. “When playoff time comes, we’ll approach it then, but we know we’ve got, three more games before we close out the regular season.”
The Ramblers have games against Brunswick on Friday and Oak Hill on Oct. 14, before finishing the regular season Oct. 16 against Lisbon, which was dealt its first loss of the season by Spruce Mountain on Monday.
Mortimer said Winthrop still has things to improve before the postseason.
“I think we’ll want to work on making moves around players, marking (players better), too,” Mortimer said. “Just working on specific skills for each player, because everyone’s unique.”
Spruce Mountain staying positive
Despite her team losing to Winthrop for the second time this season, Phoenix coach Alex Bessey saw growth in things her players have been working on.
“… Communication, energy, being ready without the ball, all those little field hockey things that I think sometimes high school players just take for granted,” Bessey said. “So just realizing how important all those little things are.”
Unsung hero
There were two instances in the fourth quarter that Spruce Mountain goalie Kyleigh Marcotte prevented Winthrop from adding to its lead. First, she made back-to-back saves off a corner. Then, in the final five minutes, she again had to stop back-to-back shots.
“She was huge for us, getting on the ground, getting dirty when she needed to,” Bessey said. “I think that’s just a huge energy boost for the rest of the team.”

• Winthrop: Evelyn Mortimer (goal)
•  Spruce Mountain: Kyleigh Marcotte (seven saves)

title: FBI says it thwarted an attack on the Mall of America by a teen it supplied with an assault rifle
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — The FBI thwarted an attack on the Mall of America by a teenager after agents supplied him with an assault rifle, authorities said Wednesday.
The 18-year-old had been under investigation for nearly two years, trading messages with a confidential informant, before agents sold him the rifle and ammunition and arrested him on the spot, they said.
“This was a radicalized young man who needed to be watched,” U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen said as he praised the FBI investigation. Agents “were able to detect a threat, and disrupt it, before the defendant carried out his intention to kill, in his words, maybe 30 to 60 people.”
Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, 18, was arrested Tuesday in a public park in Richfield, several miles northwest of the Mall of America, after he paid $600 to an undercover FBI employee posing as a member of ISIS for an AK-47 and 200 rounds of ammunition, according to the criminal complaint.
In text messages with the informant, Mohamud repeatedly affirmed his intent to carry out an attack to kill non-Muslims at the mall on Oct. 24, the date of a scheduled Hmong arts celebration, the complaint said.
It was not immediately known if the teen had an attorney who might speak on his behalf. The Associated Press could not immediately identify any of his family members to contact for comment.
Rosen said Mohamud is an American-born U.S. citizen of Somali descent. According to the complaint, in his text messages he expressed admiration for recent terror attacks as well as an interest in traveling to Somalia to join ISIS. Ultimately he decided he couldn’t afford to travel there and would attack the mall instead, it said.
The teen first came to the FBI’s attention in December 2024, the same month the source began exchanging messages with him, the complaint said. By May 2025, agents were concerned enough that they went to his home. His mother told them he wasn’t home from school yet and called the boy’s father, who declined to speak with them and said he would give their contact information to his lawyer, the complaint said.
“What I would say to parents all over Minnesota, and all over America: If you get any indication — especially if you hear from federal law enforcement — that your son or daughter is being radicalized, to the point where federal law enforcement wants to come and give you that warning, those are warnings that ought to be heeded,” Rosen said.
Tens of thousands of people of Somali descent live in Minnesota, dating back to when refugees began arriving in the 1990s. Over the years several have been charged with attempting to join ISIS or other terror groups.

title: Texas carries out nation’s first execution since Christa Pike’s failed lethal injection
text:
HUNTSVILLE, Texas (AP) — A Texas man who fatally shot a convenience store clerk was put to death Wednesday evening, becoming the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year and the first since Tennessee’s failed attempt to administer a lethal injection to Christa Pike a week ago.
Jamaal Howard, 46, was pronounced dead at 8:03 p.m. after receiving a fatal dose of pentobarbital at the state prison in Huntsville. He was convicted of killing Vickie Swartout, 42, in a 2000 store robbery caught on surveillance video.
Asked by the warden if he had a final statement, Howard apologized profusely to some members of his victim’s family, who watched through a window just feet from the death chamber.
“I wish that you accept my apology and I wish for your forgiveness,” he said, shortly before the injection got underway. “I’m sorry for what happened. I wish you can learn to forgive me one of these days.”
He also thanked his friends and family and said he loved them, adding he was “in a good state of mind to find peace and the Lord, so I thank y’all.” He concluded with: “Hey, enjoy life, and peace to y’all.”
Man took a few breaths and gasped as the drugs began flowing
As the pentobarbital began taking effect, Howard took a couple of breaths and gasped. He then began making snoring sounds, coughed and resumed the snoring sounds, each time the sound becoming quieter. Within about 30 seconds, all movement stopped.
He was pronounced dead 19 minutes later.
His sister was among witnesses watching through a window from an adjacent room and became distraught, exclaiming several times: “Get me out of here.” She was assisted by corrections officers in exiting the witness room.
Texas has executed seven people so far in 2026, including Howard, and plans two more executions later this year.
Howard’s attorneys unsuccessfully sought to block the execution by arguing that he was intellectually disabled and that he faced risks similar to those in Pike’s case because both states use pentobarbital for lethal injections.
Pike’s lawyers continue to seek more information about what went wrong after the 50-year-old woman survived two doses of pentobarbital on Sept. 30. Her lawyers said she was unconscious at a hospital after the attempt but was awake and speaking by Tuesday.
Store clerk’s killing was caught on surveillance video
Howard was convicted of capital murder in the killing of Swartout, who was shot once in the chest during the robbery. Evidence presented at trial included surveillance video showing Howard shooting Swartout.
Howard, who was 20 at the time, took $114 and a carton of cigarettes from the store in Silsbee, a small, rural town about 100 miles (160 kilometers) northeast of Houston, according to court records.
A flurry of late appeals failed to stop the execution
In bidding to halt Howard’s execution, his attorneys had filed a motion hours earlier before the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals raising concerns about the quality of Texas’ execution drugs. The court denied that request and a second filing involving the drugs without comment.
His attorneys also argued unsuccessfully to the U.S. Supreme Court that Howard’s execution should be halted because he was intellectually disabled. The Supreme Court in 2002 had barred the execution of intellectually disabled people, though it gave states some discretion in determining such disabilities.
The state told the court that Howard’s lawyers did not present evidence that would show he meets the requirements for a claim of intellectual disability.
The high court late Wednesday declined to intervene, without comment, clearing the way for the execution.
Florida leads the nation in executions this year
Florida has carried out 16 executions so far this year, the most of any state. Most states that allow executions use lethal injection as their primary method.
Tennessee Republican Gov. Bill Lee has halted the one remaining execution that was scheduled to be carried out in his state this year.
___
Stengle reported from Fort Worth, Texas.

title: Wife reports husband after finding child sex abuse material on his electronic devices, deputies say
text:
LINCOLN, Neb. (KOLN/Gray News) - A Nebraska man has been arrested for allegedly possessing child sexual abuse material.
According to the Lancaster County Sheriff’s Office, Timmy Lee Topil, 60, was arrested Tuesday after his wife reported finding suspected child sexual abuse material on thumb drives and a tablet belonging to him.
Topil and his wife reportedly were separated when the matter was reported to authorities.
Lancaster County authorities said Topil had been living in a camper near Branched Oak Lake, where the material was found in a backpack.
Lancaster County Sheriff’s Office Chief Deputy Ben Houchin said Topil’s wife shared with the department that she had an “inkling he was looking at improper things.”
Following an interview with Topil, the sheriff’s office said the content appeared to have been downloaded from the internet.
Topil was taken to an adult detention facility and booked on suspicion of possession of child sexual abuse material, a felony charge punishable by up to 20 years in prison.

title: A push to train and hire more women in the auto repair industry
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LAS VEGAS (InvestigateTV) — Most auto repair shops are staffed almost entirely by men, according to federal labor data.
A February 2026 report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics found about 1.8% of mechanics are women.
Federal data predicts about 70,000 job openings in the field by 2034 as many older workers retire. The industry is stepping up efforts to recruit and train more women to meet that demand.
Samantha Aiken is the service manager for the Midas off Tropicana in Las Vegas. The trained auto technician said some shops were skeptical to hire her. She said the family that owns the shop vouched for her, saying customer service needed a woman’s touch.
“I relate to the customers. I’m honest with them. You know, I put myself in their shoes because I was them at one point, you know,” Aiken said. “So, I just sit next to them and I show them everything. If they have questions, I bring them out here and show them the cars.”
Aiken said she has never been afraid to get her hands dirty.
After fixing cars with her boyfriend and going to parts stores by herself, she decided to pursue a new career.
Companies and shops call staff at UEI looking for students to hire. Rose White, UEI campus president, said students train in the school’s automotive lab.
“We are in the automotive lab here at my campus. This is where our students get to take the theory and the didactic part of their training and put it into hands-on, real practical practice and training,” White said.
White said students are not limited to repair work.
“They’re not looking for careers that they’re going to be sitting at a desk. You can go into the service side, into the management side, administrative,” White said. “You can break into some of the fun things like we have in Las Vegas with F1, racing. So, the sky’s the limit.”
Aiken said she hopes to go back to the classroom in the future to teach other women entering the field. “Just go for it. Don’t be afraid to get your hands dirty.”
National organizations such as Women in Automotive provide mentorship programs and connect women already working in the auto industry.

title: Swatting hoax prompted Bangor middle school evacuation
text:
The William S. Cohen School in Bangor was briefly evacuated Wednesday morning after a swatting hoax, according to the school district.
“At approximately 11:30 a.m., school administrators received a swatting hoax message related to a bomb threat,” the district said in a statement late Wednesday afternoon.
Students were moved to the Fruit Street School, according to a message sent to parents shortly after 11:30 a.m. They returned to the William S. Cohen School about an hour later.
Bangor police searched the school “out of an abundance of caution,” and nothing was found, spokesperson Jeremey Brock said.
“The Bangor School Department appreciates the continued support and understanding of families as we work together to maintain a safe and supportive learning environment for all students,” the school district said.

title: Much of the world sees tragedy in Gaza. Many Israelis see only a threat
text:
Much of the world sees tragedy in Gaza. Many Israelis see only a threat
One by one, Israelis peered through the tourist-style binoculars at the shattered Gaza town of Beit Hanoun, a distance of several football fields away, where buildings tilted in the rubble like broken teeth. The only noticeable movement was dust kicked up by Israel’s military.
Previous video coverage above: Israeli soldiers share rare accounts from Gaza, describing ongoing killings despite ceasefire
The Israelis squinted for a few moments and gestured others over. The lookout is a rare place where they can confront the Palestinian territory firsthand, and some celebrate its devastation.
An Israeli documentary released this year included one onlooker exclaiming, “Wow, destroyed beautifully.” The Associated Press heard similar sentiments there.
On Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led militants killed some 1,200 people in southern Israel and abducted 251 others, leading to a devastating war and, eventually, a fragile ceasefire.
Three years on, a visit to the communities attacked that day made clear: It’s too soon for many residents to see the Palestinians next door as anything other than a threat.
Barbecue reminds one woman of ‘the smell of hell’
The highway running parallel to Gaza, where militants gunned down people trying to flee, is dotted with memorials. Victims’ smashed and bullet-pocked cars are assembled elsewhere, rusting and piled a half-dozen high. Portraits of young female military spotters, whose warnings about a potential attack were disregarded, mark their deaths that day.
One resident, Deganit Bar Hay, said she still can’t barbecue because the smell of burnt flesh — “the smell of hell” — is a trigger.
Globally, there is shock and condemnation over how Israel has conducted the war, and how Gaza remains in ruins and cut off from the world a year since the ceasefire. Over 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry, and the vast majority of its 2 million residents live in rat-infested tent camps or among the debris.
But empathy for them is still unthinkable for many in Israel, with memories raw. Israeli media report little on the Palestinians of Gaza, and Israelis rarely, if ever, hear their voices unless they seek them out.
A new Israeli documentary, “NAZA,” in which military insiders describe what they said was the systemic killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza, has sparked outrage at the filmmakers, not the government. Everywhere in Israel — at train stations, beaches, the Gaza viewpoint — are dozens of stickers in memory of the hundreds of soldiers killed on Oct. 7 and in the ensuing war.
“We are post-traumatic, all of us,” said Ziporah Livneh, outside a cafe catering to tour groups and soldiers a short drive from Gaza. Much of her family died in the Holocaust, and she came to Israel at the age of 2.
Now, she said, the answer for Gaza is to keep believing in people’s humanity but respond strongly to acts of evil. A society and a country can’t be built on revenge, but for the world to think “we can be Mother Teresa, it is a hypocrisy.”
‘Many people around the globe don’t understand us’
Many Israelis are still turned inward. They say their story isn’t being heard or understood. They assert that Palestinians in Gaza receive more attention, even as Israel’s government still prevents journalists from entering the territory except under rare, highly managed visits — and very few Palestinians can leave.
From the day the war began, Israeli news and hearts were focused on the dead and the hostages taken into Gaza, a land that despite being an hour’s drive from Tel Aviv has long felt remote. Cross-border contact had been severely limited since Hamas seized power in 2007. Then, on Oct. 7, militants ripped the fence apart.
This is the first anniversary since the attack that all remaining hostages are out of Gaza, alive or dead.
There is rebuilding in the Israeli communities where militants went home to home, burning and shooting. There is also the insistence on keeping Oct. 7 memories alive, with hope that the outside world will come to understand how Israel’s sense of security was smashed.
“I know many people around the globe don’t understand us,” said Mor Izreal, director of an Oct. 7 virtual reality exhibit in the border city of Sderot. She said over 10,000 people have visited since it opened a year and a half ago, most from overseas. Reactions range from sadness to rage to connectedness, she said.
The first election since the war brings fresh anger
This year, for the first time since the attack, there is also an election, a momentous and angry one.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government is deeply divisive. Many Israelis accuse him of failing to prevent the Oct. 7 attack and not securing the hostages’ release sooner, before many of them were killed. He is also accused of corruption and threatening democratic institutions.
But there has been little criticism of how his government has treated the Palestinians in Gaza, where Israel’s military now controls over 60% of the territory, squeezing them into an ever-smaller space.
Next to a bullet-pocked rocket shelter outside Sderot, a man held a banner calling for an official inquiry into the security failures surrounding the attack. Netanyahu has long resisted one.
Amit Gurfinkel said he spent Oct. 7 in a safe room with his daughter in the nearby community of Netivot, holding a knife and expecting the worst.
Gurfinkel is a minority in a population that has long supported Netanyahu. Posted across Sderot are campaign banners for his far-right allies, Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben Gvir — the national security minister who has called for killing “30 to 40” people in targeted assassinations in Gaza each night.
Security is paramount, especially in Sderot, where residents have just 10 seconds to seek shelter when rockets are fired from Gaza. But Gurfinkel sees Israel’s reputation as crucial, too. He shook his head over passing drivers who shouted their support for Netanyahu, whose government is isolated over the destruction in Gaza and who has been issued an arrest warrant by the International Criminal Court.
“This is pathological. I don’t know,” Gurfinkel said. “Sociologists and psychologists will have answers in the years to come.”
There is little discussion of Palestinian civilians
Some Israelis say there are no real civilians among Palestinians in Gaza, pointing to Hamas’ entrenchment. Some Palestinians feel the same way about Israelis, noting that military service is mandatory for most Jewish men and women.
“Death to Arabs” is written inside a rocket shelter across from the Sderot police station that was besieged and then destroyed. “Hamas is still in Gaza” is scrawled on a guardrail on the highway where bodies spilled from vehicles on Oct. 7. “Make Gaza Jewish Again” is on a banner in a public square in Jerusalem’s Old City.
There is little public discussion about how everyday Palestinians are doing after three years of war.
“I think about them, and it’s complicated,” Adi Marmelstain said of the people in Gaza. She was visiting the sprawling memorial for the Nova music festival, where hundreds of people were shot dead on Oct. 7.
Her 20-year-old daughter, a member of the security forces like many young Israelis, stood in shorts and a tank top, her rifle slung across her. Both knew people who had been killed.
Marmelstain recalled waking up another daughter on Oct. 7 and sending her to war with bottled water and cookies. She later asked herself what she had been thinking. Three years later, life is not much easier to contemplate.
The world doesn’t see Israel in the right light, she said. And the Palestinians in Gaza?
“I think they have the right to live, but they choose not to,” she said.

title: Community rallies for 12-year-old girl killed after shots fired in fight over parking spot
text:
BALTIMORE (WJZ) - A Baltimore community is rallying for peace after a 12-year-old girl was killed when police say shots were fired during a fight over a parking spot near a youth football game.
Hundreds of people walked through the West Baltimore streets on Monday to remember 12-year-old Khloe Ishway, support her family and demand an end to the violence that took her life.
“Just remember her as a person, a loving person, a good family member, good sister, good cousin, good friend. Just want everyone to remember her,” said Khloe’s mother, Kristin Reese.
Baltimore Police say two men apparently got into an argument over a parking spot Saturday at Leon Day Park, which was packed for a youth football game. Shots were fired, and Khloe was caught in the crossfire. She was taken to the hospital, where she was pronounced dead.
Four other people – a 23-year-old man, a 25-year-old woman, a 28-year-old man and a 35-year-old woman – were injured.
At Monday’s rally, Reese had a strong message to anyone who knows who shot her daughter. No arrests had been made at the time.
“You don’t say nothing, then you must be a part of it, and being a part of it, you’re a clown,” she said.
The tragedy has left the youth football community shattered, asking how children can be kept safe while simply doing what they love. They hope Khloe’s name lives on and inspires positive change.
“May it live on. May some laws get changed. May security be at some football games, so these kids who aren’t in the streets, who don’t have guns, can play safe,” family friend Kevin Miller said.
On Tuesday, police announced the arrest of 23-year-old Tyree Reynolds in connection to Khloe’s death. He is facing charges including murder, attempted murder, assault, reckless endangerment and other offenses.

title: You can buy a 103-year-old urinal from this college football stadium for $3,000
text:
LINCOLN, Neb. (CNN) - People are buying century-old urinal troughs from Memorial Stadium at the University of Nebraska.
The troughs are part of a collection of memorabilia the school is selling before a major stadium renovation begins at the end of the football season.
Among the items are 300-pound troughs from the men’s rooms, priced at $3,000 each.
The company selling the items said several of the 30 available have already been sold.
The Buffalo Bills did the same when the NFL team moved out of its old stadium.
The university said everything will be thoroughly cleaned before it is delivered.

title: What is a checking account?
text:
What is a checking account?
Key takeaways
- A checking account is a bank account used for everyday transactions, such as paying bills, making debit card purchases, withdrawing cash at ATMs, writing checks, sending money to friends and family and receiving direct deposits.
- Checking accounts are often covered by federal deposit insurance.
- There are various types of checking accounts, including free checking, interest-bearing checking, rewards checking and second-chance checking.
A checking account is a bank account that’s designed to be the hub of your financial life. It holds the money you use for everyday spending, and allows you to move funds in and out with ease. You can access your money through a debit card, ATM card, checks or online transfers, and set up direct deposit and automatic billpay to keep your finances running on autopilot.
A checking account is safer and easier than carrying cash or using prepaid products. If your account is covered by federal deposit insurance, your money is protected based on the limits and guidelines, even if the bank or credit union fails. And if your debit card is lost or stolen, you can lock it and dispute unauthorized transactions. To top it off, you won’t pay for any of this protection and access with a free checking account.
What is a checking account used for?
A checking account is meant for the money you use every day, so its features are designed to help you spend, receive and manage that money. Most accounts include these tools:
- Debit card access. A checking account provides a debit card linked to the account. This makes everyday purchases — both in person and online — and ATM withdrawals possible.
- Online and mobile tracking and budgeting. Using this feature, you can check balances, transfer money, pay bills and deposit checks. Some bank apps allow you to create a budget, set alerts and access customer support.
- Overdraft protection. If you spend more than you have available, overdraft protection helps bridge the gap by covering transactions that exceed the account balance. You typically have to opt in to these programs and some charge you a fee for this privilege, though others have eliminated or reduced overdraft fees.
- Direct deposit. Direct deposit lets you have your paycheck or other income deposited electronically into your checking account. Some financial institutions even allow early access, up to two days, to funds that are deposited using this feature.
- Check writing. Although checks aren’t as popular as they used to be, they can still come in handy. For example, some landlords may still only take payment via check.
Not every account handles these features equally well, so it pays to compare Bankrate’s picks for the best checking accounts.
Benefits of checking accounts
Checking accounts keep your money safe and accessible, and they make it easy to automate your money management.
Safety
- Safer than cash. If your wallet is lost or stolen, you can lock your debit card and dispute unauthorized transactions as long as you report them quickly. Once cash is stolen, it’s often gone for good.
- Federal deposit insurance. If your account is with a federally insured bank or credit union, your money is protected if the institution fails, within coverage limits.
- Coverage limits. The Federal Deposit Insurance (FDIC) and National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund (NCUSIF) insure funds up to $250,000 per depositor or share owner, per insured financial institution, per ownership category — such as joint or single accounts.
Ease of access
- Many ways to pay. Use a debit or ATM card, checks or online payments for everything from retail purchases to rent, mortgage payments and other bills.
- Quick transfers to others. Many accounts offer peer-to-peer payments through Zelle from your phone or computer. You can also link your account to apps like Venmo.
Automation
- Direct deposit. Paychecks land in your account automatically, so you don’t have to deposit them yourself. Some banks allow you to receive your paycheck up to two days sooner through early direct deposit.
- Automatic bill pay. Regular expenses, such as credit card and utility bills, are electronically withdrawn on a recurring basis.
- Automatic saving. Splitting your paycheck between checking and a high-yield savings account allows you to “pay yourself first” and put your savings on autopilot.
Access to overdraft coverage
Overdrafts can occur when you withdraw more money than what’s in your account and your balance dips below zero. Overdraft fees the bank charges you to cover your payment can be expensive, though some banks now offer this service free of charge.
Many checking accounts offer overdraft protection, which automatically transfers funds from your savings account or a line of credit when your checking account is overdrawn. You can easily find banks that don’t charge a fee for such transfers from a linked savings account.
Checking vs. savings accounts
A checking account is best for making day-to-day financial transactions, while a savings account is a good place for funds set aside for emergencies, or financial goals such as a vacation or a new car purchase.
Bankrate insight
You can get the best of both worlds by having your checking account at a brick-and-mortar bank and a high-yield savings account at an online-only bank. This way, you’re able to walk into a bank for checking issues or to make cash deposits while earning a competitive yield on your savings at an online bank.
How to choose a checking account
Start by deciding which type of checking account fits your needs, then compare the details that affect cost and convenience:
- Monthly fees: Maintenance fees can eat away at your balance over time. Look for a free checking account with no monthly fee, or check whether the fee can be waived with either a direct deposit you would normally make or a reasonable minimum balance.
- Other fees: Check the fee schedule for overdraft fees, out-of-network ATM fees or paper statement fees. Make sure such fees are easy for you to avoid, or choose an account that doesn’t charge them.
- Minimum opening deposit: This can vary among banks, so make sure it’s an amount you’re comfortable with. Some checking accounts don’t require any set minimum deposit.
- ATM access: The total average out-of-network ATM fee is around $4 to $5. To avoid these fees, choose a bank that offers plenty of its own ATMs or is a member of a large fee-free network, or go with a bank that reimburses ATM fees.
- Branch access: If you prefer in-person banking, find a bank with branches near you, but watch for higher fees, since banks with branches tend to charge more to cover their costs. Most also offer online banking, which works well if you want a mix of both.
- Features: Consider what you’ll actually use, such as a strong mobile app, early direct deposit, budgeting tools, peer-to-peer payment options like Zelle and overdraft protection. If you want to earn interest, check whether an interest checking account’s requirements are manageable for you.
Next steps

- Checking account fees Learn the common fees and how to avoid them.
- Second-chance checking accounts Access for those whose history may prevent them from opening a standard account.
- Best interest checking accounts These accounts earn money on the funds you use for daily expenses.

title: Maine regulators reject CMP's temporary rate hike
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Maine Public Utilities Commission has denied a request to impose rare temporary electric rates on Central Maine Power customers amid a contentious debate over the company’s proposal to raise prices long-term.
The commission’s chair, Phil Bartlett, said in a meeting Tuesday that parties to CMP’s rate case could not reach an “undisputed” amount the company should be allowed to raise in the short term.
“To grant a request for temporary rates, there needs to be a clear amount that is not in dispute. In my view, that is not the case here,” Bartlett said.
CMP asked to increase its distribution prices to raise about $69 million while the commission and other parties negotiated long-term rates for the company. The proposal would have added about $7 a month to the average residential power bill, according to the utility.
Without that additional cash flow, CMP may have to delay hiring, put off important infrastructure spending and reconsider its workforce levels, according to the company.
But Bartlett noted that some of CMP’s own spending decisions contributed to its current financial straits.
“The capital spend between 2022 and 2025 significantly exceeded the forecast, by over 50%. So, to some extent, this is a problem of CMP’s own making,” Bartlett said.
A CMP spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday.
In a filing last week, CMP said that the funding it requested would pay for much-needed projects to improve reliable electric service, prepare for stronger and more destructive storms and boost its skilled workforce.
“Customers do not experience regulatory delay in the abstract. They experience it through aging transformers, deferred maintenance, postponed reliability projects, and infrastructure that continues operating long after it should have been replaced,” the company said.
The temporary rate issue is part of a bigger rate case for CMP still being negotiated through the utilities commission. The utility is asking to increase distribution prices to raise about $189 million. Opponents and critics are pushing to lower that amount, with a focus on how much profit the utility should be allowed to earn from its infrastructure investments.
The debate is unfolding as Mainers deal with high prices for energy, housing and other daily needs.
“CMP is trying to squeeze blood from a stone,” Seth Berry, a spokesperson for Fight the Hike, a coalition of consumer groups, said in a press release.
“Unlike any other business, CMP has a monopoly. This is a privilege granted to them by the state. It’s time for CMP shareholders to fund maintenance from their $160 million in annual profits— not squeeze still more from Maine families,” Berry added.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.
