title: Christa Pike is awake after failed execution as her attorneys seek more information
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Death row inmate Christa Pike has regained consciousness after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute her by lethal injection last week, and her attorneys are set to head to court Wednesday to seek more information about what went wrong.
Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital as executioners attempted to put her to death Sept. 30 for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike is believed to be the only person to survive after lethal injection drugs were administered.
Pike’s attorneys are set to appear in court Wednesday as they are seeking more information from the Tennessee Department of Correction. Chancery Court Judge I’Ashea Myles has scheduled a Wednesday morning status conference in Nashville in the case.
“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care,” attorneys for Pike said in a statement. Pike’s prognosis remains unclear and, at a minimum, she faces a lengthy recovery, the attorneys said. They said Pike’s arms were burned and blistered after the attempted lethal injection and that she is handcuffed to the hospital bed.
Pike’s attorneys are seeking a court order to require the prison system to preserve information from the attempted execution including drug lot numbers, needles, execution logs and other information.
Attorneys with the Tennessee attorney general’s office wrote in a Tuesday court filing that the court order is unnecessary because the prison system is “obliged to maintain this evidence in other cases and must assure it is preserved.” They said state officials have taken “the necessary steps to obtain medical care for Pike and ascertain what occurred.”
Republican Gov. Bill Lee called what happened “deeply disturbing” and ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred.” The governor postponed the state’s only other execution scheduled for this year.
Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on the possibility that a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue rather than entering her bloodstream. Pike’s attorneys wrote in their court filing that “apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown.”
The attempted execution got underway around 7:30 p.m. on Sept. 30 when Pike was given a chance to make a final statement. About five minutes later, Pike raised her head and said her arm was hurting. At some point she appeared to lose consciousness, but she could be heard audibly breathing until media were escorted from the witness room at 8:53 p.m. An ambulance arrived at the prison at 9:14 p.m. to take Pike to a hospital.

title: VETERANS CORNER: Attrition rate of doctors in Maine that will service Togus veterans is declining at an alarming rate
text:
Good day my fellow veterans and friends. Before I share this week’s news regarding VA and claims, I would like all of you to take a few minutes for prayer and well being to one of our own who has served us well for a number of years. Cornelius James Ware is retiring from the VFW after many years of arduous service to the veteran community. James, as we all refer to him, has performed his VFW duties in the same military manner in which he served his country as a Naval Warrant Officer II for 23 years. His honorable military history and his civilian veteran services are second to none. These past few years he has performed his duty to God, Country and our veterans through his own personal pain. He is in dire need of at least a hip replacement. We veteran advocates know what it is like to serve while dealing with personal pain. James replaced an old friend of mine, Rene Duchesne, almost two decades ago, and served veterans well. James stood outside of his office of all these years and greeted friends and said his goodbyes. Thank you James for your service, good luck with your pending surgery and may the good and loving God walk and watch over you in your retirement life with your family and friends. You have a place in the hearts of many veterans you served.
One more seat for now is vacant. VFW being a private entity, separate yet part of the VA system will most likely fill that seat in the near future. When and if they do I hope they will consider the cost of living these days as VSO’s are not paid well for their time, knowledge and effort. Organizations such as VFW, American Legion, Maine State Vets and others are underrated and under paid. The benefit package in some cases is non-existent. This needs to be addressed in the world of today. VSOs and VBAs are direly needed to protect and defend veterans; those who have given their all, truth, justice, and the American way, lives with them.
They have been overlooked and under rated for far to long and that needs to change. In the world of today to get quality you need to be able to find a way to offer, protect and accommodate the people who are placed in these positions. They are actually the backbones of the VA system. If you think about it, without them the back room may as well turn off their computers as there will be no claims to evaluate.
The sad part from where my pen stands is the decline of the VA system, yet the escalation of world turmoil. The administration has grown by leaps and bounds. Friends are moved around to service the whims of the power base. Medical departments have been all but destroyed due to the mass exodus of medical staff to the administrative side. Just ask how many have transferred or been moved from medical to administration. That group is top heavy and medical is extremely weak. Administration says they advertise but no takers and those of interest can’t work for wages offered, even with the insurance break from private practice. Why in the world is that? Is it a secret plan to make our Togus VA the administrative hub of the VA system? They say no problem they have outside doctors and hospitals who will service our veterans. I say that is a bunch of the stuff that bulls excrete. (Have to be careful these days) As I have explained before, my research shows that doctors and hospital in Maine are increasingly refusing to take “Togus” veterans. If you are a veteran with part A and B Medicare plus VA you most likely won’t have a problem. Medicare has even added onto that. How many of you receive scam calls daily from Medicare sales people propagating the Medicare enticement and lie. Many veterans, especially those who are at 100 percent Permanent and Total (P&T) don’t have Medicare, other than the mandatory part “A”.
I have told you this before but I will tell you once again, the attrition rate of doctors in Maine, that will service Togus veterans is declining at an alarming rate. I have researched this personally and can tell you for a fact, this is happening. VA is not coming close to the required fee of many of these doctors, especially Specialty Medical Service. They are expensive because the economy says they are very professional, that is reflected in their profession and the employees they need to hire. I’ve lost some myself. I went to concord, New Hampshire, last week, a three-hour drive each way to take an X-ray that could have been done at VA in five minutes. All my tolls and mileage was paid by VA. How many of us travel more than 100 miles for an exam and because of the distance and /or the procedure had to stay overnight? If Boston has availability you can stay at the “Huntington House” for free, but that still requires mileage, tolls and food. Where is the VA saving? My wife and I went there last week and it cost VA $150 for our expenses. The wear and tear on our vehicle is not even figured in. Also, there are times that the visit is less productive than that which can be attained at Togus.
If we veterans don’t get together and make calls to both Collins’s, as well as write letters explaining what you see, what is obvious, than we are going to lose the VA system we know that works. If you, who have been veterans of many years, walk through the halls of Togus today how many faces do you recognize? How many are very young, new and from other countries? I’m not saying that’s all bad; for the most part perhaps change is needed. I say this all the time; our existing medical departments are weak. For a long time we were bringing in X-ray techs from outside at a special rate to cover for emergent situations, in the department. Ridiculous. Medical specialists, well trained, have paid, and are waiting in line in the Philippines, yet no positive action from secretary Collins.
What kind of management is that? Yet we can sand blast the bricks on the back of our buildings but can’t hire and pay medical staff. Most departments have one doctor and as of July 1 Tracye Davis has shut down E.N.T. Unless doctor’s facilities, and schools receive federal funds of any kind they don’t have to take Togus veterans. Also, the quality we once enjoyed, can only be found in the pocket of administration. We need change and it’s time we stood up for ourselves, wives, and sons and daughters, the future is not bright. Some of you have done well because of a good VSO or a sharp POA, perhaps even a lawyer. VA is not following its own mandates, they can’t pay the bills, and they can’t even finish the jobs they start, why not? We have empty departments such as ENT and Rheumatology and others. We need them more than the VA hierarchy.
We do maintain a phenomenal support staff on the medical side. All active departments have great receptionists and they take the blows from the veterans who need the doctors they represent but they can’t place a vet where there is no space or no doctor. They do their jobs with cool and dignity while at times hiding a tear because they know and see the need and understand the anger and despair. “Do we ever thank them for their service?” Like the kitchen and those that keep our facility pristine, housekeeping, they go unnoticed and terribly under paid but administration is where the money is, it certainly isn’t at the “Fisher House”, where our veteran families should be staying; another black mark on administration. I have written a long letter to President Trump as well as Secretary Collins. Let’s see if it will bear fruit. I have offered myself as your guide and you know I will show them all. Beware of the broken bridge bottleneck and danger zone. God bless you all and have a safe and happy weekend. If you have difficulty or credit to share use garyek55@gmail.com.. Oh, never forget the Community Living Center. Some died waiting, who owns that?

title: These were Christa Pike’s first words after execution attempt left her unconscious for days
text:
NASHVILLE (WSMV/Gray News) - Attorneys for Christa Pike have revealed the first words she said after regaining consciousness nearly a week after the state attempted to execute her and failed.
Christa Pike was completely disoriented when she woke up in a Nashville hospital.
“Where am I and who are you?” were Pike’s first words, her attorney said in a press conference on Wednesday.
“There is still a lot of cognitive confusion. ... She is very aware that the state tried to execute. ... She is very aware up to a point,” the attorney said.
The 50-year-old was sentenced to be executed for the 1995 murder and torture of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer. She has spent over three decades on death row.
A week ago, the state of Tennessee failed to execute Pike, despite injecting her with two doses of the lethal drug pentobarbitol.
She was rushed to a hospital from Riverbend Maximum Security Institution following the injections, where she has since been receiving care in critical condition.
On Tuesday, her attorneys announced that she had woken up and was speaking, but she still requires medical treatment. It was later revealed that just hours before she awoke, they thought she was brain dead.
“She has a blood clot in her arm, she has pneumonia, she is not able to swallow so she hasn’t eaten, she can’t move her arms, her arms are both tremendously swollen,” her defense said outside a Nashville courthouse.
Pike is the only person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution, AP reported.
Many details of the execution process remain secretive, and Tennessee officials say they are investigating what went wrong.

title: This island was home to the planet’s largest penguin colony. Here’s why it just lost that title
text:
This island was home to the planet’s largest penguin colony. Here’s why it just lost that title
An uninhabited volcanic island in the Southern Ocean used to be home to the largest penguin colony in the world — but not anymore.
Scientists have discovered the staggering loss of more than half a million chinstrap penguins from the isolated outcrop.
Chinstrap penguins, named for the narrow band of black feathers under their chins, thrive in harsh locations and Zavodovski Island fits the bill perfectly. Part of the South Sandwich Islands archipelago north of Antarctica, the island is wild, craggy and windswept.
Zavodovski is home to both chinstraps and macaroni penguins, which have distinctive yellow feather plumes on their heads. In 2011, it was named the largest penguin colony in the world, but when British Antarctic Survey researchers traveled to the island in 2023, they found the chinstraps had suffered huge declines.
More than half a million have been lost since 2011, representing a quarter of the island’s penguins, according to the findings published Wednesday in the journal Current Biology. Comparing aerial surveys with satellite data, the researchers found the number of occupied chinstrap penguin nests fell by 63% between 2011 and 2025.
“It is the biggest change in community composition ever observed at a single location in Antarctica,” said Norman Ratcliffe, a penguin ecologist at BAS and the lead researcher. The decline can be linked to human-driven climate change, the report concludes.
“Chinstraps are giving quite a clear signal of the impacts of warming,” Ratcliffe said.
Zavodovski, which is about 1,200 miles from the nearest permanently inhabited settlement, is rarely visited by scientists because it’s so remote and extreme.
To reach it, BAS researchers set off from the Falkland Islands and navigated rough seas for two weeks. At points, they were forced to shelter in fjords from raging storms, before they eventually reached the only part of the island where the cliffs and swelling currents are gentle enough to allow people to scramble onto land.
They set up camp on the rocks and spent three days tracking and surveying the penguins using drones, aerial photography from a British plane stationed in the Falkland Islands and tracking devices fitted to the penguins.
Chinstrap penguin populations have experienced worrying declines in recent years. A 2020 study found drops of nearly 50% in some Antarctic island colonies compared to previous surveys in the 1980s. But, for a long time, it was believed Zavodovski Island had bucked this trend.
Instead, the BAS researchers found a sudden and dramatic decline on the island. It now has the highest rate of chinstrap penguin decline in the world. “We’re looking at annual population declines of around 7%,” Ratcliffe said, around two to three times the rate elsewhere.
The scientists ruled out a 2016 volcanic eruption as the cause, given the downward trend had started several years before and has maintained a steady pace across the years. They also found no evidence that competition for nesting space or the impact of regional krill fisheries were driving the fall in numbers.
They determined the most plausible cause is fossil fuel pollution, which is heating the ocean and disrupting the chinstraps’ key food source, krill, which rely on sea ice for food and shelter. As warming forces the krill southward, the penguins can’t follow because the water is too icy for them.
The chinstrap penguin “is quite a specialist species that’s got a very limited global range, and that range is getting squeezed,” Ratcliffe said.
There is some good news in the study. The scientists found the island’s macaroni penguin population increased by 28% between 2011 and 2016, after which it has stayed stable.
Their increase adds weight to the climate change theory, Ratcliffe said. Macaronis are happy in warmer water and have a more varied diet, so are not as reliant on the diminishing krill.
The scientists suggest that the chinstraps’ precipitous decline on Zavodovski Island, coupled with falls in other parts of Antarctica, may push them into the endangered category on the Red List of Threatened Species produced by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. They are currently designated as a species of least concern.
The findings are “really worrying news” for chinstraps as the South Sandwich Islands were thought to be their stronghold, said Noah Strycker, an ornithologist and author who was not involved in the research. “What strikes me about this study is how rapidly things are changing,” he added.
Peter Fretwell, a BAS researcher who specializes in remote sensing of penguins, said the study is yet another example “of a warming climate impacting even the most remote parts of our planet. The South Sandwich Islands are far from any humans, home to almost a third of the world’s chinstrap penguins — but not even they can escape the impacts of climate change.”

title: Susan Collins says she supports women. We saw otherwise.
text:
Debra Katz and Lisa Banks are founding partners of Katz Banks Kumin LLP. They represented Dr. Ford during the 2018 confirmation hearings of Justice Brett Kavanaugh.
In September 2018, we sat beside Dr. Christine Blasey Ford as she courageously testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee. In a packed room with more than 20 million people watching live on television, Dr. Ford raised her right hand — now an iconic image — and painstakingly recounted the sexual assault she endured by then-Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh when she was 15.
Dr. Ford came forward at enormous personal and professional cost, facing such extreme threats to her safety that she and her family were forced to leave their home and retain 24-hour security services. She did so because she believed that U.S. senators, like Sen. Susan Collins, should know the character of a man who was up for a lifetime appointment to the Supreme Court.
Ultimately, Sen. Collins did not care, and pledged fealty to President Trump in casting the
deciding vote in favor of Kavanaugh’s confirmation. She voted this way despite Dr. Ford’s testimony, which Collins described as “sincere, painful, and compelling,” and despite her own avowed support of survivors of sexual assault and the importance of reproductive rights.
Collins justified her vote by explaining that she had met privately with Kavanaugh, who, in addition to denying the assault, assured her that he would honor precedent, including Roe v. Wade. She subsequently also told CNN that with regard to Dr. Ford’s sexual assault, “I do not believe that Brett Kavanaugh was her assailant. I do believe that she was assaulted. I don’t know by whom, and I’m not certain when, but I do not believe he was the assailant.”
This preposterous explanation, while politically expedient, was offensive not only to Dr. Ford but to survivors everywhere. Conveniently forgotten by Collins was Dr. Ford’s sworn testimony that she was “one hundred percent” certain that it was Kavanaugh who had assaulted her. Also ignored was the important fact that Dr. Ford had named Kavanaugh as her assailant to her friends, therapist and husband years before his nomination.
At best, Susan Collins was duped by Kavanaugh and President Trump. At worst, her actions were duplicitous, born of a desire to assure her constituents she was a moderate and supporter of women, even if her voting record says otherwise.
Beyond Kavanaugh, Collins’ voting record includes a long history of votes for extreme judicial nominees who hold regressive positions on a shocking array of rights.
Sen. Collins voted for Joshua Dunlap, who now sits on the 1st Circuit Court of Appeals, where Maine’s federal appellate matters are heard, despite the fact that he opposed marriage equality and has a history of opposition to pro-choice laws. Collins also voted to confirm Eric Tung to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, even though he too does not believe in a constitutional right to same-sex marriage. And even though Joshua Divine, now a federal judge in Missouri, once lumped homosexuality together with bestiality, she voted to confirm him too.
In total, Susan Collins has voted for 52 out of 55 of Donald Trump’s second-term judges, while voting “no” on many of the pro-choice, pro-worker Biden nominees that she claims to find common cause with.
Collins may claim to be a moderate, but she does not vote like one. And where Dr. Ford demonstrated tremendous courage, Sen. Collins has demonstrated that she will always place politics over principle.
We hope that when Mainers go to the ballot box this November, they remember that Collins’ lack of principle has led directly to the appointment of Justice Kavanaugh, the overturning of Roe v. Wade and to President Trump stocking the federal courts with extreme jurists intent on undermining our nation’s civil rights.

title: Bedard Senior Care of Auburn announces name change
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bedard Pharmacy & Medical Supplies, the parent company of Bedard Senior Care of Auburn, announced Monday that it is changing the name of the division to Bedard Long-Term Care Pharmacy to “more accurately reflect” the breadth of patients, communities, and healthcare partners it serves.
“The Senior Care name represented an important part of who we serve, but it did not fully describe the range of communities and patients who depend on our pharmacy,” CEO Ben Nadeau said in a statement to the media. “Bedard Long-Term Care Pharmacy is a clearer reflection of what our team does today and the people we are here to support.”
Bedard said the name change is strictly for branding, and that there is no change in ownership, leadership, employees, pharmacy operations, or existing customer and partner relationships.
Bedard Long-Term Care Pharmacy provides specialized pharmacy services designed around the medication needs of long-term care communities, their residents, caregivers, and healthcare partners. Its role extends beyond dispensing prescriptions, with a focus on making medication management more organized, dependable, and easier to navigate across different care environments.
It operates at 359 Minot Ave. in Auburn.

title: New nonprofit launches campaign to preserve local newspapers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Mount Desert Islander, Ellsworth American and Bangor Historian have formed a nonprofit, Acadia Newspaper Trust, to transition the newspapers from private, for-profit ownership to nonprofit ownership.
The owner of the papers, Camden businessman Reade Brower, is planning to retire, according to Publisher Chris Crockett. As a result, newspaper leadership has been working to establish The Trust to preserve the papers’ local ownership and independent mission.
“We thought about a lot of different ways to keep the newspapers locally controlled, locally owned, and look towards the future for sustainability, growth and expansion,” Crockett said. “This made the most sense for us moving forward.”
The Trust, which is now a full 501(c)(3) recognized by the IRS, has an initial fundraising goal of $1 million, which Crockett says will allow the organization to purchase the newspapers from Brower and provide a steady financial foundation.
The Trust hopes to complete the purchase by late summer 2027.
“[Newspapers] are not a high-profit industry to begin with,” Crockett said. “Good years, newspapers can run 5 to 8% operating margins, which is literally break even. So, the non-profit will give us the flexibility to operate debt-free and explore new ways to support the work we do through philanthropy, grants and other options that are not available to us as a for-profit.”
He believes the nonprofit transition will be the most sustainable path forward for all three papers at a time when costs across the board are increasing.
“All of those pressures have mounted while our revenue remains relatively fixed,” Crockett said.
In August, multiple employees were laid off after the papers lost a major print advertiser, among other financial pressures.
“Part of this transition is to ensure that those kinds of layoffs don’t have to happen again and that hopefully in the future we can recover some of those positions and expand and grow,” Crockett said.
Acadia Newspaper Trust will be guided by a volunteer board of directors who Crockett says will not impact the day-to-day operations or be involved in editorial decisions.
He noted a “strict” conflict of interest policy for people associated with The Trust and an editorial independence policy, both of which have already been created.
“Donations will not impact what we cover, how we cover it and our core business,” Crockett said.
The board will instead direct the vision of The Trust and form long-term goals, such as expanding areas of coverage, purchasing a permanent building and increasing reader access.
Maine’s nonprofit news models
Acadia Newspaper Trust is not the first nonprofit to be formed from an existing, for-profit paper. When The Harpswell Anchor closed its doors in 2020, a group of local residents revived the paper by turning it into a nonprofit organization.
Janice Thompson, who is now director of development and operations at the paper, was one of those residents.
“We lost our way of communicating with a whole town,” she said of the closure. When they discovered the nonprofit model — they pooled resources and bought the business.
The Anchor started publishing again in June 2021.
“The rest is history,” Thompson said. “We’ve done really well.”
She said that two-thirds of The Anchor’s revenue come from philanthropy. Most of those donations are from individuals, as opposed to a large foundation.
“We pay our bills, we’re able to invest in more enterprise journalism [and] the community has come together to support us financially,” Thompson said.
She is also working with Acadia Newspaper Trust on a consulting basis.
“The community has all these building blocks that you need in order to be successful, so I have 100% certainty that the community is going to rally,” she said of The Trust.
“What are local newspapers to do?” Thompson said. “We’re sort of flipping the business model on its head to not replace advertising and subscriptions, but to augment it.”
A growing number of news organizations in Maine are becoming or popping up as nonprofits. Many daily and weekly newspapers came under the ownership of The Maine Trust for Local News in 2023.
Reade Brower previously owned the papers that now form The Maine Trust for Local News, but in 2023, he put them up for sale. Brower took an offer from The National Trust for Local News after outside companies were reportedly “circling,” according to Nieman Reports.
The Maine Trust for Local News is a subsidiary of the Colorado-based nonprofit called the National Trust for Local News. According to its website, The Maine Trust has a newsroom of 120 people and covers communities across eight counties in the state. It includes the Portland Press Herald, the Lewiston Sun Journal, the Morning Sentinel and the Kennebec Journal.
Other statewide nonprofit newsrooms include The Maine Monitor, which was formed in 2020 from the Maine Center for Public Interest Reporting, a nonprofit founded in 2009. The Monitor focuses on investigating reporting on issues impacting Maine’s communities, according to its website.
Maine Morning Star, a digital news site covering state policy and politics, is a nonprofit affiliate of States Newsroom, a national nonprofit news organization dedicated to covering state government and policy.
Other nonprofit newsrooms include those that are spun off of advocacy groups, such as The Maine Wire with the Maine Policy Institute, The Working Waterfront with The Island Institute and Amjambo Africa! with Ladder to the Moon Network, according to Nieman Reports.
Nationally, there are an estimated 550 nonprofit news organizations in the United States, according to Nieman Lab. The Institute for Nonprofit News says that nearly 400 digital-first newsrooms took in roughly $650 to $700 million in revenue in 2024, a 14% increase from the previous year.
According to Chief of Growth Programs Courtney Lewis, the Institute has over 520 members and last year, local outlets made up 51% of the membership.
“It’s increased quite considerably,” she said, adding that the growth was driven by local newsrooms.
According to Lewis, of the Institute’s members, 48% of their revenue is from foundations, 33% is from individual donors and 17% is earned revenue, meaning advertising and sponsorship.
“Funding news is a relatively new concept in the grand scheme of philanthropy in this country,” Lewis said, describing it as a “competitive space.”
“Because of that, the challenge of relying on philanthropy for news, there’s a lot of work and case making to be done,” she added.
National newsroom declines
Financial pressures have been impacting all sectors of the economy — and local news is no different. Northwestern University’s Medill Local News Initiative report tracked nearly 136 newspaper closures in 2025, up from 130 in 2024. Over the last two decades, the country has lost nearly 3,500 newspapers and more than 270,000 newspaper jobs.
As a result, the country has just 7.8 local journalists per 100,000 residents, according to a 2026 Local Journalist Index created by Muck Rack and Rebuild Local News. That’s an 81% decline since 2002, when there were roughly 40 journalists per 100,000 people.
When there are fewer journalists, newsrooms tend to preserve beats that generate more website traffic, such as crime, which can result in topics like education, health and the environment being under covered — or not reported at all.
The project also reports that states with fewer local journalists have higher rates of loneliness, higher costs for municipal borrowing and more civic gaps in measures of voting, volunteering, charitable giving and community involvement.
But while the number of local journalists is decreasing across the nation, the state of Maine has a better outlook compared to the rest of the country.
The state ranked number three in the number of local journalist equivalents per 100,000 residents at 15.28. Hancock County is above the state average with 23.83 journalists per 100,000 people.
While it’s unclear if those statistics are related to the rise in nonprofit newsrooms, they may have an impact.
“All newspapers are in danger of closing if they do not come up with a solid financial foundation to sustain them through the future,” said Crockett of Acadia Newspaper Trust. “We are starting this process now so that we can ensure that that doesn’t happen to our newspapers. If we don’t change how we do business, it’s inevitable that there’ll either be more layoffs or adjustments to what and when we publish, and the frequency at which we publish.”
He noted rising fixed costs beyond the control of the newspaper, such as fuel, postage and printing.
“The best way to be successful is to stay hyper-focused on your community,” Crockett said. “For us, our community is Hancock County, Penobscot County, Mount Desert Island. To stay focused on your community and to stay a part of your community, that’s something that we’re already good at, so it’s a matter of just continuing to push that type of culture for the organization forward.”

title: Who benefits from Susan Collins’ funding?
text:
Republican Sen. Susan Collins boasts about $1.5 billion in federal grant money she’s brought home this term. She shouldn’t be boasting.
Those grants are peanuts compared to the billions we’re losing through cuts that her Trump-controlled party enacted to federal programs, including healthcare and hospitals;
food assistance; affordable housing; infrastructure; renewable energy, environmental
protection and national parks; research, student loans and education. 
Peanuts compared to the billions we pay for tariffs and inflation, peanuts compared to the debt she and Trump Republicans have created in office.
Sen. Collins is part of the problem. Her grants amount to well-publicized handouts diverting attention from her failures of political will and leadership. Beyond that, are Collins’ grants distributed equitably? No.
Voters in the 1st Congressional District should be angry. The senator’s grants go overwhelmingly to Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, keeping her friends and neighbors there happy and beholden.
Collins takes credit for 672 grants valued at about $1.5 billion. CD2 is Susan Collins’ home turf and political base, so CD2 received the majority of the funding. In CD2’s Aroostook County, the figure is $2,900 per capita. In CD1’s Cumberland County — including Portland — the number is $355. Perhaps it matters that Aroostook County gave Collins 68% of the vote the last time she ran six years ago, Cumberland County just 38%.
Sen. Collins’ case that we should reelect her because she’s showered Maine with cash turns out to be bad policy, a sham compared to what we’re losing, and heavily skewed to reward her voters up north. It is time we retire Susan Collins.
David Chase
York

title: Lewiston councilor, also a legislative candidate, scrutinized over allegations from former tenant
text:
Key Takeaways Key Takeaways are written by Maine Trust staff and highlight the most important points of this article so you can get the gist at a glance.
- Lewiston Ward 3 Councilor Scott Harriman was accused of acting inappropriately toward a former female tenant via an interview with a right-wing website.
- Harriman denied the allegations and claimed the website was conspiring with Maine Republicans to sink his campaign for reelection to the state Legislature.
- About a dozen residents came out in protest before the City Council’s meeting Tuesday to call for his resignation.
- The meeting featured a raucous public comment period in which calls for Harriman’s resignation persisted and several came to his defense.
LEWISTON — A group of residents outside City Hall on Tuesday evening called for the resignation of Ward 3 Councilor Scott Harriman, later spilling into council chambers where Harriman’s supporters and detractors each had a say.
Harriman, who is also the state representative for Lewiston House District 94, has been accused of inappropriate contact by a former tenant. The tenant aired her alleged experience with him in an interview with the Maine Wire, a media project of the right-wing Maine Policy Institute.
Multiple attempts by the Sun Journal to contact the tenant to confirm her story have been unsuccessful.
Lewiston police said no complaints have been made directly to the department regarding the allegations.
Harriman, who is running to retain his seat in Augusta, has denied the allegations and said that he was forced to evict the former tenant in 2025.
“I take allegations like these very seriously. None of these allegations are true,” Harriman said in a Facebook post. “The person who made these allegations is a former tenant who I unfortunately had to evict last year due to several significant challenges. This included being a danger to other tenants, not paying rent, damage to the property, and breaking into other tenants’ mailboxes.”
He has also described the allegations as a conspiracy between Maine Republicans and the Maine Wire to sway his district’s election in favor of his opponent in the legislative race, Janet Beaudoin.
Harriman has released multiple pieces of home surveillance footage of Maine Wire employee Jon Fetherston speaking on the phone about Harriman while parked outside his home.
In one video, Harriman claims, Fetherston is speaking with Beaudoin on speakerphone about getting a statement from the Maine Republican Party. Fetherston had reported on the allegations for the Maine Wire.
“If it got picked up by one other news organization, why wouldn’t they?” Fetherston can be heard saying in the video. “Do they want you to win this seat?”
In another video, Harriman claims, Fetherston is speaking with another Maine Wire employee on speakerphone.
“I think the more attention we can bring on this, the better,” the voice said. “I mean, this could legitimately flip the seat. I’m with it.”
Among more than a dozen protesters outside City Hall was resident Ray Toutain. He said Harriman should resign.
“He shouldn’t be on any board, he’s been censured three times,” Toutain said. “Now, if this is true, which I believe it is, it’s time for him to sit down. … This guy, I don’t know why he’s on the board. … It’s one thing after another with him.”
Resident Renee Fortin also cited Harriman’s censures, suggested it is time for the councilor to resign, and remarked that his assignment to the Lewiston School Committee sends a bad message to youths.
“I believe that after a person’s been censured three times and he continues to be shady, I think it’s time for him to be voted out,” Fortin said. “This is not a good look for Lewiston.”
The council meeting’s public comment period ran for about one hour, with repeated disruptions and warnings from Mayor Carl Sheline for quiet in the chambers. Audience members repeatedly traded barbs and one person was escorted out of the building. More called for Harriman’s resignation, some for a full investigation. Several people came to his defense.
Ward 2 Councilor Susan Longchamps addressed the council, detailing her personal relationship with Harriman’s accuser. She said that when she learned of her friend’s experience with Harriman, she kept it in confidence. She also said she was unaware of a June email to councilors, the mayor and police detailing the accuser’s alleged experience.
The email came from Lewiston mayoral candidate Charles Soule and was addressed to former council President David Chittim, police Chief Carley Conley, Sheline, Longchamps and the Sun Journal.
“Had I known these concerns had already been reported, this discussion would have happened months ago,” Longchamps said. “I was not the only person she told, but yet I have somehow, because of the political timing, become part of an accusation as though I created this (and) convinced (her) to come forward. That is simply not true.”
Longchamps said resident Joe Philippon, who she said helped get her elected to the council, and Ward 5 Councilor Chrissy Noble have tried to discredit her in the time since the allegations became public.
“Whatever political or personal disagreement you have with me, do not make (her) allegations about me,” Longchamps said. “This is not about whether Councilor Harriman is guilty or innocent, but the question is whether this council will make sure these serious allegations are looked into professionally, independently and responsibly.”
Philippon said after the council meeting that he has not tried to discredit Longchamps, but raised a specific question about a portion of the Maine Wire’s video in which he said it sounds like someone is prompting Harriman’s accuser.
“I asked Susan directly whether that was her voice and what her involvement in the interview was, and her statement today still doesn’t answer that question,” Philippon said, adding that he never said the allegations should not be taken seriously. “My question about Susan’s involvement in the interview is separate from the merits of (his accuser’s) allegations.”
Resident Lisa Jones criticized the council for remaining silent “in the face of extremely serious accusations” against one of their peers.
“What does it communicate to the unhoused folks you see in your professional capacity when they learn you heard these allegations from their peer and you deemed them not worthy of further investigation?” Jones asked. “Short of a resignation, an independent investigation seems like the only plausible way forward.”
Several who spoke in support of Harriman said he has been responsive to his constituents, has constantly shown up for his community and is committed to the city.
Some, including resident Ifraax Saciid-Ciise Lugoole, suggested the timing of the allegations, weeks before the Nov. 3 elections, is suspect.
“He has always been there for our community and I’ve also seen him be there for the vulnerable in our community,” Lugoole said. “I’m just here to support him and to show that he has a great character. … This is political and very very disgusting and nasty … and I’m very disappointed.”
Resident Zoë Lidstrom said she was concerned that the allegations were manufactured and have become “increasingly volatile and cruel culminating in a blogger staking out Councilor Harriman’s house for hours.”
“To me, that is not acceptable, that is not politics,” Lidstrom said. “If that can happen to a councilman, it can happen to anyone in our city.”
Lewiston teacher Jae Zimmermann noted that October is National Bullying Prevention Month and that school staff are working with students to help them learn how to recognize bullying and how to stand up against it. They said it’s a lesson that a lot of Lewiston needs this month.
“It makes me sad to look around these chambers and hear the whispers, the nasty comments, to see the behavior online and know that despite all our efforts in the schools, the examples of the adults in their lives run contrary to everything we want our students to grow up and learn to be,” Zimmerman said. “It is disappointing to think this is the world my students are growing up into. They deserve better and so do we all.”
After the meeting, Sheline said he believes without more information, the whole matter seems to be a push to derail Harriman’s campaign.
“Absent further concrete details or information from the accuser, this just appears to be a political smear campaign orchestrated by the ever-bumbling Maine Wire with eager help from local Republicans,” Sheline said.
In a Facebook post Wednesday morning, council President Joshua Nagine said he is “deeply disturbed” by the “hatred, anger and fear” in Lewiston’s political discourse.
“We are a community that is attacking itself while being torn apart, and some of our residents are part of the machinery that is doing the work,” he wrote. “It feels bleak.”
“But, I’m a believer in humanity and I’m a believer in my City,” he continued. “Warts and all. So, this morning and every morning going forward, I’m going to recommit myself to being a kinder, more empathetic, and more present person.”

title: Owner of busted Madison cannabis shop, representing himself, demands trial
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA — The owner of a shuttered Madison medical cannabis shop, accused of running his business without a license and then assaulting a court marshal during a courtroom outburst last year, has said from day one he wants a trial.
And if Daniel P. Safranec, 41, does not get one soon, he says a judge must dismiss two criminal cases pending against him.
Superior Court Justice Darcie McElwee appeared unconvinced of that argument Tuesday during a hearing at the Capital Judicial Center, although she did not make a ruling from the bench.
But Safranec, who is representing himself with the assistance of a court-appointed “standby” lawyer, left the hearing with a better sense of when he may get to present his case to a jury.
McElwee set tentative dates for jury selection in November and trial in December for one of the cases. She also set another videoconference hearing later this month for Safranec to argue separate legal reasons he thinks the assault case should be dismissed and that evidence from
Safranec told McElwee, who has been specially assigned the case, he was pleased with how Tuesday’s proceeding went.
Wearing a gray sweater and jeans, Safranec brought with him a large cardboard box of documents and was cordial with both McElwee and Assistant Attorney General John Risler throughout the hearing.
Safranec’s conduct marked a sharp contrast from his initial court appearance in Skowhegan last November, when he repeatedly interrupted the judge and got into a scuffle with the judicial marshal directed to take him into custody. District Court Chief Judge Brent Davis called the outburst the worst behavior he had ever seen in a courtroom and sent Safranec to jail for 14 days for contempt of court.
Much of how Safranec’s case has made its way through the judicial system has also been unusual.
A few weeks after his initial court appearance, the case was transferred from Somerset County to Kennebec County. Then, in March, the district attorney’s office turned the case over to the attorney general’s office to prosecute because two Somerset County assistant district attorneys witnessed the courtroom altercation. Kennebec and Somerset counties are part of the same prosecutorial district, overseen by District Attorney Maeghan Maloney.
Judges also do not usually get special assignments for criminal cases, except for homicides, McElwee said.
Safranec has been representing himself since June after firing his hired attorney, Darrick X. Banda, over a March court filing to reschedule a dispositional conference.
In the filing, Banda wrote Safranec was waiving his speedy trial rights. Safranec said he had told Banda multiple times not to do that.
Safranec is charged with one Class B count of unlawful trafficking in a scheduled drug and one Class B count of marijuana cultivation. He is also charged with one Class C count of assault on an officer and misdemeanor-level counts of refusing to submit to arrest, criminal mischief and violating conditions of release.
He pleaded not guilty Tuesday to all the charges. McElwee said she and other judges who have presided over the case apparently never arraigned him after a Somerset County grand jury returned two separate indictments in January.
His legal saga began in July 2025, when Madison officials took him to court in a civil matter because his shop, Simple Twist Cannabis Co. at 97 Lakewood Road in Madison, lacked state and local licenses to sell medical cannabis.
Safranec’s caregiver registry identification card expired July 9, 2024, and regulators did not grant his renewal applications because there was missing information, Office of Cannabis Policy records show. The office officially denied his renewal application May 30, 2025, and later upheld that decision on appeal.
After a hearing — during which Safranec also represented himself and was, at times, interrupted — District Court Judge Erika Bristol ordered the shop closed until it was licensed. Bristol also ordered Safranec to pay $29,000 in civil penalties and the town’s legal fees of $2,932.09.
A week later, Safranec’s business remained open — he said at that point he had not received Bristol’s order in the mail — and the Somerset County Sheriff’s Office executed search warrants at Simple Twist and his home on East Madison Road in Madison.
Investigators seized more than 2,120 pounds of processed marijuana, 159 flowering marijuana plants, a large amount of marijuana-laced products, more than $1,800 in cash and various records, Sheriff Dale Lancaster said at the time.
Police arrested Safranec, and he posted $10,000 cash bail the next day. In November, he showed up to court in Skowhegan for his initial appearance that ended with the scuffle.
Security footage later obtained showed that Safranec had his hand and wrists across Deputy Judicial Marshal Nick Rotondi’s neck and was applying pressure to keep him from standing up, Detective Jeremy Leal of the Somerset County District Attorney’s Office wrote in an affidavit. Rotondi, who was not seriously injured, later reported it was difficult for him to breathe at that point.
Safranec’s bail was revoked, and he stayed in jail through December 2025, when he posted $50,000 cash bail. Last month, McElwee lowered bail to $10,000 per an agreement between Safranec and Risler, the prosecutor.
Bail conditions include that Safranec not use or possess marijuana.
Safranec said Tuesday that has left him unable to make a living, as he now cannot get a state cannabis license. He told McElwee that Simple Twist opened in 2019 and he has been in the cannabis business since 2003.
Safranec made his speedy trial demand at his initial court appearance and then again a month later in writing, he said. But McElwee asked whether he indicated that demand after being indicted. Safranec said he had not.
“They should’ve been ready (for trial) before they even arrested me,” Safranec said.
McElwee responded saying that’s not the case: Prosecutors have to bring the charges to a grand jury to proceed to trial in felony cases. She asked whether Safranec waived indictment, which he did not.
He said that Banda, his prior attorney, never explained that possibility to him and he would have done so had he known it was an option.
“Truthfully, your honor, Darrick Banda did not talk to me about anything else except keeping his $25,000,” Safranec said.
Risler, the prosecutor, acknowledged Safranec has made it clear he wants a trial as soon as possible and the various steps of the court process can be frustrating for criminal defendants.
But the courts often prioritize cases involving defendants held in custody, Risler said, and the state has never requested a continuance in Safranec’s proceedings.
“As soon as we were able to get on a trial docket, to my knowledge, that’s what we did,” Risler said. “There has been no willful action of the state to delay his trial.”

title: Older voters make the difference in Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
by Carl Bucciantini
AARP Maine Volunteer Congressional Liaison
Maine’s population is the oldest in the nation and Mainers age 50 and above turn out to vote in greater numbers than any other age range. In the 2024 general election there were 494,000 Mainers over the age of 50. 59.3% of those Mainers voted. AARP’s national polling over several years shows that voters 50 years and older turn out at the highest rate of any age group. This pattern holds especially true in states like Maine with older populations, where issues like Social Security, caregiving, long-term care and utility costs shape voter priorities.
Maine’s rural communities dominate the landscape and, with its accompanying slow population growth means that the political weight of older residents is proportionally greater. Younger populations are smaller, more mobile, and less likely to vote consistently. Meanwhile, Mainers like myself tend to have deeper community ties, higher rates of homeownership, and long-standing voting habits; all factors that correlate strongly with turnout.
For millions of Americans, especially those over 50, Social Security is the difference between security and uncertainty. It is the foundation that allows retirees to stay in their homes, afford medications, and maintain independence. After paying into the system for a lifetime, older voters expect leaders to safeguard it. When candidates speak vaguely about “reforms,” older voters hear potential cuts. When leaders promise to “protect” Social Security, they expect specifics. This demographic understands the stakes, and they vote accordingly.
Caregiving is an issue that rarely makes headlines, but shapes daily life for countless families. Many voters over 50 are caring for aging parents, spouses, or relatives while also supporting adult children or grandchildren. They are the quiet engine of America’s care economy, providing unpaid labor that saves the nation billions of dollars each year. Yet they often do so with little support, navigating a maze of long‑term care costs, limited home‑care options, and policies that lag behind the realities of modern family life. When older voters look for leadership, they look for someone who understands that caregiving is not a private burden, it is a public challenge that demands public solutions.
Utility costs are another issue that hits especially hard in rural states like Maine. Electricity, heating fuel, water, and broadband are not luxuries; they are necessities. But for older Mainers living on fixed incomes, rising utility bills can quickly become unmanageable. In some communities, unreliable service or high costs force difficult decisions about whether people can safely remain in their homes. Older voters want leaders who recognize that affordability and reliability are inseparable from quality of life. They want policies that keep essential services within reach.
Maine’s voters age 50 and older are stretched to the limit. They want to see politicians address their day-to-day challenges like caring for their loved ones, protecting their hard-earned Social Security and controlling rising utility costs. Older voters in Maine have power and they are not shy about making their wishes known at the ballot box. Voters 50-plus decide elections.
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!

title: Troy Jackson details personal finances in new disclosure
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson‘s primary source of income over the last two years came from two international unions based in Maryland, according to a personal financial disclosure filed this week.
Since the beginning of last year, Jackson received $90,000 from the International Association of Machinists and $48,000 from the International Union of Painters and Allied Trades for general consulting work.
Jackson’s campaign said the candidate provided consulting and organizing help for various national and local issues. Jackson is no longer providing those services, the campaign said.
“Troy’s financial disclosure reflects a lifetime of working for a paycheck,” a spokesperson said in a written statement. “He’s a logger and union member who understands what it means to worry about making ends meet — and he would bring that experience to a Senate dominated by millionaires. Susan Collins has spent nearly 30 years in Washington. Troy has spent his life fighting for people who work for a living.”
Jackson’s disclosure was filed late Monday after he received a 55-day extension. It’s the first detailed look the candidate has provided into his personal finances.
Sen. Susan Collins‘ campaign accused Jackson of not being transparent about his finances, and of taking “dark money” and corporate PAC money as Maine Senate president, despite vows to refuse that money during his U.S. Senate campaign.
“As Senate president, he was paid by three unions and a dark money group,” Collins spokesperson Blake Kernen said in a written statement. “And rather than file his disclosure on time in August, he took the latest extension possible and filed at 9:54 p.m. on the final day.”
In 2025, Jackson reported payments totaling $5,100 from the Eastern Maine Labor Council and $4,800 from Food and Medicine, a 501 (c)(4) social and economic justice group. He served as an organizer for both Brewer-based groups, his disclosure shows.
Jackson is leaning heavily on his working-class background, including his prior work as a logger, in his race against Collins, the Republican incumbent. But his disclosure does not list any income from logging.
His campaign said Jackson worked as a logger for 15 years before joining the state Legislature in 2002, at which point he continued logging intermittently.
Jackson also listed his construction and land management firm, Jackson Associates, on the paperwork. He did not list any assets for that firm, but he did report that some of his consulting income went to his company.
It’s unclear exactly how much Jackson or Collins’ total assets are worth, since they are only required to disclose minimums and ranges on the Senate financial forms.
Jackson disclosed between $147,000 and $430,000 in assets, including between $100,000 and $250,000 in state retirement benefits from his partner.
Yet Jackson’s earnings and assets pale in comparison to Collins, who earns at least $174,000 a year as a senator and receives additional income through her husband, Tom Daffron. The couple has an estimated net worth of $7.1 million and owns between $4.2 million and $10 million in assets, according to Congressstock.com.
Collins’ personal holdings include mutual funds and bank deposits. Daffron has a robust portfolio of stocks, bonds and government securities.
Jackson reported commercial real estate in Allagash owned by his longtime partner as an asset valued between $15,000 and $50,000. But he did not report any income from that property.

title: Shifting mindset — ‘Caregiving is the burden; your loved one is the blessing’
text:
(Aging Untold) — For many caregivers, social media has become a lifeline — a place to share their stories and find community. Ty Lewis is one of them.
She’s a certified dementia practitioner and content creator who cares for her mother, Gertrude, who is in the late stages of Alzheimer’s.
Lewis shares a powerful perspective shift that separates the true burden of caregiving from the loved one receiving the care.
“We have to shift our perspective”
Lewis says the mindset reframe starts with understanding what “burden” actually means.
She says it’s easy for caregivers to lose sight of that distinction on hard days.
“I think that is what a lot of us miss on this journey — that yes, it is hard. Yes, I am picking it up and carrying my cross, but also the cross is leading me somewhere special,” Lewis said. “Because our loved one depends on us so much, we have to be the ones to allow them to lean on us and help them carry that load. So, because they’re unable to do everything, we are who they need us to be. For us, caregiving is the burden. But our loved one is the blessing.”
Why some caregivers find joy — and others don’t
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said that reframing can change a caregiver’s entire outlook.
“That is a powerful perspective, and that just kind of changes your whole mood,” Ambrose said. “I think that’s the difference between people that find joy in being a caregiver versus the ones that don’t. They recognize what an honor it is, and that you do get unexpected gifts and blessings.”
See our full interview with Ty Lewis
The newborn comparison
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck said she’s taught this distinction for years, and she compares it to how people respond to a new baby.
“That’s the basis of my teaching, and it always has been — that the person is not the burden, work is. The definition of burden is that it’s work,” Cradduck said. “When you come home with a brand-new baby, how many people look at a newborn and go, ‘Man, you’re a burden’? There’s a lot of work that goes along with having a brand-new baby — there’s a ton of work — but you never impart that over on the child. You see the workload is the burden.”
She said that same logic gets lost when it comes to caring for aging loved ones.
“When we go to the aged community, we oftentimes get them confused. We hear so many of our aged community say, ‘I don’t want to be a burden.’ Honey, you can’t be a burden,” Cradduck said.
Holding both the burden and the blessing
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said caregivers don’t have to choose between the two realities — both can be true at once, drawing on her own experience caring for her father.
“I like that she said there’s a burden and there’s a blessing, that you can carry both of those things at the same time,” O’Rourke said. “I know when I was looking out for my dad with the rest of the family, there were days when I was so exhausted, I felt burdened. But then I would have times with him that I felt, ‘Oh, I’m so happy he’s with me, and I’m getting all these connections with him.’”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said she sees that same duality reflected in both ends of caregiving, from newborns to aging parents.
“I like both analogies — the newborn baby and then the elder person with whatever ailments they have. It really is the perspective,” Rogers said. “When you can shift your perspective to really zone in on the blessing — there’s a lot of people who would love to have their father or their mother, even if they have the late stages of Alzheimer’s, but they would physically be present here. And that’s the blessing.”
Grief versus joy in the caregiving role
Cradduck said the real difference between caring for a newborn and caring for an aging loved one comes down to emotional framing, not workload.
“With the newborn child, the workload is tough and you’re exhausted. There’s not a brand-new mother or father out there that aren’t exhausted, they’re tired — but they’re not imparting that over to the child, because you see that child with joy. You see that child with hope,” she said.
On the other hand, when you are caring for an older adult, you are also grieving, Cradduck said.
“When you’re over here in your caregiving, you’re grieving. That’s what changes and allows the perspective to put the burden on the person. ... When we see the person is still a human, always — the workload is the burden — then we can always see the blessing in what we’re doing. That’s what we’ve got to get back to.”
That mindset applies no matter which side of caregiving someone is on, Rogers and Ambrose added.
“I like the perspective of looking at — we’re going to be whatever they need us to be, whether that’s a child or the older person,” Rogers said.
“You’re just going to make your burden worse if you don’t make that mindset shift. Be open to the blessings that come out of it, because they are unexpected, and they are beautiful sometimes,” Ambrose said.
Key takeaways
- The workload is the burden — not the person. Ty Lewis says reframing caregiving starts with separating the tasks and stress of caregiving from the person receiving care.
- Burden and blessing can coexist. Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said caregivers don’t have to pick one feeling — exhaustion and gratitude can show up on the same day.
- The newborn comparison reveals a double standard. Parents absorb the exhaustion of caring for a baby without blaming the child. Gerontologist Sam Cradduck says aging loved ones deserve that same grace.
- A mindset shift can change a caregiver’s whole outlook. Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers who recognize caregiving as an honor are more likely to experience joy rather than only exhaustion.
- Being “who they need us to be” is a form of leadership. Lewis describes caregiving as servant leadership — stepping in for a loved one who can no longer do everything on their own.

title: Argentina bids Messi farewell in final national team match, ending an era
text:
BUENOS AIRES (AP) — Argentina is confronting a once-unimaginable reality: a national team without soccer great Lionel Messi.
On Tuesday, 39-year-old Messi bid farewell to international soccer after 21 years, 126 goals, two Copa América titles and a World Cup championship, scoring a penalty and setting up Argentina’s other two goals for a 3-0 victory over Benin. What was otherwise an unremarkable friendly against the West African nation became a moment that this soccer-crazed country had long dreaded.
“It feels like an era is ending, knowing he won’t play for the national team anymore,” said Valentino Ruso, 17, who was heading to a friend’s house in Buenos Aires to watch the game. “I’m sad. I think everyone is upset today. He will be missed.”
Argentines had an intense, often unforgiving relationship with the shy boy who left his hometown of Rosario at 13 for the youth academy of Spanish club Barcelona. As he grew into a global icon of near-mythical stature, his compatriots adored and abused him, sometimes questioning his commitment to his home country and accusing him of indifference to it.
But by the time he ended his dazzling international career, his devotion to Argentina was no longer in question. Nor was Argentina’s devotion to its most famous export, whose triumphs reminded the country of its capacity for greatness through years of political and economic instability.
“Argentines often say, ‘Thank God I was born at a time when I could experience the miracle of watching Messi play,’” said Andrés Rabinovich, a University of Chicago scholar who has researched soccer’s role in Argentine culture. “It’s hard living in Argentina. Soccer is often one of the few things that offers you some respite, some joy.”
For years, Argentines had debated when and how Messi should leave the world stage. His Aug. 31 announcement that he’d be retiring from the national team, weeks after Argentina’s loss to Spain in the World Cup final, prompted an outpouring of gratitude and grief — even as Messi will continue to light up Major League Soccer with Inter Miami.
“I don’t know if there has ever been a love story between a player and a nation as great as the one you built,” his teammate Rodrigo De Paul wrote on Instagram.
The Argentine soccer federation turned Tuesday’s game — Messi’s 208th — into a national farewell billed as “the last tango.” More than 85,000 tickets to Buenos Aires’ largest stadium sold out in 90 minutes, seats that were originally priced around $60-$300 later fetching over $2,500 on resale sites. Players from Argentina’s 1978, 1986 and 2022 World Cup-winning squads returned to see him off.
After the final whistle, Messi’s eyes glistened as his teammates gathered around him, applauding. A rumbling chorus of “Olé, olé, olé, olé, Messi, Messi” rose from the stands as tens of thousands of fans jumped, sang and bowed toward him as if in worship. A banner at midfield proclaimed him the “Eternal Captain.”
“The truth is, I’m talking more than I ever have. I don’t want to leave here, I don’t want to leave this field,” Messi told the crowd, which roared as if he had scored. “I just want to tell you that I love you, I’m going to miss you, and I’m grateful to God to be Argentine.”
Winning over his own
During the 2000s and 2010s, Messi amassed trophies with his club and won diehard fans from Barcelona to Bangladesh. Yet a major championship for his own country eluded him.
Where the world saw a supernatural talent, some at home saw an outsider who had never played professionally in Argentina and seemed to buckle under the weight of their expectations. Argentine crowds chanted “Diego, Diego,” invoking Diego Maradona, the larger-than-life hero of Argentina’s 1986 World Cup victory, and reminding Messi of a standard he had yet to meet. Messi’s quiet reserve, so at odds with Maradona’s defiant swagger, fueled doubts about his patriotism.
After Argentina lost a third consecutive final in 2016, Messi briefly quit the national team.
“There’s some resentment by the people that stay in Argentina for those who leave, this sense of, ‘They think they’re better than us,’” said Rabinovich, adding that he identifies with Messi as a fellow teenage migrant. Rabinovich said he moved to Canada during Argentina’s 2001 economic crisis, around the time Messi left for Europe. “The old-school Argentines would say, ‘Diego is the Argentine. Messi is soft, a little Spanish boy.’”
The turning point came in 2021, when Argentina beat Brazil to win the Copa América, South America’s championship, for the first time in 28 years. Messi collapsed to the turf as his teammates, delirious, ran to hug him. The player long accused of feeling too little could not stop sobbing.
“Winning clearly disarmed his critics. That’s how soccer works in Argentina,” said Diego Murzi, a sports sociologist at Conicet, Argentina’s national scientific research council. “Criticism of things off the field goes hand in hand with defeats on it.”
The World Cup victory the following year in Qatar sealed his place as a national hero. Messi had delivered the one prize that had eluded him, and millions of Argentines poured into the streets in collective ecstasy, his name in their chants and his No. 10 on their backs.
“I’ll never forget it. I’d never experienced anything like that, being out there with everyone, celebrating together,” said Antonia Correa, 70, a kiosk owner, recalling that day as she waited for a bus in Buenos Aires on Tuesday. “We saw that he wasn’t just an extraordinary player, but an excellent human being.”
In recent weeks, newspapers have hummed with nostalgic tributes and murals celebrating Messi have sprung up across the country. La Nación, a leading Argentine daily, released “Immortal,” a documentary chronicling his final World Cup run, and published a 196-page special edition devoted to his career. Since June, a 26-meter (85-foot) statue of Messi kneeling with the World Cup trophy has towered over passing motorists in Patagonia. On Tuesday, Buenos Aires’ landmark Obelisk glowed sky blue and white, the colors of the national flag, while news sites live-blogged every minute of the Benin friendly as if it were a World Cup final.
A jersey without an heir
Across Argentina, fans who grew up watching Messi as their parents watched Maradona have covered their skin with tattooed tributes to the soccer great, portraits of him kissing the World Cup trophy. It was easy to believe the world’s greatest player would always be one of their own.
“I don’t think we’ll have somebody like him again, somebody with that sort of enduring power,” said Pablo Brescia, a University of South Florida professor who writes about Argentine culture and soccer. “Like Maradona, he’ll be unique — a figure that can’t be repeated.”
Messi’s contract with Inter Miami runs through the 2028 season. But the ritual of watching him carry Argentina’s hopes and anxieties into every match is over.
“Watching Messi play, you felt anything could happen,” Murzi said.
When Tuesday’s match finally ended, the crowd remained, their ovation roaring through the stadium. Messi took a final lap, a tiny figure beneath the lights, soaking it in. At the tunnel, he paused to lift his arms toward his fans one last time. Then he was gone.

title: Landry/French gains infrastructure expertise with acquisition of T Buck Construction
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Scarborough-based Landry/French Construction is expanding its range of services with the acquisition of T Buck Construction, a contractor specializing in bridge and water and wastewater facilities construction.
The new partnership gives Landry/French an established infrastructure operation and experienced team, expanding its market capabilities and creating additional opportunities throughout Maine and northern New England.
The Turner, Androscoggin County-based firm, founded by Terry Buck in 1989, will continue operating as T Buck Construction, a Landry/French company. It will maintain the staff while gaining access to Landry/French’s broader leadership, financial, technology and operational resources.
“T Buck has built an outstanding reputation over decades, with tremendous expertise and, most importantly, a talented team of people,” said Kevin French, chairman and CEO of Landry/French. “Our goal is to build on what they have created, not change it.”
“T Buck has tremendous growth potential, and we are excited to invest in that potential,” French added. “We see an opportunity to build on the company’s strong foundation and support its continued growth.”
Richard Wentworth, president of T Buck Construction, said “This is a very positive move for T Buck and our employee-owners,” said Wentworth. “By joining Landry/French, we gain additional resources and support that will help us build on Terry’s legacy while positioning our people and our company for the next generation.”
Landry/French was founded in Maine in 2010 as a general contractor and construction management company. Over the past few years, the firm has expanded operations into Florida, with the acquisition of Melbourne-based M.H. Williams Construction Group and with the opening of a Landry/French office in St. Petersburg.
Both Landry/French and T Buck are 100% employee-owned companies.

title: Parents Navigate Communication Gap As Bangor School Clears Threat On Garland Street
text:
It was a nerve-wracking morning for parents who have kids that attend the William S. Cohen School in Bangor.
Word began to circulated via social media around 11:30 AM that a local school was being evacuated due to a threat. This was confirmed just before noon by the Bangor School District, when they alerted parents that students from the school had been moved from the school and that authorities were on- hand conducting an investigation.
Parents were notified that all the children had been taken from the Cohen School on Garland Street to the safety of a nearby facility, while authorities swept the school space for any dangers.
Raymond Phinney, spokesperson for the Bangor School Department says authorities ultimately deemed the threat to be a hoax, and when the school was deemed safe, were the students brought back. Their parents also had the option to pick them up directly.
"After completing their evaluation, first responders determined there was no credible threat and confirmed that the building was safe for students and staff to return...
The well-being of students remains the highest priority. School counselors, teachers, and administrators will be available to provide support to any student who would like to discuss today's events. The Bangor School Department appreciates the continued support and understanding of families as we work together to maintain a safe and supportive learning environment for all students."
Many parents took to social media to voice their concerns and frustrations with Maine's new "Bell-to-Bell Personal Electronic Device Policy", or as many call it school cell phone ban, stating that they couldn't reach their children and did not have details as to what was happening.
Read More: Bangor Schools Explain New Cell Phone Rules By Grade Level
Others responded by saying they were relieved the kids didn't have their phones, as the possibility of panic that would ensue from the misinformation disseminated by unverified or undearage sources was of real concern.
Mike Missbrenner, Principal of the William S. Cohen School, expressed his appreciation for the students and the staff for doing an exceptional job under intense circumstances Wednesday.
Read More: How A Former Bangor Tire Shop Is Becoming A Music Studio
"We are incredibly proud of our students for the way they responded during a challenging situation. Their cooperation, patience, and resilience were
outstanding. I also want to thank our faculty and staff for their professionalism in following emergency procedures and supporting our students throughout the day."
Throughout the day, school officials updated parents via communication avenues like email, text and the Bangor app, when they had confirmed information to share, or instructions to give.
