title: Don’t let Elon Musk buy Maine’s vote
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Thom Moore writes and consults in Scarborough. He is a member of Third Act.
The world’s richest person is funding Sen. Susan Collins’ campaign.
This is part of the GOP’s decades-long effort to make our government work for its wealthiest citizens. As Graham Platner noted, and Troy Jackson also appreciates, the wealthy mean to own everything and rent it to the rest of us. They already rent us the money to run our government, charging us a trillion dollars a year in interest. They should instead pay a fair share of the bills, about 24% of our GDP, especially those who made their money within our economy.
When we are paid less than we are worth, when staple prices are raised endlessly out of greed or because of unproductive wars and tariffs, when resulting inflation raises interest rates, money trickles upward.
Even when taxes are cut, deficits increase, benefits decrease and interest is paid by us to those who finance the debt, padding their estates at low risk. Those estates steadily appreciate in value from the upward trickling, and that unrealized income escapes taxation as it is passed to heirs by our wealthiest, most senior citizens.
But we must resist any impulse to make age an issue in this election, nor should we exploit, for political purposes, Sen. Collins’ exceptional seniority and respect among the most corporate-sponsored members of the U.S. Senate. She was influential in bringing defense work to Maine, but she also voted for the reduction of medical care and research support for working-class Mainers. Troy Jackson brings a fresh perspective on the kinds of development that create opportunities to keep Maine “the way life should be.”
We cannot ignore the current escalation in prices, driven by corporate profits, wars, tariffs and wasteful ego projects. Sen. Collins has done nothing to stop this. Maine’s domination by corporate utilities has caused our power costs to be among the highest in the nation. Accusations that renewable energy raises our costs are lies. Power sources get dialed back when supply exceeds demand, namely the most expensive ones, the gas plants. Who pays to oppose the transition to sustainable energy? The fuel industry and power utilities, that’s who.
Sen. Collins and the GOP oppose working-class collective bargaining and a fair minimum wage. Troy Jackson defends the right of employees to organize and assert their economic value. Maine has more than its fair share of rural poverty and hardship. The remedy for that is new businesses offering good jobs that pay a living wage. Troy Jackson understands that workers must often organize to win fair wages and working conditions from larger businesses.
Sen. Collins supported the obscene increase in the economic power of ICE. It is used to infiltrate our communities in the name of ferreting out, and in some cases assassinating, immigrants, whether properly documented or not. This is an intrusion into state and local affairs that Troy Jackson will not tolerate.
Sen. Collins supports the GOP belief that healthcare is a corporate profit center that is only for those who can afford it. They believe that profits should flow from prices determined by demand, rather than reflecting what is affordable. They do not think that the government should pay any costs. Healthcare is a trivial expense for the ultra-rich, but they want to limit what kinds of medical care everyone else can receive, including personal reproduction and body choices. Troy Jackson opposes these intrusions into privacy matters and accepts government responsibility to mitigate hardships where practical.
The government money that Sen. Collins has brought to Maine would continue to favor her corporate donors, at the expense of working-class Mainers. Troy Jackson would help working-class Mainers receive a fair share of the wealth that their work produces, in the form of higher wages and reduced expenses.

title: Driving simulator helps spinal cord injury patients regain independence
text:
Driving simulator helps spinal cord injury patients regain independence
A new driving simulator in Baltimore is helping spinal cord injury patients regain independence by learning adaptive driving techniques.
Jean Hudson, a patient at the Kennedy Krieger Institute, was diagnosed with transverse myelitis nearly 10 years ago. It's a rare neurological disorder caused by inflammation in the spinal cord. After losing feeling in her legs, she was hospitalized and underwent therapy to learn how to walk again. She credits the institute with helping her make further progress in her recovery.
"This is where they actually got me further than where I was at. I was in therapy, and now, I'm ready to drive," Hudson said.
Hudson, who used to drive regularly, said giving up her independence and relying on others was difficult. When she saw the driving simulator, she immediately expressed interest.
"I asked the therapist, I said, 'Y'all got a driving machine?' And she said, 'Yes.' I said, 'I want to learn how to drive,'" Hudson said.
Jenna Shipley, an occupational therapist at Kennedy Krieger Institute, said many patients were unaware of driver rehabilitation programs that use adaptive equipment to help them regain their licenses.
"I was looking at how we could help," Shipley said.
Shipley researched programs and equipment, discovering that the driving simulator costs around $90,000. She applied for a grant, which was funded by the Samuel and Margaret Gorn Foundation.
"What I find is that patients are nervous – going back to driving a different way using the hand controls, or they're not confident in their abilities. They don't think they're going to be able to do it, so this device is really nice to show them what they're capable of doing," Shipley said.
The simulator arrived in July, and Shipley has since worked with about 10 patients, focusing on strength and coordination as they learn to use hand controls or a left pedal. Hudson has completed approximately 12 sessions.
"It was great. The first two, I ran into the pole, and the only reason why is cause I was getting used to using the hand controls," Hudson said.
Hudson described the International Center for Spinal Cord Injury as a place that offers hope to patients.

title: The Best New Movies to Watch at Home This Weekend
text:
The Best New Movies You Can Watch at Home This Weekend
New movies are coming to streaming this week and every week, at a faster pace than ever before. As always, ScreenCrush has your back, with a weekly guide to the latest releases on streaming (and digital rental or purchse) that deserve your attention. Sit back, relax, and check out what’s coming to a TV or computer (or, sigh, a phone) near you.
Then you’ve got all weekend to watch up with these titles. The theater is still the best, of course, but some weekends you just can’t muster the energy to get off the couch and haul yourself to the multiplex.
New Movies Streaming This Week and Weekend
This week you can swing into a brand new day with Spider-Man, check out a brand new Netflix movie starring and directed by Ben Affleck, or see Steven Spielberg’s latest sci-fi film about extraterrestrial life in the universe.
If these titles don’t do it for you, you can also check out some other recent streaming releases here. Or just keep scrolling, and see the new movies you can stream or rent on digital at home this weekend.
Spider-Man: Brand New Day
The biggest movie of 2026 to date makes its debut on premium VOD. Tom Holland’s fourth Spider-Man adventure sees the friendly neighborhood web-slinger struggling with loneliness in a world where no one — including his former best friends — knows he exists. Brand New Day also features appearances from Jon Bernthal’s Punisher, Mark Ruffalo’s Hulk, and a mystery villain that is such a big deal that Marvel hid their identity from view right up until the film’s release in theaters.

Steven Spielberg’s career-long fascination with alien life may have reached its conclusion with this sci-fi chase movie about a meteorologist (Emily Blunt) and a hacker (Josh O’Connor) united by a mysterious past and an equally mysterious government agent (a surprisingly terrifying Colin Firth) who will stop at nothing to capture them. The Housemaid

The film’s got plenty of twists, including the fact that it was directed by Paul Feig, who got his start creating comedy shows like Freaks & Geeks and then directed Bridesmaids and a bunch of other Melissa McCarthy films, but has gradually shifted toward darker material with stuff like this and A Simple Favor.
Where to watch The Housemaid: HBO Max, starting on 10/9.

The life and career (and secret passions) of actor and comedian Martin Mull are the subject of this Netflix documentary co-directed by the late, great comic Bob Saget.
Where to watch Who Is Martin Mull?: Netflix.

title: Aroostook man charged with sex crimes against an 8-year-old is out on bail
text:
An Amity man remains free on $2,500 cash bail after being charged with multiple child sexual assault counts.
Kevin Ledger, 39, was arrested and charged on Sept. 29 by Maine State Police with three felonies and two misdemeanors for sexually related acts against two young girls on Sept. 5 in Aroostook County.
In the first felony count, Ledger was charged with attempted gross sexual assault, a Class A felony. Police said Ledger engaged in conduct that “in fact constituted a substantial step toward its commission and did attempt to engage in a sexual act with an 8-year-old child.”
Because it was an attempt of a Class A crime, Ledger was charged with a Class B felony for the alleged act.
In count two, Ledger allegedly attempted unlawful sexual contact, a Class C crime, by attempting to engage in a sex act with a 9-year-old child, according to court records.
The third count against Ledger – exposing his genitals to a 9-year-old child and making the child expose her genitals to him with the purpose of gratifying a sexual desire, is a Class C crime.
Unlawful sexual touching and assault, recklessly causing bodily injury, both misdemeanors, were committed against an 8-year-old child, police said in the arrest affidavit.
If convicted, Ledger faces up to 22 years in prison and $34,000 in fines.
In Maine, Class B crimes carry a maximum penalty of up to 10 years in prison and a fine up to $20,000, Class C crimes carry a maximum penalty of up to 5 years in prison and a fine up to $5,000, and Class D crimes are misdemeanors carrying a maximum penalty of up to 364 days in jail and a fine up to $2,000.
The conditions of Ledger’s release prohibit direct or indirect contact with the two children and an 8 p.m. to 5 a.m. curfew.
His first hearing is slated in Aroostook County Court in Houlton at 1 p.m. on Jan. 5 before Judge Rob Langner.

title: Three Shutouts, 18 Wisdom Goals Highlight Tuesday County Soccer
text:

Shutouts were the story of the day Tuesday as several Aroostook County girls soccer teams turned in impressive defensive performances.
Presque Isle, Katahdin and Central Aroostook each earned 4-0 victories, while Wisdom piled up 12 goals in another shutout win. On the boys side, Katahdin picked up another close victory over Ashland, while Wisdom also kept a clean sheet.

Presque Isle put together a complete performance on the road, shutting out Orono 4-0.

title: Scattered Showers But Not A Washout Thursday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Warm front crossing the region tonight will bring the chance for scattered showers mostly in the north that will work their way closer to the coast Thursday morning. Overnight lows will be much warmer, ranging from the mid 40s to low 50s.
Thursday: AM showers, afternoon storm chance
Scattered showers are possible Thursday morning, especially along the coast and Downeast. Shower chances ease by midday, with some clearing. Highs will range from the upper 50s in the north to the 60s for most, with a few low 70s in southern Maine.
A cold front moving west to east Thursday afternoon could bring pop-up showers and an isolated thunderstorm. The freezing level will be relatively low, so any storm that develops could produce very small hail.
Rainfall totals will remain light and provide little to no relief from drought conditions. A few spots could receive up to 0.5 inch.
Friday and Saturday: Drier, brighter and breezy
Mostly sunny skies are expected, with highs in the 50s and low 60s. Northwest winds will continue, with gusts up to 25 mph.
Sunday: Pick of the weekend
Sunday looks warmer and less windy, with highs in the upper 50s to low and mid 60s.
Next week: Watching rain chances
The remnants of Tropical Storm Isaias will be worth watching Monday, as it could graze the region and bring some showers.
An area of low pressure could also bring beneficial rainfall Tuesday and Wednesday; the forecast will depend on its track.
First Alert 7-Day Forecast
TONIGHT: Increasing clouds with scattered showers in the north. Lows will range from the mid 40s to the low 50s. SSW wind 5-15 mph.
THURSDAY: Mostly cloudy with scattered showers and isolated storms possible. Highs in the 50s, 60s, and a few low 70s. WSW wind 10-20 mph.
FRIDAY: Mostly sunny with highs in the 50s and low 60s. NW wind will gust to 25 mph.
SATURDAY: Mostly sunny with highs in the 50s. NW wind will gust to 25 mph.
SUNDAY: Partly cloudy with highs in the 60s.
MONDAY: Mostly cloudy with showers possible. Highs in the 60s.
TUESDAY: Rain possible. Highs in the 50s and low 60s.

title: Even retirees deserve a day off once in a while
text:
Vicki Sullivan of Portland is a retired English instructor and writing tutor.
Occasionally, when I was teaching, I would enter a classroom and be greeted by a student who would ask me, “Can we do nothing today?”
I’d reply sarcastically, “No work, no pay,” which invariably got the answer, “We’re not getting paid; we’re paying.” Or I might say, “That’s what you do every day,” to which the response would be a “Ha, ha” or an extended fake laugh.
But for those of us who have worked hard all our lives, that question can make you wonder.
For some days I wake up and ask myself, “Can I do nothing today?” And maybe I’m really asking myself for permission.
We, offspring of Depression Era parents, had a strong work ethic instilled in us. Our parents worked hard for their success and expected us to do the same. My mother frowned upon a sick day from school and personal days off from work were unheard of then.
I can hear my father saying, “Keep on digging” to anyone who might listen!
And a coach who coached at the University of Delaware with my father told his football players who complained about practicing on a holiday, “On Labor Day you labor.”
Doing nothing or having nothing to do was not looked upon favorably. Therefore, many of us who have retired expect ourselves to keep busy and have a purpose.
A friend of my father gave my father advice when he was going to retire. “Plan every day,” he suggested. My father didn’t and he found retirement a difficult transition.
Although I’m still trying to adjust to retirement three years later, I do plan every day. I make a to- do list as if I have a corporate job and cross off my completed tasks. Granted, they might be small items — mailing something or emptying the dishwasher — but at least I have accomplished something.
My friend Michael, a retired antiques shop owner, and I often text back and forth, discussing how productive we have been that day — his day spent cleaning out and organizing the many items in his garage and mine downsizing holiday items and “death cleaning.”
A former co-worker of mine, who had retired from the police department, had a full-time teaching job, a part-time consulting job and other short-term projects in his field. I remember laughingly commenting to him once, “You run around as if the devil were after you.”
He replied, “I don’t like to be idle.”
My friend Gladys,now deceased, lived to be 98. Before her death she was living independently, still keeping house and cooking, and driving. We laughed over an incident many times. At 97,at a doctor’s appointment, she told her physician that she didn’t seem to have much ambition. And her physician replied, “Why do you need to be ambitious at 97?” She was so used to keeping busy.
The only time most of us gave ourselves permission to do nothing was during COVID-19 when we really couldn’t do much of anything. I wasn’t working, as I was laid off during the spring semester when COVID hit.
However, of course, doing nothing has different meanings for different people.
But, whatever your definition, to those of us who’ve worked hard and deserve a day off, I say, “Let’s do nothing today.”

title: Happy birthday, ‘Arthur’: Beloved children’s TV show first aired 30 years ago
text:
Happy birthday, ‘Arthur’: Beloved children’s TV show first aired 30 years ago
PBS Kids’ beloved aardvark Arthur turns 30 Wednesday, marking three decades since the animated series made its television debut on Oct. 7, 1996.
The first episode, “Arthur’s Eyes,” introduced viewers to Arthur Read and his friends in Elwood City.
Based on Marc Brown’s children’s books, the show became a fixture of public television, following the characters through school, family life and everyday challenges.
Across its 25-season run, Arthur explored topics including friendship, learning and growing up.
PBS announced the show would conclude with its 25th season in 2022, but it did not give a specific public reason for ending the series.
The final episode, “All Grown Up,” offered a glimpse of the characters as adults, with Arthur pursuing his dream of becoming a graphic novelist.
Though the television series wrapped, PBS said the characters would remain available to viewers through reruns and new digital content.

title: REVIEW POTPOURRI: Movies, Maine and musical legends
text:
Mob Land
A 2023 film, Mob Land, revolves around a small Southern town festering with drug addiction and families scraping by. A mechanic, Shelby, and his brother-in-law, Trey, rob a local pill mill , very mistakenly thinking it would be a piece of cake.
Of course, all hell breaks loose when the so-called Dixie Mafia sends a vicious enforcer, Clayton Minor, using whatever methods he favors to punish the perpetrators.
Stephen Dorff’s portrayal of Minor was for me the main attraction in the range of nuanced detail he brought to his characterization of a mostly evil individual (No spoilers on his unexpected moments of redemption.).
However, as Clayton is wandering out and about the community, whether settling his bill with a waitress at the local diner or paying the owner of a convenience store for his gas, he asks the same question with faintly ominous eye contact – “What do you want to be when you grow up?”
Towards the end , he revisits the diner and asks the question again of the waitress only to have her ask him what he wants to be. His answer – “Quiet!”
The cinematography of the barely breathing sun-baked landscape is captivatingly harrowing.
Ashley Benson’s performance as Shelby’s wife Caroline was also quite good but Shiloh Fernandez’s Shelby and Kevin Dillon’s Trey were much too overblown while the very elderly looking John Travolta sleep-walked his way through the film as the very weary Sheriff.
PS: For a number of years, Travolta has been a summer resident on Islesboro.
Ben Ames Williams
Searsmont summer resident Ben Ames Williams (1889-1953) wrote quantities of novels and short stories, more often than not set in Maine.
I first heard about his 1941 novel The Strange Woman during the early winter of 1973, when I was student teaching sophomore English courses at Westbrook High School, from my supervising teacher, the late John Ackermann, who was a huge fan of this book.
Its setting is Bangor of from 1812 to about 1865, the city then considered, according to an observer, “one of the wildest, toughest towns in the country….More fortunes were made in Bangor than in any other town in the United States.”
The novel centers around Jenny Hager, a woman who seems the embodiment of elegance, beauty, intelligence, integrity but proves to be a sociopath; it’s divided into seven sizable chapters, each dealing with a man whose life is impacted by her behavior.
Bangor’s wild tough dog eat dog years, and one of the most colorful examples of Ames’s writing , is most exemplified in the following example of the large number of businesses that provided food, drink and feminine companionship to those seeking to satisfy such needs:
“Ma Hogan ruled her customers – sailors from the vessels at anchor here or lumbermen just in from the river or the woods – with a fist as heavy as a man’s; and for allies she had two husky individuals who did not scruple to use clubs when clubs were needed. Unruly men were apt to find themselves quickly and decisively spilled out of a door on the water side of the wharf and they usually emerged from the river with their belligerent ideas effectually cooled. If now and then it proved that one of those subjected to this treatment could not swim, no one was likely to discover the fact; and unless he could save himself, the river might carry him quietly to sea. ‘Them as can’t stand a ducking,’ Ma Hogan used to say, with a fine philosophy, ‘had best behave theirselves the way a gentleman should.’ “
In 1946, Hollywood produced a movie version of The Strange Woman, starring Hedy Lamarr and George Sanders.
Two musical tigresses
Edith Piaf – More Piaf of Paris, Capitol T 10283, LP, recorded early 1960s.
Dinah Washington – Where are You; You’re Nobody ‘Til Somebody Loves You. Roulette R-4424, seven inch 45, recorded 1962.
Two very vibrantly alive musical tigresses were the emotionally intense French songstress Edith Piaf (1915-1963) and the incisively biting Dinah Washington (1924-1963), both of whose above-mentioned recordings have merited hearing for more than sixty years.
One gem on the Piaf album is the sweetly arranged Non, Je Ne Regrette Rien while Dinah’s rendition of You’re Nobody…is one rivetingly swinging rendition.
More likely than not, these recordings can be heard on YouTube.
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!

title: ‘Saved by the Bell’ star Dennis Haskins’ cause of death revealed
text:
BURBANK, Calif. (CNN) - A cause of death has been released for Dennis Haskins, who was best known as Principal Belding on “Saved by the Bell.”
The Los Angeles County Department of Public Health listed Parkinson’s as the 75-year-old actor’s immediate cause of death.
Haskins died Sept. 27, in Burbank, California.
He had been living in an assisted living facility and had not publicly disclosed his diagnosis.
Haskins played Principal Richard Belding throughout the original “Saved by the Bell” run and later reprised the role in “Saved by the Bell: The New Class.”
His career also included appearances on “Mad Men,” “Hot in Cleveland” and “New Girl.”

title: Christa Pike’s attorneys to ask evidence to be preserved following failed execution
text:
Christa Pike's attorneys call recovery 'medically unprecedented' as judge rules execution evidence be preserved
Attorneys for Christa Pike, who survived Tennessee’s attempt to put her to death via lethal injection last week, were in court Wednesday as they sought to preserve relevant evidence in her twice-botched execution, which a judge granted.
See a news conference from Pike's attorneys following Wednesday's court hearing in the video player above.
Pike has been hospitalized for nearly a week after being injected with two ostensibly fatal doses of pentobarbital, her attorneys said. On Tuesday, her attorneys said, she was finally conscious and speaking – though she continues to receive critical medical care and suffered “severe damage” to her arms.
“Her recovery is medically unprecedented,” the attorneys said in a statement Tuesday evening. “Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery.”
Pike had been speaking "limitedly" when she became conscious, according to reports.
Her attorneys spoke about Pike's condition on Wednesday, after Judge I'Ashea Myles granted Pike's motion to preserve all state materials relevant to her failed execution.
"I was not in the room when she woke up, so I don't want to speculate too much," said Randy Spivey, one of Pike's attorneys. "Our understanding was the first thing she said when she woke up were 'Where am I?' and 'Who are you?' There's still a lot of cognitive confusion."
Spivey said they had believed that she was brain dead as of Monday night, but woke up on Tuesday "to the shock of everyone." He also noted that Pike's hands and arms are severely swollen and she is still unable to swallow.
Dr. Joel Zivot, an anesthesiologist, told the BBC that Pike was able to recall her name but believed it was still September.
"She has some memories of being in the hospital but no memory, I believe, of the execution attempt," Zivot said.
"Her memories may continue to evolve," he told PEOPLE. "I think she knew who she was, where she was, when she was told."
Preserving evidence
Pike’s lawyers filed the emergency motion last week to ensure the preservation of evidence, alleging the Tennessee Department of Correction inflicted “a cruel and unusual punishment” on Pike “through its deliberate indifference to her basic medical needs and reckless disregard of basic medical practices and their own lethal injection protocol.”
Those administering the lethal injection attempted to gain IV access to Pike using "at least seven needles," the emergency motion reads. “One needle was bent in a 90-degree angle when it was removed.”
See a clip of the court hearing in the video player above.
The attorneys first alerted the state about its duty to preserve evidence at 1:09 a.m. ET on Thursday, hours after Pike’s botched execution, the emergency motion points out. Pike’s legal team is now looking to preserve relevant physical, written and electronic evidence.
When Pike arrived at the Nashville-area hospital, her attorneys said in the motion, her arms were “swollen, burned, and blistered.” Pentobarbital “burns upon contact, including skin, tissue, and veins,” they said.
Pike was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death for the brutal 1995 killing of Colleen Slemmer, a fellow student at a job training facility.
The state Attorney General’s Office hasn’t indicated whether it will seek to put her to death again, Stephen Ferrell, one of Pike’s attorneys, told CNN on Sunday. Pike’s lawyers have called on Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute her sentence to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
After Pike’s failed execution, Lee suspended executions for the rest of the year, announcing Thursday a third party will do “a thorough and comprehensive” review of her case. Lee on Saturday also announced Correction Commissioner Frank Strada would step down later this month following backlash over Pike’s failed execution.
Republican U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who is running to replace Lee as governor in January, called to bring back the electric chair and “deliver justice for these victims swiftly.”
“The state of Tennessee has got to start telling its people exactly what it is doing, so that in the democratic process, the people of Tennessee can decide if that’s what they want to be done in their name,” Ferrell, one of Pike's attorneys, said Sunday. “This torturous execution leaves so many questions that the state of Tennessee will refuse to answer.”

title: CES school committee reviews early budget estimates
text:
BAR HARBOR — In its final meeting in the library of the old Emerson building, before switching to a room in the brand-new Conners Emerson school building for its meeting next month, the school committee took a look at some very early budget estimates for the 2026-27 school year.
While the budget process has been difficult due to the uncertainty surrounding costs associated with the transition into the new building, school officials are anticipating an increase of $25,708 in revenue from what was budgeted and a decrease of $35,663 in expenditures, resulting in a positive difference of $61,371.

title: Poland and Greely girls soccer battle to draw
text:
POLAND — After Poland began its season with six wins and a tie through seven games, Juan Bustamante knew that some difficult opponents still awaited the Knights.
Among those teams was Greely, and when the Class B South foes did finally meet on Wednesday, the result was a 2-2 tie.
“It was a tough game,” said Bustamante. “We’re happy to honestly come away with a tie with that. We wanted to win, though. We came out fast. But yeah, good competitive game.”
Poland (8-1-2), ranked third in the Class B South Heal point standings, has three games remaining, against Old Orchard Beach, North Yarmouth Academy and Waynflete. Sixth-ranked Greely (5-3-2) plays Gray-New Gloucester next and finishes with games against three of the region’s top five teams — Cape Elizabeth, Freeport and Yarmouth.
“It was a little bit of a battle, but at the same time, (to) get out of here with the points is important in the tie, so overall, happy with the kids for battling,” Greely coach Neil Carroll said. “It’s something we haven’t faced yet, so happy with them to do that.”
The Rangers also played region-leading Cape Elizabeth to a draw on Saturday.
HOW IT HAPPENED
Poland got on the scoreboard first, about six and half minutes into the game. Greely keeper Rylee Begin tried to kick the ball away from the goal, but it defected off Julia Paradis as she leaped into the air and wound up in the net.
Just over five minutes into the second half, Tess Waterhouse scored the equalizer for the Rangers. After a corner kick by Waterhouse, the ball bounced back to her and she lofted it into the far corner from a sharp angle.
It took Poland just 51 seconds to regain the lead, as Leksi Langevin scored from close range after a direct kick by Phoebe Paradis.
Greely had several looks at another equalizer, but it didn’t come until a little over 18 minutes later, again off a corner kick, as Simone Couture set up Victoria Zandan.
The Rangers nearly scored late in the first overtime, but Payton Seekins missed wide left. Late in the second overtime, a header by Poland’s Davis Hill hit the crossbar.
HEARD IT HERE FIRST
• “The girls are really hungry, and we want a home (playoff) game, so that’s what we’re looking for.” — Poland coach Juan Bustamante
• “In the last couple weeks, (the players have) kind of found a little bit different energy, and the culture has changed a little bit in our first year. And give props to the captains, really. They’ve done a great job helping us create that.” — Greely coach Neil Carroll
STATISTICAL LEADERS:
• Poland: Julia Paradis (goal), Leksi Langevin (goal)
• Greely: Tess Waterhouse (goal), Victoria Zandan (goal), Simone Couture (assist)

title: Why your retirement plan shouldn’t depend on an inheritance
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Millions of Americans are expecting an inheritance someday, but Matt Schulz, a consumer finance analyst with LendingTree, said that money should not replace a personal savings plan.
“It’s a luxury if you have it,” Schulz said. “But it’s really, really important for people to not have that be their entire retirement plan.”
LendingTree found that homeowners 65 and older could transfer $17.2 trillion between 2026 and 2045. About a third of Americans younger than 65 expect to receive some of that money as an inheritance or financial gift, and of those expecting a payout, 43% say their retirement plan depends on it arriving.
Schulz said that money is not guaranteed to be there when it’s needed.
“It’s important for people to not assume that all the money that’s there now is going to be there in the future, because the cost of health care, the cost of assisted living and so many other things that we face when dealing with elderly parents or our own aging are so expensive,” Schulz said. “And a lot of that would-be inheritance money can go away in a pretty big hurry.”
Despite the financial stakes, Schulz said many families avoid discussing inheritance planning, even though those conversations need to happen well in advance.
“There’s so much that goes into it. Whether you’re talking about just family dynamics, but there’s also legal ramifications and tax issues and all that,” Schulz said. “And that’s all the kind of stuff that needs to be discussed going down the line here, whether that’s with professionals or with siblings or with family or what have you.”
Schulz said the bottom line is to build a retirement plan around current savings, not around money that might be passed down in the future.

title: Grants fund traditional Wabanaki art, harvest practices: ‘Now that’s connection’
text:
MOTAHKOMIKUK — Standing at the narrows that separate Big and Long lakes, Matthew Dana II curled his fingers around the base of a sweet flag shoot and pried its root from the boggy earth.
He snapped it in two to reveal its light interior and release its earthen scent.
Once dried, flag root — or kiwhosuwasq, which translates to muskrat root, given the rodent’s affinity for the plant — is a traditional Passamaquoddy medicine used to treat, among other things, colds and indigestion.
Dana learned to harvest it in this patch of wetland from his late uncle.
Today, he’s teaching the next generation.
And though working with Passamaquoddy youths has been a passion of his for years, he’s made it into a full-time job thanks in part to a $25,000 grant from the Wolankeyutomone Kisi Apaciyewik Fund.
The fund, the name of which translates to “let us take good care of what has been returned,” is an endeavor of the Wabanaki Commission on Land and Stewardship and First Light.
The commission is composed of representatives of all five Wabanaki communities in Maine: the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians, the Mi’kmaq Nation, the Passamaquoddy at Motahkomikuk Indian Township, the Passamaquoddy at Sipayik and the Penobscot Nation. First Light is a group of allied nonnative organizations.
Together, they are accelerating the return of land to Wabanaki Nations.
The Penobscot Nation regained control of 11,000 acres last month and the Mi’kmaq Nation’s holdings nearly doubled when the tribe obtained title to 3,400 acres in June. These are all part of a plan to return 50,000 acres to tribal governments.
“Just getting the land back doesn’t mean that our communities are going to be properly resourced to be able to go out there and engage with the land,” said Frances Soctomah, the fund manager.
That’s where the grants come in.
Wabanaki individuals, nonprofits and governments are eligible to apply for grants of $25,000, $50,000 and $75,000, respectively. In the first two years, the fund has distributed a total of $1.35 million in 32 grants across all five communities. Projects support work around anything from food sovereignty to cultural tourism to trail building.
The fund itself, designed to support Wabanaki self-determination, breaks the mold of traditional nonprofit fundraising. Soctomah and First Light plan to grow it into a multimillion-dollar self-sustaining endowment that will support this kind of work in perpetuity.
Conservation organizations, Maine and national philanthropic foundations and individual donors all contributed in equal part in the initial fundraising. Donors in Maine included the Elmina B. Sewall Foundation, Maine Coast Heritage Trust, the Onion Foundation and the Quimby Foundation.
The application is low barrier, the grants are unrestricted and the use of donations to the fund is often undefined from the outset because it is intended to support self-determination. That’s sometimes difficult for nonnative donors to wrap their heads around.
“We are integrating more of a trust-based philanthropy approach,” Soctomah said.
But on a recent visit to Motahkomikuk, one of the two Passamaquoddy communities in Washington County, it’s not hard to find evidence of the grants at work.
QUILLS PUT A POINT ON IT
Piece by piece, Donald Soctomah can walk you through the Passamaquoddy Tribal Museum and the myriad artifacts and artworks collected there.
These things just have a way of coming home, he said.
There’s a case of stone tools people have found at their camps and, below it, a small Revolutionary War cannon gifted to the tribe by the state in 1820, in gratitude for the service of Wabanaki warriors. The cannon was once lost in the lake, discovered by a fisherman and taken to Maryland, then returned again decades later.
There are baskets, woven by artisans both famous and obscure, and a drum used by the Passamaquoddy Brass Band that toured with Buffalo Bill.
Soctomah, 71, is the Passamaquoddy Tribal Historic Preservation Officer, a former tribal state representative and Frances Soctomah’s father.
He’s been involved in three grant-winning proposals since Wolankeyutomone Kisi Apaciyewik was launched, including one that supported cultural activities through the museum he manages.
With that grant, Soctomah hired a local artist to lead workshops in porcupine quill art; he was a financial benefactor of this year’s community days to celebrate Passamaquoddy culture with drumming, dancing and a slate of native vendors; and he paid the portage drivers for the ancestral canoe journey, an annual event in which tribal members paddle from Motahkomikuk down the St. Croix River to Sipayik.
These are traditions that run in his DNA. They are traditions, he said, that must be supported.
“It’s the right thing to do,” Soctomah said.
At community days, Alisia Morin, 34, said she spotted a road-kill porcupine as she crossed Passamaquoddy lands that very morning.
She was eager to attend several of the quill workshops Soctomah organized. There, she learned to dye and soften the tubular spikes, and then thread them into a backing to create ornately detailed patterns.
“I’ve always been drawn to how beautiful quill work is,” Morin said.
She grew up in Texas and was not exposed to traditional Passamaquoddy art as a kid. Now, raising her own kids on her ancestral homelands, Morin said it’s important that they have more exposure than she did.
So when she spotted the porcupine carcass, she braked.
If Morin had a shovel, she would’ve taken the whole thing. Instead, she and her daughter, Eliana McGinley, 6, plucked just enough quills to make some earrings.
Hudson McGinley, 22 months old, shows off the medallion his mother made by threading dyed porcupine quills through a birch bark backing, at left. At right, Alisia Morin hit the brakes when she spotted the porcupine carcass that morning. (Daryn Slover/Staff Photographer)
“Mom got stuck,” McGinley pipes in, before admitting, “I was a little scared to do it.”
When she pulled out a quilled medallion she made in the workshop, her 22-month-old son Hudson insisted he wear it, and toddled back to the event grounds grasping it with both hands.
ALL ABOUT RESPONSIBILITY
That evening, Eric Bacon steadied the gunwales of his birch bark canoe as a teenager lifted the hem of her ribbon skirt and swung her leg into the shaky hull.
Bacon, who is 49 and has no kids of his own, paddled out into the channel connecting Lewy Lake to Grand Falls Flowage and made a circle.
His 23-year-old birch bark canoe was made by master builder Steve Cayard, a mentor of Bacon’s. These boats, constructed in the traditional Wabanaki style, are feather-light.
But the boats have enough gravity to pull the the course of Bacon’s life into their orbit.
He crossed under the bridge and looped back around before drifting up to the rocky shore.
“Let me get out first,” he instructed.
The girls giggled and ran off.
“I’m trying to plant the seed,” Bacon said as he strapped the boat back on his pickup.
In 1981, he dragged his mother by the hand across the grounds at Mihku Lodge to see a birch bark canoe. He was 4.
In a way, everything Bacon has done since has been about trying to nurture that passion.
He received a $25,000 grant to remodel a garage he owns and turn it into a canoe building and birch bark art space where he can host workshops.
The garage isn’t done yet, and Bacon has instead spent some of the money to rent gear for public paddling events. It’s what the community told him it wanted.
Unlike with some other grants, that’s exactly what grantees are supposed to do, Frances Soctomah said. She wants them to have the ability to pivot according to the needs of their community.
Other grant programs often come with burdensome restrictions — food distribution is often off-limits. In one case, Soctomah recalled a funder telling her they wanted to support a basket-making program, but at the 11th hour said the money couldn’t be used on sharp axes, critical tools for harvesting and processing ash trees.
Now, the fund she manages can help fill the gaps for grantees who are constrained by other programs.
There’s a new skiff parked in Matt Dana’s yard. He bought it with the grant money and, from it, harvested a porpoise as part of his goal to gather 500 pounds of protein with Passamaquoddy youth.
For Dana, all of this is about fulfilling a responsibility.
As a boy, he learned to trap muskrat from a neighbor, and from his father learned to call them in with birch bark; as a young man, Dana learned to harvest ash and weave baskets from Jeremy Frey, a nationally recognized basket-maker; in his 40s, Dana has sought out elders who can still recall how to hunt seals and process their hides.
After he was awarded a grant in 2025, Dana decided to make this a full-time job.
He’s secured funding from numerous nonprofits in Maine to support the work of Mecimi-te Nihtawehtunen — the name of his organization, which means “we have always remembered.” It’s a phrase implying that the traditions not only exist, but will continue to.
Matthew Dana made a crown from ash and sweetgrass for his 4-year-old granddaughter, Sage Dana, to wear during the community days celebration, at left. At right is sweetgrass on Dana’s kitchen sink. (Daryn Slover/Staff Photographer)
Coils of ash splints sat bound in a box outside his kitchen, and there are locks of sweetgrass in the sink.
“It’s got to be preserved,” Dana said. “The generations coming after us need to know it.”
He harvested his first moose at 11. By 18, he was out hunting with his cousins and 10 siblings, then his kids and grandkids. In the woods, Dana said placing his palms down flat on the table, he feels grounded.
Two years ago, Dana took his 21-year-old nephew out hunting and guided what was then a timid young man as he harvested his first buck. Last year, they went out again.
Dana’s nephew tracked a buck into the woods as Dana sat listening.
“And then I heard — I heard the shot.”
When they reunited, there was no more fear. There was pride and confidence and joy. His nephew shared the meat with elders in the community.
“It’s ceremony, it’s prayer, it’s connecting with the ancestors,” Dana said. “The feeling of doing something that my DNA has done for over 15,000 years in this same place? Now that’s connection.”
Reuben M. Schafir is a Report for America corps member who writes about Indigenous and rural communities for the Portland Press Herald.
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 7 to correct the amount of money that the Wolankeyutomone Kisi Apaciyewik Fund has distributed.

title: This Maine actor’s career has taken her from Camden to London
text:
Caitlin FitzGerald always finds a little bit of Maine, wherever she is.
She cornered Portland native Anna Kendrick at a party in London so she could talk about Maine with her. When the iconic true-life book “Lost on a Mountain in Maine” was made into a movie a few years ago, FitzGerald just knew she had to play the lost boy’s mother. She had read the book in grammar school, like most Maine kids.
And this year, while filming the second season of the Prime drama “We Were Liars” in Nova Scotia, FitzGerald was introduced to Elysia Roorbach, who will be playing the younger version of her character, Penny Sinclair. Roorbach grew up in Farmington, in Maine’s western mountains.
“I love Maine so much, it feels like such a part of who I am and it’s such a special place,” said FitzGerald, while filming in Nova Scotia this summer. “So it’s wonderful to meet people who understand.”
FitzGerald, 43, has traveled and worked all over the world during her 20-year career in film, TV and theater. She’s currently living in London and recently starred as Desdemona in a West End production of Shakespeare’s “Othello,” which was filmed and released to theaters in March.
She’s currently starring as one of the adult sisters of a wealthy, secrets-laden family in the Prime drama “We Were Liars,” based on the best-selling novel by E. Lockhart. The first season premiered in the summer of 2025 and the second season is slated for sometime next year. FitzGerald also had a recurring role on the hit HBO show “Succession,” playing Tabitha Hayes, girlfriend of Roman Roy (Kieran Culkin). About a decade ago, she played Libby Masters, the first wife of pioneering sex researcher William Masters, in the Showtime series “Masters of Sex.”
“We Were Liars” focuses on a wealthy family that spends the summer on a private island off the Massachusetts coast. FitzGerald’s character, Penny Sinclair, is the mother of Cadence Sinclair Eastman, part of a tightknit group called the Liars. Cadence suffers from memory loss due to a mysterious accident.
MAINE CONNECTIONS
The second season flashes back two decades, so new actors were cast to play the younger versions of the main characters. In a weird bit of Maine karma, Roorbach was cast to play the younger Penny. So there are two Maine actors on the show playing the same role. Earlier this year Roorbach made her TV debut playing an emergency room patient in two episodes of the hit HBO drama “The Pitt.”
FitzGerald said she didn’t know Roorbach, 26, until she was cast in “We Were Liars.” The two quickly found they had much in common, besides being from Maine. They both studied acting at New York University, and both did a semester abroad in London, focused on Shakespeare.
“There aren’t a lot of people from Maine in this industry, so it’s great that she’s here,” said FitzGerald of Roorbach. “I’m so pleased I get to work with her.”
FitzGerald lived in Lincolnville as a small child, then moved to Camden. Her father, Des FitzGerald, started a company called DuckTrap River Fish Farm, which became a nationally known purveyor of smoked fish. Her mother, Pam Allen, was the editor of a knitting magazine and started her own line of yarn, Quince & Co.
FitzGerald says she fell in love with acting in a kindergarten play, an adaptation of Rudyard Kipling’s “How the Elephant Got his Trunk.” She got involved with area children’s theater productions, including at Camden Civic Theatre.
FitzGerald says she really wanted to study the craft of acting, instead of just driving to Los Angeles and looking for work, like many people do. She chose the Tisch School of the Arts at NYU because it combined classroom academics with stage training. Being from Maine, she says living in New York City during college was also an education.
Though she’s worked steadily for two decades, FitzGerald says her career has ebbed and flowed. One of her early breaks was being cast in the 2009 romcom “It’s Complicated,” starring Meryl Streep and Alec Baldwin. She played Streep’s daughter.
“She was my hero, so I was definitely nervous to work with her, I had no idea what I was doing,” said FitzGerald. “I probably embarrassed myself a lot in front of her, but she was very generous.”
In one of those odd full-circle moments, FitzGerald is now sharing scenes with Streep’s daughter, Mamie Gummer. Gummer plays a sister of FitzGerald’s character on “We Were Liars.”
One of FitzGerald’s favorite roles was playing Libby Masters on “Masters of Sex” over four seasons. She says the writers created for her character “an amazing journey” from a typical 1950s housewife, who happens to be married to a sex researcher, to a more a indepedendent and complicated character. She eventually goes to Woodstock and also studies law.
But maybe her most personal role was playing the mother of Donn Fendler in “Lost on a Mountain in Maine.” Fendler was 12 when he got separated from his hiking party on Mount Katahdin in 1939 and survived nine days alone, lost in the woods.
The search for Fendler and his eventual rescue sparked stories in newspapers around the country. Within months, a book co-authored by Fendler and Joseph B. Egan, “Lost on a Mountain in Maine,” was published. For decades the book was taught in Maine schools as part of a lesson on Maine history. Fendler himself spoke to hundreds of classes and community groups over the years. He died in 2016, at the age of 90.
FitzGerald said she has vivid memories of the book, which portrays the danger, fear and hope of a young, lost boy. She said when her agent told her about the movie, and the part of Fendler’s mother, she said, “I have to do that one.”
Before opening in theaters nationally, the film premiered at the Maine International Film Festival in Waterville in the summer of 2024. FitzGerald attended the premiere and said she loved seeing so many teachers from around Maine who had taught the book to kids like her for years.
“It was such a lovely homegrown moment and I was really proud to be a part of it,” she said. “It was an honor to tell that story.”

title: Christa Pike survived 2 doses of an execution drug. How is that possible?
text:
(AP) - Christa Pike regaining consciousness and speaking a week after receiving two doses of execution drugs in Tennessee has astonished even some medical professionals and left many people wondering: How did she survive?
Attorneys for Pike, 50, called her recovery “medically unprecedented” after she was placed on a ventilator following the bungled Sept. 30 attempt to make her the first woman put to death in Tennessee in 200 years. On Wednesday, they said Pike was confused, “speaking limitedly” and could not move her arms, one of which had a blood clot.
Pike, who was convicted in the 1995 torture and killing of classmate Colleen Slemmer, is the only person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Many details of the execution process remain secretive, and Tennessee officials say they are investigating what went wrong.
Still, medical experts raised a few possibilities that could explain how Pike was able to survive, including the potential drug quality and the placement of IV lines. Tennessee’s executioners had difficulties earlier this year with IV lines for another execution, leading to it being called off.
Only a small amount of the drug may have entered her bloodstream
The 5-gram dose of pentobarbital used in executions is many more times the amount that should put someone in a medical coma, said Dr. Jonathan I. Groner, a retired pediatric general surgeon at Ohio State University College of Medicine who has studied lethal injections.
“The fact that she woke, on one hand, says she got really little of it into her system. So that’s kind of shocking,” Groner said. “It says how badly they botched the execution.”
At high doses, the potent barbiturate should make a person lose consciousness and stop breathing.
Groner said the IV might have been placed improperly, or Pike’s veins could have been fragile and ruptured, causing the drug to seep into the surrounding tissue instead of flowing through the bloodstream. Pike’s attorneys have said she was poked with needles at least seven times in the state’s death chamber and that she has a blood disorder that makes it tough to get needles into her veins.
Sourcing of drugs for executions is shrouded in secrecy
Another possible problem could be the drug quality, said Michaela Almgren, a South Carolina pharmacist and educator who has consulted on several lethal injection cases.
Many major pharmaceutical companies refuse to supply drugs for lethal injections, which has raised questions about how states get them. Court orders have revealed that some states have turned to compounding pharmacies, which create custom drugs from raw ingredients and operate with less regulatory oversight.
Tennessee does not disclose its drug supplier and has not said where Pike’s supply came from. Almgren said that makes it difficult to track if a drug was prepared, tested, handled and administered properly.
That also means the public may never know exactly what happened in Pike’s case.
Pike’s attorneys asked a court to require the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence, including drug lot numbers, communications and other material from the attempted execution. A judge told prison officials on Wednesday that they must preserve “anything that was in the actual room.”
Outgoing Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has paused executions and ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred.” It’s unclear whether the state will try executing Pike again.
Hospital treatment likely involved flushing the drug from her system
Before the execution attempt, Pike’s attorneys told courts and prison officials that she had medical conditions that could complicate a lethal injection and make it agonizing.
Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike’s legal team, said Pike has a blood-clotting disorder that causes her body to produce an excess of platelets. Her lawyers had argued that the condition could cause clotting at injection sites or bleeding that could affect her lungs.
State protocol calls for a second dose of pentobarbital if the first doesn’t result in death, but it doesn’t spell out what to do if an inmate survives the second injection.
The attempted execution got underway around 7:30 p.m. At some point Pike appeared to lose consciousness, but she could be heard breathing until media were escorted from the witness room at 8:53 p.m. An ambulance arrived at 9:14 p.m. and took Pike to a hospital.
Once there, doctors likely tried to stabilize her breathing, checked how much pentobarbital was in her system and worked to quickly flush it out, said Dr. Michael Baden, the former chief medical examiner of New York City.
Pike’s lawyers said the failed attempt left her arms burned and blistered. She was unconscious and on a ventilator for several days.
“She was very fortunate that there was enough (pentobarbital) to put her into a deep sleep, but they were able to keep her breathing going and they were able to start flushing it out,” Baden said.
___
Associated Press writers Kim Chandler in Montgomery, Alabama, and Kristin M. Hall in Nashville contributed reporting.

title: Lewiston councilor, also a legislative candidate, scrutinized over allegations from former tenant
text:
Key Takeaways Key Takeaways are written by Maine Trust staff and highlight the most important points of this article so you can get the gist at a glance.
- Lewiston Ward 3 Councilor Scott Harriman was accused of acting inappropriately toward a former female tenant via an interview with a right-wing website.
- Harriman denied the allegations and claimed the website was conspiring with Maine Republicans to sink his campaign for reelection to the state Legislature.
- About a dozen residents came out in protest before the City Council’s meeting Tuesday to call for his resignation.
- The meeting featured a raucous public comment period in which calls for Harriman’s resignation persisted and several came to his defense.
LEWISTON — A group of residents outside City Hall on Tuesday evening called for the resignation of Ward 3 Councilor Scott Harriman, later spilling into council chambers where Harriman’s supporters and detractors each had a say.
Harriman, who is also the state representative for Lewiston House District 94, has been accused of inappropriate contact by a former tenant. The tenant aired her alleged experience with him in an interview with the Maine Wire, a media project of the right-wing Maine Policy Institute.
Multiple attempts by the Sun Journal to contact the tenant to confirm her story have been unsuccessful.
Lewiston police said no complaints have been made directly to the department regarding the allegations.
Harriman, who is running to retain his seat in Augusta, has denied the allegations and said that he was forced to evict the former tenant in 2025.
“I take allegations like these very seriously. None of these allegations are true,” Harriman said in a Facebook post. “The person who made these allegations is a former tenant who I unfortunately had to evict last year due to several significant challenges. This included being a danger to other tenants, not paying rent, damage to the property, and breaking into other tenants’ mailboxes.”
He has also described the allegations as a conspiracy between Maine Republicans and the Maine Wire to sway his district’s election in favor of his opponent in the legislative race, Janet Beaudoin.
Harriman has released multiple pieces of home surveillance footage of Maine Wire employee Jon Fetherston speaking on the phone about Harriman while parked outside his home.
In one video, Harriman claims, Fetherston is speaking with Beaudoin on speakerphone about getting a statement from the Maine Republican Party. Fetherston had reported on the allegations for the Maine Wire.
“If it got picked up by one other news organization, why wouldn’t they?” Fetherston can be heard saying in the video. “Do they want you to win this seat?”
In another video, Harriman claims, Fetherston is speaking with another Maine Wire employee on speakerphone.
“I think the more attention we can bring on this, the better,” the voice said. “I mean, this could legitimately flip the seat. I’m with it.”
Among more than a dozen protesters outside City Hall was resident Ray Toutain. He said Harriman should resign.
“He shouldn’t be on any board, he’s been censured three times,” Toutain said. “Now, if this is true, which I believe it is, it’s time for him to sit down. … This guy, I don’t know why he’s on the board. … It’s one thing after another with him.”
Resident Renee Fortin also cited Harriman’s censures, suggested it is time for the councilor to resign, and remarked that his assignment to the Lewiston School Committee sends a bad message to youths.
“I believe that after a person’s been censured three times and he continues to be shady, I think it’s time for him to be voted out,” Fortin said. “This is not a good look for Lewiston.”
The council meeting’s public comment period ran for about one hour, with repeated disruptions and warnings from Mayor Carl Sheline for quiet in the chambers. Audience members repeatedly traded barbs and one person was escorted out of the building. More called for Harriman’s resignation, some for a full investigation. Several people came to his defense.
Ward 2 Councilor Susan Longchamps addressed the council, detailing her personal relationship with Harriman’s accuser. She said that when she learned of her friend’s experience with Harriman, she kept it in confidence. She also said she was unaware of a June email to councilors, the mayor and police detailing the accuser’s alleged experience.
The email came from Lewiston mayoral candidate Charles Soule and was addressed to former council President David Chittim, police Chief Carley Conley, Sheline, Longchamps and the Sun Journal.
“Had I known these concerns had already been reported, this discussion would have happened months ago,” Longchamps said. “I was not the only person she told, but yet I have somehow, because of the political timing, become part of an accusation as though I created this (and) convinced (her) to come forward. That is simply not true.”
Longchamps said resident Joe Philippon, who she said helped get her elected to the council, and Ward 5 Councilor Chrissy Noble have tried to discredit her in the time since the allegations became public.
“Whatever political or personal disagreement you have with me, do not make (her) allegations about me,” Longchamps said. “This is not about whether Councilor Harriman is guilty or innocent, but the question is whether this council will make sure these serious allegations are looked into professionally, independently and responsibly.”
Philippon said after the council meeting that he has not tried to discredit Longchamps, but raised a specific question about a portion of the Maine Wire’s video in which he said it sounds like someone is prompting Harriman’s accuser.
“I asked Susan directly whether that was her voice and what her involvement in the interview was, and her statement today still doesn’t answer that question,” Philippon said, adding that he never said the allegations should not be taken seriously. “My question about Susan’s involvement in the interview is separate from the merits of (his accuser’s) allegations.”
Resident Lisa Jones criticized the council for remaining silent “in the face of extremely serious accusations” against one of their peers.
“What does it communicate to the unhoused folks you see in your professional capacity when they learn you heard these allegations from their peer and you deemed them not worthy of further investigation?” Jones asked. “Short of a resignation, an independent investigation seems like the only plausible way forward.”
Several who spoke in support of Harriman said he has been responsive to his constituents, has constantly shown up for his community and is committed to the city.
Some, including resident Ifraax Saciid-Ciise Lugoole, suggested the timing of the allegations, weeks before the Nov. 3 elections, is suspect.
“He has always been there for our community and I’ve also seen him be there for the vulnerable in our community,” Lugoole said. “I’m just here to support him and to show that he has a great character. … This is political and very very disgusting and nasty … and I’m very disappointed.”
Resident Zoë Lidstrom said she was concerned that the allegations were manufactured and have become “increasingly volatile and cruel culminating in a blogger staking out Councilor Harriman’s house for hours.”
“To me, that is not acceptable, that is not politics,” Lidstrom said. “If that can happen to a councilman, it can happen to anyone in our city.”
Lewiston teacher Jae Zimmermann noted that October is National Bullying Prevention Month and that school staff are working with students to help them learn how to recognize bullying and how to stand up against it. They said it’s a lesson that a lot of Lewiston needs this month.
“It makes me sad to look around these chambers and hear the whispers, the nasty comments, to see the behavior online and know that despite all our efforts in the schools, the examples of the adults in their lives run contrary to everything we want our students to grow up and learn to be,” Zimmerman said. “It is disappointing to think this is the world my students are growing up into. They deserve better and so do we all.”
After the meeting, Sheline said he believes without more information, the whole matter seems to be a push to derail Harriman’s campaign.
“Absent further concrete details or information from the accuser, this just appears to be a political smear campaign orchestrated by the ever-bumbling Maine Wire with eager help from local Republicans,” Sheline said.
In a Facebook post Wednesday morning, council President Joshua Nagine said he is “deeply disturbed” by the “hatred, anger and fear” in Lewiston’s political discourse.
“We are a community that is attacking itself while being torn apart, and some of our residents are part of the machinery that is doing the work,” he wrote. “It feels bleak.”
“But, I’m a believer in humanity and I’m a believer in my City,” he continued. “Warts and all. So, this morning and every morning going forward, I’m going to recommit myself to being a kinder, more empathetic, and more present person.”

title: Maine Conservation Voters hosts online Lunch & Learn event
text:
Reading Between the Ship’s Ribs: Introducing Interco(a)stal
What: Maine Conservation Voters hosts regular, free, one-hour webinars focused on important and timely topics. On Friday, Oct. 9 from 12 to 1 p.m., MCV will host a conversation about the Interco(a)stal project, a collaborative effort bringing together researchers, artists, Wabanaki knowledge keepers, museums and community organizations to explore the histories embedded in Bath’s maritime landscape.
One week ahead of The Interco(a)stal Walk on Oct. 18, project leaders Adilah Muhammad (The Third Place), James Eric Francis, Sr. (Penobscot Nation), Andrea Francis (Bomazeen Land Trust) and Meadow Dibble (Atlantic Black Box) will share the project’s origins, creative collaborations and evolving vision for reimagining the Wyoming Evocation, a monument to Maine’s shipbuilding and seafaring heritage at Maine Maritime Museum. Together, they’ll explore how research, art, and community participation can challenge incomplete historical narratives, recenter Black and Wabanaki histories, and open new possibilities for participatory public memory.
When: Friday, Oct. 9, 12-1 p.m.
Where: Online. This is a free event, but you must register to join. Register here.

title: Man arrested after 130 mph motorcycle chase across 3 counties, deputies say
text:
HINESVILLE, Ga. (WTOC/Gray News) - A man is facing multiple felony charges after leading deputies on a high-speed motorcycle pursuit through three southeast Georgia counties, authorities said.
Long County deputies were patrolling Georgia Highway 196 near Joe Kennedy Road at about 9:25 p.m. on Oct. 3. That night, a sergeant spotted a black Yamaha MT-07 motorcycle heading west at a high rate of speed, according to the sheriff’s office.
A sheriff’s office corporal farther ahead saw the motorcycle pass another vehicle in a no-passing zone and clocked it at 90 mph in a posted 55 mph zone. When the corporal tried to pull the motorcycle over near Hay Field Road, the driver accelerated and fled, reaching speeds up to 130 mph.
The chase continued into Tattnall County and then turned left onto U.S. Highway 301, with another corporal taking over as the lead unit. The chase ended on Key Howard Road in Long County when the driver, later identified as Victor Tavarez of Fort Stewart, brought the motorcycle to a stop.
As deputies tried to arrest him, Tavarez tried to flee again and struck a corporal and his patrol vehicle with the motorcycle, authorities said. He lost control after the collision and was taken into custody. The corporal was treated for minor injuries.
Tavarez was charged with:
- Wrong class of driver’s license
- Improper passing on the left
- Reckless driving
- Speeding (2 counts)
- Felony fleeing or attempting to elude
- Felony obstruction of a law enforcement officer
- Aggravated assault against a law enforcement officer

title: Mount Desert Selectboard discusses TIF districts
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MOUNT DESERT — Proposed Tax Increment Financing districting was the topic of a workshop presented by Alyssa Tibbetts from Tibbetts Law, at the beginning of Monday’s Selectboard meeting.
A TIF district is created by a municipality to encourage economic development by capturing the difference in property taxes after development in the district. The Town of Ellsworth, which currently has four TIF districts, describes a TIF district on their website as, “a designated geographic area where local governments use future increases in property tax revenue, generated by new development, to fund public improvements and economic revitalization projects within that district, effectively paying for infrastructure by capturing the ‘increment’ of new value created, rather than relying on current taxes.”

title: FDA: Pre-workout recalled over ingredient linked to heart and blood pressure problems
text:
FDA: Pre-workout recalled over ingredient linked to heart and blood pressure problems
A popular pre-workout dietary supplement powder has been recalled nationwide, with FDA officials saying it may contain a stimulant linked to potentially serious heart and blood pressure problems.
Leader Formulas, LLC is recalling one lot of its Rapture pre-workout dietary supplement powder after FDA testing found it contained DMAA.
Related video above | How to stay ahead of recalls
When sold at the consumer level, DMAA -- or 1, 3-Dimethylamylamine – can result in elevated blood could lead to cardiovascular problems, including heart attack, shortness of breath and tightening of the chest, according to federal officials.
The powder was sold in 450-gram round plastic containers with red and black lettering and a rhinoceros image on the lid. It comes in three flavors:
- Rainbow Twist — UPC 710154236506
- Electric Lemonade — UPC 710143236513
- Berry Mojito — UPC 710154236544
The product was sold nationwide in stores and online from January 29, 2025, through May 25, 2026.
The company says it has received no reports of people becoming ill in connection with the recall.
Consumers should contact their physician or healthcare provider if they have experienced any problems that may be related to taking or using the product.

title: Residents raise concerns over Juniper Ridge Landfill expansion in Old Town
text:
OLD TOWN, Maine (WABI) - Residents brought their concerns to a Juniper Ridge Advisory meeting in Old Town Tuesday night about the landfill’s potential expansion.
They wanted to know how the expansion would positively impact the local community.
Some brought up that the proposed expansion includes three acres of wetlands.
Officials said the primary contributors of PFAS at the landfill are construction and demolition debris, the highest percentage at around 35 percent, as well as ash from incinerators, special waste including discharge from fuel trucks, and asbestos.
PFAS treatment at Juniper Ridge will be centered primarily around leachate and won’t focus on other contaminants.
That leachate would be transported 20 miles down the road from Juniper Ridge to another wastewater treatment facility.
Some residents raised concerns that expansion into the wetlands, as well as transporting the leachate, could create potential hazards for the community.
“I have really deep concerns about any, I don’t think there’s any way that the landfill could expand into a wetland area and have the type of rainfall that we have these days, which is pretty sometimes very heavy, and not have runoff from the site go down into the waters. If the leachate is going to be moved from Juniper Ridge, is it going to be treated and trucked back or is it just going to stay where it’s trucked to,” a resident said.
“After it’s been treated, it will either be taken by pipeline to a wastewater treatment facility or be trucked to its further destination of a wastewater treatment facility. So they have to say, they have to get the phone up and say to us, okay, we’re putting this on bypass, something that we started doing in 2000,” an official said.
Officials stressed they would remain compliant with regulations, prioritizing public safety and taking caution when transporting cancer-causing materials like leachate.
There’s no stipulation on where the PFAS treatment will take place due to the public benefit determination under Maine law.
Juniper Ridge accepts about 52% of the state’s municipal waste.

title: Woman reported missing from work found alive after falling down 100-foot embankment
text:
Woman reported missing from work found alive after falling down 100-foot embankment
A 72-year-old woman is in critical condition days after she was rescued from a remote hiking trail in Shasta County, California, after falling down a 100-foot embankment.
Related video: Pond rescue operation in Minnesota
Mary Beth Granbery, a resident of Mount Shasta, California, left for a multi-day camping trip on Sept. 28 but didn’t show up for work on Oct. 2, according to the Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office.
Her family filed a missing person report, and the following day, Granbery’s van was discovered along the Cabin Creek Trail on the border of Shasta and Siskiyou counties.
Sage Milestone, public information officer for the Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office, told SFGATE that about 25 search and rescue personnel from the Siskiyou and Shasta counties' search and rescue teams fanned out along the trail in the Shasta-Trinity National Forest.
Granbery was found on Sunday near a creek at the bottom of a 100-foot embankment. The area was about three miles from the trailhead and about 300 yards from the trail.
“A team around 10:30 a.m. on [Oct. 4] was covering one of the drainages in the search area and came across her,” Milestone said.
Due to her location and the severity of her injuries, Granbery was evacuated by helicopter and taken to a local hospital for treatment, where she remains in critical condition.
Milestone said investigators on the case believe Granbery was on a day hike while camping in her van when she ventured off-trail, potentially to go fishing, and fell down the embankment.
While it’s unknown exactly how long she was left in the outdoors without shelter, Milestone said it’s possible she was out there for days.
The woman suffered significant injuries, including a severe knee injury, and was found with signs of exposure. She was disoriented and “nonverbal” when she was found, Milestone said.
Milestone said two factors helped Granbery, an experienced hiker: She was wearing layered clothing, and the weather has been on the warmer side. Milestone advised anyone heading into the wilderness to alert friends and family about where they are going and when they will be back.
“We’ve had several missing person searches this summer with experienced hikers that knew the area they were hiking in and still wound up getting lost, getting into trouble. In her case, she was injured,” Milestone said. “If there’s not a clear plan with somebody back home that knows when you’ll be back, and especially what to do if you don’t come back, that can really delay the search.”
Milestone said the team is glad that Granbery’s family was able to alert authorities and identify her vehicle in time to rescue her.
“Depending on when she got injured, she could have been out there, you know, four or five days injured,” Milestone said. “… Whatever she did to get herself through this ordeal is extremely impressive, and we’re just so grateful that we found her. She’s a strong lady for sure.”

title: September’s Municipal Meetings

text:
The Town’s Ordinance Committee met on Monday, Sept. 14, at the Gorham Municipal Center, with all three members present, along with Town staff and several members of the public.

Town Manager Ephrem Paraschak reported that the Town Attorney is working on data sets to frame the ordinance and suggested scheduling a full Town Council workshop once a legal framework is established. On the agenda was an update on the traffic improvements around Gorham High School. Recent and potential future improvements were discussed with Town staff.
The Planning Board held a second September meeting on Monday, Sept. 28, to address agenda items that had been carried over from its Sept. 14 regular monthly meeting due to lateness rules.
The first agenda item was discussion of the final subdivision and site plan for Thistle Petite Condominiums, comprising 30 units of multifamily housing with associated infrastructure on County Road. The board moved to approve with conditions: 4 Ayes, 2 Absent (Walsh, Delaney), 1 Vacancy.
A request for subdivision plan pre-application review for a proposed 6-lot residential subdivision, part of a mixed-use project located at 239 County Road, was discussed, but no vote was taken.
The board also discussed an amendment to the Land Use and Development Code zoning map to create a new University District zone to implement the Comprehensive Plan, and moved to send the amendment to the next available Comprehensive Plan Implementation Committee meeting for review: 4 Ayes, 2 Absent (Walsh, Delaney), 1 Vacancy.

title: 3 adults, 1 teen charged after throwing pineapple at passing Tesla, police say
text:
WEST CHESTER TOWNSHIP, Ohio (WXIX/Gray News) — Four people have been charged after allegedly throwing a pineapple at another vehicle in Ohio, police said.
Jacob Braun, 18, Bronson Moore, 18, Danden Schlake, 18, and a 17-year-old were charged after West Chester Township police responded Thursday night to a report of criminal damage to a vehicle.
A man told police that he was driving his Tesla on a roadway when a gray Chevrolet traveling in the opposite direction threw a pineapple at his car, hitting the front windshield and causing “significant” damage.
Police said the call was the third report of people throwing objects from a car that night, with several callers reporting eggs and ice being thrown.
Police spotted the suspect vehicle a short time later and made a traffic stop. Police said the officer noticed egg yolk dried all over the vehicle when approaching it.
Braun, Moore and the juvenile were all charged with complicity and vehicular vandalism, while Schlake was only charged with complicity.
West Chester police and the Warren County Sheriff’s Office are investigating.
