title: The Latest: Trump doesn’t commit to repaying federal funds already spent on controversial ads
text:
A day after President Donald Trump said he would start paying for controversial taxpayer-funded ads with a campaign account, there’s no sign he plans to refund the millions of federal dollars already spent on them. A White House official insisting on anonymity said Trump’s promises don’t mean there’s any reimbursement coming for the $12 million worth of ads that have already aired as part of a $20 million campaign using money Congress appropriated for the Department of Homeland Security.
The White House also sought to clarify Trump’s comments that the U.S. should let Iran attack Los Angeles and San Diego, saying that the president wants to protect the US from nuclear war. Democrats and military veterans say no president should suggest that it’s OK to consider Americans collateral damage.
And Trump on Tuesday said he has a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss a possible case of plague at a Siberian research institute. Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump said he would be talking with Putin about the case “very soon.”
The Latest:
Money alone doesn’t translate into victory
Democrat Kamala Harris entered the final stretch of the 2024 campaign with significantly more money than Trump only to lose every critical swing state and the White House. Elon Musk’s $25 million didn’t lift his preferred candidate to a Wisconsin Supreme Court seat. And Tom Steyer didn’t advance in the California governor’s race despite spending $216 million of his own money.
The $1 billion that Republicans have amassed compares with roughly $579 million held by a comparable collection of major Democratic groups.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said his party is facing an “obscene” amount of spending that could swamp them in the midterms.
“We’re never going to have as much money as them,” Schumer told the AP. “I sum up the election in this sentence: Can a massive Republican advantage in money beat a massive Democratic advantage in better candidates and political climate? I bet it can’t.”
Republicans are paying for their spending delays
The challenge is acute in places like Texas, where Trump will travel on Wednesday for the second time in a week to stump for Republican Ken Paxton’s Senate campaign. The state hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1988, yet MAGA Inc. has spent more than $22 million in the past month, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact.
Texas PAC, which is aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, has spent more than $83 million on advertising in the past month, an extraordinary amount to protect what’s normally a safe Republican seat. But while Texas PAC was charged $450,000 to air a single spot in the Austin market, Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico’s campaign paid $50,000 for a spot during the same game in the same market, according to AdImpact.
GOP fears grow that even $1 billion may not buy midterm victory
Republicans are increasingly anxious that the $1 billion at their disposal may not be enough to fend off sweeping midterm election losses as the party reckons with Trump’s unpopularity, persistent cost concerns and the fallout from the war in Iran.
The cash advantage, spread out across a half-dozen groups, is driven largely by the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc., which had nearly $416 million on hand at the end of August and increased its spending on critical races in September.
But that money may have come too late, forcing the president’s group to pay much higher rates because of the shrinking availability of air time. Four Republican Senate campaign officials said groups that reserved advertising time last spring paid much lower rates than MAGA Inc. and its affiliated groups. Now, the Trump-connected organizations are sometimes paying more than five times what they would have spent if they had acted earlier.
Families of some US troops killed in the Iran war’s deadliest strike absent from White House event
Relatives of some soldiers killed in the Iran war joined dozens of Gold Star families from prior U.S. conflicts Tuesday at the White House, where Trump offered words of comfort and candles were lit for the fallen service members, according to one of the widows who attended.
Not all families of the six soldiers killed March 1 in the deadliest attack of the Iran war opted to attend. Troops who survived the attack have raised questions about why they were stationed at a site that didn’t have sufficient air protection and was viewed as a likely target.
Michelle Tietjens and other relatives have said they are angry the Army still hasn’t answered questions over whether enough was done to protect their loved ones. But Tietjens and her teenage son traveled from Bellevue, Nebraska, to attend the event to honor her husband, Master Sgt. Noah Tietjens, who was killed along with five other Army Reserve soldiers by an Iranian drone strike in Kuwait.
Tietjens said the reception “didn’t change my feelings on them giving me answers,” and added that she spoke with someone at the White House who offered to try to help.
Trump says he has call scheduled with Putin to discuss possible case of pneumonic plague in Russia
Trump on Tuesday said he has a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss a possible case of plague at a Siberian research institute.
Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump said he would be talking with Putin about the case “very soon.” Health authorities are investigating after the death of an employee at an anti-plague institute, which authorities attributed to pneumonia with an unknown cause.
Asked what the U.S. intelligence community was saying about the case, Trump said the U.S. is in “very deep discussions” on the topic. “We’ll be able to report about it, probably tomorrow,” Trump said.
The World Health Organization on Tuesday said the case presents a “very low” risk outside Russia. The United Nations agency said it was in contact with Russian authorities following reports of the death last week of a woman who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
Trump did not call for attacks on US cities but explained how he’s preventing them, aide says
The White House clarified Donald Trump’s comments at a Monday night rally, explaining that the president was not insinuating that he wanted Iran to attack U.S. cities but instead wanted to prevent Tehran from having that capability.
White House Communications Director Steven Cheung said on social media Tuesday that the president’s comments have been misunderstood and misrepresented in a “media freakout” that is “not rooted in reality.”
Trump was discussing the Iran war and the resulting high gas prices that have become a midterm liability for Republicans during his remarks in Nebraska when he mentioned the possibility of an Iranian attack on U.S. soil.
“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe,” he said of the war and its economic fallout. “They can take out a city. Let ’em take out Los Angeles, let ’em take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay.”
The commentary was delivered in the familiar meandering style that he uses at campaign rallies, when he speaks for extended periods — often an hour or more — and is only occasionally following prepared remarks on a teleprompter.
Trump doesn’t commit to repaying federal funds already spent on controversial ads
A day after President Donald Trump said he would start paying for controversial taxpayer-funded ads with a campaign account, there’s no sign he plans to refund the millions of federal dollars already spent on them.
Nearly $12 million worth of ads have already aired, according to AdImpact, as part of the $20 million the Department of Homeland Security tapped for the contract.
But Trump’s plan to pay for the ads with MAGA Inc. doesn’t mean there’s any reimbursement coming, said a White House official who was not authorized to talk publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Speaking to reporters Tuesday, Trump said the ads were “really good” and “promotion for the country, done by many presidents before.” Asked whether he’d repay the funds already spent, he said, “We’ll decide.”
The ads, which began airing in late September, glorify Trump and echo his political messaging going into the midterms. Republicans and Democrats alike have said the ads aren’t an appropriate use of U.S. government money.

title: Army study found shock gloves purchased by ICE cause pain, compliance and fear
text:
(AP) - The shock gloves immigration agents could soon use to control detainees and protesters worked so powerfully during a military exercise that participants felt intense pain, stopped fighting immediately and feared additional exposures, according to a previously unreleased Army study.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement leaders were aware of the findings before signing a $16.7 million contract to purchase 6,000 pairs of shock gloves in August, according to records obtained by the watchdog group American Oversight and shared with The Associated Press.
The shocks had a profound impact on Army employees who played the role of combative prisoners during the exercise, which took place at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas in October 2024. The participants, several of whom were large-statured men, stopped resisting seconds after officers applied shocks by touching gloves to their skin, and were left with “fatigue, soreness and excessive apprehensiveness to being shocked again,” the study found.
“After experiencing the effects of the GLOVE, ... participants stated just seeing the GLOVE was enough to make them want to comply,” the authors wrote.
Watchdog says gloves cause pain and raise safety concerns
ICE has called the gloves “distraction and de-escalation devices” that will be safer than other non-lethal options to subdue targets for arrest and deportation and protesters who create civil disturbances. The agency has argued the rapid compliance they cause will keep officers safer and prevent incidents from requiring potentially lethal force.
But critics have warned the gloves will give ICE another weapon to intimidate and brutalize people even as the agency is under fire for excessive force that has left a trail of deaths and injuries across the nation. The gloves, they note, are easy to discharge, do not leave a mark and have not been extensively used in settings outside of jails. The manufacturer warns they should not be used on high-risk populations such as kids, pregnant women or disabled people.
“The military assessment in ICE’s own files shows that these gloves can cause ‘intense pain’ and force compliance. It does not establish that they are safe,” said Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight. “Everyone should be alarmed that ICE is preparing to deploy a tool designed to inflict, at best, intense pain, without showing that it is safe for the people who will be subjected to it.”
ICE released the study and other documents to American Oversight as part of the group’s Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the agency seeking records related to its use of force.
Army study found shock gloves triggered ‘immediate’ compliance
The military prison study assessed whether the gloves could be used effectively to forcibly remove combative prisoners from their cells, to respond to disturbances in common areas and to transport uncooperative inmates. Role-playing employees conducted several scenarios with and without the gloves to test their impact, including violent encounters in which inmates were to fight as hard as they could.
The study found the devices “increased the efficiency” of teams carrying out forced cell extractions and responding to disturbances by reducing the length of physical encounters, keeping guards from becoming exhausted and preventing injuries. They did not “significantly change” the time it took to control inmates during escorts but required less effort.
“GLOVE provides a boost in confidence to smaller or less trained members,” the study found. “Inmate compliance was immediate” compared to other methods, it added.
The electric jolt does not cause the body to freeze like a Taser shock does, but instead “works by overloading the peripheral nerve endings” of the skin to cause pain, the study said. Participants who were wet or had oil on their skin described even more powerful shocks, with one reporting discomfort for 30 minutes afterward.
Senator says ICE hasn’t responded to demand for details on glove use
ICE’s contract requires the manufacturer, Compliant Technologies LLC, to deliver the gloves within six months. Its owner, Jeff Niklaus, said he was unavailable for an interview, citing a busy workload.
White House border czar Tom Homan has said it could “be awhile” before the gloves are in the field because ICE is still ironing out training and policy issues. A statement released Tuesday by ICE did not address questions about the study and the status of the rollout, but said “officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics.”
U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said ICE has not responded to an Aug. 27 letter in which she and 15 other Democratic Senate colleagues called for ICE to abandon its plan to buy the gloves or explain how they would be used and managed to avoid abuse. She said she still wants answers.
“Without ICE’s responses to legitimate questions from 16 United States Senators, the American public is being left in the dark about how these electric shock gloves are being deployed and what, if any, training the agents who use them have received,” she said.

title: FBI says it stopped a Mall of America terror attack by a teen after agents sold him an assault rifle
text:
FBI says it stopped a Mall of America terror attack by a teen after agents sold him an assault rifle
FBI agents thwarted a terror attack by a teenager on the Mall of America after supplying him with an assault rifle following months of text messages, authorities said Wednesday.
The 18-year-old had been under investigation for nearly two years, trading messages with a confidential informant, before agents sold him the rifle and ammunition and arrested him on the spot, they said.
"This was a radicalized young man who needed to be watched," U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen said as he praised the FBI investigation. Agents "were able to detect a threat, and disrupt it, before the defendant carried out his intention to kill, in his words, maybe 30 to 60 people."
Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, 18, was arrested Tuesday in a public park in Richfield, several miles northwest of the Mall of America, after he paid $600 to an undercover FBI employee posing as a member of ISIS for an AK-47 and 200 rounds of ammunition, according to the criminal complaint.
Mohamud appeared in a yellow jail uniform for his initial hearing Wednesday in federal court in St. Paul.
In text messages with the informant, Mohamud repeatedly affirmed his intent to carry out an attack to kill non-Muslims at the mall on Oct. 24, the date of a scheduled Hmong arts celebration, the complaint said.
It was not immediately known if the teen had an attorney who might speak on his behalf. The Associated Press could not immediately identify any of his family members to contact for comment.
Rosen said Mohamud is an American-born U.S. citizen of Somali descent. According to the complaint, in his text messages he expressed admiration for recent terror attacks as well as an interest in traveling to Somalia to join ISIS. Ultimately he decided he couldn't afford to travel there and would attack the mall instead, it said.
The teen first came to the FBI's attention in December 2024, the same month the source began exchanging messages with him, the complaint said. By May 2025, agents were concerned enough that they went to his home. His mother told them he wasn't home from school yet and called the boy's father, who declined to speak with them and said he would give their contact information to his lawyer, the complaint said.
"What I would say to parents all over Minnesota, and all over America: If you get any indication — especially if you hear from federal law enforcement — that your son or daughter is being radicalized, to the point where federal law enforcement wants to come and give you that warning, those are warnings that ought to be heeded," Rosen said.
Tens of thousands of people of Somali descent live in Minnesota, dating back to when refugees began arriving in the 1990s. Over the years several have been charged with attempting to join ISIS or other terror groups.

title: Tropical Storm Isaias forms in the Gulf. Here’s what to know as it moves toward US
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - Tropical Storm Isaias formed Wednesday in the warm waters of eastern Mexico, and mandatory evacuations were issued for some coastal areas in Florida as forecasters predicted it would strengthen into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season before striking the U.S. Gulf Coast.
Communities in Isaias’ potential path moved quickly to prepare with landfall forecast as soon as Friday evening. Some Gulf oil wells paused production, and at least four Florida school districts canceled classes for later in the week while Okaloosa County announced mandatory evacuations for some coastal areas. Governors in Florida and Alabama declared a state of emergency for dozens of counties.
As it moves inland, Isaias might also disrupt Saturday’s college football showdown between rivals Georgia and Alabama — a game President Donald Trump has planned to attend.
Isaias could become a major, Category 3 hurricane with winds of 111 mph (178 kph) or stronger before it strikes land, said Michael Brennan, director of the U.S. National Hurricane Center.
“We’re expecting multiple dangerous, life-threatening impacts along portions of the northern Gulf Coast beginning Friday and continuing into the weekend,” Brennan said in a video briefing Wednesday.
The storm was on track to tie or break a 121-year-old record as the latest arriving initial hurricane of the Atlantic season. According to the National Weather Service, the record dates to 1905, when the first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8.
The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year because of a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over that ocean. Storm activity has been above average in the Pacific, where Tropical Storm Simon formed Wednesday off Mexico.
Storm surge threat extends from Louisiana to Florida
The Miami-based hurricane center issued a hurricane watch for the northern Gulf Coast from Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, to Indian Pass on the Florida Panhandle. The watch means hurricane conditions are possible within 48 hours.
Brennan said dangerous storm surge could affect an even wider area, from southeast Louisiana to Florida’s Big Bend. Heavy rains of 3 to 7 inches (7 to 18 centimeters) could trigger flash flooding near the coast, with accumulations of 1 to 3 inches (3 to 8 centimeters) as far inland as Tennessee and the western Carolinas.
Isaias was centered about 200 miles (325 kilometers) west-northwest of Progreso, Mexico, and about 480 miles (775 kilometers) south-southwest of the Mississippi River’s mouth, according to the hurricane center. It had maximum sustained winds of 65 mph (100 kph) and was moving east-northeast at 8 mph (13 kph).
Isaias (pronounced ees-ah-EE’-ahs, according to the hurricane center) was forecast to become a hurricane by Thursday as it turns northward toward the Gulf Coast. Though its path and timing could shift, the storm was expected to make landfall late Friday or early Saturday.
Isaias was expected to strike along a wide swath of coastline that is no stranger to major hurricanes. One of the 20th century’s worst storms, Hurricane Camille, killed more than 250 people after hitting land near Waveland, Mississippi, in 1969. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 ravaged neighborhoods in Mississippi, flooded New Orleans and killed nearly 1,400 people. And Hurricane Michael leveled homes and buildings near Panama City, Florida, in 2018.
Oil production and tourism already affected
Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the U.S.
As of Wednesday about 25% of the oil production in the region was temporarily halted, taking about 511,000 barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said eight of the Gulf’s 371 manned oil platforms were evacuated.
With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.
“I would characterize the oil market risk as moderate, but rising,” Burkhard said in an email.
In Gulf Shores, Alabama, organizers canceled the National Shrimp Festival, which had been scheduled for Thursday through the weekend. The event drew an estimated 325,000 people last year. Gulf Shores and Orange Beach issued a statement encouraging people in low-lying areas to voluntarily evacuate.
Gulf Shores resident Maranie Adams gathered water and other supplies as her family moved belongings, including a hot tub motor, to higher ground.
Adams said she, her husband and two adult sons planned to ride out the storm at home, roughly a half-mile from shore, sheltering indoors alongside their flock of chickens.
“We’re having to get crates to bring them into the house so they don’t blow away,” Adams said. “It’s going to be noisy.”
Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties, saying on the social platform X that, “While I hope for minimal impacts, we must take preparations seriously.”
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared one for 25 counties in the Panhandle and Big Bend regions. The declaration activates the state’s emergency management plan for hurricanes, allowing officials to deploy disaster responders and equipment. The state also planned to deploy a Miami-based urban search and rescue task force.
In Pensacola, electric utilities were pre-positioning crews to quickly repair any power outages. City officials provided sand for residents to fill sandbags to protect their homes against flooding. And Mayor D.C. Reeves urged people to check on older adult neighbors and others who might need help.
“Obviously no need to panic at this point,” Reeves told a news conference. “This is really about preparation.”
___
Rico reported from Atlanta, and Collins from Hartford, Connecticut. Associated Press journalists Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, Julie Walker in New York and Hallie Golden in Seattle contributed.

title: Donald M. Tomlin
text:
Donald M. Tomlin, Don, passed away May 18, 2026, in Damariscotta, Maine.
Born on Dec. 17, 1943, in Atlanta, Georgia, and raised in Buckhead, Don lived a full and meaningful life shaped by family, friends, good humor, and a deep appreciation for the places and people he loved. Don graduated from the Georgia Institute of Technology with a degree in mechanical engineering and began his career with Arthur Andersen & Co. in its Information Technology Division. He became a partner in 1977. After many successful years there, he moved to Miami Beach, Florida in 1994 and joined his friend, Rob Tabb, at Ryder Systems, Inc. Their division was outsourced, and Don continued his career with Florida Power & Light.
Don was married to Ellen Sutter Tomlin, and together they had four children: David, twins Jennifer and Deborah, and Scott. They have 12 grandchildren and 5 great-grandchildren. Following a divorce, Don met Claire Wilson Tomlin, who worked in the Arthur Andersen Tax Division. Claire's daughter, Evi, became like a fifth child to Don.
Don and Claire built a wonderful life together in Miami Beach, where they bought a home on the Venetian Islands and enjoyed their subtropical garden. Don especially enjoyed the view across his pool to the colorful bougainvillea. He was active in the community, serving on the board of the Miami Beach Community Development Corporation and as its chairman for five years. In addition, he played an important role in The Market Company, Inc., Claire's South Florida business, which she started in 1996 and continues today.
In 1994, Don and Claire traveled to Southwest Harbor, Maine, with their good friends, Rob and Anita Tabb, and stayed in a house beside the Mansell Boatyard near the Hinckley Barn. The Wooden Boat Show was taking place in the harbor, and they were immediately smitten with Maine. They returned every year on vacation and, in 2014, bought a cottage in Boothbay Harbor near the Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens, which became one of their favorite attractions. They joined the Boothbay Harbor Yacht Club in 2015 and Don served on the board for two consecutive terms. He became the club's certified ACBL Bridge Director. Don loved bridge and was a marvelous teacher, always happy to share what he knew. In May 2025, Don and Claire moved into their new home on Southport Island. Don knew Claire would love her home and garden just as he loved her.
During the pandemic, Don's friendship with Paul Schacknow deepened. Rarely a day passed without their having a conversation, no matter where either was.
Don was an eternal optimist, inspiring all who knew him with his belief in a righteous and moral world. He also had a marvelous sense of humor and frequently emailed friends jokes, cartoons, and funny aphorisms that brightened their day. He is remembered for his intelligence, warmth, wit, and loyalty, as well as for the love he gave so freely to his family and friends.
Don leaves behind a rich life in relationships, accomplishments, and cherished memories. We all miss him deeply.
At the Celebration of his Life at the Boothbay Harbor Yacht Club on Monday, Aug. 17 at 4 p.m., all of Don's children will attend, giving them a glimpse of his love for Maine.
Hall’s of Boothbay has care of arrangements. To leaveonline condolences, please visit hallfuneralhomes.com.

title: SCORES OUTDOORS: Signs of approaching winter
text:
OK, this is the time of year when I stick out my neck, and defy all the experts when it comes to predicting the upcoming winter – I was right last year and they were wrong. All of the ads on TV and radio this past month or so were reporting a tough and harsh 2026-27 winter for Maine. The one common denominator in all of these brainwashing advertisements is that the sellers were pushing snowblowers, snowmobiles, ridiculously large trucks with plows, home heating materials, etc. Get the drift?
Well, I have come up with something that contradicts even the usually reliable publications on that subject.
As in the past, if you have read this column, I rely more on Mother Nature to provide me with the signs of the impending winter months.
First, we will go to the annual cicadae, you know, the little guy you never see that gives off that loud buzzing sound during the hot summer months. Old farmers lore says that from the date you first hear its call, the first killing frost will occur 90 days later, following the full moon. We have a little controversy on that issue this year. Traditionally, you will hear it anywhere from early to late July, bringing the first killing frost in October. This year, with the strong objections from my wife, I have yet to hear one. However, she claims she heard them back around July 26, and continues to insist she has heard them. Their sound is usually quite distinct. If they have been buzzing, they are extremely faint. My wife has claimed for some time now that I am going deaf, much to the differing opinion of my doctor.
It is called the annual cicadae because it makes an appearance yearly, as opposed to the periodical cicadae, that you hear about in the news, that occurs in large swarms only every 13 – 17 years.
Cicadaes typically live in trees, feeding on sap, and laying their eggs in a slit in the bark.
Cicadaes have been featured in literature since the time of Homer’s Iliad, and as motifs in art from the Chinese Shang dynasty. They are also eaten in China, where the nymphs are served deep fried in Shandong cuisine.
But, I’m venturing from the topic.
The second indicator of what I am believing will be another mild winter is the placement of bee hives. All summer, I have heard reports from various people of finding the hives in the ground or at the bottom of trees and tree stumps. Many have been stung while mowing their lawns. That is a usual telltale sign of below normal snowfall. When we have winters with higher than normal precipitation, bee hives are usually located higher, sometimes in trees or under eaves of outbuildings. I actually had two bee hives constructed under the floor boards of my deck at camp. Pretty low to the ground, about 10 inches.
A third sign is the common yellow onion. My mother told me many years ago you can tell the severity of an upcoming winter by how the onion peels and its strength. The easier it is to peel, and the milder the taste, the more tame the winter. If an onion is really strong, and is difficult to peel, it means a harsh winter. My wife and I have onions often, so we have peeled our share, and they have peeled awfully easy this summer, and the juices that irritate the eyes have been pretty mild .
Finally, old faithful, the wooly bear caterpillar. For those who don’t know, old folklore states the wider the red band on a wooly bear, the milder the winter. Usually by now, early October, you would have seen many of these fuzzy little creatures. So far, I have seen only one, and the rust-colored band on this particular one was very long, occupying possibly one-half to two-thirds of its body. I’m predicating my prediction on this one sighting, which, scientifically, is a small sample size. (See the October 1, 2026, issue of The Town Line, page 7).
So, with all the evidence presented, I will make a bold prediction that we are facing another mild winter ahead of us. But, I can’t tell you whether it will be as mild as last winter, but relatively speaking, milder than an average Maine winter.
Just don’t tar and feather me if we end up with mounds of snow and consistent below zero temperatures. I can only foretell based on what the natural data suggests.
Roland’s trivia question of the week:
Prior to this season, who and when was the last pitcher to win 20 games in a season for the Boston Red Sox?
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!

title: Midcoast Maine braces for a pricey winter
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Like many midcoast residents, Camden resident Electa Cerce anticipates having to tighten her budget this winter.
The 70-year-old retiree plans to cut back spending on Christmas gifts and holiday festivities. She may cancel the MLB.TV subscription she purchases for her grandson. And she will have to spread out payments to MaineHealth for the cost of her husband’s recent surgeries instead of paying it all at once.
She hopes these adjustments allow her to purchase the heating oil she needs to keep her family warm in the coming months.
“If oil prices don’t go any higher, we should be OK,” Cerce said. “But it will be tricky.”
Many others will be forced to choose between going cold, dipping into savings, turning to unsafe heating sources or seeking financial assistance from the state, which hopes to have enough funding to help everyone who needs it.
“We are in an unprecedented territory,” said Celina Cunningham, the acting commissioner of the Maine Department of Energy Resources. “The prices are going up just as it’s starting to get colder.”
The average price of heating oil in the state hit a record high of more than $6 per gallon last month — and as of Sept. 28, was up 80% over the same time last year, according to the department, with prices in the midcoast trending slightly above the statewide average.
That equates to an extra roughly $725 to refill a standard 275-gallon tank, which might need refilling every few weeks in the winter.
Maine is more dependent on home heating oil than most of the country, with roughly half of households using fuel to heat, making Mainers especially susceptible to the fuel’s cost volatility.
The price increase has been driven by the U.S. and Israel’s ongoing war with Iran, which has disrupted oil supplies worldwide. The previous record for heating oil of $5.92 per gallon was set in the spring of 2022 after Russia invaded Ukraine. But that spike came toward the end of the heating season in late spring and prices fell again relatively quickly. This time, the spike is coming before many Mainers have filled their tanks for the winter.
“People have been paying attention to gas prices going up, but not so much to heating oil,” said Mary Ellen Eagan, who’s the board president of WindowDressers.
The organization produces low-cost and custom insulating window inserts, which Eagan said provide increased comfort and reduced fuel costs. The inserts have to be requested well ahead of winter so they can be measured over the summer and built in the fall. But Eagan anticipates there will soon be an uptick of people looking for custom inserts.
“We’re trying to organize an emergency sort of sprint build for this,” she said.
Heating assistance
The price jump will be particularly difficult for lower-income households and seniors on fixed incomes to navigate. Many already turn their thermostats down and let their houses run cold. They’ll have to make difficult decisions about how much money to direct toward different necessities, said Anne Saggese, a volunteer and board member at the Waldo County Woodshed.
“It’s kind of an impossible choice,” she said.
The nonprofit distributes free firewood to people who rely on wood for heat and always runs out before the cold season is over.
“We expect that this year is going to have a higher need, and we’re going to run out earlier,” she said.
The state encouraged residents struggling with heat costs to apply for aid through the Home Energy Assistance Program, which is administered by MaineHousing and funded by the federal government.
Eligibility for the once-per-season subsidy is determined by household income and size. Applications remain open until May 29 or funds are exhausted, but the state encouraged residents to apply early. Applications are already up 5%, the state said.
“It’s not designed to pay a household’s full fuel bill,” explained Sarah Johnson, who manages HEAP for MaineHousing. “It’s a one-time annual assistance.”
The average benefit last year was $570, and it’s projected to increase this year, with Johnson hoping for around $700. At current prices, that would still purchase fewer gallons of oil, however.
The funds are distributed through nine community action agencies and usually go directly to fuel vendors. Locally, those agencies are the Waldo Community Action Partners and the Rockland office of Penquis Community Action.
Last year, MaineHousing was able to provide assistance to every eligible Mainer who applied to HEAP, Johnson said. That was about 44,000 people.
“We do try to manage as best as possible to assist as many households statewide,” Johnson said.
Johnson recognized that households will have greater needs this winter because of the rising costs. She still encouraged everybody who’s eligible for HEAP to apply. The program will move to a waitlist if necessary, she said.
The federal government has not yet released funding for this year’s Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, which funds the state’s program. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services is required by law to release 90% of the money by Nov. 1.
A bipartisan group of lawmakers, including U.S. Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King, recently urged the department to distribute the funding well before the deadline.
“State agencies and tribes are already activating their LIHEAP programs for the coming winter. A quick release of funding will ensure no gaps in assistance,” the lawmakers wrote in a letter last month.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly tried to eliminate the program, which he called “unnecessary” in his official budget proposal for the next fiscal year, saying he would “instead support low-income individuals through lower energy prices and an America First economic platform.”
Earlier this year, Trump fired the staff that administers the federal program and withheld funding for heating assistance that had already been appropriated, which ended up later being released.
Maine’s heating assistance program has not been affected by Trump’s actions and threats, Johnson said, noting the program has strong bipartisan support and has been funded stably.
Still, candidates in both parties have called for more heating assistance as they campaign ahead of the critical November election.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree has called on the federal government to double its funding for Maine’s heating assistance program to meet the “unprecedented need.”
“Providing relief this winter will be urgent and with this war continuing to push prices, the state and federal government needs to step up,” she wrote in a statement last month.
Gov. Janet Mills also asked Congress to provide the state with additional home heating assistance.
Bobby Charles, the Republican nominee for governor who has aligned himself with Trump, has proposed tapping the state’s “rainy day fund” to supplement LIHEAP funding.
Charles also voiced support for Collins and King’s request that Trump release home heating oil from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve, which the senators have said would help ease oil prices.
Another staunch Trump ally, Republican former Gov. Paul LePage, now running for the open 2nd Congressional District seat, said he would personally call Trump to make sure the administration distributes LIHEAP money on time since “they did not do that last year.”
In addition to applying for HEAP, eligible households can apply for Maine’s Energy Crisis Intervention Program, which offers emergency fuel assistance. And, Johnson said, they should utilize the state’s Low Income Assistance Plan to receive credits on their electric bills.
Alternative heating options
The fuel prices have some Mainers turning to other sources for warmth in the coming months.
Matt Wagner, who owns Upright Energy, said he’s seen an uptick in interest in heat pump installations over the past few months as people look to take advantage of Efficiency Maine rebates.
“A lot of people have already transitioned to heat pumps,” he said. “They’re going to benefit.”
Electricity prices have risen as well, but heat pumps’ efficiency still gives them the edge. According to the latest state data on fuel prices, a kerosene furnace costs about $72 to produce one million units of heat, while a heat pump produces the same amount for just under $35.
Some heat pump and insulation contractors have growing backlogs because of the public’s anxiety over oil prices, said Bridget Gifford, a senior program manager at Efficiency Maine.
Residents should also prioritize weatherizing their homes and keeping cold air out, she said. Efficiency Maine recommends insulating windows, installing door sweeps and sealing cracks with caulk or spray foam. The state Department of Energy Resources has more resources in its Home Heating Guide and tracks current prices of a wide range of heating options throughout the winter, from electricity to cordwood.
Local fire departments are concerned about the expected increase in people heating with wood or turning to risky improvised methods, like kitchen ovens or using space heaters in ways they were not designed.
Belfast Deputy Fire Chief Chris Kulbe said the department is “acutely aware” there could be more fires this winter, anticipating that people who have never burned wood before or haven’t in years might use appliances that have not been inspected or are unsafe.
Chimneys need regular cleaning and inspection, he said, urging Mainers burning wood to make sure they have working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors.
“If you’re going to do something different, please seek the help of a professional,” he said. “Make sure you understand what you’re doing and what the risks are.”

title: In first Maine Senate debate, Sen. Collins seeks to distance herself from President Trump
text:
Maine (AP) - Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins distanced herself from President Donald Trump during her first Maine Senate debate with Democrat Troy Jackson, arguing she has maintained her political independence by repeatedly voting against Trump’s agenda and saying that she’s “not exactly his favorite senator.”
Democrats are trying to flip the Maine Senate seat as they work to win control of the Senate. President Trump lost the state in 2024, giving Democrats hope of defeating the five-term moderate Republican, who has been targeted by Democrats in previous elections and survived.
During the hourlong debate, Jackson focused largely on attempting to connect Collins to Trump. He kicked off the night by pointing out she cast a critical vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Trump nominee who eventually helped overturn the constitutional right to abortion. Collins supports abortion rights and said Kavanaugh assured her it was settled law, but she has said recently that she does not regret her vote to confirm him.
“Would you trust her to pick the next Supreme Court justice?” asked Jackson, a former state lawmaker and logger.
He also repeatedly brought up her procedural vote to advance the president’s 2025 tax and spending bill — though Collins ultimately broke with her party to vote against it.
Collins countered that she has voted against Trump more than she did Joe Biden when the Democrat was president, and has pushed back against Trump on tariffs, immigration enforcement and the war in Iran.
“I voted against my party more than another other senator on either side of the aisle,” Collins said.
The attention on Trump comes as only 31% of U.S. adults approved of how the Republican is handling the presidency, according to a September AP-NORC poll. That’s well below where his approval stood when he took office last year.
The president has started holding rallies around the country in an effort to help GOP candidates win in November, telling voters to pretend he is on the ballot. At Tuesday’s debate, a moderator noted Trump has floated the idea of campaigning in Maine, and asked Collins if she would stand beside him if he does.
“I’m not exactly his favorite senator,” she said, adding “I would say that he’s not coming to Maine.”
Collins, who has said she didn’t vote for Trump in 2016, voted to convict the president after his 2021 impeachment over his role in the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. In January, Collins joined a handful of Republican colleagues in backing a failed effort to limit the president’s ability to unilaterally use force in Venezuela. The move prompted Trump to say on social media that they “should never be elected to office again.”
Collins argued that her seniority and experience in the Senate have resulted in money and resources for Maine, saying: “Leadership matters in Washington.”
She also spent Tuesday evening attempting to turn the focus of Maine’s high cost of energy and housing on Jackson, arguing that he had a larger role in making a difference when he was the state Senate president and criticizing “Augusta’s failed policies” as a way to connect Jackson’s to the state’s struggle to address affordability.
Other moments showed how the two candidates were approaching their appeal to working class Maine voters. For example, as Collins touted her ability to remove certain items from Trump’s trade war with Canada, including pulp, concrete and road salt. Jackson pushed back by quipping “we can’t eat road salt.”
Jackson and Collins are scheduled to participate in three more debates later this month.

title: Death Notice: Linda A. Elwell
Democrat files ethics complaint against Susan Collins over alleged pay-to-play scheme
text:
A former Democratic candidate for Cumberland County District Attorney on Wednesday filed a formal ethics complaint against Republican Sen. Susan Collins over pay-to-play allegations involving a defense contractor.
Attorney Valerie Adams asked the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Ethics to conduct an investigation into the allegations outlined in a recent ProPublica report that Collins agreed to steer millions of dollars in contracts to the Hawaii-based firm Navatek in exchange for political donations from its CEO, Martin Kao.
“It is difficult to conceive of behavior more improper than accepting campaign contributions in return for directing taxpayer funded government contracts to an out of state company,” Adams said in a letter to Chairman James Lankford, R-Okla., and Vice Chairman Christopher Coons, D-Del., obtained by the Portland Press Herald.
“The reporting from ProPublica suggests Senator Collins may have done just that,” she continued. “It is the Committee’s duty to get to the bottom of this.”
Collins and her campaign have repeatedly denied the allegations outlined in the ProPublica article, calling them “outrageous.”
It’s unclear what — if anything — will become of the ethics complaint. Such complaints can be filed by anybody online. The ethics committee is a bipartisan body, with three Republicans and three Democrats. Most such complaints get dismissed, although the committee has investigated senators in the past, probing then Democratic Sen. Al Franken for alleged sexual misconduct in 2017, and then-Sen. Robert Menendez of New Jersey in 2018 for improperly accepting gifts.
“This is getting to be pathetic,” Collins campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen said in a statement. “For the third consecutive week, a recently failed Democratic candidate has parroted false charges that they know nothing about against Susan Collins.”
The filing comes as Democrats are working to amplify the corruption allegations against Collins. In doing so, they are trying to put a negative light on her central argument for reelection — that she is wielding her power as chair of the appropriations committee to benefit Maine.
In her letter, Adams asked the committee to “urgently investigate whether Senator Collins engaged in improper conduct that reflects discredit upon the Senate” by:
- Steering $8 million in contracts to Navatek in exchange for political donations;
- Knowingly accepting contributions made in the name of another in violation of campaign finance law; or
- Working with President Donald Trump to stop the investigation.
In an interview Wednesday, Adams dismissed any suggestion that the complaint was politically motivated or aimed at influencing voters in Maine’s U.S. Senate race. She described herself as a former Collins supporter.
Adams said she was troubled by what ProPublica reported and believes the allegations should be looked into.
“There’s never been a more important time to demand the best of our elected officials,” Adams said. “And I truly believe that.”
In a televised debate on Tuesday, Collins said she began working with Navatek in 2017 — the year before she received any donations from Kao. The company was partnering with the University of Maine on a project for the U.S. Navy that sought federal funding.
“I worked very closely with the university. We advanced that proposal,” Collins said. “The head of Navatek at the time, unfortunately, was a crook. He is now in jail, where he belongs.”
ProPublica reported that Kao told FBI investigators that Collins would not meet with him in 2018 unless he donated to her reelection effort. But Collins’ campaign on Tuesday showed a timestamped photo of Collins and Kao meeting in the senator’s office in February 2018 — months before Kao made a donation to her campaign.
The ProPublica article also detailed how Kao told investigators that he worked with the leader of a Collins-aligned super PAC to exchange a six-figure donation to her 2020 reelection effort for millions in government contracts.
Kao made an illegal $150,000 donation to the Collins-aligned 1820 PAC through a shell company, since federal contractors are barred from contributing to campaigns. ProPublica reported that Kao told Scott Reed, the head of the pro-Collins Super PAC, about his plan to use a shell company to make the donation.
Kao pleaded guilty to charges involving money laundering and bank fraud in 2022, and is currently in federal prison. He had been cooperating with federal investigators in an effort to get his sentence reduced. Collins’ team has said he is not credible, pointing to his convictions.
Collins’ campaign manager Steve Abbott said on Tuesday that neither Collins nor her campaign were accused of wrongdoing after answering questions about Kao in 2021 — and that nobody in the senator’s office was contacted about any new investigations thereafter.

title: UMaine football players must step up after firing of offensive coordinator
text:
Something had to be done.
The University of Maine’s football team went from showing intriguing promise after a 21-18 win at Towson in its season-opener to facing the prospect that its first victory could be the only one of the season.
There is plenty of blame to go around in all areas of the game: offense, defense and special teams.
The first victim of the 1-5 campaign was offensive coordinator/quarterbacks coach Mikahael Waters, who was fired Monday.
As the adage goes, it’s easier to fire one coach than jettison dozens of players.
The numbers validate the decision as the offense ranks 90th or worse among 124 Football Championship Subdivision teams in seven offensive categories, including points scored per game (14.5, 118th) and yards gained (270.2, 115th).
Since scoring three touchdowns in the second quarter of the win over Towson, the Black Bears have had 66 offensive possessions and tallied just six touchdowns and six field goals in those 66 series.
“We have a very talented roster. We have done a lot of good things, but we have to be more consistent. We need to score more points,” UMaine fifth-year head coach Jordan Stevens said Tuesday. “We have to spread the ball around and put it in the the hands of the guys who can make plays. This is a production business. We have to win football games.”
First-year running backs coach Sean Green, who led Portland and Cape Elizabeth high schools to state championships, will take over as offensive coordinator/quarterbacks coach, but Stevens was quick to point out that Green will get plenty of help from the rest of the staff.
“It all starts with me, and I have to do a better job. I have to coach better. We need to put our players into better position to make plays, and that’s from a confidence standpoint and an execution standpoint. When we talk about execution, that’s not on the players. That’s on us,” Stevens said.
“We have to make sure the guys can execute at a high level, and that’s blocking, tackling, catching the football, throwing the football, and, on special teams, it’s about catching punts, catching kickoffs and covering kicks. It’s about playing complementary football. That’s how you win games,” he said.
The Black Bear offense has been conservative and unimaginative, and that, in turn, has made it more predictable and easier to defend.
UMaine began the season with a veteran offensive line that was supposed to be the strength of the team. Four interior starters returned.
But the line has underperformed.
Making the line’s job more difficult has been the fact opposing defensive coordinators have been loading up the box at the line of scrimmage to take away UMaine’s running game and forcing its two inexperienced quarterbacks to make throws to beat them.
And the completion rate of Eddie Buehler and Caden Drezek is 52%, which ranks 113th in the FCS. Buehler has been intercepted six times.
In addition, the receivers have had countless drops, including a crucial one that could have set UMaine up inside the Sacred Heart-20 yard line late in the 24-16 loss to the Pioneers on Saturday. That was the scoreline at the time of the drop.
UMaine’s offense has to become more diversified and adventurous.
Part of the reason it was conservative is you have two quarterbacks with little or no experience, and flooding them with a packed playbook could be counter-productive.
But you still have to throw in a reverse or two or a flea flicker, where a quarterback gets the ball back from a running back after first handing the ball off to him and then the quarterback throws a pass. You can also mix in a different formation or two like UMaine did against Sacred Heart by lining up four players in an I-formation before they branched out before the snap.
It created a productive play.
These types of plays make a defense uncomfortable and tentative. They can’t be as aggressive because that could leave them out of position and incapable of making a play.
Running backs Rashawn Marshall and Nick Laughlin came into the season off injuries, and the current bye week should help both continue to get back to 100%. Marshall is UMaine’s leading rusher, and Laughlin is its top receiver.
Marshall has had a recent resurgence, averaging 86 rushing yards per game over his past two games after averaging 58.7 in his first three.
Waters may have been too conservative, but it is ultimately up to the players to do their jobs and they haven’t been. They need to take a look at themselves and step up.
Waters is a class act and will land on his feet, somewhere.
The defense and special teams aren’t absolved from blame either.
For the most part, the defense has been respectable and has kept the team in games, but it has also been unable to come up with stops at critical times.
The defense was stout for 24 minutes in the loss to Sacred Heart, and it appeared UMaine’s 9-0 lead might even be able to stand up.
But the Pioneers promptly strung together drives of 79 and 81 in the second quarter to take a 14-9 lead into the intermission, and they promptly marched 75 yards to open the second half and built the lead to 21-9.
In the previous week’s 43-17 loss to Elon, the UMaine defense surrendered touchdown plays of 57, 55 and 39 yards.
In the 23-14 loss to Merrimack, UMaine pulled within 14-11 with 3:50 left in the third period with a touchdown and a two-point conversion, but the Warriors scored on their next possession to regain the momentum.
The special teams have received a perfect 8-for-8 showing on field goals from Sam Tremblay, but they have had three punts blocked, an extra-point blocked and they have fumbled away a punt and a kickoff.
Stevens stressed they are committed to finishing strong and winning football games and time will tell if the offense can become consistently productive with an interim coordinator with some new ideas.
UMaine plays again when it hosts Bryant at 1 p.m. Oct. 17.

title: Oversized again: Second load to start journey from Jay mill
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
JAY, Maine (WMTW) - The first delivery of oversized equipment from the former mill in Jay to South Portland was completed on Tuesday morning. Crews will start to move the second so-called superload on Wednesday night. There are a total of nine loads to be moved the nearly 100 miles.
Barnhart Crane & Rigging will be the moving contractor for each delivery, and each load will follow the same route and timeline. Drivers should expect the same traffic impacts, delays and closures that they faced during the first transport over the last week.
The equipment, a heat recovery steam generator, is coming from the former Pixelle/International Paper mill in Jay. The property is now owned by JGT2, the company that wants to turn the site into a data center.
A heat recovery steam generator (HRSG) is an energy recovery heat exchanger that captures hot exhaust gases from a gas turbine or industrial process to produce high-pressure steam
Police said the load is just over 219 feet long, 20 feet wide, 19.5 feet high and has a gross weight of 683,530 pounds. Due to the size, the load and support team will take up most, if not all, of the road in several areas and crews from Central Maine Power will be lifting and moving power lines out of the way.
“We’ve got a tractor pulling and a tractor pushing because the magnitude of the load would be too great for one tractor to pull and take care of on its own,” said Lucien Richard, site manager for JGT2 Redevelopment.

title: 3 adults, 1 teen charged after throwing pineapple at passing Tesla, police say
text:
WEST CHESTER TOWNSHIP, Ohio (WXIX/Gray News) — Four people have been charged after allegedly throwing a pineapple at another vehicle in Ohio, police said.
Jacob Braun, 18, Bronson Moore, 18, Danden Schlake, 18, and a 17-year-old were charged after West Chester Township police responded Thursday night to a report of criminal damage to a vehicle.
A man told police that he was driving his Tesla on a roadway when a gray Chevrolet traveling in the opposite direction threw a pineapple at his car, hitting the front windshield and causing “significant” damage.
Police said the call was the third report of people throwing objects from a car that night, with several callers reporting eggs and ice being thrown.
Police spotted the suspect vehicle a short time later and made a traffic stop. Police said the officer noticed egg yolk dried all over the vehicle when approaching it.
Braun, Moore and the juvenile were all charged with complicity and vehicular vandalism, while Schlake was only charged with complicity.
West Chester police and the Warren County Sheriff’s Office are investigating.

title: Waterskiing squirrel wraps up stint at state fair
text:
Waterskiing squirrel wraps up stint at state fair
Waterskiing squirrel wraps up stint at state fair
Visitors to a fair in North Carolina got to catch Twiggy the waterskiing squirrel in action.
Twiggy wows people with her ability to navigate the waters, making waves across the nation.
The squirrel has been featured in movies, TV shows and even music videos.
"It's like training a dog or cat," said Twiggy's owner, Chuck Best Jr. "We do the training during the show."
But beyond the fun and delight of the waterskiing squirrel lies a deeper story.
Twiggy promotes water safety. That stems from a terrible accident nearly 30 years ago.
"My dad lost his life in a boating accident in '97, saving my grandfather," said Best. "So, my mom put a life jacket on the squirrel to promote water safety."
The show is a family affair that honors his dad's memory, while also spreading joy to everyone who experiences it.
Twiggy's final show at the Carolina Classic Fair this year was Tuesday night. She's now heading to South Carolina.

title: Christa Pike survived 2 doses of an execution drug. How is that possible?
text:
Christa Pike regaining consciousness and speaking a week after receiving two doses of execution drugs in Tennessee has left a stunning question: How did she survive?
Attorneys for Pike, 50, called her recovery “medically unprecedented” after she was placed on a ventilator following the bungled Sept. 30 attempt to make her the first woman put to death in Tennessee in 200 years. On Tuesday, they said her prognosis is uncertain and they expect a long recovery.
Many details of the execution process remain secretive and Tennessee officials say they are investigating what went wrong.
Still, medical experts raised a few possibilities that could explain how Pike was able to survive the injections, including the potential drug quality and the placement of IV lines. Tennessee’s executioners had difficulties earlier this year with IV lines for another execution, leading to it being called off.
Only a small amount of the drug may have entered her bloodstream
The 5-gram dose of pentobarbital used in executions is many more times the amount than what should put someone in a medical coma, said Dr. Jonathan I. Groner, a retired pediatric general surgeon at Ohio State University College of Medicine who has studied lethal injections.
“The fact that she woke, on one hand, says she got really little of it into her system. So that’s kind of shocking,” Groner said. “It says how badly they botched the execution.”
At high doses the potent barbiturate should make a person lose consciousness, stop breathing and stop their heart.
Groner said the IV might have been placed improperly, or Pike’s veins could have been fragile and burst, causing the drug to seep into the surrounding tissue instead of flowing through the bloodstream. Pike’s attorneys have said she was poked with needles at least seven times in the state’s death chamber and that she has a lifelong blood disorder that makes it tough to get needles into her veins.
Sourcing of drugs for executions is shrouded in secrecy
Another possible problem could be the drug quality, said Michaela Almgren, a South Carolina pharmacist and educator who has consulted on several lethal injection cases.
Many major pharmaceutical companies refuse to supply drugs for lethal injections, which has raised questions about how states get them. Court orders have revealed that some states have turned to compounding pharmacies, which create custom drugs from raw ingredients and operate with less regulatory oversight.
Tennessee does not disclose its drug supplier and has not said where Pike’s supply came from. Almgren said that makes it difficult to track if a drug was prepared, tested, handled and administered properly.
That also means the public may never know exactly what happened in Pike’s case.
Pike’s attorneys are seeking a court order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence, including drug lot numbers, records and other information from the attempted execution.
Outgoing Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee paused executions and ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred” with Pike.
Hospital treatment likely involved flushing the drug from her body
Before the execution attempt, Pike’s attorneys told courts and prison officials that she had medical conditions that could complicate a lethal injection and make it agonizing.
Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike’s legal team, said Pike has a blood-clotting disorder that causes her body to produce an excess of platelets. Her lawyers had argued that the condition could cause clotting at injection sites or bleeding that could affect her lungs.
State protocol calls for a second dose of pentobarbital if the first doesn’t result in death, but it doesn’t spell out what to do if an inmate survives the second injection.
The attempted execution got underway around 7:30 p.m. on Sept. 30 when Pike was given a chance to make a final statement. About five minutes later, Pike raised her head and said her arm was hurting. At some point she appeared to lose consciousness, but she could be heard audibly breathing until media were escorted from the witness room at 8:53 p.m. An ambulance arrived at the prison at 9:14 p.m. to take Pike to a hospital.
When Pike arrived at the hospital, doctors likely tried to stabilize her breathing, checked how much pentobarbital was in her system and worked to quickly flush it out, said Dr. Michael Baden, the former chief medical examiner of New York City. Doctors may have also been dealing with muscle damage, both from the effects of the pentobarbital and because some may have entered muscle tissue near the injection site, he said.
Pike’s lawyers said her arms were left burned and blistered from the failed attempt. She was unconscious and on a ventilator for several days.
“She was very fortunate that there was enough (pentobarbital) to put her into a deep sleep, but they were able to keep her breathing going and they were able to start flushing it out,” Zivot said.
___
Associated Press writer Kim Chandler in Montgomery, Alabama, contributed to this report.

title: Poland and Greely girls soccer battle to draw
text:
POLAND — After Poland began its season with six wins and a tie through seven games, Juan Bustamante knew that some difficult opponents still awaited the Knights.
Among those teams was Greely, and when the Class B South foes did finally meet on Wednesday, the result was a 2-2 tie.
“It was a tough game,” said Bustamante. “We’re happy to honestly come away with a tie with that. We wanted to win, though. We came out fast. But yeah, good competitive game.”
Poland (8-1-2), ranked third in the Class B South Heal point standings, has three games remaining, against Old Orchard Beach, North Yarmouth Academy and Waynflete. Sixth-ranked Greely (5-3-2) plays Gray-New Gloucester next and finishes with games against three of the region’s top five teams — Cape Elizabeth, Freeport and Yarmouth.
“It was a little bit of a battle, but at the same time, (to) get out of here with the points is important in the tie, so overall, happy with the kids for battling,” Greely coach Neil Carroll said. “It’s something we haven’t faced yet, so happy with them to do that.”
The Rangers also played region-leading Cape Elizabeth to a draw on Saturday.
HOW IT HAPPENED
Poland got on the scoreboard first, about six and half minutes into the game. Greely keeper Rylee Begin tried to kick the ball away from the goal, but it defected off Julia Paradis as she leaped into the air and wound up in the net.
Just over five minutes into the second half, Tess Waterhouse scored the equalizer for the Rangers. After a corner kick by Waterhouse, the ball bounced back to her and she lofted it into the far corner from a sharp angle.
It took Poland just 51 seconds to regain the lead, as Leksi Langevin scored from close range after a direct kick by Phoebe Paradis.
Greely had several looks at another equalizer, but it didn’t come until a little over 18 minutes later, again off a corner kick, as Simone Couture set up Victoria Zandan.
The Rangers nearly scored late in the first overtime, but Payton Seekins missed wide left. Late in the second overtime, a header by Poland’s Davis Hill hit the crossbar.
HEARD IT HERE FIRST
• “The girls are really hungry, and we want a home (playoff) game, so that’s what we’re looking for.” — Poland coach Juan Bustamante
• “In the last couple weeks, (the players have) kind of found a little bit different energy, and the culture has changed a little bit in our first year. And give props to the captains, really. They’ve done a great job helping us create that.” — Greely coach Neil Carroll
