• Poland: Julia Paradis (goal), Leksi Langevin (goal)
• Greely: Tess Waterhouse (goal), Victoria Zandan (goal), Simone Couture (assist)

title: Obituary: Lorraine (Mohrman) Hepler
text:
GORHAM – Lorraine (Mohrman) Hepler, of Gorham, died peacefully at home on Sept. 29, 2026.
Born in St. Louis, Mo. to William and Alice Mohrman, Lorraine was the first in her family to attend college. After graduating from Jennings High School, she earned a bachelor’s degree in education from Southeast Missouri State Teachers College. She taught at Ferguson High School during the final year of segregation and the first year of desegregation, then continued her education at Columbia University, earning a master’s degree in education. While living at International House in New York City, N.Y., she made friends from around the world, beginning a lifelong appreciation of other cultures and the stories of people from every background. She later pursued a PhD at the University of Iowa.
Lorraine began her career teaching Physical Education at the University of Maine at Orono, where she met Paul Hepler, a horticulture professor. He won her over with fresh tomatoes and vegetables from his garden. They married on Sept. 7, 1959.
After leaving UMO, Lorraine devoted herself to raising their four rambunctious children. She eventually returned to teaching and coaching at the high school level before beginning a long, successful career in school fundraising.
Determined, independent, curious, and adventurous, Lorraine traveled extensively well into her 80s. Her home was a welcoming gathering place for international students, travelers, and friends, many of whom became like family. She believed in giving back, generously supporting causes that reflected her deep concern for the world around her.
She was wonderfully feisty, with a quick wit, an ever-ready joke, and an ability to be both formidable and deeply warm. Lorraine had a gift for making connections, and her generosity, humor, curiosity, and independent spirit left an indelible mark on those who knew her.
Lorraine was predeceased by her husband, Paul; brothers William and Roland Mohrman; her Danish international student son, Bent Fuglsbjerg; and beloved border collies Bacchus and BJ.
She is survived by her children, Sharon Hepler, MD, of Plymouth, Minn., Raymond Hepler and wife, Karin, of Healdsburg, Calif., Allen Hepler and wife, Kathrine, of Stetson, Bruce Hepler of Gorham, and Chilean international student son, Luis Morales Delannoi of Santiago, Chile. She also leaves behind grandchildren Rebecca and husband, Mike, Sarah, Eric, Irja, Ada and husband, Josh, Sophie, William, Joseph, Rose, AJ, Lydia and husband, Stephen, and Alexandra; as well as great-grandchildren Harper, Keller, Palmer, Porter, and baby Stephen.
Following a weekend of reminiscing, story-telling, and laughter, with family who had gathered from around the country, Lorraine slipped away quietly, off to her next great adventure.
Please join us for a Celebration of Life on Nov. 7 from 12 p.m. to 3 p.m. at the White Rock Grange, 33 Wilson Rd., in Gorham.
In lieu of flowers, please consider donating in her name to International House (www.ihouse-nyc.org), the Reed Allen Community Fund (ReedAllen.org), or any cause aligned with your friendship with Lorraine.

title: A pair of late-night earthquakes shook Maine
text:
A pair of earthquakes rattled Maine late Sunday night.
The first temblor, a magnitude 1.5, shook the ground at a depth of more than 6 miles about 1 mile west-southwest of the Waldo County town of Jackson about 10:23 p.m., according to the U.S. Geological Survey.
That was followed by a magnitude 1.6 quake that hit nearly 4 miles deep about 4 miles south of the Piscataquis County town of Sebec at 10:59 p.m., the U.S. Geological Survey reported.
Since 1997, there have been more than 170 recorded earthquakes in the state, according to the Maine Geological Survey.
The strongest quake in recent memory occurred on Oct. 16, 2012, when a 4.5 magnitude earthquake shook the ground in East Waterboro, according to the Maine Geological Survey. But Maine has felt the impact of much larger earthquakes that hit as far away as Plattsburgh, New York, and Quebec City.
Recorded quakes tend to be clustered near Passamaquoddy Bay, the Dover-Foxcroft-Milo area and southwestern Maine. Of course, earthquakes have been felt across Maine, even as far north as the St. John Valley, according to a Maine Geological Survey report.
Every so often quakes happen in clusters. That happened off York Harbor between Jan. 27 and Feb. 2, 2024, when three quakes ranging from magnitude 2 to 3.8. It happened again near Jonesboro between Aug. 11 and Sept. 1, 2022, when about nine earthquakes ranging from magnitude 1.7 to 3 shook the ground. Before that there was the cluster of six quakes east of Cadillac Mountain on Mount Desert Island from Sept. 22 to Dec. 29, 2006, the strongest of which measured a magnitude 4.2.
Correction: An earlier version of this report misstated where the first Sunday quake was reported.

title: ICE watchers stand guard all day, every day outside Scarborough facility
text:
SCARBOROUGH — On Sept. 28, at 8:19 a.m., two cars with black windows leave the Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility at 40 Manson Libby Road.
Two people standing outside quickly jot down the license plate numbers and note the time.
“They’re going hunting,” one of them says.
At 8:21 a.m., five more cars suddenly appear, heading in the same direction.
The watchers scramble. On clipboards and yellow legal pads, they document everything Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents do, taking photos of the cars, shouting out license plate numbers, reaching for their pens. They mutter curses to themselves.
Then the alerts go out.
They have a meticulous information-gathering and distribution network, as they call it, in the southern Maine immigrant community. It’s a careful system that requires constant monitoring of ICE’s only facility in the state, a small, unassuming building on a quiet road near Route 1.
Residents across southern Maine have formed groups like this to monitor ICE activity — following federal vehicles, standing guard at school bus stops, filming agents, watching out for their immigrant neighbors — since the January enforcement surge in Maine.
But after an ICE agent killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford on July 13, many have intensified their efforts. And about five core watchers have made monitoring the ICE facility their full-time job.
They’re not protesting, they said, but they’re not just watching. They’re giving immigrants rides, buying groceries, watching their kids, driving people’s cars home after they’ve been detained, and connecting them with legal resources.
Two of those watchers agreed to speak with the Portland Press Herald about why they’re doing this work, but asked not to be fully identified out of fear for their safety. Others who followed and documented ICE activity in January reported being followed home by agents, intimidated and threatened with arrest.
THE WATCH
For almost three months, K and Allisandra have spent about 10 to 14 hours a day watching the facility. On Sept. 28, Allisandra said she felt especially tired. She had been at the facility from 5 a.m. to around 7 p.m. for several days.
They are scrupulous, almost obsessive with their notetaking. They have to be, they said, lives are on the line.
They have a printed sheet with 39 license plates they’ve seen at the facility. They know if the cars are there, hidden behind a fence covered in black fabric, or if they’re out “hunting.”
On separate sheets, they track the immigrants who come in, and those who don’t come back out.
Age. Sex. Race. Height. Hair color. Clothing. Cars. Are they carrying an umbrella? A bag?
The watchers don’t know most of their names, whether they have a family or children waiting for them to come home, friends, a lawyer.
“If there’s nothing else that we can give people, we know what happened to them,” Allisandra said.
THE NUMBERS
In August, the group said they observed about 2 ½ detainments per day. That decreased to about 1.8 per day in September. Between both months, they observed 101 detainments.
Of those, they believe eight were arrested during routine check-ins.
“This is an every-day emergency,” K said, sitting in a lawn chair across from the facility last month. “ICE is detaining people every single day. People don’t realize it.”
ICE did not respond to requests for comment or questions about the number of people detained at the facility or about the watchers.
The numbers have been decreasing, the watchers said, not because there are fewer detainments, but because they believe ICE agents have increased efforts to conceal their operations.
Before a black mesh fence was installed around the facility a few weeks ago, the watchers could see detainees with shackles locked around their feet being brought inside the facility from SUVs with tinted windows.
Sometimes, they have seen cars come and go by driving over a small ditch. There often aren’t enough watchers to have someone stand guard by that area, so they don’t know how often cars leave that way or when.
A MORNING ON THE WATCH
There are about 10-12 check-ins at the facility every day, watchers said, usually between 8-11 a.m. On the morning of Sept. 28, a reporter witnessed 12 people walk in.
It was a rainy, gray day, the impacts of a fall nor’easter still lingering. But the watchers are always there, regardless of the weather.
Normally, they set up lawn chairs across the street. On rainy days, they work out of K’s car. Allisandra rolled down the window of the back seat to get a better look, regularly wiping the car door soaked from the rain pouring in.
Throughout the morning, immigrants waited outside in the rain, sometimes for half an hour. Watchers said they have seen sick and pregnant immigrants wait for hours.
Sometimes, people are inside for just a few minutes. When immigrants are inside for half an hour or more, the watchers start to worry.
That morning, an immigrant they knew went in for a check-in.
“Have you seen him come out yet?” Allisandra asked after half an hour, panicking. They called the man’s wife, promising to let her know as soon as he returned.
After 50 minutes, when he finally came back out, they waved to him frantically, sighing with relief.
Still, they worry that each check-in could mean another detainment.
“The fear just doesn’t end,” Allisandra said. “ICE says, ‘Come back in a week, come back in a day.’”
When others they didn’t recognize left the building, Allisandra hurriedly ran out in the rain to hand them a printed list of resources.
K said she knows immigrant families with newborns who have never seen the outside of their house since the ride back from the hospital.
“One person detained means one family irreparably damaged,” K said.
“Why is this on us? We’re just a couple of weirdos sacrificing everything to be out here,” she added.

title: Army study found shock gloves purchased by ICE cause pain, compliance and fear
text:
(AP) - The shock gloves immigration agents could soon use to control detainees and protesters worked so powerfully during a military exercise that participants felt intense pain, stopped fighting immediately and feared additional exposures, according to a previously unreleased Army study.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement leaders were aware of the findings before signing a $16.7 million contract to purchase 6,000 pairs of shock gloves in August, according to records obtained by the watchdog group American Oversight and shared with The Associated Press.
The shocks had a profound impact on Army employees who played the role of combative prisoners during the exercise, which took place at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas in October 2024. The participants, several of whom were large-statured men, stopped resisting seconds after officers applied shocks by touching gloves to their skin, and were left with “fatigue, soreness and excessive apprehensiveness to being shocked again,” the study found.
“After experiencing the effects of the GLOVE, ... participants stated just seeing the GLOVE was enough to make them want to comply,” the authors wrote.
Watchdog says gloves cause pain and raise safety concerns
ICE has called the gloves “distraction and de-escalation devices” that will be safer than other non-lethal options to subdue targets for arrest and deportation and protesters who create civil disturbances. The agency has argued the rapid compliance they cause will keep officers safer and prevent incidents from requiring potentially lethal force.
But critics have warned the gloves will give ICE another weapon to intimidate and brutalize people even as the agency is under fire for excessive force that has left a trail of deaths and injuries across the nation. The gloves, they note, are easy to discharge, do not leave a mark and have not been extensively used in settings outside of jails. The manufacturer warns they should not be used on high-risk populations such as kids, pregnant women or disabled people.
“The military assessment in ICE’s own files shows that these gloves can cause ‘intense pain’ and force compliance. It does not establish that they are safe,” said Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight. “Everyone should be alarmed that ICE is preparing to deploy a tool designed to inflict, at best, intense pain, without showing that it is safe for the people who will be subjected to it.”
ICE released the study and other documents to American Oversight as part of the group’s Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the agency seeking records related to its use of force.
Army study found shock gloves triggered ‘immediate’ compliance
The military prison study assessed whether the gloves could be used effectively to forcibly remove combative prisoners from their cells, to respond to disturbances in common areas and to transport uncooperative inmates. Role-playing employees conducted several scenarios with and without the gloves to test their impact, including violent encounters in which inmates were to fight as hard as they could.
The study found the devices “increased the efficiency” of teams carrying out forced cell extractions and responding to disturbances by reducing the length of physical encounters, keeping guards from becoming exhausted and preventing injuries. They did not “significantly change” the time it took to control inmates during escorts but required less effort.
“GLOVE provides a boost in confidence to smaller or less trained members,” the study found. “Inmate compliance was immediate” compared to other methods, it added.
The electric jolt does not cause the body to freeze like a Taser shock does, but instead “works by overloading the peripheral nerve endings” of the skin to cause pain, the study said. Participants who were wet or had oil on their skin described even more powerful shocks, with one reporting discomfort for 30 minutes afterward.
Senator says ICE hasn’t responded to demand for details on glove use
ICE’s contract requires the manufacturer, Compliant Technologies LLC, to deliver the gloves within six months. Its owner, Jeff Niklaus, said he was unavailable for an interview, citing a busy workload.
White House border czar Tom Homan has said it could “be awhile” before the gloves are in the field because ICE is still ironing out training and policy issues. A statement released Tuesday by ICE did not address questions about the study and the status of the rollout, but said “officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics.”
U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said ICE has not responded to an Aug. 27 letter in which she and 15 other Democratic Senate colleagues called for ICE to abandon its plan to buy the gloves or explain how they would be used and managed to avoid abuse. She said she still wants answers.
“Without ICE’s responses to legitimate questions from 16 United States Senators, the American public is being left in the dark about how these electric shock gloves are being deployed and what, if any, training the agents who use them have received,” she said.

title: Grants fund traditional Wabanaki art, harvest practices: ‘Now that’s connection’
text:
MOTAHKOMIKUK — Standing at the narrows that separate Big and Long lakes, Matthew Dana II curled his fingers around the base of a sweet flag shoot and pried its root from the boggy earth.
He snapped it in two to reveal its light interior and release its earthen scent.
Once dried, flag root — or kiwhosuwasq, which translates to muskrat root, given the rodent’s affinity for the plant — is a traditional Passamaquoddy medicine used to treat, among other things, colds and indigestion.
Dana learned to harvest it in this patch of wetland from his late uncle.
Today, he’s teaching the next generation.
And though working with Passamaquoddy youths has been a passion of his for years, he’s made it into a full-time job thanks in part to a $25,000 grant from the Wolankeyutomone Kisi Apaciyewik Fund.
The fund, the name of which translates to “let us take good care of what has been returned,” is an endeavor of the Wabanaki Commission on Land and Stewardship and First Light.
The commission is composed of representatives of all five Wabanaki communities in Maine: the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians, the Mi’kmaq Nation, the Passamaquoddy at Motahkomikuk Indian Township, the Passamaquoddy at Sipayik and the Penobscot Nation. First Light is a group of allied nonnative organizations.
Together, they are accelerating the return of land to Wabanaki Nations.
The Penobscot Nation regained control of 11,000 acres last month and the Mi’kmaq Nation’s holdings nearly doubled when the tribe obtained title to 3,400 acres in June. These are all part of a plan to return 50,000 acres to tribal governments.
“Just getting the land back doesn’t mean that our communities are going to be properly resourced to be able to go out there and engage with the land,” said Frances Soctomah, the fund manager.
That’s where the grants come in.
Wabanaki individuals, nonprofits and governments are eligible to apply for grants of $25,000, $50,000 and $75,000, respectively. In the first two years, the fund has distributed a total of $1.35 million in 32 grants across all five communities. Projects support work around anything from food sovereignty to cultural tourism to trail building.
The fund itself, designed to support Wabanaki self-determination, breaks the mold of traditional nonprofit fundraising. Soctomah and First Light plan to grow it into a multimillion-dollar self-sustaining endowment that will support this kind of work in perpetuity.
Conservation organizations, Maine and national philanthropic foundations and individual donors all contributed in equal part in the initial fundraising. Donors in Maine included the Elmina B. Sewall Foundation, Maine Coast Heritage Trust, the Onion Foundation and the Quimby Foundation.
The application is low barrier, the grants are unrestricted and the use of donations to the fund is often undefined from the outset because it is intended to support self-determination. That’s sometimes difficult for nonnative donors to wrap their heads around.
“We are integrating more of a trust-based philanthropy approach,” Soctomah said.
But on a recent visit to Motahkomikuk, one of the two Passamaquoddy communities in Washington County, it’s not hard to find evidence of the grants at work.
QUILLS PUT A POINT ON IT
Piece by piece, Donald Soctomah can walk you through the Passamaquoddy Tribal Museum and the myriad artifacts and artworks collected there.
These things just have a way of coming home, he said.
There’s a case of stone tools people have found at their camps and, below it, a small Revolutionary War cannon gifted to the tribe by the state in 1820, in gratitude for the service of Wabanaki warriors. The cannon was once lost in the lake, discovered by a fisherman and taken to Maryland, then returned again decades later.
There are baskets, woven by artisans both famous and obscure, and a drum used by the Passamaquoddy Brass Band that toured with Buffalo Bill.
Soctomah, 71, is the Passamaquoddy Tribal Historic Preservation Officer, a former tribal state representative and Frances Soctomah’s father.
He’s been involved in three grant-winning proposals since Wolankeyutomone Kisi Apaciyewik was launched, including one that supported cultural activities through the museum he manages.
With that grant, Soctomah hired a local artist to lead workshops in porcupine quill art; he was a financial benefactor of this year’s community days to celebrate Passamaquoddy culture with drumming, dancing and a slate of native vendors; and he paid the portage drivers for the ancestral canoe journey, an annual event in which tribal members paddle from Motahkomikuk down the St. Croix River to Sipayik.
These are traditions that run in his DNA. They are traditions, he said, that must be supported.
“It’s the right thing to do,” Soctomah said.
At community days, Alisia Morin, 34, said she spotted a road-kill porcupine as she crossed Passamaquoddy lands that very morning.
She was eager to attend several of the quill workshops Soctomah organized. There, she learned to dye and soften the tubular spikes, and then thread them into a backing to create ornately detailed patterns.
“I’ve always been drawn to how beautiful quill work is,” Morin said.
She grew up in Texas and was not exposed to traditional Passamaquoddy art as a kid. Now, raising her own kids on her ancestral homelands, Morin said it’s important that they have more exposure than she did.
So when she spotted the porcupine carcass, she braked.
If Morin had a shovel, she would’ve taken the whole thing. Instead, she and her daughter, Eliana McGinley, 6, plucked just enough quills to make some earrings.
Hudson McGinley, 22 months old, shows off the medallion his mother made by threading dyed porcupine quills through a birch bark backing, at left. At right, Alisia Morin hit the brakes when she spotted the porcupine carcass that morning. (Daryn Slover/Staff Photographer)
“Mom got stuck,” McGinley pipes in, before admitting, “I was a little scared to do it.”
When she pulled out a quilled medallion she made in the workshop, her 22-month-old son Hudson insisted he wear it, and toddled back to the event grounds grasping it with both hands.
ALL ABOUT RESPONSIBILITY
That evening, Eric Bacon steadied the gunwales of his birch bark canoe as a teenager lifted the hem of her ribbon skirt and swung her leg into the shaky hull.
Bacon, who is 49 and has no kids of his own, paddled out into the channel connecting Lewy Lake to Grand Falls Flowage and made a circle.
His 23-year-old birch bark canoe was made by master builder Steve Cayard, a mentor of Bacon’s. These boats, constructed in the traditional Wabanaki style, are feather-light.
But the boats have enough gravity to pull the the course of Bacon’s life into their orbit.
He crossed under the bridge and looped back around before drifting up to the rocky shore.
“Let me get out first,” he instructed.
The girls giggled and ran off.
“I’m trying to plant the seed,” Bacon said as he strapped the boat back on his pickup.
In 1981, he dragged his mother by the hand across the grounds at Mihku Lodge to see a birch bark canoe. He was 4.
In a way, everything Bacon has done since has been about trying to nurture that passion.
He received a $25,000 grant to remodel a garage he owns and turn it into a canoe building and birch bark art space where he can host workshops.
The garage isn’t done yet, and Bacon has instead spent some of the money to rent gear for public paddling events. It’s what the community told him it wanted.
Unlike with some other grants, that’s exactly what grantees are supposed to do, Frances Soctomah said. She wants them to have the ability to pivot according to the needs of their community.
Other grant programs often come with burdensome restrictions — food distribution is often off-limits. In one case, Soctomah recalled a funder telling her they wanted to support a basket-making program, but at the 11th hour said the money couldn’t be used on sharp axes, critical tools for harvesting and processing ash trees.
Now, the fund she manages can help fill the gaps for grantees who are constrained by other programs.
There’s a new skiff parked in Matt Dana’s yard. He bought it with the grant money and, from it, harvested a porpoise as part of his goal to gather 500 pounds of protein with Passamaquoddy youth.
For Dana, all of this is about fulfilling a responsibility.
As a boy, he learned to trap muskrat from a neighbor, and from his father learned to call them in with birch bark; as a young man, Dana learned to harvest ash and weave baskets from Jeremy Frey, a nationally recognized basket-maker; in his 40s, Dana has sought out elders who can still recall how to hunt seals and process their hides.
After he was awarded a grant in 2025, Dana decided to make this a full-time job.
He’s secured funding from numerous nonprofits in Maine to support the work of Mecimi-te Nihtawehtunen — the name of his organization, which means “we have always remembered.” It’s a phrase implying that the traditions not only exist, but will continue to.
Matthew Dana made a crown from ash and sweetgrass for his 4-year-old granddaughter, Sage Dana, to wear during the community days celebration, at left. At right is sweetgrass on Dana’s kitchen sink. (Daryn Slover/Staff Photographer)
Coils of ash splints sat bound in a box outside his kitchen, and there are locks of sweetgrass in the sink.
“It’s got to be preserved,” Dana said. “The generations coming after us need to know it.”
He harvested his first moose at 11. By 18, he was out hunting with his cousins and 10 siblings, then his kids and grandkids. In the woods, Dana said placing his palms down flat on the table, he feels grounded.
Two years ago, Dana took his 21-year-old nephew out hunting and guided what was then a timid young man as he harvested his first buck. Last year, they went out again.
Dana’s nephew tracked a buck into the woods as Dana sat listening.
“And then I heard — I heard the shot.”
When they reunited, there was no more fear. There was pride and confidence and joy. His nephew shared the meat with elders in the community.
“It’s ceremony, it’s prayer, it’s connecting with the ancestors,” Dana said. “The feeling of doing something that my DNA has done for over 15,000 years in this same place? Now that’s connection.”
Reuben M. Schafir is a Report for America corps member who writes about Indigenous and rural communities for the Portland Press Herald.
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 7 to correct the amount of money that the Wolankeyutomone Kisi Apaciyewik Fund has distributed.

title: Work to restore waterways in the Magalloway reaches far downstream
text:
Conservation work carried out by the Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust seeks to strengthen the resiliency of two waterways in the Rangeley region by replacing aging river crossings and correcting straightened waterways.
In July, more than 78,000 acres around the Magalloway River in northern Oxford County was conserved in a joint effort by four groups, Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust, Forest Society of Maine, The Nature Conservancy and Northeast Wilderness Trust, which formed the Magalloway Collaborative in spring of 2025.
The four groups have worked together to raise the $62 million needed to buy the development rights to the land.
Although the development rights have been secured by the collaborative, there is still conservation work to be done in the Magalloway, namely in its rivers and tributaries.
WORK TO BE DONE
Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust has identified many undersized or failing stream crossings that hinder the movement of fish in the preserve, which have been in place on logging roads for decades.
Brook trout are one of the dominant species in the Magalloway and Kennebago rivers. Preferring cold water, they will move upstream in the summer months as the waters warm, choosing rivers and ponds in the higher elevations on the surrounding mountains. The culverts sever access to streams in these higher elevations.
The culverts often sit high off the riverbed, meaning a fish hoping to move up or downstream would have to jump into the pipe and work their way to the other side.
“A lot of studies have shown that, you know, perhaps a few individuals that are more determined can make it through them, but the vast majority don’t,” said Jason Latham, conservation biologist for Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust.
Latham said that in surveys done by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, one side of a culvert on a brook in the nearby Kennebago conservation area, which has seen much of the same conservation techniques, held more than 130 fish while the opposite side had only two. The culvert cut off nearly four miles of upstream habitat from the majority of fish in the system.
“It was clearly a barrier,” he said.
The organization is moving to replace the culverts, opting instead to install open-bottom bridges that mimic a natural stream bed, which allow fish to freely swim through the miles of tributaries.
“By replacing these culverts and building these open-bottom bridges and replicating sort of that natural condition of the stream, we’re essentially reconnecting miles of upstream habitat for species like brook trout,” he said.
Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust has replaced nine crossings in its Kennebago preserve, with three left in the trust’s property. Work in the Kennebago will act as a model for the restorative conservation that will take place in the Magalloway in the coming years.
Replacing culverts also strengthens the area’s resiliency to heavy rains and flooding events.
When heavy rain hits the forest, like in the storms that drenched the region in 2023, the culverts can only handle so much water at a time. Latham said that when the region gets hit with multiple inches of rainfall, all of the water is moved down the mountainside and into the blocked streams.
These culverts can become overwhelmed by the water, causing soil to erode from around the pipe and polluting the downstream area with deposits from the crossing.
LOGGING LEGACY
Decades ago, lengths of rivers across Maine were straightened by logging companies. This allowed for timber harvested in the surrounding woods to easily float to the mills downstream. But now, years after the last log drive, the rivers in the region still show scars.
Stretches of water along the Magalloway and Kennebago were subject to the same treatment, creating long, channel-like stretches where water has little obstruction.
Latham said that healthy rivers often aren’t straight. Instead, they meander, with fallen trees and rocks slowing the flow of water and providing shelter to aquatic life under the surface. Above the surface, waters spill over to create floodplains that are vital to the surrounding habitat.
To correct straightened sections of water, Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust plans to fell trees into portions of waterways to help create the natural barriers the Magalloway needs for a thriving ecosystem. Similar actions were taken on the Kennebago and have been a success, Latham said.
River restoration isn’t solely benefiting the forests of the Rangeley Region. It acts as one of the first lines of defense against flooding and poor water quality in communities along the Androscoggin River.
“Everything flows down to the communities that are even more populated below us,” said Molly Shaw, communications director for Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust.
Communities such as Bethel, Rumford, Livermore Falls and Lewiston all receive water that enters the system through the Magalloway.
The Magalloway begins at the confluence of the river’s West Branch and Third East Branch in Bowman Township at the northern tip of Oxford County. It stretches 40-plus miles through the five unorganized territories south Bowman, then into New Hampshire before crossing back into Maine to become a tributary to Parmachenee Lake, Aziscohos Lake and the Androscoggin River, which flows into Merrymeeting Bay.
“There’s a million different sorts of threats to really good clean water quality that could happen up here at the top of the watershed that impact so many people downstream,” Latham said.
“The Magalloway is the source of fresh water that feeds down to Merrymeeting Bay and dumps into the Gulf of Maine,” he added.
“We have the opportunity, I’ll say, and the responsibility to practice good forest management up here,” Latham said.

title: Democrat files ethics complaint against Susan Collins over alleged pay-to-play scheme
text:
A former Democratic candidate for Cumberland County District Attorney on Wednesday filed a formal ethics complaint against Republican Sen. Susan Collins over pay-to-play allegations involving a defense contractor.
Attorney Valerie Adams asked the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Ethics to conduct an investigation into the allegations outlined in a recent ProPublica report that Collins agreed to steer millions of dollars in contracts to the Hawaii-based firm Navatek in exchange for political donations from its CEO, Martin Kao.
“It is difficult to conceive of behavior more improper than accepting campaign contributions in return for directing taxpayer funded government contracts to an out of state company,” Adams said in a letter to Chairman James Lankford, R-Okla., and Vice Chairman Christopher Coons, D-Del., obtained by the Portland Press Herald.
“The reporting from ProPublica suggests Senator Collins may have done just that,” she continued. “It is the Committee’s duty to get to the bottom of this.”
Collins and her campaign have repeatedly denied the allegations outlined in the ProPublica article, calling them “outrageous.”
It’s unclear what — if anything — will become of the ethics complaint. Such complaints can be filed by anybody online. The ethics committee is a bipartisan body, with three Republicans and three Democrats. Most such complaints get dismissed, although the committee has investigated senators in the past, probing then Democratic Sen. Al Franken for alleged sexual misconduct in 2017, and then-Sen. Robert Menendez of New Jersey in 2018 for improperly accepting gifts.
“This is getting to be pathetic,” Collins campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen said in a statement. “For the third consecutive week, a recently failed Democratic candidate has parroted false charges that they know nothing about against Susan Collins.”
The filing comes as Democrats are working to amplify the corruption allegations against Collins. In doing so, they are trying to put a negative light on her central argument for reelection — that she is wielding her power as chair of the appropriations committee to benefit Maine.
In her letter, Adams asked the committee to “urgently investigate whether Senator Collins engaged in improper conduct that reflects discredit upon the Senate” by:
- Steering $8 million in contracts to Navatek in exchange for political donations;
- Knowingly accepting contributions made in the name of another in violation of campaign finance law; or
- Working with President Donald Trump to stop the investigation.
In an interview Wednesday, Adams dismissed any suggestion that the complaint was politically motivated or aimed at influencing voters in Maine’s U.S. Senate race. She described herself as a former Collins supporter.
Adams said she was troubled by what ProPublica reported and believes the allegations should be looked into.
“There’s never been a more important time to demand the best of our elected officials,” Adams said. “And I truly believe that.”
In a televised debate on Tuesday, Collins said she began working with Navatek in 2017 — the year before she received any donations from Kao. The company was partnering with the University of Maine on a project for the U.S. Navy that sought federal funding.
“I worked very closely with the university. We advanced that proposal,” Collins said. “The head of Navatek at the time, unfortunately, was a crook. He is now in jail, where he belongs.”
ProPublica reported that Kao told FBI investigators that Collins would not meet with him in 2018 unless he donated to her reelection effort. But Collins’ campaign on Tuesday showed a timestamped photo of Collins and Kao meeting in the senator’s office in February 2018 — months before Kao made a donation to her campaign.
The ProPublica article also detailed how Kao told investigators that he worked with the leader of a Collins-aligned super PAC to exchange a six-figure donation to her 2020 reelection effort for millions in government contracts.
Kao made an illegal $150,000 donation to the Collins-aligned 1820 PAC through a shell company, since federal contractors are barred from contributing to campaigns. ProPublica reported that Kao told Scott Reed, the head of the pro-Collins Super PAC, about his plan to use a shell company to make the donation.
Kao pleaded guilty to charges involving money laundering and bank fraud in 2022, and is currently in federal prison. He had been cooperating with federal investigators in an effort to get his sentence reduced. Collins’ team has said he is not credible, pointing to his convictions.
Collins’ campaign manager Steve Abbott said on Tuesday that neither Collins nor her campaign were accused of wrongdoing after answering questions about Kao in 2021 — and that nobody in the senator’s office was contacted about any new investigations thereafter.

title: TOO CUTE: Four-legged wedding videographer named Swayze steals the show
text:
TOO CUTE: Four-legged wedding photographer steals the show
A Wisconsin bride turned her sheepadoodle into a wedding videographer, and the resulting GoPro video ended up stealing the show on social media.
Emily Cowles, a Door County, Wisconsin, native, said she and her husband chose to have their wedding there because it feels like “heaven” to her.
"Door County is just like heaven. It's my happy place. So, we go back frequently. And yeah, that's where we wanted to get married," she told WBAY's Grace Johnson.
She said she also wanted their dog, Swayze, to be part of the day because he is “goofy,” “a great snuggler,” and a “bright light” to everyone who meets him.
On Aug. 22, the couple strapped a GoPro onto Swayze so he could film the celebration from a dog’s-eye view.
Cowles said the video’s popularity grew quickly, with shares rising online and major outlets reaching out.
And while the family has had fun seeing Swayze get all the attention, the bride says that for her, the viral fame isn't the best part of the video.
She said one of her favorite moments involved Swayze spending time with her 91-year-old grandmother.
"He like took refuge in spending time with her for like 20 minutes. It was so sweet. And you can just hear him talk or her talking to him. And it was just so, so sweet to watch back," she said.
Cowles said she and her husband plan to look back on the footage for years, especially as time passes.
"There's going to be a day when not all those people are going to be around. And especially Swayze. Um, so we're going to be able to look back, and it's just going to bring a smile to our face for the rest of our lives."
And don't worry, Swayze hasn't changed because of the fame.
"He's so humble. We're trying not to let it go to his head," Cowles joked.

title: Man charged with murder that happened near Tukey's Bridge claims self-defense
text:
Man charged with murder that happened near Tukey's Bridge in Portland claims self-defense
The man accused of stabbing a woman to death near Tukey's Bridge in Portland in the summer is claiming he acted self-defense and told a judge he was the victim in this case.
Glen Rodney, 58, was arraigned Wednesday and then a bail hearing was held Cumberland County Superior Court.
During the bail hearing, Rodney's lawyer presented a photo that showed his client was battered and bruised, and said Rodney was the one who was attacked back on Aug. 5 while riding his bicycle along the Bayside Trail near the bridge.
"It was them approaching Mr. Rodney and continuing the conflict. Mr. Rodney says he was attacked by them," said Jim Howaniec, Rodney's lawyer. "There's certainly corroborating medical evidence that he was assaulted."
Howaniec said Rodney fought back with a knife in self-defense, killing 21-year-old Juju Nadeau. Officials said Nadeau died from a single stab would to the heart.
Portland Police Detective Aaron Curlee took the stand and told a completely different story.
Curlee said Rodney was the perpetrator who kicked Nadeau as he passed by on his bicycle, because he was angry that she and her three friends were in his way.
"Mr. Rodney started yelling at the group for taking up the path. He was yelling profanities at them, threatened to kill them," Curlee said.
The judge eventually ruled that Rodney continue to be held without bail as the case moves forward. Rodney is being held at the Cumberland County Jail in Portland.

title: Who benefits from Susan Collins’ funding?
text:
Republican Sen. Susan Collins boasts about $1.5 billion in federal grant money she’s brought home this term. She shouldn’t be boasting.
Those grants are peanuts compared to the billions we’re losing through cuts that her Trump-controlled party enacted to federal programs, including healthcare and hospitals;
food assistance; affordable housing; infrastructure; renewable energy, environmental
protection and national parks; research, student loans and education. 
Peanuts compared to the billions we pay for tariffs and inflation, peanuts compared to the debt she and Trump Republicans have created in office.
Sen. Collins is part of the problem. Her grants amount to well-publicized handouts diverting attention from her failures of political will and leadership. Beyond that, are Collins’ grants distributed equitably? No.
Voters in the 1st Congressional District should be angry. The senator’s grants go overwhelmingly to Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, keeping her friends and neighbors there happy and beholden.
Collins takes credit for 672 grants valued at about $1.5 billion. CD2 is Susan Collins’ home turf and political base, so CD2 received the majority of the funding. In CD2’s Aroostook County, the figure is $2,900 per capita. In CD1’s Cumberland County — including Portland — the number is $355. Perhaps it matters that Aroostook County gave Collins 68% of the vote the last time she ran six years ago, Cumberland County just 38%.
Sen. Collins’ case that we should reelect her because she’s showered Maine with cash turns out to be bad policy, a sham compared to what we’re losing, and heavily skewed to reward her voters up north. It is time we retire Susan Collins.
David Chase
York

title: Former corrections officer allegedly killed his wife and forced his kids to help
text:
CALLAWAY COUNTY, Mo. (KOMU) - A former corrections officer from Missouri is facing charges for allegedly killing his wife 10 months ago and forcing his kids to help.
Jonathan G. Houston, 44, is charged with first-degree murder and first-degree kidnapping in his wife’s death, according to the Callaway County Sheriff’s Office. Investigators learned about the alleged crimes after receiving a 911 call Sunday morning from one of his seven children.
Whispering during the call, the child claimed her father had “captured” her and her siblings for five years and physically abused them, according to court documents.
Authorities traced the call to a hotel in Kingdom City, where they found Houston – who is a former corrections officer – and his kids.
One of the kids told deputies that Houston had allegedly killed her mother, who was also the suspect’s wife, by strangling her at the hotel on Dec. 1, 2025, while some of the siblings were in the room.
Houston allegedly directed one child to pour hot water down the victim’s legs while she was being strangled, and another covered her mouth. Prior to this, he allegedly put the three youngest children in the bathroom and played music to muffle the victim’s screams, according to court documents.
The victim was never reported missing. Houston allegedly disposed of her body in a trash bag that was tossed into a dumpster on hotel property, the probable cause statement states.
During an interview with investigators, Houston allegedly admitted to killing his wife and planning it ahead of time, according to court documents.
Houston is being held in jail without bond. He is also under prior investigations for sexual assault and the assault of other victims.
Authorities say his kids were all placed into protective custody.

title: How the 2026 midterms could determine control of Congress
text:
How the 2026 midterms could determine control of Congress
With less than four weeks to go until the 2026 midterms, the battle over who controls Congress is ramping up in a heated patchwork of races across the country.
How the 2026 midterms could determine control of Congress
With less than four weeks to go until the 2026 midterms, the battle over who controls Congress is ramping up in a heated patchwork of races across the country.
The 2026 midterm elections are less than four weeks away, with control of Congress at stake in several critical races across the country.
Control of the House or Senate—or both—provides the majority party with access to critical power in oversight and budget committees, as well as the ability to stall or block legislation, including bills pushed by President Donald Trump.
"You can be pretty sure that most of the things proposed by Trump will not get through Congress," director of the University of Virginia's Center for Politics Larry Sabato said, "be stopped by one or both houses, depending on how much the Democrats control."
Historically, experts say the president's party tends to lose House seats in midterm elections, and many predict this year will be no exception.
But the Senate has shown a different pattern.
The Get the Facts Data Team found the Senate has flipped control three times since 1990—in 1994, 2006, and 2014.
To gain control of the Senate in 2026, Democrats need to pick up four Republican seats. Tight races in states like Texas, Maine, North Carolina, Michigan, and Kansas could play a decisive role.
Experts say the economy and the Iran war are among the issues President Trump will need to address to help Republicans maintain their majorities in the Senate and House.
Still, some surprising shifts have emerged ahead of the midterms, many favoring Democrats, experts say. States with Senate races that were once considered Republican strongholds—such as Alaska, Texas, and Kansas—are now seen as toss-ups or even lean Democratic. Experts say the changes likely reflect voter sentiment over President Trump's performance during his term.
Currently, Republicans hold majorities in both chambers, with 218 seats in the House and 53 in the Senate. Experts say the margin of control is crucial. A wider margin could make it easier for the majority party to pass or block legislation, while a tighter margin complicates the process, especially in overriding a presidential veto.
President Trump rallied in Texas Wednesday as part of a nationwide push to energize supporters ahead of the midterms.

title: Aging Untold: How to find support when trauma resurfaces with age
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we explore how trauma can resurface later in life and look at where to find essential support for managing symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder.
Plus, find out how to make peace with shifting priorities and move forward without guilt when lifelong friendships begin to fade.
Later, meet a dedicated South Carolina volunteer bringing unexpected comfort to hospital waiting rooms through the soothing sounds of her harp.
Trauma doesn’t simply fade with time, and symptoms can become more noticeable during major life changes, including retirement, illness or loss.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said trauma does not have to come from something dramatic. It’s an “invisible suffering,” and the body tries to move past something that the brain is not allowing.
The Aging Untold hosts are sharing tips on how therapies, from massage and trauma-informed therapy to service animals, could help.
Breaking up with a friend you have had for decades can be as painful as a romantic breakup, but the loss is often grieved in silence.
“Nobody’s bringing you casseroles or sending you flowers usually, and it can be really tough,” aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said.
The Aging Untold hosts are sharing their experiences and how to move forward after a friendship ends.
Caregiving can be overwhelming.
Ty Lewis, a certified dementia practitioner and content creator who cares for her mother, is sharing how a powerful shift in perspective can separate the burden of caregiving from the person receiving the care.
Lewis is a caregiver for her mother, Gertrude, who is in the late stages of Alzheimer’s disease. Her outlook is that the workload is the burden — not the person.
“We have to shift our perspective. The care, that’s the burden, the financial piece, that is the burden. Us not being able to find resources, that’s the burden. But taking care of our loved one, being a servant leader, that is the blessing,” Lewis said.
Peg Mann fills the waiting room at McLeod Seacoast Hospital in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, with gentle notes of harp music.
She is a hospital volunteer and her music provides soft, calming sounds over the monitors and footsteps.
She begins her shift by escorting patients and pushing the comfort cart before setting up to play for patients and families waiting for answers.

title: Wrong ballots distributed in one Maine House District
text:
OXFORD, Maine (WMTW) —The Maine Secretary of State’s Office confirmed that some incorrect ballots were distributed to voters in Oxford.
The Secretary of State’s Office says a resident contacted the Oxford town clerk on Tuesday after, “receiving an incorrect ballot style, and it was addressed by the clerk.”
State officials say the clerk identified that, due to a packaging error at the printer, “a small number of incorrect ballots were received and sent out.”
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said she believed nine wrong ballots distributed.
Town officials were working to contact any voters who may have received an incorrect ballot.
The state said every voter will have the chance to vote the correct ballot. Anyone who receives an incorrect ballot, or who makes a mistake on their ballot, may request a new one.
Voters should have received ballots with the candidates for House District 80, which includes Republican Ernest Fitts.
Azalea Cormier, who is not registered in a party, is also running for the House District 80 seat. There is no Democrat in the race.
District 80 includes the towns of Buckfield, Hebron, Otisfield and Oxford.

title: A Story of Courage and Loss With Anne Frank Exhibit
text:
For two weeks this fall, the story of a teenage girl who hid from the Nazis in an Amsterdam attic was being told at Gorham Middle School by students not much younger than she was when she wrote her diary.
The traveling exhibit,“Anne Frank: A History for Today,” ran at Gorham Middle School from Sept. 24 to Oct. 7. The exhibit was created by the Anne Frank House in Amsterdam with the University of South Carolina’s Anne Frank Center, and it is brought to schools in the region by the Institute for Holocaust Education.
The exhibit’s 32 panels, printed in English and Spanish, trace Anne Frank’s life, her family’s years in hiding, and her death in the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp in 1945, set against the wider history of the Holocaust.
What sets the exhibit apart is who lead the tours. Rather than adults, visitors were guided by 20 Gorham Middle School eighth graders serving as trained docents. Before the exhibit opened, the students spent two full days in training. They studied the history of the Holocaust and the details of Anne Frank’s life and death, and they practiced leading groups through the panels and answering visitors’ questions.
The peer-guided model is central to the program: young people learn the material deeply enough to teach it, and their audiences hear the story from someone close to Anne’s own age. Bringing the exhibit to Gorham was the work of Heather Whitaker, an alternative education teacher at Gorham High School, who arranged for the district to host it.
The exhibit drew a steady stream of visitors. Every social studies class at Gorham Middle School toured it, as did three Gorham High School Holocaust and Human Rights classes. Community showings opened the exhibit to the public, including a visit from a group of senior residents of the Inn at Village Square, who learned about Anne Frank’s story from the student docents. For many in that group, the history on the panels falls within their own lifetimes, and the exchange between generations gave the visit added weight.
The exhibit’s themes reach beyond the past. According to the Institute for Holocaust Education, it asks students to examine prejudice and discrimination, practice empathy, and consider the importance of standing up for others. A central message is that one young person’s voice can inspire generations, an idea the Gorham docents are putting into practice with every tour they lead.
The costs of bringing the exhibit to Gorham were graciously covered by local businesses. Aaron Chadbourne of Demetria Real Estate led the fundraising effort and was joined as sponsors by Maine Community Bank and Treworgy & Baldacci Real Estate Closing Services. Their generosity allowed Gorham students and residents to experience the exhibit close to home.

title: Cornell students stage sit-in to protest university's handling of alleged 2024 gang rape
text:
ITHACA, New York (AP) — Some Cornell students staged a sit-in at a dining hall and vowed not to spend money on campus Wednesday to protest sexual violence and how the university has handled complaints, in the latest expression of outrage over an alleged 2024 gang rape at a fraternity house.
A handwritten sign reading “Justice for Jane Doe ” — the name under which the accuser is suing — was propped on an empty table in the dining hall in the afternoon. Some students sat around the room without eating, while others lunched. Another small group sat outside holding signs with messages such as “we are Jane Doe.”
Groups organizing the demonstration intended to keep the sit-in going for seven hours.
The demonstrations were meant to spotlight complaints that the university is slow to respond to reports of sexual assault while quick to protect its reputation. Among other demands, the groups want the university to retool disciplinary procedures for addressing complaints and expel or revoke the degrees of anyone involved in the alleged October 2024 sexual assault.
Jane Doe, who was a student then, alleges that Chi Phi members plied her with alcohol and drugs and several sexually assaulted her. One man sent others a message inviting them to participate, according to a lawsuit she filed last month against Cornell, the fraternity, seven men who were Chi Phi brothers and others.
Lawyers for two of the men have denied they participated in a sexual assault. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the others or their representatives have been unsuccessful. Some of the men who underwent a university disciplinary hearing in 2024 told investigators that the sexual activity was consensual or said they were not involved.
The woman went to Cornell police in November 2024, though no criminal charges resulted. In the wake of her lawsuit, the state attorney general is conducting a renewed criminal investigation.
Cornell closed down the Chi Phi campus chapter in 2024 and says it expelled some students and suspended others after an investigation under the federal Title IX law.
This week Cornell trustees brought in former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to review how the school investigates sexual assault and sexual harassment, how the disciplinary process works, campus police response and more.

title: Maine Military Museum honors Vietnam War POWs
text:
SOUTH PORTLAND — Six and a half years — 2,402 days.
That’s how long Col. Michael Brazelton was held in captivity as a prisoner of war while serving as a fighter pilot in the U.S. Air Force in the Vietnam War.
More than a half-century later, he visited the Maine Military Museum and Learning Center in South Portland, which houses a collection of artifacts and exhibits about American military service. Brazelton was there to speak about his experience alongside John Borling, a retired Air Force major general who lives in Illinois.
The pair were astonished by the museum’s collection.
“They seem to tell the POW story,” Brazelton said. Lee Humiston, the late founder of the museum, was known as a keeper of the flame, preserving the stories and memories of POWs.
Thomas Lundy, a volunteer with the museum, recorded videos of the veterans telling stories of their service while they were visiting.
Brazelton said he knew he wanted to be a pilot since the seventh grade, went to engineering school and got his pilot’s license when he was 19. He was assigned his first combat mission when he was 23, and after more than a hundred missions, was shot down — the first in his squadron. Borling lost one-third of his squadron in six months.
“One day, you’re standing at a bar,” Brazelton said. “The next, you’re in a little cell by yourself.”
He remembers crying in his cell, which was no bigger than the small area rug in the reading room of the museum. The days were long. Soldiers kept up morale by tapping through the walls, Borling said, a form of communication that was met with brutality.
Borling remembers being punished for refusing to write letters home that said he was a war criminal, what he described as “propaganda.”
“Our expressed desire was to survive and survive with honor,” he said. “We wanted the people back home to be proud of us.” People like his wife who refused to believe he was dead. His daughter who was 3 months old when he entered the service and grew up to be just like him.
Both Borling and Brazelton returned to the skies as pilots (and lamented that they weren’t able to advance through the ranks while they were in captivity).
“Life goes on,” Borling said. “You still have to march.”
Brazelton said that his life turned out all right. “I have all of my fingers, I married a beautiful woman and I have three daughters,” he said.
Many U.S. prisoners of war, like Borling and Brazelton, retain a tight camaraderie. They have created a POW group, attended reunions (like one hosted at the Maine Military Museum years ago) and published an electronic newsletter.
A framed photo of Brazelton and Borling will be placed near the Vietnam War POW exhibit at the Maine Military Museum and Learning Center, near a re-creation of the sort of prison cells they were held in.

title: Maine’s 3 must-watch high school football games this week
text:
Playoff positioning and solidifying your current record. Those are the two themes for this week’s three must-watch high school football games in Maine.
Massabesic (4-1) at South Portland (3-2), 7 p.m. Friday
The Mustangs and Red Riots — ranked No. 8 and No. 10 in the latest Varsity Maine poll — have already shown that they are playoff-worthy teams. But South Portland is currently fifth in the Class A South Crabtree standings, one spot out of the playoffs, with a tough final four games. After this week, they play at Noble, which is ranked fourth in the Crabtree standings, then they host one-loss Winnacunnet of New Hampshire, followed by Portland (4-1).
South Portland’s Chris Salamone ran over Sanford for 227 yards last week and has been productive in every game, totaling 99 carries, 783 yards and 10 TDs. But no one has put up big numbers against Massabesic’s run defense, which is allowing 70 yards per game and stuffed Noble last week for 28 yards on 22 carries.
South Portland has the edge in the passing game. QB Shea Healy (45 of 87, 661 yards, 6 TDs, 3 interceptions) has effectively teamed up with tight end Jacoby Jellow (14 catches, 216 yards) and sophomore wideout Ben Dube (15 catches, 203 yards).
Massabesic has thrown for 215 yards total. It relies on its inside running game, with fullback Alex Harriman (100 carries, 627 yards) doing most of the work and Dustin Maley (41 carries, 278 yards) complementing him as a big-play threat, as he showed with a 75-yard sprint against Noble.
With a win, Massabesic would be in great position to finish third. A move into second would even be possible if either Thornton Academy or Bonny Eagle, the top two teams in the Varsity Maine poll and the league standings, stumble down the stretch. The Mustangs’ lone loss is to Bonny Eagle. They have winless teams Lewiston and Scarborough up next after South Portland before ending the year with a home game against Thornton.
Oxford Hills (4-0) at Bonny Eagle (5-0), 7 p.m. Friday
This game should tell us the validity of Oxford Hills’ unblemished record. Bonny Eagle’s isn’t in doubt, as the Scots beat playoff contender South Portland, Noble and Massabesic in their first three games and are averaging 34.6 points, with an a victory margin of nearly 23 points.
The Vikings, who had a Week 4 bye, have played weaker opponents in Windham (2-3), Deering (1-4), Edward Little (2-2) and Lewiston (0-5). That said, we’ve heard several coaches say something like, “Oxford Hills is looking tough.” Behind the play of dual-threat quarterback Toby Oufiero and top back Keegan Ridley, Oxford Hills has averaged 34.8 points, and the defense has allowed just 27 points total.
The Vikings are likely to have a tough time slowing a Bonny Eagle offense that is starting to hit on multiple cylinders. The Scots have theirs own dynamic QB in Lucas Klehn. Running backs Ben Noe and Ben Havu are improving weekly. Drew Gervais is a big-play threat as a receiver.
Cape Elizabeth (4-1) at Spruce Mountain (3-2), 7 p.m. Friday
Back in the preseason, Cape Elizabeth’s players were convinced they would be much better than last year’s team that went 1-7 and gave up a hideous 51.25 points per game. The Capers are certainly better under first-year coach Issiah Bachelder (though they did give up 82 points to Varsity Maine’s No. 1 eight-man team, Yarmouth).
Spruce Mountain, meanwhile, is the defending Large School South champion. Four of the six teams in Large School South make the playoffs. Right now, it looks like both Cape and Spruce will be in that mix. This game could determined which team is going to be No. 2 behind Yarmouth and get to host a playoff game.

title: Bill Harris, one of Patty Hearst’s kidnappers in the 1970s, dies at 81
text:
Bill Harris, who helped kidnap newspaper heiress Patty Hearst in the 1970s, dies at 81
Bill Harris, a member of the domestic terrorist group that kidnapped newspaper heiress Patricia "Patty" Hearst in the 1970s, has died at 81, The New York Times reported.
Harris died of a heart attack on Sept. 10 in San Francisco, his wife, Rebecca Young, confirmed to The New York Times.
Harris was a member of the Symbionese Liberation Army, a radical militant organization, when he and two others kidnapped Hearst from her apartment in Berkeley, California, on Feb. 4, 1974.
Hearst was the daughter of Randolph A. Hearst, the chairman of the Hearst Corporation, and the granddaughter of William Randolph Hearst, who founded the Hearst Corporation in 1887.
The SLA kidnapped Hearst because she was a "symbolic target," according to Harris. "Her family was in control of a media empire that we viewed as an arm of propaganda for the United States government."
After taking Hearst as a "prisoner of war," the SLA demanded that her family fund a food giveaway in California to feed the poor. The Hearst family pledged $2 million, which the kidnappers found to be not enough, according to NYT.
Two weeks after her kidnapping, Hearst participated in a bank robbery in San Francisco. She later said that she was coerced into joining the SLA and she feared that she would be killed if she refused, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.
Hearst was convicted of armed bank robbery in 1976 and sentenced to seven years in prison. After she served about 22 months in prison, former President Jimmy Carter commuted her sentence.
Harris reached a plea deal in the Hearst kidnapping and spent about eight years in prison. Harris was convicted of additional crimes throughout his life, including armed robbery and auto theft. He pleaded guilty to second-degree murder after a woman was shot and killed during a SLA bank robbery in 1975.

title: InvestigateTV+: Help for overwhelmed animal shelters
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ digs into what is driving the surge at animal shelters nationwide and unique solutions giving pets a second chance.
Then, why heart disease is too often missed in women, the diagnostic bias behind it, and how women can advocate for lifesaving care.
Plus, a group of seniors stitches together a sisterhood, creating quilts of comfort that strengthen their community.
Geography plays role in overwhelmed animal shelters
Many animal shelters across America are overwhelmed, and where animals are located is a big reason why.
In regions like the South, shelters are under-resourced and over-capacity, packed with dogs and cats waiting for adoption. For many, that wait can be fatal. In 2024, U.S. shelters euthanized more than 600,000 animals.
Experts say homes often exist for these animals, but the animals are in the wrong place.
Women advocating for themselves
Heart disease is the biggest threat to women’s health, though studies show many people still believe it is primarily a men’s health issue.
That misconception can be dangerous, as symptoms in women are sometimes mistaken for stress or something else minor, leading to delays in care.
A 2022 study published in the Journal of the American Heart Association found women who went to the emergency room with chest pain waited, on average, 11 minutes longer than men to receive medical attention.
Recruiting for the auto repair industry
Most auto repair shops are staffed almost entirely by men, according to federal labor data.
A February 2026 report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics found about 1.8% of mechanics are women.
Federal data predicts about 70,000 job openings in the field by 2034 as many older workers retire. The industry is stepping up efforts to recruit and train more women to meet that demand.
Quilting for a cause and for fun
A group of seniors meets every Thursday morning at Cedarhurst of Tesson Heights to sew quilts from fabric scraps.
The quilting club was the idea of activities coordinator Glenette Nothum.
“I love to quilt, and I think word got out. Then the ladies were like, we wanna quilt, and I was like really...wow,” Nothum said.

title: QUINN QUESTIONS: What did sidekicks do?
text:
If you grew up in the 1950s through 1970s, television westerns introduced you to a thankless career.
Here’s the job description. You work for a cowboy who travels constantly and appears to have no source of income.
You don’t decide how you spend your day. You’ve got no house or apartment.
Have you guessed your profession? Yes, that’s right…you are a sidekick.
Because sidekicks live in the 1800s Wild West, they’ve got no car, bicycle, taxi, or access to public transportation.
They ride a horse most of the time. They rarely change clothes, because their entire wardrobe is rolled up behind the saddle.
Gender equality? Forget it. All the heroes – except for one notable exception – are males. And the folks they hire for sidekicks are guys too.
The worst part is the social life. There’s no Top 40 music, unless they can create it on a harmonica or accordion.
They spend days chasing bad guys, and nights next to a campfire drinking stale coffee. They can’t call a lady for a date, because she ain’t got a phone, she doesn’t live nearby, and it’s hard for a sidekick to smell good if he hasn’t bathed since April.
So, to sum up: No car. No phone. No bed. No bath. No soap. No shampoo. No deodorant. No cologne. No clean clothes. No music. No dance. No dates.
What could make a guy want to be a sidekick? The only advantage I can see is…he would live forever in reruns.

It is also expensive!

title: Troy Jackson details personal finances in new disclosure
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson‘s primary source of income over the last two years came from two international unions based in Maryland, according to a personal financial disclosure filed this week.
Since the beginning of last year, Jackson received $90,000 from the International Association of Machinists and $48,000 from the International Union of Painters and Allied Trades for general consulting work.
Jackson’s campaign said the candidate provided consulting and organizing help for various national and local issues. Jackson is no longer providing those services, the campaign said.
“Troy’s financial disclosure reflects a lifetime of working for a paycheck,” a spokesperson said in a written statement. “He’s a logger and union member who understands what it means to worry about making ends meet — and he would bring that experience to a Senate dominated by millionaires. Susan Collins has spent nearly 30 years in Washington. Troy has spent his life fighting for people who work for a living.”
Jackson’s disclosure was filed late Monday after he received a 55-day extension. It’s the first detailed look the candidate has provided into his personal finances.
Sen. Susan Collins‘ campaign accused Jackson of not being transparent about his finances, and of taking “dark money” and corporate PAC money as Maine Senate president, despite vows to refuse that money during his U.S. Senate campaign.
“As Senate president, he was paid by three unions and a dark money group,” Collins spokesperson Blake Kernen said in a written statement. “And rather than file his disclosure on time in August, he took the latest extension possible and filed at 9:54 p.m. on the final day.”
In 2025, Jackson reported payments totaling $5,100 from the Eastern Maine Labor Council and $4,800 from Food and Medicine, a 501 (c)(4) social and economic justice group. He served as an organizer for both Brewer-based groups, his disclosure shows.
Jackson is leaning heavily on his working-class background, including his prior work as a logger, in his race against Collins, the Republican incumbent. But his disclosure does not list any income from logging.
His campaign said Jackson worked as a logger for 15 years before joining the state Legislature in 2002, at which point he continued logging intermittently.
Jackson also listed his construction and land management firm, Jackson Associates, on the paperwork. He did not list any assets for that firm, but he did report that some of his consulting income went to his company.
It’s unclear exactly how much Jackson or Collins’ total assets are worth, since they are only required to disclose minimums and ranges on the Senate financial forms.
Jackson disclosed between $147,000 and $430,000 in assets, including between $100,000 and $250,000 in state retirement benefits from his partner.
Yet Jackson’s earnings and assets pale in comparison to Collins, who earns at least $174,000 a year as a senator and receives additional income through her husband, Tom Daffron. The couple has an estimated net worth of $7.1 million and owns between $4.2 million and $10 million in assets, according to Congressstock.com.
Collins’ personal holdings include mutual funds and bank deposits. Daffron has a robust portfolio of stocks, bonds and government securities.
Jackson reported commercial real estate in Allagash owned by his longtime partner as an asset valued between $15,000 and $50,000. But he did not report any income from that property.

title: Biddeford graffiti demands strong condemnation
text:
The vandalism of Sen. Susan Collins’ Biddeford office should be a moment of clarity in this U.S. Senate race. Somebody spray-painted the door with a degrading, sexist slur, and a disturbing number of people online have applauded it.
That kind of politics doesn’t care about fixing Maine’s problems; it cares only about winning the fight, using whatever illegal or criminal means available.
Troy Jackson, and the national Democratic establishment backing his campaign, should condemn this clearly and without qualification. Silence, or a vague statement about “heated rhetoric on both sides,” will tell the voters all they need to know about the kind of campaign we can expect over the coming weeks.
In her nearly 30 years of serving the people of Maine in the Senate, Sen. Collins has found common ground in her diligent and unwavering advocacy of the people in our great state. I know she will not be intimidated by the reprehensible tactics being undertaken by her adversaries — and neither should Maine voters.
Theodore Politis
Biddeford

title: Road worker, 24, dies after being hit by 2 trucks in work zone crash, troopers say
text:
BENTON TWP., Mich. (WILX/Gray News) - A road worker was killed while on the job Tuesday afternoon in Michigan.
According to Michigan State Police, troopers were called around 2:30 p.m. to Lansing Road near Nixon Road for a reported crash in a roadwork zone.
Road crews had temporarily closed Lansing Road to northbound traffic for construction work, officials said. Flag workers were directing traffic while road commission trucks were parked at the scene.
Troopers said the crash occurred when a pickup truck was stopped on Lansing Road at the direction of a flagger, and a Kenworth sanitation truck, unable to stop while approaching the pickup, struck the back of the pickup.
The impact pushed the two trucks into an unoccupied road commission truck. Authorities said the 24-year-old worker, who was directing traffic, attempted to avoid the trio of trucks but was hit by the pickup and the sanitation truck.
The flagger was pronounced dead at the scene, according to police who called the crash heartbreaking.
“Yesterday’s tragic crash in Eaton County is a sobering reminder of the dangers our road crews face every day,” Michigan State Police Lt. Rene Gonzalez said.
The driver of the pickup and his passenger were taken to University of Michigan Health-Sparrow Hospital with injuries. The sanitation truck driver and his passenger were not injured.
“We urge every driver approaching a work zone to slow down, stay focused, and give workers the space they need to do their jobs safely. A few extra seconds of caution can save a life,” Gonzalez said.
Investigators noted that alcohol and drugs did not appear to have been factors in the crash.

title: Collins campaign pushes back on ProPublica report on claims of pay-to-play scheme
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (WMTW) - The campaign for Sen. Susan Collins is making a renewed effort to push back against recent reporting and PAC ads that claim she accepted a big campaign donation in 2019 as part of a pay-to-play scheme.
In a report published on Sept. 22, ProPublica said that Collins, R-Maine, steered millions of dollars to defense contractor Martin Kao, the former CEO of Navatek, in return for donations to her 2020 reelection campaign. More specifically, ProPublica reported that the Collins campaign told Kao that he needed to make a campaign donation before meeting Collins, and that Kao was awarded millions in federal contracts after donating to the senator’s campaign.
The Collins campaign denied the corruption allegations on the day the ProPublica report was published, and on Tuesday, the campaign again vehemently denied ProPublica’s allegations, calling Kao a convicted felon and a liar.
On Tuesday, the Collins campaign presented what it said was proof that the ProPublica report is not true and that the senator did not accept money for favors. The Collins campaign presented a picture of Collins in a meeting with Kao, which was taken by a U.S. Senate photographer and had a timestamp of Feb. 15, 2018. The senator’s campaign said that meeting — which was held to discuss a contract Navatek had been granted through the University of Maine — took place months before Kao made any donations to Collins’ campaign.
“ProPublica reported that Martin Kao used the Navatek method: get the meeting, make the big initial donation, then have the high-priced lobbyists swoop in. As you can see, we were working with Navatek, through their partnership with the University of Maine, for two years before the big initial donation showed up,” said Steve Abbott, Collins’ campaign manager.
On Sept. 23, ProPublica published a follow-up report stating that some of the statements made by Collins and her representatives denying any wrongdoing were not accurate.

title: Chick-fil-A has no plans to add AI to its drive-thru ordering service despite other rivals doing so
text:
ATLANTA (Gray News) - Chick-fil-A leadership says customers can continue to expect to be served by its team members at restaurant locations and not artificial intelligence.
Chick-fil-A CEO Andrew Cathy recently shared in a CNBC interview that it’s not pursuing AI voice ordering in its drive-thru lanes.
Cathy stated that the company is exploring opportunities to use AI but just more behind the scenes.
“From our experience, we really want that hospitality to be human to human,” Cathy was quoted in the interview. “We’re not gonna substitute that interaction with technology, because we feel like that hospitality is so important to create that warm environment for consumers.”
The popular chicken chain’s stance against using AI in its drive-thru lanes comes as some of its fast-food competitors move forward with their automated order-taking plans.
McDonald’s shared that it plans to test its drive-thru AI assistant called Archy, while Wendy’s has also rolled out its AI drive-thru ordering assistant called FreshAi.
Earlier this year, Forbes shared a survey conducted by SurveyMonkey that found that 79% of customers said they would prefer interacting with a human versus some sort of automated customer service.
Chick-fil-A’s enduring focus on customer service has made it the fast-food leader when it comes to customer satisfaction. Ranking in the top two spots on the American Customer Satisfaction Index for more than a decade and has been the clear leader in the fast-food chicken category.
