title: ‘That scares me a bit’: Bow hunter shot in chest by target shooter just days into hunting season
text:
LANSING, Mich. (WILX/Gray News) - Days into bowhunting season in Michigan, questions about safety are being raised after a hunter was shot in the chest.
The hunter was hit by an errant round from a target shooter while they were sitting inside a hunting blind, according to officials.
The injured hunter ended up being taken to an area hospital.
Brent Langenbacher, a lifelong hunter and manager at Moose Creek Sports, said what happened is concerning.
“I hunt up in Clinton County, so that scares me a bit. I hunt right up there,” Langenbacher said.
Langenbacher added that hunting blinds carry their own safety risks.
“Those are fully camouflaged. Unless you have some orange on there, someone could shoot you while you’re sitting in there and they would have no idea they even shot you,” Langenbacher said.
Michigan law requires hunters to wear bright orange, although there are exceptions, including for bow hunting.
According to the Michigan Department of Natural Resources (DNR), this is because typically there are fewer people in the woods, and the arrows hunters shoot won’t travel as far as bullets or penetrate as deeply.
Langenbacher said changes to a hunting blind could help improve visibility.
“Put a blaze orange hat on top of your hut. You can just do that, and that would let people know someone is in there hunting,” Langenbacher said.
The Michigan DNR noted that hunters do have that option.
“If you’re a bow hunter and you’re concerned that somebody is on a neighboring property, or you want people to know you’re out there, there’s nothing that says you can’t wear orange,” Michigan DNR Lt. Richard Nickols said.
State officials said all hunters are responsible for their rounds and where those rounds end up. If a shooter causes damage or recklessly fires rounds, they could be held criminally responsible.

title: Reese’s pumpkins come with a new disclaimer after lawsuit
text:
Reese’s pumpkins come with a new disclaimer after lawsuit
Hershey has added a new disclaimer to its Reese’s Peanut Butter Pumpkins this spooky season.
A front-of-package disclaimer now reads "Carving not on actual product," appearing beneath the image of a pumpkin-shaped candy with a carved jack-o'-lantern face.
The messaging replaces the previous “Decorating suggestion” label on the seasonal candy’s packaging following a lawsuit accusing Hershey of misleading customers.
That lawsuit claimed the packaging was misleading, as the peanut butter pumpkins did not show a jack-o'-lantern face, as the wrappings showed.
One plaintiff said he bought multiple bags of the pumpkins in 2023 expecting them to have carved eyes and a mouth, but found plain pumpkin-shaped chocolates, multiple news outlets report.
The plaintiffs sought $5 million, also citing other Reese’s holiday shapes, including ghosts, bats and footballs.
A federal judge dismissed the case for a second time in September, saying the plaintiffs had not shown a concrete economic injury.
The judge described their complaint as “subjective disappointment.”
Hershey has not publicly explained why it changed the disclaimer, and the plaintiffs’ attorneys have said they were considering an appeal.

title: Read the poem ‘La Cathédrale Engloutie’ by Richard Foerster
text:
This week’s poem, Richard Foerster’s “La Cathédrale Engloutie,” or “The Sunken Cathedral,” takes its title from a piano composition by Debussy, which is itself inspired by a Breton myth of a submerged cathedral that rises from the sea on days when the sea is very clear. (The italicized phrase in the first stanza, which translates as “in a sweetly sonorous fog,” is the composer’s musical instruction for how to play the piece.) I love this poem’s imagery at once of wounds and sky, and the awe with which it limns the nearness of beauty to terror.
Foerster is the author of nine poetry collections, most recently “With Little Light and Sometimes None at All”(Littoral Books, 2023), which received a Gold Medal at the 2024 Independent Publishers of New England Book Awards. He lives in Eliot.
Poets, please note that submissions to Deep Water are open now and through the end of the year. Deep Water is especially eager to share poems by Black writers, writers of color, indigenous writers, LGBTQ+ writers, and other underrepresented voices. Find a link to submit your credits at mainewriters.org/deep-water.
La Cathédrale Engloutie
The horizon at dusk, a sutured scar
barely visible, though unhealed:
thus the overworld of perception fades
to a calmness like the sleep daylaborers
might find freed of ache dans une brume
doucement sonore, till something immense
returns, dawning through the thinnest gash
that centers sacredness within searing
flame. A body cannot endure for long
this surging through its veins, the sublime
beauty that horror is often mistaken for.
Open your eyes now. Another day has come.
What do you glimpse receding, like an echo,
each time inside that music’s sunken nave?
— Richard Foerster
Megan Grumbling is a poet and writer who lives in Portland. title: Washington unearths 50-year-old time capsule; buries new one
text:
The town of Washington celebrated the country’s 250th anniversary with the Washington Historical Society at their annual Heritage Day event on August 21 and 22, 2026. Fifty years ago in 1976 the town’s bicentennial committee and the newly-formed Washington Historical Society buried a time capsule behind the Welcome to Washington sign in the town park. Their directions were for it to be dug up 50 years later and opened in 2026.
Taking on the project the town’s select board and historical society members set the date to dig for Friday, August 21. Jesse Casas and Jeff Ginnell were tasked with overseeing the unearthing of the 13x16x9- inch cement box. They along with Chris Moody, Matt Shannon, Don Bowman, Scott Foster, Gus Nelson and Barry Peabody, all a bit older than when they originally gathered at the sign post in 1976, eventually were successful with finding and removing the capsule from its deeper than expected underground location. After about an hour and a half of teamwork and cheering on from the large crowd watching, the heavy, tar and burlap covered, sealed cement box was moved to Jeff’s truck to be pressure washed at Don Bowman’s garage. The plan was to break the seal the next morning at the WHS Razorville Hall Museum.
Saturday morning Jeff and Don carefully lifted the heavy cover to expose the capsule’s contents. “OH NO”, were the next words heard! The box was filled with very smelly water, but not giving up, Wendy Carr, Jeff, Don, and Matt carefully began pulling wet papers and items from the box. Papers were handled carefully and spread out to dry and inspect. 1976 pennies and quarters were found along with the two matchbox vehicles Jeff Grinnell and Patrick Whalen donated to the cause 50 years ago. Patrick’s car was later returned to his mother, Carol, to be added back to complete his collection for his family. Pictures were found, town paperwork, and a very wet copy of the Welcome to Washington formerly Putnam book the WHS published in 1976. Thankfully we have copies still at the WHS office and refer to it often for town history. The items have been left to dry and see what may be saved.
Later a 2026 PVC pipe Time Capsule, measuring eight inches in diameter and 24 inches high, constructed by Don Grinnell and Cyd Zeigler was filled. Hazel Kopishke from the WHS, showed all the items that were going in from the town office, WHS, Prescott Memorial School, Community Auction, Village Church, Evening Star Grange, Washington’s 2011 Bicentennial, Washington Lakes & Watershed, the Fire Department and Auxiliary, Recreational Trails Committee, Gibbs Library, Medomak Camp, Washington General, Hill & Gully Snowmobile Club, Masons, and the Minnie Weaver Scholarship. Blueberry Fields contributed a small bottle of maple syrup, Two Rock Ridge added an empty bottle for maple syrup, Washington General put in two gift cards and a bandana, Dave Martucci added a new Washington flag, and the WHS added a Washington Maine, Est. 1811 T-shirt. Also included were a 2025 penny, a 2026 dime and nickel, along with four 1976 pennies. Additionally, many town business cards, flyers, menus, stickers, and other items were included. Kate Grinnell packed the capsule with a little assistance from Jack and Ginger Kenefick who added two new hot wheel vehicles at the very top. We hope they will be there to see it unpacked 50 years from now! The capsule was carefully sealed by Cyd with Eric Kenefick and Jesse Casas assisting.
At one o’clock the group proceeded back to the town park and the capsule was placed back in the hole dug the night before. Jeff Ginnell made his way back into the hole one last time to receive the capsule from the next generation of young people. Micheal and Grace Garnett, Charlie and Halas Lutz, and Jack and Ginger Kenefick worked to complete the task of filling the hole covering the capsule for another 50 years when hopefully they will take part in the next unearthing in 2076.
Earlier at Heritage Day before the opening of the capsule, Edward and Marjorie Ludwig’s children Valerie, Joanne, and Michael and granddaughter Lindsey shared memories of their family’s history in the town. Their grandfather Fred grew up in South Liberty but lived most of his life in Washington. He owned and operated the Ludwig General Store for years, once located in the now empty lot next to the Washington Post Office. He and later his son Edward were post masters for many, many years. Edward bought the family store and ran it until selling it to Robert and Patricia Ross. The Ludwig siblings shared family stories, memories from the store, and growing up in Washington bringing back memories to many in the audience.
The sweetest part of the day was consuming slices of pie from the “Tasty Pie Contest”. This years’ bragging rights go to pie bakers Cheri Garnett and Deb Zeigler. Slices were sold as a fundraiser for the WHS.

It is also expensive!

title: This Maine actor’s career has taken her from Camden to London
text:
Caitlin FitzGerald always finds a little bit of Maine, wherever she is.
She cornered Portland native Anna Kendrick at a party in London so she could talk about Maine with her. When the iconic true-life book “Lost on a Mountain in Maine” was made into a movie a few years ago, FitzGerald just knew she had to play the lost boy’s mother. She had read the book in grammar school, like most Maine kids.
And this year, while filming the second season of the Prime drama “We Were Liars” in Nova Scotia, FitzGerald was introduced to Elysia Roorbach, who will be playing the younger version of her character, Penny Sinclair. Roorbach grew up in Farmington, in Maine’s western mountains.
“I love Maine so much, it feels like such a part of who I am and it’s such a special place,” said FitzGerald, while filming in Nova Scotia this summer. “So it’s wonderful to meet people who understand.”
FitzGerald, 43, has traveled and worked all over the world during her 20-year career in film, TV and theater. She’s currently living in London and recently starred as Desdemona in a West End production of Shakespeare’s “Othello,” which was filmed and released to theaters in March.
She’s currently starring as one of the adult sisters of a wealthy, secrets-laden family in the Prime drama “We Were Liars,” based on the best-selling novel by E. Lockhart. The first season premiered in the summer of 2025 and the second season is slated for sometime next year. FitzGerald also had a recurring role on the hit HBO show “Succession,” playing Tabitha Hayes, girlfriend of Roman Roy (Kieran Culkin). About a decade ago, she played Libby Masters, the first wife of pioneering sex researcher William Masters, in the Showtime series “Masters of Sex.”
“We Were Liars” focuses on a wealthy family that spends the summer on a private island off the Massachusetts coast. FitzGerald’s character, Penny Sinclair, is the mother of Cadence Sinclair Eastman, part of a tightknit group called the Liars. Cadence suffers from memory loss due to a mysterious accident.
MAINE CONNECTIONS
The second season flashes back two decades, so new actors were cast to play the younger versions of the main characters. In a weird bit of Maine karma, Roorbach was cast to play the younger Penny. So there are two Maine actors on the show playing the same role. Earlier this year Roorbach made her TV debut playing an emergency room patient in two episodes of the hit HBO drama “The Pitt.”
FitzGerald said she didn’t know Roorbach, 26, until she was cast in “We Were Liars.” The two quickly found they had much in common, besides being from Maine. They both studied acting at New York University, and both did a semester abroad in London, focused on Shakespeare.
“There aren’t a lot of people from Maine in this industry, so it’s great that she’s here,” said FitzGerald of Roorbach. “I’m so pleased I get to work with her.”
FitzGerald lived in Lincolnville as a small child, then moved to Camden. Her father, Des FitzGerald, started a company called DuckTrap River Fish Farm, which became a nationally known purveyor of smoked fish. Her mother, Pam Allen, was the editor of a knitting magazine and started her own line of yarn, Quince & Co.
FitzGerald says she fell in love with acting in a kindergarten play, an adaptation of Rudyard Kipling’s “How the Elephant Got his Trunk.” She got involved with area children’s theater productions, including at Camden Civic Theatre.
FitzGerald says she really wanted to study the craft of acting, instead of just driving to Los Angeles and looking for work, like many people do. She chose the Tisch School of the Arts at NYU because it combined classroom academics with stage training. Being from Maine, she says living in New York City during college was also an education.
Though she’s worked steadily for two decades, FitzGerald says her career has ebbed and flowed. One of her early breaks was being cast in the 2009 romcom “It’s Complicated,” starring Meryl Streep and Alec Baldwin. She played Streep’s daughter.
“She was my hero, so I was definitely nervous to work with her, I had no idea what I was doing,” said FitzGerald. “I probably embarrassed myself a lot in front of her, but she was very generous.”
In one of those odd full-circle moments, FitzGerald is now sharing scenes with Streep’s daughter, Mamie Gummer. Gummer plays a sister of FitzGerald’s character on “We Were Liars.”
One of FitzGerald’s favorite roles was playing Libby Masters on “Masters of Sex” over four seasons. She says the writers created for her character “an amazing journey” from a typical 1950s housewife, who happens to be married to a sex researcher, to a more a indepedendent and complicated character. She eventually goes to Woodstock and also studies law.
But maybe her most personal role was playing the mother of Donn Fendler in “Lost on a Mountain in Maine.” Fendler was 12 when he got separated from his hiking party on Mount Katahdin in 1939 and survived nine days alone, lost in the woods.
The search for Fendler and his eventual rescue sparked stories in newspapers around the country. Within months, a book co-authored by Fendler and Joseph B. Egan, “Lost on a Mountain in Maine,” was published. For decades the book was taught in Maine schools as part of a lesson on Maine history. Fendler himself spoke to hundreds of classes and community groups over the years. He died in 2016, at the age of 90.
FitzGerald said she has vivid memories of the book, which portrays the danger, fear and hope of a young, lost boy. She said when her agent told her about the movie, and the part of Fendler’s mother, she said, “I have to do that one.”
Before opening in theaters nationally, the film premiered at the Maine International Film Festival in Waterville in the summer of 2024. FitzGerald attended the premiere and said she loved seeing so many teachers from around Maine who had taught the book to kids like her for years.
“It was such a lovely homegrown moment and I was really proud to be a part of it,” she said. “It was an honor to tell that story.”

title: Top teams in Varsity Maine football polls are dominating
text:
Thornton Academy has been the unanimous No. 1 in every Varsity Maine football poll this fall, and for good reason. title: Why women should advocate for themselves after delays in heart disease diagnosis
text:
GREENVILLE, S.C. (InvestigateTV) — Heart disease is the biggest threat to women’s health, though studies show many people still believe it is primarily a men’s health issue.
That misconception can be dangerous, as symptoms in women are sometimes mistaken for stress or something else minor, leading to delays in care.
A 2022 study published in the Journal of the American Heart Association found women who went to the emergency room with chest pain waited, on average, 11 minutes longer than men to receive medical attention.
The study also found women were less likely than men to have an echocardiogram, a non-invasive ultrasound test that evaluates heart structure and function.
A runner’s warning signs
Courtney Pace, a South Carolina mother, used to run a few miles a day. In 2024, even walking caused her pain.
“It felt like I was having chest pain, it would go down my arm, like a heart attack,” Pace said.
Pace went to the emergency room, where doctors gave her an EKG, a test that checks the heart’s electrical activity. Her results came back normal. Pace said doctors suggested stress or a hard workout might be the cause and sent her home.
“I left crying,” she said.
Research by the National Institutes of Health shows that during a cardiac event, women are less likely than men to be referred for cardiac diagnostic testing, receive timely treatment or be taken seriously. As a result, heart disease in women is often detected later, when it is more advanced and harder to treat.
UNC Health cardiologist Dr. Essraa Bayoumi said some of the pattern is rooted in historic thinking.
“Cardiovascular disease was seen more as a man’s disease and that women were somehow protected. And so that thought has been ingrained. So it unfortunately is true. We’ve really been behind in understanding and diagnosing and treating cardiovascular disease in women,” Bayoumi said.
Bayoumi said women are also consistently under-represented in landmark clinical trials.
A 2022 study published by the National Library of Medicine found that guideline recommendations for the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease are based on predominantly male participants.
Bayoumi said when tests come back normal, women’s symptoms are sometimes dismissed as something else, like anxiety or “just stress.”
“We use stress as sort of an excuse for their symptoms which is a double-edged sword because truly, stress is actually a risk factor for cardiovascular disease,” Bayoumi said.
Bayoumi said advocating for yourself starts with knowing personal risk factors, including family history, autoimmune disease, pregnancy-related complications like preeclampsia or gestational diabetes, and menopause-related changes.
“And that’s because they’ve lost that estrogen, which we believe is protective,” Bayoumi said. “And that’s why women who have menopause much earlier are at a much higher risk of having cardiovascular disease.”
Cardiologists and experts say women don’t always show “classic” chest pain, which can slow a diagnosis.
In addition to chest pain or discomfort, women may experience nausea and vomiting, unexplained weakness or tiredness, upset stomach, or pain in the shoulder, back or arm.
Experts say because some of these symptoms do not fit the standard heart attack narrative, they are frequently mistaken for panic attacks, acid reflux or bone and joint issues.
A Kentucky mother’s experience
In 2025, it took six stairs for Vivian Tandy to realize something was wrong.
She experienced shortness of breath and chest pain, which interfered with her daily routine. Doctors asked her to wear a heart monitor, but after it came back normal, Tandy still did not feel “right” and expressed her concerns to her doctor.
Her doctor listened and eventually found the cause. In October 2025, Tandy underwent open heart surgery to fix a rare genetic heart disorder.
“They essentially did what’s called an unroofing, and they literally shaved a piece of my heart — it’s really cool,” Tandy said.
Tandy said her decision to keep advocating for herself was connected to her mother, who died at age 47 from heart disease.
“I look in the mirror, and I see that scar, and I look at myself, and I’m like if it wasn’t for my mom, I wouldn’t have done the things that I did to fight for the answer, so I am super proud of my scar,” Tandy said.
A specialist finds answers
Back in South Carolina, Pace’s chest pain persisted, and she returned to the emergency room. This time, she asked to see a specialist. Interventional cardiologist Dr. Vincent Gacad had a hunch of what was going on.
Gacad performed a specialized type of catheterization, which detected coronary microvascular disease, or CMD, a condition that affects tiny vessels that deliver blood to heart tissue that a resting EKG often cannot detect.
“Traditionally, when we see chest pain we think about coronary artery disease or large vessel blockage,” Gacad said.
CMD causes prolonged chest pain, called angina, and increases the risk for heart attack, according to the Cleveland Clinic. It is more common in women, especially those with lower estrogen levels.
Thanks to medication and her treatment plan, Pace said she is feeling much better and has returned to exercising.
“I just got into more of a walk run, this weekend I did two miles, so I am starting to pick up the pace and get back into it,” Pace said.
What experts recommend
Experts suggest that if you suspect something is wrong with your heart, be persistent. Ask your doctor for further heart testing, such as an EKG, a stress test, a blood test for heart markers like troponin levels, or an echocardiogram.
Experts also recommend bringing an advocate, such as a trusted friend or family member, who can help reinforce your concerns.
If symptoms are dismissed, experts say do not hesitate to see another doctor.
Women who feel unheard can also request a female doctor or seek out a specialist, such as a cardiologist with expertise in women’s heart health.

title: Trump uses anti-trans slur to attack Democratic US Senate candidate
text:
CHARLESTON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — President Donald Trump used an anti-transgender slur to refer to Annie Andrews, a Democratic Senate candidate in South Carolina.
In a post on Truth Social this week, Trump wrote, “Annie ‘Tr*nnie’ Andrews is running against our wonderful Darline Graham for the Senate in South Carolina.”
Trump used the slur three times in referring to Andrews, adding that Andrews was “in favor of transgender for everyone” and that she was “not for South Carolina.”
Andrews, who is a pediatrician, has previously stated that she supports transgender children and is a supporter of gender-affirming care.
The Senate candidate also said that she does not think that biological men should play in women’s sports, while not supporting gender surgery when it comes to minors.
Trump called Darline Graham, who is running against Andrews as the Republican candidate following the death of her brother, Lindsey Graham, “a high-quality person” who has his “complete and total endorsement.”
Andrews did not immediately address Trump’s comments directly, but posted on Monday that she is in the Senate race to fight for her patients, her children and South Carolina.
Former South Carolina Gov. David Beasley called Trump’s comments “abhorrent,” saying that while South Carolinians can disagree, they can do so civilly.

title: Canada's EPA cracks down on U.S. demo debris
text:
Boothbay Region Refuse Disposal District (BRRDD) will no longer be able to sell its demo chips (demolition debris ground into small woodchips) to Canada, due to the stricter regulations from that country’s Environmental Protection Agency, Operations Manager Will Johnson said during a directors' meeting July 8.
In a post-meeting interview, Johnson said Canada has become stricter in multiple categories, including the presence of lead paint, arsenic, treated wood, etc. Johnson was told by BRRDD’s broker that most of his other clients are also failing to meet these new standards.
BRRDD is working on getting certification to have demo chips burned in Livermore Falls’ landfill. Sending chips to Canada had been free, but disposal will now cost BRRDD between $2 and $5 per ton. BRRDD generates 950 tons per year, so the estimated cost is $1,900–$4,750. Johnson is waiting for the final figure.
In other business, Johnson reported that the Giles Rubbish truck involved in a June 16 accident required $27,000 of repair work and should be on the road again by month’s end. The truck hit and snapped a utility pole near the intersection of Route 96 and Dodge Road near Smuggler's Cove Inn in East Boothbay.
The board approved spending $25,000 to pay down a $125,000 COVID loan. Until now, the district’s prior management had just been paying the interest, according to Johnson.
Jody Lewis was reelected chair; Curt Crosby, vice chair; JD Warren, secretary; and Julia Latter, treasurer.

title: A picture speaks volumes about Susan Collins
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Shoshana Hoose recently retired after 27 years with the Portland Public Schools. Prior to working for the Portland schools, she was a reporter for 20 years for newspapers in Virginia, Minnesota, New Hampshire and Maine.
Maine Sen. Susan Collins brought a photograph of a three-year-old girl to show the audience gathered at a Portland synagogue last July. Collins told us that she carries the photograph everywhere to remind her of the horror that the girl has survived, including the death of her father.
Just three days had passed since ICE agents surrounded, shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, an immigrant from Colombia with no criminal history who was living in Biddeford. The agents were l ooking for someone else, not Guerrero; he was shot by mistake. When his possessions were returned to his family, they found a bullet fired into the car seat used by his three-year-old daughter, Dulce.
One might expect that Collins was showing us Dulce’s picture as a reminder of the terror inflicted on Maine residents by a federal agency out of control. But no, Collins wanted to draw our attention elsewhere.
The photo that she carries in her purse shows an Israeli girl, Abigail Mor Edan, whose parents were killed in the Hamas raid on Oct. 7, 2023. Abigail was held hostage in Gaza for more than a year. Collins told us about Abigail to show her own steadfast support for the government of Israel. It was at the heart of Collins’ pitch that day to win support from the Jewish audience.
Abigail survived a horrible ordeal. But I want our U.S. senator to show at least as much care and concern for the children in her own state who are terrified by ICE. Last winter, hundreds of Maine children didn’t dare go to school for fear of getting caught up in the ICE raids underway.
Immigrants who follow every law have been arrested by the agency. The loss of income from a main breadwinner puts families at risk of eviction, even if the person is eventually released. And that’s on top of the trauma that an ICE arrest causes those held in inhumane conditions, plus everyone in their family and community.
At the Portland meeting, I had the rare opportunity to ask Collins an unscripted question. Given all of the missteps by ICE, I asked, why did she vote in June to give the agency an additional, unrestricted $38 billion dollars of taxpayer money?
I recall Collins began by blaming Senate Democrats, who had forced an up or down vote on an omnibus bill that provided funding for the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Customs and Border Protection as well as ICE. She noted that due to her efforts, money was included in the bill to buy body cameras for ICE agents, although none were worn by the agents involved in the Biddeford shooting.
Collins assured us that she had spoken to the head of Homeland Security to demand a complete investigation of the Biddeford incident. More than three months later, the Department of Homeland Security has yet to provide any details about what happened. In fact, it’s not even clear if they are conducting an investigation.
Meanwhile, the ICE agent who allegedly shot and killed Guerrero was identified by family members as David Brouillette, a mentally disturbed man with a history of violent behavior. Brouillette’s problematic past kept him from getting hired as a police officer in Hallowell. ICE apparently didn’t know or care about the warning signs that he was unfit for the job.
In August, I visited the moving memorial created spontaneously on the Biddeford street corner where Guerrero died. Among all the tributes, one item stood out: an orange traffic cone bearing a sign that says “Migration is an act of courage.”
I believe Susan Collins has failed to show courage by standing up to the Trump administration and demanding an end to ICE atrocities. She should carry a photo of Guerrero’s daughter Dulce to remind her of the consequences of failing to rein in a rogue agency that’s terrorizing her constituents.

title: 3 of Nolan Wells’ friends sue NFL Hall of Famer Terrell Owens for defamation
text:
JACKSON, Miss. (AP) — Three friends of Nolan Wells, a Black college student who went missing from a Mississippi island during a Fourth of July celebration and was later found dead, are suing NFL Hall of Famer Terrell Owens for defamation.
The lawsuit was among a handful of defamation claims the friends filed this week against content creators. They also previously indicated their intent to sue the Rev. Al Sharpton and “The View” co-host Sunny Hostin for comments they made while discussing Wells’ death.
The fathers of the three friends, who are under 21 and considered minors under Mississippi law, filed the federal lawsuit Monday on their behalf.
The lawsuit alleges Owens defamed the three friends after posting on X: “ARREST THEM IMMEDIATELY!!” Owens’ post also linked to an Instagram video, which theorized the three friends killed Wells and tampered with his phone, according to the lawsuit. The post was made days after a Mississippi grand jury declined to recommend charges in Wells’ death.
Owens has 1.2 million followers on X and had previously pledged $25,000 to a reward fund for information leading to an arrest and conviction in Wells’ death.
“Not only is he defaming them, he’s basically saying to the mob, get your pitchforks, get your torches,” said Edward Paltzik, a defamation and media attorney representing the three friends.
The Associated Press attempted to contact Owens through social media and SMAC Entertainment, which, according to its website, manages Owens, but did not immediately receive a response.
The three were part of a group of 30 friends, including Wells, who rode to Horn Island on three boats on the Fourth of July. Wells’ friends said Wells did not return to the mainland with them, choosing instead to stay behind to talk with a girl, a claim his family has disputed. His body was found two days later off the island’s coast.
Neither state nor independent autopsies have not determined Wells’ cause of death, though the grand jury found his death was “consistent with drowning.” Wells’ family and their lawyers disputed the grand jury’s findings, pointing to unexplained bruising on the back of his head and noting that his airways and stomach were devoid of water.
Images showing Wells with white friends the day he went missing fueled online speculation that racial dynamics played a role in his death.
Two of the three friends who are suing Owens were singled out online in part because they appear in a photo with Wells and one other friend on a boat, which was circulated on social media after his disappearance. The third called Wells’ mother and the U.S. Coast Guard to report Wells missing.

Associated Press reporter Hallie Golden in Seattle contributed to this report.

title: Obituary: Ronald W. Limington
text:
LIMINGTON – Ronald W. Morris, 80, of Limington, returned home to the Lord peacefully on Oct. 2, 2026. Born Aug. 1, 1946, to Leon and Shirley (Merrifield) Morris.
Ron spent his early years raising hell in Bath, Maine. He gave four years of his life to the Navy, serving aboard the USS Myles C. Fox during the Vietnam War. Ron later became a master plumber, operating his own business for decades while never truly retiring.
Ron enjoyed spending time outdoors hunting, boating, snowmobiling, and fishing. He was a collector of toy cars and enjoyed showing off his Corvettes at car shows all around. Ron and his wife, Rose, spent many years traveling south to Florida and enjoyed visiting all the amusement parks and beaches it had to offer. Ron and Rose enjoyed camping north at their favorite spots in Jackman and the West Forks with family and friends. Ron loved antiquing and yard-sailing with his dear friend and always made it back to Bath on Fridays for coffee with the guys.
Ron was a character who will be dearly missed by all who had the privilege of knowing and loving him.
Ron is survived by his children, Herb Ring, Jessie Waterman and her partner, Bob Gryspeerd, Justin Grass, and Zachery Grass and his wife, Sonya. He also leaves behind six grandchildren; three great-grandchildren; and several wonderful lifelong friends.
Ron was preceded in death by his parents; four siblings; and his loving wife, Rose Morris.
Visitation will be held from 9 a.m. to 10 a.m. on Saturday, Oct. 10, with a memorial service to follow at 10 a.m. at Dolby Blais & Segee, 434 River Rd., Windham.
In lieu of flowers, please consider making a donation to St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital,
as Ron was a donor for several decades.

title: Tropical Storm Isaias to threaten Gulf Coast as a dangerous hurricane
text:
Tropical Storm Isaias to threaten Gulf Coast as a dangerous hurricane
Tropical Storm Isaias formed in the southwestern Gulf on Wednesday morning and is primed to "rapidly strengthen" into a dangerous hurricane en route to landfall on the northern Gulf Coast.
Related video: As super El Niño strengthens, study suggests that climate change is intensifying El Ninos
"Rapid strengthening is forecast over the next day or two," the National Hurricane Center said.
For now, Isaias has sustained winds of 40 mph and is located about 600 miles south of the mouth of the Mississippi River. The storm is expected to push east above Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula and then turn sharply north toward the northern Gulf Coast as it strengthens.
It could peak as a Category 2 with 110 mph winds by Thursday night or early Friday before weakening a little before landfall as a dangerous hurricane.
Hurricane and storm surge watches, which warn of 74 mph or stronger winds and life-threatening coastal flooding within 48 hours, are likely to be issued for parts of the northern Gulf Coast sometime on Wednesday.
Isaias will usher in flooding, rain, powerful winds, and storm surge to areas from southern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle beginning on Friday. The storm could also spin up several tornadoes as its rainbands lash the coast.
This will be the first hurricane of the year in the Atlantic basin, ending a record-long wait tied to the effects of a likely record-strong El Niño.
Exactly where the storm could track or how strong it will be when it approaches land are still not set in stone, but anyone along the Gulf Coast from Louisiana to Florida's Big Bend should monitor the forecast closely.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency for 25 counties Tuesday ahead of the storm, urging residents to prepare disaster plans and stock hurricane supply kits. State emergency teams are staging generators, fuel, food, water and flood barriers in the Tallahassee and Santa Rosa areas to support the response.
Oil companies are also taking precautions in the Gulf. Shell is evacuating nonessential personnel from six offshore platforms, while BP is removing nonessential workers and securing its offshore facilities, the companies said Tuesday.
Forecast uncertainty
This storm is making a run through El Niño-influenced atmospheric conditions that have largely stymied tropical systems throughout the Atlantic hurricane season so far. Gulf waters are record warm for this time of year, providing plenty of fuel, but that's only part of the equation.
The bane of Atlantic tropical systems this season has been wind shear. This refers to winds blowing at different speeds and from different directions at several levels of the atmosphere. Wind shear can tear tropical storms and hurricanes apart.
This new system is benefitting from low wind shear in the southern Gulf, but it'll find higher wind shear guarding the Gulf Coast to the north, threatening to shred the storm as it makes its approach.
But the system is also forecast to move quickly, so its exposure to the higher wind shear may be limited. If the storm were to move slower, it could weaken quickly as it meanders in hostile conditions.
The storm's strength and path are also intertwined. A stronger storm's circulation extends higher into the atmosphere, allowing winds at those heights to steer it differently than a weaker system. That path, in turn, will determine how long it spends over warm water and how much hostile wind shear it encounters, shaping how strong it is when it reaches the coast.
No matter its final fate, heavy rain is a concern on the Gulf Coast and in other parts of the South by late this week. The storm could bring 3 to 6 inches of rain, with localized rainfall up to 10 inches in spots, from southern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend. The downpours could start to ramp up along the coast as soon as Friday and then continue to soak the region while creeping farther inland through the weekend.
As this year has already shown, it doesn't take a hurricane-strength system to cause significant impacts, particularly in a warming world that's making tropical systems wetter.
Tropical storms Arthur and Edouard didn't last long, but their heavy rain resulted in significant flash flooding and water rescues. Parts of Louisiana and Mississippi took the brunt of Arthur's flooding while Edouard dropped over 20 inches of rain in eastern Texas.
Pinning down the location and severity of any storm surge flooding, strong winds and tornadoes along the northern Gulf Coast is even more difficult this far out in time because we need to know how strong the storm will be and exactly where it will track. The earliest those impacts could arrive is Friday or early Saturday.
What's typical in October and November
Four named storms — that's tropical storm strength or greater — typically form in October and November, but some hurricane seasons can have a stronger finish while others quiet down.
The last few years illustrate this year-to-year ebb and flow. Seven storms formed during October and November in 2024, but just two formed during the same time in 2023.
Late-season storms tend to form closer to the United States, including in the Gulf, Caribbean and off the Southeast coast, which makes them more likely to impact land.
While there are usually fewer storms, they can still be destructive.
Last year, Category 5 Hurricane Melissa devastated Jamaica in October's final week.
Hurricane Michael roared into the Florida Panhandle on October 10, 2018, becoming the latest landfalling Category 5 on record in the US.
Hurricane Sandy may be the most notorious of all: It morphed into a hybrid superstorm in late-October 2012 and walloped the East Coast.
Super El Niño's grip on the Atlantic basin means a repeat of notorious late-season hurricanes is less likely this year. Its storm-killing wind is the main reason this season could go hurricane-free for the first time in reliable records.

title: Seth Glier: Songwriting as a tool for positive change
text:
Singer-songwriter Seth Glier will be playing the Opera House at Boothbay Harbor on Wednesday, July 22 at 7:30 p.m. He will be accompanied by fiddle player, and long-time friend, Kelly Halloran.
Glier, a Grammy-nominated artist from Western Massachusetts, says, “I think music is just, it's one of the great magic tricks of life when it comes to building whatever you need, whether it's a bridge or whether it's community, whether it's support or just a container for pain for all kinds of things.”
Recently, he has turned his musical gaze to the natural world, channeling nature’s longing for communion with humanity into song. His new album "Everything" is a collection of eight songs inviting listeners to imagine a future in which humans and the planet are re-aligned into mutual restoration. Each song presents a practical climate solution with concrete optimism.
The album’s title track was inspired by an experience Glier had while foraging. “When I picked up the chanterelle mushroom and brought it towards my nose," he says, “I first smelled sweet apricot and then my spine straightened suddenly. The feeling was like déjà vu. It was a ‘first time,’ yet somewhere inside of me I had done this once before. I was reconnecting to a knowledge I had already known.”
Glier is thrilled to be returning to Maine: “I get to come to beautiful places like Boothbay Harbor and play the Opera House. I've been playing there since I was 19 or 20 years old.” His first show here was with Livingston Taylor. “Livingston was a mentor of mine at Berklee College of Music. When I dropped out, he kind of took me out on the road, and the mentorship kind of continued. I learned a lot about stagecraft from him, everything from, like, how do you treat people when you walk into the venue to what is your sort of collegialness?” Concert veterans of his shows will attest to the fact that he has translated those lessons into his own style of welcoming and intimate shows.
Glier has shared the bill with a diverse list of artists ranging from the likes of Ronnie Spector, James Taylor, Ani DiFranco, to Glen Campbell. As a producer, music director, or studio musician he has collaborated with Sophie B. Hawkins, Tom Rush, Antje Duvekot, Richard Shindell, Doctora Qingona, Dar Williams, Nick Carter, and Cyndi Lauper. Seth Glier is a five-time Independent Music Award winner and received a Grammy nomination for his album "The Next Right Thing."
Most recently, Kelly Halloran has been touring with Foreigner. Last fall she finished a North American tour with Noah Cyrus, playing violin, acoustic guitar, and singing background vocals. She also performed with the Goo Goo Dolls at Stagecoach 2025 along with cellist Dave Eggar, and Nikki Lane.

title: I was being merciful'
Missouri offensive lineman DJ Jones needs heart transplant ‘in a hurry,’ coach says
text:
(AP) - Missouri freshman offensive tackle Johnnie “DJ” Jones needs a heart transplant and is hospitalized at the Mayo Clinic in Jacksonville, Florida, coach Eli Drinkwitz said Tuesday.
Missouri staff initially detected an issue with Jones’ heart over the summer during freshman intake testing, an emotional Drinkwitz said at a news conference in Columbia, Missouri.
The team’s medical staff sought out a second opinion with the Mayo Clinic when they weren’t getting a resolution or answers after two weeks of observation.
Doctors at the Mayo Clinic detected a much more serious heart problem, Drinkwitz said. The coaching staff was told last week that Jones needs a transplant.
“We found out that Johnnie’s now on a heart transplant list, and he’s in Mayo, and it’s tough right now. Our thoughts and prayers are with him and his family as they go through this,” Drinkwitz said. “You’re just not prepared for that kind of news. Our team wasn’t prepared for that kind of news. We’re praying for him.”
The seventh-year coach asked Mizzou fans to join in that prayer, saying the 18-year-old “needs help in a hurry.”
Drinkwitz first referenced Jones during his postgame interview after Missouri’s win over Florida on Saturday. He explained Tuesday that he knew Jones was watching the game, which moved the Tigers to No. 14 in the AP Top 25.
Jones is receiving care in his home state. He graduated from Venice High School on Florida’s Gulf Coast and signed with Missouri as a four-star recruit.

title: In its 5th year, Portland’s Festival Champlain celebrates French language films from across the world
text:
Rarely do people witness an aspiring filmmaker, a housewife with 1 million trading stamps, a man completely indifferent to the world around him and an obstinate Canadian customs agent at the same event.
Maine’s only French-language film festival is giving people the opportunity to do just that.
“It’s a very unique event,” Lisa Scali, executive director of the Alliance Francaise du Maine, said about the fifth annual Festival Champlain, which runs Oct. 15-18 at the Portland Museum of Art.
The event has grown from 2022, when six films were screened across two days. This year, it features eight films across four days.
Festival Champlain’s schedule reflects Maine’s close, complex relationship with the French language. Maine remains the state with the highest percentage of French speakers and people with French ancestry.
Over the years, organizers have diversified their selection, searching for films from outside of Canada and France. Last year, two films from Cape Verde were screened. Of this year’s eight films, three are Canadian, three are French, one is Gabonese and one is Tunisian.
They don’t just strive to represent Maine’s French-speaking communities; festival organizers made a concerted effort to find films relevant to the whole state, Scali said.
“We are looking to speak to various communities within Maine, and if a film we think in general is relevant for the state of Maine, we’re going to choose that as well,” she said.
One movie, “Promised Sky,” which screens Oct. 16, features an Ivorian pastor living in Tunisia who allows two women to seek refuge in her home. An unconventional family is formed when the group takes in a young orphan who survived a shipwreck.
For Scali, the film touches on contemporary issues Mainers are familiar with, exploring community, relationships and immigration.
“I think this movie is important for everyone to see,” Scali said.
Scali also emphasized changes to programming outside of the screenings. This year three of the films will be followed by a series of conversations with either directors or the deputy director of the Portland Museum of Art.
There will also be a gala reception from 6-8:30 p.m. Oct. 17 at State Street Church in Portland’s West End. It is free, but people are asked to register so organizers know how many guests will attend.
Previously the gala has welcomed special guests, such as Gov. Janet Mills and members of the French and Canadian consuls.
‘A CULTURAL OFFERING’
Throughout the year, the Alliance Francaise du Maine works to promote the French language throughout Maine, hosting classes, events and trips to Canada and France. While the festival is geared toward people who enjoy French, previous attendees say the event offers films that often aren’t easily available.
“I really enjoy the Francophone African films because I don’t know those films, and I wouldn’t necessarily have access to them,” Chelsea Ray, a professor of French language and literature at the University of Maine at Augusta, said.
Watching these films is important, Ray said, highlighting the variety of “different cultural perspectives” they offer.
Scali wants to continue growing the festival.
“There’s such a creative community here in Maine, and I think a cultural offering like a film festival is attractive to that creative community,” Scali said.
Ray mentioned several of her students living near Portland have attended the festival. She hopes it grows too.
“It’d be great to grow it to make more films available at UMA because there is an interest in doing that,” Ray said.
WHERE TO BUY TICKETS
Tickets to the event can be purchased online through the Alliance Francaise du Maine’s website at afdume.org. The festival pass offers access to all films for $45 for the general public and $30 for members of the Alliance Francaise du Maine or the Portland Museum of Art. Tickets to individual films are also available for $10 for the general public and $7 for members.
Every third Thursday of the month the Portland Museum of Art offers free entry to all exhibitions, so tickets to Thursday’s screenings are available for free.
There is a reduced rate for high school and college students. They are eligible to buy a $10 festival pass which allows them to see three films. The individual ticket rate for high school and college students is $5.

Susan Collins doesn’t back down from Brett Kavanaugh vote in 1st debate with Troy Jackson
The first debate between U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson happened to fall on the eighth anniversary of Collins’ 2018 vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, and the Democratic challenger didn’t miss the easy hook, asking the five-term Republican, “What will it take for you to admit you’re ever wrong?”
Kavanaugh’s appointment was expected to result in the Court overturning Roe v. Wade, and it did, three years after he told Collins it was “settled law,” with Kavanaugh in the 5-4 majority.
Collins said Tuesday that she doesn’t agree with how he voted, but she defended her process of vetting judges before turning the attack back on Jackson, saying there’s “only one of us on the stage who’s always been pro-choice, and that’s me,” a reference to his anti-abortion record earlier in his career.
The debate didn’t get any less pointed, and viewers might have come away with a better idea of how Jackson’s unpolished style would look under the bright lights and how Collins would field direct attacks.
The candidates will be back at each other’s throats Thursday in the second of four planned debates. With control of the U.S. Senate on the line, it’s bound to get uglier.

title: Army veteran Ron Russell looks to unseat Rep. Chellie Pingree
text:
Army veteran Ron Russell looks to unseat Maine Congresswoman Chellie Pingree
Army veteran Ron Russell served in the military for 30 years, and now he is looking for a new way to represent his country. Russell is set for a rematch against incumbent Congresswoman Chellie Pingree, a Democrat, for Maine’s 1st District seat in the U.S. House of Representatives.
“It’s really trying to get the United States of America back on track to something that I remember from my earlier days,” Russell said.
The Green Beret grew up in Fort Fairfield before heading to West Point. He commanded the Special Mission Unit at Fort Bragg.
“I really enjoyed being involved in what the nation was doing,” Russell said.
Russell is a proud father of three and is now a grandfather of six.
The Kennebunkport resident secured the Republican nomination back in June, defeating newcomer Joshua James Pietrowicz.
Russell already knows what it's like to go against Pingree. He lost to her in the 2024 election.
"She's a nice person, but the policies that she supports are not policies that I would support, and I think those are exactly what needs to change," Russell said.
A win for the Army veteran would flip the seat red and help Republicans keep their majority in the U.S. House.
The Republican nominee said he agrees with a lot that President Donald Trump has done in his administration, but Russell adds that doesn't mean he'll always vote in the president's favor.
"I'm not beholden to President Trump, nor Mike Johnson, nor the Republican Party, candidly," Russell said. "I'm beholden to the 547,000 people who will vote in November, the registered voters in Congressional District Number One."
If Russell takes over Pingree's House seat, he says he wants to respond to constituents and build relationships across the aisle.
"The biggest problem we have in Washington, D.C., is this divisiveness that is currently present," Russell said. "No one's talking across the aisle, and I intend to fix that."
Immigration has been a watched topic during the midterms. Russell said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement needs reform but should not be dismantled.
"We don't need to do away with ICE. That doesn't make any sense at all," Russell said. "ICE has done some wonderful things here in the last couple of years."
Russell is keeping an eye on everyday prices, saying costs will drop once the war in Iran is resolved.
"When the cost of fuel goes down precipitously, I think we can expect the cost of all consumer goods can go down the same way to include gas," he said. "Gas and diesel are too high."
Russell said he wants to commercialize medicine when it comes to healthcare and does not want Medicare for all.
“The worst of it is the government does not do anything well when it runs a particular program, and we have so many examples of that happening,” he said. “To put them in charge of everyone's healthcare, I think, would be disastrous.”
As voters head to the polls, Russell said he does not want them to pick a candidate solely based on party affiliation.
“Don’t vote for a person just because he has an R or a D behind his name,” Russell said. “Look at the person, how he falls down on different policies, and pick the best person for the job.”
Election Day is Nov. 3.

title: Russia keeps a tight lid on suspected case of pneumonic plague as global concerns mount
text:
(AP) - Russian authorities are keeping a tight lid on information about last week’s suspicious death of a lab worker in Siberia that has been surrounded by secrecy and claims that it could have been caused by pneumonic plague.
While the case has raised global concerns, Russian state TV and other national state-controlled media have steered clear of the subject. Some state-sponsored news outlets withdrew earlier reports about the case.
Russia’s public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said Sunday the lab worker was diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” meaning its origin was not known.
In its official, tersely worded statements, it does not link the case to pneumonic plague, saying only that “extensive” testing found no evidence her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
A state TV station in Irkutsk reported she died Oct. 2 in a hospital in Shelekhov, a town just outside Irkutsk.
Officials have quarantined a hospital and are monitoring the contacts of the worker, who died of what unconfirmed media reports said could have been pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person.
Moscow informed the World Health Organization that no case of plague has been registered in the Irkutsk region in southeastern Siberia.
President Donald Trump said Tuesday he would speak about the issue “very soon” with Russian President Vladimir Putin and report about it “probably tomorrow.” Wednesday is the Kremlin leader’s 74th birthday.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday that a Putin-Trump call hasn’t been set yet but could be organized quickly.
Trump said the U.S. stands ready to help Russia. Asked what the U.S. intelligence community was saying about the case, Trump said the U.S. is in “very deep discussions” on the topic.
Russia is prodded for more information
In response to the WHO’s request to clarify the situation in view of media reports alleging pneumonic plague as the cause of death, Russia has declared that no case of plague had recently been registered in the Irkutsk region, the U.N. organization said.
Russian health authorities reported a full range of preventive measures had been carried out — including tracing the dead woman’s contacts, medical monitoring and lab tests, the WHO said Wednesday. The Russian note relayed to The Associated Press by the WHO said the test showed “no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens in any of the contacts.”
The Geneva-based organization said it has requested further information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures, and media reports that a second employee had pneumonia of undetermined cause.
The organization said it has remained in contact with Russian health authorities and offered technical support.
The Kremlin and other officials stay tight-lipped
Peskov referred all questions to Rospotrebnadzor, which does not mention suspected plague in its reports.
In its latest statement Tuesday, the agency said “the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region, the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov is calm.” Authorities were completing a “complex of prophylactic measures and medical observation over contacts,” it said, adding that so far they have found two cases of COVID-19 and two cases of rhinovirus.
“No other infectious pathogens have been found among contacts,” it said.
Judy Twigg, professor of political science at Virginia Commonwealth University, noted that while the measures taken by Russian health authorities “have been swift and serious,” officials sought to play down the situation and “any statements that strayed from that party line ... were edited or deleted within hours.”
“What we are watching is less a failure to respond than a failure of candor,” Twigg said in written comments.
Vasily Vlassov, professor at the department of healthcare administration and economics at Russia’s Higher School of Economics, said the measures taken appeared “sensible,” focusing on treating the sick, isolating them and their contacts, looking for new cases and carrying out final disinfection.
But he said it wasn’t clear whether more transparency was possible if those dealing with the situation didn’t have enough certainty, and “maybe, they still don’t.” Deceiving the public in these cases “always turns out to be harmful,” he added, and distrust of Russia’s official narrative is “natural” and “almost inevitable.”
In the Soviet era, crises with dangerous outbreaks of infection had “a thick veil of secrecy — people were told nothing.”
The “massive” restriction and isolation measures were “almost always completely successful,” he said.
The lab worker who died was described as highly diligent
The news outlet Lyudi Baikala — or “People of Baikal” — identified the dead lab worker as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova and said she first was hospitalized with cold symptoms Sept. 29 and died three days later.
It quoted her colleagues as saying she was a highly qualified and diligent researcher. They also emphasized that security rules at the facility, established in the 1920s to monitor and study the plague that is endemic to southeastern Siberia, are extremely strict.
The report quoted Shipilova’s neighbors as saying a team of disinfection experts did several cleanups of her apartment, leaving a strong antiseptic smell.
Shipilova’s mother, who worked as a doctor in the past, described her daughter as hard-working and dedicated to her job, according to independent Russian news outlet Glubina, adding that she had not gotten official documents describing the cause of death.
Irkutsk Gov. Igor Kobzev said she died of a “particularly dangerous infection” and everyone who came into contact with her has remained under medical supervision.
The hospital where she died was under quarantine, no longer admitting or discharging patients, although its outpatient clinic has continued operating, according to Mayor Maxim Modin.
Twigg noted that Russia has criminalized “false information” about threats to public safety in 2020 amid the COVID-19 pandemic, “so silence is the one safe move for everyone below the top.”
“Personalist regimes without electoral accountability tend to treat bad news as a loyalty problem rather than focusing on the actual problem to be addressed,” she said.
She warned that “a government that is not believed when it says ‘there is no outbreak’ will not be believed when it must actually say ‘there is one; do the following.’ We saw this with COVID.”
Pneumonic plague and the more well-known bubonic plague — also called the “Black Death” — are caused by the same bacteria, said Simon Clarke of the University of Reading in the U.K.
Pneumonic plague results from breathing in the bacteria, causing an infection in the lungs. Bubonic plague is spread by flea bites from rodents carrying the bacteria called Yersinia pestis. It had not been eliminated, but it’s not spread very easily and it is treatable with antibiotics.
“People think the plague is gone. It was something that occurred 500 years ago, and it’s not. It’s here amongst us,” Clarke said. “Unless you get rid of those wild animals, which of course is not possible, then you’re not going to get rid of the bacteria. It’s just something that is with us.”
The incubation period for pneumonic plague — the disease’s most virulent form — can be as short as 24 hours, the WHO said. The lung-based illness is a less common but severe form of plague that can spread between people via respiratory particles. If untreated, the illness can be fatal, but recovery rates are high if detected and treated in time, it said.
__
Dasha Litvinova in Tallinn, Estonia, and Jamey Keaten in Geneva contributed.

title: Mainers hiking the trails of Grand Manan in Canada
text:
Sea kayaking was the primary focus for many of us who participated in an August week of outdoor adventures on Grand Manan Island in the Bay of Fundy. However, our sizeable group of Mainers with the Penobscot Paddle & Chowder Society included some whose primary goal was hiking. My wife, Nancy, was one of them and I planned to join her on treks when not kayaking.
When we exited the ferry in North Head on the day of arrival, our first stop was North Head Drugstore to purchase a copy of “Heritage Trails and Footpaths on Grand Manan Island.” The compact guidebook contains maps and descriptions of the popular island hiking trails and easily fits in the side pocket of a daypack.
While at the store, we met two fellow Chowderheads, Laurie Wunder and Tom Meredith, who were also purchasing their copy of the guidebook. Since it was several hours before we could check into our accommodations at Castalia Marsh Retreat, we decided to hike in Anchorage Provincial Park located in the southeastern sector of the island.
Route 776 is the only major road on Grand Manan Island. The paved artery weaves along the east side of the island from North Head to Southwest Head. We followed the highway south through the village of Grand Harbour to a left turn into the park. Long Pond Road leads to Anchorage Park Beach, and trailheads for Red Point and Great Pond Trails.
We hiked easily on well-maintained, gravel Red Point Trail that twists along the coast of scenic Long Pond Cove. Early on, we traversed an extensive, wooden boardwalk. Light rain interrupted our hike about halfway to Red Point so we donned raingear for the remainder of the trek. Red Point provides excellent views of Seal Cove Sound and Wood Island farther out in the Bay of Fundy. Two covered picnic tables offered protection from the precipitation and a dry location for a respite.
Leaving Red Point, we completed a short loop hike on nearby Hudson Trail, a scenic coastal path named for a beloved islander, Gene Stanley Hudson. The light rain continued to the Anchorage Beach trailhead. Red Point Trail is an excellent choice for hikers looking for a relatively short trek with convenient access.
On our third day on Grand Manan, Nancy and I joined longtime friends Allen and Marion Gaskell for a trek on Southwest Head Trail. Beginning at the southern end of Route 776 next to Southwest Head Lighthouse, patchy fog was hovering in the area when we arrived.
We followed a wide trail in open terrain along towering cliffs. Side paths led to spectacular overlooks that required careful negotiation to avoid life-threatening falls.
Beyond the high cliffs, the trail leads away from the shoreline and narrows in a dense spruce forest. Progressing on a sometimes damp path, we arrived at remote Bradford Cove Pond, a picturesque location with a couple of small cottages. The fog had completely lifted when we backtracked to the lighthouse.
That afternoon, Nancy and I took the ferry to Whitehead Island for some hiking and biking. Located a few miles east of Grand Manan, a half-hour ferry ride transports vehicles and passengers to the small island. Our destination was Long Point Lighthouse on the southern end. From the ferry landing, we drove a short distance to a small parking area for the lighthouse trail.
The rough, rocky trail follows along the ragged shoreline to the lighthouse. As the name implies, the functioning lighthouse is situated at the end of a narrow peninsula that extends out into the Bay of Fundy. After completing the trek, we returned to the ferry landing and parked our vehicle in line to ensure we caught the final ferry of the day. I still had time for a pleasant bike ride around the island.
Nancy and others completed several additional hikes on Grand Manan. They included Ross Island Trail, paths along the massive cliffs of North Head with visits to Hole-in-the-Wall and Swallow Tail Lighthouse, treks out of Dark Harbor that follow alongside cliffs on the western side of the island, Great Pond Trail in Anchorage Provincial Park and Castalia Marsh Trail.
Grand Manan is a great destination for hikers in search of adventure.
Read about many more excellent hikes closer to home in my book, “Maine Al Fresco: The Fifty Finest Outdoor Adventures in Maine.”
The author of “The Great Mars Hill Bank Robbery” and “Mountains for Mortals – New England,” Ron Chase resides in Topsham. His latest book, “Maine Al Fresco: The Fifty Finest Outdoor Adventures in Maine” is available at North Country Press and through online retailers. Visit his website at ronchaseoutdoors.com or he can be reached at [email protected].

title: Peaks Island writer explores the human consequences of immigration policy
text:
Eleanor Morse uses the shock of United States immigration policy to jumpstart her fifth novel, “This Foreign Land.” When Vincent Ottley hears a 2018 radio broadcast describing children being separated from their parents at the border, he turns to his sister Bryn and asks, “What are we? Savages?” Though he lives outside of Augusta, he secretly heads south on foot, wanting to help. Bryn is left to care for Vincent’s beloved donkeys, her class of fragile third-grade students and her own faltering self. Meanwhile, Dolores, a young Ecuadorian widow, and her daughter are also walking to the border, fleeing from danger. The characters’ literal and metaphorical journeys make for a beautifully wise, quirky and moving book.
Morse spoke with the Press Herald about what inspired her characters, the purpose of imagination and activating compassion in others.
Let’s start with Vincent. He’s a deeply compassionate, luminously perceptive character who has bouts of psychosis when under profound stress. He sees things ‘askew and true,’ as you write of a different character. How did you come up with him and his backstory?
My father had a brother, Uncle Dwight, who had schizophrenia. I got to know him fairly well. I think Vincent partly grew from Uncle Dwight. But I was very comfortable inside Vincent’s head, and I loved writing scenes with him. I slipped into his brain, and I liked being there. Toward the end of his life, I became Uncle Dwight’s guardian, though he didn’t want me to be. He said I wasn’t beautiful enough. He wanted Rita Hayworth.
Vincent’s journey involves many curious stops. I was particularly struck by the woman in a tarpaper shack who puts Vincent up for the night and how he offers to bury her husband’s ashes.
Vincent is a character who has a holy fool aspect to him. He activates compassion in people that he meets, partly because of his oddity and the things that he says. But that scene is one of my favorite scenes in the book, too. I had an image in my head of an old piano that had music in it still, but nobody had played it in years and years. In a sense, that’s who the woman was. She had music in her and she hadn’t really spoken much in years. There was something about Vincent that activated her sense of humanity. I loved what happened between them. It wasn’t something that I planned out. It was something that I just followed the thread of, which often happens in the way that I write.
In Vincent’s absence, Bryn becomes close with an arborist named Ollie. What made you want to develop that plotline?
Oddly enough, sometimes it’s easier for me to develop a male character than a female character. With a female character, I feel the closeness of gender. But Ollie is a very different woman than I am. I don’t climb trees for a living. But I love that she did. I knew her name right away, Ollie Dobson. I always thought of her as having those two names attached to her, and I could see her up in the treetops where she was really risking her life every day.
Speaking of difference, did you have any concerns about writing Dolores, who is a different ethnicity than yourself?
I grappled with it and finally came to think, “Well, what do we have an imagination for? What do we have compassion in our hearts for if not to try to understand human beings who grow up differently than ourselves?”
What kind of research did you do for this novel?
I did a lot of different kinds of research about donkeys for one thing. What they eat, how to trim their hooves, that kind of thing. I did research about lightning strikes, about schizophrenia. Even though I knew something about schizophrenia from my own family, I learned quite a bit more about it.
I went to the southern border because I needed to know more than I knew. I met people while I was in Texas who had come through the Darién Gap, which is the most dangerous migration route in the world. There was a mother I remember who had three children with her — older children — and they had lost everything except the clothes on their backs. I learned so much from everybody that I spoke with. I feel if I hadn’t gone to Texas and crossed the border and spoken to people who were kind enough to speak to me, that I would not have had the right to tell any part of Dolores’s story.
Given the subject, how did you keep your book from becoming a polemic?
Moral outrage, when it’s on the page, gets tiresome very quickly. I didn’t want to write that kind of book any more than I would want to read it. But it felt like the utmost cruelty to use parents and their children politically. I couldn’t think of anything more cruel. I didn’t anticipate what we would be facing now. I knew that I had to take it on in some way. Vincent kind of saved me because he felt grief in his heart, but it didn’t come out as outrage. It came out with his odd connections with people. He set out because his heart told him to. And that’s kind of how I set out: because my heart told me to.
Debra Spark is the Zacamy Professor of English at Colby College. Her most recent novel is “Discipline.”

title: New African restaurant opening in downtown Portland
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A restaurant specializing in Central African cuisine is slated to open on Brown Street on Oct. 17.
Owner Joceline Lesso and her husband, General Manager Patric Lombo, aim to open the 90-seat Chez Biso at 11 Brown St. The space formerly housed Tokyo Sushi Ramen.
Lesso used to run a restaurant in the Congo, and also operated a catering business out of a commissary kitchen in Maine, according to Heritier Nosso, business advisor to Lesso and Lombo. Nosso said after Lesso ended her catering business, clients urged her to open a restaurant.
“Because many African people, not just from the Congo, but from Angola, Rwanda-Burundi, and Central Africa, they love Congolese dishes,” Nosso said. “It’s so difficult to find these dishes (locally), so she decided to open an African restaurant.”
Chez Biso’s menu will include specialties like fumbwa (wild spinach stew), liboke ya mbisi (fish steamed in banana leaves) and pork feet simmered in beans. They’ll also offer stateside classics like smashburgers, fish and chips, spicy wings and lobster rolls.
Chez Biso means “at our home” in Lingala. “She wants people not to feel like they’re at a restaurant, but like they’re eating from their home, food made by somebody who cares about your health and wants to make sure you’re satisfied,” Nasso said.
Nasso noted that a former Washington Avenue restaurant named Chez Biso na Biso had different ownership and is unrelated to Lesso and Lambo’s venue.
Chez Biso will be open seven days from noon until 10 p.m.

title: Opal Lee celebrates her 100th birthday by kicking off construction of Juneteenth museum in Texas
text:
FORT WORTH, Texas (AP) — Opal Lee celebrated her 100th birthday Wednesday by kicking off the start of construction of a museum in her Texas hometown dedicated to telling the history of Juneteenth, the holiday commemorating the end of slavery in the U.S.
“It was important for us to do this on this date because everything we’ve done for the last several years, everything we continue to do, is built around the spirit of the venerable Miss Opal Lee,” said Jarred Howard, CEO of the upcoming National Juneteenth Museum in Fort Worth.
Lee, founding board member of the museum, became known as the “grandmother of Juneteenth” after spending years rallying to get federal recognition for June 19. When then-President Joe Biden in 2021 signed a bill into law making Juneteenth a federal holiday, Lee was by his side.
The holiday marks the day in 1865 when Union soldiers arrived in Galveston at the end of the Civil War with an order declaring the freedom of the enslaved people in Texas. It was about 2 1/2 years after the Emancipation Proclamation freed the enslaved people in the still rebellious states of the Confederacy. Six months later, the ratification of the 13th Amendment permanently ended slavery in the United States.
Lee expressed her happiness and gratefulness at the Wednesday event, where a crew began demolishing a building to clear the way for the construction of the planned 50,000-square-foot (4,600-square-meter) project in a historically Black neighborhood.
The event included an announcement that the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints would be donating $3 million toward the museum’s construction and the creation of a genealogy center in it.
“I’m so happy I could do a holy dance, and these old legs won’t respond, but let me tell you how thankful I am and that this deed won’t go unnoticed,” said Lee, who spoke after the announcement.
Lee has been a force in Fort Worth, where she worked for decades as a teacher, counselor and community activist.
Lee has said she has cherished childhood memories of celebrating Juneteenth with food, music and games, and as an adult, she was involved in planning the celebration in Fort Worth.
“Long before there were historic walks, cameras, books and well-deserved national acclaim, my childhood memories are filled with you making sure that Fort Worth remembered,” U.S. Magistrate Judge Renee H. Toliver said at the event.
She told Lee, who was sitting in the crowd, that she remembered her planning community events, parades and festivals.
“You always reminded us that history is not something you leave behind, it’s something you actively protect,” Toliver said.
The future site of the museum is not far from the home that was built for Lee a couple of years ago on the same tree-lined corner lot that her family had been driven from by a racist mob when she was a young girl.
Lee was 12 when, on Juneteenth in 1939, a white mob of hundreds descended on her Black family’s home, days after they moved into a white neighborhood. The mob smashed windows and furniture, according to newspaper reports from the time.
The celebration of Lee’s birthday continues Wednesday evening as the museum hosts a conversation with former first lady Michelle Obama at the city’s convention center.

title: These were Christa Pike’s first words after execution attempt left her unconscious for days
text:
NASHVILLE (WSMV/Gray News) - Attorneys for Christa Pike have revealed the first words she said after regaining consciousness nearly a week after the state attempted to execute her and failed.
Christa Pike was completely disoriented when she woke up in a Nashville hospital.
“Where am I and who are you?” were Pike’s first words, her attorney said in a press conference on Wednesday.
“There is still a lot of cognitive confusion. ... She is very aware that the state tried to execute. ... She is very aware up to a point,” the attorney said.
The 50-year-old was sentenced to be executed for the 1995 murder and torture of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer. She has spent over three decades on death row.
A week ago, the state of Tennessee failed to execute Pike, despite injecting her with two doses of the lethal drug pentobarbitol.
She was rushed to a hospital from Riverbend Maximum Security Institution following the injections, where she has since been receiving care in critical condition.
On Tuesday, her attorneys announced that she had woken up and was speaking, but she still requires medical treatment. It was later revealed that just hours before she awoke, they thought she was brain dead.
“She has a blood clot in her arm, she has pneumonia, she is not able to swallow so she hasn’t eaten, she can’t move her arms, her arms are both tremendously swollen,” her defense said outside a Nashville courthouse.
Pike is the only person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution, AP reported.
Many details of the execution process remain secretive, and Tennessee officials say they are investigating what went wrong.
