title: Susan Collins’ approach to governing is the right approach
text:
Stephen Diamond is a retiree who lives in Topsham.
If Sen. Susan Collins is politically vulnerable, it is not because she has changed, but because the country has.
We live in a time when what divides us greatly overshadows what unites us. What used to be legitimate policy differences now degenerate into ugly personal attacks, and rather than push back against this development, some in public office seem happy to fan the flames of discord.
This change in our political climate has even led to calls to fundamentally transform the nature of our country, ranging from those advocating a white supremacist Christian theocracy to those arguing for a transition to socialism. Our struggle to make our religion-neutral, free-market democracy work has emboldened the advocates of extreme solutions.
Maine, along with the rest of New England, was once the ideological center of the country with little to separate Democrats from Republicans, but now Sen. Collins, as the only Republican member of Congress from this region, remains the sole heir to this tradition. Should she be voted out of office, it will be the final nail in the coffin of New England pluralism.
As someone who has known Sen. Collins for many years and who served on her staff (but who voted for the Democrat in every presidential election since 1968), I think that in addition to her legendary work ethic, her approach to governing can be summarized in three words: civility, compromise and compassion. Her civility reflects her manner of working with others, even unpleasant colleagues holding dramatically different views.
Without civility, compromise becomes impossible, and without compromise, progress becomes impossible, with our government either experiencing paralysis or vacillating between conflicting policies. Her consistent ranking as the least partisan member of the Senate and her effectiveness as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee attest to the senator’s understanding that compromise is essential to effective governing.
A less recognized feature of Sen. Collins’ approach to governing is her compassion for persons facing difficult challenges, as manifested in the importance she attaches to helping constituents dealing with personal setbacks as well as in her support for programs designed to assist those genuinely in need. A government insensitive to the suffering of persons facing hard times is not a government worth having.
What arguably most distinguishes Sen. Collins from others holding elected office is that she is a frequent target of both the extreme left and the extreme right. Ironically, nothing demonstrates more convincingly the importance of her voice.
When Rep. Jared Golden, with his impressive military record, expresses concern for the safety of his family, the problem in Washington has gone beyond mere incivility. It may be that Sen. Collins is of the old school, with an approach to governing reminiscent of that practiced by Sens. Muskie and Cohen, but we have much to learn from a past when political opponents treated each other with respect, the result of which was a functioning government.
Whether Sen. Collins is reelected has serious consequences not only for Maine but for the country. Hers is among the lonely voices in Washington pushing back against the dangerous partisanship that undermines our constitutional order. Simply put, a vote against Sen. Collins is a vote to perpetuate our national polarization while a vote for her is a vote for a healthy, civil and effective democracy.

title: In first Maine Senate debate, Collins seeks to distance herself from Trump
text:
In first Maine Senate debate, Collins seeks to distance herself from Trump
Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins distanced herself from President Donald Trump during her first Maine Senate debate with Democrat Troy Jackson, arguing she has maintained her political independence by repeatedly voting against Trump's agenda and saying that she's “not exactly his favorite senator.”
In first Maine Senate debate, Collins seeks to distance herself from Trump
Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins distanced herself from President Donald Trump during her first Maine Senate debate with Democrat Troy Jackson, arguing she has maintained her political independence by repeatedly voting against Trump's agenda and saying that she's “not exactly his favorite senator.”
Democrats are trying to flip the Maine Senate seat as they work to win control of the Senate. Trump lost the state in 2024, giving Democrats hope of defeating the five-term moderate Republican, who has been targeted by Democrats in previous elections and survived.
During the hourlong debate, Jackson focused largely on attempting to connect Collins to Trump. He kicked off the night by pointing out she cast a critical vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Trump nominee who eventually helped overturn the constitutional right to abortion. Collins supports abortion rights and said Kavanaugh assured her it was settled law, but she has said recently that she does not regret her vote to confirm him.
“Would you trust her to pick the next Supreme Court justice?” asked Jackson, a former state lawmaker and logger.
He also repeatedly brought up her procedural vote to advance the president’s 2025 tax and spending bill — though Collins ultimately broke with her party to vote against it.
Collins countered that she has voted against Trump more than she did Joe Biden when the Democrat was president, and has pushed back against Trump on tariffs, immigration enforcement and the war in Iran.
“I voted against my party more than another other senator on either side of the aisle,” Collins said.
The attention on Trump comes as only 31% of U.S. adults approved of how the Republican is handling the presidency, according to a September AP-NORC poll. That’s well below where his approval stood when he took office last year.
The president has started holding rallies around the country in an effort to help GOP candidates win in November, telling voters to pretend he is on the ballot. At Tuesday's debate, a moderator noted Trump has floated the idea of campaigning in Maine, and asked Collins if she would stand beside him if he does.
“I’m not exactly his favorite senator,” she said, adding “I would say that he’s not coming to Maine.”
Collins, who has said she didn’t vote for Trump in 2016, voted to convict the president after his 2021 impeachment over his role in the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. In January, Collins joined a handful of Republican colleagues in backing a failed effort to limit the president’s ability to unilaterally use force in Venezuela. The move prompted Trump to say on social media that they “should never be elected to office again.”
Collins argued that her seniority and experience in the Senate have resulted in money and resources for Maine, saying: “Leadership matters in Washington.”
She also spent Tuesday evening attempting to turn the focus of Maine’s high cost of energy and housing on Jackson, arguing that he had a larger role in making a difference when he was the state Senate president and criticizing “Augusta’s failed policies” as a way to connect Jackson’s to the state’s struggle to address affordability.
Other moments showed how the two candidates were approaching their appeal to working class Maine voters. For example, as Collins touted her ability to remove certain items from Trump’s trade war with Canada, including pulp, concrete and road salt. Jackson pushed back by quipping “we can’t eat road salt.”
Jackson and Collins are scheduled to participate in three more debates later this month. The next one is Thursday and starts at 8:00 p.m. on Maine's Total Coverage; the hour-long debate will also stream live here on WMTW.com.

title: Obituary: Sally (Fletcher) Hotham
text:
ALBION – Sally (Fletcher) Hotham, 76, of Albion, passed away on Sept. 27, 2026, surrounded by family, after a long battle with Parkinson’s.
Sally was born on August 29, 1950, in Benton to Byron and Rosella Fletcher. She graduated from Lawrence High School in 1969 and shortly after married her high school sweetheart Steve, who went on to enjoy 57 years of marriage together. They settled in Albion where they raised their two children, Dina and Travis.
Sally held several jobs over the years where she met many of her life-long friends, but her main focus was raising her children, making sure they made it every practice, game and event without ever being late. After retirement she enjoyed “puttering around” with her sisters and being a proud Mimi to Avery and Bennett, where she could always be found at a field, court, event, or with them having a sleepover at Mimi’s house.
Sally is survived by her husband Steve; her daughter Dina (Brad) Giggey, her son Travis (Katie); her grandchildren Brad, Damien, Samantha, Ryan, Avery and Bennett; great-grandchildren Zachary, Elise and Grace. She is also survived by her sisters (Mimi’s friends) Karen (Linwood) Doughty, Donna (Blaine) Bunker and Beth Stanhope, sisters-in-law Judy Hotham and Charleen Grotten; many nieces and nephews; as well as close friends Tobey and Cheryl.
She was predeceased by her parents, her brother David and her twin sister Sandra.
Our family would like to give a special thanks to Shelly Oullette for her amazing care, compassion and friendship she showed our mom throughout their time together.
A celebration of life will be held on Saturday, Nov. 7, at the VFW in Winslow from 1 to 4 p.m. To celebrate Sally please wear a pop of color or some “bling!”

title: This election is about reclaiming the federal government
text:
The ongoing Susan Collins vs. Troy Jackson debate is a great example of not seeing the forest but for the trees. The real issue for the upcoming midterm election is not which senator should represent Maine, but how do we, the citizens, wrest control back from an administration exemplified by cruelty, incompetence, corruption, self-aggrandizement and self-enrichment.
As much as I respect Sen. Susan Collins (I have voted for her in past elections), electing a Democrat to the Senate would move us closer to flipping the balance of power in the Senate. Reducing the Senate Republican majority to minority status is a prerequisite for reclaiming our government. A government of decency, fairness, competence and sanity.
As we head to the polls, let us step out of the trees so we can see the forest.
Larry O’Rourke
Sumner

title: Susan Collins’s committee bought trucks the Army didn’t want. Then campaign donations poured in.
text:
The U.S. Army announced last year that it had enough of a specific model of armored vehicle and that any more deliveries would be “excess.” But even so, Congress found a way to keep funding alive for the vehicle — and executives at the company that produces the vehicle found a way to flood key members of Congress with campaign donations.
In the weeks after this year’s appropriations bill passed, employees of AM General or its parent company donated tens of thousands to key appropriations committee members in both chambers, Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Rep. Ken Calvert, R-Calif.
Collins is separately facing scrutiny over a report from ProPublica that the FBI investigated an alleged pay-to-play scheme involving a major donor, an ex-defense contractor. Collins’ office denied that there was any kind of pay-to-play arrangement and said she fully cooperated with the FBI. There is no indication that AM General’s donations were part of such a scheme, but the giving nonetheless demonstrates how Collins’ campaign account has grown with help from employees at defense contractors doing business with the government.
Before the Army put the future of the vehicle in jeopardy, Collins was not a frequent beneficiary of contributions from the company’s workers. She last received campaign funds from AM General or its parent company’s employees more than a decade ago. But after the Army’s “excess” announcement last year, employees and the company’s PAC donated over $58,000 to committees associated with Collins.
One observer of money in politics said that appropriators receiving money from government contractors is a long-standing problem.
“Members of the appropriations committees in Congress are extremely powerful. These lawmakers can steer huge sums of money to private companies. Government contractors today routinely try to leverage a broken campaign finance system to their advantage,” said Michael Beckel, money in politics reform director at Issue One.
The revival of the Army’s order was supported by lawmakers in both parties, including the top Democrat on the House Appropriations defense subcommittee, Rep. Betty McCollum, D-Minn. Collins’ office said that in the Senate, decisions on the program were made not by her but by defense subcommittee chair Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and vice chair Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del. McConnell did not receive donations from employees at AM General or its parent company this election cycle. Coons received $2,500 from its employee PAC.
“Sen. Collins was not involved in this decision. The final decision was made by the Chairs and Ranking Members of the House and Senate Defense Appropriations Subcommittees,” said a Collins spokesperson, Phoebe Keller.
AM General’s CEO, John Chadbourne, said in an email that the company does not comment on campaign donations, “all of which fully comply with FEC rules and regulations.”
He added, “AM General’s focus is on the Warfighter and providing the best light tactical vehicle capabilities to the Joint Forces.”
Congress steps in
AM General is most famous for producing the Humvee, the iconic military vehicle that trawled the streets of Baghdad during the Iraq War. In 2023, the Army selected the company to produce 20,000 units of a more heavily armored successor known as the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle. The company was ramping up its production line in Indiana when then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll announced in May 2025 that he would cancel its order, saying the additional deliveries would result in an “excess.”
Driscoll’s announcement was part of a larger effort to “eliminate waste and obsolete programs.”
“Yesterday’s weapons will not win tomorrow’s wars,” he said.
The military does not always have the last say on its contracts, however.
Congress has for decades swooped in to save pricey programs with political appeal. Soon after the Army moved to kill the vehicle contract, Congress mobilized to save it.
AM General had backing from members of Congress in Indiana, thanks to the jobs on its production line there. It also found backing from legislators in states far from its home.
The House moved first: In June 2025, the House Appropriations Committee’s subcommittee on defense proposed spending hundreds of millions on the vehicle for the Army. By the time the final version of the defense spending bill passed this February, the Army had been provided with $345 million for procurement of a vehicle it said it did not need.
A joint statement from the House and Senate, which Collins’ office said was produced by the defense subcommittees, sounded a skeptical note about the Army’s decision to cancel further orders of the vehicle. The statement said that the Army had provided “inadequate supporting analysis.” One concern was that without the efficiencies from a larger order that included the Army, the cost-per-unit price of vehicles that the Marines still wanted would rise.
McCollum, the House Democrat with an influential role in the process, said in a statement that she was one of numerous members of Congress to question the Army’s decision.
“Appropriators felt the Army failed to do adequate due diligence to justify their rash budget decision to cut the JLTV program and explain the full impacts on the Army, and especially the Marine Corps, which had not been consulted,” she said.
By the time the final version of the defense spending bill passed this February, the Army had been provided with $345 million for procurement of a vehicle it said it did not need.
Collins’ campaign committees had received some money after the Army announced that it wanted to cancel the project.
In the weeks after Congress passed the appropriations bill on Feb. 3, Collins and Calvert, one of her counterparts in the House, both received a burst of donations from AM General employees and the company’s political action committee.
After the appropriations bill went through, donors associated with AM General gave a total of $50,000 to Collins’ fundraising committees.
The donors included Chadbourne, the company’s CEO, and two of KPS Capital’s managing partners. (Private equity firm KPS Capital Partners acquired AM General in 2020.) All gave money to a committee raising money on Collins’ behalf at the end of February or start of March.
Calvert, the California representative with the defense appropriations post, has also benefited from similar donations. Both AM General employees and KPS Capital employees have given $14,285 in direct contributions to Calvert for Congress this election cycle.
The AM General employee PAC has given a combined $20,000 to Ken Calvert for Congress and Eureka Political Action Committee, Calvert’s leadership PAC.
Most of the donations to Calvert associated with AM General came in the weeks immediately after Congress passed the appropriations bill. His office did not respond to a request for comment.
Those contributions put Collins and Calvert in the same league as the Hoosier politicians who were natural supporters of AM General. A fundraising committee associated with Republican Sen. Todd Young received $36,000 from AM General or KPS Capital employees. The AM General employee PAC donated another $10,000 to his main campaign committee. A Marine Corps veteran, Young has been a vocal proponent of the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle.
His Republican colleague Sen. Jim Banks’ leadership PAC received $14,375 total from AM General’s employee PAC and Chadbourne, the executive. Meanwhile, Rep. Frank Mrvan, a Democrat representing northwest Indiana, received $33,050 from AM General or KPS Capital employees, and another $10,000 from the AM General employee PAC, according to FEC filings.
A ban that isn’t
On her campaign website, Collins notes that she serves as chair of the “powerful” appropriations committee.
“This committee decides how federal dollars are spent each year, from national defense and infrastructure to medical research, education and public safety. Susan’s position gives Maine an outsized voice at the table when critical decisions are made which allows her to deliver serious results for Maine,” her website states.
Collins’ office said that in the case of the AM General vehicle, she had nothing to do with the funding decision. A spokesperson said the decision-making in the Senate was up to McConnell, the defense subcommittee chair, and Coons, the vice chair.
McConnell announced his pending retirement in February 2025. His campaign committee and leadership committee have not received donations from either KPS Capital or AM General employees this election cycle, FEC records show. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Coons’ campaign committee received a $2,500 donation from the AM General employee PAC on March 5, according to FEC records. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
McCollum’s leadership PAC received $5,000 from the company’s employee PAC last October, according to FEC records.
Government contractors have been banned from donating directly to candidates for decades. In practice, however, that ban does nothing to prevent company PACs or individual employees from giving to campaigns — even if they serve as company executives.
The contributions associated with AM General represent a sliver of the $15.8 million Collins had raised this election cycle through July, according to data compiled by the watchdog group OpenSecrets. Yet every dollar could help her in what is expected to be a tough fight with Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate candidate with a slight lead on her in recent polls, in November.
The contributions also illustrated a trend among the top contributors to her campaign. Many of them are from people affiliated with government contractors, according to OpenSecrets. Two defense contractors, General Dynamics and RTX, are also on the list of her top organizational contributors.
AM General’s owner, KPS Capital Partners, is the sixth-largest organizational donor to Collins’ campaign committee and leadership PAC, according to the group’s data.
Although AM General has cultivated connections in Congress, members appear to be growing increasingly skeptical of the JLTV vehicle program. In June, House appropriators signaled that they wanted to find a new contractor for the vehicle, citing production delays. AM General was 2,000 vehicles behind on orders from the Marines, the defense subcommittee said.
Chadbourne, the company’s CEO, issued a statement in June defending its performance and blaming a previous contractor for delays.
“Healthy competition, transparency and accountability strengthen America’s defense industrial base,” he said. “AM General remains fully committed to continue earning the trust placed in us by the Army, the Marine Corps, Congress, and the American taxpayer through performance, quality, and disciplined execution.”
By Matt Sledge and Jorge Medellin. Originally published on October 5, 2026. Republished

journalism. Sign up for The Intercept’s Newsletter.

title: Teen’s resilience shines in senior photos taken amid rubble of home lost to wildfire
text:
SPOKANE, Wash. (KXLY) - A high school senior in Washington state has turned the devastation of losing his home to a wildfire into a symbol of resilience.
Weeks before his senior year of high school, Becks Bird lost his childhood home in Spokane to the Old Trails fire in August. He grew up with Riverside State Park as his backyard, and the plan was to use it as a natural backdrop for his senior photos.
“I probably ran over a thousand miles back in those trails, biked a lot with my friends,” Becks said.
But while he still needed senior photos, the backdrop had changed.
“There’s always been such good lighting there. But this year, there was no flowers. Normally, there’d be flowers,” he said.
Still, Becks chose to have his senior photos taken by what remained of his home on the morning of his last first day of high school. He stood along charred trees and debris, capturing his senior year the best he could.
Photographer Jenna Starr says the session was especially emotional for Becks’ family. One photo shows all four of them standing near the remains of their home.
“I couldn’t really look at his mom because it was so emotional for her. That was the forest her son was raised in,” Starr said. “But Becks is just resilient. He’s tough. He’s always been kind of tough.”
Like many in the Rifle Club neighborhood, the Bird family only had minutes to evacuate as the fire moved through the area. Becks, a cross-county athlete, was able to grab his medals before leaving. Those medals were also included in his senior photos.
Now, as Becks moves through his senior year and looks ahead to the future, he’s already learned some of life’s hardest lessons – and is more resilient for it.
“Don’t run away from it. You gotta live in it. You’ve got to move on at some point, so might as well make it now. So, you can get on with it faster, start trying to live a normal life again,” he said.
The Bird family is currently rebuilding their home in the Rifle Club neighborhood. More than 900 structures were damaged in the Spokane Complex fires.

title: Missouri offensive lineman DJ Jones needs heart transplant ‘in a hurry,’ coach says
text:
(AP) - Missouri freshman offensive tackle Johnnie “DJ” Jones needs a heart transplant and is hospitalized at the Mayo Clinic in Jacksonville, Florida, coach Eli Drinkwitz said Tuesday.
Missouri staff initially detected an issue with Jones’ heart over the summer during freshman intake testing, an emotional Drinkwitz said at a news conference in Columbia, Missouri.
The team’s medical staff sought out a second opinion with the Mayo Clinic when they weren’t getting a resolution or answers after two weeks of observation.
Doctors at the Mayo Clinic detected a much more serious heart problem, Drinkwitz said. The coaching staff was told last week that Jones needs a transplant.
“We found out that Johnnie’s now on a heart transplant list, and he’s in Mayo, and it’s tough right now. Our thoughts and prayers are with him and his family as they go through this,” Drinkwitz said. “You’re just not prepared for that kind of news. Our team wasn’t prepared for that kind of news. We’re praying for him.”
The seventh-year coach asked Mizzou fans to join in that prayer, saying the 18-year-old “needs help in a hurry.”
Drinkwitz first referenced Jones during his postgame interview after Missouri’s win over Florida on Saturday. He explained Tuesday that he knew Jones was watching the game, which moved the Tigers to No. 14 in the AP Top 25.
Jones is receiving care in his home state. He graduated from Venice High School on Florida’s Gulf Coast and signed with Missouri as a four-star recruit.

title: The Date You Can Expect to See First Snowfall in 4 Maine Cities
text:
For most people across Maine, they've already awoken to the first frost of the year. The evening temperatures are cooling and the heat is likely coming on overnight.
Those are the typical signs that winter is approaching for Maine. While the state has seen some warmer winters in recent years, the snow always falls at some point.
As winter closes in, here's a snapshot of how the snow adds up in four major cities throughout Maine, courtesy of How Much Will It Snow and Current Results.
The following data shows the average day where the first snowfall hits, the amount of snowstorms (1-5 inches) happen in each city as well as how major snowstorms (6+ inches) occur in each setting.
The First Snowfall Date For Portland, Maine, is Predicted For November 19
First Snowfall Date: November 19
Snowstorms Per Winter: 16
Major Snowstorms Per Winter: 5
For most people who live in and around Portland, Maine, it probably feels like winter keeps showing up a little bit later each year.
There's some truth to that, as the average date for the first official snowfall keeps creeping later on the calendar each year. 50 years ago, Portland's first snowfall date averaged out to be November 15.
The record for first measurable snowfall in Portland was October 10, 1979.
The First Snowfall Date for Augusta, Maine, is Predicted For November 21
First Snowfall Date: November 21
Snowstorms Per Winter: 20
Major Snowstorms Per Winter: 6
Central Maine's weather doesn't vary a whole lot from that of major cities in southern Maine. Augusta sees a handful of additional snow events that Portland doesn't, and is privy to an additional major snow event or two throughout the coldest months of the year.
The First Snowfall Date for Bangor, Maine, is Predicted For November 14
Date of First Snowfall: November 14
Snowstorms Per Winter: 20
Major Snowstorms Per Winter: 6
Bangor's data is a bit misleading because over the last five winters, the town has averaged only 15 storms per winter, four major snowstorms, and about 50 inches total snow.
The outlier was the winter of 2022-2023, where Bangor got hit with nearly 90 inches of snow.
The First Snowfall Date for Presque Isle, Maine, is Predicted For October 29
First Snowfall Date: October 29
Snowstorms Per Winter: 28
Major Snowstorms Per Winter: 8
While the mountains get the headlines when it comes to snow in Maine, 'the County' takes the brunt of the pain.
Presque Isle's first snowfall date happens well before the winter solstice, and their last snowfall date happens well after the spring solstice.
That leads to a long, grueling winter for northern Maine that features a ton of snowstorms and the most major snowstorms of any region in the state.

title: 2 lawsuits challenge Trump’s taxpayer-funded ads, alleging they violate propaganda law
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Two lawsuits filed Wednesday challenged President Donald Trump’s recent series of federally funded television advertisements, which promote his political message while costing taxpayers millions of dollars.
The Democratic National Committee was first to sue the Republican administration, alleging the ads are illegal government-sponsored propaganda and accusing Trump of personally directing them. Later Wednesday, a coalition including the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause filed a separate lawsuit, also alleging an illegal misuse of funds.
Both complaints asked federal judges to stop the use of federal funds to pay for the ads. The lawsuits represented the first legal challenges to the TV spots, which have faced bipartisan backlash for glorifying Trump and promoting his campaign message with November’s midterm elections less than a month away.
The ads, which began airing in September, already have cost more than $12 million to run, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact. The Department of Homeland Security awarded a $20 million contract for the campaign.
Responding Monday to the criticism, Trump defended them as “positive promotion for our Great U.S.A.” but said he’d start paying for them using his MAGA Inc. super PAC going forward.
But on Tuesday, a fifth ad began airing with a notice it was paid for by the U.S. government. It promoted Trump’s military actions to capture Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela earlier this year. The same day, Trump made it clear he hasn’t committed to reimbursing any money that has already been spent, telling reporters “we’ll decide.”
DNC Chair Ken Martin said in a statement that Trump is misusing taxpayer dollars in “a last-ditch attempt to save Republicans in November.”
“Americans deserve better than to have their hard-earned tax dollars used for Trump’s illegal schemes,” he added.
A person familiar with the ad campaign who was not authorized to speak publicly said the ad buys placed prior to Trump’s pledge to start paying for them with his super PAC will end this week. Outside groups will begin to pay at that point, the person said.
The second lawsuit was filed by the legal advocacy group Democracy Forward on behalf of Common Cause, a New York public employee union and a Democratic state legislative candidate in Alabama.
Taxpayers “shouldn’t have to foot the bill for the president’s politics,” said Skye Perryman, who leads Democracy Forward.
Omar Noureldin, senior vice president of policy and litigation at Common Cause, said his organization doesn’t trust that Trump will stick to outside money for future ads. He cited Tuesday’s new ad as proof that the government-sponsored ads were still being scheduled.
“Even if he said that moving forward, he plans to have his super PAC pay for this, that’s not enough for us,” Noureldin said. “We are not going to take the president’s word for it.”
Legal experts have suggested the ads run afoul of a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda,” and potentially other federal laws. The Homeland Security money tapped for the ads comes from a $175 million package Congress gave to the department as part of Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda.
The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have done to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren’t aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs. One of the ads is a near replica of a 2024 ad that Trump ran during his presidential reelection campaign.

title: Texas set to execute man for fatally shooting a convenience store clerk during robbery in 2000
text:
DALLAS (AP) — A Texas man who fatally shot a convenience store clerk is set to die by lethal injection on Wednesday in what would be the nation’s 30th execution this year.
Jamaal Howard, 46, was found guilty of capital murder in the 2000 killing of Vickie Swartout, 42, who was shot once in the chest. He is set to receive a lethal dose of pentobarbital in the first scheduled execution in the U.S. since Tennessee’s failed attempt at putting Christa Pike to death last week.
Pike’s attorneys said Tuesday that she was awake and speaking as she received treatment at a hospital.
Texas has executed six people so far this year, with two more scheduled after Howard.
A killing caught on surveillance
Swartout was fatally shot during the robbery at the store in the small, rural town of Silsbee, located about 100 miles (161 kilometers) northeast of Houston. Evidence presented at the trial included the store’s surveillance video, which showed Howard shooting Swartout.
Howard, who was 20 at the time, took $114 and a carton of cigarettes from the store, according to court records.
His attorneys have argued that Howard is intellectually disabled and his execution should be halted. The state said that he has not presented evidence that would show he meets the requirements for a claim of intellectual disability.
He has an appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court pending to stop the execution.
The Supreme Court in 2002 had barred the execution of intellectually disabled people. But it has given states some discretion in how they determine such disabilities.
Executions in the U.S. this year
Florida has carried out 16 executions so far this year, the most of any state. Most states that allow executions use lethal injection as their primary method.

title: Obituary: Norma Nivison
text:
OAKLAND – Norma Nivison was born on Jan. 11, 1946, the daughter of Leland “Bud” and Maefred (Thomas) Thing. She attended Waterville High School, graduating with the class of 1964. Norma went on to work at Thayer Hospital, where she dedicated nearly 40 years of her life before retiring in 2011.
In 1966, Norma married Melvyn D. Nivison. Together, they enjoyed many years of marriage and shared a number of adventures and special memories. They loved snowmobiling, taking long trips together on their trike, and accompanying Mel as he performed with his band, “The Entertainers.” Norma also enjoyed ceramics and was known for cooking wonderful holiday dinners for her family and extended family, creating traditions and memories that would be cherished for years to come.
Norma was a devoted mother, grandmother, sister, and friend. She will be remembered for the love she had for her family, the joy she found in spending time with those close to her, and the many memories she created throughout her life.
Norma was predeceased by her parents, Leland “Bud” and Maefred Thing; her beloved husband, Melvyn; and her sister, Nancy Thing.
She is survived by her daughter, Margo Nivison; her son, Kurt “Bubba” Nivison; her granddaughter, Sarah Briganti; her brother, Robert “Bob” Thing and his wife, Shirley; her brother-in-law, William “Bill” Nivison; her cousin, Charlene Mushero; and her lifelong friend, Paula Mitchell.
The family would like to extend a special thank you to the staff at D’Youville Manor for the excellent care they provided Norma over the past two years. They would also like to express their heartfelt appreciation to Norma’s loving roommate, Beverly Donahue, who made sure that “Big Boy” and “Princess” were always by Norma’s side.
The family will be holding a private burial in the coming weeks.

title: ICE reviewed tens of millions of voter records looking for noncitizen voters, records show
text:
ICE reviewed tens of millions of voter records looking for noncitizen voters, records show
The Department of Homeland Security’s sweeping election fraud operation has drawn on tens of millions of records, scrutinized dozens of nonprofit voter registration groups and considered deploying undercover agents to investigate organizations suspected of helping noncitizens register to vote, according to newly obtained internal documents.
Video above: The Trump administration will comply with Supreme Court's mail-in ballot order
The 166 pages of records, released on Wednesday by the advocacy group Democracy Forward, offer a detailed look inside one arm of the Trump administration’s escalating election integrity campaign, which has marshaled federal investigators, immigration databases and voter records in an effort to identify noncitizens suspected of illegally registering or voting.
They show the extensive infrastructure the administration has built within its immigration enforcement agency to pursue probes aligned with Trump’s election fraud beliefs, with multiple layers of data reviews, dozens of organizations investigated, primary elections tracked and weekly reports summarizing the progress of the various projects.
Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative division of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, described the undertaking as a phased national initiative involving voter-roll acquisition, data analysis, investigative leads and field investigations.
The operation drew on extraordinarily large pools of data. A June 1 HSI report said investigators had ingested 50.6 million records from a Justice Department dataset and another 48.4 million records that Heather Honey, a senior counselor to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, had obtained through what the report called "independent sources of information."
The document does not identify those independent sources, but the data may include public voter lists from California, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Nevada that DHS purchased and analyzed around this time.
In July, Mullin announced that his department found roughly 250,000 noncitizens registered to vote in just those four states — claims that officials in those states have repeatedly challenged.
The 50 million Justice Department records may include unredacted voter lists voluntarily handed over by more than a dozen Republican-led states in the months prior. DOJ has sued 30 other states to force them to share their unredacted rolls for audit.
In a statement, a DHS spokesperson said: "DHS has been incredibly transparent about the acquisition and the analysis of publicly available voter files conducted by the Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate of USCIS. DHS and DOJ are laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of US citizens."
Democracy Forward president and CEO Skye Perryman said in a statement: "It appears the president and his allies want to pick their voters, as opposed to the way things are supposed to function in a democracy where voters pick their leaders."
The documents suggest that the Trump administration is using data-review products offered by the controversial software company Palantir for its reviews of voter rolls. The agency is using a Palantir tool known as ELITE to process state voter rolls, according to a July election probe progress report in the trove. Palantir’s website describes ELITE as a "data integration" tool with the purpose of "identifying the location of known foreign nationals who meet criteria for removal." CNN has reached out to Palantir for comment.
Probing voter registration organizations
The documents also show that investigators were looking well beyond individual suspected voters. An internal comparison said HSI was adopting a "network-based investigative approach, prioritizing organization and facilitation analysis over individual leads." Investigators reviewed dozens of nonprofits and voter registration organizations in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and other states and examined organizations linked to an Ohio company suspected by investigators of voter registration fraud.
Many of those reviews turned up no evidence of wrongdoing. Investigators said they found no derogatory information on dozens of New Jersey groups they examined, found no suspicious financial activity in another nonprofit review and closed a separate Ohio inquiry after exhausting its investigative leads.
But the records show that by late May, HSI and the FBI were developing investigative plans involving seven Ohio companies that investigators described as "consolidation centers" associated with Black Fork Strategies, a progressive canvassing firm that HSI alleged was connected to several noncitizens registered to vote in Cuyahoga County. On June 8, ICE notified senior officials that agents planned to execute federal search warrants and interview more than 100 current and former employees as part of their investigation into fraudulent voter registration and illegal voting.
The heavily redacted records do not explicitly identify Black Fork as the target of those warrants. But three days later, federal agents raided the Ohio Organizing Collaborative, a progressive organizing group with extensive ties to Black Fork.
HSI contemplated more aggressive investigative tactics as well. A June report said officials were exploring whether to use undercover agents to engage with organizations suspected of encouraging or facilitating illegal voter registration by noncitizens. New Jersey and Pennsylvania were identified as areas of focus. The document said undercover agents could be used to gather evidence and trace financial backing if investigators determined an organization was actively recruiting noncitizens to register.
The records show that HSI also monitored this year’s primary elections for "trends, vulnerabilities, or indicators" that agents believed "may impact election integrity."
Updates on voter fraud probes shared with White House
The bulk of the documents contain status updates on HSI’s voter fraud-related investigations.
Most of the details are redacted, but the documents offer insights into how HSI and other DHS components were focused on trying to find voter fraud cases to prosecute.
In June, HSI officials wrote that their investigations were focused on five states: New Jersey, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Minnesota and Ohio.
Among the various voter fraud topics, HSI was investigating "Counties with 2020 Results" and "Voter Machines," according to a May update on the probes.
It’s not clear what specifically was being investigated, though earlier this year, HSI agents contacted Arizona state officials with questions about the 2020 election in the state’s largest county, Maricopa. A set of DHS talking points included in the new trove described those interactions as "routine law enforcement coordination and information sharing."
Mullin sent letters in August to the White House and Justice Department arguing that foreign-made components in voting machines could "potentially compromise election infrastructure at any stage of the supply chain."
The investigative status updates were shared with White House officials beginning in July, according to emails from the documents.
The records also reveal how immigration enforcement gave the administration another avenue to pursue suspected noncitizen voters when a criminal case could not be brought. Internal legal guidance distributed to ICE attorneys in December 2025 said that "in cases in which the evidence is insufficient to support a criminal prosecution," suspected unlawful voting could nevertheless make a noncitizen subject to immigration consequences.
The guidance noted that certain immigration law provisions covering unlawful voting do not require a criminal conviction and, in some circumstances, do not require proof that the person knew the vote was unlawful.
ICE’s Office of the Principal Legal Advisor sent out guidance about illegal voting following July reports that New Jersey mistakenly added 6,600 non-citizens to its voter rolls, and nearly 400 cast ballots.
ICE officials wrote noncitizens who voted could be deported under the Immigration and Nationality Act. "There is no requirement that the alien have knowledge that he or she has illegally voted, and no conviction is required," the guidance stated.
"HSI is heavily working these cases," ICE Deputy Director Charles Wall wrote in a July email.
The records also detail separate investigations of "anti-ICE" groups in Minnesota, where a massive federal immigration-enforcement operation earlier this year sparked widespread protests, particularly after federal agents fatally shot two Americans. Internal reports describe undercover agents infiltrating and surveilling activist groups as HSI investigated alleged stalking, doxing and other activity targeting immigration officers.
By late May, HSI had opened 418 voter-fraud cases and made 64 administrative arrests. But 318 of those cases had not been referred for prosecution. Investigators had also distributed more than 1,500 leads generated from immigration records to field offices across the country.

title: The seniors make quilts for foster children and veterans
text:
ST. LOUIS, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - A group of seniors meets every Thursday morning at Cedarhurst of Tesson Heights to sew quilts from fabric scraps.
The quilting club was the idea of activities coordinator Glenette Nothum.
“I love to quilt, and I think word got out. Then the ladies were like, we wanna quilt, and I was like really...wow,” Nothum said.
People started donating fabric and sewing machines, and the quilting club was formed.
The club includes 71-year-old Barb Jackson, who has sewing experience.
“My mother was a sewer, she taught me how to sew,” Jackson said.
It also includes 81-year-old Doris Lake, a newcomer who was convinced to join by Jackson.
“I said, ‘I can’t sew like that.’ She says, ‘Come on everybody,’ and now I just love my machine,” Lake said.
Not every member of the club sews, but all members contribute.
The quilts are donated to those in need, including children in the foster care system.
“Today is a baby quilt for the foster care system,” Nothum said.
“Whoever may need it, we give it,” Lake said.
Some quilts were also given to veterans at the Jefferson Barracks VA Hospital, who sent the quilters a letter of thanks.
“The veterans love them,” Nothum said.
Club member Barb Jackson said the group is “just giving back to the community.”

title: University of Arizona suspends fraternity activities as reports of misconduct persist
text:
University of Arizona suspends fraternity activities as reports of misconduct persist
The University of Arizona has suspended activities at its fraternities following persistent reports of misconduct, including assault, hazing and drug- and alcohol-related behavior, a university official said.
Related video above: Former Northern Arizona University fraternity leader sentenced last week in student’s hazing death
Just seven weeks into the fall semester, the university's Dean of Students Office was investigating multiple misconduct reports involving nearly half the school's Interfraternity Council chapters, Dean Chrissy Lieberman said Monday in a letter to the school's fraternities and sororities announcing the suspension.
The reports follow misconduct findings against some interfraternity chapters in the spring and multiple criminal investigations, according to the letter.
“The number of cases under investigation and the severity of the concerns is egregious,” Lieberman wrote.
University spokesman Nick Prevenas did not immediately respond to a request for more information about the criminal investigations.
He also did not say whether the suspension was triggered by recent public outcry over how Cornell University handled allegations that multiple fraternity brothers sexually assaulted a woman in 2024. Lieberman's letter noted that “the value of the Greek experience is under scrutiny nationwide.”
The suspension prohibits fraternities from hosting, attending, participating in and sponsoring any organizational activities at least until their advisers have met with Lieberman at one of three meetings that were scheduled for Tuesday, Wednesday and Oct. 12, according to the letter.
The letter said the dean's office had reached “capacity” to investigate misconduct reports, and that reports continued even after the university’s president warned Interfraternity Council presidents at an August meeting about the possibility of additional consequences.
“It is time for the University of Arizona Greek community to step up and set an example for good,” the letter said. “It is time to have difficult conversations with each other and the members of the community.”
The university had previously suspended activities at the Sigma Tau Gamma fraternity after new members last year were reportedly forced to consume large quantities of alcohol and live goldfish and subjected to screaming, degradation and threats, according to a Sept. 2 letter from a university official to the fraternity.
An email and a phone message at the fraternity's national headquarters were not immediately returned.

title: In the Broccoli: Worm Problem Prompts Commons Changes
text:
On Sept. 16, students and other Commons-goers ate broccoli with worms in it for nearly two hours at lunch. At 12:30 p.m., JJ Rocha ‘28 stood on a chair in Commons and warned fellow diners not to eat any more.
On Oct. 5, a similar scene unfolded. Rocha again stood on a chair, saying, “Do not eat the broccoli. There are worms in them.”
How did the infested broccoli make it into Commons and onto the plates of Bates students, faculty and staff?
Associate Vice President for Dining, Conferences and Campus Events (DCCE) Christine Schwartz shed light on the incident in an interview with The Student. She described the supply chain Bates uses and the steps DCCE is taking to keep this from happening again.
As reported earlier this week, Bates’ food distribution chain is relatively simple. Bates’ primary vendor, NorthCenter, which operates throughout Maine and New Hampshire, sends food to a secondary vendor that cuts, trims, and cleans food before it reaches Commons.
Commons staff cooked the broccoli after it arrived, Schwartz said. “It had an innocuous worm on it, sort of part of the growing process, which means it wasn’t cleaned the way it should have been,” she said. Schwartz noted that it is not unusual for food to have some sort of impurity, but that is “why we pay to have it cleaned.”
Why didn’t Commons staff notice the worms before serving the broccoli?
Schwartz said that it can be difficult to spot “because the bug is a darker color … Once it’s cooked, the bug lightens up slightly.”
Regardless of how it landed on lunch plates, precautionary measures took effect immediately. Schwartz shared that Common’s staff took a sample of the bug to pest control, and “they confirmed it was a run-of-the-mill [bug].”
Among students in Commons, the scene was far more turbulent. Rocha recalled some of his teammates, who he was eating with at the time, “laughing and saying that they were pleased about the worms due to the broccoli containing extra protein.”
Others, he said, were more concerned: “letting the placebo take over, saying that they felt sick or … that they can’t believe they just ate worms.”
After the second incident, DCCE decided to make long-term changes. Schwartz said that moving forward, “we’re going to just use a high-end frozen broccoli floret, which will ensure that there’s no issue.”
As for the secondary vendor tasked with cleaning the broccoli, Schwartz said that hopefully whatever issues the secondary vendor is having can be remedied. However, for the foreseeable future, Bates will cut, trim and clean broccoli in-house.
Commons serves around 5,000 meals a day for students, events, faculty and staff, Schwartz said, and she takes pride in both the scale and quality of that work.
Schwartz stressed that the bugs were not harmful and emphasized the steps DCCE has taken to prevent similar issues with broccoli going forward.
Above all else, Schwartz wants students to trust Commons to consistently provide quality food. She shared, “We want to be … an important part of your life.” The steps DCCE has taken following the broccoli incidents are an important part of building that trust.

title: Youth pastor dies after collapsing during marathon days before his birthday, family says
text:
PORTLAND Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - A 24-year-old youth pastor in Portland died after collapsing during a marathon, according to his family.
Thousands flocked to the Rose City for the annual Portland Marathon on Sunday, including Treyton “Trey” Lara.
His wife, Audrey Shin-Lara, said he trained for the marathon for several months.
“I think he’s just always just enjoyed running as just a way to like relax and release,” said Audrey.
Everything was going great that morning.
“I saw him at 18, 19. He ran over and was able to smile and give me a kiss, and then he ran off, and he looked good,” Audrey said.
Then around mile 20, Audrey said Trey collapsed.
Doctors told her he went into cardiac arrest.
Trey Lara was taken to the hospital, and Audrey said doctors did all they could to save him, but it was too late.
“The grief is coming in waves where one moment it still doesn’t feel real where we’re like I’m just gonna wake up, and he’s gonna be over there,” Audrey said.
Trey was a youth pastor. Most recently, his wife said, he was working with other youth pastors and leaders, hoping to make a change in the community around him.
“Besides loving Jesus, he loved his friends and family. He was the best big brother, Tio to so many cousins, and some of our friends’ kids would call him Uncle Trey,” Audrey said.
Audrey said Trey recently helped open a youth camp called Camp Genesis over the summer.
It was one of the many goals he had for himself.
Audrey said that, besides ambition, Trey was full of love.
And it’s the love from all those who knew Trey that’s getting Audrey through this heartbreaking time.
“He’s the love of my life, always will be. And we’ll see him again,” said Audrey.
She said Trey was as healthy as could be, with no underlying medical issues, so this loss is sudden and shocking.
A GoFundMe page has been set up to help the family during this heartbreaking time.
The fundraising page said Trey was days short of his 25th birthday on Oct 15.

title: Gorham, Thornton Academy tie in Class A South boys soccer matchup
text:
GORHAM — The Gorham boys soccer team looked like a championship contender in the first half. Thornton Academy took on that form in the second half.
A matchup that looked on paper like one between the two best teams in Class A South played out that way on the field as well.
Sabri Ninziza and Cohen Landry scored highlight-reel goals less than 10 minutes apart, and Gorham and Thornton Academy tied 1-1 on Wednesday night in a showdown between the two teams atop the Class A South Heal point standings.
Gorham, in the No. 1 spot, moves to 8-2-1. Thornton remains undefeated at 8-0-2. The Golden Trojans are ranked third in the Varsity Maine poll, while the Rams are fifth.
“We’ll take the tie. On grass, we’ll take it for sure,” Thornton coach George Sherry said. “They played well. I think they had us for a while … and then I thought there were times we had our chances.”
From the Gorham bench, coach Nick Viola saw the benefit of the draw as well.
“Clearly, we matched up pretty well,” he said. “Playoff atmosphere here tonight, nothing could separate us. Just a really good game between two really good teams. … I think a tie in this league is a positive result, especially against a top-four team.”
Trading blows
• While Gorham started faster, Thornton got on the board first. On the Trojans’ second corner kick, Ephraim hit an arcing cross to the back corner of the box, and Ninziza headed it over a leaping Corbin Wilson for a 1-0 lead with 13 minutes left in the first half.
“I always go behind … and I saw the ball coming in, and I just had to make sure I headed it in the right corner,” he said. “It was amazing. This is what I was waiting for, and this was what we worked for.”
• The Rams pulled even just before halftime. Moises Ntango raced down the left wing and ripped a cross to the far side of the box, and a sliding Landry met the ball and redirected it into the goal with 3:42 to go.
“He’s always telling me to cut back, because he’s going to keep it in the air longer,” Landry said. “I kind of scissor-kicked it. I’m not sure what happened in the moment.”
Momentum shift
• Early on, the Rams had the run of play. Ntango, an electrifying dribbler and playmaker, generated one chance after another in the first half, and Gorham outshot Thornton 7-2 in the first 25 minutes.
It was just the urgency Viola wanted to see, two games after what he called a “difficult” 1-0 loss to Scarborough.
“I think we were hungry to just get off to a good start,” he said. “The emphasis was just getting into our attacking third early, trying to find the net early, and we were very, very close.”
• In the second half, the play tilted Thornton’s way. The Trojans marked Ntango more closely, generated the best chances, and even had a few good looks in overtime.
One opportunity went by the wayside when Santiago Macias Olivar lost his footing while racing in, causing a weakened shot that was saved by Wilson. Later, Andres de Haro found Mambueni going in alone, but the play was whistled dead for offsides.
“A couple of calls I thought could have gone our way but didn’t,” Sherry said. “But what can you do? That’s part of the game, for sure.”
Unsung heroes
• Griffin Ayers provided the Trojans with tenacious 1-on-1 defending and had a big moment in the 62nd minute when he won a battle for the ball with Ntango and denied the dynamic junior a look at a go-ahead goal.
• Antoine Dube, who Viola called the Rams’ “heart and soul,” was just as effective on defense for Gorham, providing a resilient last line of defense and almost single-handedly derailing a Thornton corner in the 66th minute.
Stat leaders
• Gorham: Cohen Landry (goal), Moises Ntango (assist), Corbin Wilson (five saves)
• Thornton: Sabri Ninziza (goal), Ephraim Mambueni (assist), Lucas Stolf (eight saves)

title: Chick-fil-A has no plans to add AI to its drive-thru ordering service despite other rivals doing so
text:
ATLANTA (Gray News) - Chick-fil-A leadership says customers can continue to expect to be served by its team members at restaurant locations and not artificial intelligence.
Chick-fil-A CEO Andrew Cathy recently shared in a CNBC interview that it’s not pursuing AI voice ordering in its drive-thru lanes.
Cathy stated that the company is exploring opportunities to use AI but just more behind the scenes.
“From our experience, we really want that hospitality to be human to human,” Cathy was quoted in the interview. “We’re not gonna substitute that interaction with technology, because we feel like that hospitality is so important to create that warm environment for consumers.”
The popular chicken chain’s stance against using AI in its drive-thru lanes comes as some of its fast-food competitors move forward with their automated order-taking plans.
McDonald’s shared that it plans to test its drive-thru AI assistant called Archy, while Wendy’s has also rolled out its AI drive-thru ordering assistant called FreshAi.
Earlier this year, Forbes shared a survey conducted by SurveyMonkey that found that 79% of customers said they would prefer interacting with a human versus some sort of automated customer service.
Chick-fil-A’s enduring focus on customer service has made it the fast-food leader when it comes to customer satisfaction. Ranking in the top two spots on the American Customer Satisfaction Index for more than a decade and has been the clear leader in the fast-food chicken category.

title: 17-year-old accused of stabbing another student repeatedly in the neck at school, police say

Michiganders had mixed views about President Donald Trump's approach, but told us that the trade war won't sway their vote.
Will the US-Canada trade war sway elections in border state battlegrounds? What Michigan voters said
Michiganders had mixed views about President Donald Trump's approach, but told us that the trade war won't sway their vote.
President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada shows no signs of letting up ahead of midterm elections, at a time when the balance of power in the Senate hinges on races along the border between the United States and its northern neighbor.
In a new campaign ad posted on Wednesday, Michigan's GOP nominee, Mike Rogers, became the latest swing-state Republican to distance himself from the president on the issue. His Democratic opponent, Abdul El Seyed, has spoken out against the tariffs for months.
Before the ad was released, we spoke to Michiganders on the newly opened Gordie Howe International Bridge, a 1.5-mile crossing that connects Windsor, Ontario, to Detroit, Michigan. Hundreds of millions of dollars in trade move through the corridor each day, but now, those economic bonds are being tested by the trade war.
"Well, I think it's stupid. I mean, what are we fighting about?" said Steve Leonard, a Democrat voter.
"Especially for our dairy products, things like that, we were being overcharged, nobody likes to be overcharged, and it didn't just happen for a couple of months. It's been going on for years and years and years," said Earl Elliott, a Republican voter.
That's what Trump argued when he launched the latest phase of the trade war in August by slapping 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports, which Canada soon matched dollar for dollar on U.S. products. The retaliatory cycle has continued since, ramping up tensions that were already high over Trump's earlier duties on major cross-border industries like steel, aluminum, autos, and lumber.
"Whether a two-by-four is $2 or $5, I don't know, and I don't blame that on the trade war," said Bruce Francis, who said he's still undecided in the Senate race. 
Allen Silver, who plans to back Rogers, said the trade relationship with Canada needed to be "adjusted," but he is concerned about added costs from the tariffs.
"I think everyone is," Silver said. "I look at the younger people, and right now, housing is expensive for people. You know, for cars and stuff, everything has gone up in price, and the trade war has something to do with that, you know, being that we are in Detroit."
A recent analysis from the conservative group Advancing American Freedom Foundation found that Michigan is among the states that could be hit hardest by the feud based on its annual trade with Canada, alongside other border states like Maine and Ohio. All three are home to some of the midterm's most competitive Senate races.
In Ohio, Republican Senator Jon Husted has defended the president's pursuit of a better deal with Canada. The Democratic nominee, former Sen. Sherrod Brown, described the tariffs on Canada as a disaster.
Like Rogers in Michigan, Maine's Republican Senator Susan Collins has called for an end to the tariff war with Canada, though the state's Democratic nominee, Troy Jackson, argues she has not gone far enough in her opposition.
A POLITICO poll finds about a quarter of Americans believe Trump was right to introduce new tariffs on Canada, while more than half feel he was wrong. Even among self-described "MAGA Trump voters" who support his tariff strategy, 40% said he should've waited until after the midterms to avoid jeopardizing elections in border states like Michigan and Maine.
Yet the Michigan voters we spoke to said that the trade war with Canada wouldn't impact their decision-making.
"I don't think that the trade war is impacting my vote, but you know I'm more of a conservative-leaning voter," said John Vanalst.
"I don't like Trump. I don't like any of his policies. I think he is destroying the country and the world. So I'm gonna vote democratic no matter what," Leonard said.

title: 7-month-old child dies after being kicked by pony, authorities say
text:
HARMONY, Minn. (KTTC/Gray News) - A 7-month-old girl in Minnesota died after being kicked in the head by a pony, according to authorities.
The Fillmore County Sheriff’s Office said it happened on Tuesday around 2 p.m.
According to the initial investigation, the child and an adult family member were both riding in a wagon pulled by a pony when the animal spooked and kicked the child.
Deputies responded to the scene along with Harmony Ambulance, the Harmony Fire Department and the Preston Police Department.
Authorities are still looking into the situation.

title: Portland man pleads not guilty in Tukey’s Bridge killing
text:
PORTLAND — A Portland man has pleaded not guilty to murder in a fatal stabbing on Tukey’s Bridge in August.
Glen Rodney, 58, was arrested and charged in the death of 21-year-old Julian “Juju” Nadeau, following what police described as an altercation on a walking path near the bridge.
Rodney is being held without bail at the Cumberland County Jail, and a judge is considering whether to grant him bail following a hearing Wednesday.
Prosecutors requested that Rodney continue to be held without bail, citing a public safety risk if he is released. Assistant Attorney General Mark Rucci described the killing as a “stranger-on-stranger assault.”
Rodney’s attorney, Jim Howaniec, argued that the stabbing was self-defense and that Rodney should be allowed to be released from jail to live with his parents.
Investigators say that on the night she was killed, Nadeau was walking with friends to open packs of Pokemon cards underneath the bridge.
Somewhere along the path near the bridge, Rodney approached the group on his bicycle, allegedly kicking Nadeau. Howaniec said they exchanged some words, but “nothing that would justify (the argument) continuing on beyond that.”
Then, Nadeau and her friend continued walking on the bridge in the same direction as Rodney “while the verbal altercation was still occurring,” Portland police Detective Aaron Curlee said during the hearing.
Rodney then pulled out a knife and chased Nadeau and her friend along the trail on the southbound side of Interstate 295. According to court documents, he jumped on top of Nadeau and stabbed her once in the chest. She was pronounced dead at the hospital.
Nadeau’s friend, Liz McGehee, told investigators that she hit Rodney after the stabbing. Howaniec questioned whether that assault occurred before or after the stabbing.
“I think that there’s evidence that the other individuals were the ones who initiated the conflict,” Howaniec said. He added that Nadeau and her friend were holding a leash that was found with blood on it, which is still being processed in the state crime lab.
Rucci said when police found and arrested Rodney that night — about a mile from the crime scene — he was carrying a bloody knife and some of Nadeau’s clothing, and he was wearing her hat.

title: 84-year-old accused of creating and selling explosives from home, deputies say
text:
LAKE CHARLES, La. (KPLC/Gray News) - An 84-year-old man in Louisiana was arrested for allegedly creating and selling explosives from his home, according to deputies.
On Oct. 2, detectives searched the home of John W. Sinkankas in relation to an ongoing joint investigation.
Investigators say Sinkakas was manufacturing and selling explosive devices from his home, which is also 500 feet away from a school.
Detectives initially learned the devices were manufactured to resemble fireworks, but after further investigation it was discovered that the devices contained an illegal amount of explosive materials.
During the search, detectives found several pounds of explosive powders, around 18 pounds of explosive precursors, numerous homemade explosives, and materials used to assemble them.
Sinkankas was arrested and booked into the Calcasieu Correctional Center and charged with manufacture & possession of delayed action incendiary device.
He was released the following day on a $150,000 bond. The investigation is continuing and more charges are possible.

Mortgage rates jump to three-year high, blow past 7.5%

Monthly mortgage payment at today’s rates
The national median family income for 2026 is $106,800, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, and the median price of an existing home sold in August 2026 was $429,100, according to the National Association of Realtors. Based on a 20% down payment and a 7.53% mortgage rate, the monthly principal and interest payment of $2,407 amounts to about 27% of the typical family’s monthly income.
Meanwhile, home prices are still rising — the National Association of Realtors reports the median home price was up 1.6% over the past year, and the median of $429,100 was an all-time high for the month of August. However, values have begun to dip in many formerly hot markets. Still, signs are mixed. The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller index released in late September showed national home prices grew 1.9% in the year ending in July, marking an acceleration.
What will happen to mortgage rates in the rest of 2026?
Inflation held at 3.4% in August, although the Fed’s preferred measure, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) index, was 3.0% for September. Oil prices have spiked amid the conflict in Iran, pushing inflation up and lifting mortgage rates from their 2026 low of 6.09%. Rising inflation has been the main driver of higher mortgage rates — the consumer price index has pushed well above the Fed’s 2% target, and 10-year Treasury yields topped 5.3% this week, well up from earlier in the year.
“The 10-year Treasury has been battered over the last six weeks, climbing from 4.66% to 5.36% on Wednesday, a striking 70-basis-point jump,” says James Sahnger of C2 Financial Corp. “The 10-year hasn’t been this high since April 2002, and 30-year fixed rates haven’t been this high since August 2000. Normally, favorable personal consumption expenditures numbers and weak jobs data would bring at least some improvement in rates. Right now, though, too many crosscurrents and concerns are weighing on the markets for any relief to take hold.”
Housing economists no longer expect mortgage rates to fall below 6% in the near future, and even a return below 7% seems a stretch. That reality that’s affecting home sales. Higher mortgage rates, still-record home prices and persistent inflation are likely to put the brakes on home sales. Instead, rates have risen sharply, a situation only exacerbated by the Fed’s Sept. 16 rate hike.

title: Bangor students learn restaurant skills through SOAR Store club visit to Moe’s Barbecue
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Fourth- and fifth-graders from Bangor’s Fairmount School got a taste of the restaurant business today.
Members of the SOAR Store after-school club visited Moe’s Barbecue to learn what it takes to run a restaurant, from preparing food to welcoming customers at the register.
The club teaches students about customer service and marketing.
They put those skills to work by selling items to their classmates on Thursday and Friday mornings.
“So we sell items and use the money to help the school. We do snacks, and then there’s a care closet, and then we do a whole bunch of other fun things,” said Duncan Simpson, a Fairmount fifth grader.
“I think it’s fun to be really nice to your customers, like, hey, how are you doing? I think it’s really fun to do that, and I wanted to learn more about it,” said Mirabelle Christopher, a Fairmount fourth grader.
The student-run club uses its profits to restock and support the school.
Students also take on leadership roles, including shift leader.

title: State says ‘packaging error’ caused ‘small number’ of incorrect ballots to go out in Oxford County
text:
Editor’s note, this story was updated on Oct. 8 to correct information about the ballots and where they were sent.
Several Oxford voters received incorrect ballots this week for the November election.
The Department of the Secretary of State said the Oxford town clerk was notified by a resident on Tuesday that that they had received a ballot meant for another town.
A relative of Ernie Fitts, who is running for an Oxford-area Maine House seat, noticed the candidate was missing from the ballot and raised the alarm on social media.
Jana Spaulding, deputy secretary of state for communications, said Wednesday afternoon that the situation had already been remedied.
“A resident did contact the Oxford town clerk yesterday after receiving an incorrect ballot style, and it was addressed by the clerk,” Spaulding said.
“The clerk identified that due to a packaging error at the printer, a small number of incorrect ballots were received and sent out. Oxford is working quickly to contact any resident who could have possibly received an incorrect ballot.”
She said anyone getting an incorrect ballot will be given a proper one.
“Every voter,” Spaulding said, “will have the chance to vote the correct ballot.”
