title: What voters should know about the Augusta Farrington School expansion project
text:
This November, Augusta residents will vote whether to approve funding for the $53 million renovation of Farrington Elementary School, resulting in the closure of the Lillian P. Hussey Elementary School.
As school enrollment is projected to decline in Augusta over the next decade, the proposed plan would consolidate elementary students who live east of the Kennebec River into the renovated Farrington building.
While plans for the consolidation have been in the works for several years, the matter is finally landing on the ballot for Augusta voters. Here are some key details to know about the project before heading to the polls.
WHY IS THE HUSSEY SCHOOL CLOSING?
The Hussey school was built in 1954, making it the oldest of the city’s four elementary schools. It has been on a list for reconstruction for more than 10 years, said Augusta Superintendent Mike Tracy.
Hussey was selected to be replaced in 2017, but the pandemic eventually halted progress, Tracy said. The Department of Education approved funds for Hussey’s replacement in 2023.
The school department is opting to close Hussey rather than replace the building as a result of projected enrollment declines over the next 10 years. Tracy said it would be a more efficient model to consolidate students under one roof, rather than continue operating four schools as the population continues to decrease.
Farrington, built in 1988, was selected for expansion over Gilbert Elementary School, Lincoln Elementary School and Cony due to a combination of factors, including current building conditions, available land and feasibility and cost.
WHAT’S NEXT FOR THE HUSSEY SCHOOL?
The school department does not yet have official plans for the Hussey school building if students transition to the expanded Farrington School. The building is owned by the city, so it would be up to city officials to make a decision in the future, Tracy said.
WHAT WILL THE PROJECT COST?
The projected cost of $53,571,590 will be fully funded by the state with no cost to Augusta taxpayers, if the November referendum passes.
The project funding was approved before July when a new law went into effect requiring school districts looking for state-funded construction to help pay for it with a local share. Tracy said the project could be the last one to be 100% state-funded before the law changed.
“It makes the most sense financially to take this project on now because if the voters decline to do it, they’re still on the hook for replacing the Hussey school, because that building is becoming less and less usable,” Tracy said.
Voters will choose whether to borrow the $53 million for the project in Question Two on the ballot. If the referendum does not pass, the school district would likely have to apply for the funding again under the new rules, adding a new local cost to the project.
However, the school department is also hoping to raise $1 million to fund upgraded equipment, such as playground equipment or a larger kitchen freezer, as state-funded school construction projects are only built to the state’s minimum standards for things like equipment.
WHAT IS THE TIMELINE FOR CONSTRUCTION?
If funding is approved by voters, construction would begin in the summer of 2028 and finish in the summer of 2030, allowing students to start at the new school in the fall of 2030.
Students at both schools will still be able to attend school during the construction period, as it will be completed in phases. Parts of the Farrington School may be closed off during the school year while undergoing construction, but spaces students need to access will be redone during the summer, so school operations are not interrupted.
The Farrington expansion would add 32,750 square feet to the current 48,000-square-foot building and include 19 new classrooms and updated existing classrooms, six classrooms for universal pre-K, a new science technology engineering and math learning space and a new cafeteria, among other building improvements.
The expanded school would accommodate approximately 525 students in pre-K through grade 6.
“I think it’s an opportunity to have a brand new facility that’s modern,” Tracy said. “It’s going to be a wonderfully built facility that will help us engage families well, well into the future.”

title: House and Senate control has flipped often in midterms since 1990
text:
Republicans control Congress now. Here's how midterms have shifted power since 1990
The U.S. midterm elections are less than a month away, with both political parties hoping to retain or gain control of Congress.
Midterm elections occur halfway through a president's term, giving voters an opportunity to express their approval or disapproval of the president's agenda by supporting candidates from the president’s party or opposing them.
Currently, the Republican Party controls both congressional chambers. In the House of Representatives, there are 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one Independent and two vacant seats, giving Republicans a slim majority. In the Senate, Republicans hold 53 seats, Democrats hold 45 and two are held by Independents.
The Get the Facts Data Team looked at previous midterm elections dating back to 1990 to see how party control of the two congressional chambers shifted historically. Chamber division counts reflect initial election results and do not account for retirements, deaths, resignations or party changes after elections.
House of Representatives party shifts
In the House of Representatives, every seat is up for election every two years, making it easier for voters to determine which party controls the chamber.
The president's party tends to lose political power during midterm elections. Party control of the House flipped five times in the nine midterms since 1990, according to the data team's analysis.
The president's party did not hold a majority in the House after eight of the last nine midterm elections. The 2002 midterm was the only election in which the president's party retained control of the House. Republicans gained eight seats that year, giving them a total of 229 seats in the chamber.
The largest party shift was in 2010, when Democrats lost 64 seats, leaving them with 193 seats in the chamber.
Senate party shifts
Unlike House representatives, senators serve six-year terms, so about one-third of the Senate is up for election every two years.
Since the 1990 midterm elections, party control of the Senate has flipped three times: 1994, 2006 and 2014.
Even if a party retains control of the Senate, its majority can still be slim. Democrats had 47 senators in the chamber after the 2022 election, but four independents caucused with the party, giving them the majority. Democrats flipped one Senate seat in Pennsylvania that midterm election.
Sometimes, a politician switching parties after elections can shift the balance of power. After the 2000 presidential election, Republicans held a majority in the Senate, with Vice President Dick Cheney able to cast the tie-breaking vote. But in 2001, then-Sen. James Jeffords switched from Republican to Independent and caucused with Democrats. 
To gain control of the Senate this year, Democrats would have to pick up four Republican seats. Competitive races include Republican-held seats in Maine, Texas and North Carolina, as well as the Democratic-held seat in Michigan.
More than 80 congressional members are set to leave their seats after the midterm elections, either choosing to retire, run for another office or having lost their reelection bid.

title: Another superload is heading toward Maine's coast
text:
Another superload will begin crawling toward the Maine coast Wednesday evening.
That follows the successful delivery to South Portland of a nearly 684,000-pound piece of machinery from the old Androscoggin Mill in Jay.
The next load will depart from Jay for Turner beginning at 6 p.m., the Maine State Police said Tuesday afternoon. Once in Turner, it will wait until Thursday evening before continuing to Oxford, where it will remain until Sunday night.
On Sunday night, it will depart from Oxford to Gray. Then on Monday night, it will travel to Buxton, where it will stay until Tuesday night, when it will crawl the final leg to South Portland.
The state police warned drivers to expect rolling delays as the convoy makes it way along the route.
The first load was originally expected to reach South Portland on Sept. 29 after a two-night journey. But after departing from Riley Road in Jay, it failed to reach a key bridge in time. It then began making a more painstakingly slow journey, traveling from Turner to South Portland over several nights.
This is the second of night super oversize loads expected to travel this route in the coming weeks.

title: October events with Friends of Sears Island
text:
Constellation exploration activity kits available for kids from Friends of Sears Island
Friends of Sears Island has created free constellation-themed activity kits for kids that will be available for families to pick up at Carver Memorial Library beginning Friday, Oct. 16. In autumn, it is getting dark earlier each day, which gives us plenty of time to stargaze! This activity kit will allow your child to explore the night skies by creating their own star wheel, glow-in-the dark stars to make constellations at home, star beads for bracelet making, and ID cards that can also be used to project each constellation onto the wall with a flashlight! Project instructions and educational handouts about constellation mythology will also be included. Families who enjoy these kits are also encouraged to attend FOSI’s virtual star party on Oct. 27 at 6:30 p.m., led by John Meader of Dark Sky Maine. To sign up for this Zoom visit https://tinyurl.com/virtual-star-party.
These kits are intended for children ages 5-12. Donations to Friends of Sears Island are always gratefully accepted to allow the organization to continue to offer programming to all at no cost. Activity kit quantities are limited and will be distributed to families on a first-come, first-served basis. Pre-registration is no longer required to receive a kit- simply stop by Carver Memorial Library in Searsport when they are open (beginning Oct. 16) and request a kit for your child while supplies last!
Friends of Sears Island’s children’s programs and activity kits are sponsored by First National Bank. To learn more about Friends of Sears Island check out www.friendsofsearsisland.org or facebook.com/friendsofsearsisland.
____________________________________________________________
Virtual Star Party Zoom Presentation with John Meader
On Tuesday, Oct. 27 at 6:30 p.m. Friends of Sears Island will host a Zoom presentation given by John Meader. Using Stellarium software to create a virtual sky, Meader will lead participants on an exploration of the stars, constellations, visible planets, and a few deep sky objects that you can easily find in the autumn sky with binoculars or a small telescope.
Meader is the owner-director of Northern Stars Planetarium and Educational Services, and he just finished his 39th school year traveling to schools and libraries across Maine. He also regularly leads outdoor star parties with telescopes for schools, museums, libraries and land trusts in Maine. John has been an astronomy educator since 1979 when he got his start as the student director of the planetarium at the University of Maine in Orono. From 1983-88 he was the planetarium director at the Francis Malcolm Science Center in Easton, before starting his own astronomy education business in 1987. He is a fellow of the International Planetarium Society and the Middle Atlantic Planetarium Society. He was a founder, past vice president, past secretary and active board member of Dark Sky Maine. He also serves on the board of the Friends of the LC Bates Museum in Hinckley and the Eagle Hill Institute Astronomy Center in Steuben. Meader is a Registered Maine Guide, a canoeist and a photographer.
Please visit https://tinyurl.com/virtual-star-party to sign up. Registered participants will receive a link to the Zoom prior to the event.
If you’d like to learn more about the work of Friends of Sears Island, visit friendsofsearsisland.org, and to learn more about Dark Sky Maine, check out darkskymaine.com.

title: Disaster relief funding is creeping into Trump's midterm rhetoric. Critics say it has no place there
text:
Disaster relief funding is creeping into Trump's midterm rhetoric. Critics say it has no place there
President Donald Trump has turned emergency relief into a campaign talking point in the final sprint to the midterm elections, approving disaster declarations in consequential states and coupling endorsements with funding announcements.
As the country braces for a major hurricane barreling toward the U.S. Gulf Coast, the moves have revived questions about whether the administration is politicizing disaster recovery.
The latest example came Wednesday, when Trump voiced support for Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany in Wisconsin's governor race while pledging millions to help with recent storms.
In addition, the president recently joked that he would cut off money to North Carolina, which is still healing from Hurricane Helene two years ago, if Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley lost. And the day before an Ohio campaign rally with Sen. Jon Husted last Saturday, Trump approved a disaster declaration for the state while leaving 15 other requests pending.
Disaster survivor advocates say they want elected officials to prioritize their recovery — not wield it as a political tool.
"Recovery isn't partisan," said Sierra Lindsey-Kos, co-founder and co-executive director of Extreme Weather Survivors, an advocacy nonprofit.
"Neighbors help each other without asking who anyone voted for, and that's exactly the way it should be," she said.
The White House rejected accusations that it's injecting politics into disaster recovery. "There is no politicization to the president's decisions on disaster relief," spokesperson Lauren Bis said Tuesday.
Trump has frequently mentioned disaster support in social media posts about the midterms, sometimes announcing new funding in conjunction with reminders of endorsements for Republican candidates like Ashley Hinson in Iowa and Andy Barr in Kentucky.
On Wednesday, Trump posted that he'd spoken to Tiffany, "who has my Complete and Total Endorsement to be the next Governor of the Great State of Wisconsin," and told him about $17.9 million in disaster funds were coming to the state. "18 Million Dollars should help, A LOT," Trump wrote.
A spokesperson for Democratic Gov. Tony Evers said their office had not been informed about the money, and Evers responded to the announcement on social media.
"Clearly, President Trump and Congressman Tiffany are continuing to play politics with emergency aid that's meant to help communities recover in the wake of disasters like tornadoes and floods."
Tiffany is up against Democratic nominee David Crowley in Wisconsin's governor's race.
Even creating the perception that disaster relief and votes are connected has traditionally been "out of bounds," said Rafael LeMaitre, FEMA spokesperson under former President Barack Obama.
"It diminishes the integrity of the disaster management system and it erodes trust in the way the government addresses disasters generally," he said.
When Trump held a rally in North Carolina for Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley, the president acknowledged the state was still waiting for billions of dollars in federal recovery funds for Hurricane Helene.
"Now, if Michael loses, I'm not sending it," he said. "No, I'm only kidding, you're getting it," he added.
Republican Jennifer Balkcom, a congressional candidate in a western North Carolina district, later defended Trump's comments.
"I don't know if he was being funny," Balkcom told WLOS ABC News 13. "I think he was trying to persuade voters to vote for Michael Whatley."
While the joke might not faze Trump's most dedicated supporters, others found it off putting, said Jon Council, who works for the organizing group Down Home North Carolina.
"That just doesn't strike me as a person or administration that's taking the conditions on the ground here seriously, and taking the responsibility to the American taxpayer seriously," Council said.
Trump also brought up disaster relief funds at a campaign rally in Ohio last Saturday, telling supporters in a high school gymnasium in Vandalia that he had signed a "special" disaster declaration for the state after August severe weather.
"You had some bad storms, and Jon and everybody wanted me to help, and I took care of it," Trump said, referring to Republican Senator Jon Husted, who is running a tight reelection race against Democrat Sherrod Brown.
The major disaster declaration for Ohio authorizes direct assistance to residents of seven of the 23 counties requested by Republican Governor Mike DeWine. It came while 15 other requests from states, tribes and territories remain pending, including two from Hawaii, which experienced back-to-back hurricanes in August and September.
Trump did not answer pending disaster requests before rallying in two other Republican states last week with less consequential races, Oklahoma and Nebraska.
Andrew Rumbach, a senior fellow at the Urban Institute who tracks presidential disaster declarations, said politicians "have always tried to use disasters to their advantage." However, he said this White House's behavior has been "unusual and frankly concerning."
An Associated Press analysis in July found that Trump has approved more than three-quarters of the requests from states that voted for him in the 2024 election but less than half the requests from states that did not.
A FEMA spokesperson said Tuesday that "any suggestion that disaster decisions are politically motivated does not reflect how this process works or how FEMA carries out its mission."
Politics has permeated recent communications from FEMA itself.
A September news release about preparations for a nor'easter storm listed 18 Republican members of Congress with whom it said agency leadership was "working closely" during the weather event, omitting mention of any Democrats despite the states mentioned being Democrat-led.
A FEMA spokesperson did not address questions about why only Republican representatives were named.

title: Maine parties are propping up independents where their own brands have eroded
text:
Stephen Carey vows to “audit the books in Augusta,” lower energy and other costs and “protect biological girls’ sports, scholarships and spaces” on his campaign website.
In that way, the Maine Senate candidate from Bangor fits right in with Republicans running for office at all levels across the country. But his material is clear that he’s not in a party.
The Senate Republican campaign arm has spent nearly $40,000 to help the independent win an open Bangor Senate seat with no Republican on the ballot against Rep. Amy Roeder, D-Bangor. The Republican money behind him is nearly 60% of all outside spending to help independents this year, according to Maine Ethics Commission filings.
It’s one of 24 legislative races where an independent will face only one major party candidate, more than twice as many as in any election since at least 2010. Six independents are getting help from partisan groups. Others are raising money from notable partisans ranging from sitting Democrats to a Republican megadonor who lives in Maine seasonally.
Many of these districts follow the lines of Maine’s political realignment. Democrats have lost ground across much of rural Maine, while Republicans have lost support along the coast and in cities and suburbs. In a growing number of districts, parties that can’t win under their own label are getting behind people who reject them.
The most closely watched of these races may be in the Belgrade area, where first-term Rep. Sharon Frost, an independent who ousted a Republican incumbent in 2024 by just 43 votes, is defending a swing seat against Republican Dexter “Buzz” Bridges Jr. of New Sharon.
Groups aligned with Democrats have spent more than $10,000 to help Frost keep the seat, but more than twice as much has been spent against her by Republicans. Democrats hold the House by a razor-thin margin and may need help from Frost and other independents to govern next year.
Most of their allies’ help for House independents has come from the Planned Parenthood Maine Action Fund PAC, with smaller amounts from Rebuild Maine, the Maine Democratic Party and a political group led by Rep. Marc Malon, D-Biddeford. Two other independent House candidates — Shawn Saindon of Warren and Sam Pfeifle of Gray — are seeing outside money as well.
In a House district spanning part of Mount Desert Island, Deer Isle and Vinalhaven and Swan’s Island, independent Clifford Noyes of Southwest Harbor is aiming to unseat Rep. Holly Eaton, D-Deer Isle. His campaign is quiet, but he did raise hundreds from a conservative foundation and the conservative legal architect Leonard Leo, who has a home in Northeast Harbor.
Some Democratic lawmakers have also given money directly. In a Pittsfield-area district Republican Rep. Amanda Collamore won easily in 2024, independent Zachary Lejonhud got seed money as part of Maine’s taxpayer-funded Clean Election program from Reps. Scott Harriman of Lewiston and Mike Ray of Lincolnville, both Democrats.
Lejonhud, a union electrician, has also been endorsed by the Maine AFL-CIO, which usually backs Democrats. He said he is “not a secret Democrat.”
“I don’t want to position myself in a way that closes off anybody who’s right-leaning from wanting to work with me, or anybody who’s really left-leaning from wanting to work with me,” he said. “People just get a little too defensive, a little too tribal about their party.”
While Democratic support is flowing to independents in the House, Republicans are focusing on the Senate. The party has struggled in the Bangor district vacated by Democratic Sen. Joe Baldacci, who defeated their nominee by more than 15 points in 2022 and 2024. Both Carey and Roeder are running as Clean Election candidates.
Will Parmacek, who directs the Senate Democratic Campaign Committee, said he thought Senate Republican leadership was “playing a game of smoke and mirrors.” But he declined to comment on his party’s strategy in the House, where party-aligned groups have spent more than $20,000 to help independents where no Democrat is running.
The House Democratic campaign arm did not respond to a request for comment. Zach Lingley, a Republican strategist working on races in both chambers, would not discuss strategy. Carey and Frost did not respond to requests for comment.
In the Biddeford area, lawyer Jason Litalien is running as an independent against Sen. Henry Ingwersen, D-Arundel, who won by 17 points in 2024. Litalien has gotten $5,200 in outside help from the conservative group Common Sense for Maine. Donors to his campaign include Rep. Wayne Parry, R-Arundel, and former Maine Republican Party Chair Demi Kouzounas.
“I don’t really think that a party makes all that much of a difference,” Litalien said. “I think, regardless of what is next to my name, I think I’d win Biddeford anyway, simply because I know the people in Biddeford.”
Daniel O’Connor is a Report for America corps member who covers rural government as part of the partnership between the Bangor Daily News and The Maine Monitor, with additional support from BDN and Monitor readers.

title: Who needs a win, and more Week 6 high school football storylines
text:
We talk a lot about the teams at the top of the Crabtree standings. This time of year, though, the games that define seasons are often not between the top teams but between those fighting for their lives.
So, what are some key showdowns this week that involve teams teetering on the brink? Let’s dive into that and Maine high school football’s other top storylines for Week 6.
Who needs a win?
Early in the season, many people tabbed Cheverus as a potential favorite in Class B. Instead, after a shocking loss Saturday against Gorham, the Stags are in last place at 1-4.
That means Cheverus would be on the outside looking in if the playoffs were to begin today. The Stags could use the points that would come with a win over Marshwood (5-0) on Friday. Otherwise, they’ll have to beat at least one of Deering or Biddeford in the final two weeks.
In Class C, York (1-4) is ninth in a statewide field that will send eight to the playoffs. The Wildcats would benefit from a win Friday against Class D Oak Hill (1-4). Belfast, meanwhile, is one spot behind Oak Hill in D South, and should the Raiders lose, the Lions have a chance to move up with a win over Madison.
In eight-man, a Large School North playoff berth might be on the line Saturday when Waterville (1-4) travels to Houlton (0-5). With both teams having tough schedules down the stretch, the winner will have the inside track to the No. 4 seed, while the loser is in peril.
If you think we forgot Class A, we didn’t — but with many key games remaining and an extra week on the schedule, these teams have more breathing room. Still, South Portland (3-2) could use a win Friday when it hosts Massabesic (4-1) or next week at Noble (2-3) as he tries to move higher than fifth place in the South.
Thursday night lights
With 11 of them having already taken place, Thursday games have been a fixture in 2026. That continues this week with five Thursday games, the most since a six-game slate back in Week 1.
A crossover clash in Freeport between Class C Wells (3-2) and Class D Freeport (4-1) highlights Thursday’s schedule. Other games feature Camden Hills (1-4) at Cony (4-1), Brewer (1-4) at Hermon (5-0), Poland (1-4) at Morse (3-2), and Traip Academy (1-4) at Old Orchard Beach (5-0).
If it seems there are more Thursday night games these days, that’s because there are. In all, 18 regular-season high school football games will be played on Thursdays in 2026. There were 12 Thursday games in 2025 and 13 in 2024. In 2023, there were only six.
Why? Dean Plante, Old Orchard Beach’s coach and a member of the Maine Principals’ Association Football Committee, believes it’s two-pronged. Sure, there’s an officiating shortage, but Plante also believes that, when OOB got permission from the MPA to open the 2019 season on a Thursday against Telstar, it started a trend.
“That was the first year of eight-man, so we wanted to showcase eight-man by having it as the first game of the season, and it kind of took off,” Plante said. “I think it’s cool; you get to be one of the only games — maybe the only game — and that gets a little exposure for the kids.”
Cony coach B.L. Lippert said the Maine Association of Football Officials asked his team to move either this week’s game or next week’s against Brunswick to a Thursday night. Because next week is senior night for the Rams, the team chose this one.
“I don’t know specifically how dire the referee shortage is, but it seems like that’s obviously an issue,” Lippert said. “It might not be 50-50 Thursday-Friday, but there might be 10 Thursday games a week next year, is what I’ve heard.”
Can the upstarts keep winning?
Every year, teams that weren’t on many radars at the start of the season capture the state’s attention. A few meet the mark in 2026: Massabesic, Biddeford, Maine Central Institute and Cape Elizabeth are all 4-1, and Lisbon is 3-2. So, what to expect from those teams in Week 6?
MCI, 2-7 a year ago, might have the toughest task of the five. The Huskies host defending Class D North champ Winslow (4-1) in a matchup between the top two teams in the region. The rivals had some fun Big 11 Conference battles between 2017-22.
Massabesic, which missed the playoffs at 3-6 last year, has the aforementioned clash with South Portland. That’s a challenging road showdown for the Mustangs against an opponent whose only losses were hard-fought defeats to Bonny Eagle and Thornton Academy — the top two teams in the Varsity Maine poll.
Cape Elizabeth, Biddeford and Lisbon all went 1-7 last year. Cape Elizabeth (at 3-2 Spruce Mountain) and Biddeford (at 3-2 Skowhegan) make long trips north to face tough opponents on Friday, while Lisbon hosts Mattanawcook Academy (2-3).

title: Maine Democrats call out Bobby Charles for his views on the war in Iran
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - On Wednesday the Maine Democrats hosted a press conference to call out Republican candidate for governor Bobby Charles on his views regarding the war in Iran.
They say the war has had a negative impact on Mainers citing a survey from the Maine Department of Energy Resources showing the average price of heating oil is up 80% from a year ago.
While Maine Democrats acknowledged the Governor of Maine would have no power to end the war in Iran, they attacked Charles for not staying consistent in his viewpoint on the war.
“For me, what’s the most upsetting about Bobby Charles is he won’t stand by his original comments. Like I said, his values have changed with the wind. And Hannah has been consistent. She has been outspoken against the war. I have been outspoken against the war. Most of my colleagues have been outspoken against the war. I think it’s most important to know that when you’re electing somebody to be governor, you’re electing somebody who has principles that they’re not afraid to stand behind,” said Rep. Amy J. Roeder.
A spokesperson for the Charles campaign responded by stating: “Bobby Charles isn’t running for president. He’s running for governor, to fix what Janet Mills and Hannah Pingree have broken. After eight years of their policies, Mainers pay some of the highest energy costs in the country, their taxes have gone up, and their property tax bills keep climbing. Maine Democrats can’t stop talking about the president because they can’t defend their own record. The question for Maine Democrats is simple: when will they hold Janet Mills and Hannah Pingree accountable?”

title: Trump uses anti-trans slur to attack Democratic US Senate candidate
text:
CHARLESTON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — President Donald Trump used an anti-transgender slur to refer to Annie Andrews, a Democratic Senate candidate in South Carolina.
In a post on Truth Social this week, Trump wrote, “Annie ‘Tr*nnie’ Andrews is running against our wonderful Darline Graham for the Senate in South Carolina.”
Trump used the slur three times in referring to Andrews, adding that Andrews was “in favor of transgender for everyone” and that she was “not for South Carolina.”
Andrews, who is a pediatrician, has previously stated that she supports transgender children and is a supporter of gender-affirming care.
The Senate candidate also said that she does not think that biological men should play in women’s sports, while not supporting gender surgery when it comes to minors.
Trump called Darline Graham, who is running against Andrews as the Republican candidate following the death of her brother, Lindsey Graham, “a high-quality person” who has his “complete and total endorsement.”
Andrews did not immediately address Trump’s comments directly, but posted on Monday that she is in the Senate race to fight for her patients, her children and South Carolina.
Former South Carolina Gov. David Beasley called Trump’s comments “abhorrent,” saying that while South Carolinians can disagree, they can do so civilly.

title: Leslie Anne Wellington
text:
Leslie Anne Wellington, 79, died Sept. 26, 2026, at her home in Southwest Harbor. She was born April 9, 1947, in Bar Harbor, the daughter of John C. and Lucille M. (Harper) Wellington.

title: China TIF committee decides on consultant to help program
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
China Tax Increment Financing Committee members decided at a Sept. 28 meeting that they need a consultant to help them draft a revised TIF program for the town.
China is currently on its Third Amended TIF Program. It has an ample supply of money, Town Manager and Treasurer Rebecca Hapgood assured committee members. Their questions were about distributing the money.
The first issue raised was funding for recreational trails. The Four Seasons Club and the Thurston Park Committee both submit annual requests; for the last few years, the two requests have exceeded the money allocated for trails (and the two groups’ representatives have amicably split the funds).
Trail funding could be changed and increased in a fourth TIF, committee member Jamie Pitney suggested.
Another issue was the state’s rejection of the town’s using TIF funds to repair the church parking lot near the causeway at the head of China Lake’s east basin. Committee members thought it should have been eligible because many users of the recreational area park their vehicles there.
A major China TIF project was rebuilding the bridge over the inlet stream and creating the shoreline recreational area. More work is planned.
Joann Austin wanted China’s libraries to be eligible for TIF funds.
Pitney suggested China’s current TIF districts, shown on maps on the TIF document, could be revised.
Hapgood wondered if emergency services could be added as eligible for TIF funds. The purpose of the program is to promote economic development, and businesses need good emergency services, she argued.
A broader issue is whether China still needs a TIF program. It is funded by taxes Central Maine Power Company pays on its north-south power line through town and its South China substation.
The TIF is an engine for economic development, and also – primarily, Pitney said – a tax shelter. If the CMPC taxes were paid to the town, making China richer, its state aid to education and state revenue sharing income would decrease, and its county tax and school bills would increase.
Perhaps, Pitney suggested, it is time for an expert to evaluate whether getting the CMP taxes would more than cover the changes resulting from ending the TIF.
If they are to consider a Fourth Amended TIF Program, committee members decided they need help from a consultant who specializes in TIF. They unanimously approved Austin’s motion to ask the select board to issue an RFP (request for proposals) to seek such a consultant.
Hapgood said she would add the request to the agenda for the Oct. 5 China selectboard meeting.
TIF Committee members scheduled another meeting for 6 p.m., Monday, Oct. 26, in the China town office meeting room.

title: Letter: I’m voting blue because I’m worse off under this administration
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
Before voting I ask if I am better off under the current administration. I am not.
Living: My property taxes have skyrocketed, gas is $4.51 a gallon, heating oil $6.05, and groceries prices have risen sharply as I avoid food recalls due in part to DOGE cuts.
Detentions: My physician was detained at the border in Canada for five months with no reason and no apologies. Hispanic people are also detained here from downstate, only to be released as a mistake.
Health care: Primary and specialty care, if available, have long waiting lists. Homebound elderly are expected to drive long distances. I have one specialist 420 miles away. At age 62, my health care premiums were $2,875 per month. We need Medicare for all. I believe only Democrats understand medical care should not be for profit.
Preventable deaths: Women without reproductive care. The unvaccinated. People of color. Neighbors by ICE. Civilians and Americans in the Iran War. Ukrainians. The nameless due to the abrupt cessation of USAID.
Our government should not be a version of Lord of the Flies. Every day brings a new outrage leaving Mainers to clean up the mess. I believe Democratic candidates offer integrity and alternatives. Vote blue!
Dale J. Gordon
Caribou

title: This election is about reclaiming the federal government
text:
The ongoing Susan Collins vs. Troy Jackson debate is a great example of not seeing the forest but for the trees. The real issue for the upcoming midterm election is not which senator should represent Maine, but how do we, the citizens, wrest control back from an administration exemplified by cruelty, incompetence, corruption, self-aggrandizement and self-enrichment.
As much as I respect Sen. Susan Collins (I have voted for her in past elections), electing a Democrat to the Senate would move us closer to flipping the balance of power in the Senate. Reducing the Senate Republican majority to minority status is a prerequisite for reclaiming our government. A government of decency, fairness, competence and sanity.
As we head to the polls, let us step out of the trees so we can see the forest.
Larry O’Rourke
Sumner

title: Susan Collins’ approach to governing is the right approach
text:
Stephen Diamond is a retiree who lives in Topsham.
If Sen. Susan Collins is politically vulnerable, it is not because she has changed, but because the country has.
We live in a time when what divides us greatly overshadows what unites us. What used to be legitimate policy differences now degenerate into ugly personal attacks, and rather than push back against this development, some in public office seem happy to fan the flames of discord.
This change in our political climate has even led to calls to fundamentally transform the nature of our country, ranging from those advocating a white supremacist Christian theocracy to those arguing for a transition to socialism. Our struggle to make our religion-neutral, free-market democracy work has emboldened the advocates of extreme solutions.
Maine, along with the rest of New England, was once the ideological center of the country with little to separate Democrats from Republicans, but now Sen. Collins, as the only Republican member of Congress from this region, remains the sole heir to this tradition. Should she be voted out of office, it will be the final nail in the coffin of New England pluralism.
As someone who has known Sen. Collins for many years and who served on her staff (but who voted for the Democrat in every presidential election since 1968), I think that in addition to her legendary work ethic, her approach to governing can be summarized in three words: civility, compromise and compassion. Her civility reflects her manner of working with others, even unpleasant colleagues holding dramatically different views.
Without civility, compromise becomes impossible, and without compromise, progress becomes impossible, with our government either experiencing paralysis or vacillating between conflicting policies. Her consistent ranking as the least partisan member of the Senate and her effectiveness as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee attest to the senator’s understanding that compromise is essential to effective governing.
A less recognized feature of Sen. Collins’ approach to governing is her compassion for persons facing difficult challenges, as manifested in the importance she attaches to helping constituents dealing with personal setbacks as well as in her support for programs designed to assist those genuinely in need. A government insensitive to the suffering of persons facing hard times is not a government worth having.
What arguably most distinguishes Sen. Collins from others holding elected office is that she is a frequent target of both the extreme left and the extreme right. Ironically, nothing demonstrates more convincingly the importance of her voice.
When Rep. Jared Golden, with his impressive military record, expresses concern for the safety of his family, the problem in Washington has gone beyond mere incivility. It may be that Sen. Collins is of the old school, with an approach to governing reminiscent of that practiced by Sens. Muskie and Cohen, but we have much to learn from a past when political opponents treated each other with respect, the result of which was a functioning government.
Whether Sen. Collins is reelected has serious consequences not only for Maine but for the country. Hers is among the lonely voices in Washington pushing back against the dangerous partisanship that undermines our constitutional order. Simply put, a vote against Sen. Collins is a vote to perpetuate our national polarization while a vote for her is a vote for a healthy, civil and effective democracy.

title: Death Notice: Norma Nivison
Susan Collins says she supports women. We saw otherwise.
text:
Debra Katz and Lisa Banks are founding partners of Katz Banks Kumin LLP. They represented Dr. Ford during the 2018 confirmation hearings of Justice Brett Kavanaugh.
In September 2018, we sat beside Dr. Christine Blasey Ford as she courageously testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee. In a packed room with more than 20 million people watching live on television, Dr. Ford raised her right hand — now an iconic image — and painstakingly recounted the sexual assault she endured by then-Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh when she was 15.
Dr. Ford came forward at enormous personal and professional cost, facing such extreme threats to her safety that she and her family were forced to leave their home and retain 24-hour security services. She did so because she believed that U.S. senators, like Sen. Susan Collins, should know the character of a man who was up for a lifetime appointment to the Supreme Court.
Ultimately, Sen. Collins did not care, and pledged fealty to President Trump in casting the
deciding vote in favor of Kavanaugh’s confirmation. She voted this way despite Dr. Ford’s testimony, which Collins described as “sincere, painful, and compelling,” and despite her own avowed support of survivors of sexual assault and the importance of reproductive rights.
Collins justified her vote by explaining that she had met privately with Kavanaugh, who, in addition to denying the assault, assured her that he would honor precedent, including Roe v. Wade. She subsequently also told CNN that with regard to Dr. Ford’s sexual assault, “I do not believe that Brett Kavanaugh was her assailant. I do believe that she was assaulted. I don’t know by whom, and I’m not certain when, but I do not believe he was the assailant.”
This preposterous explanation, while politically expedient, was offensive not only to Dr. Ford but to survivors everywhere. Conveniently forgotten by Collins was Dr. Ford’s sworn testimony that she was “one hundred percent” certain that it was Kavanaugh who had assaulted her. Also ignored was the important fact that Dr. Ford had named Kavanaugh as her assailant to her friends, therapist and husband years before his nomination.
At best, Susan Collins was duped by Kavanaugh and President Trump. At worst, her actions were duplicitous, born of a desire to assure her constituents she was a moderate and supporter of women, even if her voting record says otherwise.
Beyond Kavanaugh, Collins’ voting record includes a long history of votes for extreme judicial nominees who hold regressive positions on a shocking array of rights.
Sen. Collins voted for Joshua Dunlap, who now sits on the 1st Circuit Court of Appeals, where Maine’s federal appellate matters are heard, despite the fact that he opposed marriage equality and has a history of opposition to pro-choice laws. Collins also voted to confirm Eric Tung to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, even though he too does not believe in a constitutional right to same-sex marriage. And even though Joshua Divine, now a federal judge in Missouri, once lumped homosexuality together with bestiality, she voted to confirm him too.
In total, Susan Collins has voted for 52 out of 55 of Donald Trump’s second-term judges, while voting “no” on many of the pro-choice, pro-worker Biden nominees that she claims to find common cause with.
Collins may claim to be a moderate, but she does not vote like one. And where Dr. Ford demonstrated tremendous courage, Sen. Collins has demonstrated that she will always place politics over principle.
We hope that when Mainers go to the ballot box this November, they remember that Collins’ lack of principle has led directly to the appointment of Justice Kavanaugh, the overturning of Roe v. Wade and to President Trump stocking the federal courts with extreme jurists intent on undermining our nation’s civil rights.
